access|osimertinib.t: PA for osimertinib alone is routine now; the chemo add-on is where questions start.
Denials for the combo keep citing 'not standard of care', honestly exhausting.
Copay foundation support came through within days for her.
Specialty pharmacy delays are eating start dates, mostly at first fill.
Not sure buy-and-bill economics even matter for an oral agent.
Peer-to-peer usually flips the denial if we land the right reviewer.

Small community practice, so our nurse navigator handles nearly every PA herself. She says osimertinib approvals are predictable, usually a few days. The chemo add-on sits on a separate authorization track, which doubles the paperwork.

One patient on a high-deductible plan hit the January reset and nearly walked away from therapy. Our social worker found assistance, but it took about three weeks and he was off drug in the gap. I think this happens more often than we track.

The academic site has a financial counselor who runs benefits checks before the visit. Because of that, most newly diagnosed EGFR patients leave clinic with a start date in hand. It makes the team more comfortable considering the combination.
A payer step edit asked if we'd tried an earlier-generation EGFR TKI first, which felt outdated. We pointed to the guideline listing and it cleared on appeal. Probably a one-off, but not sure.

The pemetrexed side worries the practice manager. Buy-and-bill margins are thin and a few payers reimburse slowly, so a long payment lag matters to the business. She said that isn't clinical preference, but it nudges conversations anyway.
Testing authorization comes up before any drug discussion, since if NGS isn't covered the whole path stalls. Once the mutation is confirmed the osimertinib approval is usualy smooth.
Letters of medical necessity built on the FLAURA2 rationale have mostly been accepted, which surprised her. The few combination appeals they filed were resolved at the first level.

Hospital-based clinic, so site-of-care rules are different from the independent offices nearby. Chair time for the infusion portion is allocated by the hospital rather than the oncologist, and that sometimes decides the schedule more than the patient's preference does.

After a long conversation, the oncologist called the combination clinically attractive but administratively heavy. Every pemetrexed and platinum cycle needs scheduling, chair time, and in some plans a separate authorization that expires on a different date than the oral drug's. Her staff spends hours on appeal letters, often repeating the same argument for different reviewers. She wasn't sure payer attitudes will shift without more real-world experience. For now she sometimes leans toward osimertinib alone in older patients, partly for access reasons, though she said that is not the only driver.

Rural practice, and the patients drive a long way, so anything that adds infusion visits is a real burden. The physician said coverage was rarely the barrier for the TKI itself. Transport and time off work are what stop people from choosing the combination. He wasn't sure if payers or travel cost more, honestly, and he thought it depended on the patient. Overall he described access as workable but uneven.

She was upbeat about how copay assistance has worked lately for her EGFR patients. Enrollment is mostly done online by the office staff in one sitting, and approvals usually arrive before the first fill. She mentioned one patient who was worried about cost and ended up paying very little out of pocket. She still wonders what happens when those programs reach their annual limit, but so far it hasn't come up. Overall it has made starting osimertinib much less stressful.

Her recent case was a patient with brain mets who needed to start quickly, and the first PA was denied because of a documentation gap. The appeal took nearly two weeks, and for much of that time the family was anxious and calling the office daily. She said the clinic ended up bridging with samples, which isn't sustainable. In her view the problem is not the drug decision but the timing of the payer process. She thinks urgent cases need a faster pathway and is skeptical one will materialize.

Payer mix at this center is split, with a lot of older patients on government plans and a smaller commercial group. Approvals for osimertinib seem similar across both, but the combination gets more scrutiny on the commercial side. I think that is because of the added chemo costs, though he wasn't certain. Appeals take effort either way. He summed it up as manageable if you have the staff and painful if you dont.

The pharmacist I spoke with described authorization renewals as the quiet problem. Initial approval is fine, but renewals come up at odd intervals and sometimes lapse without anyone noticing until a refill is rejected. Patients then call the clinic upset, and staff scramble to fix it the same day. She said a tracking system would help but the practice has no one to maintain it. A good chunk of her week goes to these gaps, which she finds frustrating for a drug people should stay on continuously.
PA for osi approved first pass, no peer-to-peer needed.
Chemo add-on PA = biggest headache right now.
Copay card covers most commercial pts; Medicare pts still have a gap.
Denials for the pemetrexed combo keep coming back, appeals eat staff time.
Foundation assistance came through fast for an uninsured pt.
Unsure how their payer will treat osimertinib combo vs mono, still waiting on policy.
Community onc clinic, maybe 2 PAs/wk for EGFR tx. Staff says osi mono is routine now, combo needs extra docs (path report, brain MRI). Turnaround about a week, I think.

Practice mgr worried about buy-and-bill on the infusion side. Platinum/pemetrexed reimbursement lags and cash flow is tight for a small group. Might nudge some pts toward oral-only just for that reason.
Academic HCP says their specialty pharmacy handles the osi PA end to end. Pt starts within a few days, no gap in tx. Called it one of the easier orals.
Medicare pt hit the coverage-phase cost jump mid-year on osimertinib. Nearly stopped tx until SW found a foundation grant. HCP says this happens w/ every oral TKI, not just this one.
Step edit wanted the EGFR test report before approving, HCP thinks that's fair. NGS was already in the chart so no delay. Concern is pts with only a liquid biopsy result.
Payer denied osimertinib + chemo as 'not medically necessary', wanted mono first. HCP did peer to peer and won on 2nd try. Says its exhausting evrey time.
Hospital outpatient infusion center says combo reimbursement is workable once auth is in hand. Their pharmacy pre-verifies benefits before the pt ever sits in the chair. Few surprises so far.
Tumor board now has a nurse navigator who flags auth problems before the tx decision is final. HCP likes it, says fewer last-minute switches. Not sure other sites do this.

Rural practice HCP frustrated. Every combo start needs PA for osimertinib plus separate auth for the chemo and the infusion visits. Different reviewers, different forms, and one piece often gets approved before the others. Pt waits, anxious about progression. Staff time is the real cost, not so much the drug itself.

Large cancer center HCP described a split. Commercial pts mostly sail through with copay assistance, Medicaid pts take longer, and a few have to appeal. Overall she sees access as okay but uneven. Biggest variable seems to be which payer, not which clinical picture. Not sure that will change soon.

Very upbeat on access. HCP said once the payer added the combo to its pathway, PAs became mostly a checkbox exercise. Pharmacy team has a template letter citing guidelines and it works most of the time. Pts rarely wait more than a few days. Copay support covers most of the out-of-pocket for insured pts. Osi is not the issue in their clinic.

Site-of-care economics came up. HCP said the independent clinic loses margin on infusion when payers pay late or downcode. Some docs are quietly steering to hospital outpatient sites for combo pts. That adds travel for pts and delays. HCP worried about unequal access for pts far from big centers.

HCP noted prior auth for osi alone is basically settled, a few days, rarely denied. Combo is different. Payer policies seem to lag guidelines, and some require documented reasons like CNS disease or high-risk features. She's fine with documenting but wants consistency. Pts who need fast start are the ones affected. Probably improves as policies catch up.

Financial toxicity was the main theme. Pt with good PFS on tx but copays for scans, chemo visits and supportive meds stacking up. HCP said some pts skip cycles or ask to stop chemo for cost. Assistance programs help but have income caps and paperwork. She feels the system quietly rewards the cheaper regimen regardless of what the tumor board favored.
Prior auth for the combo takes forever, every single time.
Osimertinib alone gets approved fine; adding pemetrexed is where it gets messy.
Copay card helps until the deductible resets, then it's a scramble
Our specialty pharmacy handles the osimertinib PA better than we ever did, frankly.
Denied once, overturned on peer-to-peer within days; system worked, barely.
Not sure payers read appeal letters, but some do get overturned.

We're a small community practice, so buy-and-bill for pemetrexed and platinum is a cash flow worry. Osimertinib itself goes through specialty pharmacy so that part doesn't touch us. I think the infusion side is what makes us hesitate on the combo, probably more than the clinical question.

Step edit asked for a different EGFR TKI first in one case, which makes no sense for someone with a confirmed exon 19 deletion. Took a peer-to-peer and about two weeks. Patient was sitting there with brain mets waiting.
Look, in my experience the approvals for first-line osimertinib have been mostly smooth once the biomarker report is attached. I don't love the paperwork but it's rarely a fight anymore.
Patients on osimertinib under Part D get hit with a big out-of-pocket early in the year. A few just skipped fills until the foundation grants came through. Nobody tracks that gap.
Our academic center has a financial navigator who deals with the combo regimen auths. Without her I think we'd be drowning. Not every clinic has that luxery tho.

Payer wanted documentation that the chemo was 'medically necessary' on top of the targeted therapy. Basically asking us to justify the whole combination line by line. Frustrating when the TKI indication itself is clear.
Site-of-care rules are pushing some of our infusions to home or an outside suite. Works for a few patients, but the coordination is a mess and I'm not convinced it saves anything.
Once the assistance program enrolled the patient, copay was basically a non-issue. Took maybe a week. Credit where due.

We had a patient with L858R, good performance status, ready to start. Prior authorization came back denied for 'insufficient documentation' even though we'd sent the pathology and NGS report. The appeal dragged on, and the patient nearly went on chemo alone because we couldn't wait. I get that payers want controls, but this is a clear biomarker indication for osimertinib. It feels like denial is the default and the appeal is the real review.

Mixed bag for us. Osimertinib monotherapy is routine, the auth is basically a template now. The combo is different because you have several drugs, each with its own rules and infusion codes. I think our billing staff spend more time on it than the nurses spend in the chair. Chemo reimbursement is okay I guess, but margins are thin, so I'm not sure it's sustainable at volume.

The financial toxicity conversation is the part nobody wants to have. Patients ask about cost before they ask about side effects. Folks who were fine with an oral TKI copay see the bills jump once infusions and coinsurance get added. A couple declined the combo for that reason alone, I think. We point them to foundation help but the funds run out and it's not predictable.

I'll give credit here: our last few starts went through without a fight. We front-load the NGS result, the stage, and a note on why we chose the combo, and the PA tends to come back within a few days. Peer-to-peer was needed once and it was short. I'm still skeptical it holds, since policies change every year, but right now it's workable.

Hard to say whether denials are more about the drug or about how we submit. Some I've seen were just clerical, wrong code or missng date. Others were real policy, like wanting an older regimen tried first. I'd guess half our headaches are self-inflicted. Still, nobody on the payer end is helpful when you call.

Buy-and-bill is a gamble for pemetrexed in the combo. If the claim gets denied after we've already infused, we eat it. Our practice admin told us to hold off until auth is in hand which delays starts by days. For a patient we're supposed to move on quickly, that delay is just irritating. The oral side through specialty pharmacy is less painful, honestly.
PA for osimertinib usually clears within a few days at their practice.
Copay card covers most of it, patients rarely complain.
Chemo add-on is where the denials start.
Appeals take too long, nothing else to say really
Not seeing step edits on first-line EGFR TKIs so far.
Pharmacy benefit vs medical benefit confusion again, depends on the plan.

Community clinic running osimertinib with pemetrexed and carboplatin said the payer wanted a separate prior authorization for each piece. Their nurse navigator says it basically doubles the paperwork and delays the first infusion.
The academic center's specialty pharmacy handles the osimertinib PA in-house and turnaround is predictable. Only hiccup is in January when patients switch plans and everything restarts.
Practice administrator said buy-and-bill for the chemo part is workable, margin is okay but not great, I think. It hasn't changed any treatment decision so far.

A Medicare patient was worried about out-of-pocket costs late in the year and the foundation grant had closed for the month. The social worker bridged her with free drug for a few weeks. Physician called it stressful for everyone.

Denial came back for the combination saying chemo plus the TKI wasn't covered as first-line. Peer-to-peer overturned it, but the whole thing took about a week. Physician said he expects to do that again.
Infusion chair time for the combo is a scheduling issue at their small site, but the administration reimbursement apparently covers it. Not sure how that holds with other payers.
Rural clinic patients drive a long way, so the mailed oral drug from specialty pharmacy helps a lot. Occasional delays when a signature is needed at delivery and teh patient is at work.
Financial counselor finds manufacturer assistance enrollment quick for insured patients. Uninsured or underinsured ones still get stuck waiting on documentation.

At a hospital-based lung clinic, a handful of patients had their osimertinib start pushed back because the plan asked for the biomarker report again after already receiving it. Staff resubmitted and it was approved, but each time it cost several days. The physician said patients with a known driver mutation shouldn't be waiting like that. She also noted the pharmacist spends a good part of the week just on this.

This oncologist said access to osimertinib has been mostly smooth in his community practice. Most commercial plans approve with the pathology report and stage attached. Copay assistance takes care of the rest for most patients. He thinks the clinic's dedicated authorization coordinator is the main reason.

Clinic is split on the combination. Medical benefit billing for the chemo means they front the drug cost, and a couple of staff worry about delayed payments. On the other hand the physician feels the clinical case is strong enough to push through the paperwork. Probably they'll keep offering it case by case depending on payer.

Physician at a community site described a patient with a commercial plan that required a trial of a different EGFR TKI before approving osimertinib. The appeal went through two levels and the patient waited almost a month. Meanwhile the family was calling the office daily. She said she doesn't see that as appropriate for a patient with a known mutation, and the staff time was a big burden.

Pharmacist at a large cancer center said their prior authorization team now has a template for the osimertinib plus chemo request, and approvals come back quickly. Denials are rare and mostly clerical. Patients get connected to copay support at the first visit. They consider access a non-issue for most of their EGFR patients.

Small practice owner worried about site-of-care economics if payers push the infusion part to hospital outpatient settings or to a preferred infusion vendor. He said patients on the combination would then be split between places, which complicates the oral and infused pieces. I think he is more concerned about the future than what is happening now. Right now he is just absorbing the extra admin cost.
PA for osi basically rubber-stamped at our site now.
Chemo add-on is where denials start, not the TKI itself.
Copay card covers most commercial pts, gap is the uninsured ones.
Peer-to-peer every single time for the combo, exhausting.
Not sure how their specialty pharmacy times refills tbh
Foundation grant came through in under a week for one pt.

Community practice, two oncologists. Pemetrexed and platinum are buy-and-bill so they carry the float, but osimertinib goes thru specialty pharmacy, which splits the workflow and sometimes pushes cycle 1 back a few days.
Payer wanted the EGFR report plus a trial of single-agent first before approving the combination. Doc said thats backwards for someone with heavy disease burden. Appeal dragged on for weeks.
Their PA coordinator has a template for the osimertinib plus chemo request now and approvals come back quick. Says quoting the FLAURA2 label language in the letter helps a lot.
Academic site with a 340B pharmacy, so infusion margins are less of a worry. Bigger issue is pts sent to outside infusion for pemetrexed because of plan site-of-care rules, I think.
Part D copay during the deductible phase is brutal for oral TKIs. A few pts delayed their first fill until assistance got sorted. Nurse navigator spends a big chunk of her week on this.
Pharmacist said most denials are paperwork, like missing biomarker docs, and get overturned on resubmission. Still costs prob a few days each time.
Hospital finance team seems comfortable with the combo economics. No pushback at tumor board on reimbursement, which surprised me.
Quick note, main worry from admin is chair time. Chemo days plus extra visits for the combo strain throughput and payment at the rural satellite clinic, and they dont have spare capacity.

Small private practice, very frustrated. Commercial plan denied osimertinib with chemo as 'not medically necessary' even though the pt had a clear exon 19 deletion. They did the peer-to-peer, lost, then filed a written appeal. Pt waited almost a month and the doc said she nearly started chemo alone out of desperation. Staff time on this was huge and unreimbursed.

Mixed picture at this center. Single-agent osimertinib is easy, PA is usually approved first pass and the copay program works for most commercially insured pts. The combo needs extra steps, mainly coordinating two pharmacy channels and getting infusion auth lined up. Practice manager thinks it will smooth out once they've done a handful. Not sure about uninsured pts, they didnt have a clear answer.

Positive chat with the oncology pharmacist. They built a checklist for biomarker docs, staging and ECOG, and PA submissions are now mostly one-and-done. Their financial counselor gets pts into assistance programs before the first fill. Fewer treatment delays than last year, I think. She felt payers are getting more familiar with the combo regimen.

Appeals were the theme today. Doc said when a plan denies the combo, the letter cites 'off-pathway' and wants a reason why not osimertinib alone. Each appeal eats nurse time and sometimes a physician call. Meanwhile pts on the fence about chemo get anxious waiting. Recieved no clear sense of whether the plan reverses more often on second level.

Buy-and-bill discussion with a practice administrator. Their concern is the upfront cost of pemetrexed and the lag before payment arrives, which affects cash flow if several combo pts start at once. They're fine with it at current volumes. If volume grows they might look at a hospital-affiliated infusion arrangement, but nothing decided.

Mostly neutral on access, a bit worried about step edits coming. Doc heard a regional plan may require a trial of an earlier-line option before osimertinib combo, nothing confirmed. For now her pts get through, though sometimes with a delay for paperwork. She wants to see how it plays out before changing how she presents the combo.
Said the PA for osi plus chemo takes too long to clear.
Reports prior auths for single-agent osimertinib basically go through now without a fuss.
Not sure how payers will handle the pemetrexed add-on yet, per this oncologist.
Copay card maxes out mid-year for several patients, and then they scramble. Oncologist's words, roughly.
Appeal was overturned in under a week, which surprised the physician.
Thinks buy-and-bill margins on the chemo backbone are thin but workable.

A nurse manager at a community practice explained that the team now sends the prior authorization and the biomarker report together, which cut the back-and-forth. For the combination, though, they still get asked for a peer-to-peer fairly often. She wasn't sure if that's payer-specific or just whoever the reviewer is.

Rural clinic oncologist said patients on high-deductible plans hesitate when infusion visits get layered on top of the oral drug. He worries some will recieve the option that looks cheaper out of pocket rather than the one he'd prefer.

According to an academic physician, their financial navigator files foundation assistance applications within days, so almost nobody has waited to start therapy. She credited having a dedicated person more than any payer change.

Mentioned a denial that cited 'not standard first-line' for the combination, so they appealed with the trial publication attached. It took a few weeks, and the patient started osimertinib alone in the meantime.

Practice administrator felt the specialty pharmacy handoff for the oral piece is smooth, but lining it up with infusion scheduling is a headache. Probably a workflow problem rather than a policy one, in their view.

Step edits haven't really been an issue for EGFR-mutant patients, as far as this oncologist can tell, because the mutation result is accepted as the justification. Only the occasional odd plan asks for more.

Doctor at a hospital outpatient clinic said site-of-care rules are pushing some infusions to a freestanding center. That complicates the combination schedule for patients who live far away, and a couple had delays because of transport.
Thinks payers are probably still working out how to write policy around the FLAURA2 regimen. For now each case seems to get decided one at a time, so the team just documents everything thoroughly.

Independent practice oncologist said buy-and-bill is what keeps him up at night. Stocking the chemo for the combination ties up cash while claims sit pending, and if a payer denies after the fact the practice absorbs it. He'd feel more comfortable adding chemo if reimbursement timelines were predictable. Right now he stays cautious and picks patients carefully.

Academic thoracic oncologist described a good process: biomarker report, imaging and a templated letter go in with every PA. Most osimertinib approvals come back quickly, and the combination ones usually do after a short delay. Patients are linked to copay support at the first visit. She felt access doesn't limit her regimen choice, though she acknowledged her setting is better resourced than most.

Said access is a mixed bag depending on the plan. Commercial patients generally get approved once the paperwork is right, but it can take a couple of rounds. Public plan patients seem easier on the oral TKI and harder on anything with infusion. He wasn't sure why, only that scheduling depends on knowing the answer first. Overall he'd call it manageable but unpredictable.

Oncologist described an older patient on a fixed income with a public plan who was told her share of the oral drug would be unaffordable once she reached the coverage gap. The clinic's social worker spent weeks looking for assistance, and the patient nearly skipped doses meanwhile. He said this scenario worries him more than the prior auth itself. A few similar patients have quietly stopped treatment, he thinks.

Clinic pharmacist said the main time sink is documentation for appeals, not the appeals themselves. Once they built a standard packet with the mutation report and the relevant trial data, turnaround got a bit better. Still not sure whether outcomes changed or just the effort. She felt that for the combination, payers want more justification than for osimertinib alone.

Community physician said one payer wanted a different EGFR TKI tried first, which he found hard to accept for a patient with brain involvement. They filed an expedited appeal and it was eventually reversed. But the delay meant the patient sat untreated for a stretch, and the staff were frustrated. He said he doesn't feel confident this won't happen again with the next plan.
Not sure yet if PA turnaround changes with the chemo add-on.
Seems like denials are creeping up for the osimertinib combo, but hard to say.
Copay card apparently covered most of it for her, so probably fine.
Buy-and-bill for the chemo side worries the admin more than the TKI.
Would need to see how their payers handle the doublet first.
Osimertinib alone gets approved pretty quickly I think, no real fuss.

Community practice nurse said the peer-to-peer for osimertinib plus a platinum doublet took a couple of weeks last time, which may have delayed cycle one. She wasn't sure whether it was the payer or just paperwork on their end.

Pharmacy lead at a hospital-based clinic thinks the oral TKI is mostly handled through specialty pharmacy, so the access hurdles seem modest. The infusion portion is where it may get complicated, but they haven't had enough cases to judge.
Oncologist mentioned that appeals with the FLAURA2 data attached seem to get overturned more often than not, at least in her experience. Not sure if that holds across payers though.

A practice manager said patients on high-deductible plans may delay starting because of the out-of-pocket for the first fill. She thinks foundation assistance helps but the timing is unpredictable, so it's a mixed picture.
Academic physician says step edits requiring a prior first-gen TKI appear less common now for first line, but he's not certain. Would need to look at their last few denials to confirm.

Infusion center director is worried the reimbursement for the added chemo visits may not cover chair time and nursing. Probably will limit how many patients they offer the osimertinib combination to, though nothing is decided.
Fellow noted the copay assistance enrollment is done by a navigator at the same visit, so patients seem to leave with a plan. Probably helps adherence, I think.
Rural clinic doc said travel to infusion is the bigger issue than coverage, honestly. Coverage seems okay so far for the few patients she's tried.

Seems like the denials we hear about are mostly for the combination rather than osimertinib by itself. One community oncologist thought the payer wanted a clear rationale for adding chemo, maybe tied to disease burden, and the first submission didn't have it. They resubmitted and I think it eventually went through, but the start was pushed back. She isn't sure whether that's a payer policy thing or just how her staff wrote the letter. Either way, she'd rather not repeat it.

Honestly hard to generalize. At the group practice, the oral drug goes through specialty pharmacy and the team says it's mostly routine, though refills sometimes lapse when a plan reauthorizes. Pemetrexed and carboplatin are buy-and-bill, so the finance lead is watching how the margins look after a few cycles. She may be fine with it, but would need to see actual remits before saying. For now it's wait and see.

Pleasantly surprised by one large cancer center's workflow. A navigator starts the prior authorization the day the biomarker result lands, so by the visit it's often already moving. Patients get screened for copay help at the same time, which seems to prevent a lot of surprise bills. The physician thinks this is probably why few of her EGFR patients have gone without therapy. Not sure it would scale to smaller clinics.

Appeal fatigue came up a lot. The nurse coordinator said one patient's appeal took multiple rounds adn she spends more time on that than on actual teaching. Peer-to-peer slots are short and the reviewer sometimes seemed unfamiliar with the combo regimen, I think. She may stop pursuing the doublet for borderline cases if that continues, though she wasn't certain.

Site-of-care came up with a physician in an independent office. Hospital outpatient infusion might be reimbursed differently, and payers may push them toward one setting, but he wasn't sure which direction. If the combination means several infusion cycles plus the oral drug, he worries the office would carry the drug acquisition cost before payment arrives. Would need to see how long payments take. He said he's open to it if the numbers hold.

A social worker described a patient who got oral osimertinib approved but then hesitated over the infusion cost share on top. She thinks the combined out-of-pocket may be more than people expect, though she couldn't say how much for sure. The patient took a few weeks to decide, and that delay seemed to worry the family more than the cost itself. Foundation help may not stack neatly, apparently, and she didn't recieve a clear answer from them.

access|pembrolizumab.t: Prior auth for pembro in resected gastric has mostly gone through without drama at their site.
Denials on the perioperative lung regimen are eating the nurse navigator's whole week.
Copay program covers most patients, but the uninsured still fall through the cracks.
Peer-to-peer is the only thing that overturns the step edit, and its slow.
Buy-and-bill margin is fine for them, so no hesitation on starting anyone.
Not sure how the 340B side changes the picture for pembrolizumab here, never really looked.

Small community practice, two oncologists. Auth usually comes back in a few days when they cite the label, but the stress point is lining it up with the surgery date. Probably needs to be started before neoadjuvant cycle one, not after.

The payer wanted CPS documented before approving the gastric indication, and the pathology report didn't have it in the format they asked for. Resubmitting cost close to two weeks. Patient started chemo alone in the meantime, which the physician was clearly unhappy about.
Foundation copay grants have been reliable for their lung patients, I think. The financial counselor handles it at the first visit, so patients rarely delay treatment over cost.

Said the adjuvant phase after neoadjuvant pembrolizumab sometimes gets treated as a brand new request by the payer. Reviewers then ask for the original auth number and the surgical path report agian. Annoying paperwork but it usually clears eventually.

Hospital outpatient infusion suite versus a freestanding clinic came up. Some payers are nudging toward the lower-cost site, which the doctor sees as reasonable for stable patients. He worries about the first cycles, where he wants the patient in the setting with the most monitoring.

Older patients on government plans rarely hit prior auth in her experience, while commercial plans are where the friction sits. She said that split shapes which patients get scheduled first, though she wasn't comfortable calling that a formal policy.
High-deductible plans early in the year are brutal; patients balk at the first infusion bill.
Approvals for the gastric first-line combination have been quick lately, no real complaints.

Cash flow is the real worry for this small group. They buy the drug up front, and when a claim gets denied weeks after administration, the practice often absorbs the loss or spends months on appeal. Pembrolizumab is expensive enough that a couple of bad claims in a quarter would hurt. He said they now check auth twice, before ordering and again before the patient sits down. It works, but it ties up a staff member nearly full time.

Her view was mixed after we talked for a while. Approvals for the lung perioperative setting are mostly smooth now that the payers have seen enough requests. The step edits in gastric are less predictable, with some plans wanting chemo documented first and others not asking at all. She thinks it depends on the individual reviewer more than on any written policy. Appeals do succeed, but timing is the issue, since a delay of even a week can push surgery scheduling around.

They hired a dedicated pharmacy auth coordinator last year, and she described it as the best thing they did for access. Submissions now go out with the biomarker results, staging, and a short letter attached, so most come back approved on first pass. Denials are rare enough that the team treats them as exceptions. Patients also get connected to assistance programs before the first dose rather than after the first bill. She credits the workflow, not the payers, and said smaller sites might struggle to copy it.

Rural gastric patients are the ones he worries about. Even with approval, the travel to the infusion site is a cost that no copay program touches, and some payers won't cover the closer, smaller site. A long course of treatment means lots of trips, and a few patients have quietly dropped the immunotherapy and stayed on chemo alone. He said that's rarely documented as an access problem, so it probably goes undercounted.

We spent a lot of time on financial toxicity. The oncologist said the cost conversation now happens in the same visit as the treatment-choice discussion, which feels uncomfortable but necessary. Assistance programs help a good chunk of patients, though the paperwork burden falls on people who are already exhausted. She wasn't sure whether the programs are generous enough for those just above the income cutoffs. Overall she's cautiously okay with the current state but wouldn't call it solved.
PA turnaround for pembro is usually a few days at his clinic, no real complaints.
Denials on perioperative requests keep coming back and the appeals eat up staff time.
Not sure how the copay card applies once patients are in the neoadjuvant phase.
Buy-and-bill margins on infusions are getting thinner, per the practice manager.
A foundation grant came through in under a week for her uninsured gastric patient.
Mostly no coverage problems, just waiting on paperwork.

Community clinic with two infusion chairs said the payer wants the pathology report and PD-L1 result attached to the prior authorization for gastric. Once the staff upload both, approval comes back fast. They have it down to a routine now.

Most of their patients go to the hospital outpatient infusion site because the payer prefers it. The patients' coinsurance is usually higher there, though. The pharmacist thinks that's just how it is for now.

A step edit asked for chemo-only first in a perioperative lung case, and it came up once so far. The doctor needed a peer-to-peer to get it overturned, and surgery scheduling slipped in the meantime. I think the reviewer didn't grasp the neoadjuvant intent.

Their financial navigator handles all copay assistance, and the physician admitted he doesn't know the details. His impression is that commercially insured patients are generally fine. The uninsured or underinsured are the hard ones.

One plan makes the clinic use white-bagging through a specialty pharmacy, and the nurse manager dislikes it. If a dose changes or the patient gets admitted, the drug is wasted and nobody gets reimbursed. Pembrolizumab is probably not the only drug affected.
NP said appeals on gastric requests were overturned most of the time once they cited the compendia listing. It takes one extra letter, but she called it manageable.

Academic center pharmacy runs benefits verification before cycle 1. Sometimes the neoadjuvant and adjuvant phases are authorized separately, so they resubmit midway through the regimen. It hasn't caused a gap yet, but they watch the calendar.

Patient on a high deductible plan started in January and hesitated over the first infusion bill, so the start got pushed back about two weeks. The oncologist felt that delay mattered for a resectable case. Clinic only caught it after the patient called to say they were worried abuot cost.

Small rural practice owner is worried about cash flow on buy-and-bill. He fronts the cost of the drug and then waits weeks for payment on some claims. A single denial on a high-cost infusion can really hurt that month. He's thought about referring new starts to a bigger center. I don't think he wants to, but the math is getting hard.

For perioperative lung, the PA was approved for the neoadjuvant portion without trouble. The adjuvant phase needed its own request, and the clinic isn't sure whether the first approval carries over. The coordinator keeps a tracker so that nothing lapses after surgery. Pembrolizumab is covered, but the process is fragmented. She said it's more annoying than blocking.

This gastric clinic has a dedicated PA coordinator and the difference is obvious. She submits the request the same day the biomarker result lands and follows up with the payer by portal. Approvals mostly come back before the patient's first chemo visit. The physician said he rarely thinks about access anymore. He also said that probably wouldn't be true without her.

A payer denied a gastric request citing the biomarker threshold, even though the report was attached. The appeal took a few weeks. The patient started chemo alone in the meantime, and the physician wasn't happy about it. They're not sure whether the denial was a reviewer error or a policy rule. Staff are now adding a cover note that spells out the PD-L1 result.

Practice administrator described the site-of-care question as mostly economics. The office-based infusion suite makes money on some drugs and breaks even on others. Payers sometimes push toward home infusion or the hospital depending on the contract. For checkpoint inhibitors she said the schedule is convenient, which helps, but reimbursement still drives where patients go. She didn't give specifics, only that it varies by plan.
Prior auth for pembro still eats two days of my nurse's week.
Depends entirely on the payer, honestly.
Copay foundation covered my last three patients without a fuss.
Denials keep coming back citing 'not medically necessary' for perioperative use.
Buy-and-bill margins are thin, I think, once you count the admin burden.
Appeal got overturned in under a week, surprisingly.

We're a small community practice, so floating drug cost for two months before reimbursement lands is a real cash flow issue. Probably manageable with the volume we have on pembro, but I worry about the next new agent.

Gastric patients with borderline PD-L1 get the worst of it. The payer wants biomarker documentation attached to the PA, then bounces it anyway for a missing pathology addendum. It usually gets approved on resubmission, just late.
Honestly our infusion pharmacist has the PA process down. Perioperative lung approvals through most commercial plans come back within a few days now, which wasn't true a year ago.
Step edits asking for chemo-first documentation make no sense when the label and guidelines say otherwise. I end up spending peer-to-peers arguing about what's already in the compendium. Frustrating.
Some plans favor hospital outpatient for site of care, others push us toward office or home infusion. Patients get shuffled around and I'm not convinced it saves anybody anything.

Patients on high-deductible plans just stop showing up for cycle 2, in my experience. Copay assistance covers the drug but not the infusion admin fees so they still get a bill. Not sure anyone explains that upfront
Neoadjuvant authorization is the tricky part since the adjuvant phase needs a separate approval. We sometimes get one but not the other, and then scheduling gets awkwrad.
For uninsured or underinsured gastric patients, manufacturer assistance is the only route and the paperwork is brutal. It takes weeks, and weeks matter.

The appeals process is a time sink. Last month a perioperative lung patient got denied on the first PA, so we did a peer-to-peer and then a written appeal. Surgery got pushed because nobody wanted to start without coverage confirmed. I get that payers want controls, but delaying a curative-intent regimen over paperwork is hard to defend. Not sure what the real denial rate is but it feels like a lot lateley.

We run buy-and-bill and it's okay but not great. Reimbursement per unit on pembro is solid, though the money tied up in inventory is scary for a small clinic. Vial waste isn't a huge issue since dosing is fixed, I think. The bigger problem is when a claim gets denied after the fact and we eat the cost. So, mixed, and it depends on how clean the front end is.

I'll give credit where due: the manufacturer hub support has been decent. Benefits verification usually happens before the patient is even scheduled, so I rarely see surprises. For gastric, the PA templates are fairly standard now and approvals mostly follow the label. I still wish the copay program had fewer hoops, but it's smoother than I expected.

Our health-system specialty pharmacy mandate is a mess. Some payers insist on white-bagging, so the drug arrives with no guarantee on timing or storage. When a cycle gets delayed because the shipment didn't show, who's accountable? Not the payer. We also can't bill the usual way, so the clinic loses margin on the visit. I'd rather they just let us buy and bill.

We're academic, so we have a financial navigator team. They tell me most gastric approvals go through, but a good chunk need a second submission. Older patients on fee-for-service coverage seem to have fewer step edit problems than commercial folks. I'm not certain why. Maybe the commercial plans just have more internal rules.

Surprisingly positive lately. A resectable lung patient got approved in a day, no peer-to-peer, and copay assistance was enrolled the same visit. Our PA coordinator thinks the payer updated its policy to match the perioperative indication. If that holds, it removes the biggest headache I had last year. Cautiously optimistic, but I won't believe it until I see a few more.
PA for pembro usually sails through here, couple days tops.
Copay assistance covers most pts, so cost rarely comes up.
Denials on periop lung tx still happen, but fewer than last yr.
Peer-to-peer needed almost every time for neoadjuvant start.
Not sure about payer side, their PA team handels all of it.
Buy-and-bill margin on pembro is thin but practice absorbs it.
Community clinic, small practice. Since the payer added pembro to its gastric pathway, PA turnaround dropped a lot. HCP said it's basically just a form now.
Pt w/ resectable NSCLC waited ~2 wks for PA, surgery slot almost lost. HCP worried delay eats into the neoadjuvant window and nobody on payer side seems to care.
Step edit on one commercial plan wants chemo-only first for HER2-neg gastric, I think. HCP documents PD-L1 status w/ pembro request and it usually clears on appeal.
Foundation grant money dries up mid-yr, then pts w/ big copays during adjuvant phase start hesitating. Clinic pharmacist flagged it, not sure how common across the practice.
Academic center, hospital-owned outpatient infusion. Site-of-care rules push some commercial pts to a cheaper site or home infusion, which HCP finds annoying but workable.
Dedicated fin counselor enrols pts in assistance at first visit. HCP says pts dropping pembro tx over cost is rare now.
Tumor board picks periop pembro but payer calls it off-label for a gastric subset w/o PD-L1 cutoff met. Appeal letter takes the NP hours to recieve a decision, overturned maybe half the time?
Rural oncologist, buy-and-bill. Cash flow is the real worry when claims get held for auth mismatch, otherwise fine w/ pembro.

Big concern for HCP = delays. Neoadjuvant pts need tx started fast, but PA wants staging docs, path report and tumor board notes. Miss one doc and it bounces back, staff spends a lot of time chasing. Pt anxiety goes up during the wait. HCP thinks some practices probably skip the periop regimen if payer looks hard.

Access fine per HCP at large community network. Central PA team submits within a day of tumor board decision. Denials only a handful per yr, mostly paperwork errors not coverage. Copay card plus foundation support covers most commercial pts on pembro. Underinsured pts are the tricky group, handled case by case.

Mixed picture per HCP. Commercial plans mostly approve per label, but govt plan pts see more variation in timing. Adjuvant continuation after surgery needs a second PA at some plans and staff sometimes forget. Not sure if that's payer policy or local workflow. Overall tx rarely cancelled, just delayed.

Reauth cycles frustrate HCP. Pt on pembro 1L gastric got auth for only a few cycles at a time, then had to resubmit w/ scans. Missed one renewal, infusion pushed a week and pt was upset. Staff now use a tickler system. HCP feels it's admin burden w/o clinical value.

Site-of-care economics came up. Hospital system wants pts infused in-house for margin reasons while payers steer toward lower-cost sites, HCP caught in the middle. Pt travel and AE monitoring matter too, so HCP prefers keeping complex periop pts at main center. Not sure how it plays out next yr.

High-deductible pt got hit w/ a big bill after first pembro infusion early in the yr. Assistance enrollment took weeks to retro-cover. Pt nearly stopped tx. HCP says Jan-Mar is the worst stretch and nurse navigators get swamped.
PA turnaround still the biggest headache for periop starts.
Pembro approvals have been pretty smooth lately, honestly.
Copay foundation funds dry up fast, then everyone just waits.
Denials mostly tied to neoadjuvant timing, not sure why
Their PA team handles everything, docs barely notice it.
Buy and bill margin is ok but thin, really depends on payer mix.

Community practice, gastric pt, payer wanted chemo-alone first before approving the PD-1. Took two peer-to-peers and almost 2 wks, which pushed the start date. Doc said that delay is hard to explain to the pt.

Says pembrolizumab approvals hinge on whether the biomarker documentation matches the label. If the PD-L1 result is in the chart up front it usually goes through, if not it bounces back. Probably a paperwork issue more than a coverage one.
Academic site has a pharmacist who does benefit verification before the first visit. Thinks thats why they rarely see surprise denials on periop lung. Wants to keep that workflow as is.
High deductible pt got a huge bill after the first infusion and nearly skipped adjuvant. Social worker scrambled to find assistance. Not sure it would have been caught otherwise.

Site-of-care policies from a couple of payers are nudging them toward hospital outpatient infusion instead of the office. Not clear yet if that helps or hurts them financially. Still sorting through the numbers.
Appeals for off-pathway gastric use mostly get overturned if the letter cites guidelines, I think. But it eats nurse time. One-person team so it adds up.

Manufacturer assistance program moved quickly for an uninsured pt with gastric cancer, drug on the shelf within days. Clinic manager was surprised how little back and forth there was. Would use it again.
One payer is pushing specialty pharmacy over buy-and-bill. They see pros and cons, less cash tied up but less control over scheduling, so undecided.

Big issue for periop lung is continuity. Payer approves the neoadjuvant phase, then reviews the adjuvant phase as a totally separate request. Pts are post-surgery and waiting, and some get anxious about the gap. Staff said they now submit both requests together but approval is still hit or miss. Frustrating since the plan was set at tumor board.

Mixed feelings on buy-and-bill with Keytruda. Reimbursement is okay when claims pay on time, but the drug cost is so high that one slow or denied claim hurts cash flow. Practice admin said they probably wouldn't stock more than a couple of patients' worth. Still prefers it to the alternatives for most commercial pts, though.

Pretty positive overall. Financial counselor meets every new immunotherapy pt before cycle 1 and runs through copay card eligibility and any foundation options. Docs rarely hear about cost anymore because it's handled upstream. A few pts on government plans still have gaps, but she said those are manageable. Thinks this is why their abandonment rate is low, though no hard data.

Rural clinic, and cost hits twice, copay plus travel. Hospital-based infusion is the only covered site for some plans, so pts drive a long way for each cycle. Nurse said a couple of pts just stopped coming, and she's not sure whether it was cost or distance. Docs feel stuck, they cant fix the payer rule.

Re-authorization comes up every few months and they never quite know when. Sometimes it's a rubber stamp, sometimes they have to resend the same notes. Pembro pts on maintenance usually fine, but a lapse in auth can delay a dose by a week. Staff built a tickler system to track it, which helps a bit.

Small independent practice feels squeezed. Claims for pembrolizumab sit for weeks, and the practice has to float the drug cost in the meantime. Owner said they've talked about referring new gastric pts to the hospital instead, which they hate doing. Denials plus slow payment make it hard to justify stocking. Not sure how long they can keep this up.
Said PA turnaround is usually a few days, nothing dramatic.
Peer-to-peer requests for perioperative lung are becoming routine, per the clinic pharmacist.
Felt copay assistance has covered nearly all of his patients so far.
Denials on gastric cases can sit for weeks, and it wears the whole team down.
Not sure whether the payer step edit even applies to neoadjuvant use.
Described buy-and-bill margins for pembro as acceptable in their practice.

A community oncologist explained that the infusion center fronts the drug cost and then waits on reimbursement, so a denial after administration really hurts cash flow. He thinks smaller practices might hesitate to start perioperative patients because of that exposure.

Mentioned that the nurse navigator builds the prior authorization packet, usually staging plus PD-L1 results. Approvals mostly come back fine, but gastric cases sometimes trigger a second request for biomarker paperwork.

According to the HCP, the hospital financial counselor enrolls patients in a manufacturer assistance program the same week as the consult. Patients rarely walk away over cost, which she called a relief.

Uninsured and underinsured patients are the real worry, she said, since foundation funds tend to run dry midyear. Pretty sure a couple of people had surgery planning pushed back while waiting on coverage

Reported that the academic center routes perioperative lung patients through an in-house specialty pharmacy rather than buy-and-bill. In their view it simplifies things for payers but adds a lag before cycle one. Overall a wash, probably.
Complained that appeals drag when a plan treats the neoadjuvant-plus-adjuvant sequence as not covered. They usually win in the end, but the window before surgery can close first.
Noted that since the label expanded, payers seem more aligned with guidelines and approvals feel smoother. Probably true for gastric too, though he sees fewer of those patients.

Site-of-care policies are nudging some patients from hospital outpatient to office or home infusion, he said. Patient preference varies a lot, and he isn't sure the economics favor the practice either way.

The HCP described a resectable lung patient who was approved for the neoadjuvant phase, but adjuvant continuation needed its own authorization. That second request lagged, and the patient nearly missed a scheduled cycle. Staff spent hours on the phone confirming the approval carried over. He called split approvals clinically nonsensical. His wish was that payers would authorize the entire perioperative course at once.

Said their 340B status makes the buy-and-bill math work reasonably well, but independent practices don't have that cushion. I think he said the lag matters most when payment trails acquisition cost. He doesn't see pembrolizumab as a loss leader, but not a big winner either. The pharmacy team reviews denial rates monthly, and so far nothing alarming.

Walked through their workflow with evident pride: the pharmacist flags a new perioperative start, the navigator submits the authorization the same day, and the financial counselor screens for assistance in parallel. Most patients are cleared before the first infusion chair slot opens. She said denials are a handful per year and typically overturned on first appeal. Credits the dedicated staff more than any payer change.

Patients on high-deductible plans get hit alot in the first months of the year, he said. Even with assistance programs, some are confused by paperwork and give up halfway through enrollment. He worries a few never start treatment because of the out-of-pocket estimate they were quoted. Social work helps, but they are stretched thin. In his words, cost conversations now happen before the clinical ones.

Reported that one plan asks for documentation of prior systemic therapy before approving certain gastric regimens, which reads like a step edit even though it isn't labeled that way. The team has a template letter that usually clears it. Turnaround is inconsistent, though, from a couple of days to over a week. She isn't sure whether policies differ by employer group or by plan. Either way, she keeps a tracking sheet to stay ahead of it.
Pembro approvals have been smooth for us, just the copay card paperwork drags.
Perioperative PA usually clears in days, if the staging note is airtight.
Great drug, but peer-to-peer requests are eating my nurse's week.
Buy-and-bill margins are probably fine for now, I think.
Denials landing after the neoadjuvant start are what worry me most.
Foundation support came through fast for our uninsured gastric patient, huge relief

Honestly thrilled with how pembro is working in our resected lung patients. The only wrinkle is that one payer wants a separate auth for the adjuvant phase even though the neoadjuvant was approved, so we resubmit and wait.

Our infusion center has a dedicated auth coordinator and it has made a big difference. Most gastric requests that include PD-L1 documentation go through on the first pass. The caveat is that anything that looks even slightly off-label gets kicked to medical review.

I'm a big believer in perioperative immunotherapy, but a regional commercial plan keeps denying for 'criteria not met' when the stage is borderline. Appeals take weeks and the surgery date doesn't wait for them.

We're a community practice, so buy-and-bill is just our reality. Reimbursement for the PD-1 is probably still OK, though carrying that much inventory makes our practice manager nervous. I love being able to offer it locally, I just wish the cash flow were less lumpy.
Medicare patients have been easy, which is great. Supplemental plans are where we sometimes see copay surprises and I'm not sure why. Patients get a bill and call us teh same day.

Step edits that require chemo first in some gastric plans drive me nuts, since I want to start with the immunotherapy combination. We usually win on appeal, but it costs us time and the patient is anxious the whole while.

Patient assistance enrollment is wonderful when it works. Income cutoffs confuse the patients who are just over the line though, and I think a few of them quietly drop off. We try to catch it early but it isn't systematic.

Site-of-care policies pushing patients toward lower-cost infusion sites haven't hit us yet. I'm very excited about where this drug is going in lung and gastric. I'm just a bit worried the hospital outpatient setting gets restricted down the road.

Pembro in the KEYNOTE-671 setting has become routine for us, and access has been better than I feared. Our pharmacy team preloads every PA with histology, staging and the surgical plan. A good chunk come back approved within a few days. Prior auth for adjuvant continuation is the one caveat, because some payers ask for pathology response documentation that we simply don't have on the day of the request. Still, I'd call it a net win for our patients.

I'm very supportive of using it, but access keeps me up at night. A few of my gastric patients waited longer than I'd like for a determination, and one had to recieve a delayed first cycle. Our staff spends hours on forms and phone trees. I worry that smaller practices without a dedicated coordinator will just give up on the harder cases. The science is compelling, so the friction feels especially frustrating.

Copay and assistance have been a mixed bag for us. Commercially insured patients generally do fine with the manufacturer copay program, and our navigator enrolls them at the first visit. Medicare patients depend on independent foundations, which open and close unpredictably. I'm enthusiastic about offering perioperative treatment to everyone eligible. But the financial side is uneven, and I think it shapes who gets it more than we admit.

Being a small independent clinic, we absorb a lot of risk on buy-and-bill. When a payer denies after we've already administered, we're often left chasing the claim for months. I love what pembro offers my lung patients, truly. The caveat is that I've had to be pickier about timing and verification before the first dose. Some partners in the practice wonder if we can sustain it if denials increase.

Gastric access has surprised me in a good way. Most of our HER2-negative patients with the right biomarker documentation get approved without drama. When a denial does come, a short letter plus peer-to-peer usually turns it around. Our pharmacist tracks every case, which helps a lot. I'd just flag that the process works because we have that person, and I'm not sure it would elsewhere.

Site-of-care economics are something we're thinking about more. Our hospital outpatient infusion suite is convenient and patients like it, but some payers seem to prefer the physician office or home settings. I'm excited about the drug and don't want logistics to dictate where patients are treated. That said, I understand why the payers do it. We're probably going to need to rework scheduling and chair capacity if more plans push this.

access|sacituzumab govitecan.t: SG PA usually clears first pass, few days turnaround.
Medicare Advantage denial, peer-to-peer pending.
Copay foundation covered pt quick, no tx delay.
Buy-and-bill margin on ADCs razor thin, admin nervous.
PA nurse handles all of it, HCP doesn't see the details.
Payer step edit wanted two prior chemo lines documented, so delays.
Community onc, HR+/HER2- pt post-CDK4/6 and endocrine. Trodelvy PA approved on label basis, tumor board note helped. Tx started within the week.
Payer questioned urothelial use, I think compendia status was unclear to them. Appeal took weeks and pt progressed in the meantime. HCP now hesitant to even try in that setting.
Academic center, infusion pharmacy deals with PA in-house. Denials rare per HCP but appeals eat staff time. Not sure how 340B plays into their margin.
Medicaid pt, state plan slow on auth. Had to bridge with single-agent chemo, HCP frustrated. Would have preferred SG at progression.
Copay assistance enrollment is routine now. Pt w/ high deductible still balked before C1, social worker sorted it I think.
HCP says payer policies now seem to mirror the TROPiCS-02 population so PA is mostly a checkbox. Fewer peer-to-peers than last yr. Probably helps that office has a template letter.
Independent practice worried abt cash flow, ASP lag plus buy-and-bill = float risk. If denials stack up they might send pts to hospital outpatient. Not thrilled about losing continuity.
Rural pts face travel burden, site-of-care is hospital outpatient only for this tx accoridng to HCP. Payer doesn't push home infusion for SG. Reimbursement itself not the main barrier there.

Small oncology group described denials as 'whack-a-mole'. One payer wants PFS data from prior lines, another wants AEs history from earlier ADC exposure. Staff spends hours on appeals per pt. HCP thinks some pts just never get offered SG because the paperwork seems daunting. Frustrated but still pushes for it in select pts.

Mixed picture at this hospital system. PA approvals fine for HR+/HER2- after endocrine and chemo, but timing is unpredictable, sometimes 2 days, sometimes 2 weeks. Specialty pharmacy vs buy-and-bill decision depends on payer. HCP isn't sure which route is better financially, finance team decides. Pts mostly OK on copay once foundation support is in place.

Large practice with dedicated auth team, HCP very upbeat. Said PA for SG is now routine, approvals come back fast when notes cite prior endocrine and chemo lines. Copay support covers most commercial pts. Buy-and-bill is manageable since volume is steady. Honestly access is not what stops them from using it, more AEs mgmt and chair time.

HCP described a pt with commercial coverage denied for 'not medically necessary' despite meeting criteria. Appeal letter, peer-to-peer, then second-level review, over a month total. Pt had rapid progression, PS dropped, no longer fit for tx. HCP thinks payers underestimate the cost of delay. Said it left the team demoralized.

Safety-net hospital, many uninsured or underinsured pts. Drug is expensive so pharmacy committee wants a clear case each time, usually reviewed at tumor board. HCP said manufacturer assistance helps some but paperwork is heavy. Probably fine for insured pts, case by case for the rest.

HCP pleasantly surprised by recent access. Last two pts got PA approved same week, and financial counselor enrolled both in copay help before C1. No gaps in tx. Thinks payers are getting more comfortable with the TROP2 ADC after wider use. Would still keep a backup plan ready for denials.
PA approvals for SG have been coming back fast lately.
Copay card covers most of their commercial patients, so cost rarely stops anyone.
Denials mostly come down to line-of-therapy documentation, not the drug itself.
Buy-and-bill margin on this one is thin, honestly.
Unsure how their payers handle it after endocrine therapy plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor.
Peer-to-peer needed nearly every time and it wears the staff down
Community practice PA coordinator said approvals usually land within a few days if the note lists prior endocrine therapy and the CDK4/6 inhibitor. The only snags are missing documents.
For urothelial, the payer wanted proof of prior platinum and a checkpoint inhibitor before approving. The clinic sent both and it went through, but it added about a week before cycle 1.
Hospital outpatient infusion pharmacy said the drug cost sits heavily on their budget. They float inventory for weeks until the payment comes back, and a denial leaves them holding it.

One retired patient on a fixed income balked at the coinsurance estimate. Treatment was delayed about two weeks until a foundation grant recieved approval. The nurse navigator said this happens a lot with older patients.

Practice manager doesn't think site-of-care policies pushing patients to home infusion will apply here, given premeds and monitoring. Not sure if the payers see it the same way. They are watching for any policy change.

Oncologist said one plan has a step edit requiring another chemo first in HR+/HER2- disease. They appeal citing the label and I think it gets overturned at the second level. It's extra paperwork but not a blocker.

Financial navigator at a small clinic said manufacturer support enrollment is simple and the forms come back quickly. Most patients are sorted on copay before the first chair time. She called it one of the easier drugs to get started.

Got a denial as 'not medically necessary' for a patient who clearly met the label criteria. The appeal took close to three weeks. The physician was frustrated because the patient was symptomatic while waiting, and it made him hesitant to offer SG early.

Academic center has a dedicated PA team that pre-checks every SG order against payer criteria. The team gathers pathology, prior regimens and dates of progression into one packet. Turnaround is typically under a week. Where it stalls is secondary payers, which seem to be handled separately. The oncologist says the team does the heavy lifting and he rarely sees the process.

Rural clinic nurse said the closest specialty infusion option is far away, so most patients stay with them. Their buy-and-bil exposure worries the owner, especially when a claim rejects months later. They have thought about limiting how many SG patients they take at once. The physician says he would rather refer out than risk the cash flow, though that isn't ideal for the patient.

Pharmacist at a mid-size oncology group said access has gotten smoother since they built a standard checklist for SG. Commercial plans mostly approve on first submission, and the copay assistance covers the rest. Their reimbursement has been steady, and the drug no longer feels like a financial gamble. A couple of appeals still come up, but they are manageable.

Several payers in the region keep sending step-edit letters asking for a taxane or another chemo before SG in HR+/HER2- disease. The practice answers with the label and prior-therapy history, and that usually works. The office manager said it eats a few hours of staff time per case. The oncologist thinks this is just the cost of doing business with a newer ADC and doesn't expect it to ease soon.

Some payers at a large group push white bagging through specialty pharmacy, while others allow buy-and-bill. The group has to track which patient falls under which rule, and scheduling gets awkward when drug delivery is late. The physician said clinical use isn't affected but the logistics are annoying. He probably prefers buy-and-bill when the margin works.

Nurse practitioner said patients started on SG at her clinic rarely drop out for cost reasons. The financial counselor does a benefits check at the first consult, so patients know their copay before scheduling. Most are comfortable once they see the assistance numbers. She thinks the early conversation is the reason there are few surprises later.
PA turnaround is killing us, honestly.
Peer-to-peer every single time for Trodelvy, exhausting.
Once the PA clears, copay support has worked fine for us.
Appeals mostly get overturned eventually, just painfully slowly.
Reviewers clearly haven't seen the TROPiCS-02 data. Zero familiarity.
Depends entirely on the payer, some approve in days, some stall for weeks.

We're a small community practice and buy-and-bill for this drug scares our administrator. Reimbursement lag can run weeks, and a denied claim means we eat the cost of the vial. Probably why I send some patients to the hospital infusion center instead.

Step edits want prior endocrine therapy and chemo documented, which for HR+/HER2- is fine because those patients have all been through it. It's the paperwork that trips us up, not the criteria themselves.
Our navigator gets benefits verification back fast, and the copay card basically zeroes out the commercial patients. I'll admit I expected worse with SG.

Urothelial is murkier than breast. Reviewers sometimes ask why we didn't use an EV/pembro combo first, which is fair, but then they don't know how to read the label for post-platinum, post-checkpoint patients. Usually gets sorted after a call, so more annoying than blocking.

I think site-of-care economics matter more than anything drug-specific. Our hospital outpatient setup cushions the margin, but the independent clinic down the road can't do that. Not sure how they manage.
Patient got denied for 'not medically necessary' after we sent the full data package. The appeal took about three weeks and she progressed in the meantime. Frustrating doesn't cover it.
Our payer mix is mostly one big regional plan and they've been pretty reasonable with sacituzumab. Approvals typically come through without a peer-to-peer if the notes are clean.

Copay assistance foundations run dry every few months and then the patient is just left waiting. We've had people delay cycle one while we hunt for another fund. Its not a drug problem, its a system problem.

Every SG start eats hours of staff time. Our PA coordinator submits, gets a request for more records, resubmits, and then I do the peer-to-peer explaining prior lines to someone who isn't an oncologist. If it's denied, the appeal letter lands on me. I've honestly wondered whether it's worth starting when the clock matters. Not sure other practices feel as strongly, but we're stretched thin.

Vial wastage comes up in our pharmacy meetings. Weight-based dosing means rounding and some leftover, and I'm not sure every payer reimburses the discarded portion. Our hospital outpatient site absorbs it okay, but I think a smaller clinic would feel it alot. Otherwise the buy-and-bill margin seems fine, not great, not terrible. I'd guess it's the main reason a few colleagues refer patients to the hospital.

Medicare Advantage is where we get burned. Approval comes through, the patient gets two cycles, then a retrospective review flags something and the claim bounces. Nobody told us the auth had a narrow window. We've written off a couple of those, which a practice our size can't do often. I'm skeptical the plans even read the criteria they publish.

Credit where it's due: this has been smoother than I feared. The support program does benefits checks fast, and for HR+/HER2- patients after endocrine therapy and chemo the criteria line up with what we'd do anyway. We've had a handful of denials but most flipped on first appeal. Still annoying paperwork, but it hasn't stopped anyone from getting treated in my practice.

Step edits for sacituzumab in breast haven't bothered me much. Plans want CDK4/6 and endocrine therapy documented plus a couple of chemo lines, and our notes already capture that. We built a template for the PA packet, so submission takes minutes now. The urothelial side is still a coin flip, I think.

Patients ask about out-of-pocket cost before they ask about side effects. Commercial patients with the copay card are mostly fine. Medicare patients without supplemental coverage are the ones who hesitate, and we point them to foundation funds that may or may not be open. Some go ahead anyway. I just wish the cost conversation were less of a lottery.
Prior auth turnaround is usually fine for us, just slower on Fridays.
Denials for the ADC keep citing missing step therapy that the chart already shows.
Our financial navigator sorts copay assistance before cycle one, honestly a lifesaver.

After a long chat, the main theme was that coverage itself isn't the problem, it's the friction. At their academic center every sacituzumab request goes through a central auth team that doesn't know the HR+/HER2- treatment sequence, so it bounces back asking for prior endocrine and chemo lines again. The physician thinks this costs about a week, which matters for patients progressing fast. Peer-to-peer slots are limited and tend to land when clinic is full. Frustrated overall, but not planning to avoid prescribing it.

We're a mid-size community group, and once the pathway was set up, SG approvals in pretreated HR+/HER2- disease have mostly gone through first submission. I think documenting the endocrine and CDK4/6 history up front in the note is what makes the difference.
Buy-and-bill on this drug scares our practice administrator.

Honestly this was one of the more upbeat access conversations I've had lately. The practice built a standard packet (pathology, prior lines, progression scans) and submits it the same day the decision is made. Most commercial plans have approved with little back-and-forth, and the assistance programs have covered nearly all the copay worries. The doctor credits a dedicated pharmacy tech who tracks every case. Appeals are rare now, maybe a handful in the past year.
Medicare Advantage plans are our pain point. Two or three patients got approval for a limited number of cycles and then needed reauthorization mid-treatment, which risks a gap in therapy.
Not sure how payers read SG against the label versus compendia, seems to vary by plan.

For urothelial, I think most of us are unsure what payers will accept with sacituzumab, since the indication picture has been shifting. We just submit the prior platinum and checkpoint history and wait to see what comes back.

The practice manager's biggest worry is cash flow. They buy and bill, and with a drug this expensive one denied claim after administration can sit on the books for months. A couple of retrospective denials last year made the partners much more cautious, and now they insist on written auth before even scheduling. I think that has delayed starts for some patients, which the physician hates. Underpayment relative to acquisition cost came up too, though no specifics were given.
Patients on high-deductible plans are the ones who worry me. Foundation funds run dry fast, and a few have put off starting because they couldn't face the first bill.

Site-of-care came up a lot. This physician runs a small rural clinic and said the cost makes the practice nervous about stocking the drug, so some patients get referred to a regional hospital infusion center a couple of hours away. Payers seem fine with that, I think, but patients carry the travel burden. They'd rather treat locally if reimbursement were more predictable. Not sure a different contracting arrangement would change that.
Copay enrollment takes our navigator maybe twenty minutes and nearly every commercially insured patient has been covered. That has taken the money conversation out of the exam room for the most part.

Our payer mandates white-bagging for some patients and coordination has been smoother than I feared. The drug shows up on time, though the nurses now spend extra effort verifying labels and chain of custody.
Peer-to-peer requests always seem to arrive after the patient has waited two weeks and recieved nothing.
Appeals do work eventually, usually at second level, but it eats a lot of staff time. Our nurse manager says its mostly the ECOG and prior-line documentation that gets requested again and again.

From the pharmacist side, step edits mostly want prior endocrine therapy, a CDK4/6 inhibitor and some chemo tried first, which is roughly what the patients already have, so it's rarely a hard wall. The messier part is vial waste and dose rounding, since some payers reimburse discarded drug and others don't. Not sure how consistent that is across plans. She keeps a spreadsheet of each payer's quirks and called it tedious but manageable.

Younger patients with employer plans get caught in a bad spot. The plan approves, but specialty-tier coinsurance is steep, and when the out-of-pocket max resets in January, a fall start means the patient pays twice. The oncologist said assistance programs help commercial patients but government-insured ones are left to charity foundations that often have closed funds. One patient reportedly asked to stretch the interval, and the doctor refused. I think financial toxicity is quietly shaping decisions here.
PA approvals for SG have come back quicker than I feared, honestly.
Denied twice, overturned on peer-to-peer. Exhausting.
Copay assistance covers most of my patients, so cost rarely stops anyone.
Step edit through endocrine therapy and a CDK4/6 is basically automatic, no surprise there.
Nobody at my front desk knows how to track these appeals.
Buy and bill margin on this one is razor thin, thats all I'll say.
Community site, so we usually get the PA back in about a week, but the paperwork is a lot for one drug. Our nurse navigator basically lives on hold with the plan. Once it's approved things run fine.

Urothelial is where I get stuck. Plans want proof of prior platinum and checkpoint therapy, and records from outside systems are never complete, so the denial comes back as 'insufficient documentation'.
Our pharmacy team built a PA template for sacituzumab and it cut the back and forth a lot. I think that's the main reason we've had so few denials lately.
Not sure how much of our denial problem is the drug versus the plan. Some approve straight off the label, others ask for line of therapy in writing three separate times.
Honestly the supportive care costs worry me about as much as the drug. Growth factor needs its own auth sometimes, and patients get hit with separate copays they never saw coming.
Academic center here, so we have a discounted drug pricing arrangement that cushions buy-and-bill. The smaller practices I refer to probably don't have that luxury.
Appeals take weeks and these patients don't have weeks. I've had people progress while we waited on a letter of medical necessity and I'm not convinced the plan cares
Foundation grants have come through fast for my uninsured and underinsured patients. The free drug program paperwork is annoying but it does work.

We're a small community practice and the buy-and-bill economics on this drug keep me up at night. Acquisition cost is high, reimbursement lags, and if a claim gets denied after the infusion we eat it. I've told my administrator we may have to send some patients to the hospital outpatient setting. That isn't what I want for someone doing well on treatment, but I can't carry that kind of exposure. The plans don't seem to register that at all.

Breast side, the PA question is nearly always about prior lines. Most plans want endocrine therapy, a CDK4/6 inhibitor and a couple of chemo lines documented, which matches the TROPiCS-02 population more or less. When our notes are clean it goes through. When someone dictated sloppily it bounces, so the problem is partly us, I'll admit.

One plan insists on white bagging through its own specialty pharmacy and it's a mess. Shipments arrive late or at the wrong site. If labs change the dose I can't use what was sent. We wasted a chair slot twice last month because of it. I think mandating that for a dose-adjusted infusion is just bad policy.

Surprisingly smooth so far. Most commercial plans approve off the label and the PA comes back in a few days. Our financial counselor gets copay card enrollment done the same day the order is signed. I expected way more friction given the price tag. Maybe we've just been lucky.

Patients on government plans have a different experience from the commercially insured. The older ones often have a supplemental plan, which helps, but those without it face coinsurance that's scary.
