We refer to foundations, but funds open and close unpredictably. I'd say access is okay for most and rough for a few.

Coverage in bladder cancer feels murkier to me. I think it follows the label, but reviewers seem less familiar with the drug in that setting and ask basic questions. Peer-to-peer usually settles it, though it eats time I don't have.
PA turnaround still the bottleneck, days lost every single time.
SG approvals mostly smooth at their site lately.
Copay assistance enrolled same day usually but varies by plan
Buy-and-bill on sacituzumab = cash flow headache for a small practice.
Not sure what payers want for step edits post-CDK4/6.
Nurse navigator handles PA, HCP called it basically routine now.
Community onc, 2 pts delayed last month waiting on PA. Peer-to-peer eventually overturned both, but tx start slipped a couple wks and pts were anxious about progression.
Payer step edit wants prior endocrine plus at least one chemo in met setting, I think. HCP says TROPiCS-02-type pts usually fit, so approvals mostly OK. Documenting prior lines is what trips them up.
Hospital-based infusion center, 340B in place so economics fine. HCP not worried about acquiring SG. Site-of-care a non-issue for them.
Medicare pt w/ no supplemental, copay exposure scary. Foundation funds were dry when HCP tried to refer. Pt opted to hold off on tx.
Urothelial use mostly after EV/pembro, so some plans may treat PA as off-label-ish. HCP unsure how payers view it. Probably case by case.
Denial last quarter for HR+ pt, reason listed only as 'not medically necessary' w/ no detail. Appeal took forver, and staff spent hours on letters.
Copay program works great for commercially insured pts, HCP said most pay little out of pocket. Only hurdle is the enrollment paperwork.
Practice admin debating keeping SG in-house vs referring to hospital outpatient. ASP reimbursement lag is the worry, not sure how it shakes out.

Small private practice, 2 oncs. HCP says buy-and-bill for SG ties up a lot of capital since vial cost is high and payment lags. One claim denied post-infusion because PA had lapsed, practice ate the cost. Now they won't dose until auth is in writing. Thinks some colleagues just refer pts out. Concerned about delays for pts who could benefit.

Academic center, dedicated PA team plus a pharmacist. Turnaround quick, most SG requests approved first pass citing NCCN listing. Appeals rare. Fin counselors screen for copay help at first visit. HCP said access isn't limiting there, though they're probably lucky vs community sites.

HCP mixed on access. Commercial pts fine, Medicaid pts slower, varies by state I think. Underinsured need the mfr assistance program, slow but usually comes through. Tumor board flags insurance early so PA is lined up before scheduling. A handful of pts still fell through cracks.

Rural clinic, nearest infusion site is far. HCP unsure if payers will push site-of-care shifts for SG, as they have with other drugs. Pts already travel a long way. Copay plus travel costs make some decline. HCP felt access is a real barrier even when PFS benefit looks attractive.

Payers keep asking for rationale after 2 prior chemo lines, even when pt clearly eligible. HCP frustrated w/ repeated recerts, every few months I think, and staff time adds up. Also said AEs mgmt (G-CSF, extra visits) triggers more auth questions, teh paperwork snowballs.

Tx sequencing at tumor board now includes 'will it get covered'. In HR+, HCP often waits to confirm PA before finalizing the plan post-CDK4/6 and endocrine. Pts w/ good commercial coverage start within days, others wait. Probably gets easier as payers get used to SG. Not sure how long that takes.
PA turnaround is the bottleneck here, not the clinical decision.
Our hub turns approvals around fast, so SG starts rarely slip.
Copay card covers most commercial patients; the Medicare folks are the question mark.
Denials after second-line step edits on SG keep eating our nurse's whole week
Honestly haven't seen one denial yet but it's a tiny sample.
Buy-and-bill float on this drug makes the finance people nervous.

In their hospital outpatient infusion center the buy-and-bill margin is acceptable because the 340B arrangement softens acquisition cost. Pharmacy models it every quarter and so far SG hasn't been a money-loser.

Peer-to-peer calls are where they win or lose. Reviewers keep asking why not single-agent chemo first, even for a heavily pretreated HR+/HER2- patient who has already been through endocrine therapy and a CDK4/6 inhibitor. I think the reviewers just aren't current on the label.

Independent community practice, so they only route to specialty pharmacy when buy-and-bill gets blocked. Not sure that's the right call for sacituzumab. Probably depends on the payer more than anything.
High-deductible plans are brutal early in the year, patients arrive and get sticker shok at the copay estimate and a few just push back cycle 1 while they sort out the foundation paperwork

For urothelial the access picture is different because most patients are older and on a government plan, so less PA drama. The worry is coinsurance on an infusion drug like sacituzumab, and whether supplemental coverage picks it up.
Foundation grants came through quickly for a couple of her patients. The social worker handles it end to end, which is why she doesn't lose sleep over cost.
Appeals usually get overturned in the end, I think, but 'in the end' can mean three weeks. For someone progressing fast that delay is a real cost.

Their payer mix leans on step edits that need documented progression on a taxane before sacituzumab is approved. That's awkward in urothelial, where the sequence of enfortumab and checkpoint inhibitors is already crowded. They get through it, but it takes extra letters and a lot of patience.

We talked a long while about why SG uptake is slower at their center than the data might suggest. The physician's view is that it isn't efficacy, it's paperwork: every start needs a PA, a letter of medical necessity, often a peer-to-peer, and then a re-auth after a few cycles. One nurse navigator is basically full time on this. They said they'd probably start fewer patients if she left. I got the sense the clinical enthusiasm is real but fragile.

This was the most upbeat conversation I've had on access. Their health system has an oncology pharmacy team that submits the PA the same day the order is signed, with label language and prior therapy history already templated. Denials are rare, and when one happens the appeal is mostly a formality for sacituzumab. They did say smaller sites in their referral area probably have it harder. Overall coverage isn't a barrier for their HR+/HER2- patients.

Mixed picture, in her words. Commercial patients mostly sail through once the PA is in, and the manufacturer copay program takes care of out-of-pocket. Government-plan patients are fine on coverage but can't use that program, so they lean on independent foundations whose funding opens and closes unpredictably. The practice manager worries about the lag between administering and getting paid given the cost per vial. No losses so far, but they watch receivables closely.

Small private group, and the buy-and-bill discussion was frank. Acquisition cost is high enough that one denied claim hurts and they have no buffer. Two patients last year got Trodelvy before the approval formally posted, and I think the claims bounced afterward. Now the rule is no infusion without written authorization, which delays starts by a few days. The physician sees that as the safe choice financially but not necessarily for the patient.

What stood out after a long chat was how much access varies by site of care. Hospital-based infusion has more leverage with payers and better margins, while office-based docs feel squeezed. This physician has considered sending patients to the hospital campus just for infusions, though that creates continuity-of-care headaches. Not sure it's worth it. Probably depends on how many starts they'd realistically have in a year.

Coverage hasn't been the story for them, to be honest. They've started a steady handful of HR+/HER2- patients on Trodelvy after chemo, and approvals mostly come back within a few days. Their authorization specialist keeps a checklist of prior lines and the documentation payers ask for, which cuts the back-and-forth. Copay assistance has worked for the commercial patients. The doctor said she'd probably feel differently if they were buy-and-bill with thin margins, but their group sits inside a larger network, so overall it's manageable.

access|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: PA turnaround usually 2-3 days now, no complaints.
Copay card covers most pts, rarely a barrier in our clinic.
Denied twice for HER2-low, still waiting on peer-to-peer.
Not sure what payer wants for HER2-low documentation tbh.
Buy-and-bill cash flow is the practice's big worry w/ T-DXd.
Medicaid pts, slower approvals but nothing unusual.

Community onc, small group. Upfront drug cost is huge vs their margin, and admin keeps asking if they can really float it. HCP will probably refer some pts to the hospital outpatient infusion instead.
PA team built a template w/ IHC report + prior tx lines attached. Approvals mostly smooth since they started that. HCP said it saves alot of back-and-forth.
Step edit wants prior endocrine tx before the ADC in HR+/HER2-low, which HCP finds kind of reasonable. Only concern is delay if pt is symptomatic. Depends on payer I think.
Appeal letters eating NP time, an hr or more each. HCP feels peer-to-peer reviewers don't really get HER2-low as a category. Overturns happen eventually but pt waits wks.
Site-of-care split: hospital clinic w/ 340B handles it fine, private practice doesn't want the inventory risk. HCP thinks this shifts where pts get tx. Unsure if good or bad.
Foundation assistance got an uninsured pt on drug within a week, HCP impressed. Social worker does the heavy lifting. Wishes more pts knew to ask.
Medicare pt w/o supplemental hit the coinsurance wall and was scared of out-of-pocket. Cycle 2 got delayed while financial counselor sorted it. HCP worried this happens more than we hear about.
Tumor board now does a quick coverage check before committing to T-DXd. Slows things a bit but avoids surprise denials, I think.

Rural practice, one infusion nurse. Reimbursement lag on buy-and-bill is 'killing us' per HCP, drug ordered and paid months later sometimes. Pt w/ HER2-low mets progressing on chemo got PA fast, but claim came back underpaid. Practice manager now hesitant to stock. HCP would use more T-DXd if cash flow weren't an issue, probably sends to regional center.

Payer variability is the theme. One plan approves off label + compendium w/o fuss, another wants chart notes, imaging and HER2 IHC scoring detail. HCP's staff keep a cheat sheet per payer. Not a dealbreaker, just admin burden. Overall approvals eventually come through for most pts.

Since the HER2-low use became routine, PA mostly approved first pass when staff cite label and compendium. HCP said the fear of denials was bigger than the reality. Infusion scheduling is now the bottleneck, not coverage. Pts start tx within days of the decision. Honestly happy w/ how access has gone lately.

HCP unsure how payers will handle IHC 0 w/ faint membrane staining. Heard of a denial for 'not HER2-low' in a colleague's pt. Wants clear payer policy before ordering broadly. Pathology wording on the report probably matters a lot.

Manufacturer copay card can't be used for gov insurance pts, and that's where HCP sees the gap. Older pts on Medicare often have a big share of cost and no supplemental. Charity funds run dry mid-year. HCP has seen pts decline tx over this, which frustrates her. Says pt cost conversations now happen before efficacy talk.

Academic center, payer-mandated white-bagging came up. Specialty pharmacy ships drug, but timing mismatches cause wasted chair slots and sometimes missed dosing windows. HCP prefers buy-and-bill for control but pharmacy leadership disagrees. Mixed feelings, workable w/ a good coordinator.

Dedicated pharmacy navigator in the clinic changed everything. She runs benefits verification before the first visit, files PA same day and tracks appeals. HCP says denials are rare now and copay help is lined up early. Pts rarely delay tx for financial reasons. Would love every clinic to have one.
PA turnaround is killing us, especially for HER2-low.
Denied twice, still waiting on a peer-to-peer slot.
Honestly, approvals for Enhertu have been smoother than I expected.
Copay card helps, but only commercially insured patients qualify.
Buy-and-bill margin on these ADCs? Depends entirely on how fast they pay.
Payer wants chemo first, then maybe they'll consider it. Apparently.
We're a small community practice and stocking T-DXd upfront is scary. If a payer denies after we've already mixed it, we eat the cost. I think that's why a couple of our docs hesitate to start it.
PA usually goes through for HER2-low after endocrine therapy, but the paperwork is a mess. Our infusion nurse probably burns half a day per case chasing documentation.
Once we built a pathway template, approvals became fairly routine. Our coordinator knows exactly which notes the payer wants for HER2-low. Not perfect, but way better than last year.
Payers keep asking for the IHC 1+ versus 2+/ISH-negative documentation again and again, even when its right there in the pathology report. Feels like a stall tactic to me.
High-deductible plans are what worry me. Foundation help comes through sometimes, other times the fund is just closed for the month and the patient is left hanging.

Appeals take weeks, and in metastatic disease weeks matter. I had a patient progress on her current regimen while we waited for an overturn. I'm not convinced anyone at the payer even opened the chart.
Hospital outpatient sites get reimbursed differently than our office, so I tend to send T-DXd patients there. It's not ideal for continuity, but the economics kind of force my hand.
The manufacturer's assistance team has been responsive, I'll admit. Copay questions got answered within a day or two.

The step edit is what really gets me. The label supports T-DXd after endocrine therapy for HER2-low and ultralow, yet the reviewer wanted documented chemo first, which makes no sense in slow-growing hormone-positive disease. We sent the guideline pages and they still said no. The peer-to-peer was a ten-minute call with someone who clearly hadn't read the file. I'm tired of fighting for something that's on label.

We've gone back and forth on buy-and-bill versus white-bagging through specialty pharmacy for Enhertu. Buy-and-bill gives us control of scheduling, but the cash tied up in inventory is real and reimbursement lag is unpredictable. Specialty pharmacy shifts the risk off us, though a shipping delay means an empty chair. I think we stay with buy-and-bill for now, but our administrator isn't thrilled.

Older patients on government coverage with a supplemental plan fall through the cracks. The manufacturer copay card doesn't apply to them, and independent charity funds seem to run dry fast. I've had two or three patients decline treatment outright after hearing the out-of-pocket estimate. It's frustrating because they'd probably benefit. Our social worker does what she can, but its patchwork.

I'll give credit where due: our financial navigator has made T-DXd access much less painful. She starts the benefits check at the first discussion, not after the order, so the PA is usually in before the scan results are back. Denials still happen but we overturn most on first appeal. I'd still call the system clunky, but for us it works.

Claim rejections after the infusion are the worst part. We gave the drug, then the payer bounced the claim over a coding mismatch and wastage billing for the partial vial. Our billing team resubmitted twice and it took months to resolve. A small practice can't float that for a drug this expensive. It makes me hesitant to start new patients on it at all.

Coverage for HER2-low seems to be settling down. Early on every case was a fight, now most payers appear to have a policy in place. Ultralow is still a grey area and I'm not sure how reviewers treat it, but I'm cautiously optimistic.
PA turnaround is fine for us, usually a few days.
Denied twice on a HER2-low patient, still waiting on the peer-to-peer.
Copay program has covered basically everyone we've enrolled so far.
Buy-and-bill margin on T-DXd is thin and finance keeps flagging it.
Honestly it depends on the payer, I can't see a single pattern.
Nurse navigators now spend more time on auth paperwork than on patient education.

Their PA coordinator says approvals go through cleanly when the pathology report plainly states IHC 1+ or 2+/ISH-negative. She isn't sure that holds once volume grows, though. So far it has been smoother than she expected for a new ADC.

One regional plan keeps applying a step edit that wants a chemo line before T-DXd, even in patients who already progressed on endocrine therapy. The physician feels that conflicts with how she would sequence treatment. Appeals do eventually win, but it costs weeks the patient may not have.

The hospital-based infusion center barely worries about reimbursement because of its 340B margin. The community satellite clinic down the road refers patients over for cost reasons alone. He wasn't sure that's good for continuity of care.

A patient with a high deductible started in January and got an out-of-pocket estimate that scared her badly. The foundation fund she was referred to had already closed for the quarter. The team ended up delaying cycle one while they hunted for alternatives, which the doctor hated.
Billing staff are unsure which diagnosis code to use for HER2-low, and the PA sometimes bounces on that alone. Once it's corrected and resubmitted it usually goes through.
Hiring a dedicated benefits verification person changed things for them. They now know the coverage answer before the patient ever sits in the chair, and fewer starts get postponed.

Patients on the state Medicaid plan wait noticeably longer for T-DXd approval. One patient missed her planned date while paperwork bounced between the plan and a delegated review vendor. The clinic has no good escalation route and mostly just keeps calling.

Peer-to-peers are tolerable if the payer reviewer is an oncologist and miserable if not. He said the outcome often turns on whether the reviewer understands HER2-low as its own category. Roughly half the time he walks away feeling heard.

We talked for a long while about denials, and she kept returning to the same frustration. For T-DXd, the payer's medical policy seems to lag behind how oncologists actually use it in HER2-low disease, so the first submission is often rejected as not medically necessary. Her staff now pre-build an appeal letter and attach the guideline excerpt up front. It works eventually, I think, but she estimates one appeal costs several hours of a nurse's week. She worries smaller practices without that capacity simply give up and switch regimens.

After a long chat, his overall view was more upbeat than I expected. His practice built a standard PA packet with pathology, prior therapy history and a short rationale, and approvals for T-DXd have mostly come back first pass. The copay assistance process is also routine now, and patients rarely raise cost as a reason to hesitate. He admitted the practice got lucky with a couple of cooperative payers, so he isn't sure it generalizes. Still, he called access a manageable problem rather than a barrier.

Her take was mixed and she kept qualifying it. Commercial plans in her area approve fairly predictably, though some want a repeat PA after a dose reduction, which seems unnecessary. Government-sponsored plans are slower but usually land in the same place. The big unknown for her is how site-of-care policies will shift; some payers nudge infusions toward home or non-hospital sites. She's not sure her clinic's economics survive that if drug acquisition costs stay high.

We spent a while on buy-and-bill. The pharmacy director thinks T-DXd ties up a lot of working capital because of drug cost and the lag in payment. If a claim is denied after administration, the practice eats a very large loss. They haven't refused anyone, but leadership now wants PA confirmed in writing before any order is placed. He sees that as prudent and a bit of a drag on speed at the same time.

The doctor described a patient scenario that stuck with him: a younger woman with HER2-low disease who was approved quickly, with assistance covering most of her cost share. Treatment started within about a week of the decision, which he said wasn't always the case with other new agents. He credited a payer that had updated its policy and a financial counselor who knew the foundation process well. He doesn't assume that is typical, and he repeated that it took infrastructure to get there. Even so, it left him more optimistic about access for the next patient.

Mostly neutral overall, and he said so himself. Prior auth is a nuisance but predictable; denials happen, mostly around documentation of HER2 status rather than the drug itself. Their financial counselor handles assistance applicatons and he rarely hears about it unless something goes wrong. What he cares about more is whether payers will keep the criteria stable, since changing rules mid-year confuses everyone. Beyond that, he said access hasn't changed his prescribing much.
PA turnaround is still the main bottleneck, usually several days.
Approvals for T-DXd have been routine at their site lately.
Copay card covers most of their commercial patients, not sure about the rest.
Denied twice for T-DXd in HER2-low, appeal pending.
Infusion center pharmacist handles all the paperwork so there's no real burden on the docs.
Buy-and-bill margin is thin but they absorb it for now.

Community practice with two infusion chairs said the upfront cost of T-DXd is hard to carry when payments lag. They have one claim sitting unpaid for a couple of months. The owner is thinking about sending new starts to the hospital outpatient department instead.
Academic breast clinic said the plan approved HER2-low use on the first submission once the IHC 1+ pathology report was attached. Their nurse navigator thinks that documentation is what matters most.

Oncologist said prior auth for trastuzumab deruxtecan usually goes through, but the peer-to-peer step adds a day or so. Probably acceptable, though it depends on the plan. Medicaid patients seem slower.

One patient on a high-deductible plan faced a big out-of-pocket amount before a foundation grant came through. Her start slipped about two weeks. The doctor said that delay worries her more than anything on the clinical side.
Hospital-based clinic can't do buy-and-bill, and a couple of plans require white-bagging from a specialty pharmacy. Late shipments create scheduling headaches. The pharmacist thinks it's manageable.
Front desk at this clinic enrolls T-DXd patients in the financial assistance program, usually same day. Patients rarely bring up cost concerns afterward.
A step edit requiring prior endocrine therapy before an ADC in HR+/HER2-low came up. She said it doesn't match how she would sequence and it eats time in appeals. Not sure if every plan does this.
Rural oncologist said the long drive to the infusion site is a bigger barrier than the copay for some patients, though both matter. The social worker helps with transport vouchers and copay forms.

Large community group keeps a spreadsheet of T-DXd denials. A good chunk of the early ones were for HER2-low because the plan policy only referenced HER2-positive disease. They won most on appeal, but it took weeks and a letter of medical necessity every time. The practice manager said staff time is the hidden cost. I think they'd like a standard appeal template.

Nurse at a freestanding infusion center described a smooth process. Benefits verification is done before the first visit, and the PA goes in the same day as the order. Most approvals come back within the week. For the few denials the appeal usually works on the first try. She said reimbursement is acceptable and they don't ration chair time because of it.

Practice administrator said T-DXd economics depend heavily on payer mix. With mostly commercial patients buy-and-bill is fine. Older patients on government plans with supplemental coverage pay more unpredictably. They keep a cash buffer for that. Not sure what happens if volume grows with HER2-low, so they're watching it quarterly.

Hospital pharmacist flagged that authorizations sometimes expire mid-course and nobody tells the clinic until the claim bounces. Last month a patient arrived for infusion with a lapsed auth. The chair was held but the dose slipped a day. She sees it as a workflow gap more than a payer policy issue. Staff now check expiry dates weekly.

Oncologist in a mid-size group said patients who change plans in January are the real headache. Re-authorization starts over, and the new plan sometimes asks for fresh HER2 documentation. They try to get a cycle in during December when possible. Overall she thinks most get sorted out, just not smoothly.

Social worker at a cancer center said copay assistance for T-DXd covers most commercial patients but not those on government plans. For those they lean on independant foundations, and the funds open and close unpredictably. She spends a fair bit of time just checking which funds are open. Patients are usually grateful but anxious while waiting. Overall she called it workable.
PA turnaround too slow, delays C1 for symptomatic pts.
T-DXd approvals mostly smooth now, honestly.
Copay assistance covers most pts. Uninsured gap still unclear.
Denied at first pass, peer-to-peer overturned it. Every time.
Not sure how payers will word HER2-low vs ultralow criteria.
Site fin assistance team handles everything, huge relief for HCP.
Community practice, buy-and-bill. Cash tied up waiting on reimbursement for T-DXd vials is the admin's big worry. HCP said they'd probably limit new starts if payment lag gets worse.
Step edit in some plans requires prior HER2-directed tx or chemo before approval, others don't. Pretty inconsistent. HCP thinks DB-06 data may help with criteria but waiting to see.
Academic center, in-house PA pharmacist preps letters of medical necessity. HER2-low pts post-endocrine mostly clear on first submission. HCP very happy w/ this workflow.
Commercial-plan pt denied for HER2-low IHC 1+ because path report wording was vague. Appeal ate up a few wks and pt was progressing meanwhile. HCP frustrated, wants clearer path reports upfront.
Site-of-care edit pushes infusions to hospital outpatient for some plans. Convenience vs cost-sharing tradeoff for pts. HCP unsure which is better overall.
Copay for infusion visits adds up even w/ foundation help, and funds run dry mid-year I think. HCP knows of a handful of pts who stopped tx over cost. Worrying for those w/ good response so far.
Tumor board now includes nurse navigator who flags PA issues before the tx plan is final. Fewer surprises, less rework for the team.
Older pts on gov't plans see fewer PA hurdles, but supplemental coverage gaps decide whether they can afford the ADC. HCP says financial counselor visit is now routine before C1.

Small rural clinic, buy-and-bill only. HCP says T-DXd acquisition cost is hard to carry, and payment lag from payers makes it worse. Practice manager has raised referring pts to a bigger center. Pts then travel far, which HCP thinks hurts adherence. No clear fix from their side, just stuck.

Appeals workflow at this community site: MA submits PA, nurse tracks status, HCP does peer-to-peer if denied. Most get overturned eventually, I think, but it's time-consuming. HCP estimates a chunk of staff hours go to this each week. Not a reason to avoid T-DXd, just a cost of doing business.

Payers in region want chemo first in HR+ HER2-low even after endocrine progression. HCP argues this contradicts DB-06 context and delays an effective option. Pts get a worse-tolerated or less useful tx while appeal is pending. Some plans do accept exceptions but it's not predictable. HCP feels the step edit is outdated.

Pretty positive experience lately. PA for T-DXd in HER2-low went through in a few days for the last several pts. HCP credits a standard template w/ biomarker results, prior lines and rationale attached. Financial assistance enrolled pts quickly too. Only teh occasional denial, resolved after one call.

Debate at the practice on specialty pharmacy vs buy-and-bill. SP reduces financial risk but adds scheduling delays if drug arrives late. HCP prefers buy-and-bill for control of timing. Admin side worries about margins, not sure how it nets out. Probably depends on payer mix.

HCP raised financial toxicity: pts with high deductibles hit big bills early in the year. Foundation support helps but isn't guaranteed. Some pts ask to delay C1 until next plan year, which HCP finds hard to hear. Mentioned that social work is stretched. Overall access feels uneven depending on the pt's insurance.
Prior auth turnaround is the bottleneck, not the drug.
Denied twice for HER2-low, still waiting on a peer-to-peer.
Honestly our PA person has T-DXd approvals down to a routine now.
Copay card works, but only for the commercially insured patients.
Nobody tells us the step edit rules untill the denial lands.
Buy-and-bill margin is thin, I think we roughly break even.

We're a community practice and we front the drug cost for weeks before payment comes back. For something this pricey that is a real cash flow hit. Our administrator keeps asking whether HER2-low patients should just be sent elsewhere.
Appeals usually go through for us if the IHC and ISH documentation is attached. But each one eats a nurse's afternoon. Not sure that's sustainable if volume grows.

Approvals for the endocrine-resistant HER2-low patients have been smoother lately, I think because the label language is clearer. Fewer calls from the payer asking us to justify T-DXd over more chemo.

One payer wanted another chemo tried first even though the patient progressed quickly on endocrine therapy. That step edit makes no clinical sense to me. The ADC start slipped by about two weeks because of it.
Foundation assistance funds dry up every few months. When they reopen we scramble to re-enroll everyone who's waiting. It's basically a game of timing.

Hospital outpatient sites get reimbursed better than our office infusion suite, so some payers steer patients over there. Patients hate the extra drive. I get the economics, but it's annoying and probably costs us continuity.
Our benefits verification person is excellent. Most T-DXd cases clear in a few days and copay support covers the bulk of what patients would otherwise face.

We had a HER2-low case denied as 'not medically necessary' with a one-line rationale. The peer-to-peer was with a reviewer who clearly wasn't an oncologist and kept asking about older regimens. We appealed with a long letter and the pathology report. Eventually it was overturned, but the patient lost close to a month. Frankly I shouldn't have to write a novel to get a labeled therapy covered.

On buy-and-bill, T-DXd is a mixed bag for us. Reimbursement does eventually cover acquisition, but the carrying cost and the occasional underpayment make me nervous. Our pharmacy manager wants tighter inventory, which is hard when patients' schedules shift. I think the margin is acceptable only if denials stay rare, and I'm not convinced they will.

A patient hit her high deductible in January and was looking at a huge bill before reaching her out-of-pocket max. She seriously considered delaying cycles. Assistance programs helped eventually, but the enrollment paperwork took longer than anyone admitted. I find it unacceptable that financial toxicity is part of the treatment conversation.

Being at an academic center helps a lot. We have a dedicated financial navigator who handles auths, appeals and copay enrollment before the patient even sees me. T-DXd requests mostly sail through now. I still get the odd surprising denial, but it's the exception and not the rule.

Rural clinic here, so we deal with a patchwork of payers. Authorizations seem to expire after a set number of cycles and nobody reminds us. Twice we've had a lapse right when the patient was due for the next infusion. I'd say approval itself is okay, it's the reauthorization tracking that trips us up.

Payer behavior is wildly inconsistent. One approves HER2-low on the IHC 1+ report alone, another wants repeat testing or an explicit ISH-negative result. A handful of our patients were stuck because the original pathology report was vague. I can't tell if the criteria are really written down anywhere, and that uncertainty makes planning treatment sequence a headache.
Surprisingly, my last appeal for the ADC was overturned within days. Credit goes to the letter template our team refined. Still not something I'd count on every time.

We spent a good while on how T-DXd approvals actually play out in their community practice, and the main frustration is unpredictability. Prior auth for HER2-low usually comes back approved eventually, but the IHC documentation seems to trigger a peer-to-peer more often than it should. The nurse navigator said the delay is typically a week or so, which matters when the patient is symptomatic. I think they've accepted it as a cost of doing business, though not happily. Not sure the DB-06 data has shifted anything on the payer side yet.
Auth came back in two days, no peer-to-peer needed.

Buy-and-bill is the sticking point for their small infusion suite. Cash tied up between administering T-DXd and getting paid is manageable for now, but the physician said a couple of denials in a row would make them rethink stocking it.
Copay assistance runs dry mid-year for a few of the patients.

Overall this was one of the more upbeat access conversations I've had. Their hospital-based infusion center has a financial counselor who starts benefits verification as soon as T-DXd is discussed, so the auth is usually in hand before the treatment-planning visit. The physician credited that workflow for very few treatment gaps. She still said commercial and government plans behave differently, but she felt the process is predictable enough now that cost rarely changes her treatment choice.
A step edit asking for prior endocrine therapy documentation came up for HR+ HER2-low patients. The physician said chart notes usually satisfy it, so it's more a paperwork burden than a true barrier.
Denials for HER2-low keep citing 'not medically necessary' then get overturned on appeal.

The pharmacist walked me through their thinking on specialty pharmacy versus buy-and-bill, and honestly they're split. Some payers push white bagging, which she dislikes because of scheduling risk if a patient's labs change the day of infusion. Others reimburse well enough that buying in-house is fine. She thinks the answer is probably payer-by-payer rather than one policy for the whole clinic. Nobody on her team has resolved how to handle vials that arrive and then aren't used.

Appeal turnaround is what worries her most with T-DXd. One patient waited nearly three weeks for an overturn and the disease moved in the meantime, so now they open the appeal the same day as the denial, wich helps a bit but doesn't fix it.
Honestly the foundation support for copays has been smoother than I expected.
Depends heavily on the payer; some approve in a day, some drag.

This was a more sobering conversation. Most of her older patients are on government coverage with a supplemental plan, and she said the out-of-pocket exposure for T-DXd is what makes them hesitate, even when the clinical case is clear. Charitable funds that cover copays seem to close without warning, and her staff spends a lot of time hunting for the next open one. She said she's had patients decline or delay treatment over cost, not many but enough to remember. I think she'd like a more reliable safety net, not just case-by-case rescues.

Site-of-care policy pushed their T-DXd infusions to a lower-cost freestanding clinic and it worked fine. Chair time is the only real constraint, and the physician didn't see any clinical downside to the move.
Baseline and surveillance chest CTs sometimes need their own auth, which stacks another step on top of the T-DXd approval. The nurse said it's rarely denied, just one more thing to track.

They're a smaller practice and mostly avoid stocking T-DXd, referring patients to the hospital outpatient department instead. It works and approvals go through there, but the referral adds several days. The physician said it's a reasonable trade-off given their cash flow, though not ideal for the patient.

The practice manager described a very organized setup. They keep a templated letter of medical necessity for T-DXd that cites the label and guideline listing, and a dedicated staffer submits it the day the order is signed. She said most requests clear on first pass and the denials they do see tend to be clerical, like a missing HER2 test report. I got the sense they're proud of it. She did add that it only works because they can afford a person whose full-time job is auth.
Not sure yet how payers will handle HER2-ultralow requests.

Weight-based dosing leaves partial vials, and the physician wasn't sure every payer reimburses the discarded portion. If they don't, the practice absorbs the loss on each patient. That makes the finance team nervous about stocking it.

This one was mixed. The clinic's billing lead said coding for T-DXd is straightforward now that they've done it a number of times, and claims mostly pay without rework. Where it gets messy is when a patient switches plans mid-treatment, since the auth doesnt carry over and a new one has to be started. She thinks that's probably rare but it hits hard when it happens. Overall she'd call access acceptable, not great, and heavily dependent on having experienced staff.
Every new HER2-low start still feels like a fight with the payer, and the staff are tired of it.

barrier|osimertinib.t: PA turnaround for the combo. Payer slow, pts wait wks.
Chemo add-on logistics, mainly infusion chair availability.
No real barrier. Osi is the 1L default in his clinic.
Worried about AEs w/ chemo in older pts.
Wants OS data first, not just PFS. Waiting on that.
Brain MRI surveillance slots tight, scheduling is a hassle but manageable.
Community onc, no in-house NGS. Send-out results take too long, so some pts start chemo before the mutation result is back. HCP says that's how osi gets missed up front.
Copay assistance paperwork is heavy, per HCP. Thinks a few pts drop off tx because of it. Staff time is the issue, not the clinical case.
Main hurdle is getting pts to accept q3w infusions. Once they hear the PFS story most agree, per HCP.
Not sure the FLAURA2 combo fits everyone. Probably reserves it for high-burden or CNS mets pts, rest stay on osi mono.
Tumor board split on adding platinum/pemetrexed. Some see tox as too much for the gain, I think that was the gist. Hard to reach consensus so mono often wins by default.
Payer pushes back on the combo and wants mono tried first. Appeals eat clinic time and pts sit untreated meanwhile.
Rural site, pts drive far. Extra chemo visits = transport problem, and that sways the tx decision more than efficacy does.
Coverage is fine in her setting, PA approved quick. Only real barrier is awareness among referring docs w/ new dx pts, so some arrive late.

Tox monitoring is the sticking point. Combo means more labs, more visits, more cytopenia mgmt. HCP says the nurses are already stretched. Not against the regimen, but unsure the clinic can safely run it for many pts at once. Probably would limit it to fit, younger pts.

HCP says reflex testing isnt consistent at the referring path labs. Some pts get tissue NGS, others only liquid biopsy, and a negative plasma result gets over-trusted. Re-biopsy is sometimes needed and delays tx. Once EGFR is confirmed, starting osi is straightforward. Barrier is the front end, not the drug.

Academic center, multidisciplinary clinic. Coverage rarely an issue, PAs go through. HCP uses the combo in pts w/ brain mets or heavy burden and mono in others. Main barrier is just deciding who benefits most. Would like more guidance on selection but feels positive overall.

Concern re ILD and cardiac effects. Echo monitoring is hard to schedule, esp for pts w/ prior cardiac hx. HCP admits pts w/ comorbidities often get mono or another option instead. Also unsure how adding chemo changes AE overlap. Wants clearer real-world experience before pushing combo more.

Biggest question for HCP is what comes after progression. Resistance mechanisms vary and next-line options feel limited. That said, doesnt hold him back from using osi up front. Sees it as a minor barrier, more of a planning issue than a reason to avoid it.

Infusion nurse capacity is the bottleneck. Combo needs chair time every 3 wks plus anemia and nausea mgmt, and the clinic is already booked. HCP also mentioned pt fatigue w/ frequent visist. Thinks uptake stays low until staffing improves. Drug itself isnt the problem.
Prior auth for the chemo combo takes too long.
Chemo add-on tolerability in older patients is my hesitation.
Not much of a barrier now, osimertinib is first choice for most of mine.
Infusion chair capacity at our community clinic
Waiting for the OS data to mature, I think.
Scheduling regular brain MRI follow-up is a hassle but manageable.
Tissue turnaround for the molecular panel is the sticking point at our small practice. Sometimes we start treatment early if the patient is symptomatic, but that makes teh whole plan feel rushed.

Pemetrexed plus platinum every three weeks means more chair visits for patients who live far away. Several have said they'd rather stay on the pill alone. I think that limits how often I offer the combination.
Coverage hasn't been an issue for osimertinib alone in our hospital clinic. For the combination, the pharmacy team handles the paperwork so it goes fairly smoothly.
Not sure there is just one barrier. Payer approval for the add-on chemo varies, and so does how comfortable the infusion nurses are with the pemetrexed schedule.
Cost to the patient. Copays on the oral drug are steep for a few of my retired patients and they sometimes delay the first fill.
Familiarity was the main thing and that's mostly gone now. Our tumor board has discussed the combo for high-risk cases a few times, so referral to infusion is routine.
Cytopenias with the combination mean extra bloods in the first cycles. Our rural satellite site can't always draw labs locally, so that's a bit of a hurdle.
Plasma testing isn't covered consistently, so some patients start something else while we wait on tissue. By the time the result lands the plan has often moved on

Most of my EGFR patients are older with a few comorbidities, so adding chemo to osimertinib is a harder sell. I'll consider it if they have a big tumor burden or brain mets and are otherwise fit. The data look interesting but I'm not sure how much I'd be adding for a frail 78-year-old. It mostly comes down to a chat in clinic about how much time they're willing to spend in the infusion suite.

Our payer wants a peer-to-peer for any regimen that isn't a single-agent TKI. That adds a week or more before we can start, and patients with symptomatic disease don't want to wait. Staff time on appeals is also a real cost for a small practice. Sometimes I just go with the TKI alone to avoid the delay. Not ideal but practical.

Honestly the barrier is smaller than it used to be. Our oncology pharmacist built an order set for osimertinib with pemetrexed and carboplatin, and the nurses are comfortable with it. Younger patients worried about brain progression are usually keen. The remaining issue is just finding infusion slots, which we can usually sort out.

Monitoring burden worries me. Between infusion visits, labs, and ECG checks for the TKI, patients who work full time struggle. A couple dropped off the combination after cycle two because of time off work. I think logistics, not efficacy, is what stops me offering it more widely. Transport is also a problem for those coming from outlying areas.

Tough to name one. Testing at diagnosis is better than before, but a good chunk of our referrals still arrive with no EGFR result, so the first visit is spent waiting. Once the result is back, osimertinib is easy to start. The combination takes more coordination. I'd say delay in getting mutation status is the main one.
Prior auth for the combo takes forever, honestly.
Chemo add-on toxicity is my worry. A lot of my older patients probably won't tolerate it.
Infusion chair capacity, plain and simple.
Few barriers for me. Osimertinib alone is easy, I just want more survival follow-up.
Waiting on NGS results sometimes three weeks and by then they have already started something else
Still not convinced the progression-free gain justifies the added chemo burden.

Pemetrexed plus platinum on top means anemia, nausea, and a lot more visits. In my community practice patients often live an hour away, so that's a hard sell. Not sure the extra benefit is worth it for most of them.
Payers usually approve single-agent osimertinib without fuss. The combination is a different story, and I get denials citing immature survival data. Probably improves once guidelines catch up.
Tissue. A good chunk of my biopsies come back QNS, and then we wait on plasma, which can miss things. It delays the whole start.
With brain mets I'm happy to use it, no real hesitation there. My only gripe is cost-sharing for patients on high-deductible plans, which still bites.
Monitoring burden, I think. Echo for cardiac, ILD vigilance, and labs around the chemo cycles all stack up, and my nurses are already stretched thin.
Nobody can tell me how to sequence after progression if they've had chemo up front. That uncertainty keeps me on TKI alone. Frustrating when the data feel incomplete.
Getting the pharmacy to stock it was the biggest hurdle, and that's sorted now. Beyond that I'm comfortable.
Resistance after progression, we dont have a clear next step beyond chemo. Makes me hesitant to commit to anything heavy early on.

Honestly the barrier is the whole logistics chain around the combo. Somebody has to schedule infusions, arrange growth factor or transfusion support, and keep the oral drug going on time. Our tumor board talks about it a lot but nothing changes on the ground. I end up defaulting to the simpler option because the clinic just can't absorb the extra workload. It's not that I doubt the idea, it's that I can't execute it reliably.

Think about the 75-year-old with borderline performance status and a few comorbidities. I'm supposed to recieve her into a platinum doublet plus a TKI? No thanks. Frankly the trial population doesn't look like my waiting room, and nobody has convinced me otherwise. Until I see something for frail patients I'll keep the combination for the fit ones only.

Reflex testing isn't set up where I work, so pathology waits for me to order it. By the time EGFR comes back the patient has often been sent home with a plan for chemo-immunotherapy. Sometimes we switch, sometimes the first cycle is already given. Fixing that workflow would do more for uptake than any new data, I think.

I'm a skeptic by nature, but osimertinib has earned its place in my clinic. The only real barrier now is payer pushback on the combination. Appeals work eventually, they just eat staff time. Once that eases I'd use the combo more in higher-risk patients, especially with CNS disease.

Cost and access, no question. Specialty pharmacy delays leave patients waiting weeks for the first fill, and a handful have simply gotten worse in that gap. Copays are brutal for anyone without good coverage. I spend more time on financial navigation than on the clinical decision, and that's wrong. Add the chemo costs and the combo feels even further out of reach for many.

Evidence is the thing I keep coming back to. Overall survival is still maturing, so I'm cautious about overselling the combo to patients. That said, I'm already using it in selected cases with high-risk features and the early experience is encouraging. More follow-up would let me widen that group with confidence.
Pemetrexed-platinum add-on means more chair time, and our infusion suite is already full.
Payer approval timing for the combination, mostly.
No real barrier with osimertinib now, access is smooth in our setup.
Frail older patients, I worry they can't tolerate the chemo backbone.
Waiting for more mature survival data before I change habits.
Tissue turnaround, though it's improving; sometimes we start something else meanwhile.

Mostly the logistics of getting brain MRIs on schedule for patients on the combination. Radiology slots in her community practice are weeks out, so surveillance drifts later than she'd like. Not sure that's unique to them.

Prior auth has become routine for him, honestly. Once the first-line EGFR indication is cited for osimertinib the approvals come back quickly, so the real limit is just deciding which patients need the added chemo.
Cost sharing for patients. Even with insurance the add-on drugs plus extra infusion visits mean copays that some families cant carry, and she has had people decline outright.

I think the barrier is deciding who actually benefits from intensification. Without a clear marker he defaults to single-agent osimertinib in most patients and saves the combination for those with high-risk features such as CNS disease.
Rural patients driving a long way every few weeks for infusion is a hard sell. Some would rather stay on the pill and accept the uncertainty.
Their tumor board is very receptive, so the main thing is educating the referring community oncologists. Once those colleagues understand the CNS protection rationale they tend to come around fast.

Toxicity monitoring, mainly. Rash and diarrhea are manageable, but with chemo layered on top the nurse call volume goes up and the clinic is short staffed. Probably needs a dedicated navigator, she said.

Insurers keep asking for a peer-to-peer on the combination, which eats clinic time. Several requests were denied at first and then overturned on appeal, and that delay is the barrier for him, not the clinical question.

After talking it through, the sticking point for her is really the evidence horizon. She likes the FLAURA2 concept and has used the combination in a couple of younger patients with brain mets, but overall survival isn't mature enough to justify extra toxicity for everyone. She'd probably use it more if she could identify the subgroup that truly gains. For now single-agent osimertinib remains her default and she doesn't feel uncomfortable with that.

Main concern is the testing pathway upstream. In her practice plasma and tissue NGS are ordered inconsistently, so a lot of patients start chemo-immunotherapy before EGFR status is back. By the time the result arrives they've had a cycle already and switching feels messy. She thinks osimertinib would be used more if reflex testing were reliable. Not a drug problem, she stressed, more of a systems one.

He feels the barrier is shrinking. Coverage was the headache a year ago, but his pharmacy team now handles the paperwork and patients start within a reasonable time. The remaining issue is infusion chair capacity, which the center is addressing by adding an extra weekly slot. He said he's keen to offer the osimertinib combination to fit patients and just needs capacity to catch up.

She kept coming back to tolerability in real-world patients. Trial populations look fit, but her clinic sees people with comorbidities, poor performance status, sometimes renal issues that complicate platinum. She worries about admissions for anemia and nausea that then interupt the TKI itself. I think she'd rather protect the oral therapy than risk gaps, especially in patients who recieve care far from home.

He split it in two. For osimertinib monotherapy there's essentially no barrier, it's on formulary and everyone knows the side effect profile. For the combination it's the monitoring burden and how long to continue pemetrexed maintenance, which he said nobody has given him a clear answer on. He's not against it, just unsure. Practical guidance on duration would help his comfort level.

Looking back over the discussion, she said the main barrier is simply awareness at the smaller satellite clinics, not the drug. Patients there often get referred late, after progression on something else. Once they are sent early, osimertinib is started without trouble and the combination is discussed openly. She feels it's an education gap that is very fixable.
Probably the chair time for the chemo add-on, not sure our infusion suite can absorb it.
Seems like payer coverage for the combo is still murky.
Not sure yet, maybe just waiting on longer follow-up.
I think there's no real barrier for osimertinib alone in our clinic.
Would need to see overall survival mature before I push the doublet harder.
Honestly the extra toxicity in frail pateints may be what holds me back.
Biggest thing seems to be getting NGS back fast enough, but once the result is in, starting osimertinib is easy. Our tumor board usually agrees on it quickly. So I'd say access is mostly fine for us.

Hard to say, maybe the monitoring burden. Adding platinum-pemetrexed means more labs and more visits, and I'm not sure which patients really need it. I'd probably reserve it for those with higher-risk disease.

Prior auth for the combination seems to drag on for weeks at our community practice. I think some patients may start single-agent just to avoid the delay. Not sure that's ideal, but it's what happens.

Brain mets data look reassuring, I think, but I'm unsure how much that changes my default. It may depend on whether the patient has CNS disease at baseline. Would need to see a clearer subgroup signal before changing anything for the rest.
Seems the main hurdle is just awareness among referring docs. Once they see the progression-free benefit story, I suspect uptake would grow. Our pulmonologists are already asking about it.

Likely the cost and travel for older patients living far from the cancer center. Every extra infusion visit may mean a long drive, and some families probably can't manage it. I worry they'd drop out of the combo early.

Not totally sure, but I think it's mostly about patient selection. Some of my patients are doing great on osimertinib alone, so it's hard to justify adding chemo without knowing who gains the most. Maybe a biomarker like ctDNA clearance would help someday.
Probably nothing major on my side. Our pharmacy has the regimen built into the order set and nursing seems comfortable with the pemetrexed schedule. I may see more use as the team gets used to it.

Reimbursement seems to be the sticking point for us. The combination may not be covered in the same way across payers, and I'm never sure until the denial comes back. Our staff spends a lot of time on appeals. Some patients seem to give up waiting. I think that probably shapes my choices more than the evidence does.

I think the question for me is the tradeoff. The combo seems promising, but anemia, nausea and fatigue may add up, especially in the first few cycles. I'm not sure how patients feel about it long term. I'd want a better sense of quality of life before using it widely. For now I discuss it case by case.

Honestly, I think the barrier is shrinking. Testing at diagnosis seems more reliable now, and osimertinib is familiar to the whole team. The combo discussion may take longer in clinic, but patients seem open to it when I explain the rationale. Mostly I'd say it's about time and scheduling rather than a real obstacle.

Monitoring, I guess. Between ILD vigilance, cardiac checks and now chemo labs, I'm not sure our small clinic has the bandwidth. We probably miss some of the early symptoms in patients who call instead of coming in. I worry that something like pneumonitis could be caught late. That makes me cautious about adding more complexity.

I'd say it's the evidence gap on sequencing. If the combination is used first, I'm not sure what the best next step is after progression. Resistance testing at that point may help, but access to repeat biopsy or liquid testing is spotty here. I'd probably need clearer guidance. Until then I lean on single-agent for most.

Likely timing. Patients often come in with symptoms and want to start something right away, and I'm not sure waiting for full molecular results always feels acceptable. I sometimes begin chemo first and then switch once the EGFR result returns. That may muddy how I think about adding platinum to osimertinib later on. It probably varies by site.
Big fan of osimertinib; copay burden is the only thing that slows me down.
Prior auth for the chemo combo takes forever, that's it.
Mostly ctDNA turnaround - tissue is slow when we need to start.
Infusion chair capacity, honestly. Can't fit more combo pts right now.
Older patients and the added chemo toxicity, I think.
Happy to use it more, just need payers to stop questioning the add-on.
I'm very keen on the FLAURA2 approach for high-burden disease. The sticking point is that my community site sends chemo patients to a separate infusion center, so coordination gets messy.

Frankly the concept excites me, but I can't get the platinum-pemetrexed piece approved quickly for symptomatic patients. By the time the insurer answers, we've often already started single-agent therapy.
Osimertinib is a no-brainer for me in newly diagnosed disease. Only caveat is making sure NGS is back befor the first-line decision, which doesn't always happen in our clinic.
Really enthusiastic about intensifying up front, I just don't know which patients truly need it. Without clearer selection I tend to hedge and go with the TKI alone for many of them.
Monitoring burden worries me with the combo: more labs, more visits, more cytopenia checks. Rural patients travel a long way, so its probably the biggest hurdle for us.
Love the CNS activity of osimertinib. The barrier is mostly reimbursement for the frequent brain MRIs I'd want to order.
I'm excited but cautious. Our hospital formulary review is the hurdle for the combination, and pharmacy keeps asking for longer follow-up before adding it to the pathway.
I use it a lot already. The main thing is education for referring oncologists who still see chemo as too toxic to pair, which limits who gets sent my way.

Enthusiastic about osimertinib plus chemo for the right patient, honestly. My caveat is tolerability in real-world practice. Our patients are older and frailer than trial populations, I think. Anemia and nausea have led a few to stop early. Until I'm confident picking the fit ones, I'm not offering it widely.

The combo makes sense biologically and I like it. Logistics are the issue: three-weekly infusions plus a daily tablet means scheduling gymnastics for working patients. Our nurses are already stretched thin. If we had a satellite infusion option I'd probably use it more. Not a deal-breaker, just friction.

Very positive on osimertinib overall. Patients with brain mets do well in my hands and families love the oral option. The one hurdle is reliable baseline testing, especially when the biopsy is small and the sample is insufficient. We sometimes wait on a repeat sample, which delays starting. Once results are in it's smooth sailing.

Don't get me wrong, I like where this is going. But our payer wants documented progression criteria for anything beyond single-agent osimertinib, and appeals eat up staff hours. A couple of patients last quarter gave up waiting and we began standard therapy. The admin load is wearing the team down.

The progression-free signal excites me, qualitatively speaking, but maturity of the survival picture is what I keep coming back to. Tumor board colleagues ask whether the extra toxicity is justified without more follow-up. It's a fair question. I'd use the combo more once that is clearer, and for now I reserve it for high-risk presentations.

Tolerability of osimertinib itself is easy, patients do fine. The barrier for me is the combination in people with poor kidney function, since platinum gets tricky. A good chunk of my clinic is older with comorbidities, so I end up dropping the chemo. I'd love to offer it to more people but safety comes first.

barrier|pembrolizumab.t: Prior auth turnaround, takes weeks at our practice.
Honestly no real barrier now, pembro is already on our pathway.
Waiting on PD-L1 results before anyone commits to anything.
Infusion chair capacity in the community clinic.
Not sure how to sequence pembrolizumab with the adjuvant phase after surgery, still unclear to the team.
Toxicity worries in older patients, mostly colitis and pneumonitis
Biomarker turnaround is the sticking point for them. HER2 and CPS come back at different times, so the first-line decision sometimes slips a week or so.
Payer pushback on the perioperative regimen in resectable lung cancer, especially when neoadjuvant chemo was already started elsewhere. Staff spend a lot of time on appeals.
Main hurdle is getting surgeons and med onc aligned on timing. Once the tumor board agrees, pembrolizumab goes ahead without much fuss.
Rural patients drive a long way for q3w infusions. Some drop off, I think, because of travel more than anything else, though the ones who stay do fine.
The lower CPS gastric group is what he keeps coming back to. He isn't against using it, probably just selective until the picture is clearer for those patients.
Nobody owns irAE follow-up between cycles at her clinic. Patients call the front desk with diarrhea or a rash and it can take a day to reach a clinician.

Many of his lung patients struggle to get through the adjuvant phase after surgery. Recovery drags on, some recieve fewer cycles than planned, and a few just say they are done. He likes the neoadjuvant part but feels the whole sequence is hard to finish in a regional hospital setting. Better post-op support would probably help more than anything on the drug side.

At their large cancer center the use is already routine for both gastric and perioperative lung. The remaining issue is education of referring pulmonologists, who sometimes send patients late or not at all. The tumor board is trying to fix that with a simple referral form. She feels that once patients reach the right clinic, uptake is smooth.

Cost to the patient is the main thing she raises. Several people on high-deductible plans hesitate when they hear about the copays across a year of treatment. The social worker helps with assistance programs, but the paperwork is slow. I think a few patients choose a shorter course or delay starting, and she finds that frustrating.

Small gastric biopsies are the problem in his practice. Pathology sometimes reports not enough tissue for PD-L1 and HER2 together, so a repeat endoscopy gets discussed. Most of the time they wait, but it adds delay and anxiety. He did say the testing itself is not hard once tissue is adequate.

He worries about patients progressing during neoadjuvant therapy and losing the chance for surgery. In his mind that risk makes some of the thoracic surgeons nervous about the whole approach. Imaging gaps between cycles do not help, since scans sometimes get scheduled late. He said he would use pembrolizumab more if the restaging process were tighter, but right now it feels like a gamble for borderline cases.

Order sets are built and the pharmacy knows the regimen, so the day-to-day is pretty smooth. Only real friction is drug prep time on busy infusion days, which pushes some starts to the afternoon. She called it a minor annoyance. Patients and staff seem comfortable with pembro overall.

Biggest barrier now is just the paperwork, which is manageable. Her team has a dedicated coordinator for prior auths on pembrolizumab, and approvals mostly go through. She would like faster responses but is not blocked.

Follow-up imaging and labs between visits add up for him. For the community patients, that means extra trips and sometimes missed appointments, probably more than the drug itself. He is not sure there is an easy fix.
PA turnaround. Delays neoadjuvant start.
Pts dropping off before adjuvant phase, HCP's biggest worry.
Honestly none at his site, payer approves pembro fast.
CPS not reflexed by path here, so everything waits on a re-request.
No real barrier now, chair capacity ok. Just referral awareness.
Not sure how much the adjuvant part adds, so hard to push pembro for every pt.
HCP says barrier mostly gone since pathway built into tumor board. Only friction left is getting surgeon to agree on timing. Pembro itself is easy to sell to pts.
Payer denials for periop use when stage documentation is thin. Office spends a lot of staff time on appeals, multiple touches per pt. Some pts give up waiting and recieve chemo alone.
Worried about irAEs in older gastric pts w/ poor PS. Would use more if monitoring (TSH, LFTs, cortisol) was easier to coordinate w/ PCP. Not sure who owns labs between cycles.
Surgeons reluctant, fear IO AEs will delay resection. HCP thinks it's more cultural than data-driven but it still blocks use in his tumor board.
Biomarkers (HER2, MSI, PD-L1) all needed before 1L decision and send-outs can take a couple wks. Pt often starts chemo alone then IO gets added later, I think. Bottleneck is path not the drug
Convinced by evidence in resectable NSCLC, barrier is just bandwidth. No nurse navigator to track pts from neoadjuvant through adjuvant. Pembro uptake would probably rise if that existed.
Cost to the system for full-course pembro. Hospital pharmacy committee wants pharmacoeconomic data first. HCP expects it will pass eventually, just slow.
Rural pts travel far for q3w infusions. Many prefer to stop after neoadjuvant, esp. when fatigued post-lobectomy.

Pt selection in gastric unclear. HCP only uses IO when CPS positive, feels benefit below cutoff is weak. Path reports often lack CPS so he re-requests, and pt is symptomatic meanwhile. Would use more if CPS reporting was standardized. Doubts that's happening soon.

Small community practice, 2 NPs. AE triage is the issue: pts call w/ cough or diarrhea and it's unclear if pneumonitis, colitis or post-surgical. Needs after-hours protocol. Doesn't want to over-steroid. Probably would treat more pts if triage was clearer. Pembro itself not the problem.

HCP enthusiastic about periop lung tx. Barrier now is awareness among referring pulmonologists and surgeons, many still send straight to resection. Weekly tumor board helps. He said pts who see teh whole plan upfront accept it better. Wants more joint education.

Separate PA for adjuvant continuation after surgery, pt can wait wks w/ no tx. HCP frustrated, says payer treats it as new request. Staff chasing forms. Pts anxious, some lose PS during gap. Feels pembro access is fine on paper only.
Wants longer f/u before changing practice. Unsure on PFS vs OS maturity, esp. in PD-L1 low pts. Peers at tumor board split. Not against pembro, just cautious. Will likely revisit when more data out.

Elderly pts w/ comorbidities or autoimmune hx are the sticking point. HCP afraid of serious AEs that wipe out surgical benefit. Tends to defer to chemo only in those pts. Says no good guidance on who is too frail, so he errs on the safe side.
Prior auth. Every single time, and the delays eat into the surgical window.
Honestly, waiting on biomarker results before anyone will commit.
Nobody trusts the adjuvant half, patients just vanish after surgery.
Barrier? Only chair time. The drug itself I'm fine with.
Cost conversations with admin, pretty much end of story.
Still unsure which patients actually need both phases.

PD-L1 CPS reporting is a mess in our community setup. Results come back late or with no score at all, and by then the gastric patient has already started chemo. Pembrolizumab ends up bolted on late or not at all.

I think the data are fine, my problem is surgeons. Some won't move the OR date for neoadjuvant immunotherapy in resectable lung, and I can't totally blame them. Still, when they cooperate it works well enough.
Grudgingly, it works well enough that my main gripe is logistics. Getting EGFR/ALK results back before starting perioperative IO is slow, but once that's cleared we go ahead.
Toxicity follow-up. Who is checking endocrine labs six months out? Our clinic has no endocrine support and the PCPs dont want to own it.
Payers keep asking for MSI/MMR and HER2 before they'll even look at the request. That's fair, but pathology turnaround is slow. Mixed feelings, pembro isn't the issue here.

Frankly the evidence for gastric outside the higher CPS group feels thin to me. I'm not going to push it on a frail 75-year-old when the benefit looks marginal and I worry about colitis. Probably I'd use it more if that were clearer.
Biggest hurdle now is just getting patients scheduled. Infusion slots fill up and perioperative regimens need tight timing. Otherwise I'm happy to use it more.
Rural patients driving hours for every q3w infusion. Some drop out for that alone.

Honestly the attrition after surgery is what kills it for me. We start perioperative pembro in resectable lung, the patient does the neoadjuvant part fine, then they get a complication or a slow recovery and the adjuvant cycles never happen. Nobody follows up systematically, the surgeon assumes oncology has it, and oncology hears about it weeks late. I don't have a nurse navigator to chase this. The regimen ends up half delivered and I can't tell if that's even worth it.

Pneumonitis worries me more than people admit. In lung we're treating patients with poor reserve, often smokers with emphysema, and the CT read from outside radiology is vague about baseline ILD. If they get short of breath at home it's anybody's guess whether it's infection, progression or the PD-1. I've held treatment on soft grounds before. Until there's a cleaner pathway for that, I'm cautious about offering it broadly.

Tumor board is the choke point. Gastric cases get discussed, everyone nods, then there's no clear owner for ordering PD-L1 and HER2 or deciding sequence with surgery. I think it's more a process problem than a drug problem. Some weeks it flows, other weeks a patient sits for a week or more waiting on someone to pick up the phone.

I'll say it's better than it was. Approvals for pembrolizumab in the perioperative lung setting go through faster than a year ago, and our pharmacy knows the drill. What still bites is pathology, since molecular and PD-L1 results trickle in separately from different labs. If those landed together I'd start more patients on time and wouldn't have much else to complain about.

Not sure I can pin it on one thing. Part of me wonders how much benefit comes from the neoadjuvant phase versus the adjuvant phase, adn the data doesn't really split that out for me. Then there's coverage for the adjuvant cycles, which sometimes gets questioned separately. So I hesitate to commit patients to the full year when I'm not certain they'll all get through it.

Gastric is confusing right now. Between CPS cutoffs, HER2 status, MSI and what the payer accepts, I spend more time on eligibility than on the patient. I think pembrolizumab has a role, but the label and the testing requirements don't line up cleanly in my head or in the EHR order sets. Residents get it wrong all the time.

After talking it through for a while, the thing that keeps coming back is PD-L1 turnaround in gastric. Her site sends CPS testing out, and results often land after the first chemo cycle is already planned, so the decision gets made without it. She'd use pembro more readily if the result were reliably back by the first tumor board. I think she also feels the scoring variability between labs makes borderline results hard to lean on.
Payer approval timing, mostly. Varies a lot by plan.

Honestly not much of a barrier for him now. Perioperative pembrolizumab is on their pathway and the infusion team is comfortable, so it comes down to getting patients through surgery fit enough for the adjuvant phase.
Worried too many patients won't make it to the adjuvant portion.

Coordination between surgical and medical teams is where it gets stuck, she said after we'd gone around it a few times. The drug is clearly accepted, but timing of surgery relative to the last neoadjuvant cycle gets negotiated case by case. Theatre slots in her hospital are tight, so a delay of a few weeks isn't unusual. She isn't sure it matters clinically, yet it makes her uneasy. A shared scheduling protocol would probably help, though nobody owns that right now.
Immune-related toxicity monitoring eats up nurse time the clinic doesn't have.

Prior auth for the neoadjuvant setting is the sticking point. Her office has had a couple denied at first submission and then overturned on appeal, which pushes the start back by weeks and she doesnt always want to wait.

Pretty upbeat overall after a long chat. His limit is awareness among referring surgeons, since a few still send patients straight to the OR without a medical oncology consult. Once cases come through multidisciplinary review, uptake of the perioperative regimen is easy. He thought better referral habits would be the single biggest unlock and said the evidence itself doesn't hold him back.

Biomarker selection in gastric is the open question for him. He's unsure how much to lean on CPS versus MSI status when deciding, and wants clearer guidance before extending use to lower-expressing patients.

He raised surgical difficulty as the real worry. In his thoracic group a few surgeons feel inflammation after neoadjuvant IO makes the hilar dissection harder, and I think that shapes who gets offered it. He isn't against the approach but is cautious with borderline-resectable stage III disease. Without more local surgical experience he expects referrals to stay conservative.
None really; the pathway is set and eligible patients get it.
Extra visits for the long adjuvant schedule, patients get worn out.
Pharmacy budget pressure. Day-unit spend on IO is under scrutiny and he expects pushback from administration if volumes rise.

She framed it as an evidence question in subgroups. For the older or frail gastric patients she sees, she's not sure the data really apply, so she often defaults to chemo alone. She doesn't see it as a coverage problem. I think she'd welcome more on how to select patients, particularly anyone with a comorbid autoimmune condition. Until then her use stays selective.
Mainly molecular testing bandwidth, and that is getting better. Once EGFR and ALK results come back reliably he's happy to go with pembro in everyone else, and his team has become quicker at it.
Reimbursement uncertainty in gastric outside the narrow label.
Travel is the issue for his rural patients, who go a long way for three-weekly infusions. Shared care locally would suit many of them, but the nearest unit isn't set up to manage IO reactions.

Her concern was what happens when a patient relapses after the perioperative course. Sequencing after pembrolizumab feels unclear to her, and she worries that using it early limits what she can offer later. I think that makes her slower to adopt in younger, fitter patients where she'd rather keep options open. It's not a deal breaker, just a nagging doubt, and her tumor board hasn't taken a clear stance.

Right now the barrier is internal logistics, and he sounded fairly optimistic about fixing it. They're building a nurse-led toxicity phone line and a standard order set for the pre-op cycles, which he expects will let them treat more eligible patients without swamping clinic. Coverage hasn't really been a problem for his patients.
Getting pathology to report PD-L1 consistently on both resection and biopsy specimens, i think. It's a small thing but it holds up decisions in a few cases.
Biomarker turnaround, honestly. We often can't wait for the full panel before the first cycle.
Prior auth delays for the perioperative regimen, every single time.
Not much now, pathway is set. Just chair time on busy days.
Thoracic surgeons worry about delayed surgery and more complications after neoadjuvant immunotherapy.
For pembro in gastric, the evidence outside the metastatic setting still feels thin to him.
Community nurses arent confident triaging irAE calls after hours, so he holds back on referring patients out.

Pembrolizumab uptake in resectable lung is mostly smooth at her center since the tumor board agreed on a shared pathway. The one friction is getting EGFR and ALK results back quickly enough that nobody has to hold the first infusion.
He thinks the main barrier is the long adjuvant phase. Patients are worn out after surgery, and I think he's unsure how many really stay on treatment to the end, though he had no numbers to share.

Reimbursement in their system covers only certain stages, and the pharmacy committee keeps asking for more justification. For gastric he said it is basically a non-starter outside metastatic, CPS-selected patients.
Rural patients are the issue. Three-weekly infusions mean long drives, and the local clinic can't give it, so a few decline. He sees it as a travel problem more than a clinical one.

CPS testing in gastric isn't standardized in his lab. Scoring seems to vary by pathologist and he's not sure which result to trust. Until that is sorted he stays cautious about who gets pembrolizumab, and he wasn't sure it's coming soon evn.
Payer approval used to be the biggest hurdle. Since the team built a template appeal letter, most requests go through. What's left is mainly scheduling around theatre dates.

Frail older gastric patients are where he hesitates. He feels the perioperative burden is already high, and he isn't sure adding immunotherapy is wise for them. No single obstacle, just a case-by-case judgment call.

She was fairly upbeat about the data. Her only real barrier is infusion suite capacity, since the perioperative schedule adds a lot of chair slots. They are extending hours, which she thinks will mostly solve it.

Monitoring is what worries him most. Their clinic is small and has no on-site endocrinology, so thyroid and adrenal problems can be picked up late. Patients also often present to the ER first, where staff don't recognize immune-related toxicity. He said that gap makes him think twice before offering it widely. He'd use it more if there were a clear shared-care protocol, but nothing like that exists at present.

In perioperative lung, he keeps coming back to what happens after surgery. If a patient has a very good pathologic response, he isn't sure whether to continue the adjuvant phase in full. He also can't tell how much each phase contributes, and he wants more clarity. Not a refusal, more a nagging uncertainty that slows his decisions. Tumor board seems split on it too, I think.

She said the clinical story is convincing for her team, and logistics are the only real brake. Medical oncology, thoracic surgery and pathology all need to line up within a few weeks, and early on that coordination fell apart. They now have a nurse navigator who tracks every case, and referrals flow much better. She feels the barrier is largely solved locally, though she knows other centers lack that support.
