Budget is the story at his hospital. The drug spend is capped, and every new perioperative immunotherapy start competes with other priorities. He has to justify each case to the committee, and approvals take weeks while patients wait. He thinks the clinical case is strong enough, but admitted he stops pushing when the process gets this heavy. Frankly it wears the team out and thats his main obstacle.

In gastric the sequence of testing slows things down. HER2, then CPS, then MSI, and sometimes the samples are scant after biopsy so repeats are needed. Some patients deteriorate before the results come back. He likes the idea of earlier immunotherapy but feels the workflow isn't built for it. He thought reflex testing at diagnosis might help but wasn't sure the lab could manage the volume.

His biggest concern is losing patients between neoadjuvant therapy and the operation. A handful have developed side effects or progressed and never made it to surgery, and that stays with the team. Patients also grow anxious about the delay and ask to go straight to resection. He said it makes him selective about who he offers pembrolizumab to. I think he'd feel differently with better tools to predict who is at risk.

barrier|sacituzumab govitecan.t: Prior auth turnaround, takes weeks at our community practice.
Neutropenia and sorting out G-CSF support, I think.
Not much really, coverage has been smooth for us so far.
Sequencing. Unsure where it fits after CDK4/6 and endocrine therapy.
Chair time. Our infusion suite is booked out and scheduleing day 1 and day 8 is tough.
Mostly referral timing, supply hasn't been an issue for this clinic.
Mostly the payer side. Our infusion center gets breast approvals fairly easily, but urothelial requests come back more often, probably because of the line-of-therapy criteria.
Diarrhea management worries the nurses on our unit. Patients call on weekends and we don't have a good after-hours triage process.
Once the paperwork is done it's fine. The oncologists here are comfortable with sacituzumab after enfortumab, so the limiter is just remembering to consider it earlier.
Some of the docs want more follow-up in later-line urothelial before moving it ahead of other options. I think that's the hesitation, not safety. Not sure how soon that changes.
Frail elderly patients at our rural clinic. Travel for two visits in three wekks is hard and families can't always bring them in.
UGT1A1 testing came up. Nobody orders it routinely and the group wasn't sure results would change dosing, so it stays a grey area.
Buy-and-bill ties up a lot of cash in our small practice. The admin team likes the drug clinically but worries about the reimbursement lag.
Biggest hurdle was nurse education and that's mostly done now. The team feels fine with premeds and infusion reactions. They'd use it more if eligible patients showed up sooner.

Hair loss is the thing patients bring up. A few women with HR+ disease in our clinic said they'd rather stay on endocrine-based options than lose their hair. I explain it's manageable, but some decline anyway. Nurses say the conversation takes a while. It isn't about efficacy for them, it's about quality of life during treatment.

At our academic tumor board the discussion is usually about logistics. Everyone agrees it's an option after prior chemo and endocrine therapy. The question is who owns toxicity follow-up between cycles. Right now it falls on the breast nurse navigator, who is already stretched. If that were sorted I think usage would go up a bit.

Monitoring between cycles is the sticking point. Our patients often live far from the clinic and local labs don't send CBC results back quickly. That makes the team nervous about neutropenia going unnoticed. Sacituzumab is on the shortlist, but they hold off when they can't be sure of labs. Fixing the lab loop would help more than any new data, in their view.

Honestly the barrier is small for us. The evidence in the HR+/HER2- setting is persuasive to our group, and they like having an option after endocrine therapy and chemo. Pharmacy has the ordering sorted. If anything it's just waiting for the right patient, usually someone with good performance status who has progressed quickly.

The group is unsure which ADC to use first in HER2-low patients. Some lean toward T-DXd and keep SG for later, others aren't certain either way. They said sequencing guidance is thin. Until that is clearer I think they'll keep choosing case by case, so use stays modest.

Payer step-edits. We usually need a peer-to-peer, and the first answer is often a denial. Each round costs a week or two, which matters in a patient who is progressing. Our office staff spend a lot of time on appeals. A couple of patients got worse while waiting, and that makes the doctors less willing to start the process at all.

We spent a good while on this and it kept coming back to neutropenia. In their community practice there is no easy way to get mid-cycle CBCs for patients who live far away, and they worry a febrile episode will land in a local ED that doesn't know the regimen. They would use SG earlier in HR+/HER2- disease if primary G-CSF were reliably covered and a nurse triage line were in place. For now they hold it back for patients who live close and are very reliable.
Prior auth turnaround, mostly. Sometimes a week or more.

Honestly, not much of a barrier is left in their view. Early on the infusion nurses were nervous and the first few patients took a lot of hand-holding. After that the team settled into a routine with premeds, diarrhea instructions and a day 8 check. They think the only thing still limiting use is remembering to consider it at the right line, and I think that will fade as more patients go through the clinic.
Diarrhea management scares the nursing staff more than the drug itself.

Sequencing, really. After a CDK4/6 inhibitor and a couple of endocrine lines they aren't sure whether SG or a HER2-low directed ADC should come first, and the evidence doesn't settle it for them. Probably they default to whatever the payer approves fastest.
Chair time. Day 1 and day 8 slots are hard to find.

In urothelial they see this as a real option once patients have progressed on enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab, because there is not much else to offer. The barrier they named is late referral. Community urologists tend to send patients over only after performance status has already slipped, and by then the window for a toxic-ish ADC is gone. They said earlier conversations with referring colleagues would probably do more than any new data. Otherwise they are happy to prescribe it.
Not sure yet, probably payer step edits in urothelial.

Cost to the practice. Buy-and-bill exposure on an ADC like this is significant for a small independent group, and a denial after the fact would really hurt. They said they would rather refer out than carry that risk.

The conversation circled around dose reductions and quality of life. They are comfortable starting SG, but they find it hard to predict who will need to drop a dose level by cycle two or three, and they don't want to promise patients a smooth ride. Fatigue and GI effects seem to matter as much to them as the labs. I think they would use it more if they had a clearer picture of the real-world tolerability pattern in patients who aren't trial-fit. Until then they pick patients carefully and keep the follow-up visits tight.
Honestly none; once the patient is lined up it is easy to start.

Mainly the thinner evidence in urothelial compared with breast. They said they feel fine using SG in HR+/HER2- disease after chemo-exposed lines, but in bladder they want more mature data before moving it up. The toxicity trade-off feels harder to justify in an older, often renally impaired population. A couple of their patients were cisplatin-ineligible and also frail, which adds to the hesitation. So for now it stays a late option, and they don't see that changing soon.

They wondered whether UGT1A1 testing is needed up front. Nobody in their lab offers it with a quick turnaround, so they tend to just start at the labeled dose and watch closely. Not sure if that is the right approach and would like clearer guidance.

The main hurdle was the pathway, and it has been fixed. Pharmacy built an order set with premeds and G-CSF, and uptake went up afterward. What remains is identifying the right patients early enough, before they are too many lines in.
Patients balk at hair loss, honestly more than anythng.

This clinician mostly treats older patients and said frailty is the real limit. They are not against the drug, but they hesitate to start it in anyone over a certain age with comorbidities, because they expect cytopenias and GI effects to cause admissions. Family members also tend to push back on weekly visits. I think they would reach for it sooner if there were a clear dosing approach for borderline-fit patients. For now they favor oral options or single-agent chemo with an easier schedule.
Travel. Many of their patients live well over an hour from the clinic, and the day 8 visit is where they drop off. Some families just decline once they hear about the weekly schedule.

Referral timing, they said. By the time patients reach their center they have had several lines and performance status is marginal. SG would probably be considered more often if the handoff happened one line earlier.

Coverage has been fine in their experience, so the only real constraint is bed availability. When someone develops neutropenic fever they need an inpatient bed quickly, and that is not always possible. They still plan to use SG more in HR+/HER2- disease.

They keep asking whether TROP2 expression matters. With no biomarker to point to, it is hard to answer payers who want clear selection criteria. They also feel uneasy telling patients it works regardless of expression, though they use it anyway when other options have run out.
PA turnaround. Takes too long, pts progress while waiting.
Neutropenia mgmt. Not sure their clinic has G-CSF logistics sorted.
Honestly no real barrier now, payer approves fast for HR+ pts.
Buy-and-bill risk for the hospital pharmacy, cost mainly.
Wants more OS data before moving SG earlier in sequence.
Pts scared of hair loss + diarrhea, a handful decline outright
Community practice, limited chair capacity. Day 1/day 8 schedule is hard to fit with current staffing. HCP would probably use SG more if the schedule were simpler.
Worried re AEs in older urothelial pts, esp. diarrhea and neutropenia. ECOG 2 pts usually go to other options. Not sure where SG fits after EV.
Tumor board is supportive once pt has progressed on endocrine + CDK4/6. Only hurdle is getting pt scheduled quickly. Otherwise happy w/ the PFS story.
Sequencing unclear vs other ADCs in HR+/HER2-low. HCP thinks T-DXd goes first for those pts, SG after. Waiting on guidance, I think.
Insurer denied first PA, needed peer-to-peer. Staff time burden is big. Only one person in the office handles auths so delays happen
No barrier in their large center, has dose-mod protocols and a nurse navigator. Main question is pt selection and the TROP2 role. Thinks use will grow over the next year.
Mostly the AE mgmt workload. Pts need close f/u in first cycles, lots of fever calls. HCP thinks it gets easier once team is used to it.
Hospital P&T hasn't added it to formulary yet, so every case is an exception request. Slows everything down and pts wait.

Financial toxicity is the issue. Copay is high for a lot of pts even w/ coverage, and assistance paperwork is slow. HCP said some pts on fixed income just say no before starting. Not sure what the social worker can do. Would offer it more often if cost wasn't part of every conversation.

No biomarker needed for SG, which HCP sees as both good and bad. Easier workflow, no waiting on testing. But unsure how to pick pts most likely to benefit, so tx choice becomes gut feeling. Wants better markers or clinical features. Barrier is more about confidence than access, I think.

HCP likes SG for pretreated HR+/HER2- pts after endocrine and chemo. Biggest barrier is referral awareness, since many outside oncologists still think of it as TNBC only. Tumor board discussions are helping. Once pts get to HCP's clinic it is mostly smooth. Wants more case-based education for community colleagues.

In urothelial HCP feels evidence is thinner, mostly single-arm so far. Wants confirmatory data before using it routinely. Payers also push EV and IO first, so SG is a later option anyway. PA denials are more likely outside HR+ breast. Cautious for now, but open if more data comes.

Rural catchment, pts travel a long way for day 1 and day 8 infusions. Labs can be done locally but results come back slowly. HCP says a few pts stopped tx just from travel burden, not AEs. Clincal benefit is fine, logistics is the limiter. Would consider SG more if satellite infusion was possible.

Monitoring uncertainty. HCP unsure whether to do UGT1A1 testing and whether to use primary G-CSF prophylaxis. Dose delays are common in their experience, which makes pts and nurses anxious. No clear local protocol yet. Probably holds off on more pts until pharmacy and nursing agree on a plan.
Prior auth for SG takes forever and then they deny it anyway.
Neutropenia management, mostly. I don't have the staff to cover it.
Efficacy I'm fine with on sacituzumab; only the paperwork holds me back.
Sequencing. Nobody can tell me where it really belongs versus the other options.
Infusion chair time in our community clinc, but patients on sacituzumab do well once started.
Diarrhea calls at 2am land on me, though we manage.
Every payer wants something different for SG, and my staff burns hours on peer-to-peers. By the time approval lands, the patient has often progressed or gone to hospice. That's the barrier for me.

UGT1A1 testing before SG is the sticking point. I'm not convinced it changes what I do, so it doesn't get ordered routinely, and I'm not sure what the label expects. Probably creates some hesitation in my group.
Look, in pretreated HR+ patients I'll reach for it when I can. The only real friction is that we're a small practice and buying and storing it upfront ties up cash. Reimbursment lag is the issue.

Evidence in urothelial feels thin to me, mostly single-arm data and extrapolation. I'm skeptical about using sacituzumab ahead of enfortumab in anyone. Until there's something randomized I'm cautious.
Patients hate the alopecia more than I expected, and some refuse it up front. That limits uptake in younger women. Beyond that, the day 1 and day 8 schedule is a hassle for people who travel far.
G-CSF support is basically mandatory in my hands, which adds cost and yet another authorization. Nobody mentions that when they pitch the drug. Frustrating.
Honestly it's the competition. With other ADCs and oral agents around, I don't see a clear reason to pick SG first, and the toxicity trade-off makes me hesitant.
Biggest thing is awareness among my referring docs. Once a patient lands with me they usually get treated, but late referrals are the problem. I'd use it more if people sent them earlier.

Monitoring burden is what kills it for me. Frequent labs in the first cycles, CBC checks before day 8, and a toxicity phone line that rings constantly. We're a two-doc clinic with one triage nurse. The drug looks fine on paper, but I can't safely run more patients on sacituzumab without more staff. Sometimes I just choose something simpler.

For breast, the barrier is mostly who gets it and when. I tend to use chemo options I'm comfortable with first, and by the time I think of SG the patient's performance status has dipped. Then I worry about tolerability in someone frail. I'm probably too conservative, I'll admit. If I felt more sure about it earlier in the line I'd move it up.

Cost and coverage, no contest. Our hospital pharmacy flags it as a high-cost infusion and every new start goes through a committee. That adds a week or two, sometimes longer, and I've had patients drop out of the queue. Honestly it feels like the system is designed to make me give up. Off-site infusion centers seem even worse about it.

I'm a fan once patients are on it, which surprises me given how skeptical I was. The sticking point is first-cycle anxiety: I want dose-reduction plans and clear stopping rules, and the guidance I've seen is vague. With a cleaner algorithm for neutropenia and diarrhea I'd start more people. Right now I lean on my own judgement and that makes some colleagues nervous.

Hard to pin to one thing. Part of it is that the urothelial data I know come from a heavily pretreated group, and my patients rarely look like that. Part of it is TROP2 expression, which nobody tests for, so I don't know who benefits. Not sure it matters but it nags at me. Mostly I'm waiting for more in that setting.

We got burned by a denial last quarter and the patient had already been told it was coming, so now I hesitate to even propose sacituzumab. Appeals take weeks and the documentation requirements keep shifting, from what my coordinator tells me. Meanwhile the patient is sitting there with progressing disease and a lot of questions. I get that it's costly but the delays are the real barrier. I end up defaulting to cheaper chemo.
Said prior auth turnaround is the sticking point, usually a week or more.
Neutropenia management is what worries the infusion nurses most.
Felt the only real hurdle is getting the team used to the dosing and G-CSF routine, nothing deeper than that.
Thinks the urothelial data are still too thin to use it earlier.
Chair time, basically. The day 1 and day 8 schedule is hard to fit in.
Mentioned that copay assistence paperwork is what stalls most starts, though it usually gets sorted eventually.
A community oncologist said the biggest issue is the day 1/day 8 schedule for patients who live far from the clinic. Thinks transport is probably a bigger problem than anything clinical.

Reported feeling quite comfortable with SG after TROPiCS-02 and sees it as a clear option once a patient is through endocrine therapy and CDK4/6. The only friction is payer paperwork, which the office has now streamlined.

Brought up diarrhea and the need for an atropine and loperamide plan up front. The phone triage calls take staff time that isn't reimbursed, so the clinic is cautious about adding patients. Still sees the drug as worthwhile for the right person.
Not sure where it sits in the sequence for HR+/HER2- disease, especially relative to other ADCs. Wants more real-world experience before moving it earlier, I think.
Pointed to buy-and-bill exposure as the main block. The drug is expensive, and if a claim is denied the practice absorbs the loss.
Said no TROP2 testing requirement makes this easier to offer than some other options. What slows uptake is awareness among referring urologists, who don't always send patients back in time.
Felt the barrier is selecting older, frail urothelial patients. Isn't sure who will tolerate the myelosuppression, so tends to reserve it for fitter pts.
According to this HCP, the hospital formulary committee hasn't added it for the urothelial indication. Every case needs an exception request, and it takes weeks while thier patients keep progressing.

Said patients are the problem more than the system. Hair loss and fatigue make a lot of women hesitate, especially if they are still working. Even when counseled, some choose to stay on chemo they already know. The doctor felt the conversation takes a lot of time and doesn't always land. Thinks better patient education materials would matter more than any new data.

Described lab monitoring as the main logistical headache. Patients in outlying areas have to get CBCs drawn locally and the results don't always reach the clinic quickly. That makes dose delays and G-CSF decisions feel less safe. Said it's manageable in town but hard to scale beyond the main site. Thinks a clearer monitoring schedule would help.

Reported that the institution built an order set and a nurse-led toxicity pathway, so use has grown steadily. Said the main barrier now is just keeping infusion slots open. Felt the team is confident with early diarrhea and neutropenia management. Sees it as a fairly routine later-line option now, and would use it more if chairs allowed.

Said the evidence is the issue for them. In urothelial especially, they want clearer comparisons against what they already use before changing practice. The survival benefit in breast looks real but modest to them, so they weigh it against the toxicity. Probably waits for longer follow-up and more subgroup detail. Not hostile, just unconvinced for now.

Said coverage has been smoother than expected, with most approvals coming through on first submission. Main barrier is simply the occasional patient whose plan wants a peer-to-peer. Felt that's an annoyance rather than a true block. Would use it more if referrals came earlier.

Told me the infusion side is stretched, with premeds, observation and the long chair time all adding up and not enough nurses to cover it. Said they've had to turn down starts some weeks. Wants it for more patients but the capacity just isnt there

barrier|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: Prior auth fights eat weeks, and patients progress while we wait.
ILD risk. I just don't love the monitoring burden that comes with T-DXd.
Honestly, HER2-low IHC 1+ vs 0 reads are inconsistent in my hands.
Only chair time, really. The drug itself I'm happy with.
Nausea managment. Patients dread it and I'm the one getting the calls.
Scan schedule for pneumonitis surveillance, logistics mostly.

We're a community site with no quick access to pulmonology or high-res CT. When a patient starts coughing I'm stuck deciding whether to hold T-DXd or send them to the ED. That uncertainty makes me hesitate to start it.
I think the evidence is fine for HER2-low after endocrine therapy, but I'm not sure where it sits against another endocrine-based combo first. Sequencing is the question for me, not the drug itself.
Our pathology lab still reports HER2 as just positive or negative, so low never gets flagged. I have to ask them to re-read slides, and that takes forever.
Coverage has mostly been fine for us lately, which surprised me. The remaining issue is chair time, since infusion days run long with observation. I'd take that trade for the right patient.
Specialty pharmacy delays. Drug shows up late, the patient gets rescheduled twice, and they start losing faith in the plan.
Out-of-pocket cost for older patients, probably. Some manage fine, others just walk away from treatment. Hard to predict which until we're already talking about it.

Echo checks plus the ILD surveillance feel like a lot for someone who's otherwise doing OK on endocrine therapy. I'm skeptical the extra visits are worth it for earlier-line use of T-DXd. Maybe the data will change my mind, I'm not there yet.
Biggest hurdle is getting my partners comfortable. They've seen a couple of bad pneumonitis cases and now they're gun-shy. I've been fine with it when we catch things early.

Payers. Every single start turns into a peer-to-peer. Last month one patient waited almost three weeks for approval, and her scans looked worse by the time we got the green light. My staff spends more time on appeals than on patient education. If the paperwork were simple I'd use this a lot more. As it stands I sometimes pick the easier regimen just to avoid the fight.

The HER2-low testing situation is murky. Some of my biopsies are old and from the primary, and I'm not convinced the score still reflects the current disease. Re-biopsy is a big ask for a patient who's already tired. I think a lot of potentially eligible patients get missed because of this. It's not a deal-breaker, but it slows everything down.

Tolerability in real life, not the study setting. Hair loss, fatigue and nausea add up, and my patients are honest with me about it. I'm not saying it's unmanageable, but quality of life matters when someone has been stable on oral therapy. I usually spend a whole visit just on counseling. That conversation is where a good number of them decide to wait.

The data are persuasive for the right patient, and I'll say that even as a skeptic. What holds me back is staff readiness. Our nurses needed real training on spotting early respiratory symptoms, and the phone triage had to be rebuilt. Once that was in place things got smoother. So the barrier was internal workflow more than the drug.

Step edits. Several plans want chemo first for HER2-low, so I have to document failure of regimens I wouldn't have picked. Denials come back with vague wording and no real clinical rationale. Appeals eventually work, but only if I push, and I don't always have time to push. Frankly it's the biggest reason this gets used later than it should be.
T-DXd prior auth delays, usually a week or more.
Honestly none right now, T-DXd approvals come through fast for us.
Getting CT slots for ILD checks on schedule is tough
Mostly unsure how to read IHC 1+ vs 0 on older samples.
Pharmacy wants the T-DXd order two days ahaed, which limits add-ons.
Only thing is chair time, otherwise happy to use it more.

In our community practice the biggest hurdle with T-DXd is nausea and vomiting in the first cycles. Patients call the office a lot and we don't have a dedicated nurse for that. So I tend to hold off in frail patients.
Insurance usually says yes for HER2-low after endocrine therapy, but the appeal letters for T-DXd eat staff time. It's not a dealbreaker, just slow.
The pathology team now reports HER2 IHC with the low category spelled out, so the testing barrier has mostly gone away for us. Occasionally a pt still needs a re-biopsy.
I'm worried about pneumonitis with T-DXd, particularly in older patients with COPD. Pulmonary follow-up is far away for a lot of my rural patients.
Sequencing is the question for me. I'm not sure where T-DXd fits after CDK4/6, so it probably needs more real world experience before I move it earlier.
Co-pay assistance for the T-DXd infusion is the sticking point. A handful of patients have declined after the cost conversation.
Our infusion center is booked out so adding a new q3w patient means waiting. Once a slot opens people go ahead.
Evidence is convincing enough for me in the endocrine-resistant HER2-low group. The main thing is getting the echo done on time before starting, which is just a scheduling issue.

Biggest barrier is the monitoring burden with T-DXd. We need regular imaging, symptom check-ins between cycles and a clear plan if a cough shows up. With one NP covering the whole clinic, that's a lot to absorb. I think some colleagues avoid it for that reason alone.

Payer rules vary. One plan wants documented HER2 IHC 1+ or 2+/ISH-negative on the pathology report itself, and some of our reports just say 'HER2 negative'. We end up calling the lab for addenda. That adds maybe a week. Once the paperwork is right, approval is typically fine.

Not much holding me back at this point. My patients who've progressed on endocrine therapy tolerate T-DXd reasonably, and the team knows the antiemetic plan. If anything I wish referrals from the community oncologists who send patients to us were quicker. Mostly a logistics thing.

Honestly, uncertainty about long-term safety. Patients ask how long they'll be on the drug and what happens to their lungs, and I don't have a great answer. Also the guidance on dose delays seems fuzzy to some in my group. Until that's clearer I'd stay conservative.

Testing is the thing. Our lab sends out IHC and results take over a week, and the tumor block from years ago is sometimes unusable. We then wait on a new biopsy, which the patient doesnt love. After that, the drug side is straightforward.

Transport. A lot of our patients live far from the hospital-based clinic and come in with volunteer drivers. Every three weeks plus extra visits for labs or scans is too much for some. We also lose track of people if they get admitted elsewhere for side effects and we don't hear about it.
PA turnaround. 2+ wks, pt progreses while waiting.
HER2-low IHC 0 vs 1+ calls, HCP not confident in path reads.
Minimal barrier per HCP. T-DXd is first choice once HER2-low is confirmed.
ILD fear. First thing out of his mouth.
Infusion chair capacity, esp. certain days of the wk.
Payer denials for HER2-low, earlier lines esp, I think.
Community clinic, no easy pulm/rad access for ILD workup. HCP would use T-DXd more if CTs could be scheduled fast between cycles. Not sure how they'd set that up.
Barrier is mostly awareness among referring docs. Once a pt w/ HER2-low result hits her tumor board, tx choice is easy in her words. Wants low expression flagged clearly on path reports.
N/V in older pts, HCP says they drop off early. Premeds add chair time. Probably holds back T-DXd in frail pts, but willing in fit ones.
Unsure re sequencing after CDK4/6i vs going to chemo first. Says data is there but guidelines lag in his practice. Waiting on tumor board consensus.
Buy-and-bill cash flow w/ T-DXd. Small practice, cant float the cost for long. Admin told him to limit # of pts.
Testing no longer an issue, path lab reports IHC 1+/2+ routinely now. Main thing left is counseling pts on AEs, which she thinks is manageable.
Pts live ~2 hrs away. q3w visits + scans + labs = big burden. HCP worries about missed visits and late AE catches. Rural practice.
Echo/LVEF slots hard to get, cardiology backlog maybe 3 wks. Not a dealbreaker but tx start delayd.

Main worry is ILD. HCP had a pt w/ grade 2 pneumonitis before and says it shook the whole team. Now every cough = hold tx and CT, which clogs the schedule. Pts also read about it online and refuse. Thinks he'd use it earlier in line if there were a clear monitoring protocol. For now sticks w/ chemo in borderline pts.

HER2-low status is the bottleneck. Archival tissue often old, sometimes IHC 0 on old block but pt clearly different now. HCP debates rebiopsy, but pts hate it. Not sure retest is worth it. Says if the result were reliable he'd just go ahead and use T-DXd.

Honestly no big barrier at her site. Pharmacy set up a pathway, PA team knows the drill, tumor board flags eligible pts. Only gripe is chair time on infusion days. She'd like to move it earlier in HR+/HER2-low since PFS benefit seems clear to her.

Payer step edits. Plan wants 2 prior lines of chemo before approving, even where HCP thinks label supports earlier use. Appeals take forever and peer-to-peer is a coin flip. Staff time wasted. A few pts just switched to capecitabine to avoid delay.

Trial competition at the center. Several HER2-low pts are on studies so T-DXd use is limited by enrollment priorities. HCP not against it, just says trial slots come first. Real-world use will probably rise once those close. Unclear when.

Nurses are key. Infusion RNs got trained on AEs and early ILD signs, and HCP feels comfortable now. Remaining barrier is pharmacy supply timing, drug sometimes arrives late. Thinks that is solvable. Wants T-DXd in more HER2-low pts.

We talked for a good while and he kept coming back to ILD. He is comfortable with T-DXd on paper, but his clinic has no easy route to a pulmonologist and CT slots are slow, so he worries about catching early pneumonitis late. I think he would use it more if the monitoring workflow were already built. For now he reserves it for patients who live close and who he trusts to call early.
Prior auth denials for HER2-low, mostly after endocrine therapy.

Honestly, not much stands in the way for her. The main thing is infusion chair availability on a couple of days a week, which she says is solvable. She'd happily move more HER2-low patients to it earlier.

Pathology is the sticking point in this community practice. The reference lab reported HER2 as 1+ one week and 0 on a repeat, and she is not sure which result a payer will accept. The borderline patients are the ones she hesitates over, since a 0 call closes the door. She said she'd probably treat more if IHC scoring felt more reproducible. Until then she tends to default to chemo for the unclear cases.
Nothing major; the evidence convinced the team, it's just chair time.
Cost to the patient, mostly, from what he sees. Copay assistance covers some of it but the paperwork lands on his nurses, so T-DXd tends to get pushed later in the queue.

Sequencing is what he kept returning to. After a CDK4/6 inhibitor and a couple of endocrine lines he sees a clear place for T-DXd, but earlier than that he is unsure whether to hold it back for later. Tumor board is split, roughly half wanting it right after progression and half wanting more chemo-free time first. He thinks more real-world experience will settle it. No hard objection, just uncertainty about the best slot.
Nausea and vomiting; patients dread it before they even start.
Her worry is the monitoring burden, frequent scans and visits for patients who already feel over-tested. A few older patients decline T-DXd once they hear the lung risk, and thier families back them.

Overall he is enthusiastic and said the real barrier is only internal. His center is still building a standard order set for premedication and a symptom check call between cycles. Once that exists he expects to offer T-DXd to almost every eligible HER2-low patient. He added that payers have mostly approved on the first submission. So for him it is logistics, not evidence.
Probably the lack of clarity on HER2-ultralow, he isnt sure how to test or who qualifies
The drug is fine, staffing isn't. Infusion nurses are stretched and T-DXd needs closer observation, so he caps how many new starts he does each week.

Mostly the testing pathway, as she sees it. Many referrals arrive with only an old primary biopsy, HER2 status may have shifted, and re-biopsying a bone-only met is hard. She thinks it would be used more if archival results were accepted more flexibly.
Only the wait for approval; once T-DXd is cleared, patients do well.
I think it's the unknowns around brain mets for him. He has a few patients with stable CNS disease and isn't sure he can lean on this option there, so he keeps other choices in the mix

Payer step edits are what stop him. One plan wants documented failure of two chemo lines before it will release trastuzumab deruxtecan, which doesn't match how he'd like to sequence. Appeals take weeks, and in that time a symptomatic patient may need to start something else. He said he's tired of the back and forth.
Mostly awareness among referring general oncologists, he feels. Once they see how it fits for HER2-low he expects uptake to climb. T-DXd is already his go-to after endocrine failure.

Long chat, and the theme was toxicity in a frail population. Her patients are often elderly with lung comorbidities, so T-DXd ILD risk feels heavy to her. She also mentioned cardiac function checks adding yet another appointment. She will prescribe it for fitter patients but not routinely, and would rather keep it rare than see a serious event.
Rural clinic, so the practical issue is distance. Patients would need to travle for scans and any pulmonary workup, which she isn't sure they can manage. Telehealth check-ins help a bit.
Buy-and-bill exposure; the practice is wary of the upfront drug cost.
Honestly just the prior auth turnaround, everything else I can live with.
ILD monitoring burden on a small clinic like ours with T-DXd.
Love the drug, only snag is getting restaging scans booked on time.
HER2-low scoring is still inconsistent between pathology reports, I think that's what stops people.
Nausea management. Patients dread it more than anything else.
Payer denials for the ultralow group, mostly.

T-DXd has been a great fit for my chemo-naive HR+ patients once endocrine therapy stops working. The one thing holding me back is the pathology side. I'm not sure our lab reliably separates a 0 from ultralow, so I hesitate to push.
We're a community setting, so infusion chair time is the real issue. We can do it, but squeezing a q3w slot in next to everything else gets tricky.
Biggest issue is fear of pneumonitis, among the nurses and some of the older patients. I'm enthusiastic about T-DXd's efficacy, but I spend a lot of visit time just on counseling about that risk.
Really impressed with how my patients do, so for me the barrier is awareness among referring docs. Some of the general oncologists still reach for another chemo first out of habit.
Coverage varies a lot by plan with trastuzumab deruxtecan. Some approvals come through in a few days, others bounce back twice before anyone reads the label.
Cost to the hospital pharmacy, since we carry the drug upfront. I'd use T-DXd more if the reimbursement lag wasn't such a worry, probably.
I'm all in on the data, but baseline cardiac and lung workup slows us down. Echo slots are scarce here so patients just wait. By the time they are cleared the window has sometimes moved.

Pathology, mainly. Our reports say HER2 1+ one time and negative the next on a rebiopsy, and then the payer questions it. I really want to use it more but that mess makes it hard teh whole way through.

I'm very positive on T-DXd, it's become one of my go-to options for the right patient. My caveat is the monitoring schedule. Regular imaging and symptom checks need staff time that we don't really have. I think a dedicated nurse for ILD follow-up would change things. Until then I'm choosy about who I start.

For T-DXd the barrier is patient finances and travel. A lot of my patients live far from our infusion center and the copays worry them even with assistance. I'm excited about what the drug can do. But several have simply declined once they heard about the cost and the drive every three weeks. Social work is stretched thin, so it's hard to catch everyone.

Sequencing is what I keep coming back to with T-DXd. I like it and would use it earlier, but I'm not sure where it best sits relative to the other options after CDK4/6. We just don't have much head-to-head guidance. So I tend to decide case by case, which is slower. A clearer sequencing framework would probably help me commit.

My worry with T-DXd is delayed symptom reporting. Patients don't call when they get a cough, they wait until the next visit. I'm enthusiastic about the benefit, but a missed early ILD sign scares me. We don't have the staff for weekly phone check-ins. Maybe telehealth would help, I'm not sure.

Our tumor board is firmly behind T-DXd for eligible patients, and the team is excited. The main barrier now is specialty pharmacy supply, because delivery delays have pushed back a few starts. When it does arrive on time everything runs smoothly. it's frustrating to lose a week over paperwork and shipping

I'd say long-term data in the lower-expression patients is my caveat with T-DXd. The early signal is encouraging and I'm keen to use it. But patients ask about hair loss and fatigue over many months, and I can't answer fully. Some of them want more certainty than I can give. I'd guess comfort will grow as follow-up matures.
PA delays. Pts waiting weeks for approval, sometimes longer

IHC scoring at the low end is the sticking point for her. Local path reports often just say negative or 1+ with no real comment, and she doesnt fully trust the borderline calls. She would order repeat testing more often if turnaround were quicker. Not sure how many of her older pts even have usable blocks left.
Mostly awareness from referring general oncs, I think. Once pts land in her clinic with HER2-low documented, T-DXd is an easy conversation. She just wants the community docs to flag them earlier.
ILD worry, plain and simple. They had one grade 2 case last year and the whole team got spooked. Now everyone wants baseline CT plus regular scans, and radiology cant always fit those in.
Not sure where it slots after CDK4/6 + ET

Payer is the biggest hurdle for her. Commercial plans keep asking for another chemo first even when IHC 1+ is clearly documented. Appeals eat up nurse time and peer-to-peers are hit or miss. Honestly she has stopped fighting for some pts, which she admitted feels bad. Medicare pts are mostly fine.
Nothing major, team is comfortable. Just need more chair slots.
Nausea management is what slows him down. He uses T-DXd but wants a tighter antiemetic routine before he moves it earlier. Says the pts who vomit once tend to dread cycle two.
Pts scared off by the pneumonitis warning, hard conversation to have

Cardiac monitoring is more of a nuisance than a true barrier in his view. The nearest echo lab is far from his rural site, so pts often have to travel for a baseline LVEF. He said he skips it less often than he used to, but it still delays starts. Probably fixable with better scheduling, though no one owns that problem right now.

She'd honestly use it more if she could. The only thing holding her back is getting HER2-low status documented early in the metastatic setting. When the report is in hand, approvals go through smoothly and pts start quickly. She feels the evidence is convincing enough for her group. It's mostly a workflow gap between pathology and the oncology team.
Frailty in older pts. He worries about tox in 75+ and tends to default to endocrine or oral options. Not convinced the benefit holds up for the more fragile ones.
Waiting on longer f/u for OS before shifting it earlier

Rebiopsy is the problem for him. A lot of his pts only have primary tumor tissue from years ago, and HER2 status can drift. IR is booked out and some pts refuse another core. He sometimes treats on the old result and hopes for the best, which he doesnt love. Wants a simpler way to confirm low expression.
Pharmacy buy-in was the thing. Once the committee signed off on the formulary addition, uptake got much easier. Nursing training for infusion reactions is done as well.

Cash flow for a small practice. Buy and bill on an expensive ADC ties up money, especially when payers are slow to reimburse. Says clinically hes fine with it, it's the finance side that makes the partners nervous.
Hair loss and nausea make some younger pts hesitate, others dont care at all. Mixed.

Sequencing is what he keeps coming back to, esp for HER2+ pts who have several options after first line. Tumor board discussions go back and forth on whether T-DXd should come before or after other HER2 agents. He doesnt see a clear consensus and the guidelines are not specific enough for him. For now he decides case by case, and a good chunk of his pts end up on something familiar.
Fewer concerns than a year ago. Remaining issue is just the scan schedule logistics for ILD surveillance. Probably manageable once the clinic builds a standard order set.

Confusing path language. Reports say things like HER2 0 with faint staining or ultralow and her group doesnt agree on what that means for eligibility. It leaves her unsure whether pts would be covered, so she tends to hold off.

biomarker|osimertinib.t: Reflex NGS at dx now built into path workflow. HCP very happy w/ it.
Still waiting 3+ wks on tissue NGS, frustrating.
Plasma first, tissue only if neg. Standard for this HCP.
No reflex testing at the community sites that refer to him.
Liquid bx TAT finally predictable, helps get osimertinib started on time.
PD-L1 scoring varies path to path but HCP says moot once EGFR+.
Tissue often insufficient after diagnostic core bx, esp small peripheral lesions. Ends up repeating bx or sending plasma, tx start slips by a couple wks. Not thrilled.
Thoracic clinic runs tissue + plasma concurrently at baseline. HCP says the osimertinib +/- chemo decision can be made at first tumor board w/o waiting on anything.
PA for NGS panel sometimes needed, depends on the plan. HCP thinks ordering itself is fine once pt is stage IV, but admin burden is real.
Reflex gaps: some outside labs only run single-gene EGFR/ALK, so rarer alterations get missed. HCP worried pts start tx w/ an incomplete picture.
Not sure a negative plasma can be trusted. I think HCP usually confirms w/ tissue if clinical suspicion is high. Uses liquid mainly when pt too frail for rebx.
Small community onc practice, one order set for send-out NGS, results back in a week or two which is OK for them. Said fewer pts get chemo by default while waiting. Osi decision feels cleaner now.
Tumor board keeps debating whether co-mutations like TP53 should push osimertinib alone vs w/ chemo. Reports differ lab to lab on what gets flagged, so hard to compare pts.

At progression HCP prefers plasma first for resistance, tissue if plasma neg. Probably will do more of this as the FLAURA2-type pts start progressing. Osi pts mostly get rebx only if plasma is unclear.

Rural clinic, everything is send-out. TAT is long, sometimes 3-4 wks, and pts w/ symptomatic disease get chemo while waiting. HCP then switches to osimertinib once EGFR result lands, but worries about AEs from chemo the pt maybe didn't need. Says path often doesn't have enough tissue to begin with. Wishes reflex was automatic, right now depends who reads the slide

PD-L1 IHC still ordered at baseline by habit. HCP notes assay and scorer variability is a known thing, esp near cutoffs. But for EGFR+ pts it rarely changes tx, so HCP doesn't sweat it. Main focus is making sure NGS comes back complete. Overall mixed, more annoyed by redundancy than by the variability itself.

Large center, reflex NGS at dx plus plasma drawn same visit. Results usually back by first consult, which HCP loves. Lets them discuss osimertinib alone vs w/ chemo, thinking about PFS and AEs, with the full molecular picture. High-burden pts get most of the combo discussion. HCP feels the whole workflow finally matches how fast pts need tx.

Payer denied repeat NGS at progression twice last quarter. PA appeals take wks and plasma coverage is inconsistent between plans. HCP sometimes just skips testing and changes tx empirically, which he doesn't like. Pt on osimertinib w/ clear progression waited a month. Says this is the biggest testing barrier right now, more than the tech itself.

Lab reports are inconsistent on how they call exon 19 del vs L858R vs uncommon muts. HCP reads them carefully but VUS wording is vague, so a few go to tumor board just to interpret. Not a huge problem, just time. Thinks standardized reporting woudl help. Otherwise comfortable w/ the panels being used.

In-house molecular path is quick, results usually before the pt even returns. HCP uses tissue as default and adds plasma if bx is thin. Osimertinib start is rarely delayed now. Feels team trust in the results is high, and tumor board spends less time arguing over whether the testing is adequate.
Reflex testing still doesn't happen here, so osimertinib waits on a manual EGFR order.
Plasma first, honestly, since tissue takes forever to come back.
NGS turnaround is finally under two weeks. About time.
PD-L1 scoring varies reader to reader and we all know it.
Tissue is still king for me, plasma negatives don't count for osimertinib decisions.
Our in-house panel now catches the uncommon EGFR variants, which is a relief.
We're a community site, so everything goes out to a reference lab. By the time teh report lands the patient has often started chemo already, and then we're debating a switch. Drives me nuts.
I send ctDNA at the same time as the biopsy request, not instead of it. If plasma shows an EGFR driver I'll start osimertinib, but I want tissue to back it up eventually.
Since pathology set up reflex NGS on every new nonsquamous lung sample, I stopped chasing orders. Honestly it's the one thing that has gotten better this year.

Insurance denied the broad panel on a never-smoker last month and said single-gene testing was enough. We lost weeks, the osimertinib start slipped, and I'm not even sure the single-gene test would have caught an exon 20 insertion.
Before chemo plus a TKI is even on the table I want the baseline mutation status nailed down. Tissue quantity is the usual limiter, small core biopsies run out fast and then everyone shrugs.
Liquid biopsy gets sold as the quick fix, but a negative result tells me very little. I've had patients with clean plasma who turned out positive on tissue. I don't trust it to rule anything out.
We're at an academic-affiliated clinic, so NGS comes back in about a week, I think. The bigger problem is that pathologists disagree on whether a sample has enough tumor cells to run.
Ordering plasma at diagnosis has been useful for frail patients who can't tolerate another biopsy. Osimertinib started sooner than it would have otherwise, and I'll admit that surprised me.

We still have no real reflex process. The oncologist has to remember to tick a box, and if a different service did the biopsy the box never gets ticked. I've seen two cases this year where the pathology report sat for days with no molecular request. Then the family calls asking why treatment hasn't begun. It's a system problem, not a patient problem.

I do both tissue and plasma most of the time. Plasma gives me an answer in days, which matters when someone is symptomatic. Tissue gives the full picture, including co-mutations like TP53 that I think might influence whether I add chemo to osimertinib. The catch is the two don't always agree, and then I'm guessing which one to believe. Probably tissue, not sure.

PD-L1 scoring bugs me. Same slide, two readers, a diffrent category, I've seen it. In EGFR-mutant patients it barely changes what I do, yet it eats time and tissue. I'd rather the sample go to NGS first, though in wild-type cases I accept it matters.

Honestly our current workflow is decent. Pathology triggers reflex NGS on the diagnostic sample, and plasma goes out in parallel if tissue is scant. Results usually land before the first clinic visit. I'm still skeptical of some send-out vendors, whose reports are bloated and hard to read. But for getting osimertinib started quickly, it works.

Rural practice, so we depend on couriers and a distant lab. Tissue samples get lost or sit over a weekend. Re-biopsy at progression is even harder, so I lean on plasma for resistance testing even though I know it misses things. Osimertinib is easy to prescribe; getting the right result in time to prescribe it is the hard part.

Payer rules are inconsistent. Some plans cover NGS on tissue but not plasma, others the reverse, and prior auth can take days. I've stopped predicting which will go through. Our staff now submits both requests and sees what sticks. Not elegant, probably wasteful, but it keeps patients moving toward osimertinib or whatever else fits.
Plasma first, tissue only if plasma comes back negative.
Reflex testing still doesn't happen reliably in the community clinics she covers.
Osimertinib decisions now wait for NGS here, and everyone accepts that.
Tissue is often insufficient after the diagnostic core biopsy, honestly.
Turnaround is fine when in-house, painful when sent out.
PD-L1 scoring varies between their pathologists, though that matters less for osimertinib decisions.

We run broad NGS on tissue at diagnosis for essentially every non-squamous case, and results usually land before the first oncology visit. That makes the osimertinib conversation, with or without chemo, much easier at the first consult. He credited the pathology lead for building that workflow.
Honestly, the payer pushes back on repeat NGS at progression, so they sometimes settle for a plasma assay and hope it picks somthing up. Not sure how many resistance mechanisms get missed that way.

Liquid biopsy is her go-to when the patient is frail or the lesion is hard to reach. A negative plasma result isn't fully believed, so they usually try for tissue anyway. I think that's fairly standard now.

Send-out testing took long enough that two patients last quarter started chemo before the EGFR result came back. They then had to change course. It's frustrating, especially when the FLAURA2-type regimen discussion hinges on that result.
The lab they use reports exon 19 deletions and L858R clearly, but rarer variants get a vague comment. Then the team debates whether it's actionable for osimertinib. Probably ends up at tumor board.
Since the hospital switched to reflex testing on all new lung adenocarcinoma specimens, the ordering gaps have basically vanished. Oncologists no longer have to remember to ask for it.

Small biopsies from the interventional team run out of tissue fast. By the time IHC and PD-L1 are done there's little left for NGS, so the oncologist ends up asking for plasma. Seems like a stewardship issue nobody owns.
Our rural satellite clinic orders plasma testing because it's quicker for the patient, then sends tissue later in parallel. Timing of results differs a lot week to wek.

Sequencing of tests dominated the conversation. Her group sends tissue NGS and plasma at the same visit when the patient looks symptomatic, mostly to avoid waiting. Plasma comes back in a few days and tissue closer to two weeks, I think, though she wasn't certain of the exact numbers. When the two disagree she leans on tissue unless the sample was poor. She felt osimertinib start dates are driven by whichever result lands first.

The main frustration was reflex testing gaps. Pathology will reflex EGFR on some specimens but not on cytology cell blocks, so those patients fall through until someone notices. She thought a good chunk of delayed starts trace back to that. Nobody owns the handoff between pathology and the oncology office, and she adimtted it's partly her own team's fault. Drug access isn't the problem, it's getting a result in time.

He was upbeat about how testing has changed in the last couple of years. Their lab validated a broad NGS panel covering EGFR, fusions and MET in one run, so serial single-gene tests are rare. Plasma is used at baseline while tissue is pending, and he finds it reassuring that the two usually agree. For osimertinib plus chemo discussions he likes seeing co-mutations upfront. He still wants better TP53 interpretation but called that a refinement.

Scoring variability came up repeatedly, mostly around IHC for MET and PD-L1. He said two pathologists in the same group can read the same slide differently, which makes him reluctant to let those results shape treatment alongside osimertinib. He wasn't sure whether central review would help or just slow things down. Referral reports also arrive in inconsistent formats, making comparison harder. Overall he sounded worried that interpretation noise is bigger than people admit.

She described a split workflow. Patients seen at the main center get tissue NGS up front, while those in outreach clinics usually get a plasma panel first because the biopsy is harder to schedule. She thinks that's reasonable but admits plasma panels probably miss some cases, likely low-shedding tumors. At progression she tries tissue again if it's safe, otherwise plasma. Insurance approval for the repeat sometimes takes a while and varies by plan. Not sure there's a clean answer.

He felt testing is one of the things his community is now doing well. Samples go for NGS the day the diagnosis is made, and the lab phones EGFR results to the oncology nurse, so turnaround rarely holds up a start. That has made conversations about osimertinib with chemotherapy much more straightforward, since he knows the full picture early. Plasma is the backup when tissue is scant and it has worked fine so far. His only wish is that rebiopsy at progression were as smooth.
Community clinic still waits close to two weeks for NGS tissue results.
Plasma ctDNA first at their site, osimertinib started on a positive result.
Reflex EGFR testing exists on paper, not always triggered in practice
Not enough tissue left after the diagnostic biopsy, again.
Osimertinib decision now made the same week thanks to the in-house panel.
Mostly sends out NGS, uses PCR for EGFR only when urgent.

Thoracic group at a regional hospital orders a broad NGS panel on all new nonsquamous cases. They run plasma alongside if the biopsy is small. Results usually land before the first oncology visit, so osimertinib can start without a gap.

Private practice oncologist said pathology sends PD-L1 and molecular as seperate requests, so he often has PD-L1 back and no EGFR result for days. He feels pushed to begin chemo-immunotherapy in the meantime. Probably a workflow issue more than a lab issue, not sure.

Liquid biopsy is their go-to when the patient is frail or the lesion is hard to reach. If plasma is negative they still repeat with tissue, since they don't fully trust a negative. Osimertinib gets started on a positive plasma result without waiting.

Academic-affiliated clinic, where a nurse navigator chases NGS reports by hand. Reports somtimes get lost in the portal between pathology and the oncologist. Hard to say how often, a handful of cases this quarter.

Insurance prior auth for the larger panel is the sticking point at his clinic. The smaller PCR panel gets approved fast, so that is what he uses first, then NGS later for the rest. For patients who might get osimertinib plus chemo he wants the full picture before deciding.

Pathologist said EGFR calls are generally fine but classification of rare variants varies between labs, I think. He sometimes gets different answers on uncommon insertions depending on which vendor ran the sample.
Every new lung adenocarcinoma at their cancer center now goes straight to NGS via reflex, set up last year. Oncologists rarely have to ask anymore.
Mixed bag with tissue versus blood at his community site. Blood is quicker, about a week, but he trusts tissue more for co-mutations like TP53 when deciding whether to add chemo to osimertinib.

Small rural clinic, so all biopsies are done elsewhere and sent out. The oncologist said tissue often reaches the reference lab with too little tumor, and a repeat biopsy means another procedure for the patient. Turnaround is long enough that some patients start chemo first. She would like plasma to be the default, but the payer only covers it after tissue fails. Overall she thinks the testing gaps cost them time with EGFR-mutant patients.

Hospital-based thoracic clinic with a molecular tumor board every week. Pathology reflexes NGS on every new nonsquamous sample, and plasma goes out the same day for stage IV. Results are usually back in time for the first treatment visit. Because of that the physician feels comfortable offering osimertinib alone or with chemo straight away. Only complaint is the occasional sample with insufficient tissue.

He said PD-L1 scoring is where he sees the variability, less so EGFR. Different pathologists in the group read the same stain a bit differently, so he asks for a second read on borderline ones. EGFR itself comes off the NGS panel and seems consistent. Not sure that holds for less common variants. It doesn't change what he does with osimertinib in the end.

The gap, as he described it, is ordering. The surgeon biopsies, pathology confirms adenocarcinoma, and nobody orders molecular unless the oncologist asks. If the patient comes through the ED, the oncologist sometimes meets them after the block has gone to storage. He thinks a handful of patients a year end up on non-targeted therapy instead of osimertinib for that reason. A standing order would fix it, but that hasn't happened.

Their lab moved to an in-house NGS panel this year. Turnaround dropped to a few working days, which she said changes the conversation with patients. They still use plasma when the patient is too sick for a biopsy. She is happier now about starting osimertinib quickly, with chemo added case by case.

Tissue versus liquid is a constant argument at their tumor board. Radiology wants plasma to avoid another needle, pathology worries about false negatives, and the oncologist is stuck waiting. In one recent case a patient with a suspected EGFR mutation sat for a couple of weeks while they debated. She felt the delay was avoidable. Nobody seems to own the pathway.
Said plasma ctDNA first has changed how fast they can start osimertinib.
Reflex NGS still isn't automatic in their lab, he said.
Thinks tissue is still the gold standard, liquid just as backup, accoding to this HCP.
Community oncologist reported results come back quickly now, no real complaints.
Told me turnaround is the biggest pain point, full stop.
Mentioned IHC scoring differs reader to reader, but EGFR PCR calls feel clear-cut.

She said her pathologists send broad NGS up front on any new nonsquamous case, so the EGFR result is usually there by the first visit. That has made the FLAURA2 conversation about adding chemo with osi much easier to have early.
Often gets a tiny core biopsy, and the tissue runs out after the PD-L1 stain, per this physician. Then they go to plasma and wait, and occasionally a repeat biopsy is needed.

According to this HCP, the payer in their region only authorizes NGS once the diagnosis is confirmed, so there's a lag before testing even begins. Not sure if that is policy or just paperwork, but approvals do usually come through.

Explained that a negative plasma result doesn't mean negative, so with never-smokers they follow up with tissue as a matter of routine. Seems comfortable with that, the workflow is clear to the whole team.

A rural clinic physician noted samples go to an outside reference lab and the wait is probably a week or two. He only starts osi early if the patient is very symptomatic, otherwise he waits for the report.
Felt the in-house NGS panel has been a real upgrade, with turnaround under a week or so, he thinks. Tumor board now sees the EGFR status before anyone discusses osimertinib or chemo combinations.

Described inconsistent lab reporting of exon 19 deletions versus rarer variants. Uncommon mutations sometimes come back as 'variant of unknown significance', which leaves him unsure whether osimertinib applies. He would like clearer, more standard reports.
Said at their larger center they run tissue and plasma in parallel for advanced cases, mostly to save time before starting the TKI. Cost is a minor concern but nobody pushes back.

Said reflex testing is inconsistent across their network. Some pathologists automatically order EGFR, ALK and the rest of the panel on any lung adenocarcinoma, while others wait for the oncologist to request it. He recalled a couple of patients who began chemo-immunotherapy because the molecular result hadn't come back and nobody chased it. He thinks that's a systems problem rather than a lab quality one. Would love a hard-wired order set, but IT apparently moves slowly.

She reported that since adding plasma alongside tissue, most of her newly diagnosed stage IV patients have a result in time for the first treatment visit. For FLAURA2-style discussions she likes knowing the exact alteration up front, since she would be deciding about platinum-pemetrexed with osimertinib. She still sends tissue when plasma is negative. Overall she called the workflow smooth and credited the nurses who coordinate the samples.

Talked about liquid biopsy sensitivity and said he trusts a positive but not a negative. Brain-only or low-shedding disease is where he thinks plasma misses things, so for those he insists on tissue even if it delays things a bit. Not sure how colleagues handle this. He also retests with plasma first at progression because repeat biopsies are hard on frail patients

Raised concern about variability between labs: one reports EGFR by a quick hotspot PCR, another by a large NGS panel, and results don't always line up on rarer variants. He has seen discordant reports on the same patient, probably from different sample sites or tumor content. Hard to know which to trust. He didn't think this gets discussed enough.

Described her private practice workflow: IR does the biopsy, pathology confirms, then she orders molecular herself because the lab doesn't reflex. It usually takes around two weeks, which she considers acceptable but not great. Patients get anxious waiting. She would consider osimertinib upfront if results arrived earlier, otherwise she just waits.

Said tissue quantity is the main bottleneck, especially after EBUS samples. Cytology cell blocks sometimes fail QC and then he needs plasma, which adds days. He mentioned a patient who deteriorated while waiting and ended up in hospital. Honestly, he said, the delay bothers him more than anything about the drug itself.

biomarker|pembrolizumab.t: Tissue only for us; liquid biopsy is rare, mostly when tissue is exhausted.
CPS results often land after the first visit, which is too late.
Reflex PD-L1 on every new lung biopsy now, ahead of pembro planning. Works well.
No reflex HER2 on gastric biopsies so we still have to ask for it
Community practice sends everything out, so turnaround depends on the reference lab.
Pathology here reads CPS the same way most weeks, no real complaints.
Their gastric patients usually start chemo before CPS is back, which makes the pembro decision awkward. The send-out takes more than a week, I think. Surgeons don't want to wait either.

Small community group orders PD-L1 and EGFR/ALK together on lung specimens, but neoadjuvant biopsies are often too small. Then they either re-biopsy or work with what they have. Not sure how often it actually delays things.

Thoracic clinic with a molecular tumor board gets the full panel back before the first neoadjuvant cycle in most cases. They like that NGS and PD-L1 come off the same block. Pembrolizumab planning feels straightforward there.
Worried about CPS variability near the low cutoff. Different pathologists in their group have called the same borderline slide differently. Not sure how often that changes who gets pembro.
They use liquid biopsy for lung when tissue is scarce, mostly for EGFR. A negative plasma result isn't trusted though, so they usually push for tissue anyway and dont bother with it in gastric.
MMR/MSI testing in gastric isn't reflexed. It only gets ordered when someone remembers, sometimes after the first cycle, and the result is recieved late by then.

Gastric surgeon-oncologist at a large hospital says pathology now runs HER2 and PD-L1 together on every new gastric biopsy. Turnaround is a few days, which fits the pre-treatment visit. Happy with how it runs.
Payer prior auth in their clinic wants the PD-L1 report attached, so a missing report delays the pembro start. Otherwise the testing side is fine.

Rural oncology clinic sends all biomarker testing to an outside reference lab. Blocks go by courier and reports can take over a week, longer if the block needs recutting. Symptomatic gastric patients can't wait, so chemo starts first. Pembrolizumab gets added later only if CPS comes back supportive, I think. They find the whole process frustrating.

Lung oncologist described a mixed picture. EGFR, ALK and PD-L1 are reflexed automatically for stage IV, but for resectable disease it's inconsistent and depends on who did the biopsy. Bronchoscopy samples usually get the full set, while outside imaging-guided cores often don't. They end up calling pathology to add stains before perioperative pembro. Probably a process gap more than a lab problem.

Medical oncologist at a mid-size hospital finds liquid biopsy a useful add-on in lung when the core is thin. Plasma results come back faster than tissue NGS. Tissue is still the main source and PD-L1 needs it anyway. Overall they're happy with the combination because there are fewer repeat procedures.

Pathology-minded HCP said CPS in gastric is harder to score than PD-L1 in lung, mainly because of counting immune cells in small endoscopic fragments. Heterogeneous samples mean the result can depend on which piece was cut. They think different readers and assays probably give inconsistent calls, though they had no numbers. Concerned some patients get missed.

GI tumor board has a standing order set so HER2, MMR/MSI and PD-L1 CPS get requested at diagnosis. Turnaround is about a week, which they consider acceptable. Gaps show up when the biopsy was done at an outside facility, since slides have to be requested and sometimes testing repeated. Claudin 18.2 was added recently but not on every case.

Nurse navigator at a lung clinic tracks every biomarker result on a shared sheet, so nothing is missing at the pre-op visit. Results are normally back before neoadjuvant start. The team feels confident choosing the pembrolizumab regimen because the PD-L1 and driver mutation results are already in the chart. Said it took some setup but it's been smooth.
CPS scoring depends way too much on which pathologist reads it.
Reflex testing? Not here, we still have to ask for everything separately.
Tissue first, always; plasma only if the biopsy is a bust.
Our in-house NGS turnaround is finally decent, honestly.
Waiting on EGFR and ALK results delays the neoadjuvant start sometimes, but we live with it.
Liquid biopsy for gastric: not convinced yet, still mostly tissue.

We order HER2 and MMR upfront on gastric biopsies, but PD-L1 CPS gets added later, usually after the first MDT. I think that's just habit. Not sure it changes much for pembro decisions in HER2-positive disease, but the sequencing is messy.
Community practice, so everything goes out to a reference lab. Results trickle back in pieces over a couple of weeks, and by then the patient is staged and wants to start pembrolizumab. Frustrating.

For resectable lung we set up a pathway where the pathologist reflexes PD-L1 TPS plus the driver panel on every new NSCLC biopsy. Took some arguing with admin, but it works now. Surgeons like knowing before tumor board.
EBUS samples are often scant, so we sometimes run out of tissue after PD-L1. Then it's a rebiopsy or plasma, and I don't fully trust plasma negatives. Probably a case-by-case call.

Payer wants prior auth for the broader NGS panel, which adds days we don't have in the perioperative setting. I end up ordering single-gene tests just to get things moving before pembro. Makes no sense scientifically.
Honestly the 22C3 CPS read in our gastric patients has been consistent when the same two pathologists do it. We double-read the borderline ones. Helps me feel okay about using pembro near the cutoff.
Plasma saved us on a frail patient who couldn't tolerate another biopsy, so I'll give it credit. I still treat it as supportive, not a replacement.

Nobody agrees on what counts as tumor cells versus immune cells in CPS, and I'm tired of pretending it's objective. Two reads, two answers on the same slide. Then we're deciding on pembrolizumab eligibility off that.

Biggest gap for us is that nothing is triggered automatically. A gastric adenoCA biopsy comes in, the pathologist does H&E and maybe HER2, and then someone has to remember to request PD-L1 and MMR. Half the time that someone is me, a week later. By then the block is back in storage and we wait again. We lose a good chunk of time on paperwork, not on the assays.

In our lung clinic we do tissue for PD-L1 and the driver genes, and I'm fairly firm on that. Plasma gets used if tissue fails, and I know some colleagues lean on it earlier, not sure that's wise for patients headed to surgery. NGS turnaround is the sticking point; sometimes the OR slot is booked before the report lands. A few times we started chemo-immunotherapy while waiting, which makes me uneasy if an EGFR alteration turns up later.

Since we moved to a single combined order set on the biopsy, things got much smoother. Gastric patients get HER2, MMR and PD-L1 CPS ordered together. Results are usually back before the first oncology visit, which is a first for us. I was skeptical it would hold up and there are still odd weeks, but I wouldn't go back. Pembro conversations are easier with the numbers in hand.

I don't trust PD-L1 numbers as much as people pretend. Different antibodies, different labs, different cutoffs on the report, and sometimes the report doesn't even say which assay was used. For a patient near the threshold I end up second-guessing everything. Pembrolizumab access can hinge on that single number. Rant over.

Small-town practice, so most testing is sent out. Gastric tissue goes for HER2 and MSI, and I've started asking for Claudin 18.2 too, though I'm unsure how it fits with checkpoint therapy sequencing. Turnaround is all over the place, sometimes quick, sometimes forever (dont quote me). Liquid biopsy is an option for the sicker ones but we rarely get to it.

Perioperative lung is where this hurts most. Patient comes in with a mass, the biopsy is tiny, PD-L1 uses up most of it and the NGS fails for insufficient tissue. Then we're begging for another sample or sending plasma while the surgeon asks why we're not moving. I get that KEYNOTE-671 context doesn't hinge on every biomarker, but I can't safely skip driver testing. Teh system just isn't built for speed.

We went through the whole workflow for new gastric adenocarcinoma, and what came across was that HER2, MMR and PD-L1 CPS are all requested but rarely at the same moment. The pathologist said the biopsies are small, so by the time HER2 is finished there is sometimes little tissue left for the rest. Pembrolizumab decisions then end up waiting on CPS, which I think is the step that gets bumped. He didn't see it as a disaster, more a sequencing annoyance that adds days.
CPS reads differ between our pathologists, honestly.
Reflex testing for lung went in about a year ago and it has made a real difference. EGFR and ALK are now back before the neoadjuvant pembrolizumab discussion at tumor board, so nobody is guessing.

She was frustrated about community referrals. Biopsies arrive from outside hospitals with a diagnosis and no biomarker orders, and then someone has to chase the block. For resectable lung patients that chase eats into the pre-surgery window, and she worries some people start chemo-immunotherapy before EGFR/ALK is back. Not sure how often it happens but she has seen it more than once. Pembro is only part of it, the real gap is that nobody owns the ordering
Tissue first, liquid only if the block is inadequate.
Said ctDNA is useful when the biopsy is scanty, but he doesn't trust a negative result in the perioperative setting. He would still re-biopsy if feasible.

Turnaround for send-out NGS is the pain point, usually a couple of weeks. Surgeons won't wait that long for stage II-III disease, so they operate first and the molecular results arrive afterwards, sometimes after pembro has already been planned.
In-house IHC means PD-L1 is back within a couple of days.

Long chat about gastric scoring. She feels CPS is harder than TPS because you have to count tumor and immune cells and decide what counts, particularly in tissue with a lot of inflammation or necrosis. Inter-observer differences matter most near the cutoff, and I think she would welcome a second read for borderline cases. She wouldn't hold back pembrolizumab on a single borderline read if everything else supports it, but she wants the consensus documented.
Nobody reflexes MMR on gastric biopsies here; we ask later.

Pleased that the lab bundles HER2, MMR and PD-L1 on every new gastric biopsy as one order set. Oncologists get a single report, and she said the first-line pembrolizumab conversation is much cleaner for it.

Payer friction came up again. For liquid biopsy, prior authorization is inconsistent, so patients are sometimes denied when tissue is insufficient and a repeat endoscopy becomes the only route. He said older gastric patients with poor performance status suffer most from this. By the time approval or the repeat procedure comes through, treatment has often started on partial information. He thinks it's a systems problem rather than anyone's fault.

Rural clinic, so everything is sent out. She is fine with the send-out turnaround as long as PD-L1 is flagged urgent, but its not always flagged, and then nobody knows the result until the visit when the PD-1 start is discussed.

He felt the testing landscape has improved a lot for lung. In his practice the pathology team routinely runs PD-L1 TPS together with the molecular panel on the diagnostic biopsy, so by the first oncology visit the results are generally there. That lets him discuss perioperative pembrolizumab knowing EGFR and ALK are negative. He still worries about very small biopsies, but said that is rare. Overall he is happy with the process.
Main failure point is tissue quantity, not the assay.
Asked whether liquid biopsy has a role pre-surgery, she said probably not routinely and she would want clear guidance first. Right now it's an add-on when tissue fails.
Pathology reports often just say 'PD-L1 positive' without the actual CPS number, which is useless for deciding anything. I think it's a template problem, and she has to call the lab to get teh score.
Appreciated that the molecular tumor board reviews discordant PD-L1 results together before pembro is started. It cuts down on arguments and gives her more confidence in the cutoff-based decision.

Discussion on repeat testing. He said he occasionally re-tests PD-L1 on a resection specimen versus the biopsy because heterogeneity in gastric tumors is real, but he isn't sure it changes anything once perioperative therapy is planned. Different blocks can give different scores, which he thinks is probably down to sampling. He would rather test the best block once and carefully than run several. Reimbursement for repeats is also unclear, so it's rarely done.
Honestly, timing of HER2 and PD-L1 results matters more than which assay.
CPS read varies by path; HCP re-sends borderline cases for 2nd opinion.
No reflex EGFR/ALK ordering at community site yet.
In-house NGS panel = results back before tumor board. Very happy.
Liquid bx only when tissue insufficient, HCP still cautious on negatives.
Turnaround for PD-L1 is a few days, no issue delaying pembro neoadjuvant start.
Payer PA keeps stallng send-out NGS orders.
Academic thoracic clinic now runs reflex PD-L1 plus EGFR/ALK on every new NSCLC biopsy. Pt hits tumor board with everything in hand. HCP said this made periop pembro decisions much smoother.
Gastric pts often get tiny endoscopic biopsies, so tissue runs out after HER2 and IHC. HCP thinks CPS gets skipped or delayed in a good chunk of cases. Not sure who owns the re-biopsy request.
MMR IHC upfront in all gastric per HCP, MSI by PCR only if IHC equivocal. Likes the speed for pembro eligibility. Says CPS is still the bottleneck bc of send-out.

TAT for send-out comprehensive panel too long for resectable lung pts, surgery gets scheduled first. Sometimes pt starts tx w/o full molecular and pembro gets added after. Accepts that if PD-L1 is at least back.
Community onc, I think they use plasma ctDNA when pt too frail for repeat bx. Probably fine for EGFR but HCP unsure how to read a negative in the periop setting.
Since path group did an internal concordance review, HCP feels CPS reads are more consistent. Fewer discordant calls at tumor board. Still sends truly borderline ones out.
Claudin 18.2 and HER2 both needed in 1L gastric but ordering is piecemeal. Surgeon sends one, med onc adds the rest later and pt waits. HCP calls it a workflow mess.
Different antibody clones for lung PD-L1 TPS across labs bug HCP a bit, not sure it changes tx though. Mostly just goes with the report as written.

Rural practice, no on-site path. Blocks shipped to reference lab so PD-L1 and molecular come back at different times. HCP said stage III lung pts often seen before results land, then visit #2 needed. Reflex EGFR/ALK not set up, nurse has to remember to order. Thinks some pts probably slip through without it.
