Large GI program, HCP very happy w/ current setup. Biopsy at endoscopy triggers reflex HER2, MMR and PD-L1 CPS on one requisition. Results usually in hand by first med onc visit. Tumor board reviews slides together when CPS is near cutoff. Says pembro eligibility talks are way faster than before.

Tissue vs liquid: HCP split. For lung periop, tissue first always since PD-L1 can't come from plasma. Would use ctDNA for driver check if tissue exhausted, though sensitivity worries remain. Gastric ctDNA seems less established so rarely ordered. Payer coverage for plasma inconsistent.

Scoring variability is the main gripe. HCP had a gastric pt whose CPS differed between bx and resection, which changed the pembrolizumab conversation. Also worries small bx misses tumor heterogeneity. Not sure what to do besides repeat sampling. Feels path reports dont always say which cells were counted.

Surgical onc perspective. Wants PD-L1 and EGFR/ALK back before choosing neoadjuvant chemo-IO but doesn't want to lose the OR slot. Usually waits a few days and accepts it. If result is late, pt probably starts chemo and they sort out IO after. Thinks a clear TAT target would help.

Reflex gaps mostly in gastric, honestly. HCP said MMR/MSI often not run on initial bx, only added after pt progresses. By then tissue is gone. A MSI-H pt would have had a different tx path. HCP thinks path labs need a standing order.
CPS read differs between our two pathologists more often than I'd like.
Liquid biopsy only when tissue is insufficient, per this oncologist.
Reflex PD-L1 and HER2 on every new gastric biopsy; pembro talk starts sooner.
Waiting on send-out NGS again, nearly three weeks.
Pembro decision waits for EGFR/ALK results, otherwise no real delay.
No reflex MMR at their community site so it gets ordered ad hoc if someone remembers

Small community oncology practice told me their lab now runs PD-L1 and MMR together on all gastric biopsies. Results are usually back within a few days, so the first-line plan is set by the first visit. Pembrolizumab discussion happens with the data in hand.

Academic thoracic clinic orders EGFR and ALK on the diagnostic biopsy when there is enough tissue. Not sure that's consistent across proceduralists. For perioperative pembro they said it mostly doesn't hold up treatment.

Gastric biopsies from endoscopy are often tiny, and HER2, CPS and MMR all compete for alot of the same few blocks. The pathologist said they sometimes have to prioritize one. Re-biopsy is rarely offered.
Community oncologist uses a ctDNA panel when the patient is too frail for repeat endoscopy. Finds it helpful but doesn't trust a negative result. Tissue is still the default.

Payer at their clinic wants documented PD-L1 before approving pembrolizumab in gastric, which adds a few days when the result is stuck at an outside lab. They said it's the lab handoff, not the test itself, that slows things down.
Hospital-based GI group has an in-house IHC platform, so CPS comes back quickly. They like that the same two pathologists read every case. Pretty happy with it overall.
Said claudin 18.2 is being added to the gastric panel, but only some patients get it depending on who's covering that day. Seems like a workflow issue more than a lab issue.
Surgeon sends specimens to a reference lab and nobody tracks them. Sometimes the team only learns at tumor board that HER2 never got run.

Thoracic oncologist at a regional hospital said the biggest gap is that EBUS samples are often scant and the lab uses most of it for diagnosis. Reflex EGFR and ALK isn't automatic there, so someone has to remember to request it. Last month a patient was almost scheduled for neoadjuvant pembro plus chemo before a driver alteration came back. They added a checklist, but I think uptake is patchy. Liquid biopsy is occasionally used as a backup, though turnaround isn't fast either.

Large cancer center lab runs reflex testing for gastric: HER2, MMR and PD-L1 CPS from the same biopsy at diagnosis. The oncologist said the report arrives as one combined summary, which makes tumor board straightforward. Turnaround is typically about a week, which they consider acceptable. Pembrolizumab eligibility gets discussed at the first visit rather than a second appointment. Main remaining issue is the occasional borderline CPS near the cutoff.

Private practice oncologist orders tissue first and liquid biopsy only if tissue fails. For perioperative lung they said tissue matters more because early-stage disease probably sheds little ctDNA, I think. Gastric is different since many patients present with advanced disease and plasma sometimes picks up HER2 changes. Still, they don't treat a plasma result as final. Coverage for liquid testing varies and they aren't sure what's reimbursed.

Told me scoring is what worries her most. For PD-L1 in gastric, CPS near the cutoff gets read differently depending on who is at the scope, and she has seen a repeat stain change the call. Different antibody assays at outside labs make it worse. She definately wants to know which lab scored the slide before relying on it for pembro. Not sure how other clinics handle this.

Medical oncologist at a rural satellite clinic: tissue goes to a central lab, so turnaround is typically over a week. For gastric they start chemo while waiting and add pembro once PD-L1 is back if appropriate. For lung they would rather wait for molecular results before neoadjuvant therapy. Said it's a tradeoff but a manageable one.

Pathology lead at a mid-size hospital described a recent change: lung biopsy and resection specimens now get PD-L1, EGFR and ALK ordered automatically at accessioning. Before, the oncologist had to request each one and some got missed. Now results are usually in before the multidisciplinary meeting. For perioperative pembrolizumab planning that means fewer surprises. They still send ctDNA only in rare cases.

biomarker|sacituzumab govitecan.t: Community practice here sends HER2 IHC out; results usually back within a week.
Nobody reflexes HER2-low scoring unless we ask for it specifically.
Their in-house NGS panel has been quick enough for sacituzumab planning.
Liquid biopsy keeps coming back with not enough ctDNA in low-burden patients. Frustrating.
Honestly TROP2 testing isn't on anyone's radar, SG gets chosen on clinical grounds.
Pathology reports now spell out HER2 0 versus low, which helps a lot.

At the academic center, breast pathology does reflex HER2 IHC with a low versus zero call on every HR+ biopsy. That makes the post-endocrine conversation about sacituzumab much easier because the score is already in the chart.

Urothelial patients in this community clinic mostly get NGS on the TURBT specimen, tissue only. Turnaround is about two to three weeks I think, so by the time results land some have already started platinum.

Rural oncologist said archived tissue from the original primary is often years old and sometimes used up. Re-biopsy of a bone-only met is hard, so they end up guessing on HER2 status before even considering sacituzumab.
Practice uses ctDNA when tissue is insufficient, mostly for ESR1. Not sure it changes sequencing before an ADC, probably more relevant for oral options.
Prior auth at this infusion center sometimes stalls waiting on the biomarker report. Two patients last quarter waited extra days just for a pathology addendum.
Medical oncologist was pleased the reference lab report now lists the HER2 IHC category plainly ahead of SG discussions. Fewer calls back to pathology, he said.
Pathologist at a small hospital admitted HER2-low reads at the 0 and 1+ boundary can differ between colleagues. They may send borderline cases out for a second look, but that adds time.
Mixed feelings on liquid biopsy at this practice. Convenient for frail urothelial patients, but the team still trusts tissue first and only uses blood when the sample fails.

Oncology nurse navigator at a large community clinic described the biomarker workflow as scattered. Breast cases go to one reference lab and bladder cases to another, each with its own requisition. Reflex testing exists on paper but rarely triggers for metastatic recurrences, so someone has to remember to re-request HER2. She thinks a few patients reached later lines, even before sacituzumab, without an updated result. Turnaround is variable, sometimes under a week, sometimes closer to three.

Breast tumor board at a regional cancer center now requires an updated HER2 IHC on any new metastatic biopsy. They said the habit took a few months to build but it's routine now. Results usually return in under a week, which fits the visit schedule. When a patient progresses on CDK4/6 plus endocrine therapy, the team already knows HER2-low status and can discuss sacituzumab govitecan versus other chemo without waiting. Overall pretty satisfied.

Urologic oncologist explained that for advanced urothelial they order FGFR3 testing early, mostly through NGS on tissue. Blood-based testing is used if the TURBT block is too small. He's not sure how a TROP2-directed agent would fit into any testing algorithm since no biomarker is required. Wait times are the main complaint, probably two weeks or a bit more. He would not delay therapy for a result.

Pathology lead said HER2 IHC scoring variability is the thing keeping her up. Different labs apply the 1+ cutoff differently, and fixation or cold ischemia time on outside blocks muddies it. Patients arrive with outside reports she can't verify. Repeating the stain is possible but eats time and tissue. In her view a HER2-zero versus low label from a poor sample isn't reliable, and that matters for any ADC discussion.

Private practice breast oncologist orders tissue HER2 on every new metastatic biopsy but rarely sends liquid. Says ctDNA is reserved for ESR1 and only when the bone biopsy fails. Coverage is inconsistent and sometimes the lab bills the patient. With SG he mostly relies on the clinical picture after endocrine and CDK4/6 failure, so testing doesnt drive the choice much.

Fellow at a teaching hospital noted that reflex NGS for bladder cancer isn't set up, so it depends on the attending remembering. The last few cases she saw had results back only after first-line was underway. Tissue from TURBT is often thin. She felt gaps like this make an informed sequencing talk hard, including about sacituzumab later on
Still no TROP2 test anywhere in our workflow, and nobody is asking for one.
Reflex NGS doesn't happen for urothelial unless someone remembers to tick the box.
Liquid biopsy turnaround has made SG planning easier for our frail patients.
HER2 0 versus low calls still feel like a coin toss honestly
Tissue first, always; ctDNA only when the block is exhausted.
Send-out NGS takes weeks and the patient is often progressing by then.

Our breast pathologists will re-read borderline HER2 IHC when oncology asks, and that has been really helpful. For sacituzumab it matters less since HER2 status doesn't gate use, but they like having the full picture documented before choosing the next line.

In our community practice we order ER/PR/HER2 on the metastatic biopsy if it's feasible, but many times we just rely on the primary's results. I think we probably should rebiopsy more often. Getting IR scheduled is the real bottleneck.
The outside lab reports HER2 as equivocal and then the ISH comes back a week later so the whole decision just sits there. Frustrating when the patient is symptomatic

For urothelial we send FGFR3 testing early now because the order of options depends on it. Where Trodelvy fits relative to that is something we sort out case by case, and I'm not sure there's a consensus.

Having the in-house NGS panel with a short turnaround has made it much easier to line up options in advance. I think we're ahead of most nearby practices on that, and the team likes not waiting on send-outs, especially when we're planning Trodelvy sequencing.

Payer prior auth sometimes asks for biomarker documentation even when none is required for the drug, which confuses the staff. We end up attaching pathology reports that don't really answer the question, and it mostly just costs time.
Liquid biopsy gets used here when tissue is thin, like bone-only mets. I'm not convinced it picks up everything though, so a negative result doesn't settle anything for me.
Our pathologists don't all agree on HER2-low cutoffs, and I've seen the same slide scored differently across two reads. It makes me hesitant to lean on those categories when talking to patients.

After a long talk through their workflow, the physician described a split system. Breast cases get ER, PR and HER2 on the new biopsy, plus an NGS panel when targeted options are in play. Urothelial cases mostly get nothing beyond the original TURBT pathology, partly habit and partly because options felt limited until recently. They'd like a reflex panel at diagnosis of metastatic disease, but the lab says that needs a protocol change and nobody seems to own it. For sacituzumab govitecan there's no biomarker selection, so testing doesn't hold up a start.

The HCP kept coming back to HER2 IHC scoring. Their view is that the 0 versus 1+ boundary is where things go wrong, because faint membranous staining gets read very differently by different pathologists, and reports rarely say how confident the read was. One patient had been called HER2 0 at one site and low at another within a few months. It doesn't change sacituzumab eligibility, but it muddies how they discuss ADC sequencing overall. I got the sense they're tired of the ambiguity.

This oncologist was upbeat about their setup. Pathology automatically runs ER, PR and HER2 and sends NGS on every new metastatic breast sample, so results are usually back by the first or second follow-up. They use a plasma assay when a biopsy isn't tolerable and found it good enough to guide the conversation, if not always decisive. For Trodelvy in HR+/HER2- disease after endocrine and CDK4/6 therapy, the testing is already done by the time they need to choose. They said that's probably why treatment planning feels calm.

Most urothelial specimens here come from TURBT with small, fragmented tissue, so there's often not enough left for NGS after histology. They then consider liquid biopsy, but I think they doubt it in bladder cancer since shedding seems variable. They'd order both in parallel if payers allowed it. Meanwhile, decisions about enfortumab or sacituzumab don't depend on a marker, so testing mostly serves trial screening and FGFR3.

They told me flatly that turnaround is the biggest issue. Tissue send-outs for NGS take what feels like weeks, and when the sample is insufficient they only find out at the end. Reflex testing isn't set up, so the order depends on whoever sees the patient first, and sometimes nobody does. Last month a patient with rapid progression on endocrine therapy started chemo before any genomic result was recieved, which the team saw as a missed chance to line up options. Not sure sacituzumab would have changed anything, but the delay bothered them.

A thoughtful, fairly positive conversation. They treat tissue and liquid biopsy as complementary: tissue for the baseline ER, PR and HER2 picture, plasma at progression when rebiopsy is risky or slow. Their lab turns around both quickly enough that results usually inform the next visit. They said that clarity makes it easier to discuss sacituzumab govitecan alongside other options without feeling rushed. I think the main thing they'd still like is more consistent HER2 scoring across readers, but they called it a manageable problem.
Nobody here reflexes anything; we order every test by hand and it slips.
TROP2 staining isn't required for SG, so honestly I don't test it.
HER2 0 versus 1+ is a coin flip depending on which pathologist reads it.
Liquid biopsy has saved us weeks when the tissue was exhausted.
Send-out NGS turnaround is all over the place, sometimes a week, sometimes a month.
Tissue first, ctDNA only if the block is gone, thats our rule.

Our community site sends everything out, and the report often lands after the patient has already started the next line. I get that it's a logistics thing, but it makes the exercise feel pointless for sequencing decisions around SG.

Our academic center runs in-house NGS on every metastatic breast biopsy at progression, and results usually come back within about ten days. That lets me plan the next line before the patient crashes. I wish every clinic had it.

In urothelial, FGFR3 and HER2 testing happens inconsistently, probably because nobody owns the order. When I do get results they rarely change what I'd do before SG, so I'm lukewarm on the whole panel.
Prior auth for NGS is a nightmare. We often wait longer on the payer than the lab takes to run the thing, and the patient just sits there.
I think ctDNA is fine for ESR1 but I dont trust a negative in a low shedder. If it comes back negative I still go back for tissue, which adds delay.

The pathology group here changed how they report HER2-low and suddenly a bunch of patients I'd called 0 are now 1+. Not sure which version is right. Makes any HER2-directed conversation before SG feel shaky.
Adding reflex HER2 IHC to the ER/PR on every new breast biopsy was a good fix here. We stopped missing the low expressers. Pretty happy with that, though recuts on old blocks still lag.
Bone-only mets are the usual headache. Decalcified tissue gives garbage biomarker results, so we lean on liquid biopsy, which works okay but not perfectly. Either way it slows things down.

Reflex testing is where we lose people. ER/PR/HER2 gets done on the primary, but nobody repeats it on the metastatic biopsy unless I ask. NGS is then a separate order, a separate form, sometimes a separate lab. By the time it all lines up, the patient has often progressed again. For SG it matters less, honestly, but it's the same broken process for everything else.

We're a mid-size community practice and mostly use tissue NGS when there's enough sample. When there isn't, we send a liquid assay, though I'm never sure how to read a negative. Turnaround on the blood test is faster, usually under two weeks, while the tissue one drags. I don't think either changes my SG decision much but they affect what I give before it

The HER2 0 versus 1+ line drives me nuts. Same slide, two pathologists, two answers, and I've seen it happen. Some patients were called 0 on the primary and 1+ on a later biopsy, and I can't tell if that's biology or reader noise. The scoring guidance is supposed to help, but I don't think anyone is calibrated for the faint-staining cases. It makes any HER2-low discussion feel shaky well before we get to SG.

Our new workflow is genuinely better. Pathology now holds extra unstained slides at the time of biopsy, so if we need NGS later we don't have to chase blocks. Turnaround for the in-house panel is mostly under two weeks. I also get liquid biopsy back quickly when tissue fails. Fewer patients are waiting around, and that's helped how I plan sequencing around SG.

In urothelial, biomarker testing is an afterthought at most places I see. FGFR3 gets ordered late if at all, and HER2 IHC is hardly standardized. Urologists often send the TURBT sample to a general lab that doesn't do molecular work, so the tissue is stuck there. Then I'm told there's not enough tumor left. I'm skeptical this gets fixed soon, and it limits how we sequence after platinum and IO.

Honestly I'm fairly happy with ctDNA now. Ordering is simple, blood comes back in about a week, and for ESR1 it's been reliable in my hands. I still prefer tissue if there's a fresh biopsy, but for progressors who can't get another core it's a lifesaver. Probably I'm overselling it, but it has changed my workflow.
No TROP2 IHC ordered at their site; HCP says not needed for SG.
Reflex NGS not set up, pt tissue just sits in path unless onc asks.
ctDNA liquid bx now routine for 2L+ mBC at their clinic, happy w/ TAT.
HER2 0 vs 1+ calls differ pathologist to pathologist, super frustrating per HCP.
Honestly just waiting on FGFR3 result before deciding sequencing in mUC pt
Tumor board gets NGS back quickly, helps w/ sequencing decisions.
Community clinic, send-out NGS takes forever, around 3 wks sometimes. Pt often progressed or too sick by the time it's back. HCP said would have moved to SG sooner otherwise.

Academic HCP does tissue NGS at mUC dx, liquid only if tissue insufficient. Thinks ctDNA is probably less sensitive in low-shed tumors, not sure though. Uses both when the FGFR question is still open.

For HR+/HER2- pts post CDK4/6 + ET, HCP re-checks HER2 on new met bx, finds HER2-low label useful for tx planning. Path is in-house and scoring seems consistent in their experience. Good workflow overall.
Reflex gap: ER/PR/HER2 on met site not auto-ordered, onc has to request it. HCP admits it got misssed a few times. Not sure if its path's job or onc's.
PA for broad NGS panel is a hassle w/ some payers. HCP says SG decision usually doesn't wait on it since no companion dx needed. Mixed feelings on value of repeat testing.
Liquid bx a win for bone-only mets pts where no usable tissue. HCP said TAT typically under a week. Would use it more if covered.
HCP doesn't trust HER2 1+ vs 0 on old archival blocks, suspects fixation issues. Sometimes requests repeat bx, which delays tx start. Pt anxiety goes up while waiting.
Urology onc: PD-L1 rarely ordered now in UC, NGS mostly for FGFR3. Asked if any TROP2 expression assay is coming; I think the answer is no but HCP seemed curious.

Rural practice, no in-house molecular, everything is sent out. Tissue shipping alone eats several days, then the vendor TAT on top. HCP said by the time HER2 and NGS are back, pt's PS has sometimes dropped. Liquid bx would help but payer denials are common. Feels like testing logistics, not the drug, decide who gets tx in time.

HCP orders ER/PR/HER2 on every new met bx but only does NGS if pt is fit for later lines. Tissue is first choice, liquid as backup when bx is risky (liver lesion, anticoag). Scoring variability on HER2-low comes up at tumor board now and then, usually resolved by 2nd path read. Overall says process is OK, nothing dramatic, just slower than ideal.

Big cancer center, reflex NGS built into the path order set for mUC and mBC. HCP says results land before first follow-up visit, so sequencing talk w/ pt happens once. Liquid bx used when tissue fails QC, and TAT is short. SG discussion is easier since pt already has full biomarker picture. HCP called it a real advantage of being at a large center.

HCP worried about the lack of standardization across labs. Same tumor could be HER2 0 at one lab and 1+ at another, and that changes eligibility conversations. Reflex testing is inconsistent too, some pts get NGS at dx and others never do. Liquid bx results sometimes come back with no actionable finding, and the HCP isn't sure whether to trust a negative. Said it feels like a patchwork.

Mixed picture in mUC. Tissue NGS ordered at dx by most of the group, but a couple of HCPs only test at progression. TAT is acceptable, roughly 2 wks I think. Liquid bx is used occasionally, mostly if TURBT tissue is scant. HCP doesn't expect any biomarker to gate SG use right now, but would want one eventually.

HCP wishes there were a validated marker to pick SG pts, but fine w/o it for now. Currently orders HR/HER2 and germline testing early so nothing holds up 2L+ decisions. Tissue is default, liquid if the pt is frail. Said repeat HER2 on met is worth it even if scoring is a bit subjective. Not a major barrier in their practice.
No TROP2 testing here, just go off HR/HER2 from original path.
NGS turnaround is still painfully slow, patients progress while we wait.
Reflex HER2 IHC now automatic for every breast biopsy, huge help.
HER2-low vs 0 scoring is all over the place between pathologists
Liquid biopsy maybe for pts who cant be rebiopsied, not routine tho
Community group says send-out panels come back fast enough now for Trodelvy candidates.

Re-biopsy after progression on CDK4/6 is a hard sell in our older pts, esp with bone-only disease. So we're stuck with primary tissue from years ago and I'm not sure HER2 status hasn't shifted. Makes sacituzumab sequencing feel like guesswork.
Urothelial side, they mostly order FGFR3 on the TURBT sample before anyone thinks about ADCs. Sometimes tissue is scant and NGS fails, then liquid biopsy is plan B. Mixed results honestly.

Our breast tumor board now requests repeat HER2 IHC at metastatic recurrence as standard. Makes the Trodelvy conversation easier since everybody is looking at the same updated data. Pathology has been really responsive.
Prior auth people keep asking for a biomarker report even though there's no companion test for sacituzumab govitecan, which confuses my staff. Ends up delaying start by several days. Frustrating.

Honestly we send NGS to an outside lab for most mets and wait about two weeks, give or take. If pt is symptomatic we pick something quick for Trodelvy-or-chemo discussions and revisit once thier results land. Not sure that is optimal.
ctDNA assays miss alot in low shed tumors, so a negative result doesn't reassure me. We still prefer tissue when we can get it. Liquid is more of a backup.
PD-L1 in UC is checked at diagnosis, I think, but not always repeated later. For TROP2 nobody asks. Probably fine given how the drug is used?
Having HR and HER2 reflexed on every new breast specimen has cut the back-and-forth with pathology. I think we rarely chase missing results anymore. Smooth workflow in our hospital-based clinic.

Biggest gap for us is HER2-low calls. Two pathologists can read the same slide and one says 1+ and the other says 0, I've seen it happen a few times. That changes whether the patient is even considered for certain ADCs down the line. We don't have a good tiebreaker, maybe a second read but that adds days. Sacituzumab doesn't need it but the sequencing conversation does.

Community practice, three oncologists, no in-house molecular. Tissue goes out to a reference lab and results land in the portal, sometimes after the patient's already back for cycle 2. For liquid biopsy we use it when the biopsy is risky, like a liver lesion with ascites. Reflex testing is hit or miss, depends which pathologist is on that day. We're okay with it but it's not tight.

Pretty happy with our testing flow lately. Metastatic breast biopsy goes to path, HR/HER2 and HER2-low scoring get done together, and NGS is added automatically if there's enough tissue. Results usually back before the second visit. With sacituzumab govitecan in the picture post-endocrine and CDK4/6, I like knowing receptor status is current. Liquid is rarely needed for us.

Urothelial testing is a mess honestly. Many pts are diagnosed on small TURBT chips, so tissue often runs out before NGS. Reflex for FGFR isn't set up, someone has to remember to ask, and sometimes nobody does. By the time we realize, pt has started platinum. Then what comes next, including sacituzumab, gets muddier.

Not sure how much biomarker work matters for sacituzumab given no selection marker, tbh. We still order HER2 IHC and sometimes ISH on equivocal cases, and ISH adds like a week. Liquid biopsy we use for ESR1 mostly, so that's a different decision point. I think TROP2 IHC probably only comes up in research settings. Pts ask about it sometimes.

Rural clinic here, so everything is send-out and shipping alone eats a few days. We lean on tissue because liquid isn't well covered by some payers, or so the billing person says. When a pt has an old block from another facility, retrieving it takes forever. Mixed feelings about how this plays into starting sacituzumab on time. Probably better than it was a couple yrs ago though.

biomarker|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: Our path group still doesn't report 0 vs 1+ consistently, honestly.
Reflex testing? Half the time nobody orders it until oncology asks.
Tissue only for us. Liquid doesn't tell me anything about HER2-low.
IHC turnaround has improved, usually a few days now.
Send-out HER2 on bone mets takes forever and decal wrecks teh sample.
Still unsure how much ultralow should change what I order.

We're a community practice and everything gets sent out. By the time the IHC comes back the patient has often already started chemo or endocrine therapy, which defeats the point. Not sure who to blame, the lab or us.
I order IHC on the metastatic biopsy when feasible, but sometimes only a primary from years ago exists. Is that block even representative? I probably use it anyway if rebiopsy is risky.
Our pathologists now report 1+ and 2+ separately, and ISH reflexes automatically on 2+. That has made T-DXd eligibility discussions much quicker. Wish it had happened sooner.
Second reads on the same slide have disagreed on 0 versus 1+ more than I'd like. That's close to a coin flip deciding access to an ADC for some patients. Nobody seems to want to own the problem.

Tried ctDNA once for a patient with no accessible lesion. It came back with nothing useful on HER2 expression, so we went back to hunting for archival tissue. Maybe I misunderstood what the panel was meant for.
Payer wanted a documented IHC score before approving, and the report only said 'HER2 negative'. Had to chase pathology for an adendum, which cost us over a week. Typical.
With in-house IHC we get results in a couple of days. I like being able to review the slide at tumor board. It makes the low vs. 0 call feel less arbitrary.
I think most of my colleagues order HER2 only at first diagnosis and never repeat it. With HER2-low now mattering that habit probably needs to change though rebiopsy burden is real

Old HR+ cases in our system just say 'HER2 negative', so I can't tell 0 from 1+. Re-staining archival blocks takes weeks, and some blocks are gone or too small to bother with. For someone progressing on endocrine therapy, that delay is hard to justify when T-DXd might be an option. Patients ask me about it and I can't answer until the lab sorts itself out. Pretty frustrating.

At our academic site the workflow is decent. Any new metastatic breast biopsy gets IHC reflexed, with ISH on the 2+ cases, before the patient even sees me. Results usually land within a few days, so the T-DXd conversation can happen at the first visit. I'd still like a consistent 0 vs 1+ read, but compared with what I hear from colleagues elsewhere we're lucky.

I'm skeptical of liquid biopsy for HER2 status in this setting. ctDNA can pick up amplification in some HER2-positive cases, but for HER2-low it's IHC, full stop, as far as I know. I'll use blood when there's truly nothing to biopsy, mostly for other alterations. Tissue is still the answer for the T-DXd decision. Not thrilled about that for frail patients with bone-only disease.

The biggest change this year is that our lab added HER2-low and ultralow wording to the report template. Before, I had to call and ask. Now the score and the ISH result are right there, which saves a lot of back and forth. There's still some variation between readers, I think, but at least it's documented and I can discuss it with the pathologist.

Scoring faint membrane staining is where it gets messy. I've seen pathologists hedge between 0 and 1+ on the same case, and honestly I don't blame them, since the cutoff is subtle. Still, T-DXd access in HR+ disease can hinge on that call. I'd rather they be candid about uncertainty than force a number. But then what do I tell the patient?

We're a rural clinic, so blocks get shipped out and the round trip alone eats several days. I usually order IHC and NGS together to avoid a second request, though NGS won't give me HER2-low anyway. If the sample is inadequate we lose another week. Not sure there's a fix besides in-house testing, which isn't happening here.
Path report just says HER2 neg, no IHC score. Useless for low.
Tissue only here, liquid bx not really used for HER2.
Reflex IHC on all new breast cores now, big improvement.
Send-out ISH TAT painfully long, T-DXd start slips.
Asked about ultralow. HCP unsure if their lab even reports it.
0 vs 1+ call = coin flip depending on pathologist, per HCP.
Community onc, 3 docs. Path now reports 0 / 1+ / 2+ explicitly w/ ISH reflex for 2+, so pt eligibility for T-DXd is clear at first visit. HCP said this smoothed out tumor board prep too.
Liver met bx came back insufficient, no repeat done, so onc defaulted to the old primary's HER2 result. Probably misses pts whose status shifted, not sure how common. HCP was frustrated about it
Academic HCP orders NGS on mets for all HR+ pts but HER2 IHC is a separate order. NGS copy number doesn't help w/ low anyway. Two orders = occasional gaps.

Payer PA wants a documented IHC 1+ or 2+/ISH neg report, not just 'HER2 negative'. Some pts delayed about a wk while office chased old path reports. Nurse nav mostly eats the admin burden, but it does get done in the end.
ctDNA comes up for other markers, not HER2-low. HCP would like a blood option for pts w/ no safe lesion to biopsy but doesn't trust it for IHC-type calls.
Seeing fewer repeat bx lately, in-house IHC TAT is quick. HCP says T-DXd vs chemo can be decided at the same visit as scan review.
Pt w/ bone-only mets, decalcified bx, HER2 stain questionable. HCP unsure whether to trust a 0 there. Would rebiopsy if feasible, I think.

Rural clinic, everything is send-out. No reflex, so onc has to remember to request HER2 re-test on older blocks and it's often forgotten til progression. Results sometimes recieve late, after tx decision already made.

Big issue is inter-pathologist variability at the 0/1+ border. Same slide read differently by 2 pathologists at their center, which matters more now w/ ultralow in the conversation. Lab has no formal second-read process. HCP thinks some pts are probably getting missed, esp. w/ faint staining. Not sure who would standardize training.

HCP at large cancer center very happy w/ workflow. Breast path does reflex HER2 IHC on every invasive ca incl. HR+, reports the score even if 0 w/ a note on staining. Results usually in system before first onc visit. Borderline cases go to tumor board. T-DXd candidates get identified much earlier now, they said. Only gap is archived cases from before the policy.

Mixed bag. HCP orders tissue first always, liquid only if bx not feasible, and then mostly for other targets not HER2. In-house IHC TAT is ok, a few days, but ISH reflex adds time. Payer sometimes wants both reports. Workable overall but depends who is on path that week.

Reflex gaps are real. HCP looked at a handful of recent HR+ pts and several had HER2 'neg' on old reports w/ no score, so nobody knew if low. Recuts from archive took weeks for some. Meanwhile pt progresing on endocrine tx w/ CDK4/6 AEs piling up, wanted T-DXd option clarified sooner. Clearly annoyed.

Asked whether HER2 should be re-checked at each progression. Currently only retested if lesion is easy to biopsy. HCP thinks heterogeneity probably matters but not sure how much. Some pts may drift between 0 and low over time, just an impression. Would like tumor board consensus on when to rebiopsy.

Positive on how T-DXd data changed lab behavior. Path team now asks onc which score cutoffs matter and added ultralow to the report template. One pt w/ IHC 0 but faint staining got a re-read and moved to T-DXd after tumor board. HCP thinks awareness is up a lot. Still some variability but direction is good.

Long conversation with a community oncologist, and she kept returning to the HER2-low question as where things fall apart in her practice. Pathology reports often say 'HER2 negative' with no IHC score unless someone asks, so she ends up phoning the lab to find out whether there was a 1+. She suspects a good number of patients labeled negative years ago were never looked at again. The original blocks are sometimes at an outside facility, and she isn't sure how to get around that. Since T-DXd access hinges on that detail, she finds it really frustrating.
IHC 0 versus 1+ is basically a coin flip between pathologists here.
Reflex HER2 on every new breast biopsy now, and it works well.

Our tumor board re-reviews the IHC on any borderline case before a treatment decision. It adds a few days, but the oncologists seem fine with that trade-off. Probably worth it when trastuzumab deruxtecan is on the table.
Tissue first, always. Liquid biopsy only if the block is exhausted.

After a long chat, a breast medical oncologist was upbeat about testing at her center. HER2 IHC is reflexed on all invasive breast samples, and the score and ISH result sit together in one report. She says that makes the HER2-low conversation easy and she rarely has to call anyone. Turnaround is usually within the week, which fits her treatment-planning visits. She still thinks reader variability at the low end exists, but felt the lab's case volume helps. Overall she's keen to use T-DXd in more of her patients.
Insurance wanted a documented IHC 1+ or 2+/ISH-negative result before approving, and the old report just said negative. We lost close to two weeks chasing the original pathology.
Nobody in our group orders ctDNA for HER2 questions, honestly.
Since the lab added the HER2 score to a synoptic template, ordering decisions got much easier. I think most of the team now knows what a 1+ looks like on paper.

We talked a while about chemo-naive HER2-low and ultralow patients who have progressed on endocrine therapy. He said the hard part isn't the drug question but knowing what the original score really was, since older reports lack detail. He would probably re-test if tissue were accessible, though he's not sure the lab would run an old block. Blood-based testing doesn't help him here. I got the sense he's waiting for clearer direction on 0 versus ultralow. He did say his pathologists are open to discussing cases.
A breast surgeon at a small regional hospital said biopsies go to a reference lab, so turnaround depends on courier days. Sometimes results land after the first oncology visit.
She said recurrence biopsies often aren't repeated and people just lean on the primary's HER2 status. She worries this misses HER2-low conversion, but bone-only disease makes re-biopsy hard.
Turnaround is fine, about a week, no complaints.

Solo-ish community physician sends everything out to a reference lab. He said the wait can run long enough that patients start the next line of chemo before the HER2 answer arrives, and asking for a slide review makes it worse. He thinks that is probably the main reason T-DXd gets considered late. It's especially worrying for fast-moving visceral disease. He has no real fix on his side yet.
Pleased with how our lab handles ISH when IHC is 2+; its automatic and quick. No more asking for it seperately.

Reflex testing is inconsistent across the three sites he covers: one does it, one doesnt, and one only if you tick a box. He thinks HER2-low is getting missed in the advanced setting because of teh variation.

A pathologist told me scoring at the 0/1+ boundary is inherently subjective, especially with faint, incomplete membrane staining. They use a second reader on borderline cases and image analysis as a helper, though not everyone trusts it. In her view fixation time and cold ischemia matter as much as the read itself. She feels oncologists underestimate how much preanalytics can move a result. She's cautiously comfortable with their process but not complacent.
Still unsure whether ultralow is something we should be reporting separately.
He uses liquid biopsy mainly for PIK3CA and ESR1, not HER2, so for ADC decisions he still falls back on tissue. He'd welcome a blood-based option for HER2 but doesn't trust one yet.

Her practice is a mixed picture: tissue is the default, but after a failed core biopsy in a frail patient she tried a blood-based panel. It gave her useful information on other targets, though nothing she could use for HER2 scoring. She said the pathology group is responsive when she calls, which softens the delays. Reflex testing exists but she isn't sure it covers metastatic samples as well as primaries. I think she'd like a clearer standard before changing how she orders.
IHC 0 vs 1+ call still feels like a coin flip on some slides.
Reflex HER2 IHC on every new breast biopsy now, big help.
Mostly tissue, liquid biopsy only when the block is used up
Nobody reflexes HER2-low scoring on older metastatic samples, as far as I know.
Turnaround is the bottleneck, T-DXd start waits on pathology.
Send-out for ISH, about a week or so I think

Community practice with two oncologists. They order HER2 IHC on the primary and rarely repeat it at recurrence. If the primary was 0 they'd probably just move on to chemo, and I'm not sure they'd rebiopsy to look for low expression.

Their academic breast group has pathology doing reflex HER2 testing, with a low-range comment added to the report. The oncologist said that makes T-DXd conversations with HER2-low patients much more straightforward. Results usually come back in a few days.

Rural clinic sends every biopsy out, and the report often just says 'HER2 negative' with no HER2-low designation. The oncologist has to phone the lab to get the actual IHC score. For T-DXd candidates that adds delay they didn't expect.

This HCP uses liquid biopsy mainly for ESR1 and PIK3CA, not for HER2. Tissue is still their standard for HER2 status. They'd consider ctDNA for HER2 if tissue wasn't available but aren't sure it's reliable enough.

A pathologist at a small hospital admitted that 0 versus 1+ scoring varies between colleagues, and there's no formal second read. The oncologist worries some patients are being missed for trastuzumab deruxtecan because of that.

Tumor board reviews every HER2 result before systemic therapy planning. For hormone receptor-positive patients who have progressed on endocrine therapy, they now check whether the IHC was 1+ or 2+ with negative ISH before choosing the next line. They said T-DXd is part of that discussion earlier than before.

The nurse navigator tracks pending biomarker results on a spreadsheat. Send-outs typically take about a week, in-house is quicker. She says it depends a lot on whether the block request goes out promptly.
At their site payer prior auth asks for a documented IHC score, but the report often only says HER2 negative. They ask pathology to addend it, which takes a few days each time, but it does get done.

Private practice, three oncologists. HER2 was tested on the original primary years ago for most of their metastatic patients, and those reports predate the HER2-low concept. There's no process to go back and re-score archived blocks. One doctor said they'd consider it for a patient running out of options, but the lab is slow with block retrievals. I think a good chunk of their HER2-negative patients have never been checked for low expression, and so aren't being considered for T-DXd.

Large cancer center with in-house pathology. Reflex HER2 IHC runs on all new invasive breast cancers, and an equivocal 2+ goes to ISH automatically. The oncologist feels this part works well. It breaks down with metastatic biopsies from outside hospitals, where scoring is inconsistent and sometimes not reported. For those they usually repeat testing on a fresh sample if the patient is fit enough.

Oncologist said the last year changed how they talk about HER2 status. Pathology now reports the IHC score and ISH result separately, and the template flags HER2-low. She orders a biopsy at progression in most cases, mostly tissue, since liquid biopsy doesn't tell her HER2 expression. Results usually come back within the week. She's comfortable that eligibility questions for T-DXd can be answered quickly.

Hospital-based clinic described repeated problems with insufficient tissue from bone met core biopsies. Decalcification seems to hurt IHC quality, so they get a lot of non-evaluable results. They sometimes try liquid biopsy as a fallback, but it doesn't answer the HER2-low question. Patients end up waiting on a second biopsy, and a few have progressed in the meantime.

Not sure what the standard is, said the oncologist, but they probably send HER2 testing to the same reference lab every time. Turnaround has been acceptible, around a week I think. They haven't had to question a score yet. They'd only ask for a second opinion on a 1+ versus 0 if the patient was otherwise a strong candidate.

Smaller regional practice that recently switched to a lab offering rapid HER2 results. The oncologist said turnaround dropped to a few days, so treatment decisions no longer sit waiting. They test tissue first and keep liquid biopsy for monitoring only. Reports now give the IHC score as a plain number. He feels more confident picking out HER2-low patients who might benefit from T-DXd.
Reflex HER2 testing on every breast biopsy? Not here, honestly.
IHC 0 versus 1+ still feels like a coin flip to their pathologists.
Turnaround is down to a few days since they moved IHC in-house.
Liquid biopsy to find HER2-low for T-DXd? Nobody he knows orders it.
Mostly tissue, with a repeat biopsy if the old block is exhausted.
Send-out ISH takes forever and patients just sit there waitng for an answer.

In their community clinic the pathology group started reporting HER2 IHC with an explicit 0, 1+ or 2+ category on every invasive breast report. That made it much easier to spot HER2-low patients for T-DXd without chasing anyone. I think it's a real step forward.

Biggest gap, in her view, is older primary specimens where the original report just says negative and nobody went back to look at the 1+ or 2+ nuance. They'd probably have to re-cut blocks for a lot of metastatic patients, and that rarely happens.

Oncologists there order tissue first, almost always, and only think about circulating DNA when the biopsy is risky, like a bone-only lesion. Even then he's not sure it says anything useful about HER2-low or T-DXd candidacy.
Payer pre-auth for T-DXd sometimes asks for the exact IHC score, and a lot of reports just don't have it. Office staff then scramble to get an addendum from the lab, which adds days to the start.
Their tumor board reviews slides when the score is borderline, which they like, but it's not scalable. For routine cases they just accept the report as written.

Digital pathology with image analysis has helped with the 0 versus 1+ calls, I think, or at least made the readers feel more consistent. She said disagreement between pathologists comes up less often now.
Rural practice, so everything is sent out. Turnaround is fine for new diagnoses but frustrating at progression, when T-DXd decisions wait on a fresh biopsy result and the patient is symptomatic.

We spent a good while walking through how HER2 testing flows in their group. The surgeon sends the core to a central lab, which runs IHC and only does ISH on 2+ cases, but nothing about HER2-low is reported unless the oncologist writes it on the requisition. Most don't. So a patient labeled HER2-negative at diagnosis can quietly be HER2-low and nobody revisits it until progression. He thinks this is probably costing them eligible patients for T-DXd but couldn't say how many.

She was fairly upbeat about where testing is heading. Their lab now reflexes HER2 on all new invasive cancers and reports the full IHC category, and they re-test a metastatic biopsy when feasible because status can shift. IHC turnaround is usually a couple of days, which fits well with treatment planning. For HR-positive patients after endocrine therapy, having the score ready before the progression visit makes the T-DXd conversation easy. Her only complaint is the occasional equivocal ISH.

We went back and forth on tissue versus liquid. His view is that liquid biopsy is great for ESR1 and other genomic questions in HR-positive disease, but for HER2 expression it's the wrong tool, since it's protein-level and mostly an IHC question. He does worry about patients who can't be biopsied safely and isn't sure what he'd do for them. Overall he sticks with tissue and accepts the wait.

Scoring variability was the main theme. He described cases where two readers landed on opposite sides of the 0/1+ line, on a small core with heterogenous staining, so it was hard to say either was wrong. The ultra-low category makes it murkier still, and he doubts reproducibility at that edge. The consequence is real because that call can decide whether a patient is considered for T-DXd. Beyond second reads he sees no obvious fix in his lab.

Small hospital oncology group that uses a regional reference lab for all breast work. Typical wait is about a week, longer when ISH is needed, and they've sort of accepted it. They'd like reflex testing for HER2-low on every HR-positive metastatic recurrence, for T-DXd eligibility, but aren't sure the lab can or will do it. I think they're waiting to see if the lab changes anything on its own.

Very positive conversation with a breast-focused medical oncologist. Her pathology department built a standing workflow: every new metastatic or recurrent biopsy gets a repeat HER2 IHC regardless of what the primary showed. She said that picked up several HER2-low patients who had been written off as negative, and it changed how she thinks about sequencing T-DXd. Turnaround is predictable and results land in the chart as discrete fields. She'd like other sites to copy this but admitted it depends on a cooperative lab.
Mentioned that NGS panels get ordered a lot but HER2 expression isn't really captured there, so people sometimes assume its covered when it isn't. Probably a training issue.

competitor|osimertinib.t: Tumor board still defaults to osimertinib mono, chemo add-on case by case.
Rep keeps pushing the combo data, HCP is tired of it.
Says nothing else touches CNS control like osimertinib, at least in his pts.
Cross-trial comparisons = apples and oranges imo, wont switch on that alone.
Amivantamab combo: infusion burden, no way in a small community clinic.
Colleagues all on osi 1L, no real debate in group.
Onc in mid-size practice would consider lazertinib/ami for pts w/ brain mets, but PA headaches worry her. Probably sticks w/ whatever the payer approves fastest.
HCP thinks the FLAURA2 vs MARIPOSA cross-trial talk is overplayed by reps. Different pt populations, so can't really line them up. Wants head-to-head data before changing anything.
Older gen TKIs (gefitinib, erlotinib) basically gone from his clinic. Says osimertinib is better tolerated in his elderly pts, fewer tx breaks.
Tumor board split. Thoracic surgeon likes chemo add-on for high-burden dz, pulm just wants single agent. No consensus yet, so they go case by case.
Mentioned afatinib occasionally for uncommon mutations, otherwise osimertinib. Doesn't really see it as a competitor.
Rep visited 3x this month w/ the same slide deck and HCP feels it's noise. Would rather have a peer discussion. Not sure which agent the rep was even pushing by the end.

Community HCP worried about chemo add-on tox in frail pts. Compared w/ the amivantamab combo, she thinks both add AEs her limited nursing staff would have to manage. Many pts drive far for infusions. I think she stays on mono for most and only adds chemo for young pts w/ big tumor burden. Not convinced the extra PFS is worth it for everyone.

Academic HCP sees osi + chemo as a reasonable step up for pts w/ CNS dz at baseline. Prefers it over moving to a bispecific combo, mainly because the AEs are familiar. Says tumor board generally agrees, though a couple of colleagues remain skeptical. Still wants longer OS follow-up before calling it standard for all.

HCP says the tumor board talks about the alternatives every few weeks. Surgeons lean toward intensification, med onc folks more cautious. Pharmacy keeps raising cost and chair time. Overall they stay with osimertinib mono unless pt is high-risk, and nobody has changed the default. HCP herself is undecided, maybe revisit after next data update.

Said payer denied PA for the combo regimen twice, pt ended up on osimertinib alone. Now his group is reluctant to even start the paperwork for alternatives. A colleague in another practice had better luck but it took weeks. He thinks access is driving choice more than the data. Frustrated, honestly.

Pt-level view: HCP has 2 pts on the ami/laz combo and says skin tox and swelling were rough. One dose-reduced early. Colleagues heard similar and are cautious. For now she keeps new pts on osimertinib and says the combo needs a clear reason, like heavy brain mets.

Cross-trial comparison came up unprompted. HCP said she reads the PFS curves but doesn't trust lining up different trials with different brain mets rates. Wants subgroup data by CNS status. Meanwhile she's fine using osimertinib +/- chemo, depending on pt fitness.
Surprised how little push from reps on other EGFR options lately. HCP says osimertinib is still the reference everyone compares against. Fine with that.
Tumor board mostly still defaults to single-agent osimertinib.
Cross-trial comparisons with the amivantamab combo just feel apples to oranges to me.
Osi alone still my comfort zone, nothing else has beaten it for tolerability.
Rep visits lately are all about the bispecific, nothing new on osi.
Dont think the lazertinib combo is even on our formulary yet.
Chemo add-on only for the fit ones, probably not my 78 year olds.

In our community clinic we have a couple of younger, fit patients on osimertinib plus platinum-pemetrexed and they seem to be doing fine so far. Colleagues are curious about it, but I think most are waiting to see how people tolerate it day to day.
Afatinib and the older first-gen drugs barely come up anymore at our conference. Occasionally someone mentions them for cost reasons when the patient is uninsured.
The amivantamab regimen worries me because of the infusion time and the rash. For a patient who lives two hours away, that's a hard sell compared with a daily pill.

Residents at our academic center keep asking how FLAURA2 stacks up against the other first-line combination trial. I tell them I'd be wary of comparing across the two populations, and honestly I'm not sure the real-world difference is that big.
Payer pushback is the real competitor here. Our prior auth team says the combinations get questioned more than osimertinib alone, so we often just don't try.

The rep for our area brought up the competitor combo again, but I stuck with osimertinib for the new brain met patient. CNS control is the reason, and I don't think anything else matches it for that scenario.
Reps keep leaving the same slide lining up curves from different trials, and it irritates me. Different eligibility, different scan schedules. You can't read across like that.

At our weekly thoracic conference the default is still osimertinib alone for most newly diagnosed patients. When someone has liver mets or a large burden, the chemo combination gets raised, usually by the medical oncologists. Radiation oncology tends to favor the TKI alone so they can treat oligoprogression later. We rarely discuss other TKIs. I think the group will shift slowly, if at all.

I'm concerned about how the competitor combination is being pitched. A rep left material last month framing it as the new standard, and a couple of my partners seemed swayed. In my rural practice the infusion chair capacity just isn't there. The skin and infusion reactions would also be tough for my older folks. I'd rather keep things simple until I see more.

I like having more options than a few years ago. For a fit 55 year old with L858R I'd now discuss osimertinib with or without chemo, and the amivantamab combination as well. Our board was fairly open to all three. Patients mostly choose based on how often they have to come in. It's a good conversation to be having.

Honestly the cross-trial talk is confusing for my team. The nurses ask why one regimen looks better on paper than another when the trials enrolled different patients. I try to say you can't line them up directly, but I'm not sure that lands. Meanwhile pharmacy asked which combination to stock and nobody had a clear answer.

A pulmonologist who refers to us asked whether ADCs are coming for EGFR after the first-line TKI. I said they're mostly later-line so far and I don't see them replacing first-line. He seemed to think chemo plus a TKI at progression is still the fallback. Our infusion center is already busy so any new IV regimen is a workflow issue. Probably wait and see

Our group moved most first-line patients to osimertinib from erlotinib years ago, and nobody wants to go back. The newer combos get discussed, but a daily pill with fewer clinic visits is hard to beat for our patients. A rep stopped by last week to talk combo data and it was a decent chat. I think the combos will be used for select high-risk cases only.

We talked for a good while about whether the chemo add-on really beats osimertinib alone, and she kept coming back to the cross-trial problem. On paper the amivantamab-lazertinib combination might have an edge on brain mets, but different populations and imaging schedules make her cautious. She would not switch a stable patient on that basis. For new starts she still leans toward single-agent osimertinib in older patients, and she discusses the chemo combo for high-burden disease. She'll probably revisit when more mature survival data land.
Tumor board defaults to osimertinib alone, chemo add-on rarely even discussed.

Small community practice, two oncologists, and they disagree. One likes pemetrexed plus platinum upfront, the other thinks it's too much toxicity when the alternative is basically an outpatient-friendly pill. They haven't settled on a shared approach.
Still sees osimertinib as the benchmark everything else gets measured against.

Reps for the bispecific antibody have been visiting much more often lately, usually with infusion-schedule leaflets and skin toxicity slides. He found it useful but felt the visits glossed over infusion chair capacity, a real constraint in his small satellite clinic. He worries the combination would push patients toward the big center, where referral pathways are slow. Honestly, he said the pressure to consider it feels louder than the evidence he can compare directly.
Aumolertinib comes up now and then, but nobody here has access.
Cross-trial comparisons drive her a bit crazy because the populations just aren't the same. When a slide puts curves from different studies side by side, she trusts the whole presentation less.

Her patients with CNS disease do well on osimertinib, and she sees little reason to move to a doublet. Colleagues at the regional meeting mostly agreed, though a couple wanted to hear more about chemo combinations for brain mets.

The payer here asks for extra justification whenever chemo is added to a TKI, and she finds that slows approvals by a week or so. Gefitinib and erlotinib are basically never considered first line anymore, except occasionally for cost reasons. Honestly the bispecific route worries her more on authorization, since infusion billing comes into it too. Her pharmacy lead seems to favor whatever is simplest to get approved.
Honestly the combo infusions are just not feasable for our patients.

Thoracic tumor board split roughly down the middle last month. Younger, fit patients with a lot of disease get the chemo combo discussed, everyone else stays on a single agent. Nobody there is using afatinib or dacomitinib anymore as far as I know.

By the end of the chat he admitted he's uneasy that newer combination regimens are framed as obviously better. He thinks the extra hematologic toxicity from chemo is under-discussed when people compare against osimertinib monotherapy. A couple of his patients stopped chemo early because of fatigue and nausea, though he couldn't say how typical that is. Colleagues in neighboring practices seem less skeptical than he is. Overall he'd rather wait.

She likes having more options now, honestly. The bispecific plus lazertinib route gives her something to offer when resistance comes up, and she sees chemo added to the TKI as a reasonable middle ground for high-risk presentations.
Waiting to see how sequencing after progression shakes out across regimens.

Of all the options pitched to her, osimertinib with or without chemo feels the most straightforward to explain to patients. The oral-only path keeps people out of the infusion suite, which matters in a rural area with long drives. She's open to adding chemo for heavy baseline burden and thinks the newer data support that. Reps from other classes visit regularly, but she hasn't changed anything because of them.
Visits from the rep for the competing combination have become frequent and he feels they push a narrative. Hasnt seen anything yet that would change his practice.
Colleagues mostly stick with what they know, i.e. single-agent osimertinib.

Tumor board members keep citing indirect comparisons between the chemo add-on and the amivantamab combination, and she thinks that's unfair to both. Without a head-to-head, the discussion just goes in circles.
Prefers the chemo combo for high-risk patients, thinks it's underused.

He framed it as three paths: monotherapy, adding chemo, or the bispecific-based combination. Patient fitness, brain involvement and distance from the infusion center drive the decision more than any single trial. He's not sure the cross-trial picture is clean enough to pick a winner. Reps have raised newer agents still in development, and he listens but doesn't act on pipeline talk. Probably stays the course for another year.
Cross-trial comparisons are apples and oranges, honestly.
Tumor board still defaults to osimertinib alone for most.
Rep keeps dropping by with the same slide deck, no new info.
Nothing else matches osi's CNS coverage in my patients.
Amivantamab combo? Interesting, but infusion chair time kills it for us.
Haven't seen anything yet that makes me abandon first-line osimertinib.
Our tumor board split on adding chemo to osimertinib upfront. Half the room thinks the progression benefit is real but not worth the anemia and nausea in elderly patients. I'm honestly undecided.

Community colleagues I talk to mostly wait and see on the lazertinib plus amivantamab option. Infusion reactions and the early weekly dosing logistics come up every time. Probably staying put until payers clarify.
Reps from the other side keep pushing cross-trial tables at me. I tell them populations differ, brain mets enrichment differs, so I don't buy it. Frustrating that nobody has done a head-to-head.
For my frail patients I still lean on single-agent osimertinib, and the tumor board backs that. It's oral, easy to manage, and I know the tox profile cold.
Payer denied the combo regimen twice last quarter, so the whole discussion is kinda moot. We end up on osimertinib mono anyway. Tired of fighting prior auth for something I'm not even sure is better.
I think aumolertinib or furmonertinib come up at conferences but nobody here can get them. So it's academic. Maybe if they showed up on formulary I'd look, but I dont expect that soon.

Honestly the chemo-add data made me rethink things for younger patients with high-burden disease and brain mets. I'd still discuss both options with them. At least the combo is a reasonable conversation now.
Sales rep visits have gotten more frequent and less usefull. Same talking points on the competitor, no answers when I ask about long-term toxicity or sequencing after progression.

Frustrated with how cross-trial comparisons get used in lunch talks. Someone shows two curves from different trials and declares a winner, and nobody mentions eligibility, imaging schedules, or how many had brain mets. I think it's misleading and I said so. We need real-world sequencing data before anyone changes practice. Until then I treat it as hypothesis only.

Our thoracic tumor board is pretty evenly divided. The medical oncologists lean toward adding platinum-pemetrexed in selected patients, while pulmonology and radiation prefer osimertinib alone and saving chemo for progression. I sit in the middle, depending on performance status and CNS disease. Honestly it seems driven by who presented last.

I've tried the amivantamab-based approach in a couple of patients. Rash and paronychia were rough, and one patient had a clot, so the team got cautious. Compared with osimertinib the tolerability just feels heavier, even if efficacy may be better. I'm not sure the extra burden is justified for everyone. Rural patients can't travel for infusions anyway.

I'll give credit where due: compared with the first-gen TKIs I used a decade ago, osimertinib is night and day for brain mets. My older colleagues who were skeptical have mostly come around. Newer competitors haven't shaken that for me. Still, I'd like to see more on what comes after progression.

One competitor rep brings reprints, another only sends emails. Neither answers my actual questions on sequencing. I told them I'd rather hear from someone medical. Probably going to keep ignoring both until there's real data.

Not sold on switching to a combo as the default. Our pharmacists flagged cost and chair-time burden, and the nurses are already stretched thin. Also, nobody can tell me how to sequence after progression if we use the heavier regimen upfront. Seems like we'd be spending our best options early. I lean conservative, but I could be wrong.
Amivantamab combo infusion burden is the sticking point for us.
Prefers the FLAURA2 regimen over older gen TKIs, no question.
Rep visited twice this month about the bispecific combo.
Cross-trial comparisons feel apples to oranges honestly
Colleagues seem comfortable adding chemo for patients with brain mets.

Two-oncologist community practice. One has started offering the chemo combo to patients with brain mets, the other sticks with single-agent. Neither has moved to the amivantamab-based option because chair time is limited.
Said afatinib and dacomitinib are basically off the table in their clinic now. Not sure why anyone would go back after the diarrhea and rash conversations they used to have.
Concerned that the competing combination brings more skin and infusion reactions, and her nurses would be the ones managing them. She'd want longer follow-up before moving anyone off osimertinib.

Academic center physician said the payer in their region approves the TKI alone without fuss but wants extra paperwork for combos. So the competitor option isn't really the issue, the platinum-pemetrexed add-on is the harder sell.
A rep from another company keeps bringing cross-trial PFS slides. The HCP finds it annoying and thinks the study populations just aren't comparable.
Thinks the chemo combo has a better story than the bispecific combo for high-risk patients. Probably would use it first in younger patients with a heavy disease burden.
Tumor board is split, I think. Radiation oncology likes the combo approach for CNS control, thoracic surgery doesn't have much of an opinion either way.
A few patients asked about the other combo after reading about it online. He wasn't sure how to compare it with osimertinib plus chemo and felt unprepared for that conversation.

Small regional hospital, tumor board meets weekly. For new EGFR cases they usually discuss osimertinib alone versus adding platinum-pemetrexed, and the amivantamab combo comes up only as a footnote. The medical oncologist said she'd probably decide based on performance status and how far the patient lives from the infusion center. Nobody on the board has strong loyalty to one option yet. She expects that to change once more colleagues have real-world experience.

Private practice doc feels overwhelmed by the number of first-line options. Reps for the competing combo stop by often with detailed handouts, and he feels the tolerability messaging is a bit one-sided. He isn't convinced either combo is clearly better than osimertinib alone for his older patients. Mostly he worries about managing toxicity with a small staff. Said he'd rather wait than switch now.

Thoracic oncologist at a large cancer center said the FLAURA2 approach fits how they already work, since pemetrexed and platinum are familiar. Compared with the newer bispecific regimen, she finds the logistics easier. Several colleagues have started it in patients with brain mets and feedback so far has been decent. She still wants to see how it holds up outside trial settings, but overall she's comfortable.

Pulmonologist who refers patients said he hears conflicting stories from oncologists about which regimen is best. A couple of patients ended up on a combination he hadn't heard of, and he only found out afterwards. He thinks cross-trial comparisons get used loosely in talks. It makes referral conversations harder, since patients ask which one is better and he has no clean answer.

Hospital drug review noted that other third-gen options like aumolertinib and furmonertinib aren't on formulary, so they rarely come up. Discussion is mostly osimertinib alone versus with chemo. The amivantamab-containing regimen is considered for fit patients who can handle the visit schedule. Pharmacy said it would revisit if oncology asks.

Community oncologist, three-physician group. Says reps from the competing regimen visit about monthly, while osimertinib visits have been less frequent lately. He thinks colleagues in the area still prefer single-agent for stable patients and save combos for high-burden disease. Payer approvals have been okay so far.

competitor|pembrolizumab.t: Tumor board defaults to nivo combo in gastric, pembro barely discussed.
Colleagues split on durva vs pembro periop, no consensus.
Prefers pembro, knows the AE profile best.
Rep visits lately all about the other PD-1s.
Unsure if tisle is interchangeable w/ pembro in 1L gastric, asked me.
Cross-trial slides irrelevant to payer, PA denied anyway.

Community onc, gets periop lung pts referred in from surgeons. Says surgeons like neoadj chemo-IO over adjuvant-only but he's not sure which PD-1 they prefer. Probably just follows whatever tumor board picks.
HCP thinks pembro has the most mature periop NSCLC data of the options. Comfortable managing irAEs, so no plan to switch.
Annoyed w/ reps lining up nivo and durva periop trials side by side. Says designs differ too much for cross-trial comparison, thinks it's overstated.
Gastric, HER2-neg, low CPS pts: HCP not sure any PD-1 adds much. Ends up choosing by PA ease rather than agent, I think.
EGFR+ resectable pt came up. HCP would skip IO and go TKI instead, so pembro not really in the picture there. Said colleagues feel the same.
Tumor board at his hospital leaning pembro for resectable stage III, mostly bc they know KEYNOTE-671 well. Surgeon is on board too, which helps workflow.
Rep came by 2x this month, both pitching durva. HCP calls it noise, no change to his tx choices so far.
Says ADCs and bispecifics in the pipeline make PD-1 in gastric feel like old news. Not sure how he'd sequnce them once available. Wants to see where pembro fits later.

Concerned that other PD-1 regimens in periop lung seem simpler to schedule. Pt travels far for infusions so fewer visits matter to him. He thinks pembro q6w helps but admits colleagues don't always know that. Tumor board seems to default to whichever option the pharmacy stocks. Feels pembro gets lost in that process.

Academic gastric clinic, HCP says nivo is the default in 1L because it was adopted first and the pharmacy order set is built around it. Pembro is used mostly when pt has a clear CPS-positive profile. He's not against pembro, just thinks inertia drives most choices. Might revisit order sets next year, not sure.

Very positive on pembro for periop NSCLC. Says in the last few months most of his tumor board has moved to it for resectable stage II-III pts. He likes that the neoadj and adjuvant phases are in one regimen. Compared w/ alternatives, thinks the safety experience is more reassuring. Only open question is long-term outcomes vs newer agents.

HCP frustrated that rep activity is heavy on competitor PD-1s and pushes indirect comparisons. He said one rep implied a competitor was better in gastric based on cross-trial reading. He knows that's not valid but worries junior colleagues might believe it. Wants clearer guidance from med affairs on what can be said. Thinks the confusion is hurting tumor board discussions.

Mixed feelings. Likes pembro in lung periop but says durva is getting traction w/ a few colleagues, mostly for pts w/ certain staging. In gastric he's watching tisle and nivo as well. Says tumor board isn't unanimous. He'd probably stay with pembro for now unless payer pushes otherwise.

Community HCP, small practice, says pembro is what he's most confident with for both gastric and periop lung. Competitors seem fine on paper, but he hasn't seen a reason to change. Most of his referring surgeons ask for pembro by name. Pt education materials are easy too.

We talked for the better part of an hour about how periop nivolumab sits next to pembro, and she wasn't dogmatic at all. Her view is that the trial designs differ enough that she doesn't trust a side-by-side read, especially on the neoadjuvant-only versus continue-after-surgery question. In her clinic the choice mostly comes down to what the tumor board is already comfortable with. She said that with borderline lung function she'd lean toward whichever regimen feels gentler to her, though she admitted that's more gut than data.
Cross-trial comparisons are basically noise, he said, but everyone still makes them.
Their tumor board defaults to pembro for resectable NSCLC, mostly because the team knows the toxicity playbook cold. Nobody has pushed for an alternative so far.

She brought up the reps from the other PD-1 and PD-L1 camps almost immediately. They've been at the pharmacy committee a lot, and she feels the messaging has gotten pushy, with lots of indirect comparisons she doesn't think hold up. She said her pharmacist now asks her to justify every non-formulary preference in writing. It hasn't changed what she prescribes, but it eats clinic time and she resents that. I think she'd welcome a more balanced conversation, but she wasn't sure that's realistic.
Waiting to see how the durvalumab data matures before judging.

This gastric oncologist has been using chemo plus a PD-1 inhibitor in HER2-negative patients for a while, and after a long chat it was clear he's comfortable with pembro. He said the other options feel interchangeable on paper, but his team knows how to manage pembro irAEs and that matters to him. When a patient has a clearly positive CPS he doesn't hesitate. He also thinks his colleagues in the region mostly share that view, though a couple of them use nivolumab out of habit. Overall he sees no strong reason to switch.

He feels the competitor's gastric label is wider in practice for CPS-low patients, and that makes pembro look restrictive. He's not sure the difference is clinically meaningful. But it comes up every time he's at the tumor board.

Small community practice, one infusion protocol set, and she says changing it for a different checkpoint inhibitor would be a hassle. So she sticks with what's built into the order sets. She'd reconsider only if a payer forced the issue.
Colleagues keep drifting toward the other agent because of simpler scheduling, I think.
Prefers pembro; most of her peers do too.

Most of our discussion was about payers. His main frustration is that one large insurer prefers a competing PD-1 on its pathway, so he spends a lot of time on prior auths and peer-to-peers for pembro. He said the staff time is real and some patients have waited days to start. He doesn't think the competing drug is better clinically, but he admitted younger colleagues sometimes just take the path of least resistance. He worries that over time this erodes how much real choice the team has.

For EGFR or ALK-positive patients they skip the IO question altogether, and the periop targeted-therapy conversations are taking up more board time. She sees that as a different lane rather than direct competition. Still, it makes her more careful about who she sends down the pembro route.
He said the bispecific and ADC buzz at congresses is making his fellows ask whether pembro is already yesterday's news. Hes skeptical but doesnt have a good answer for them yet.

The thoracic group likes that pembro has a clear periop framework they can explain to patients. Compared with the alternatives, she says the story is simpler to tell. That counts for a lot in the consent visit.

At the academic center the surgeons and medical oncologists don't fully agree. Surgeons care mostly about pathologic response and timing to the OR, and they tend to compare regimens on that alone. Medical oncology cares more about the adjuvant phase and whether patients actually complete it. She thinks both groups are cherry-picking a bit from cross-trial data. In the community network she covers, though, nobody debates it; they follow whatever the guideline lists first. She said it's probably a mix of inertia and trust.
Not convinced any one PD-1 is clearly better than another.
Tumor board is split roughly down the middle.

She told me she thinks pembro has the edge in the perioperative lung setting, mainly because the longer follow-up gives her more confidence when counseling patients. When she compares it with the other regimens in her head, she keeps coming back to how mature the evidence feels. She also said that her nurses are already familiar with the monitoring and that helps day to day. She's open to newer agents, but she'd want a clear reason to move away. I think she'd defend pembro in front of any board.

The rep visits have become almost weekly and the slides never seem to change. He feels the competitor push is mostly about convenience claims, not clinical substance. It's wearing thin with the whole department.

There's curiosity about newer gastric combinations and ADCs, but nobody on his board is changing first-line practice yet. They're waiting to see what the guidelines say. For now PD-1 plus chemo remains the default.
Cross-trial comparisons are basically noise, nobody can convince me otherwise.
Board just defaults to whatever the payer approves first.
Pembro still my go-to for resectable NSCLC, honestly nothing has shaken that.
Rep keeps showing up with the same slide deck, zero new info.
Split between pembro and nivolumab-based regimens at our board right now, no clear winner
Durvalumab data look neat, but I'm not sure they transfer to my patients.
Every time someone lines up CheckMate 77T against KEYNOTE-671 I roll my eyes. Different designs, different populations, and we all pretend it fits on one forest plot.

Our community oncologists mostly follow whatever their thoracic surgeon is comfortable with. Some surgeons like the simpler neoadjuvant-only idea, but I'm not sure that's evidence driven, probably more about scheduling.

In gastric I still reach for a PD-1 plus chemo when CPS looks decent. Zolbetuximab is interesting for claudin-positive disease, but the infusion nausea is a headache, so pembro combos feel easier to run in my clinic.
Tumor board last week went in circles on adding a PD-1 to FLOT in periop gastric. Nobody had a clean answer, and I don't trust anyone who sounded certain given how thin the data is.
Rep dropped by twice this month, once about the adjuvant phase and once about a competitor's label update. Useful-ish, but I'd rather get the actual papers than a leavebehind.
