Most of my colleagues say pembro has the longest track record, so it's what we're comfortable with. Newer perioperative options look decent on paper, I just haven't seen enough real-world use to switch.

Payer here steers us toward a different PD-L1 agent over pembro for step-therapy reasons, which has nothing to do with the clinical picture. I think half the 'preference' people quote is really formulary.
For EGFR-mutant patients I wouldn't even consider periop IO, osimertinib takes over. That makes the whole comparison moot for a decent slice of my clinic.

Honestly the toxicity conversation gets lost whenever someone compares perioperative regimens. Some patients sailed through neoadjuvant and then stalled on the adjuvant phase, a handful just stopped, and no cross-trial table captures that. I get asked whether a competitor's schedule is easier and I can't say, because the designs aren't alike. Pembro gets blamed for thyroid and skin issues that probably show up with the others too. Frustrating that the debate is all headline endpoints.

Our tumor board is roughly split down the middle. The thoracic surgeons like the regimen they've used longest, while one of the medical oncologists prefers the newer option after a recent talk. I think neither camp has looked closely at the eligibility criteria. Pembrolizumab usually wins when the case is borderline resectable, mostly out of habit. We don't have a formal way to settle it.

Coming from a busy academic clinic, I'd say pembrolizumab remains the reference point everyone else gets measured against. When a new perioperative option comes up, the first question is always how it stacks up to KN-671. That's probably a bit unfair to the newcomers, but it shows where the comfort level is. Residents know the pembro schedule cold, which makes workflow smoother. I'd be surprised if that changed within a year.

In gastric, the competitor noise is mostly about biomarkers rather than agents. HER2 and claudin results come back at different times, and by then the patient is already on chemo. Reps keep pitching PD-1 combos as if CPS cutoffs were settled, which they're not, at least not in my practice. I'm skeptical of anybody claiming one checkpoint inhibitor is clearly better there. Cross-trial reading in that space is a mess.

The rep visits have gotten more frequent and less useful. Last time I was handed a comparison chart that put two different trials side by side with no mention of population differences. I called it out and got a vague answer about 'consistent trends'. I'd rather someone just admit what we don't know. They also show up unanounced during clinic hours, which is rude.

I'll say something positive for once: pembro has held up well in my patients compared with what I've seen on other PD-1 or PD-L1 agents. Fewer surprises managing irAEs because we've done it so many times. My community colleagues seem to feel the same, at least the ones I trade cases with. Not claiming it's superior head to head, I just trust what I know.
Our board treats nivolumab and pembrolizumab as interchangeable in most cases.
Competitor rep came by twice this month with the same slide deck both times.
For perioperative lung, pembro is still my first thought.
Cross-trial comparisons in gastric are a mess, nobdy at our board trusts them.
Community colleagues mostly follow whatever the academic board picks.
Happy with pembro, no reason so far to move to durvalumab.
At her community clinic the pharmacy stocks one PD-1 for perioperative use, so the choice is mostly made before the patient walks in. She would only look at durvalumab if the stocking changed.
He said the payer in his region approves the competing gastric regimen faster, which delays starts by about a week. Pembro-based plans seem to end up in appeals more often, and that frustrates him.
The thoracic surgeon finds the perioperative pembrolizumab schedule easy to fit around OR slots compared with other options he has seen. I think the tumor board agrees with him.

Medical oncologist at a small hospital said zolbetuximab comes up for claudin-positive gastric cases, but they haven't tested many patients yet. He is waiting to see how colleagues use it before forming a view.
She is concerned that osimertinib in EGFR-mutant disease makes the perioperative IO question murky. The board now asks for mutation status before anyone discusses pembro.
A rep from another manufacturer stops by the infusion center monthly to drop off patient handouts. Nurses like the visits but nobody thinks it changes prescribing
The fellows compare every new neoadjuvant abstract to KEYNOTE-671 even when the populations differ. He thinks that is unfair and confusing, though he admits he does it too.
The academic GI group leans toward PD-1 plus chemo in first-line gastric when CPS is high. They prefer that over layering in other targeted agents, and it seems pretty settled at their board.

Two oncologists and an NP run this community practice. They said patients often arrive having read online about a competing perioperative regimen. A lot of visit time goes to explaining why the trials aren't directly comparable. One oncologist said it is hard to be confident when populations and endpoints differ. She probably still leans toward pembro but wishes the comparison were clearer.

The multidisciplinary board meets weekly with surgery and radiology present for gastric cases. Nivolumab comes up mostly when CPS is borderline, and the room is split. Some members prefer to stay with one agent for consistency, others want to follow whichever the payer approves first. Nobody seemed strongly attached to a single option.

A pulmonary oncologist at a regional cancer center said most of her peers have settled on pembrolizumab for resectable stage II to III NSCLC. She likes using the same drug before and after surgery because ordering is simpler. She has looked at alternatives and sees nothing she would switch to. Nurse navigators also find the adjuvant phase easy to schedule. Overall she is comfortable with where things are.

The hospital pharmacist said last quarter's formulary review compared several checkpoint inhibitors, and cost per cycle dominated the discussion. Pembro stayed on, but with a note requiring documented biomarker status. The oncologist felt that was a step backward. He worries that competitor discounting could tip the next review, though he's not sure how likely that is.

Their clinic gets a visit from a competitor rep roughly every other week, usualy with new cross-trial slides. The practice manager said the doctors listen politely but mostly ask about scheduling and prior auth help. One physician said she tosses the slides because the trial designs are too different. Another thinks they are useful just to know what the other side is saying.

In his rural clinic, the oncologist handles many older patients with limited access to the infusion center. He wonders if a competing agent might be gentler on immune-related toxicity, though he admits he has no data to back that up. Because follow-up visits are hard for patients to reach, any risk of a late immune event worries him. He said that makes him hesitant to start any perioperative checkpoint inhibitor in frail patients.

competitor|sacituzumab govitecan.t: Board usually goes to chemo first; SG comes up as a later option.
Honestly the rep visits for the other ADC are way more frequent.
Prefers SG over capecitabine after endocrine plus CDK4/6 failure.
Cross-trial comparisons with T-DXd make me hesitant, diffrent populations.
Waiting to see how sequencing after enfortumab shakes out
Community docs keep asking how neutropenia compares across the ADCs.

In urothelial my group goes enfortumab plus pembro up front and then really struggles with what comes next. It's on the radar, but payer pushback has made people stay with platinum rechallenge whenever they can.

I think it has a clearer role than the oral options for heavily pretreated HR+ patients. The tumor board has been fairly receptive, especially when the patient has fast-moving visceral disease and needs a response.
Our breast tumor board splits roughly down the middle between SG and T-DXd when HER2-low comes up. It depends a lot on who's in the room and whether they're more worried about ILD or GI toxicity.

Reps for the competing ADC are in clinic nearly weekly with lunch-and-learns, whereas I've seen SG materials maybe once this year. Not sure that's affecting prescribing yet, but the nurses clearly know the other product better.
Cross-trial comparisons come up constantly, mostly PFS figures pasted onto slides. I tell my fellows they aren't comparable, though honestly I still catch myself doing it.
Everolimus-based and plain chemo options are cheaper and the pharmacy committee notices. This one needs G-CSF planning and chair time, so the infusion center is lukewarm about adding it.
Pts who've had capecitabine and eribulin do reasonably well on SG in my hands, better than I expected. Peers at the regional meeting said much the same.
The community docs have a dual question: is SG really better than yet another line of chemo, and how does it stack up against the HER2-directed ADC? Most haven't decided.

We talked for a long while about where SG fits in HR+ disease after CDK4/6. I think most of the group sees it as a reasonable replacement for chemo, but they keep comparing it mentally with T-DXd in HER2-low patients, which muddies things. Nobody was confident about the right order. The board tends to pick whichever agent the presenting oncologist has used before. Probably that familiarity matters more than any trial data right now.

After a long chat the main worry was toxicity relative to the alternatives. Diarrhea and neutropenia are a lot to manage in a small clinic with no after-hours nurse line, and she said oral options just feel easier to hand to a frail patient. She also felt the competing ADCs have a simpler story to tell. Not against it, she stressed, but she'd rather keep it for later lines. Her partners feel the same.

Overall quite upbeat. He said that in pretreated HR+/HER2- patients at his academic center, SG has become his go-to once chemo has been tried, and he finds the benefit more convincing than what he sees with single-agent chemo. Colleagues on the board have moved the same way over the last year. He admitted cross-trial comparisons are shaky but felt the direction of benefit was consistent. Rep support has been fine, responsive when he had access questions.

Frustration came through about urothelial. With enfortumab plus pembrolizumab so entrenched up front, she said the evidence for it afterwards feels thin, and her board keeps asking for head-to-head data that doesn't exist. Some colleagues lean toward trials or platinum instead. She also mentioned that payers want a pile of paperwork. I think she'd consider it, but only in a narrow group, and she isn't sure her partners would.

Surprisingly positive on the competitive landscape. He feels SG has a more manageable profile than some other ADCs in his practice, especially since he worries about eye and lung issues with the alternatives. His community colleagues are warming up too, mostly after hearing from peers rather than reps. He'd still like clearer sequencing guidance. But for now it's his preference once endocrine therapy has run out and chemo is the only other choice.

Mixed feelings after a long discussion. The tumor board uses a loose algorithm: oral agents for slow disease, an ADC when things are moving, and the choice of ADC depends on HER2 status first. SG tends to win when HER2 is truly zero. He said the other ADC's reps are more visible, but he doesn't think that changes his choices. He's open to more data on sequencing.
Tumor board still defaults to chemo after CDK4/6 progression, SG only gets discussed.
Haven't seen anyone about SG in months, other ADC reps are in constantly.
Prefers sacituzumab over capecitabine in later-line HR+ if counts allow.
Cross-trial comparisons with T-DXd make me hesitant for HER2-low patients.
Colleagues split between eribulin and the TROP2 ADC, mostly decided by neuropathy history
Mostly sticks with enfortumab plus pembro first line, nothing else on radar.

Community practice, two patients so far on SG after endocrine plus CDK4/6 failure. The oncologist said it felt like a clear step up from the single-agent chemo she used before. She would still pick it over a third chemo line.

Their nurse navigator says GI tox management and neutropenia counseling take real chair time in a small infusion center. Because of that some docs drift toward oral capecitabine. Nobody there recieves much support material for the ADC options.
Says comparing TROPiCS-02 with the T-DXd studies is apples and oranges because the populations differ. Wouldn't draw conclusions from it, but likes having another option after endocrine therapy.
Payer in his region wants two prior chemo lines documented before approving SG, so he often reaches for eribulin first. Prior auth delays are the issue, not preference.
Academic breast group sequences by biomarker: HER2-low goes T-DXd first, then SG. Not sure what they'd do for HER2-zero, probably SG.
Urology-heavy practice, after EV and pembro progression she sees sacituzumab as the logical next ADC. Her colleagues generally agree and the board rarely debates it.
Reps from the other ADC teams visit often and bring lots of cross-trial slides. He finds it hard to weigh those when nothing on SG has been presented in his clinic lately.
Platinum rechallenge still comes up at the urothelial board for older pts, I think. SG gets mentioned but mostly as a later option.

Rural single-physician clinic. She said the newer ADCs blur together for her staff, and the pharmacist keeps asking which one has the easier premed and growth factor plan. She leans on whichever has the clearest toxicity handout, and right now that isn't SG. Reps for competing agents drop theirs off regularly. Cross-trial talk doesn't really change her mind.

Large cancer center HR+ breast clinic. The attending said for heavily pretreated patients SG is now her usual pick after endocrine and CDK4/6 progression, unless there's a HER2-low reason to go T-DXd first. Fellows ask about eribulin and she explains she moves away from it when neuropathy is already present. Tumor board mostly agrees. Patients ask about hair loss and counts, but versus the alternatives she thinks it's worth it.

He keeps reminding the group that cross-trial comparisons between TROPiCS-02 and other ADC studies are shaky because prior-therapy requirements differed. The fellows still quote them anyway. He wants more real-world data before changing his sequence. For now it's chemo, then the TROP2 agent, then something else by biomarker. Not totally sure where other options fit.

Hospital-based urothelial clinic. Their board prefers EV plus pembro up front, and afterward still debates trial, chemo or SG. Several docs feel the ADC space is crowded and don't want to juggle another toxicity profile. One said skin and eye monitoring for the first ADC already eats clinic time. SG feels like one more thing to them.

Mid-size community group. Reps from a couple of other oncology brands come by monthly with lunches, but the contact on SG was more of a quick email. He has no strong preference between agents. Patients are mostly sorted by insurance and seperate travel distance to infusion. He'd compare drugs more closely once the pharmacy committee asks.

A regional hospital tumor board voted to add SG to their pathway after discussing capecitabine and eribulin as alternatives. The lead said the talk was short and mainly about infusion reaction staffing and G-CSF. Most members were comfortable with it. A couple were waiting on payer language. Overall he felt it fits next to the other options.
Tumor board defaults to chemo (cape/eribulin) post-CDK, ADC option rarely raised.
Prefers SG over single-agent chemo in 3L HR+, says PFS story more convincing.
Waiting to see how EV combos setlle before changing sequencing in UC.
Rep keeps pushing T-DXd for HER2-low; HCP says SG gets crowded out.
Community colleagues increasingly asking about SG after endocrine failure.
Cross-trial comps probably don't mean much, but her pts look like the TROPiCS-02 population.
Academic HCP: in HER2-low pts T-DXd goes first, SG after. Thinks sequencing data are thin, so tumor board just goes by HER2 IHC and prior tx lines.
Worried about neutropenia and diarrhea vs oral options like capivasertib when pt has a pathway alteration. Would try the oral first in frail pts, I think.
Says SG fits better than everolimus-based combos when pt is close to visceral crisis. Expects faster response, so fewer admissions. Tumor board agreed on last two cases.
PA for SG takes longer than for generic chemo, so community HCP just starts eribulin to avoid the delay. Says this happens a lot, esp. w/ commercial payers.
UC: EV + pembro is now the 1L standard in her clinic, so SG only comes up post-platinum and post-EV. Unsure where it slots, probably waits for more data before changing anything.
Competitor ADC reps visit the oncology clinic weekly; SG visits are rare. HCP couldn't recall the last one but didn't seem bothered, says she reads the data herself.
Likes that SG has a different payload class vs T-DXd, hopes resistance doesn't overlap. Would use it after T-DXd in HR+ if pt is fit enough.
Uneasy about cross-trial comps with other ADC studies, since pops and lines differ a lot. Still sees TROPiCS-02 as relevant, because those pts were heavily pretreated like her 3L pts.

Small community practice. Most pts get cape first, then maybe eribulin, and SG only gets mentioned after 2 failed lines. HCP worried about chair time and G-CSF logistics vs orals. Nurses are also more comfortable with AEs from chemo they already know. Probably no change until a colleague shares a good SG experience.

Large center breast tumor board. Consensus: SG preferred over more chemo in endocrine-resistant pts w/ prior CDK4/6i and chemo. Members liked the PFS advantage vs physician's choice, though one said cross-trial talk about HER2-low ADCs muddies things. Neutropenia mgmt w/ dose reductions seen as doable. HCP expects use to grow.

Urology HCP, academic. Pts mostly get platinum then maintenance IO, with EV in the mix, so the sequence is already crowded. She isn't sure SG adds enough after EV progression to justify the AE burden. Colleagues are split, a couple keen, most waiting. Says trial enrollment is the easier route for those pts right now.

Says orals and T-DXd get most of the mindshare in her group, and a lot of the push comes from rep detailing. Last quarter she saw maybe one SG-related touchpoint. Colleagues assume SG is just another chemo-like ADC w/ heavy tox. She thinks that perception is hard to shift without peer experience. Not sure what would change it.

Hospital-based HCP, mixed view. Some in her group prefer eribulin in older pts because of familiarity and simpler dosing. Others lean SG for pts w/ prior CDK4/6i and fast progression. She said tumor board decisions end up depend on pt perfomance status more than on any head-to-head comparison. Wants real-world data in pts like hers.

Honestly thinks EV-based regimens are easier to sell in UC, and the community uptake reflects that. Colleagues see SG as a later-line fallback, not a priority. Worried about GI AEs and neutropenia in older, platinum-ineligible pts. Tumor board hasn't discussed it once this year, I think. Unlikely to change soon.
Eribulin is still what my group reaches for after capecitabine, habit mostly.
Tumor board mostly defaults to EV plus pembro first, SG comes later.
Post-CDK4/6, SG beats capecitabine in my mind.
Cross-trial comparisons with T-DXd are apples and oranges, frankly.
Nobody's shown me anything better than SG after CDK4/6, so it stays.
Rep keeps showing the same slide deck, nothing new.

Our board keeps asking why we'd use SG over an oral endocrine combo before chemo. Nobody has a clean answer, and the cross-trial tables the rep leaves behind don't help because the populations differ so much. I end up defaulting to whatever the room is comfortable with.
In my community practice, a heavily pretreated HR+ woman who'd already failed capecitabine did better on SG than I expected. Not saying it's a slam dunk, but I'd move it up the sequence.
Urothelial is dominated by the EV and pembro combo now, so anything TROP2 gets pushed to third line. That's probably fair, I just wish there were cleaner data after progression.
Trastuzumab deruxtecan for HER2-low just gets used first in my clinic, no debate. SG has to carve out the leftovers, and that's a tough pitch to patients who've already burned through lines.
Colleagues at the academic center I refer to lean toward clinical trials over SG for later-line urothelial. I get why, but it's not realistic for my rural patients who can't travel.
The rep came by three times this month, always pushing TROPiCS-02 against chemo. I already know that comparison. What I need is how it stacks up against the newer ADCs and nobody answers that.

Versus everolimus-based therapy or single-agent chemo, SG seems to buy my patients more time off progression, at least in my impression. Tolerability is the catch, but I'd still pick it over another round of capecitabine.
Payer wants cheaper chemo tried first so the alternatives win by default regardless of what I'd prefer. Prior auth denials for SG after only one prior line happen a lot

I'm frustrated with how these comparisons get framed. TROPiCS-02 was against physician's choice chemo, which is a low bar in my opinion. The real decision I face is SG versus T-DXd, or versus a newer endocrine agent when there's an actionable mutation. Reps hand over cross-trial slides that line up different populations side by side and call it context. I don't trust that and neither does my pharmacist.

Last month's tumor board debate was split. Medical oncs wanted SG after EV plus pembro in urothelial, but the urologists would rather try erdafitinib if FGFR is positive. I think both positions are reasonable. Someone said they'd honestly rather manage EV neuropathy than SG neutropenia and diarrhea. We left without a firm pathway.

I'll give credit where it's due. In HR+ disease after endocrine and CDK4/6 failure, SG has been the least bad option for a few of my fast progressors. Capecitabine and eribulin just weren't buying them time. I was skeptical at first and the cross-trial stuff still bugs me, but the responses I saw made me reorder my sequence a bit.

Honestly the competitor landscape moves faster than the evidence we get. Every few months another ADC shows up and the SG messaging doesn't change. My colleagues have stopped going to the rep lunches because it's the same talking points. When a patient asks me which ADC is best I can't say, and thats the real issue.

Two nurses on my infusion floor asked how SG compares with EV for chair time and toxicity calls. I said probably similar workload but different side effects, though I'm not sure. Alopecia comes up with SG and patients really dislike it, while neuropathy with the other drug is worse for some. Hard to say much without real-world head-to-head experience.

Platinum-ineligible patients in my clinic usually end up on whatever insurance clears fastest. I've seen SG sit behind avelumab maintenance and chemo even when I thought the ADC made more sense. Colleagues say the toxicity profile scares them off compared with immunotherapy, and I'm not convinced they're wrong. Mostly I feel the data to rank these options just isn't there.

competitor|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: Honestly, cross-trial comparisons here are apples and oranges.
Tumor board still defaults to endocrine plus CDK4/6 first.
Rep dropped by again, same slides, nothing new on sequencing.
For chemo-pretreated HER2-low, I'd reach for T-DXd before anything else.
Sacituzumab feels easier on my infusion nurses, thats my gripe with T-DXd monitoring.
Not sure DB06 changes much for my HR+ patients yet.

My colleagues keep quoting numbers across the HER2-low ADC data and the TROP2 data like they're interchangeable. They aren't: different populations, different lines. I think it's lazy and it muddies every tumor board discussion.

In our community clinic, T-DXd has basically become the go-to after endocrine progression in HER2-low. The oncologists I work with trust it more than rolling through another chemo. ILD vigilance is the only thing they grumble about.
Tumor board is split. Half want to push the ADC earlier after CDK4/6 failure, the other half say give capecitabine or another chemo and save it for later. Hard to say who's right.
The rep keeps calling T-DXd the obvious choice but never answers my question on how it stacks up against the TROP2 option in HR+ disease. I get brochure answers. Frustrating.

For HER2-positive after T-DM1, I weigh T-DXd against tucatinib-based regimens depending on brain mets. If CNS disease is active I lean tucatinib combos, otherwise T-DXd. Probably oversimplified but that's how I practice.

Payer keeps asking why not older chemo first, and prior auth for the ADC drags while the patient sits on a failing regimen. Once approved it goes fine, but cheaper competitor options with simple approvals win by default sometimes.

Versus the standard chemo I used for years, responses on T-DXd just look different, and patients come back looking better. I say that to colleagues. Some are still skeptical but they're coming around.

I don't buy that the newer ADCs are interchangeable, since toxicity and targets differ. Our pharmacy still lumps them into one class when building pathways, which bugs me, though to be fair the pathway is workable.

Frankly, I'm tired of cross-trial slides. Someone puts DB06 next to a TROP2 ADC trial and implies a winner, but the HER2-low and ultra-low populations, prior therapy, and endpoints don't line up. I said that to the rep and got a shrug. Our tumor board ends up arguing from screenshots. Without a head-to-head I think we're just guessing.

We see a real mix. At my academic center the younger oncologists reach for T-DXd quickly once endocrine therapy stops working, since the HER2-low label opened that door. The older ones still sequence chemo first because they know its toxicity. HER2 0 versus 1+ readouts from pathology are inconsistent, which makes choosing against other agents messy. I'd say we're still figuring out where it fits.

I'll admit I was skeptical early. But versus capecitabine or a taxane I've watched T-DXd outperform in a handful of heavily pretreated patients, and the tumor board noticed. Nausea is manageable with prophylaxis. ILD is still the worry, but compared to the alternatives I'd pick it. Colleagues in the region seem to be drifting the same way.

Reps have been in my clinic three times this month, all pitching the same comparison. None could tell me how to choose between T-DXd and the TROP2 ADC for visceral disease with low HER2. I asked about alopecia and the neutropenia versus ILD trade-off and got vague answers, definately not what I wanted. Honestly the competitor rep was more upfront about limitations. That says something.

For HER2+ metastatic, second line is where my colleagues debate most. T-DXd seems preferred over T-DM1 in most conversations I hear, though some worry about lung toxicity in older patients with COPD. Tucatinib combos come up for brain mets. Insurance sometimes pushes us toward whatever is easier to administer. I think it's case-by-case, honestly.

Tumor board last week landed on T-DXd for a HER2-low patient post-CDK4/6 without much of a fight. That surprised me, since a year ago they'd have gone straight to chemo. Maybe the DB06 discussion nudged them. I'm still not convinced about using it earlier than endocrine options, but the comfort level has grown.
Chemo first, T-DXd later. Still his tumor board default.
Rep stopped by twice this month, mostly pushing oral options.
Prefers T-DXd over sac gov for HER2-low, mainly bc familiarity.
Cross-trial comps make her nervous, wont rely on them.
Colleagues split; younger docs more open to ADCs.
Doesn't see a clear T-DXd edge over other ADCs, honestly.
Community onc. Sees T-DXd as go-to ADC for HER2-low after ET + CDK4/6 fail. Said DB06 made the tumor board talk easier. Still watches ILD closely.
HCP worried about ILD vs the tox profile of the other ADC. Thinks pts w/ lung comorbidities would get sac gov instead, no question. Not sure how many of his pts actually fit that.
PA for T-DXd in HER2-low is slow w/ the payer, so some pts get bridged on chemo. HCP said that delay muddies the comparison discussion at tumor board.
Rep keeps pitching an oral SERD-type option as 'less burdensome'. HCP felt that comparison ignores pts w/ visceral dz and fast progression.
Academic HCP: tumor board prefers to sequence, not pick one agent. T-DXd probably before other ADCs in HER2-low, but order not settled.
Likes q3w infusion vs weekly-ish chemo, pts appreciate fewer visits. Thinks PFS benefit is what colleagues remember most from comparisons
HER2+ pts do fine on current sequence w/ T-DM1 and tucatinib combos, per HCP. Sees little reason to move T-DXd earlier. Wants more data first, probably real-world.
Asked how DB06 stacks up vs trials of other ADCs. Told him cross-trial comps are shaky; he agreed but still wanted a mental ranking.

Small community clinic, 2 oncologists. Both lean on familiar chemo + CDK4/6 sequences and find the ADC space crowded and confusing. Rep visits cover several agents so no single message sticks. HCP admitted she cant keep the ADC differences straight. Probably defaults to whatever tumor board already agreed on, rarely T-DXd early.

Academic center, breast tumor board. Group now lists T-DXd as preferred option in HR+/HER2-low after endocrine tx. HCP feels PFS signal in DB06 beats what they'd expect from chemo. Compared w/ sac gov, thinks AEs are manageable once ILD monitoring is in place. Skeptics from last year are coming around.

HCP split on which ADC goes first. Likes T-DXd for HER2-low but thinks sac gov might suit pts w/ very fast disease, not sure why exactly. The other side's rep stresses oral convenience, which she finds a bit off-topic. Wants a clearer sequencing view from tumor board before committing either way.

Hospital-based HCP frustrated. Formulary committee favors cheaper chemo, so cross-trial comparisons rarely even come up. T-DXd rep activity was light, while competitors show up monthly. Thinks nobody on staff can explain ILD mgmt confidently, so pts get steered elsewhere. Unsure that changes soon.

Private practice. Pts ask about 'the new chemo' after seeing ads, usually comparing to what a friend got. HCP explains HER2-low isn't HER2-positive. Still uses T-DM1 and tucatinib combos for HER2+ pts, T-DXd mostly 2nd line there. Unsure whether to move it earlier, waiting to see what tumor board colleagues do.

After two pts did well on T-DXd, the unit stopped treating it as last resort. Response seemed quicker than chemo, which matters for symptomatic pts. Tumor board consensus now leaning toward ADC earlier. Still wants nausea mgmt protocols tightened up.
Tumor board still defaults to chemo first in HR+ HER2-low.
Says the sacituzumab rep stops by every couple of weeks.
Prefers T-DXd over capecitabine after endocrine failure, no hesitation.
Worried about ILD, so sticks with sacituzumab govitecan in older patients.
Cross-trial comparisons are apples and oranges, in his view.
Her colleagues thinks T-DXd nausea is worse than the oral options.

Community oncologist with a small infusion suite moved a few post-CDK4/6 patients to T-DXd instead of another chemo line. Her partners did the same once the first patient stayed on treatment without much fuss.

At the academic center the breast tumor board lists T-DXd and sacituzumab govitecan side by side. The choice usually comes down to HER2 IHC score and how the patient feels about hair loss versus diarrhea.
Pharmacist at a regional hospital said prior auth for the ADCs takes longer than for oral CDK4/6 or capecitabine. Because of that some docs start with the cheaper option even if they'd prefer T-DXd.

He said datopotamab is on his radar but he hasn't used it, and probably won't until his pathologists are comfortable with the newer biomarker reports. For now he just compares it in his head to what he already gives.
Doesn't trust cross-trial comparisons between the HER2-low ADC data and the TROP2 data because the populations looked different, I think. Says he won't change his sequencing based on that.

Oncologist at a rural satellite clinic likes that T-DXd is one infusion every three weeks, versus the day 1 and day 8 schedule for the TROP2 agent. Fewer long drives for patients is a real factor for him.
Nurse navigator said patients ask about the other ADC after seeing it online. Docs like having T-DXd as a clear answer so the talk stays short
Medical oncologist felt endocrine plus CDK4/6 still beats going straight to an ADC for most HR+ patients. So T-DXd rarely gets compared against anything except chemo in his clinic.

Fellow at a university clinic described a HER2-low patient with lung damage from prior radiation. The team debated T-DXd versus sacituzumab govitecan for a while. Because of the ILD risk they went with the TROP2 agent, though he admitted that's probably overcautious. He said most of their board discussions go this way for anyone with lung history. Nobody there had a clear way to rank the two.

Private practice group of four said T-DXd is now their go-to after one or two endocrine-based lines in HER2-low. They informally compared it with capecitabine and taxane options and felt the ADC controlled disease better in their own patients. Not sure how much of that is selection. Their infusion nurses are comfortable with the premeds and monitoring. The competitor ADC rep is persistent but hasn't changed their view.

Hospital P&T committee reviewing the ADCs asked for a side-by-side. The pharmacist said the cost burden looks similar, so the decision stays with clinicians. Use is mostly driven by biomarker result and prior lines. She said they'd hold off on formulary restrictions for now, but not sure that holds.

Oncologist said the DESTINY-Breast06 data are interesting but the chemo control arm doesn't match what he'd actually use now. In his clinic a CDK4/6 inhibitor would come first. He also feels rep messaging makes it sound like T-DXd should go earlier everywhere, and he doesn't buy that yet. He'll wait for more real-world data and see what his colleagues do.

Tumor board at a mid-size hospital meets every Thursday and breast cases are usually split. Surgeons lean toward whatever shrinks tumors fastest, while med onc leans on tolerability. T-DXd comes up for HER2-low, but so does sacituzumab and sometimes just more chemo. No consensus, they decide case by case.

Community doc complained that the different ADC reps contradict each other about sequencing. One says use T-DXd first, another says the opposite. He ends up reading the papers himself, which he doesn't have time for. Honestly he thinks it makes him less likely to move away from standard chemo.

After talking for the better part of an hour, her main point was that in HR-positive, HER2-low disease she still holds T-DXd until endocrine therapy plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor has run its course. She finds the DESTINY-Breast06 context interesting for chemo-naive patients but isn't convinced it beats another endocrine switch in someone with slow, low-burden disease. Her tumor board mostly sequences by symptom burden and doesn't argue much about agent choice. She admitted she may be underusing it because HER2-low hasn't come up at board in a while.
Honestly, sacituzumab feels easier to get through our pharmacy.
Against taxane-based chemo, T-DXd is what I'd pick for a chemo-naive HER2-low patient with visceral disease. Speed of response matters when someone is symptomatic.
Dato-DXd is on our radar but nobody here has used it yet.

He was fairly blunt that the community oncologists he trains with lean toward sacituzumab. They know its neutropenia and diarrhea patterns, and the supportive care is already built into their clinics. The ILD monitoring that comes with the HER2 ADC means extra scans, extra nurse calls, and a lot of anxiety about missing early symptoms. He thinks that familiarity gap, more than any efficacy argument, keeps them on the TROP2 agent. He wasn't sure how to close it.

He kept saying you can't line the trials up side by side, because prior lines, HER2-low definitions and endocrine exposure all differ. Still, the story in his head is T-DXd first and probably a TROP2 agent after.
The rep for the other ADC is in our clinic monthly, and I've seen nobody for this one.

Her tumor board has more or less converged on T-DXd as the preferred ADC for HER2-low after endocrine therapy. The pathologists now flag IHC 1+ and 2+/ISH-negative cases without being asked, which she says changed the whole conversation. Younger oncologists on the board are comfortable with the toxicity talk, and the senior ones follow along once the scan looks good. She still hears the occasional 'why not chemo first' but it's become rare. Overall she described the room as clearly in favor.
Prior auth for T-DXd in HER2-low went through without much pushback, though one payer asked why not chemo first. Colleagues in the practice are split on how hard to push back on that.
I think oral options like capecitabine still win for frail older patients. An infusion every three weeks plus nausea management is a hard sell no matter how good the ADC is
Tucatinib combinations still own HER2-positive brain mets for us.

She said competitor reps are in the building far more than anyone talking about T-DXd, and the infusion nurses know them by face. Those reps bring lunch and slide decks on the TROP2 agents, so the nurses already have a vague positive impression. Meanwhile she'd like more practical material on ILD workup and dose holds, because that's what her team actually asks about. She doesn't think the rep imbalance changes prescribing directly, but it shapes who feels confident. Probaly worth noting that her nurse manager raised it unprompted.
After progression on pertuzumab-containing therapy, the ADC is simply more convincing to me than the older HER2 regimens. Fellows on service now ask for it by default.

The T-DXd versus T-DM1 debate in HER2-positive came up repeatedly, and he stayed fairly neutral. He sees T-DXd as the stronger option in many second-line settings but says some colleagues stick with T-DM1 because they know its safety profile cold. He mentioned that tumor board discussion often turns on how fast the patient needs a response and how reliable follow-up is. In his clinic, patients who live far away tend to get the more familiar regimen. He wasn't sure that's the right call, just that it happens.
Not convinced it beats chemo plus endocrine in indolent HR+ disease.
T-DXd is my go-to ADC for HER2-low now.

Colleagues at the regional hospital where she covers lean toward sacituzumab when HER2 IHC is borderline between 0 and 1+. She thinks pathology reproducibility drives that more than any efficacy argument, and she sounded sympathetic to it.

What worries him is burning through the best ADC too early. If T-DXd goes first and the patient progresses, he isn't sure what is really left that carries the same weight. He also hears colleagues say the sequence doesn't matter much, and he disagrees but can't point to data. On top of that, his center's ILD experience is limited, and a few bad stories make people cautious. He'd rather use endocrine and chemo options first in anyone who looks stable, and said he'd probably stay there until sequencing evidence is clearer.
She likes that the ADC class is finally giving options beyond single-agent chemo, and thinks having several to sequence is good for patients. T-DXd would still be her first pick in HER2-low.

Her group still debates whether an oral SERD or T-DXd should come first in ESR1-mutant HER2-low patients. She thinks it depends on the tempo of disease and probably will until more comparative data arrive.

ctdna|osimertinib.t: Interesting for research, but I wouldn't change anything in clinic off a ctDNA result yet.
Clearance by the first couple of cycles on osimertinib alone would genuinely reassure me.
No coverage for serial liquid biopsy here so its a moot point.
An MRD-style assay for EGFR would be great, but I don't think a validated one exists for us yet.
Rising ctDNA with clean scans? Repeat it and wait, probably.
Honestly we draw plasma at baseline and then mostly leave it.

In my community practice I can see ctDNA clearance becoming the thing that lets us stop the chemo backbone sooner in the osimertinib combination. I think patients would welcome it. It just needs prospective support before I'd act on it.

My worry is the false negative. Some patients are low shedders, and a negative plasma result could falsely reassure us. Turnaround is also slow enough that the result often arrives after the treatment decision.
At our tumor board ctDNA comes up regularly, usually as an add-on comment. Decisions still follow imaging and clinical status. I'd say the board is curious but not yet persuaded.

Patients get anxious when a result has no clear action attached. If I tell someone their ctDNA is detectable and I can't say what we'd do differently, I've mostly just caused distress. That's a real cost I don't think gets discussed enough.

If ctDNA was still detectable after several cycles of the combination, I think I'd feel more comfortable continuing the chemo part rather than dropping it. A persistent signal could help identify who actually needs the extra treatment. I'd want it confirmed on a repeat sample though.

Our payer handles serial ctDNA inconsistently. Some approvals come through for progression workup but nothing for monitoring while responding. We end up ordering it only when there's a clinical reason, and that limits any real trend data.

A lot of my patients have brain mets at diagnosis, and I'm not convinced plasma reflects CNS disease well. So a negative ctDNA wouldn't make me de-escalate in that group. I'd still want MRI surveillance regardless.

Our nurse navigator already lines up blood draws with infusion visits, so adding a timed ctDNA draw wouldn't be hard logistically. The harder part is deciding what we'd do with the number once we have it. Right now the workflow exists but the decision rule doesn't.

After a long discussion my sense is that ctDNA clearance is probably the most promising way to individualize how long someone needs chemotherapy alongside osimertinib. Imaging alone tells us late and tells us little about microscopic disease. I'd welcome using it, ideally within a protocol first. The key is agreeing on timepoints and assay sensitivity. If those get standardized I think uptake would be quick, especially among the patients who dread more infusions.

I'm skeptical, and not shy about saying so. Shedding varies a lot between patients, assays differ in sensitivity, and nobody has a threshold I trust. A single blip could push someone toward overtreatment, or a quiet result toward undertreatment. On osimertinib people often do well for a long time, so I'm reluctant to disturb that on a biomarker that's still finding its footing.

We're a regional practice and plasma testing is a send-out, so results take about ten days. I mostly use it at progression to look for resistance mechanisms, not for serial monitoring. I'd be open to more if the turnaround improved. Realisticaly though, without clear guidance it'll stay a niche tool for us. Mixed feelings overall, curious but cautious.

What concerns me most is escalation. If ctDNA rises before anything shows on scans, would we really switch someone off osimertinib early? I haven't seen evidence that the next line does better when started on a molecular signal alone. The patient could lose a drug that's still working. I'd want imaging or symptoms to confirm before moving.

I like the idea of early molecular response as a reassurance marker, especially in higher-burden patients who are frightened at the start. Telling them the blood signal is falling by the first few weeks would be a real morale boost. I'd be careful not to oversell it as a guarantee. Still, I hope guidelines start acknowledging it, because clinicians are already asking about it.

The tension for me is in older, frailer patients on the combination. I'd love to use a cleared ctDNA to justify de-escalating to osimertinib alone when chemo tolerability is poor. But I'm not sure a negative result is trustworthy enough to carry that decision. I'd probably do it only with the patient's strong preference and close imaging, and I'd document the reasoning carefully.
Show me a trial where acting on ctDNA changed outcomes on osimertinib, then we talk.
Clearance on osimertinib is encouraging, but I'm not dropping chemo over it.
Liquid biopsy turnaround is too slow to change anything here.
Honestly the only ctDNA use I trust is catching early progression.
Probably useful for research, not my Tuesday clinic.
Payer denied the repeat ctDNA panel again, so why bother ordering.

We tried serial plasma testing in a handful of patients on osimertinib plus chemo. Half the time the result was negative or uninterpretable and nobody knew what to do with it. Waste of a blood draw, in my view.

I think molecular response on ctDNA might help justify stopping pemetrexed earlier in someone doing great. But there's no agreed threshold, so I'd be guessing. Tumor board would want more than a hunch.

One patient on osimertinib had a rising ctDNA signal before any scan change, so we moved the imaging up and caught progression early. That convinced me it works as a tripwire. Escalating based on it alone though, no.
Community oncologists in our network don't have easy access to MRD-type assays for metastatic disease. Send-outs take ages and the report is confusing. Hard to build a workflow around that.
Depends who's asking. Academic folks want ctDNA to de-escalate, my community colleagues just want it covered by insurance first.

If clearance at a few weeks really predicts a deep response, I'd feel more comfortable with osimertinib alone in older frail patients. We aren't there yet, but I like the direction. Would want it tested prospectively.

Negative ctDNA doesn't mean disease-free, especially with brain only disease. I've had patients on osimertinib with clean plasma and a new CNS lesion on MRI. So de-escalating off that result is scary.
Pateints keep asking if the blood test can tell them to skip chemo. I tell them it's not validated for that. Some are disappointed, others relieved to avoid one more thing to chase.

Frankly the whole MRD conversation in EGFR feels borrowed from other settings. In resected disease maybe, but here we have measurable disease and scans anyway. Assays differ, nobody agrees on the cutoff for 'cleared', and results land after I've already seen the patient. If I escalate or switch early on a blip, I own the consequences. Not doing that outside a study.

Mixed feelings. On one hand, ctDNA clearance on osimertinib seems to track with patients who do well, and I see that anecdotally. On the other, I've had shedders who stayed stable for ages and non-shedders who progressed. I'd use it as supporting info at best, never the deciding factor. Probably the combination with imaging is where it lands eventually.

Our lab sends liquid biopsy out and it takes about two weeks, sometimes longer. By then the next cycle is due and the decision is already made. Then the report lists variants of unclear significance that I have to explain to the patient. Nursing burns time on kit logistics. For now it adds work without changing management.

I'll give credit where due: for early switch, ctDNA is the one place I've seen real value. We had a patient on osimertinib with a resistance signal showing up in plasma months before imaging. We rebiopsied, found a mechanism, and got them onto a trial. Would that have happened without the blood test? Maybe later. So I'm cautiously for it in that narrow use.

Everyone's excited about using ctDNA to guide adding chemo, but who's going to pay? Our pharmacy committee wants outcome data, and we don't have any. Without that, I can't justify repeated testing every cycle. Patients get anxious waiting on each result too, and that has a cost. I'd rather rely on CT and the clinical picture for now.

My view hasn't moved much. A detectable baseline ctDNA might flag higher-risk patients who need the osimertinib-chemo combination, which sounds logical. Still, a good chunk of patients have undetectable baseline, so what then? And I'm not sure a single timepoint tells you much. I'd want serial sampling standardized before changing practice.
ctDNA clearance at first restaging = reassuring, but wouldn't change tx yet.
Liquid biopsy at progression, yes. For MRD-type monitoring, not routine.
Would love ctDNA to justify dropping chemo early on osi. We're not there.
Pts prefer a blood draw over another biopsy, big plus for monitoring.
No PA path for serial ctDNA so they just wont order it.
Clearance on ctDNA gives HCP real confidence in the plan, said so openly.
Community clinic, sends baseline ctDNA on some osi + chemo pts, mostly when tissue is thin. Repeats at a few months if pt is willing. Not sure what they'd do with a persistent signal tbh.
Turnaround is the issue. By the time the ctDNA result is back the pt is already on the next cycle, so can't really use it to adjust chemo on osi.
Academic HCP would consider using ctDNA clearance at first restaging to stop chemo after a few cycles, in a trial setting. Thinks it could spare AEs, esp. in older pts.
Worried about false negatives in low-shedding disease, brain-only esp. Would not de-escalate osimertinib combo on a negative ctDNA alone. Imaging stays.
Tumor board discussed ctDNA last month. Split: some want it for early switch, others say imaging still rules. Consensus was 'interesting, not actionable'.
Payer denied repeat liquid biopsy for monitoring, said not medically necesary w/o progression. HCP now orders only at PD.
Likes baseline ctDNA to flag higher-risk pts who might get osi + chemo instead of osi alone. Calls it a soft tool but it helps the convo w/ pt.
Private practice onc, orders ctDNA q3 mo on some pts, mostly the anxious ones. Admits it's partly reassurance, not sure it changes mgmt.

HCP had a pt on osimertinib with ctDNA rising again at the 6 mo draw but CT stable. Asked me what the field does here. I said no prospective guidance that I know of. HCP's plan was to move the next scan up and not touch tx, which I think is reasonable. Worried this will become common and generate a lot of anxious calls from pts.

Very enthusiastic HCP, thoracic focus. Thinks MRD-style thinking will eventually reach advanced EGFR disease, so deep ctDNA clearance on osimertinib + chemo could mean fewer chemo cycles. Would happily enroll pts in a trial randomizing on ctDNA. Not ready to do it off-protocol. Wants to see durability of clearance before trusting it.

Workflow chat w/ nurse navigator + HCP. Draw happens at the infusion visit, goes out to a vendor, result lands in EHR a week or two later, sometimes as a scanned PDF. Nobody owns interpretation. Reports differ between vendors, so 'not detected' on one may not mean the same on another. HCP says it needs a clear owner or it just sits.

HCP skeptical on using ctDNA to switch early. No agreed definition of clearance, assays differ in sensitivity, and pts end up paying out of pocket when coverage fails. Tumor board folks said they don't want to chase a number. Would rather stick w/ imaging + symptoms. Might revisit if guidelines ever mention it.

Oligoprogression case: ctDNA showed a resistance alteration in a pt on osi, which helped pick next line, HCP found that useful. But early switch off a ctDNA rise alone, before imaging PD? Probably not, I think HCP wants data first. Also unclear if one rising draw is real or noise. Prefers a repeat draw in a few wks to confirm.

Rural clinic, everything is send-out so ctDNA is slow. HCP uses it mainly when tissue fails at dx. Dont think they'd use serial draws for tx decisions, no one to review at tumor board locally. Said they'd consider it if osi + chemo pts could be monitored without extra visits.
Payer here won't cover serial ctDNA outside a trial, so it's not happening.
Uses ctDNA at baseline only for osimertinib patients, nothing serial yet.
Likes seeing ctDNA clearance by the first scan on osimertinib.
Wouldn't change therapy on one positive liquid biopsy, too noisy.
Community practice, send-out ctDNA, results take about two weeks.
MRD idea makes sense, but metastatic EGFR data feel thin, still waiting.

Academic thoracic clinic draws ctDNA at baseline and again around cycle 3 for patients on osimertinib plus chemo. If the EGFR signal is gone early, I think the physician would feel more comfortable stopping pemetrexed sooner. Still informal, nothing in the pathway.
Physician orders liquid biopsy mosly at progression, to look at resistance mechanisms rather than for on-treatment monitoring. Says maybe they'd do serial draws if lab turnaround got shorter.

Seen a couple of patients on osimertinib where ctDNA stayed detectable while scans looked fine, and nobody knew what to do with it. They just repeated imaging earlier. Not sure the result changed anything.

Nurse-led monitoring at a regional cancer center draws plasma with routine bloods, so adding ctDNA is easy logistically. The oncologist would use a lack of molecular response as a reason to bring the scan forward.
Worried about low-shedding tumors, especially limited or brain-only disease. A negative ctDNA there could give false reassurance, so she would never de-escalate based on it.

Would consider ctDNA to choose between osimertinib alone and adding chemo up front, but only with prospective data behind it. For now the choice rests on brain mets and performance status. Probably revisits once more data come out.
Insurance denied the repeat liquid biopsy twice last quater. The clinic ended up covering one patient from a research fund.

Hospital lung clinic with a weekly tumor board has been sending ctDNA at baseline and at first restaging for patients on osimertinib with chemo. When the EGFR signal is gone by then, the board generally feels reassured and keeps the plan. One doctor said she'd even consider shortening chemo if clearance holds, though she admitted that's just a gut feeling. Patients seem to like a blood draw instead of yet another scan.

Private practice oncologist in a three-person group tried ctDNA monitoring on osimertinib for a few patients and found the reports confusing. Nobody could say what counts as molecular response. Without a clear threshold he doesn't think he can escalate or switch early on a blood result. He went back to CT every couple of months.

University thoracic oncologist sees ctDNA as promising but not ready. She uses it when imaging is equivocal, for example small new lung nodules a few months into osimertinib. If plasma is still positive for the EGFR mutation she looks harder, but she doesn't switch on that alone. Pathology wants a tissue rebiopsy before any change anyway. Mixed overall, and she'd like guidance on timing of draws.

Medical oncologist at a mid-size center said ctDNA clearance on the first or second draw has become part of how he talks to patients about FLAURA2-style combination treatment. He thinks it helps set expectations. If it clears quickly he'd probably lean toward dropping to osimertinib alone eventually, though he wants more evidence first. Their lab turnaround is under a week, which helps.

Pharmacist and oncologist at a rural clinic both said liquid biopsy samples have to be shiped out. Turnaround is long, so the next scan is usually done before the ctDNA result is back. They felt that makes any early-switch decision pointless. Also worried about cost for patients who aren't covered. Nothing about the assay itself, just logistics.

Oncologist at a trial site uses MRD-type testing only inside the protocol and doesn't order it outside. She thinks the field will probably get to guiding escalation or de-escalation, but sees that as a few years away. Patients ask about it more than before, mostly after reading online.

Hematology-oncology clinic in a hospital system orders ctDNA when a patient on osimertinib has new symptoms but a clean scan. The result is mostly used to decide how soon to repeat imaging. It hasn't changed a regimen yet, as far as I heard.

ctdna|pembrolizumab.t: Not ordering ctDNA outside a trial. No evidence it changes outcomes.
Clearance after surgery sounds nice, but what do I actually do with it, stop pembro?
Interesting for research, not for my Tuesday clinic yet.
If ctDNA stays negative I'd be a lot happier stopping pembro early, honestly.
Turnaround is too slow, the scan is usually back before the plasma result.
Maybe useful in gastric for pembro decisions, I just haven't seen it work in practice.

Payer won't cover serial liquid biopsy in our community practice, so patients either pay out of pocket or it simply doesn't happen. I'm not going to build a monitoring strategy on something I can't reliably order.

Had a perioperative lung patient after lobectomy whose ctDNA stayed detectable once adjuvant pembrolizumab started. The surgeons wanted to escalate and I said we have nothing validated to escalate to. We ended up just watching closely with imaging.
I like molecular response as an earlier signal than CT, especially in gastric where scans get messy with peritoneal disease. Still need prospective data, but I'd enroll patients in a study tomorrow.
Negative MRD doesn't mean cured, yet half the room at tumor board treats it that way. Feels like false reassurance waiting to happen in the pembro era, especially with low-shedding tumors.
We send it on some patients mainly because they ask. Results come back, we nod, and the treatment plan doesn't change

Every vendor pitch sounds the same, tumor-informed and super sensitive. Nobody has told me how to handle a positive result after neoadjuvant pembro when the patient looks fine clinically. I'd still send it on a research basis, I suppose.

Colleagues at the academic center use ctDNA to open de-escalation discussions, and I think that's where it would be most valuable. Fewer cycles of pembrolizumab for someone persistently negative would be a real win for toxicity.
Timing is the mess. Baseline, post-neoadjuvant, post-op, every three months? There's no consensus so each clinic does its own thing and nothing is comparable.

Frustrated, honestly. We were told ctDNA would sort out who needs more immunotherapy after a KEYNOTE-671 style regimen, but in the real world I get a PDF with positive or negative and zero guidance. Extend pembrolizumab if positive? Switch? Add chemo? Nobody has answered that. Until then it's an expensive number that makes patients anxious.

I think there's something there for gastric, probably more in settings where options after progression are thin. But shedding seems variable and I'm not sure a negative result is trustworthy. I'd use it as supporting information only. An early switch based on one rising value would make me nervous, especially with clean imaging.

Had a patient last month go ctDNA-positive at the first post-op draw with clean radiology. The whole family panicked and wanted an immediate change in therapy. I couldn't justify it, and the repeat sample was inconclusive anyway. Honestly my worry is these tests being ordered casually, because we recieved chaos rather than clarity.

I'm cautiously for it. In perioperative lung, a patient clearing ctDNA on pembro would reassure me the immunotherapy is doing its job. If it didn't clear I'd want an earlier scan and a tumor board discussion. I wouldn't change drugs on it alone, but as a trigger for closer follow-up it seems reasonable.

Pathology and oncology don't even agree on who owns the sample workflow. Blood gets drawn at surgery sometimes, sometimes not, so half my patients have no baseline. Without a baseline, molecular response is meaningless. Sort out the logistics first, then we can argue about escalation.

Small win in our clinic: one resected gastric patient's ctDNA went undetectable after surgery and has stayed that way through follow-up so far. We kept the plan unchanged, but it helped the conversation about how long to push pembrolizumab. I know one case proves nothing and I'm skeptical of most hype here. Still, seeing clearance track with a patient doing well felt meaningful. If more of that accumulates I'd get on board.
No payer coverage for serial ctDNA outside trials, so basically moot for them.
Interested in MRD but won't change tx off a single draw.
ctDNA clearance after neoadj would make me comfortable de-escalating, honestly.
Turnaround too slow to matter for adjuvant start.
Community onc, no access to tumor-informed assays yet.
Persistent ctDNA+ post-surgery pt, would absolutely push for closer imaging.

HCP uses ctDNA mostly as an add-on at tumor board for borderline resectable gastric pts. Says it nudges discussion but wouldn't override imaging or path. Wants prospective data before it touches pembro duration.
Worried about false negs post-op in low-shed tumors, esp. gastric w/ peritoneal dz. A neg result could give false reassurance and pt might skip adjuvant. Not sure how to counsel on that.

Academic thoracic surgeon likes ctDNA clearance after neoadj + surgery as a response marker beyond pCR. Would consider stopping adjuvant pembro early if clearance is durable, but only within a trial. Thinks pts would welcome it.
Ordering ctDNA q3 mo in a few high-risk lung pts, mostly out of curiosity. Results haven't changed mgmt yet. PA denied twice so one pt just pays out of pocket.
ctDNA+ w/ neg scans = anxiety without an actionable plan, per HCP. No evidence he knows of that switching tx early helps PFS. Doesn't want to escalate on a number alone.
Had a pt w/ molecular response on tx and felt it supported continuing pembro thru AEs. Found it really useful for counseling, esp. w/ fatigue and thyroid issues. Wants it routine.
Path lead says assay validation varies a lot, tumor-informed vs fixed panel, so results prob not comparable between labs. Wants one standardized workflow before it goes in any pathway and not before
Surgeon asked whether pre-op ctDNA clearance could shift surgery timing. Not sure it should, thinks path stays the anchor. Open to seeing data tho.

Med onc at large community practice. Pts request ctDNA after reading online, maybe a couple per month. Orders it when pt is anxious post-resection for gastric ca. If positive, unclear what to do — add chemo? Switch? No guidance, so far just repeats imaging sooner and waits.

Skeptical on ctDNA-guided early switch. MRD+ doesn't say which tx works better, only that disease is likely there. Tumor board split, surgeons keen, med oncs less so. Worry about overtreating pts who might never relapse, plus cost of extra scans and draws. Needs randomized data, not retrospective stuff.

Very enthusiastic, keeps an informal registry of KN-671-type pts w/ serial draws. Says clearance after neoadj pembro + chemo seems to line up w/ a good course in most, a handful stay positive and recur. Thinks adjuvant will eventually be de-escalated in cleared pts. Admits sample is small, anecdotal, no control. Wants MSL to flag any upcoming trial.

Gastric focus at tertiary center. ctDNA only in research protocol, not routine. Says logistics are the hurdle: draw timing vs surgery, who orders, who reviews result. Pts generally keen. Pembro continuation still based on imaging, AEs and pt preference. I think she'd adopt if guidelines endorsed it.

Lung team tried post-op ctDNA in a few pts, results came back late and didn't match CT. One pt was ctDNA neg then relapsed within months, which shook their confidence. Now only treat it as supportive. Also insurance issue, each draw needs PA and often gets denied. Not routine for them.

Mostly older pts in his clinic, so ctDNA-guided de-escalation of pembro is appealing, fewer infusion visits and fewer AEs. But isn't sure one clearance is enough, would want two consecutive negatives. Also unsure who pays for repeated draws. Said he'd be open w/ pts about uncertainty. Cautiously interested, not ready to act.
Interesting science, but no payer here will cover serial ctDNA outside a trial.
Would want ctDNA clearance clearly defined before using it to stop anything.
Keen on MRD-guided de-escalation if the data ever matures.
Not changing adjuvent pembro based on a single positive ctDNA draw.
Tissue-informed versus tumor-agnostic assay, still undecided which they'd pick.
Turnaround is the issue, results land after the treatment decision is already made.

After neoadjuvant plus adjuvant pembrolizumab in resected NSCLC, she likes the idea that a negative ctDNA could support stopping early. Said it would help patients who struggle with immune-related toxicity and can't face finishing the full course. Still wants a prospective signal first.
Community oncologist, sends ctDNA now and then in stage III lung when imaging is equivocal. Treats it as one more data point, not a trigger. Honestly the result rarely changes what he does.
In gastric, he thinks shedding is so variable that a negative result may not mean much, especially in diffuse histology or peritoneal-predominant disease. Would not de-escalate on it.

Academic GI doctor thinks on-treatment molecular response could eventually separate patients who need chemo intensification from those fine on the PD-1 alone. Excited, but says it needs a randomized design before anyone changes practice.
Their tumor board discusses ctDNA results when they exist, but nobody agrees on what to do with a persistent positive. Probably would repeat in a few weeks and watch the trend, not sure beyond that.

Worried about patient anxiety. A positive MRD result with nothing to offer except more scans is hard to sit with. She had one patient who was frantic after a rising signal, and imaging stayed clean for months afterward.
Nurse navigator's practical question was who orders it, who tracks it, and who calls the patient with the result. Without a defined workflow she doesn't see clinic adopting it.
Insurance denials for MRD tests are common at their center and the paperwork eats a lot of clinic time, so most docs just skip it

We talked a long while about ctDNA after surgery in patients who got perioperative pembrolizumab. He sees the logic of treating clearance as a marker of benefit and a persistent positive as a flag for something more aggressive. But he's not sure what 'more' would be, since no escalation after the standard regimen is proven. He also thinks timing of the draw relative to surgery probably matters and nobody seems to standardize it. Interested, but not ready to act outside research.

For gastric he was frankly skeptical. Many of his patients are on pembrolizumab with chemo, and he sees ctDNA as too noisy in low-shed tumors to base a switch on. A negative result might just mean the assay missed disease. Scans and the clinical picture still drive decisions, so an extra blood test adds cost without a clear action. He'd want guideline support before ordering it routinely.

She was the most enthusiastic person I spoke with on this. A handful of her resected lung patients had serial ctDNA that cleared on pembrolizumab, and she felt it helped her counsel them on prognosis. She imagines clearance supporting shorter adjuvant treatment and persistent positivity prompting trial referral. She admitted that's speculation, but the direction feels right to her.

Assay quality is his main hang-up. Different vendors, different panels, different limits of detection, and he doesn't trust that a negative from one equals a negative from another. Tumor-informed tests also need tissue and several weeks of lead time, which is a problem in the perioperative window. Until there is some harmonization he treats results as hypothesis-generating at best.

Early switch came up. What if ctDNA rises before imaging shows progression on pembrolizumab? She sees the appeal, especially in advanced gastric where options are limited. But she worried about abandoning an effective therapy over a transient blip, and I think she feels the same ambiguity as with pseudoprogression applies to molecular data. Would want a confirmatory repeat draw before acting, and is open to it within a study.

Likes that it's noninvasive and repeatable, and says patients generally prefer a blood draw to yet another CT. For perioperative lung with pembro he would happily use ctDNA to support decisions once guidelines catch up. Right now he uses it mainly as reassurance.
Tumor-informed ctDNA assay takes too long to come back for our surgical timeline.
Honestly we don't use ctDNA outside of a trial yet.
Would happily stop adjuvant pembro early if MRD stayed negative, once data supports it.
Clearance on ctDNA doesn't convince me enough to drop treatment.
Sends a few liquid biopsies post-resection, mostly out of curiosity and nothing changes
Molecular response on ctDNA is a useful extra read next to imaging for me.

Community practice with two oncologists. They order a ctDNA panel at the first post-op visit for some gastric patients, but the results mostly sit in the chart because nothing tells them what to do with a positive on pembrolizumab. Payer coverage is hit or miss.

A positive MRD result after surgery would just create anxiety with no clear next step, per the lung oncologist at an academic clinic. The patient is already getting perioperative pembrolizumab, so escalating to what? Not sure there is a real option.

Tumor board lead would like ctDNA to pick out patients who could skip the adjuvant phase after neoadjuvant pembro plus chemo and a good pathologic response. Thinks that is probably where the field goes. Right now they only discuss it and don't act on it.

One gastric oncologist ordered serial ctDNA during adjuvant chemo in a few high-risk patients. Rising levels led to earlier scans, which were sometimes clean. So it changed imaging timing more than treatment.
Turnaround and cost are the problem. Patient waits a few weeks for the result and the insurer denied it twice, so the adjuvant decision is already made by then.
Said a negative ctDNA after surgery is reassuring but they still wouldn't de-escalate pembro, especially in PD-L1 positive tumors. They would only consider it inside a protocol.
Low shedding in some gastric tumors worries me, so a negative result may be falsely reassuring. Peritoneal disease especially doesnt show up well in blood, I think.

Small private oncology group now uses ctDNA after resection to decide how closely to scan patients after pembro-based treatment. If it turns positive they bring the patient in sooner. They find it useful and patients like having a number to follow.

This medical oncologist at a regional hospital says ctDNA questions come up from patients more than from colleagues. Their lab has no validated assay, so they would have to send out. Reports come back with no guidance on what a positive means for someone on pembrolizumab. They worry about changing therapy based on a test with no prospective support. For now they stick to imaging every few months and the standard schedule.

We talked about using ctDNA for an early switch in metastatic gastric cancer if levels don't fall after the first cycles. The oncologist said it sounds logical but they'd need proof that switching improves outcomes and not only predicts them. In their clinic they would still wait for the first CT. A few patients had levels checked informally and it matched the scan, I think. They'd be open to a study.

The lung team at a large cancer center is enrolling patients in an MRD-guided study after surgery. They like that ctDNA could spare some patients extended adjuvant immunotherapy. They also see it catching recurrence before symptoms start. The main hurdle is logistics, meaning blood draws at the right timepoints and getting results back in time. Overall they are quite enthusiastic.

Lab director is concerned about assay variability. Vendors use tumor-informed and tumor-naive approaches and results aren't comparable, so a patient could be cleared on one and positive on another. Until there's standardization they won't let it drive de-escalation. Timing of the draw relative to surgery is also unclear, since very early post-op samples could mislead.

Hospital-based oncologist has a mixed view. They find ctDNA helpful for prognosis talks with families but not for deciding how long to continue pembro. They tried it in a handful of resected lung patients and most were negative with no change in plan. The one positive patient had an early PET and scan that found nothing, which caused a lot of worry. They want guidance on how often to repeat testing.

A gastric oncologist in private practice says patients ask about liquid biopsy after reading online. They have sent MRD tests on a couple of resected patients to see how the process works. Results were easy to get but they didn't know how to act on them. They said they'd keep pembrolizumab and chemo plans unchanged for now. They think it could matter later for de-escalation, but not today.

ctdna|sacituzumab govitecan.t: No ctDNA assay on formulary here, so it's research only.
Uses liquid biopsy at progression only, not for monitoring.
Would welcome ctDNA clearance as an early signal on SG.
Doesn't trust MRD results enough to switch therapy.
Community practice, orders ctDNA maybe once a quarter, mostly out of habit.
Molecular response sounds nice but nobody reimburses the repaet draws.

Academic breast clinic draws ctDNA every second cycle in a few HR+/HER2- patients on sacituzumab govitecan. A falling level made her more comfortable continuing through grade 2 neutropenia. Still informal, nothing written into the pathway.

In urothelial, the tumor board sometimes asks for ctDNA after cystectomy. Results take a couple of weeks, which I think is too slow to inform adjuvant decisions. Not sure how it would apply to an ADC later on.

Oncologist at a mid-size hospital said a rising ctDNA with no change on imaging wouldn't make her stop SG. Patients would just get anxious and she'd have nothing different to offer. Imaging still rules for her.

Likes the idea of ctDNA clearance to de-escalate in early breast patients after neoadjuvant therapy. Her clinic already banks plasma at baseline, so adding timepoints would be easy. She'd use it if a payer covered it.
Private practice doc orders liquid biopsy mainly to look for ESR1 at progression. Hasn't used it to time a switch to sacituzumab, since next line is decided by scans and blood counts.

Hospital lab lead says assays differ a lot between vendors, so serial ctDNA values aren't comparable if the patient changes site. That undermines any molecular response cutoff. Infusion nurses also grumble about extra tubes on treatment days.
Nurse navigator tracks ctDNA draws in a spreadsheet for the few trial patients. Rest of teh clinic doesnt bother.
Finds MRD testing in bladder after surgery interesting, but wouldn't escalate to an ADC on a positive result alone. As far as she knows there's no data in that setting.

Large cancer center breast group started a small pilot drawing ctDNA at baseline, after cycle 1, and every third cycle for patients on SG. The aim is to see whether early clearance lines up with scan response. A couple of patients had levels fall quickly and scans later confirmed benefit. She admits it's anecdotal. Even so, she thinks an early molecular response read could spare people a few cycles of something that isn't working.

Urology group is skeptical. Tumor-informed assays need tissue, and many of their bladder patients only have small TURBT samples. Turnaround is long, so the patient has had another cycle by the time results come back. Payer denied the last two requests. She'll keep using CT and clinical status for switching decisions.

Community oncologist has mixed feelings. She sees value in ctDNA for flagging progression earlier in HR+/HER2- disease, especially in bone-only patients who are hard to image. But a rising signal doesn't tell her what to switch to, and after CDK4/6 and endocrine therapy the options are limited anyway. I think she'd move to SG earlier if the ctDNA story were convincing, but she wasn't sure. For now she orders it occasionally.

Her main worry is false reassurance. A negative ctDNA in a low-shedding tumor doesn't mean disease-free, and she has seen patients progress on scan with a flat plasma result. In her busy clinic nobody has time to explain that nuance. She'd hesitate to de-escalate anyone on a negative result, and she said clearance on SG would need to be validated first.

Lab director at a regional hospital said they could bring ctDNA in-house within a year if oncologists ask. Right now samples go out and results are slow. So far requests are mostly for resistance mutations, not MRD. She wasn't sure SG patients would be candidates for serial monitoring.

GU oncologist at a university clinic uses ctDNA after cystectomy in selected patients and says it helps counselling. A positive result prompts closer imaging and a trial discussion. She'd be open to ADC-based strategies like sacituzumab govitecan if data supported it. A negative result gives patients some peace of mind, though she hedged that it isn't proof. She thinks practice is heading that way.
Honestly, ctDNA clearance means little to me without a prospective trial behind it.
Not switching off SG over a blip in ctDNA, no way.
Would love a molecular response readout on sacituzumab that beats waiting for the next scan.
Liquid biopsy turnaround is too slow, wont change anything for us.
Interesting for MRD, but we can't act on it outside a trial.
Useful adjunct, still not a decision-maker.
Our community site sends out liquid biopsy rarely, and the payer denies it a lot of the time. Even when we do get a result, nobody agrees on what a rising level should mean for treatment.
I had one metastatic HR+ patient on sacituzumab where ctDNA dropped early and the scan later matched. Reassuring, I think, but it's one patient and I wouldn't build a pathway on it.
After cystectomy I'd consider MRD testing to decide who gets adjuvant therapy. But the assays differ so much that I'm not sure a result from one is comparable to another.
Everyone talks about early switch based on ctDNA. Where's the evidence that switching off SG actually helps the patient rather than just burning through a line of therapy?
Tumor board asked whether molecular response could tell us when to stop sacituzumab for toxicity. Nobody had an answer, so we fell back on imaging and the clinical picture.
Ive had reports come back with no variants detected in patients who clearly progressed on CT. So a negative ctDNA doesnt reassure me one bit.

For de-escalation I'm cautiously keen. If MRD stays negative in a lower-risk patient, sparing further systemic therapy would be very attractive, though we're nowhere near being able to do that safely.

We're an academic clinic and even we struggle with sample logistics. Draw timing relative to the cycle, differnces in shedding, lab backlog... by the time the report is back the patient has had the next dose anyway.

We tried ctDNA monitoring in a small group of patients on second-line sacituzumab last year, hoping to catch progression before imaging.
