In practice draws got missed, reports took ages, and a couple of results contradicted what we saw clinically. I'm frustrated because it added cost and patient anxiety without changing a single decision. Until someone shows it alters management, I'm not repeating the exercise.

My worry with ctDNA-guided escalation in urothelial is how heterogeneous these tumors are. A low-shedding tumor could look clear when it isn't. That said, if a patient on SG shows clearance and symptoms improve, I'd feel a bit better continuing at full dose. I just wouldn't take it as permission to stop or de-escalate. Probably need a lot more evidence first.

Running a busy community practice, I can't add another send-out test unless it changes management. Payers already push back on basic NGS, so liquid biopsy for monitoring is a tough sell. If ctDNA gave a clear signal to switch early off sacituzumab I'd consider it. Right now it's a nice-to-have, maybe once there's a validated cut-off and reimbursement.

I came in skeptical, but serial liquid biopsy has grown on me in HR+/HER2- disease. We use it alongside imaging, and a rising ctDNA level has made me bring scans forward a couple of times on SG. It hasn't replaced radiology and I wouldn't switch purely on it. Still, as an early warning it's been more helpful than I expected.

Post-cystectomy patients are where MRD seems most relevant to me. Detectable ctDNA could push us toward adjuvant treatment, and undetectable might let us watch. But nobody knows if treating on molecular relapse alone improves outcomes, and where an ADC would fit is unclear. I'd raise it with the patient but be honest about the uncertainty.

Fair point to the enthusiasts: molecular response on ctDNA is probably going to matter. I saw a patient on SG whose levels fell quickly and stayed low while scans lagged behind, which supported staying the course through some nasty neutropenia. It's anecdote, I know. But if prospective data confirm it, we could avoid stopping effective treatment too early and avoid dragging on ineffective treatment too.
No validated threshold, so I wouldn't switch on a ctDNA blip.
Clearance on ctDNA would make me comfortable stretching imaging intervals, honestly.
Interesting for MRD after cystectomy, but we have no access to it here.
Turnaround of three weeks makes liquid biopsy useless for a fast-moving HR+ patient.
Still just a research toy in our community practice, I think.
Rising ctDNA ahead of scan changes would honestly help me move to sacituzumab earlier.

Our payer turned down the last two monitoring panel requests, so ctDNA for molecular response is a non-starter for most of my patients. I'd love to use it to decide on an early switch to sacituzumab govitecan, but I can't justify the cost to anyone.

We send ctDNA at baseline in some HR+/HER2- patients, mainly to look for actionable changes. Whether serial draws should drive a switch after CDK4/6 progression, I'm not sure. Probably needs prospective data first.
In the urothelial clinic, post-cystectomy MRD positivity is what gets my attention. If a patient is ctDNA positive with clean imaging, I'd be keen to bring an ADC in earlier, trial permitting.
Patients ask me if a detectable liquid biopsy result means treatment is failing, and I don't have a good answer. A single result without scan correlation mostly just causes anxeity.

I think ctDNA dynamics on sacituzumab govitecan could be a decent early read on molecular response, maybe by cycle two or three. But assay variability worries me, and low-shedding tumors could give false reassurance.
Tumor board discussed using ctDNA clearance to de-escalate and the room was split. Some were comfortable in the adjuvant setting, others said no way outside a trial
Honestly, de-escalating on undetectable ctDNA scares me. Negative doesn't mean no disease, especially in bone-only HR+ disease where shedding is probably low.

We talked for a long while about whether ctDNA could tell us when sacituzumab govitecan is working. In theory, a fall in tumor fraction after the first couple of cycles would be a very practical early marker, quicker than waiting for restaging. In practice, I think most of us have no data in this setting, only extrapolation from other drugs. He'd consider it for a patient who is borderline on tolerability, to justify pushing through, but wouldn't change a regimen on it. Probably needs a prospective study before it's more than curiosity.

Her main concern was workflow rather than science. Blood gets drawn, goes to an outside lab, the result lands in the inbox weeks later, and nobody owns it. By then the patient has had imaging and the decision is already made. She also said reports differ so much between assays that she can't compare one draw with the next. Until that's sorted she doesn't see ctDNA guiding escalation or an early switch.

He's quite enthusiastic and has been using serial ctDNA in a handful of post-endocrine, post-CDK4/6 patients to track how they're doing on sacituzumab govitecan. When the signal drops quickly he feels reassured about tolerating the neutropenia and diarrhea, and when it climbs he brings scans forward. He admitted it's informal and not protocol-driven. Still, he thinks it adds confidence to conversations with patients, and he'd welcome guidance on standardizing sampling times.

Her urothelial colleague noted that MRD after surgery is where the field is heading, but metastatic monitoring is much less clear. She'd want to know whether molecular response predicts benefit with the TROP2 ADC before using it to escalate. She also wonders whether a persistent signal would make her switch earlier, and to what. I think she's open but wants the evidence first. Sequencing options are limited anyway, which blunts the value of an early warning.

Frankly, he was skeptical of the whole concept. He's seen discordance between ctDNA and imaging too many times, with clearance in blood while a lesion still grows, and the other way round. With sacituzumab he worries that stopping early because of a clean result would deprive someone of benefit, and that switching on a rising level might throw away a working line. He'd rather rely on scans and symptoms, and his patients wouldn't get testing reimbursed anyway.

She sees ctDNA as the likely future for deciding between continuing and moving on, particularly for HR+/HER2- patients who've exhausted endocrine options. Her thought is that a molecular response after two cycles of SG could allow longer imaging intervals and less patient anxiety. Conversely, persistently high levels could prompt an earlier discussion of next line. She accepts it isn't standard yet. But she'd enroll patients in any study testing ctDNA-guided switching.

Research use only for now. My pharmacist keeps asking whether SG dosing could be guided by ctDNA and I tell him not really. Maybe someday for escalation, but dose changes are driven by counts and toxicity.
No payer here covers serial ctDNA, so it's research-only for now.
Keen on ctDNA clearance as an early SG response marker, would use it tomorrow if validated.
ctDNA interesting but not changing my tx decisions yet.
Doesn't trust a single MRD-negative result enough to de-escalate anyone.
Orders liquid biopsy at progression mostly for ESR1, not for anything SG-related.
ctDNA turnaround too slow, pt already scaned by the time result is back.
Community onc, HR+/HER2- pt on SG 3rd line. HCP said a falling ctDNA level by wk 3-4 would reassure him about pushing through grade 2 AEs. Wants prospective data but sees real use.

Tumor board discussed ctDNA in mUC pts post-cystectomy. Split room: some want MRD to guide adjuvant, others say there's no standard action to take on a positive result. HCP will probably wait for more readouts.
HCP worried about false reassurance. Low shedders in HR+ disease could look 'cleared' on ctDNA while imaging says otherwise. Won't escalate or de-escalate off ctDNA alone.

Academic breast clinic sends liquid biopsy each cycle for a few pts, protocol only. Outside that, PA denials are common so they don't bother. Thinks workflow is the bigger barrier than the science tho.
Early-switch idea appeals. If ctDNA rises on endocrine + CDK4/6 before the scan shows anything, HCP would move to SG sooner. Thinks it could spare pts a cycle or two of ineffective tx.
No clear threshold for 'molecular response'. HCP pointed out each lab reports differently, so hard to build a tumor board rule around it. Wouldn't act on it until that's standardized.
Urologist said bladder ctDNA is mainly an MRD tool after surgery, not something used on SG in the met setting. Not sure how it fits there. Still interested.
HCP sends ctDNA occasionally, mostly in anxious pts who ask. A positive result with normal imaging causes distress and there's no good action to offer. Sees potential, but not routine.

Large breast center, HCP is quite positive on ctDNA for monitoring. Says clearance during SG could support staying the course when scans are equivocal. Would also like a rising signal to trigger earlier imaging. Thinks the tumor board would accept it as supportive, not decisive. Main ask is a simple, repeatable report.

Mixed view from regional hospital onc. Likes the idea of ctDNA-guided early switch in HR+/HER2- after CDK4/6, but says SG access and sequencing matter more day to day. Orders it rarely, usually when imaging is unclear. Unsure what a 'molecular non-responder' on SG should get next. Would want guidance before using it to change tx

HCP is skeptical about using ctDNA to stop SG early. Says pts have often run out of options by then, so stopping on a biomarker alone feels risky. Also worried about shedding variability across tumors. Neutropenia and diarrhea are the things that actually drive his dose decisions. ctDNA is 'a nice research toy' for now.

Concerned about equity and logistics. HCP says serial liquid biopsy means extra draws, PAs and lab coordination that a small practice can't absorb. Even if ctDNA guided escalation well, only big centers would use it. Doesn't see it fitting a busy infusion clinic. Also unsure who pays when results don't change tx.

Urothelial-focused HCP uses tumor-informed MRD in a few post-op pts, mostly to guide surveillance intensity. For SG in advanced disease, he said ctDNA is too early to use. Thinks clearance may eventually be a surrogate but isn't convinced yet. Would join an observational project if the sampling schedule is practical.

Very enthusiastic. HCP thinks ctDNA dynamics could become the earliest read on whether SG is working in HR+/HER2- pts, before the first restaging scan. Would use clearance to support continuing and a flat or rising signal to prompt a tumor board discussion about switching. Admits the evidence is thin and says he'd keep imaging as backup. Still wants it in his clinic soon.

ctdna|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: Would love ctDNA clearance as early T-DXd response marker. Not there yet.
No PA approval for serial liquid biopsy, so we don't order. Period.
MRD to de-escalate? Not comfortable, pt safety first.
HCP enthusiastic re ctDNA-guided early switch, asks how to access a protocol.
Turnaround on liquid biopsy too slow to matter tbh
Rising ctDNA + stable scan = tumor board discussion, nothing more.

Community onc sees ctDNA as a useful adjunct when imaging is equivocal in HER2-low mets. Would check molecular response at first restaging on T-DXd to reassure pt that tx is working. Wouldn't change tx on it alone though.
HCP worried about false reassurance from undetectable ctDNA, esp. in low-shed tumors. Thinks lobular pts would get missed. Imaging stays the standard for now.
Asked what 'molecular response' even means for an ADC. Which timepoint, which threshold? No consensus, so hard to build into a pathway, probably waits for guidelines.
Payer pushback is the main barrier. Two PA denials last quarter for serial ctDNA. Pts either pay out of pocket or we skip it.
Interested in MRD-style monitoring after neoadjuvant tx. Thinks it could help pick who needs escalation vs staying on current tx. Wants to see it in a trial setting first, not routine care.
Breast MDT only discusses ctDNA when pts bring results from outside. 'Interesting' but hasn't changed tx so far. Unsure how it fits with HER2-low heterogeneity.
Pt asked about a liquid biopsy after reading online. HCP explained it's not validated for stopping or switching T-DXd. Pt still anxious waiting for the next scan.
Orders ctDNA at baseline sometimes, mosly for ESR1/PIK3CA, not for monitoring. Serial draws on T-DXd for response? Probably not worth the cost, I think.

Large academic site, HCP quite positive. Uses ctDNA in research protocols to track clearance over the first few cycles of T-DXd. Thinks early non-clearance could trigger earlier imaging and a switch discussion. Would want a clear workflow, e.g. draw at C1, C2, then with each scan. Hedged though: 'a couple yrs away, I think'.

HCP skeptical. Has seen discordant cases, ctDNA up but pt clinically fine and scans stable. Worried about dropping an effective ADC too early and burning a line. AEs from next-line tx aren't trivial either. Until prospective data, ctDNA stays out of T-DXd decisions.

Private practice, two oncs. No in-house workflow for serial liquid biopsy, it's all send-out and results take a while. Nurse navigator would need to coordinate draws with infusion visits. HCP thinks q3w T-DXd cycles actually make timing convenient. PA and cost unclear, would try if reimbursed.

Asked about de-escalating after ctDNA clearance. HCP firmly no, responding pts can still relapse and there's no data on stopping early. Maybe in a HER2+ residual disease setting some day. Right now it would be reading tea leaves.

Pt-driven demand is growing. HCP says several pts ask for 'the blood test' to know early if tx is working. Sees value for shared decision-making and lowering anxiety. Would use it for an early switch if validated. Thinks ADC sequencing makes this more relevant as more options come after T-DXd.

Mixed feelings. Likes the MRD concept for escalation but unsure which assay to use, tumor-informed vs not. Lab availability varies by site. For HER2-low mets pts, MRD seems less relevant than ctDNA as a response tracker. Tumor board split, not sure it changes anything now.
Not using ctDNA to switch anyone off T-DXd, there's no validated threshold.
Liquid biopsy sits in research protocols only at our center.
Would happily see ctDNA clearance used to support de-escalation.
Payer won't cover serial MRD testing, so it's a nonstarter for us.
A couple of the docs send ctDNA at baseline, nothing after that.
Too many false negatives in low-shed tumors, honestly don't trust it

Our community practice started sending a tumor-informed ctDNA assay at first restaging on T-DXd for a few HER2-low patients. When the molecular response looked deep, it gave them comfort to keep going without adding extra imaging. Still early, but the oncologists like it.

Academic breast clinic draws ctDNA alongside scans in the trial setting only. Outside the trial they see it as interesting but not actionable. Probably will wait for prospective data before changing anything.

Turnaround of two to three weeks makes ctDNA useless for a switch decision in their infusion center. By the time the result is back the next T-DXd cycle is already booked. The nurse manager said that timing issue alone kills it for now.

One oncologist said a rising ctDNA signal would make her order imaging earlier, but she wouldn't stop treatment on that alone. She thinks of it as a trigger for a scan, not a decision tool. Not sure the payer would cover the extra draw either.

Nurse navigator set up a standing liquid biopsy draw with the pre-cycle labs. The physician finds a trend easier to discuss with patients than waiting for the next scan. He thinks ctDNA clearance after a few cycles could eventually support de-escalation.
Doesn't see how MRD fits metastatic HER2-low disease, since there's no clear residual-disease state to track. Thinks it's an early-stage concept being stretched. Wouldn't use it to escalate anything.
Small private group sends ctDNA only when imaging is equivocal. They said it helped once or twice, not a routine habit. Hedged that results probably vary a lot by assay.

Patients ask about it after reading online, and the doctor has to explain that a negative ctDNA result doesnt mean stopping T-DXd. She likes that they're engaged. But she says it adds a long counseling conversation to a short clinic slot.

Hospital-based clinic discussed ctDNA at tumor board last month for a patient on T-DXd with slow radiographic response. Some in the room wanted a molecular response readout to back up the scan, others said the result wouldn't change management. They ended up not sending it. The medical oncologist said she'd revisit if the lab offered a faster assay. Overall mixed views, I think.

Main worry is assay heterogeneity. The group uses two different vendors depending on the payer, and the results aren't comparable from one draw to the next. With T-DXd, a falsely reassuring clearance could delay a switch, and a noisy blip could trigger unnecessary worry. Cost to the patient also came up, since some plans deny repeat testing. They don't feel ready to act on ctDNA outside a study.

Rural practice with limited scanner access sees real value here. They draw ctDNA at home-visit labs and use a persistent rise to move a restaging scan forward. If a patient on T-DXd showed rising signal, the doctor said she'd be comfortable discussing an early switch. A drop to undetectable would reassure her that continuing is right. She does want some guidance on what counts as a meaningful change.

No guidelines endorse ctDNA-guided changes in this setting, and the physician said that's the end of the discussion for her. She worries about over-treating patients based on a number that isn't validated. Patients also get anxious over every result. She'd rather rely on imaging and clinical status for now.

Thinking about the HER2-low and ultralow population from DESTINY-Breast06, the oncologist said ctDNA might eventually help sort who benefits most from T-DXd. Right now she only sees it for research or at progression to look for resistance alterations. She isn't sure a baseline level would change her first-line choice. Interested, but waiting on data.

Breast oncologist at a large center is keen on ctDNA-guided de-escalation for patients with sustained clearance. She'd consider stretching imaging intervals, and maybe discussing a treatment break, if the data supported it. She thinks T-DXd toxicity, especially ILD risk, makes the case stronger for finding patients who can safely do less. Wants a prospective study first, but thinks it's coming.
Honestly, ctDNA for switching therapy is still a research toy in my clinic.
No payer here will cover serial liquid biopsy, so we just don't send it.
Interesting idea, but I'd want propsective data before changing T-DXd on the back of it.
Would love a validated MRD test to guide escalation, honestly.
ctDNA clearance on T-DXd, interesting, but I can't act on it yet.
Tumor-informed vs fixed panel, nobody agrees, so we wait.

We tried sending plasma panels on a few T-DXd patients with HER2-low disease, and the results came back after the scan had already answered the question. Turnaround kills the whole concept. I'm not changing anything based on it.
I actually think early molecular response could beat imaging for bone-only disease, probably. Thresholds are still unclear, but I'd happily join a study that tests it.

In our academic clinic we bank plasma at baseline and every cycle for patients on T-DXd. Seeing ctDNA drop early in a few of them was reassuring. I could see it supporting staying the course when imaging is equivocal.

Community oncologists here can't even get HER2 IHC scoring consistent, and now we're supposed to layer ctDNA on top? Pathology first, please. Liquid biopsy for HER2-low is a non-starter at the moment.
For de-escalation I'm not convinced. Stopping T-DXd because ctDNA is negative sounds scary to me, even with ILD worries pushing us to want a shorter course. Maybe inside a trial.
My patients ask about MRD tests they read about online. I tell them it isn't validated here and insurnce won't pay. They leave frustrated, and so am I, a bit.

Early switch on rising ctDNA before radiographic progression, sounds nice but switch to what, and is there any proof it helps anyone. Without that it's just anxiety on paper, especially on T-DXd where the next options are limited
Rising ctDNA ahead of the scan has prompted me to bring imaging forward twice. It didn't change the drug, just the timing. That's a modest but practical use, and I'd keep doing it.

Frankly the ctDNA conversation is ahead of the evidence. Every vendor pitch promises MRD detection and early switching, but nobody can show me that switching earlier gives patients more time. Shedding varies a lot between tumors too, so a flat result might just mean a low shedder. We're a small regional center and the send-out takes ages. Show me a randomized strategy trial and then we talk.

I use ctDNA in a limited way, mostly in early-stage HER2-positive when a patient is anxious after neoadjuvant therapy. If T-DXd were used post-neoadjuvant I'd imagine clearance would matter. But I'm not sure persistence after treatment justifies a switch. A positive result without a plan is just stress. Probably I'd take it to tumor board case by case.

Our tumor board argued about this last month. One colleague wanted to escalate a patient on T-DXd because ctDNA hadn't cleared after a few cycles, even though imaging showed shrinkage. I thought that was overreach, and I still do. Assays differ, timing differs, and nobody knows the cutoff. We ended up ignoring the result, which defeats the purpose of ordering it.

I'm cautiously more enthusiastic than my peers. Serial ctDNA is cheap compared with what we spend on a drug like T-DXd, and if molecular response tracked with benefit it could spare people months of ineffective therapy. We'd need clear rules though, like when to draw and what a switch looks like. Our hospital lab is already set up for it, so logistics isn't the barrier. Evidence is.

Workflow is my headache. Bloods on day one of each cycle are easy, but who reviews a ctDNA report, and when? Nurses dont want another result to chase and neither do I. If it sat in the same portal as routine labs I might try it for HER2-low patients after endocrine progression. Right now it's too clunky.

The thing that bugs me is ctDNA negativity getting treated like a cure signal. In a HER2-low patient on T-DXd, a negative plasma result while a brain lesion progresses is worthless, since CNS disease probably sheds poorly. I've seen colleagues reassured by a clean result when the scan said otherwise. Liquid biopsy has blind spots and people forget that.
Not routinely, no. ctDNA doesn't change what we do with T-DXd yet.
Would love a validated MRD trigger for early switch, honestly.
Payer won't cover serial liquid biopsy outside a trial, end of story.
Tried it twice in HER2-low, results were hard to interpret.
Turnaround time kills it for us, results land after the scan already happened
A drop in ctDNA could be a nice early molecular response signal for T-DXd responders.
We send tumor-informed assays out to a reference lab and the wait is usually a couple of weeks or more. Useful for research cases, I think, but I wouldn't base a T-DXd decision on it.

Had a HER2-positive patient after neoadjuvant therapy with persistent ctDNA positivity, and it nudged the team toward closer imaging. Felt like the assay added something real. Not sure it would drive a switch on its own though.
My worry is false reassurance. If ctDNA clears but there's residual disease in a low-shedding tumor, we could de-escalate the wrong person.
Academic center, so the tumor board discusses it case by case. Most of the group feels de-escalation based on clearance is premature, while escalation on a rising signal is easier to accept.

In HER2-low, where the biology is so heterogeneous, a blood-based readout of response is appealing. If it tracked with imaging we could probably spot non-responders on T-DXd sooner and spare them cycles of toxicity.
Patients ask about it because they read online. I tell them it isn't standard, and honestly ILD vigilance on T-DXd is a much bigger daily concern than any ctDNA result.
Would need prospective data showing that switching on a ctDNA rise beats waiting for radiographic progression. Until then its a research tool for me, nothing more.
We only use it for a few trial patients. Draws line up with cycle day 1 which is convenient, but nobody acts on the result.

The main theme was that nobody trusts a negative result enough to pull back. She described a patient on T-DXd with a great radiographic response whose ctDNA stayed detectable for months, and another with clearance who progressed anyway. Her view is that shedding varies too much across HER2-low tumors, probably more than in HER2-positive disease. She also noted that brain-only progression would be invisible in plasma. So for now it's noise until proven otherwise.

Thinking out loud, the oncologist sees two possible roles: early escalation if levels rise while imaging is still quiet, and de-escalation after sustained clearance in the adjuvant setting. He's much more comfortable with the first than the second. Logistics worry him, since repeat draws every few cycles mean extra chair time and extra billing questions. He isn't against it, just wants a clear action threshold before ordering. Not sure what that threshold would even look like, to be honest.

Genuinely enthusiastic, a breast specialist at a large cancer center. She feels ctDNA molecular response could become the earliest readout of whether the DXd payload is reaching a heterogeneous tumor. Scans every couple of months feel slow when a patient is clearly struggling. She would consider an early switch if a rising signal was confirmed on a second draw. Still wants it inside a protocol, but she'd enroll patients tomorrow.

Frustrated tone throughout. Their lab offers a tumor-informed MRD panel, but insurance denials are routine and patients end up with surprise bills. Even when approved, results arrive late enough that the next T-DXd cycle has already been given. He said the idea sounds great in a talk and falls apart in a Tuesday clinic. He won't use it outside research until payers and turnaround change.

Mixed feelings overall from this community oncologist. She orders ctDNA occasionally for HER2-positive patients after surgery, mostly to reassure them, and it has never actually changed treatment. De-escalation would definately need randomized data in her opinion. She did say monitoring would matter more if T-DXd moves earlier in the treatment course, so she's keeping an eye on it.

Interesting split in the room: the translational people wanted ctDNA clearance as an endpoint, while the clinicians cared whether it changes management. The doctor I spoke with sits in the middle. She thinks clearance after a few cycles might be a decent surrogate, but only if assays are harmonized, because different panels gave her different answers. HER2 status can also differ between tissue and plasma, which complicates things further.

early_stage|osimertinib.t: Would happily use osimertinib before surgery if it let more patients get resected.
Chemo added in the early setting is a hard sell to my surgeons.
Still waiting to see how perioperative data read out before changing anything.
Not convinced adding chemo makes sense in resected stage I.
Adjuvant TKI is routine here already so perioperative feels like a natural next step
Honestly depends on whether the tumor board is on board.

At our community clinic most resected EGFR patients go straight to adjuvant osimertinib after surgery. Moving it before surgery would need thoracic surgeon buy-in, and I think that's the bottleneck. Probably would consider it if the tumor board pushed for it.

Concerned about delaying surgery in patients who could be cured upfront. If a neoadjuvant TKI doesn't shrink the tumor much, we've lost time. Also not sure how pathologic response would even be read with a targeted agent.
Younger never-smoker with resectable stage III, EGFR+ on biopsy: this is the patient I'd want a neoadjuvant option for. Would be glad to avoid immunotherapy-chemo in that group.
Payer approval is the problem for us. Prior auth teams already push back on adjuvant duration, so a perioperative request including chemo would probably sit for weeks.

Would want disease-free survival and at least some early sense of overall survival before changing practice. Pathologic response alone feels like not enough for a TKI. Oncologist at an academic-type clinic said much the same.

Toxicity worries me in the curative setting. Adding chemo on top of osimertinib for a patient who may already be cured by surgery feels like overtreatment, and a couple of docs said they'd hesitate in older patients.
Pulmonologist said she'd send for molecular testing earlier if a neoadjuvant option existed. Right now resuts often come back after surgery, so the workflow would have to change.

Oncologist at a small practice likes the idea of a perioperative approach. Said patients are motivated and would accept a few extra months of treatment if recurrence risk drops. Wants to see it both with and without chemo.

Thoracic surgeon at the hospital clinic told me he doesn't love the neoadjuvant idea for EGFR. His worry is that a partly responding tumor still needs the same resection, so the benefit is unclear. He also thinks added chemo could delay surgery if anyone has side effects. I think the med onc side is more open than he is. Without a clear staging benefit, osimertinib before surgery is probably a no for him.

Mixed feelings from an oncologist at a regional cancer center. Adjuvant is easy to explain to patients, while perioperative is a longer story with more visits. She said the data would need to show something beyond what adjuvant already gives. If it did, she'd consider it for stage II-III. Not sure about stage I at all.

Really positive conversation with a lung-focused oncologist. A lot of her EGFR patients relapse after surgery, some in the brain, so anything that improves early control is welcome. She'd use osimertinib with or without chemo in resectable stage III if the readout were clean. Her nurse navigators already coordinate testing, so scheduling wouldn't be a barrier. Main ask is long follow-up.

Pharmacist at an infusion center raised logistics. Adding chemo before surgery means chair time, antiemetics and lab monitoring on top of a daily oral drug. Their center is already stretched. They doubt many practices outside big centers could manage it smoothly. Probably they'd stick with adjuvant TKI alone.

Tumor board summary: they take curative-intent EGFR cases one at a time. A few members want neoadjuvant targeted therapy for borderline resectable disease, others prefer surgery first and then adjuvant. Everyone agreed they need a clear readout on recurrence, not just response at surgery. Nobody wanted to commit before seeing more mature follow-up.

Community oncologist asked how early-stage results would be reported. He wants outcomes split by stage and by whether chemo was used, since his patients are mostly stage I-II. He said a single pooled number wouldnt help him decide. I think he'd also want brain recurrence called out separately. Until then he'll keep using adjuvant osimertinib after surgery and wait.
Perioperative sounds logical, but I'd want the surgical data first.
Not convinced chemo belongs in a resected stage I patient.
Neoadjuvant osimertinib is appealing for borderline resectable cases.
Tumour board would need pathologic response endpoints before changing anything.
Honestly too early for us, still waiting on DFS to mature.
Keen on any osi-based approach that downstages before lobectomy.

Most of my resected patients already go on adjuvant osimertinib without much debate, he said. Adding chemo upfront in that setting feels like a hard sell unless the benefit is clearly separated from the TKI alone.

Surgeons in her group are lukewarm about neoadjuvant TKI, mostly because they worry about delaying the operation if the response is poor. She'd probably accept it with a clear imaging checkpoint a few weeks in.
Payer pushback is what I keep hearing for anything perioperative, since reimbursment tends to follow label wording. Without a clear approval pathway he wouldn't even raise it with patients.
Interested in ctDNA-guided escalation after surgery, thinks that's where early-stage is heading. Would want osimertinib alone as the default and chemo only for high-risk residual disease.
Younger patients with stage II disease are the ones she'd consider for a more intensive plan, I think. For older or frail patients, no way; tolerability worries her more than recurrence risk.
Would be excited by a pathologic response readout that actually translates into survival, not just a surrogate. Says the field has been burned by early endpoints before.

Community pulm-onc clinic with limited multidisciplinary access said coordination is the real barrier. Surgery, med onc and pathology all need to be alinged on timing, which is hard to guarantee week to week.

Positive overall, he sees a curative-intent combination as a natural extension if osimertinib tolerability holds up. His main practical question was how many chemo cycles before surgery would be realistic.

After a long discussion she said she'd genuinely like to use osimertinib earlier, ideally before surgery in a stage III patient who is otherwise marginal. Her thinking is that shrinking the tumour could turn a debatable resection into a clean one. She'd want the tumour board involved from day one. I think she'd accept chemo being added if the preoperative window stays short and nobody loses their surgical slot. Enthusiastic, but wants the readout to show surgical outcomes, not only response.

He was quite skeptical about moving the combination into curative-intent care. His worry is that a patient who would be cured by surgery alone, or by a TKI alone, gets exposed to platinum toxicity for nothing. He also mentioned that in his rural practice infusion chair capacity is limited and patients travel far. Not sure the data will ever be clean enough to show who actually needs chemo. For now he'd stay with what he knows.

We spent a while on how early-stage data should read out. Her preference is disease-free survival as the main message, with pathologic response as supportive rather than the headline. She also wants clarity by stage and by exon 19 versus L858R, though she admitted that's probably too much to ask. Quality of life during the preoperative phase matters to her, I think more than most colleagues admit. She'd reserve judgement until she sees everything together.

She feels the early-stage conversation is running ahead of the evidence, and said so more than once. In her centre resected EGFR patients already get a TKI afterward, so a perioperative change would have to beat that bar convincingly. She worries about delayed surgery, complications, and patients dropping out before adjuvant treatment even starts. Also noted that osimertinib plus chemo toxicity in an elderly resected population is an unknown. Wouldn't change practice without longer follow up

Mixed feelings, which he was upfront about. He likes the biology argument for hitting micrometastatic disease early, but isn't sure that needs chemotherapy on top of osimertinib. Turnaround for EGFR testing is another practical point, since many of his patients are operated on before results are back. If testing were reliably done preop he'd be more open. Otherwise it stays a theoretical discussion for him.

Quite positive after we talked it through. He sees the earlier setting as where the biggest gains might sit, because patients are fit and the goal is cure. He'd happily offer a perioperative regimen if the data show a clear recurrence benefit and the surgeons are on board. Said patients in his clinic already ask about it after reading online. I think he'd move fast once guidelines caught up.
Adjuvant osi already standard in my stage II-IIIA pts, no hesitation.
Neoadjuvant? Surgeons here not convinced, tumor board split.
Wants OS before changing periop practice.
Chemo add-on in resectable disease = hard sell to pts.
Would consider perioperative approach if downstaging is clear and surgery isn't delayed
Very interested in neoadjuvant osimertinib, esp for borderline resectable.
Community onc, sees few resectable EGFR+ pts. Most get adjuvant osi once molecular results are back, wouldn't flip to neoadjuvant w/o clear benefit over that. Waiting on more data.
Thoracic surgeon at tumor board asked if neoadjuvant TKI makes resection harder (fibrosis?). Not sure there's a good answer yet. Concerned about delaying surgery if pt doesn't respond.

Pt scenario: young never-smoker, stage IIIA N2, HCP would love a TKI-first route to shrink before surgery. Thinks pts tolerate osi much better than platinum chemo. Positive, but wants pathologic response data plus survival before committing.
PA for adjuvant osi usually ok, but payer asked to justify duration of tx. Neoadjuvant would be off-label so prob denial. Clinic staff already stretched on appeals.

Academic pulm onc: EGFR testing on resected specimens is the bottleneck, not the drug. If neoadjuvant, need bx results BEFORE surgery, which is a workflow change for whole team. Pathology turnaround a worry.
Doesn't see FLAURA2-style chemo combo making sense in curative setting. Too many AEs for pts who might be cured w/ surgery alone. Prefers osi mono if anything.
Likes idea of ctDNA guiding who needs adjuvant tx. Would want that to read out alongside DFS. Not there yet tho
Pts anxious about recurrence so they ask for osi as long as possible after resection. HCP is happy w/ that and thinks earlier use is where the field is going.

Med onc, big regional center. Worried neoadjuvant data will be small and single-arm and everyone will over-read it. Surgeons will push for upfront resection regardless. Also unclear which endpoint matters, pathologic response vs EFS? I think w/o EFS or OS it won't change practice. Cost of longer osi course also a payer concern.

Strongly pro early use. Every EGFR+ resected pt in clinic gets adjuvant osi now, tolerability fine, few dc's for AEs. Open to periop if surgery timing preserved. Wants DFS and CNS relapse reported separately since brain mets are the big fear. Would enroll pts if site had access.

Tumor board discussion: rad onc wants osi after chemoradiation in unresectable stage III, med onc asking where that fits vs surgery. HCP unsure how to sequence. Thinks answer is probably pt-specific. Would like data split by stage and nodal status.

Concerned about overtreatment. Some stage I pts likely cured w/ surgery alone, so why expose them to years of TKI + AEs (rash, diarrhea, ILD risk)? Wants clearer selection. Also if recurrence happens on osi, what next? Chemo combo in early stage could burn options.

Rural clinic, pts referred out for surgery so HCP rarely controls timing. For perioperative regimen would need clear comms w/ surgeon and path re: molecular results. Probably fine w/ neo or adjuvant if data support. Main issue is pts recieve chemo cycles far from home, so prefers simple oral approach.

NP in thoracic clinic. Pts ask whether they can skip chemo entirely in early stage if osi works. Honestly not sure what to tell them. Thinks a periop design of osi alone vs w/ chemo would be most useful. Wants AEs and QoL reported clearly, not buried. Pts value staying at work.
Perioperative chemo plus TKI? Show me it beats adjuvant TKI alone first.
Not sure neoadjuvant makes sense unless the downstaging is actually meaningful.
Honestly, still waiting on survival data in the adjuvant space.
Neoadjuvant osimertinib is appealing for borderline resectable stage III, I'll give it that.
Our tumor board never agrees on who's resectable anyway.
Depends entirely on what pathologic response ends up meaning.

We get EGFR results back too late, usually after the surgeon has already operated. So the neoadjuvant conversation is moot for most of my patients. Until molecular turnaround improves it's a nonstarter here.

I already use osimertinib adjuvant after resection and it's fine. Adding chemo on top in the early setting? I think I'd need a clear benefit over the TKI alone, since tolerability was the whole worry in advanced disease.

A perioperative approach would suit my community patients who often can't tolerate adjuvant chemo after a lobectomy. If a TKI up front shrinks things and the surgeon is comfortable, I'm in. Probably need MDT buy-in first.
Payer pushback is the real wall. Prior auth for off-label neoadjuvant TKI takes wekks and by then the surgical slot is gone.
Surgeons at my center are lukewarm. They like downstaging in theory but worrry about fibrosis after a TKI and delayed operations. I'm somewhere in between.
Everyone says 'cure' but I haven't seen proof that early TKI cures anyone versus just delaying recurrence. Feels like we're selling hope with a longer pill schedule.
If early-stage readouts report CNS recurrence separately, that would sway me. A lot of my relapses go to the brain, so that matters more to me than DFS alone.

My issue with adding chemo in the curative setting is that these patients may already do well on a TKI alone. Cisplatin-based regimens knock people flat, and a good chunk of my older patients never finish them. With osimertinib I at least know the side effect profile, ILD risk aside. I'm not convinced the extra toxicity buys anything real in stage II or III. Overtreating someone we hope to cure feels worse than undertreating.

I'd want pathologic response reported clearly, but I'm honestly not sure it's a valid surrogate yet. Our group would probably accept event-free survival if the curves separate and stay separated. Overall survival will take forever and I don't think anyone is waiting for it. Mostly I want the data split by stage, because IB and IIIA are different conversations.

Trial designs for early-stage EGFR disease frustrate me. Control arms often don't match what we actually do, and nobody's selecting by ctDNA or residual disease. So even a positive readout leaves me guessing who truly needs the combination. I'd also want clear stopping rules for osimertinib, because 'until progression' in someone we hope is cured makes no sense to me.

I had one young never-smoker with bulky stage IIIA N2 where upfront osimertinib got her to surgery, and she's doing well. Not a trial, just one patient, so salt required. Still, it changed how I think about the neoadjuvant option. If formal data back it, I'd bring it to tumor board routinely. The surgeons were more open than I expected.

Finally someone is looking at the early setting with the combo instead of just copying advanced disease. I'm cautiously optimistic that adding chemo might help higher-risk resected patients, maybe those with nodal involvement. Probably wouldn't use it in IB. If recurrence drops in a way I can see, I'd happily take on the extra infusion chair time.

Workflow is the headache. Small biopsies often don't give enough tissue for NGS so we wait on plasma, and then the surgeon wants a date. Neoadjuvant osimertinib only works if pathology, molecular and surgery all line up and in my clinic they barely talk to each other
Osimertinib in resectable disease sounds neat until you ask who monitors for resistance after surgery. We have no clean plan for what happens at recurrence. Feels like the cart is ahead of the horse.

early_stage|pembrolizumab.t: Keen on periop pembro for resectable gastric, esp. if OS matures.
Wants EFS AND OS before changing anything in resectable disease.
Community onc, no thoracic surgeon on site. Periop sequencing = logistical headache, pts get lost between referral and OR. Would need a clear timeline in the data before even trying.
Tumor board already defaults to periop IO for lung, fitness permitting.
Worried about pts who never make it to surgery after neoadjuvant tx.
Honestly unsure how to read pCR without survival.
Academic med onc likes treating while tumor still in situ. Immune priming makes sense to them, but they're not sure the adjuvant phase adds much. Wants that teased apart.
Saw a pt w/ big path response on neoadjuvant pembro + chemo, surgeon was happy. HCP says cases like that are why they want a periop option in gastric too. Would use it if label allows.
PA for adjuvant continuation keeps stalling at the payer. Pt finishes surgery, then waits weeks for approval. HCP thinks the gap undermines whole periop idea.
Adjuvant-only data? meh, prefers starting before surgery
Re gastric: probably wants PD-L1 CPS subgroup readout before use. If benefit sits only in high CPS, would restrict to those pts. Not sure how tumor board would feel about that.

Surgeon, thoracic. No problems operating post-IO so far, margins and healing fine in their experience. Says dissection can be a bit stickier sometimes but nothing that changed plans. Fine to keep going.
Concerned re AEs, esp. hepatitis or thyroid issues pushing back OR date. Borderline PS pts mostly. Manageable I think, but delays in curative setting feel higher stakes than in mets.

Lots of older, comorbid pts in this clinic, many cisplatin-unfit. HCP doubts trial populations look like their waiting room. Worried that periop regimen = lots of tx for pts who might not finish it. Also unclear what happens if they stop mid-way, do they still get adjuvant IO? Would want real-world-ish data, not just selected pts.

Workflow is the sticking point for this HCP. Biopsy, staging, board review, then start tx; each step adds days. Likes the concept of periop IO. Wants readout to show time-to-surgery clearly, plus how many pts completed all phases. Said they'd decide after seeing that, not before.

Cost worries mostly. Long periop course of IO in pts who may already be cured by surgery = big spend and financial toxicity for pt. HCP not against it per se. Payer pushback expected, esp. if benefit shown only on EFS. Thinks pharmacy committee will ask for OS.

Gastric periop HCP hopes IO layers onto FLOT backbone w/o killing tolerability. Tumor board is eager, a few members already asking about it. Would like to see pts get to surgery on schedule. If the data hold up he'd switch most eligible pts. Excited, but waiting on full readout.

Lung: asks whether EGFR/ALK pts excluded, and how to handle biomarker results that come back late. Doesn't want to start neoadjuvant IO then find a driver. Thinks testing turnaround is the real bottleneck. Would want readout to say clearly who was screened out.

Skeptical on EFS as surrogate in curative setting. Overtreatment is the fear, some pts cured w/ surgery alone get exposed to IO and late immune AEs for no gain. Not sure we can tell who. Wants long f/u before calling this standard, and says pts shuld be counselled on that.
Perioperative framing makes sense to me; I'd use it routinely if survival benefit holds.
Not convinced the neoadjuvant phase is worth risking delayed surgery in frail patients.
Honestly waiting on longer follow-up before changing our MDT pathway.
Toxicity before resection worries our surgeons more than anything else.
Pembro in curative-intent gastric, yes please, if the biomarker story is clean.
Unclear whether the adjuvant phase adds anything beyond teh neoadjuvant part, needs dissecting.

Community oncologist said she'd only start perioperative immunotherapy if the surgeon is on board and an OR slot is guaranteed. Otherwise the delay just creates stress for patients. She sees it as a logistics question first and efficacy second.

Regional hospital oncologist worries about immune-related adverse events landing right before surgery, especially endocrine ones that complicate anesthesia. He'd probably stay with chemo alone for borderline-fit patients. Wants to see how many actually make it to the OR on time.

Thoracic surgeon was quite enthusiastic, since in his experience downstaging has made resections cleaner. He'd like pathologic response reported in a standardized way so teams can compare programs without guessing.

Payer approval timing came up. In her centre authorisation for neoadjuvant therapy can take weeks, which defeats the purpose of moving quickly to surgery. Not sure that's a data issue but it clearly shapes uptake.

He said the PD-L1 question in gastric is still unresolved and he dislikes treating everyone if only a subset truly benefits. Wants subgroup readouts before he commits to a blanket approach, and no, a broad label alone won't convince him.

Academic GI oncologist thinks perioperative immunotherapy is where things are heading, but MSI-high patients are a separate conversation in his mind. I think he'd want the early-stage readout split that way, with dMMR clearly shown on its own.

Tumor board lead said that after seeing a few patients with major pathologic responses in lung he is far more open to the perioperative approach. Still wants event-free survival to mature before he calls it standard.

Concerned about overtreatment: some early-stage patients would be cured with surgery alone and he doesn't want to expose them to a year of immunotherapy. He'd probably restrict use to higher-risk nodal disease until selection tools improve.

Long chat with a hospital-based oncologist who runs a busy lung clinic. He likes the idea of starting treatment while the tumor is still in place because it feels biologically logical. But he kept returning to the adjuvant year and whether every patient should continue after a good pathologic response. I think he'd want a clear signal on de-escalation before he's fully comfortable. For now he'd follow the label and discuss each case at tumor board.

Gastric surgeon was frankly skeptical. His main fear is that patients who progress or get sick during neoadjuvant therapy lose their window for curative surgery, and he has seen that with chemo already. He said adding an immunotherapy agent could make that worse if toxicity is unpredictable. He also noted that nutrition status in gastric patients is often poor to begin with. Not sure any readout would fully calm that concern unless resection rates are transparent.

This was one of the more positive conversations. The oncologist said curative-intent settings are where immunotherapy should matter most, because the immune system is still intact and tumor burden is low. She has already moved a few lung patients to a perioperative plan and the surgeons cooperated well. She'd like readouts to emphasise how many patients completed the whole sequence. If that looks reasonable, she'd expect colleagues to adopt it fairly quickly.

Pharmacist-oncologist hybrid in a smaller centre mentioned cost and monitoring burden. A year-long schedule means a lot of infusion chair time, plus labs for thyroid and liver, and their day unit is already stretched. He supports the science but worries that rural patients will recieve only the neoadjuvant part because travel is hard. He wondered whether any shorter adjuvant course could be considered. Overall more concerned than opposed.

Medical oncologist described how she'd like early-stage data presented: clear separation of neoadjuvant versus adjuvant contribution, plus patient-reported quality of life across the whole course. She thinks pembrolizumab is probably a reasonable option for fit patients already, though she isn't sure how to handle those with autoimmune history. She would also like real-world completion rates once uptake grows. Until then she's comfortable but not evangelical, and mostly wants more clarity on sequencing.
Wants biomarker-guided selection before broad use, but open to it.
Pembro periop in lung? Fine, but show me OS first.
Honestly pembro toxicity worry in curative patients keeps me cautious.
Would use pembrolizumab in resectable lung tomorrow if our pathway allowed it.
Perioperative immunotherapy has genuinely changed my resectable lung conversations.
Interested, not convinced.
Early-stage gastric data feels years behind lung, and that's frustrating.
Our tumor board argues every time about whether to give the adjuvant phase after a good pathologic response on pembro. Nobody has a clean answer, and I'm not sure the data will ever give us one.
Surgeons in my network hate the delay risk. If a patient gets neoadjuvant immunotherapy and then has an immune-related event, the OR slot dissapears and they blame us.
In resectable NSCLC I've started to see the perioperative approach as a reasonable default for fit patients. Community colleagues still hesitate, mostly because of biomarker turnaround.
Payer approval is the bottleneck for us, not belief in the concept. Prior auth for pembro in the perioperative setting takes weeks, probably longer than the window we have before surgery

I don't buy that all the benefit comes from the neoadjuvant part, but I can't prove it either. Without a design that splits the phases I can't tell who needs the post-op cycles, and thats a real problem in curative patients.
For gastric I'd want to see how pembro sits next to standard perioperative chemo before changing anything. Maybe it's a good add-on, maybe it just adds toxicity, I cant say.

Older patients with borderline fitness rarely get through the full perioperative sequence in my clinic. The pembrolizumab regimen looks fine on paper, but trials select fitter people than I actually see.
Pembrolizumab in the curative setting makes sense biologically, and I'd like pCR and EFS to read out together. If both move in the same direction I'd be comfortable using it more broadly.

I'm frustrated with how early-stage readouts get oversold. Event-free survival looks nice, but the curves are always immature when we're asked to change practice. I want overall survival, and I want to know what happened to the patients who never made it to surgery. A few of mine progressed during neoadjuvant treatment and nobody talks about them. Until that's transparent I'll treat the headline with suspicion.

We're a smaller regional hospital, so everything hinges on whether thoracic surgery, pathology and oncology can sync up. PD-L1 results back in time is hit and miss. When it works, pembro before and after surgery is straightforward enough. When it doesn't, we default to chemo alone. I think workflow is a bigger barrier than the evidence, honestly.

I'm fairly positive on the lung perioperative data, I'll admit. Several of my resected patients did well and a couple had striking pathologic responses on the specimen. What I'd want next is clarity on who can safely skip the adjuvant phase. If ctDNA or a biomarker could tell us, that would change my clinic. Compared to chemo alone, though, I wouldn't go back.

Gastric is where I'm most skeptical. MSI and PD-L1 status seem to matter a lot, yet the early-stage question gets discussed as if everybody benefits. Most of my gastric patients are frail after gastrectomy and don't tolerate the adjuvant leg anyway. I'd want honest subgroup reporting, not buried in a supplement. Otherwise I'm not sure I can justify adding pembrolizumab to an already rough regimen.

Long-term toxicity bothers me in patients we're trying to cure. Endocrine problems tend to stick around for life, and a younger patient may carry that for decades. I'm not saying don't use it, just that the trade-off should be discussed openly. Late effects reporting is usually an afterthought in these trials, in my view.

Nobody talks about cost. Our payer already pushes back on long immunotherapy courses in the metastatic setting, so I expect a fight when we ask for it in curative patients too. And if the benefit is mostly from the pre-op part, we'd be paying for adjuvant cycles that might not add much. I'd like the economics addressed upfront, not after approval.
Would use perioperative pembro in resectable NSCLC if the surgeons stay on board.
Not convinced adjuvant continuation adds much after the neoadjuvant phase.
Waiting for more follow-up on pembro before changing the tumor board default.
Worried about surgery delays, thats the main thing.
Gastric perioperative immunotherapy data still feels early to me, honestly.
Community oncologist, happy to see immunotherapy move earlier in curative lung cases.

Runs a mid-size community practice with two thoracic surgeons referring in. Likes the perioperative concept but says the referral loop has to be tight so patients don't stall between neoadjuvant cycles and the OR. Would start offering it once the pathway is set.

Has seen a few patients come back from neoadjuvant treatment with thyroid or skin toxicity, and it complicates surgical timing. Pembrolizumab itself isn't the issue, I think, it's the coordination. Wants clearer guidance on when to hold off.

Thoracic group at a teaching-affiliated clinic already treats resectable stage III with perioperative pembro. The multidisciplinary meeting now defaults to discussing it for every fit patient. Pathology response reporting is getting more consistent.

For gastric, he mostly sees older patients with comorbidities who struggle to finish perioperative chemo. Not sure adding a checkpoint inhibitor changes that. Would want subgroup reads before leaning in.
Prior auth for the adjuvant portion is slow at her infusion center. Patients finish surgery and then wait weeks for approval. She thinks that undermines the whole perioperative idea

Said he wants early-stage readouts to split PD-L1 subgroups clearly and to show event-free survival next to overall survival once mature. Otherwise it's hard to explain pembrolizumab's role to patients in clinic.
Thoracic oncologist likes that the neoadjuvant approach lets him see response before surgery. Tends to prefer it over adjuvant-only for resectable disease.
Concerned about overtreatment, since some patients would probably be cured with surgery alone. He doesn't see a practical way to pick them out upfront.

Small hospital-based oncology unit with no in-house thoracic surgery, so patients travel for resection. She said that makes perioperative regimens harder because neoadjuvant doses are given locally and surgery happens elsewhere. Adjuvant dosing then restarts back at her clinic, sometimes late. She is interested in pembrolizumab here but thinks logistics decide uptake more than data. Probably would adopt it if the surgical center sent clear instructions.

Gastro-oncology lead at a large clinic said gastric perioperative immunotherapy is hard to picture in his population. Many patients are nutritionally depleted at diagnosis and some never reach the adjuvant phase. He worries that adding a PD-1 to chemo raises dropout before surgery. He'd want a readout showing how many completed the full sequence, not just who was randomized. Not against it, just skeptical for now.

Thoracic oncologist at a regional cancer center called KEYNOTE-671 practice-shifting for her resectable cases. Her tumor board now asks about candidacy before any surgery date is booked. She said patients like that treatment starts right away. What she'd still like is a clearer read on who can skip the adjuvant part. Overall supportive.

Private practice, two oncologists, no nurse navigator. He uses perioperative pembro selectively, mostly in patients with good performance status and clear staging. Biomarker results often aren't back when the decision is needed, so the first visit gets pushed. He's fine with that tradeoff, I think. Wants readouts to say what to do when molecular testing is pending.

Radiation oncologist at a hospital clinic said the curative-intent conversation gets muddy once immunotherapy is added upfront. Some patients who would have gone to chemoradiation now get pushed toward surgical pathways. Staging disagreements at the tumor board slow decisions. He's also unsure how to sequence care if response is poor after the neoadjuvant phase. Wants cleaner algorithms.

Gastric surgeon-oncologist said they already give perioperative chemo to nearly all resectable gastric patients. Immunotherapy added to that would need to fit the same FLOT-like schedule without extra visits. He likes the idea in principle. He'd look at how toxicity affects surgical readiness before committing. For now he'd discuss it case by case.
Thoracic surgeon at a community hospital is keen to use pembro before surgery.
Worried about patients who never make it to surgery after the neoadjuvant cycles.
Wants to see more on who actually needs the adjuvant phase.
Pembro perioperative in gastric, not convinced yet and wants more data first
Already uses it perioperatively for resectable NSCLC, no complaints so far.
Tumor board still debating sequencing, honestly.

In her small regional practice the tumor board only meets every other week, which slows the neoadjuvant start. She thinks logistics matter as much as the drug itself. Probably would use pembrolizumab more if the pathway were faster.

Medical oncologist at a private clinic said payers keep asking for extra paperwork for perioperative immunotherapy in gastric cancer. Approvals can take a couple of weeks, and by then the surgery slot is often gone. Not sure it's worth the hassle for borderline resectable patients.
Surgeon at an academic center said resections after neoadjuvant treatment have felt fine in his lung patients. He's comfortable referring early and likes having one regimen from start to finish.

Wants the readout to separate the neoadjuvant contribution from the adjuvant contribution. Right now he can't tell which part is doing the work, I think. Would still offer pembro for the full course for now.

Pathology lead at a cancer centre said response reporting after neoadjuvant therapy varies a lot between labs. She doesn't trust it as a stand-in for outcomes yet. Wants event-free survival to mature before she changes practice.
For gastric he mostly sticks with chemo-based perioperative regimens and is waiting to see where a PD-1 fits. Patients with high PD-L1 might be the first he'd try it in, but he's not sure.

Older patients in his rural clinic often strugle to finish adjuvant cycles after a big resection. He's concerned that adding immunotherapy makes that worse. Would want tolerability data in frail patients before using it.

The nurse-led infusion unit has had a smooth time with perioperative pembro in lung, with mostly manageable side effects. The oncologist there said he'd be happy to extend that to gastric if the data supports it.

Thoracic oncologist at a large hospital said most of her early-stage lung patients are now discussed before any surgery is booked. She likes the perioperative approach in principle, mainly for stage III disease. What she is less sure about is patients with EGFR or ALK alterations, who she thinks probably benefit less. She'd like the data to show clearly which subgroups were included. Until then she stays selective.

A GI oncologist at a community practice said his gastric patients often arrive malnourished and surgery already gets delayed. He worries a neoadjuvant immunotherapy phase would push things back even more. Immune-related events like colitis or hepatitis could also derail the operation. He'd want clear guidance on when to stop and go to surgery. Right now the risk-benefit isn't clear to him for his population.

Oncologist at a teaching hospital said he's genuinely excited about moving immunotherapy into curative-intent settings. In lung he has seen a few patients go to surgery with very little tumor left, and that has changed how he talks to families. He'd like the gastric data to read out just as cleanly, with event-free survival as the main message. Nothing fancy, just a clear picture of who benefits. If that happens he'd adopt it quickly.

Pharmacy lead at a cancer clinic mentioned that perioperative regimens are hard to schedule because of the long gap between the neoadjuvant and adjuvant phases. They have to track who is due back and wether surgery actually happened. It isn't a deal breaker. They'd just prefer a simple flow chart. Overall neutral on the drug, it's more about workflow.

Medical oncologist said he sees too many patients finish neoadjuvant therapy and then end up too unwell for the adjuvant part. In practice the perioperative plan often becomes neoadjuvant only. He wants the data to report how many people actually got every phase. Otherwise he feels the headline benefit overstates what happens in his clinic. He's skeptical until that is shown.

From the surgical side at a mid-size hospital, he said he doesn't mind either way as long as the operation isn't delayed. Pembrolizumab before surgery is fine with him if the medical team starts promptly. He hasn't noticed much difference in the operating room so far, but he only does a handful of these a year. For gastric he'd need to hear more, and he'd like the readout to say something about surgical complications.

early_stage|sacituzumab govitecan.t: Not before we see data in patients who actually recur on standard adjuvant therapy.
Would happily use it for residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy if the data hold up.
Interesting idea, but I'd need a pathologic response signal first.
Too toxic for curative intent in my view, the neutropenia worries me most.
Perioperative bladder question still wide open; cisplatin-ineligible patients are the obvious target.
Residual disease after neoadjuvant chemo plus IO is where I'd want this tested.
Running a community clinic, I'd only consider it adjuvant if the schedule fits our infusion chair capacity. Day 1 and day 8 dosing is a big ask for patients who may already be cured.

My worry is long-term tolerability, especially diarrhea and hair loss in women treated with curative intent. People accept a lot when metastatic, much less when they've been told they're probably cured.
For MIBC patients who can't get cisplatin, I'd be very keen on a TROP2 ADC before cystectomy. Current options leave a real gap, and a strong pCR-type result would defintely get my attention.
Payers will probably want EFS or OS eventually, not just pCR, before approving anything in early disease. I'm not sure pathologic endpoints alone would move our formulary committee.
Adjuvant HR+ already has endocrine therapy and CDK4/6 options, so I struggle to see where SG fits. Maybe only post-neoadjuvant high-risk patients, but that's a small group.
Our surgeons would want to know about wound healing and any delay to the operation. If it pushes surgery out, that's a hard sell at tumor board.
I'd be open to referring patients with residual disease into a trial. A handful of my patients are quite motivated and ask about newer ADCs all the time.
Depends on the readout. If it's invasive disease-free survival in a high-risk residual disease group I'd listen, but a pCR-only story wouldn't change what I do.

Long conversation, and the overall tone was cautiously curious rather than convinced. They see the logic of moving a TROP2 ADC earlier, particularly for aggressive biology, but most of their HR+ patients do fine on endocrine therapy plus CDK4/6 so they can't picture where sacituzumab slots in. They'd want a clearly defined high-risk group, probably residual disease or high genomic risk. Quality of life should be reported up front, not buried in a supplement. I think they'd enroll patients but not prescribe off-label.

The concern kept coming back to the risk-benefit balance in curative settings. Most of their early-stage patients are 'well' and working, and they were uneasy about adding a regimen with notable myelosuppression and GI effects. They said that a small survival gain probably wouldn't justify it unless the control arm was clearly weak. Also worried about dose delays interfering with radiotherapy timing. Overall skeptical, though not closed to seeing data.

Genuinely enthusiastic after we talked it through. They feel the biggest unmet need is patients who finish neoadjuvant treatment with residual disease and are at high risk of relapse. If an ADC could be given post-surgery and show a meaningful benefit in recurrence, they'd adopt it quickly in their academic-style clinic. They'd want clear guidance on sequencing with other adjuvant agents. I think they'd also support a bladder study in the perioperative window.

They kept returning to the point that the metastatic data don't translate automatically. Different patients, different disease burden, and a much lower tolerance for toxicity. There was also a practical worry about cost: if the drug is used before surgery in many patients, budgets could be strained, and payers may refuse without hard survival endpoints. They also mentioned that nurses are already stretched with the current infusion load. So not a no, but very doubtful for now.

Mixed feelings, I'd say. On one hand, they can see that a perioperative bladder approach might spare some patients from relapse, especially those who can't tolerate cisplatin. On the other, they worry about overtreating people who'd be cured by surgery alone, and there's no good way yet to identify them. They'd like biomarker work, maybe TROP2 expression or ctDNA, built into any early-stage design. Until then they'd see it as a trial-only option.

Frankly I think this is premature. The conversation circled around how little we know about durability and late effects, and they don't want to expose curable patients to an unknown. A few patients of theirs have already asked about it after reading online, which creates pressure they find unhelpful. They'd need very mature follow-up before even discussing it with a tumor board. Until then, standard of care stays.
Would absolutely enroll pts in a neoadjuvant SG trial if one opened.
Curative setting, tox bar way higher. Not sold on SG there yet.
Need pCR AND EFS before I'd change anything.
Adjuvant HR+? Too many decent options already, honestly
Perioperative UC interest high, esp cis-ineligible pts.
Waiting on early-stage data no opinion yet
Community onc here, mostly HR+ pts post endocrine + CDK4/6. Would consider neoadjuvant use only if residual disease pts showed a clear benefit signal. Probably needs a tumor board discussion first.
Neutropenia and alopecia worry me for curative-intent pts. Someone who'd be cured with less tx won't tolerate grade 3 AEs from SG. Not sure it's worth it in low-risk HR+.
Bladder-sparing is where I see the biggest unmet need. If SG plus something shrinks tumor pre-cystectomy, our urology colleagues would be very interested.
Academic breast clinic. I think neoadjuvant SG is the logical next step after the 2L data, but I'd want DFS as primary readout, not just pCR. Surrogates in HR+ are shaky.
PA burden already heavy for 2L+ use. Extending to early-stage w/o OS or EFS data = denials galore, prob.
Surgeons asked about wound healing and timing to OR with SG. Unknown, so a washout window would need defining. Med onc more open to this than surgery side.
Residual disease pts post-surgery are the only adjuvant group I'd consider SG for, probably. Would need a clear DFS signal first. Still undecided.
Honestly dont see it in adjuvant. Pts on endocrine tx do well and ADC AEs would hit QoL hard.

Tumor board pushed back this week on ADCs in curative setting. Consensus: interesting biology, but we treat lots of HR+ pts who'd never relapse. Would want a genomic risk score or biomarker to pick high-risk pts. TROP2 expression as selector, not sure that's validated. Would watch a high-risk residual disease trial first.

Concerned about overtreatment. Most early-stage pts are cured w/ standard tx, so adding SG exposes many to tox w/o benefit. Neutropenia and GI AEs mean dose delays, which hurt schedule completion. Infusion chair capacity at our site is tight too. I'd need a clear EFS gain before even discussing.

Very excited re perioperative UC. Cis-ineligible pts have limited choices and many relapse after cystectomy. If SG showed pathologic response in neoadjuvant trial I'd refer pts right away. Urologists on our board keep asking. Would want path response plus DFS reported together, with QoL.

A few pts asked about 'earlier use' after reading online. I explain no early-stage data yet. For HR+, adjuvant is a stretch, but neoadjuvant in high-risk luminal B maybe. Payer would be the gatekeeper. Not sure what readout beyond EFS would convince me.

Readout worry: if trial uses pCR only I'm skeptical. pCR is low in HR+ and doesn't track outcomes well. Long follow-up needed, so years. Meanwhile pts ask for SG off-label with no support. Also don't want crossover muddying the picture.

Positive on moving earlier. Small private practice, our HR+ pts relapse on endocrine and burn through lines fast, so hitting disease earlier makes sense. Would want DFS, QoL and clear G-CSF guidance. I'd definately use SG in high-risk pts post-surgery if label allowed. Hope trials enroll real-world pts, not just ideal ones.
Would want DFS, not just pCR, before using it neoadjuvant.
Keen on sacituzumab for residual disease after neoadjuvant chemo, honestly.
Too toxic for curative intent unless EFS clearly moves.
Neutropenia worries me in adjuvant, those patients feel well.
Waiting on early-stage data first no opinion yet.
Perioperative use in MIBC would fill a real gap.

Community oncologist sees only a few high-risk early breast cases a month, mostly HR+. She'd consider an ADC after neoadjuvant therapy only if there's a clear invasive DFS gain over what adjuvant CDK4/6 gives. Not sure how she'd sequence it with the other options.

Academic breast surgeon said the neoadjuvant window is already crowded with chemo plus IO. Adding an ADC means another toxicity profile before surgery and maybe a delayed OR date. He'd need to see surgical timing stay unaffected.

Urothelial GU oncologist at a large center is interested in SG for cisplatin-ineligible MIBC before cystectomy. Says many of those patients get nothing neoadjuvant right now, so even a modest pathologic response signal would get his attention.
Payer issues come up first for her. Prior auth for an adjuvant ADC in the curative setting would be a headace, plus it eats infusion chair time. She probably wouldn't go off label.
Said ctDNA-guided escalation would make the most sense to him, treating only those with MRD after surgery. Not sure the assays are reliable enough in his clinic yet.

Nurse practitioner running an infusion unit said the day 1 and 8 schedule, hair loss and diarrhea management would be a hard sell to patients who may already be cured. Still thinks it depends on the size of the benefit.
He doesn't think pCR alone is enough, since it's been a shaky surrogate in HR+ disease. Wants EFS with long enough follow-up. Until then he'd keep sacituzumab in the metastatic box.

Medical oncologist in a regional hospital would happily enroll patients in an adjuvant sacituzumab study for HR+ disease with residual tumor. Says options are thin after neoadjuvant chemo and patients ask about it.

Mixed feelings from a breast med onc in a mid-size private practice. She likes the idea of an ADC after neoadjuvant therapy for patients with residual disease, since that's where she feels stuck. But she'd want to know if it replaces or adds to current adjuvant options, depending on subtype. Probably wouldn't change anything until there's a randomized readout. SG would also need to be tolerable in people who feel fine.

Urologic oncologist is worried about delaying cystectomy. Most of his patients are older with kidney issues, so neoadjuvant anything is already a stretch. He'd be concerned about neutropenic complicatons right before major surgery. Wants perioperative complication rates reported clearly, not buried in a supplement. Not convinced it fits outside a trial.

Tumor board discussion at a university hospital was fairly upbeat on sacituzumab govitecan moving earlier, especially for high-risk HR+ cases with residual disease. They liked the TROP2 mechanism and assumed the target is present in early disease too. Main ask was a clean EFS readout with patient-reported outcomes alongside. One member said that if it could spare anthracycline they'd be very interested.

Pharmacist and oncologist at a community cancer center both flagged cost. Curative-intent use means many more patients and longer exposure than metastatic, and the formulary committee would push back hard. G-CSF support and diarrhea calls would also add to nursing workload. They'd need very convincing early-stage data. For now it stays in the later-line box for them.

A surgical oncologist wanted to know how the data would read out for operability. He cares about pCR, but also breast conservation rates and time to surgery. Said it would help to see results split by HR status instead of pooled. No strong view on the drug itself yet.

Genitourinary oncologist at a network clinic said bladder-sparing is where the interest would be. If an ADC plus IO produced enough complete responses to skip cystectomy in selected patients, it would change practice discussions. But he's skeptical about durability and about how anyone would define response. He'd want long follow-up and strict endpoints before offering it, I think.
Not convinced SG belongs near curative intent until the toxicity is sorted.
Perioperative? Show me pCR and EFS first, then we talk.
Neutropenia and alopecia in someone we're trying to cure is a hard sell, even with SG.
Honestly, if SG deepens response preop I'd be interested.
Too many adjuvant trials already, nobody can enroll them all
Maybe in residual disease after neoadjuvant chemo, that I'd actually look at.

Our breast clinic is already stretched supporting metastatic patients with G-CSF and chair time. Now picture doing that with sacituzumab in a neoadjuvant population who mostly do fine on standard therapy. I just don't see the infusion capacity.
I'd be open to sacituzumab in high-risk HR+ patients who respond poorly to preop endocrine therapy. We have very little to offer them. Safety has to be good enough though, and I'm not sure it is.

In bladder, perioperative is where the action is, especially cisplatin-ineligible patients heading to cystectomy. Whether a TROP2 ADC fits there against the existing ADC-plus-PD-1 regimens, I'm not sure. Sequencing is going to be a mess.
Payers fight us on everything in metastatic already. For early-stage they'll want clear survival benefit, and a pCR bump won't cut it with them. I expect months of prior-auth pain.
I think the endpoint matters more than the drug here. If it's only pCR in neoadjuvant I'd shrug, but for adjuvant I'd want DFS at minimum and probably OS eventually.

Frankly most HR+ early-stage patients do well on endocrine plus CDK4/6, so adding SG with its GI toxicity feels like overtreatment. If someone delivers real biomarker selection for the true high-risk ones, I'd reconsider. Right now that piece is missing.

Community oncologists I hear from would welcome anything for patients with residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy. It's the gap everyone complains about. If sac gov reads out clean there, uptake would be quick.
Diarrhea management in the outpatient setting is a headache already. Doing it in patients heading for surgery, with possible delays to the OR, makes me nervous.

We've been burned before by ADCs that looked great late-line and fizzled earlier. I'm skeptical that response in heavily pretreated metastatic disease translates to curative intent.
