Dose intensity worries me too, since reductions in early-stage would undermine the point of using sacituzumab at all. And nobody has explained how UGT1A1 testing fits a preop timeline. Until then I'm not holding my breath.

If I could design the readout, I'd want separate cohorts by subtype, not a blended pile. For HR+ I'd look at event-free survival with long enough follow-up, plus quality of life measured honestly. Surgeons will want wound healing and delay data. I'm not sure the sponsor will wait for mature numbers, which frustrates me.

I'll admit I'm cautiously excited. Residual disease after neoadjuvant treatment in triple-negative gets a couple of options, but in HR+ it's thin. A TROP2 agent with real activity in metastatic disease is a logical thing to push earlier. My patients are mostly fit and motivated, so I think they'd tolerate it if supportive care is solid. Still want data before I get ahead of myself.

At our urology tumor board nobody wanted to commit patients to a perioperative ADC trial when established regimens exist. Referal pathways between urology and med onc are clunky as it is. Add the neoadjuvant window before cystectomy and half the patients are gone before enrolling. It feels like a trial that will struggle with accrual.

Not against it. Early use makes biologic sense, since TROP2 is probably expressed in primary tumors, but I don't know how much that matters. Toxicity is the big question mark, and so is cost versus what we do now. I'd consider sacituzumab for a clincal trial patient, not off-label.

Too much hype. Everyone wants the adjuvant indication for the market, not because patients are asking. Curative-intent patients will accept a lot of toxicity, sure, but only if benefit is clear, and so far we're extrapolating from advanced disease. I've watched patients quit early from fatigue and cytopenias. Sac gov data in early-stage better show most people finish the planned course.

early_stage|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: Would use T-DXd neoadjuvant in a heartbeat if pCR data hold up.
Not de-escalating from TCHP on pCR alone, needs iDFS first.
Interested, but ILD risk in a curative pt makes this HCP nervous.
Tumor board wants HER2-low neoadj data before even discussing it, nothing yet.
Adjuvant after residual disease = obvious niche, if PA doesnt block it.
Too early to say, waiting on readouts.
Community onc, 2 MDs. Both say curative setting = low tolerance for tox, esp. pneumonitis monitoring w/o easy CT access. Would probably refer out to a bigger center for early-stage tx.
HCP thinks HER2-low early stage is a real unmet need, esp. HR+ pts w/ residual disease after neoadj chemo. Not sure how a trial would be designed tho. Wants EFS, not just pCR.
Onc working closely w/ breast surgeons is keen on T-DXd pre-op for node+ HER2+ pts. Thinks downstaging could change the surgical plan. Wants imaging response data alongside path.
Payer worry. Off-label neoadjuvant = PA denial, pt waits weeks, surgery gets delayed. Not worth the headache for this clinic.
Said probably reserve for pts w/ residual disease post-neoadj, not upfront. Needs to beat current standard on recurrence, whatever endpoint ends up being used.
Concern re nausea and fatigue stacked on surgery recovery. Thinks pts in curative intent accept fewer AEs than mets pts. Would want clear QoL data.
Excited about the ADC moving earlier, mets benefit makes it logical to this HCP. Would enroll pts in an investigator trial if the site is eligible.
Raised sequencing: if T-DXd used early, what's left at recurrence? No good answer yet. Tumor board split on this.

Large practice, mostly HR+/HER2-low. HCP calls early-stage use 'interesting but premature'. Wants pts w/ residual disease after neoadj chemo studied first since that's where need is clearest. Asked about duration, fixed cycles vs until tox? Thinks adherence to q3w infusions plus monitoring could be an issue in adjuvant.

Skeptical overall. Curative setting means most pts do fine on existing regimens, so bar for anything new is high. Would need DFS benefit and a clean safety profile, esp. ILD and cardiac. Worried about overtreating pts who'd be cured anyway. Doesn't trust pCR as a surrogate, not sure regulators do either. Wouldn't change practice off a small or single-arm study.

Positive tone. HCP sees T-DXd as natural next step for HER2+ pts w/ residual disease, where options feel limited. Would want a clear stopping rule and an ILD monitoring plan up front. Said if the data are clean, tumor board would adopt fast. Mentioned pts ask about it already after hearing of mets results.

Infusion center capacity is the bottleneck, per this HCP. Adding perioperative T-DXd means more chair time, baseline and serial scans, and pulmonary check-ins. Staff already stretched with current neoadj regimens. Thinks smaller sites simply couldn't run it. Also unclear who owns ILD surveillance, onc or surgeon.

Asked how data should read out: wants EFS or iDFS, split by HR status, and HER2-low vs ultralow if possible. Also OS eventually but knows that takes years. Would like pCR reported but not as primary. Said without nodal status breakdown it's hard to apply to clinic pts. Neutral on whether to adopt, depends entirely on the readout.

Academic HCP, undecided. Likes the biology rationale for earlier use but worries about cumulative tox vs benefit in pts who may be cured. Thinks a de-escalation angle, fewer cytotoxic agents, could be attractive. Not sure the design exists yet. Will revisit when more early-stage data emerge.
Not touching it in a curative setting until I see a real EFS signal.
Neoadjuvant interest is there, honestly, but only if pCR holds up.
ILD risk in someone we're trying to cure? Hard sell.
Would use it for residual disease after neoadjuvant, yes, if the data back it.
Call me when there's actual early-stage data, not before.
Perioperative sequencing is the big unknown for me imo

Our tumor board already asks about T-DXd for patients with residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy. If a trial reads out clean I think we'd move fast, because the current post-surgical options feel tired.

Community practice here, and infusion chair time is already tight. Adding scheduled scans for ILD surveillance in adjuvant patients who feel fine is a workflow headache, though I'd do it if the benefit were clear.
Payers will balk at anything in early stage without mature survival data. We'd be fighting prior auths for months, and I'm not sure my staff can absorb that.
The metastatic HER2-low data don't translate for me. Different biology, different risk tolerance, and I'm not extrapolating to curative intent just because the ADC works later on.
I'd want pCR read alongside long-term outcomes, not as a standalone surrogate. Not sure the field agrees on that though, and I think too many people are sloppy about it.
For high-risk node-positive HER2+ patients, putting an ADC upfront makes sense on paper. I'd enroll without hesitation if a trial were open near us.
Cardiac and pulmonary follow-up add up quick in a young adjuvant patient. My nurses are already stretched and nobody has told me who owns the monitoring. Frankly that worries me more than efficacy.
We're an academic site, so I'd probably wait for guideline inclusion. Until then it's trial only, no off-label early use, and I don't think my colleagues would disagree.

My main worry is toxicity in people who might already be cured by standard treatment. Nausea, fatigue and the lung risk are tolerable in metastatic disease, but in early stage we'd be harming some patients who never needed it. I haven't seen anyone explain how we'd pick who actually needs escalation. Until there's a de-escalation or selection strategy, I'm skeptical this belongs in curative treatment at all.

HER2-low in early stage bugs me because testing is so variable. IHC 1+ on a core biopsy versus the residual tumor can read differently, and nobody agrees which one counts. I think any trial would need a clear rule on that. Otherwise I won't know whom to treat. I'm open to it, just not convinced the definitions are ready.

I've been waiting for something better than the current post-neoadjuvant standard for residual disease. Those patients relapse more than I'd like, and I think an ADC with this kind of activity deserves a proper early-stage test. I'd accept some added monitoring if the benefit held. Honestly, I'd be annoyed if it took years to read out.

What frustrates me is trial design. Comparators in early-stage studies often feel dated by the time results come out, and endpoints like pCR get oversold. I'd want invasive disease-free survival, not just a nice pathology slide. Then we'd have to ask whether the extra toxicity was worth it. Right now I don't trust the early-stage story to be clean.

From the surgical side, I'd be fine with perioperative use if it doesn't delay surgery or radiation. Our multidisciplinary group is flexible about timing, and the real question is whether a few extra cycles before the OR change anything. If the data say yes, I think we can fit it in. Pharmacy would need to plan the supply, but that's solvable.

My patients in curative treatment are focused on getting through it and getting back to normal life. Hair loss, nausea and the fear of lung problems will make adherance hard, and I'd have to counsel them hard. I think many would stop early. It's a tough ask when they feel well, and I'm not convinced the benefit justifies it.
Would wait for the pCR and long-term outcome data before changing anything.
Keen on T-DXd neoadjuvant for node-positive HER2+ in younger patients.
ILD risk makes me hesitant in a curative setting.
Too much toxicity for patients who may already be cured with standard treatment, honestly.
Depends on what the residual disease data look like after neoadjuvant therapy.
Residual disease after neoadjuvant is where I'd want it first.

At our community practice most early HER2+ patients still get a standard neoadjuvant regimen, and nobody is asking to switch. If T-DXd showed a clear benefit pre-surgery I'd consider it, but I'd want to see how it compares head to head first.
Our tumor board treats early HER2-low disease like any other HR+ case, so I doubt an ADC would get much traction there. Payers would probably push back too. Maybe only for the very high-risk ones.

Infusion pharmacy said chair time for a q3w ADC isn't the problem, its the monitoring. We'd need regular imaging checks for ILD in people who are supposed to be cured, and that's staffing we don't have right now.

The breast surgeon in our clinic worries about delaying surgery if patients need extra neoadjuvant cycles or a dose hold for toxicity. She wants clear timing rules before anything changes. Not sure the OR schedule could absorb delays.

I'd be open to using it adjuvant for patients with residual disease who are currently on T-DM1. Those are the ones I lose sleep over, so a stronger option would be welcome. I'd still need the safety picture to be manageable in a community setting.

Said he would want some de-escalation angle too, like whether fewer cycles could work. The younger patients in his clinic care a lot about nausea and hair loss. Would look at the data first before forming a view.

Worried about cumulative toxicity in patients who will live decades after treatment. Heart and lung effects are my main concern for early-stage use. I think I'd need a very clear benefit over what we already give.

The radiation oncologist in our multidisciplinary group asked how an ADC would be sequenced with adjuvant radiotherapy, especially given lung toxicity. Nobody in the room had a good answer. They'd want guidance before offering it.

I think early-stage is where this drug could matter most. In my clinic we see a fair number of HER2+ patients who relapse after neoadjuvant therapy and surgery, and it's hard to watch. If T-DXd could reduce that, I'd happily use it, even with the monitoring burden. Patients are usually willing to accept a tougher regimen if the aim is cure.

Our hospital-based group already runs a neoadjuvant pathway with response assessment at surgery. Plugging T-DXd in for non-responders seems like a natural fit. Pharmacy and nursing are used to ADCs, so workflow wouldn't be a big hurdle. I'd be positive as long as the readout shows a real survival signal and not just pathologic response.

Mixed feelings. A strong pCR signal would get my attention, but pCR alone probably wouldn't change my practice. I'd want event-free survival, and ideally some quality of life data. Our patients are mostly treated close to home, so how complex the follow-up is matters too. I'd probably start with a few selected high-risk patients.

Nurse navigator raised the practical side: early-stage patients are often working and have young kids, so side effects like nausea and fatigue hit differently. She thinks uptake would depend on how well tolerated it is day to day. The oncologist said he is interested but wants the trial population to look like his clinic. Both said they'd wait for the full readout.

I don't see myself using it early without very strong evidence. We already have effective regimens, and a lot of patients do well on them. Adding an ADC with ILD risk feels like trading a small gain for real harm in some. Insurance approval would likely be a fight, and in our small practice we don't have the staff for it. Mostly I'd hold off.

My concern is overtreatment. In our clinic a good chunk of HER2-low early patients are low to intermediate risk, and I'd be uneasy giving them an ADC. There is no clear way to pick who truly needs it. If the data come only from high-risk groups, I'm not sure it would translate. Also the cost question in curative settings isn't small.
Would absolutely want T-DXd in the post-neoadjuvant residual disease space.
Curative setting, so my tolerance for toxicity is much lower.
Waiting for pCR and EFS data before I'd even consider T-DXd.
ILD risk is the sticking point for early disease, honestly.
Interested, but only if it reads out in HER2-low residual disease too.
A neoadjuvant ADC without a full chemo backbone would be a real change for my patients.

Tumor board in our community practice mostly defaults to standard neoadjuvant regimens, so any change would need clear support from event-free survival, not just pathologic response. I think pCR alone wouldn't move most of the room.

Honestly the nausea and fatigue worry me in a patient we're trying to cure. Younger women working full time, I'd probably hesitate to swap out T-DXd's competitors, which have a known track record, tbh.
If the neoadjuvant data hold up, I could see using T-DXd for high-risk HER2-positive patients who respond poorly to the usual approach. Pretty excited about that possibility.
Payer side is going to be the hurdle, I suspect. Prior auth for an early-stage indication usually drags, and we'd have to sort out sequencng with the adjuvant options already approved.
Not convinced HER2-low belongs in curative-intent discussions yet. The biology in early disease seems differnt, and I see no real reason to expect the same benefit as in the metastatic setting.
Subgroup reporting by hormone receptor status is something I'd want to see. Not sure how a mixed population would read out for the HR-positive HER2-low group.
Academic clinic colleagues were keen on a de-escalation angle: if an ADC allows dropping anthracyclines, that's attractive. They'd want cardiac outcomes reported clearly.
Long-term follow-up is my concern. Early-stage trials need years before we know about late toxicity like lung effects and I'm wary of adopting T-DXd before that

The conversation kept coming back to residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy. This physician felt there's a clear unmet need there, since those patients do worse and current options feel limited. They got more hesitant about upfront neoadjuvant use, mainly because of the toxicity trade-off and thin long-term safety information. I think they'd want invasive disease-free survival as the headline endpoint, with pCR as supportive. Open to T-DXd overall, but wants mature data first.

Very engaged discussion. This oncologist sees a lot of HER2-positive patients with residual disease and finds the current adjuvant choice unsatisfying. T-DXd there would be an obvious next step if the data are positive, in their words. They'd also like to see patient-reported outcomes and how many patients complete the planned cycles. Probably would adopt quickly within the first few months at their centre.

Skeptical overall. The speaker pointed out that most early breast cancer patients do well, so the bar for adding a drug with ILD risk is high. Monitoring burden matters too: CT surveillance and pulmonary follow-up are hard to organise in a community setting. I think the feeling was that benefit with T-DXd would need to be large and obvious. Also worried about patients stopping early and ending up undertreated.

Rural practice perspective, mostly about logistics. Three-weekly infusions are fine for them but anything needing extra imaging means travelling to the regional centre. They'd be open to a neoadjuvant ADC if surgery timing wasn't affected and asked whether delays before surgery were a concern. Not sure they'd be first to use it, probably wait for guidelines to include it. Wants clear guidance on antiemetic prophylaxis upfront

Lots of discussion about the pathology side. Many HER2-low tumors are borderline on IHC and reproducibility between labs is a worry, so selecting patients for a curative-intent setting feels shaky. In early disease a misclassified patient gets toxicity with no benefit. They would want a clear testing standard before using T-DXd. Also noted that tissue after neoadjuvant therapy can change HER2 status, which complicates things further.

Spent a while on how results should be presented. In their view a perioperative trial should report event-free survival clearly alongside pCR, with separate curves for patients who had residual disease. Wants adherence and dose reduction rates reported, because real-world patients rarely finish everything as planned. Said they'd read the supplement for ILD adjudication details. Would not change practice off a conference slide alone.

efficacy|osimertinib.t: PFS bump looks real on paper, but I don't see it changing much in my clinic.
Responses are deep and fast with osi, no argument there.
Waiting on OS before I get excited.
Honestly the added benefit feels modest for most of my patients.
Brain mets control has been solid in my hands.
Durability past the first couple of years still unclear to me

Community practice here, so I mostly see plain osimertinib patients who just keep going for ages. The combo curves look better, but I can't say I've watched anyone clearly outlast what I'd expect on single agent. Maybe it's just too early to tell.
Everyone quotes the PFS gain but nobody can tell me what it means for OS. If the curves end up flat I'm not sure the extra toxicity was worth it. Payers are going to ask exactly that.

I had a patient with a big primary and liver mets who shrank dramatically on chemo plus osi, and she's still on treatment. One case, I know, but that kind of response depth makes me think the combo has something.

Depth of response seems better with the combination from what I've seen, but deep doesn't always mean durable. Several of my mono patients had very deep responses too. I think it comes down to picking the high-burden ones.

Subgroup data are thin for the patients I actually treat, older folks with comorbidities. They'd probably stop pemetrexed early, and then what happens to the benefit? Nobody has given me a clear answer.
Our tumor board keeps debating whether to reserve the combo for CNS-positive disease. The intracranial story sounds encouraging but follow-up is short. We're mostly splitting on gut feeling.
Resistance shows up eventually no matter what I do. Whether the combo truly delays it or just shifts the timing, I can't tell from my own patients so far.

Patients who tolerate the combo seem to stay controlled longer, at least in my small group. I'm cautiously impressed, fewer early progressors than I expected. Still a handful of patients though, so I'm not drawing big conclusions.

My issue is that the trial population doesn't look like my waiting room. Many of mine are frail or have poor performance status and wouldn't get anywhere near full-dose chemo. So when I'm told the PFS benefit is clear, I translate that as 'clear for fit patients'. I haven't seen anything to show it holds when doses get reduced or delayed. Until then I treat the headline number with some suspicion.

I think the data are good, not great. Progression-free time is longer, fine, but the shape of the later curve matters more to me and it's immature. In clinic I see osimertinib patients doing well for a long time already, so the bar for adding chemo is high. A few of my colleagues jumped in early, and honestly I'm not sure they can point to a patient who clearly benefited more. Probably need another couple of years of follow-up.

Frustrating that we keep celebrating PFS when patients care about living longer and feeling okay. Nobody has shown me an OS signal I'd trust yet. Meanwhile the combo means more infusion visits, more cytopenias, more calls to my nurses. If the benefit is just a few extra months of control before the same resistance mechanisms appear, I struggle to sell that. My patients ask me directly and I don't have a satisfying answer.

I was skeptical, and still am about OS, but I've changed my mind a bit on early disease control. Two of my patients with heavy brain and bone involvement had really striking responses and are still on the combination well past when I'd have expected trouble. Tolerability was manageable with dose adjustments. It's anecdotal and I know that. But it's enough that I now offer it to the high-risk ones and I'm watching closely.

What I see day to day is a split. Some patients on osi alone stay quiet for a very long time, and I'd hate to overtreat them. Others progress earlier than I'd like, and those are the ones I wonder about for the combo. The problem is I can't identify them upfront with any reliability. ctDNA clearance might help but I'm not sure our lab turnaround or reimbursement supports using it that way.

Durability is the thing I don't trust. Early response is impressive with any of these regimens, yet I've had patients who looked amazing at first scan and progressed with a messy, resistant picture. The combo may push that out, but I haven't seen evidence it changes the endgame. And second-line options afterwards are still pretty limited, so I don't see the trade as obviously favorable. Show me survival and I'll listen.
Responses on osimertinib alone have been deep and long in my clinic.
Not convinced the extra PFS justifies chemo toxicity in older patients.
Still waiting on mature OS before changing anything.
Most of my EGFR patients stay on single agent for a long time, no drama.
CNS progression is what worries me most, even after a good initial response.
Combo looks appealing for high-burden disease, especially with brain mets at baseline, but I haven't used it much.

At our community practice, most EGFR patients are still on osimertinib monotherapy and doing fine on scans. The combination comes up mainly for younger patients with heavy disease burden. Hard to say yet if the extra PFS turns into an OS gain.

Pemetrexed-platinum cycles mean extra chair time and labs, and a few patients just stop early. If they drop out of chemo, I wonder how much of the PFS benefit they keep. Probably something the trial can't really answer for us.

Seen a handful of patients with near-complete radiographic response that has held a long time on osimertinib. Those tend to be exon 19, low-volume disease. Makes me comfortable with monotherapy as the default for them.
Tumor board kept debating whether to offer the combo upfront or save chemo for progression. Nobody had a firm view. Payer approval timing also plays into it

Resistance shows up eventually no matter how deep the first response is. I see patients progress with MET or other off-target changes and we're back to chemo anyway. So durability of benefit feels finite to me.

Our thoracic group likes that the combination seems to push responses deeper and keep CNS disease controlled. Fewer early progressors is the appeal. I think for the right patient it's a real step forward.
Follow-up still feels short to me for a disease where people live a long time on a TKI. PFS curves separate but OS is immature, and I say that to patients. Not sure it changes my practice yet.

Rural clinic, and patients travel far for infusions. For them tablet-only is easier to keep up with, so real-world durability depends on adherance too. I'd weigh that against the deeper responses you may get with chemo.

I've got a mix of patients. Some are on osimertinib alone for a long stretch with small stable residual lesions on every scan. A couple started the combination recently, so it's too early to say anything about duration. Response on first scan looked good in both groups. I think the real question is who needs the extra push, and we don't have a clean way to pick them.

Honestly the thing that bothers me is the gap between trial curves and my clinic. Real patients are older, more comorbid, and miss visits. When they get chemo on top, I see dose delays and some stop pemetrexed early. I'm not sure the benefit seen in the study carries over fully. I'd want OS data before pushing this widely.

Had a stage IV patient with multiple brain mets at diagnosis start on the combination. Intracranial response was quick and has held on every MRI so far. She tolerated the chemo phase better than expected. It's one case, but it shaped how I think about high-burden CNS disease. I'd lean toward combination for similar patients.

Several patients I follow had a great first response on osimertinib and then plateaued, with slow growth of a single lesion. We continued past progression with local therapy, which worked for a while. It makes me doubt how long any regimen keeps full control. The combination might delay this, but I haven't seen that proven in my own patients.

A community oncologist told me she mostly trusts the PFS data but wants OS. Her patients on osimertinib alone often stay controlled for a long time with little fuss. For those with ctDNA still detectable after a few months she'd consider adding chemo. She admitted she's not sure that's evidence-based

Infusion nurses and I have noticed fewer combo patients coming back with early progression than I'd expect. Responses seem deep by the first or second scan. It's anecdotal, just a few patients so far. Still, it's encouraging for people who would otherwise relapse fast.
Depth of response with the combo looks impressive in my hands, honestly.
Still waiting on OS before I change anything.
PFS gain doesn't feel worth the extra toxicity for most of my older pts.
Durability is the whole point for me, and the early tail looks encouraging.
CNS control on osimertinib alone has been fine so far, no obvious reason to add chemo.
Not convinced the curves separate enough to matter outside a trial.
Community practice, so my patients often stop chemo early. I worry the PFS benefit seen in the trial gets diluted when people can't stay on pemetrexed past a few cycles.

Most responses I see on single-agent osimertinib are quick and deep anyway. Hard to say whether adding platinum builds on that or just adds noise, and it doesnt seem obvious which patients gain. Probably depends on baseline burden.
Had a patient with brain mets and high-burden disease who responded rapidly on the combo and is still doing well. Anecdotal, I know, but it has shaped how I pick cases for it.
Payer pushback on the combination keeps coming up, mostly because OS isn't mature. Without that I can't really argue durability in a prior auth appeal
I think the progression-free benefit is real, but I'm unsure how much of it turns into living longer given how many later lines we have. Sequencing after progression matters a lot here too.
Resistance still shows up eventually, wahtever we add upfront. Fewer of my patients than I'd like are in the truly long-term responder group.
Radiographic response with the combination tends to be fast, which helps symptomatic patients a lot. If that carries into longer disease control I'd be very happy with it.
Tumor board discussion split down the middle: half wanted the combo for L858R with brain involvement, half preferred to wait for more follow-up. No real consensus.

We spent a good while on this and I came away with a mixed picture. The physician felt the FLAURA2 PFS result is convincing on paper and that the deeper responses match what they see. What they couldn't square was how much it matters for patients already doing well on osimertinib alone. They'd probably offer the combination to younger, fitter patients with heavy disease and keep monotherapy for everyone else. OS maturity would be what settles it for them.

After a long discussion the main theme was skepticism. The HCP said progression-free benefit is nice, but a few extra months of control, if that's what it turns out to be, may not justify weeks of cytopenias and infusion visits. They also noted real-world patients are older and more comorbid than trial populations, so they expect the benefit to look smaller in routine practice. I think they were also worried about what is left at progression, since chemo has already been used up front. Not dismissive, just unconvinced.

This was a fairly upbeat conversation. The physician described several patients on osimertinib plus chemo whose scans showed marked shrinkage early and who have stayed controlled for a long stretch, which has made them more comfortable recommending it. They especially value it in patients with CNS disease at baseline. They still want longer follow-up, but said the durability signal is the first thing in a while that has shifted their default in a subset of patients.

Long chat, and frustration came through on durability. This HCP sees plenty of patients on osimertinib who do really well for a long time, so they struggle to identify who actually needs intensification. Without a biomarker they feel they'd be overtreating a good chunk of people. They also said progression eventually comes for almost everyone and the combo doesn't seem to change that story, just pushes it out. No clear OS benefit yet adds to the hesitation.

The HCP talked through how they read the data in clinic. On monotherapy, the first scans are usually already good, so it's hard to see the incremental gain from adding chemotherapy at the bedside. They think the benefit is probably concentrated in higher-risk groups, like those with brain mets or persistent ctDNA, but weren't sure the evidence is firm there. They said they'd revisit once subgroup and survival updates come out.

Near the end of the call the HCP raised that durability on osimertinib seems to vary a lot by co-mutations, and that trial averages hide that. They lean on TP53 status informally when counseling patients, though they admitted that isn't evidence-based. Probably will keep individualizing until more data arrive.
Thinks the PFS gain with the combo is real, OS still pending.
Responses on osimertinib alone are deep enough for most of his patients.
Not convinced adding chemo to osimertinib buys enough durability to justify the toxicity.
Brain mets control has held up well, which keeps him on osimertinib
Worried that follow-up is just too immature to talk about durability.
Mixed on it: deep responses, but no clue yet who gets the long tail.

A community oncologist said most of her patients on first-line osimertinib stay on for a long stretch, and she rarely sees early progression. She thinks the combo might help the ones with high-risk features but isn't sure how to pick them.

Told me the scans after a few cycles of chemo plus osimertinib looked noticeably better than what he is used to, especially in patients with big baseline burden. He's hopeful that translates into longer control.
Academic thoracic lead pointed out that PFS gains are nice but her patients ask about living longer. Until OS matures she's hesitant to push the combination with osi, particularly in older folks.

According to him, the payer in his region wants proof of overall survival before approving the add-on chemo, so durability data are the sticking point. He personally finds the PFS signal persuasive though.
Tumor board chair said CNS progression seems less common with the combo in his experience, though it's anecdotal. He wouldn't want to over-read that from a handful of cases.
Reported that a few patients on osimertinib alone progressed quite fast after a great initial response, which shakes his confidence in durability. He now wonders if he's undertreating some of them.
Felt the duration of response in real-world practice probably mirrors the trials, but his clinic is small so its hard to tel. Needs more time to say.
The nurse navigators see fewer patients rolling over to second-line quickly since the combo started being used, and that's the clearest sign of benefit to him. Pretty encouraged.

He said the efficacy conversation with patients has gotten harder. The PFS curves look good on a slide, but in clinic he sees people stop chemo early because of fatigue and low counts, so he questions whether the benefit survives real-world dose reductions. He's not sure durability carries over if patients can't finish the pemetrexed. Also mentioned nobody can tell him yet whether OS will separate.

Oncologist at a large cancer center said she's been impressed. Her patients with brain involvement at baseline have had lasting control, and a good chunk are still on treatment well past what she'd have expected a few years ago. She thinks osimertinib already set a high bar, and the combo seems to push it further for the right patient. She still wants OS data but feels comfortable offering it now.

Mentioned that response depth is easy to see on imaging but durability is harder to judge in routine practice. Many of his patients on osimertinib get scanned on irregular schedules because of travel distance, so progression dates are fuzzy. He thinks that blurs any comparison with trial PFS. Overall he trusts the direction of the trial, just not his own clinic numbers.

His concern is what happens after progression. If the combo keeps more patients on first line longer but resistance mechanisms are the same, he doesn't see how OS changes much. He also pointed out that fewer patients may end up getting later-line chemo, so the survival comparison could get muddy. He's skeptical until the data are clearer.

Her take was that the benefit probably depends on the patient. Younger, fit, high-burden folks seem to get the most out of the combination, while frail ones do fine on the TKI alone. She has no data to prove it, just an impression. Durability in the elderly is her main unknown.

Sounded frustrated that the early curves raise patient expectations too high. He had a patient who responded beautifully on osi, then progressed within a year, and the family blamed him for not using chemo up front. He doesn't know if the combo would have changed that. Basically he feels the durability message is oversold on slides compared with what he sees, and he'd like more honest tail data.
Osi+chemo responses look deeper, he's seen it in a few pts already.
OS still immature, so no change to his practice yet.
Waiting for OS before deciding anything.
Durability worry on osi, esp in brain mets pts.
Osimertinib alone still gives long disease control for most of his pts.
Says PFS gain is real but unclear who actually needs it.
Community onc, mostly older pts. Thinks the PFS benefit with chemo is probably real but wonders if it's worth the extra infusion visits when single agent already holds for a long time.
Cites tox causing dose delays, so she doubts the full benefit shows up in real life on osi + chemo. Pts who stop pemetrexed early, no idea if they keep the advantage. Wants data on that.

Academic thoracic clinic. A handful of his high-burden pts with liver mets had rapid, deep responses on osimertinib plus platinum/pem, and they've stayed controlled longer than he'd expect from single agent.
Not sure how to read the FLAURA2 curves tbh, separation looks clear but OS is what matters to him. Will wait for another data cut.
Payer pushback is the issue, they want OS before approving the combo. So even if durability looks better on paper he cant act on it for most pts.
Likes that CNS control seems to hold up over time, fewer brain progressions in his own pts on osimertinib. Says that's what keeps people functioning.
Resistance arrives eventually whichever arm, I think. He sees the same C797S or MET stuff at progression, so 'durable' is relative.

Tumor board last week, group split on who gets chemo added. Younger fit pts with brain mets or high burden, most would offer the combo; others keep osimertinib alone and save chemo for later. Main reasoning is the PFS gain seems meaningful but nobody's sure it turns into longer survival. Said they'll probably revisit once OS matures.

Rural practice, long drive for pts. Combo means more visits and labs and she thinks alot of pts would trade some PFS for staying home. Saw one pt with a deep response who couldn't tolerate chemo past a couple cycles, then did fine on osi alone. Makes her question how much benefit is the chemo part. Not convinced for her typical pt.

Very upbeat. Has pts on osimertinib for a long time now, some well beyond what he'd have predicted in the gefitinib era. Depth of response on scans is usually obvious by first restaging. With the combo he's seen early deep responses buy time for a couple of really symptomatic pts. Durability is the main reason he's comfortable using it first line.

Concerned that post-progression options are poor, so first line durability matters more than anything. If the combo delays progression but pts are too worn down for later chemo, net benefit unclear. Also says trial pts are fitter than his clinic pts. Skeptical the curves translate, wants real world data.

Hospital-based oncologist, between clinics. Says early response looks similar either way, difference only shows later in who stays progression free, if at all. Hard to judge from so few cases. Thinks scan timing matters too since long intervals can hide early progression. Open to combo for select pts.

Spoke after clinic, rushed. Pts mostly ask 'how long will it work' and the trial numbers are hard to explain. He tells them probably longer with combo but no one knows about overall survival yet. Some hear that and pick oral only, others want everything upfront. He doesnt feel the data push him either way for most.
Sees imaging response as fast on both approaches so durability is the real discussion. Hasn't treated enough pts with the combo to form a view.

efficacy|pembrolizumab.t: Durable responders in a few pts, tail looks real.
PFS benefit not obvious in my own pts tbh.
OS still immature per HCP, wants longer f/u before changing anything.
Pembro periop: EFS signal convincing enough to bring to tumor board.
Responses dont last long enough, pts relapse fast and HCP frustrated
Depth of response varies a lot, probably PD-L1 dependent.
Community onc, gastric 1L. Sees quick radiographic response in some pts but many progress by first restaging. Not sure if that's biology or just who gets selected for tx.
Resectable NSCLC pts on pembrolizumab: path response in clinic roughly matches what HCP expected, and few recurrences so far. Caveat is small numbers and short f/u.
HCP worried EFS gain may not turn into OS benefit since most relapsed pts get IO at recurrence anyway. Says crossover muddies the whole picture.
Thoracic surgeon says pts with major path response seem to stay disease-free, but a handful recurred in brain. Unsure if benefit holds beyond a couple yrs.
PA reviewers keep pushing back on gastric, want OS not just PFS. HCP spends more time on appeals than on the tx decision itself.
Elderly gastric pt, PD-L1 high, still on tx long after anyone expected, disease stable on scans. HCP called it the case that keeps them believing in pembro. Wishes more pts looked like this.
MSI-H gastric pts do great per HCP, everyone else underwhelming. Hard to generalize from the good ones.
Rural clinic, imaging access limited so HCP can't really judge depth of response, goes mostly by symptoms and PS. Hedged that durability is probably underestimated or overestimated, can't tell which.

HCP skeptical on gastric durability. In their experience early responses look good at first scan, then a good chunk progress within months. AEs also force tx breaks in some pts, and that seems to cost them the benefit. Says the curves in papers look nicer than what walks into clinic. Would still use it for the right biomarker pt but expectations are low.

Academic thoracic onc very positive on periop pembro. Pts who got neoadjuvant then adjuvant are mostly disease-free at last visits, which is more than they saw with chemo alone. Surgeons at tumor board now ask for it by default. HCP thinks long-term OS will probably follow but admits it's early. Overall the most encouraging IO story in their lung practice.

Mixed view. HCP likes that some pts get deep, lasting responses and stay off tx for a long time. But can't predict who, and PD-L1 alone doesn't feel like enough. HCP in private practice sees a split. A few lung pts after surgery doing well, no recurrence yet, but follow-up is short. In gastric, responses are real in some yet often partial and not long. Durable responses in a few of my resected lung patients, still disease free.

He thinks the pathologic response at surgery is a decent marker for who does well. He added that his later patients just haven't had enough time yet.

Community GI oncologist described her PD-L1 positive gastric patients getting decent responses on first-line chemo plus the PD-1. Duration varies a lot, though. She isn't sure why some progress at the very first scan.

Academic med onc is concerned that the survival gain in gastric seems tied to a PD-L1 subgroup, and in her clinic that's a small slice of patients. Most of her gastric patients don't qualify, so she rarely sees the long tail people talk about.

At their lung tumor board, patients with little pathologic response after neoadjuvant therapy get flagged for tighter imaging. The group wasn't sure whether the adjuvant phase adds much durability on top of that. They plan to keep following and see.

Oncologist in a hospital-based practice said the payer keeps asking if the benefit lasts long enough to justify a full year of treatment. He couldn't offer anything beyond the published curves, and he admitted that makes the conversation awkward. He feels stuck defending durability with limited follow-up.

One gastric patient in a small private clinic has had stable scans for a long stretch on immunotherapy and is back at work. It's a single case, but the doctor said it changed how he talks about expectations with newly diagnosed patients.
He said event-free survival looks encouraging in the perioperative lung setting. He still wants OS to mature before telling patients this cures more of them.

Several of his gastric patients responded well at first and then progressed within a few months. He felt the early scan results gave patients too much hope. Now he tries to temper the first follow-up visit.

A medical oncologist at a large cancer center said the relapse pattern after perioperative treatment is what worries her most. Pulmonologist-turned-tumor-board lead said his team sees a real mix. Some resected patients are well past a year with clean scans, while others relapsed during the adjuvant phase. Overall he thinks the benefit is real but uneven. He wants better ways to identify who is in which group. Until then they just follow everyone on the same imaging schedule.

A community oncologist said that since adding pembrolizumab to perioperative care, the surgeons are seeing more tumors with major pathologic response at resection. Those patients are mostly doing well on follow-up. She finds it easier to talk about long-term control now. She still hedges, because follow-up is only so long. The oncologist talked about gastric patients whose responses looked good on paper but didn't translate into feeling better or living longer in his clinic. Per a nurse-led immunotherapy clinic lead, the patients who respond tend to keep responding, while those who don't show it early. Late progressions are rare in her experience, but the numbers are small.

This lung surgeon said the resectability and response rates after neoadjuvant therapy are better than what he used to see with chemo alone. Patients are reaching surgery in good shape, and many of them remain disease free at their check-ins. He thinks the durability signal is promising, and he is more confident referring borderline cases now. He'd still like to see longer follow-up before calling it a change in cure rates.
Durable responders exist, but I can't predict who they'll be.

Pembro in gastric: responses come, but they fade sooner than I'd like

In my community practice, post-neoadjuvant patients who reach a pathologic response seem to do well so far, but follow-up is short. I keep telling patients we're still learning what long-term really looks like.

Our tumor board has noticed that when pembrolizumab works in gastric, it tends to work for a long time. Those few patients change how I counsel everyone else.

Depth of response in gastric is hit and miss, I think. Some shrink dramatically, others just stabilize. PFS curves apparently separate late rather than early, which makes the first scan hard to interpret.
A payer asked me last month for proof that benefit lasts beyond the adjuvant phase, and I couldn't show much beyond early data. Hard to defend a full year of therapy when some relapse anyway.
An academic colleague said the pembrolizumab OS data feel reassuring but immature. She'd wait for more mature follow-up before changing sequencing.
Radiology reads after neoadjuvant therapy have been striking in a number of my patients, with very little residual tumor at surgery. That early depth makes me optimistic about durability.

Elderly gastric patients with low PD-L1 rarely get meaningful benefit in my hands, and the ones who do often lose it within a few months. Not sure the population-level signal translates to patients who recieve it in real life.

After a long discussion about perioperative lung, my sense is that this physician sees the pathologic response story as encouraging but not the full picture. Patients with a major pathologic response tend to stay disease-free so far on pembro-based treatment, which feels right intuitively. The ones with little response are the worry, because they often recur and it isn't clear the adjuvant phase rescues them. The curves probably look good overall, yet the clinic experience is more uneven than the headline. They want longer follow-up before using words like cure.

We spent a while on gastric, and the frustration was obvious. In their clinic a fair number of patients get an initial response that looks promising, then progress within the first year, and there's no good way to tell upfront. Survival gains feel modest when you're sitting across from a family. They also pointed out that chemo is given alongside, so it's hard to know how much of the durability is the checkpoint inhibitor itself. Without clearer biomarkers they'd call the benefit real but narrow.

Talking through their lung cases, this oncologist was clearly upbeat. Several patients treated before and after surgery with pembrolizumab are now well past the point where they'd normally expect recurrence, and scans remain quiet. They said it changed their expectations of what resectable disease can look like. They still hedge, since it's a small number of patients in one clinic, but the pattern matches what they've read. I think durability is the thing they'd defend most strongly to colleagues.

Their view of gastric was balanced. They use it mostly where PD-L1 expression is higher, and in that group the responses seem deeper and last longer, though they wouldn't call it dramatic every time. Outside that group they're more cautious, and some patients simply stay stable for a while, which they count as acceptable. Imaging at first restaging often isn't conclusive, so they wait for the second scan before deciding anything. Overall mixed, and leaning heavily on patient selection.

Long chat about durability in the real world and the tone was sceptical. Trial populations look nothing like their referral patients, who are older, frailer and often can't finish the planned perioperative course. So when they see early relapses they wonder whether the published curves would hold for those people. Toxicity-driven stops also make it unclear whether partial treatment still buys lasting benefit. Not sure anyone knows, alot of this is guesswork at the moment.

We wrapped up with how they'd read the survival data. They think the OS signal in lung is encouraging yet still maturing, and they're careful not to over-promise to patients. In gastric, the benefit seems clearer for a subset than for everyone. Probably the honest message is that some people do remarkably well and others get little. They'd like real-world cohorts to confirm this before it shapes routine practice.
Several of my periop lung patients are still disease-free well past a year.
Responses in gastric just don't seem to last for most.

Seeing deep responses in MSI-high gastric, some going on for years.
OS curves look fine on paper, real world is messier.

At our community practice, a couple of stage III NSCLC patients who got the perioperative regimen had clean scans at their last visits. Surgeons were happy with how many made it to resection. Hoping it holds.
Most of my gastric patients on pembro plus chemo respond at first, then it varies a lot. PD-L1 CPS seems to drive who stays on longest, I think.
Medical oncologist at a regional hospital said recurrences after neoadjuvant pembrolizumab still show up in the brain more than he'd like. He's not convinced the EFS gain means cure for everyone.
Tumor board discussion today: they like the pathologic response signal but aren't sure it predicts long-term OS. Waiting for more mature data before changing how they counsel patients.
Payer in their system keeps asking for durability evidence before approving the adjuvant continuation. The oncologist says that's hard to give while follow-up is still maturing.
Academic thoracic group says KEYNOTE-671 changed how they talk about resectable disease. Patients with a major pathologic response are doing really well so far, from what they see.
Elderly gastric patients in their clinic tend to stop early because of tox, so they doubt the trial-level benefit shows up for them. Not sure the durable responders look like their typical patient.
PFS benefit seems real to her, but she says the tail of the curve is what matters and she wants to see it. Some of her patients plateau, some progress by the first restaging scan.

Saw a thoracic surgeon in a mid-size hospital this week. He said a handful of his patients relapsed within the first year after surgery despite a good-looking pathology report. That makes him cautious about promising anyone a cure. He thinks the data are encouraging on average but individual patients are hard to predict. Wants better markers for who needs more than the standard approach.

Gastric clinic, mostly HER2-negative patients. The oncologist described a mixed picture: some get a clear response and stay on treatment a long stretch, others progress at the first scan. She thinks CPS helps but doesn't fully explain it. Pembrolizumab in first line is routine for the right subgroup now, though she still counsels about uncertainty on how long benefit lasts.

Infusion center staff and the oncologist both pointed to a few long-term gastric patients who come in regularly and remain stable. He said those cases are why he keeps offering PD-1 combinations. He admits they are a minority, but the depth of response in them is striking. Patients ask about stopping at two years and he feels more comfortable discussing it now.

Oncologist at a rural clinic said response duration is his main worry. Patients come in hoping for years of benefit and he can't promise it. Several of his gastric patients progressed after a decent initial response and had limited options after. He feels the survival signal is modest for many, and the cost conversation with payers doesnt help.

Pulmonologist-turned-tumor-board lead said they track their perioperative cases in a simple spreadsheet. So far most are without recurrence, but follow-up in their own cohort is short. He doesn't want to over-read it. Plans to revisit once they have a couple more years of data.

Radiology reads at their center often show shrinkage that looks impressive on the first scan. The oncologist said the real question is how long it lasts, and she isn't sure yet. She has a few patients who stayed responders and a few who turned around quickly. For now she treats each case individually.
Pembro responders stay responders, but I'm not convinced that's most patients.
Honestly the pembro tail is what sells it, not the median.
Too early to say if pembro EFS holds past a couple of years.
Nobody in my clinic has seen anything dramatic in gastric, frankly.
Durability? Show me five-year data in real-world patients first.
Lung periop patients I follow are mostly still disease free, so far.

Our tumor board keeps debating whether the gastric benefit is just the PD-L1 high subgroup. Everyone else seems to progress within a few scans. I don't buy that the headline survival numbers reflect what we actually see.
With pembrolizumab in gastric I see a few really deep responders and then a lot of nothing. Hard to predict who's who upfront, which is the frustrating part.
In community practice patients come in older and sicker than trial pts, so I doubt the survival gains translate fully. Maybe I'm being cynical, I'm not sure.
I'll admit KEYNOTE-671 won me over a bit. A couple of my resected patients are well past the point where I'd expect a relapse, though it's only a small handful.
Radiographic response is one thing, but I care whether they're alive and functional a year later. Pembro seems to buy time for some, not all, and the scans don't tell me which.

Relapses after periop immunotherapy are showing up and nobody has a clear plan for them. The benefit looked durable on the slides, yet in clinic I'm seeing recurrences in brain and nodes sooner than I'd like.
When pembrolizumab works in gastric it really works, and those folks just keep coming back for their infusoins with stable scans. I'd still like to know how long we're supposed to keep treating them.
Payer keeps asking for proof of durable benefit before approving periop pembro. I tell them the curves separate but honestly I'm not sure how much is surgery vs drug

I've been burned by early curves before. Gastric patients on pembro look great at first scan, then a good chunk progress by the time we'd call it durable. The publications talk about survival signals, but that's not what I see in my Tuesday clinic. Add the steroid courses and treatment breaks and I wonder what the net benefit is for the average patient. Not saying it's useless, just oversold.

In perioperative lung I'm torn. Pathologic response after neoadjuvant treatment is encouraging and the surgeons love it. But we don't really know yet if that translates into long-term survival for our patients, and follow-up is short. I also don't know what to do with the ones who had a poor pathologic response but are still on adjuvant for a year. I guess we wait and watch.

My frustration is that the data are all averages. A patient asks 'will it last?' and I've got nothing individual to tell them. In gastric, CPS helps a bit, but there are CPS-low patients who do fine and CPS-high ones who progress fast. I end up hedging, which patients hate. The biomarker needs to be better, simple as that.

I came in skeptical, I'll say that. But a few of my gastric patients with MSI-high disease are years out with no sign of progression, which I never saw with chemo alone. That's anecdotal and I know it. Still, for that group the durability seems real and I'd treat them again tomorrow. The rest of the gastric population, I'm much less sure about.

Follow-up is the issue. Everyone quotes event-free survival from the lung periop work but I want to see OS mature before calling it a win. Patients ask if they're cured and I can't say that. Some of mine relapsed within months of finishing adjuvant pembro, and honestly that's demoralizing. I think the early benefit is real but the long game is unproven.

Workflow-wise we restage every few months and the pattern is bimodal: stable for ages or progressing fast, few in between. I think that matches the trials but it makes counselling hard. Also the stopping rules, two years vs until progression, still feel arbitrary to me and I defintely see colleagues doing it differently.

efficacy|sacituzumab govitecan.t: Responses come fast but fade. Most pts progressing before any plateau.

Community onc, 3 pts on sacituzumab so far. One long responder, other two progressed quick. HCP can't predict who ends up which.
Urothelial pts post-EV/pembro: responses are real but short-lived, mostly just buying time. HCP wants OS data that actually move the needle.

Pts in visceral crisis respond fast enough to matter but it doesn't last. HCP also wary of cross-trial comparisons being oversold in slides.
HCP says TROP2 expresion doesnt seem to predict who benefits, so hard to pick pts for a durable response.

Large private practice, heavily pretreated HR+ pts. HCP says SG is the first tx in a while where she sees both tumor shrinkage and symptom relief that lasts a few cycles. A handful of pts stayed on far longer than she expected. She still says OS is the real question but the PFS signal is enough for her to offer it after endocrine and CDK4/6 failure. Pts and families seem to value the extra time.

HCP not impressed by durability in the real world. Of the urothelial pts he treated, a good chunk had a response that looked great on first restaging, then progressed by the next scan or two. He thinks the trial curves flatter the drug because of patient selection. Clinic pts are older, more comorbid, and often need dose delays, so he doubts they get the full benefit. Would like to see OS data in a population that looks like his clinic.

Mixed feelings from this HCP. In HR+/HER2- she's seen clear PFS benefit versus what she'd expect from further chemo, and a few pts had impressive depth of response. But AEs often force breaks, and she can't tell whether the benefit holds up after interruptions. She presents each case at tumor board and the group is split. Overall she'd call it useful, not transformative, and wants longer follow-up before changing sequencing.

HCP worried about the gap between response and survival. Several pts had good radiographic response yet declined within months, usually from disease in new sites or from tolerability. He isn't sure ORR is the right metric to quote to pts. He says when counseling he stays cautious and talks about time gained, not cure. Would probably still use SG, just with tempered expectations.

Positive overall from a big-center HCP. In her experience sacituzumab gives a clear PFS advantage in later-line HR+ pts, and several remained on tx through multiple scans with stable or shrinking disease. She thinks the TROPiCS-02 story holds up in clinic, mostly. The caveat is that early responders do best, so she checks at the first restaging and moves on quickly if nothing happens. She'd like more data on sequencing with other ADCs.

HCP is waiting on more follow-up. Responses look good at first, but she can't say yet how many are truly durable versus a short-lived dip in tumor burden. Payer pushback on PA is also making it hard to build her own series. She treats a few pts per quarter, so impressions are anecdotal. Says she's open to it but reserves judgment on OS until mature data are out.
Responses are real, but they don't last long enough for my liking.
PFS gain feels modest, and OS is still the open question.
SG bought one of my patients a surprisingly long stretch off chemo.

Sacituzumab has given me a few HR+ patients with a clear radiographic response who stayed on for a good while. Not everyone, but enough that I'd keep it in the sequence after endocrine plus CDK4/6 and a chemo.
The TROPiCS-02 curve separation is there, I think, but the OS story is less clear to the group I spoke with. They'd want longer follow-up before changing how they sequence.

A community oncologist said most of his patients progressed before he could judge any real benefit, mostly because delays and dose reductions for neutropenia kept eating into treatment. He isn't convinced the trial result translates to his frail, older population.

In urothelial they mostly compare it to whatever follows enfortumab vedotin. Response looks decent, but duration is hard to call with so few patients seen so far, so they're waiting for real-world data.
She described a patient with liver mets who had a quick, deep response and kept it for many cycles; every scan was a pleasure. She called it an outlier but a happy one.

Payer pushback means he often gets the drug late, after patients are already declining, so the benefit he sees looks smaller than in the trial. Probably a selection issue rather than the drug itself, he admitted.
Benefit measured in months rather than years is fine with him as long as the patient feels OK. Quality of life during response matters as much to him as the scan.
Wants better OS before calling it standard; PFS alone doesnt move him much in a heavily pretreated patient.

After a long talk it was clear she sees the efficacy as real but hard to generalize. Her tertiary-center patients tend to be fit, so responses look good and treatment goes on a while. She suspects the satellite clinics see something different, with more early discontinuation. She wouldn't say the durability is disappointing, just that it's uneven. For her the OS signal is what would settle it, and she isn't sure we have enough yet.

He kept coming back to the fact that response depth doesn't seem to predict how long the benefit lasts. He's had a few partial responders who progressed within a couple of scans, which stung after the toxicity they went through. In his view the PFS improvement is statistically nice but clinically thin for some of these patients. He also worries that OS follow-up is immature and might never show much once later lines get mixed in. Overall he's cautious and doesn't want to oversell it to families.

What stood out was how animated she got describing her HR+/HER2- patients who had run out of endocrine options. Several got a meaningful response, and a good chunk stayed on treatment longer than she expected when starting. She thinks the TROPiCS-02 data match what she sees: not a cure, but time that matters. Management of side effects keeps patients on drug, which in turn protects durability, she said. She'd happily use it earlier if access allowed.

He was frank that the clinic experience feels less rosy than the slides. Patients arrive after multiple lines, performance status is borderline, and the response, when it comes, is often brief. Honestly he thinks the median numbers hide a lot of early progressors. He'd like to see waterfall-type data in real practice populations, not just trial ones. Until then he describes the benefit to patients as a chance, not a promise.

The conversation circled around what counts as a good outcome. She said a response that holds for a handful of months can be a win in this setting, particularly if the patient avoids hospital admissions. But she also admitted she can't predict upfront who will get that, and biomarkers don't help yet. On OS she is waiting, as most of her colleagues are. She feels the data are supportive but not practice-changing on their own.

For urothelial he sees a real role post-EV and checkpoint, mainly because there is so little else that produces a response. A few of his patients had rapid symptom relief and tumor shrinkage that held for a decent period, which he values a lot. Responses are real but they don't last long enough for me.
Deep responses in a few, honestly more than I expected.

Had a heavily pretreated HR+ patient on SG who stayed on well past what I expected, probably the best response I've seen after CDK4/6. Still an outlier, and I wouldn't promise that to the next one.
Academic center here, and we see a lot of patients progress at the first scan. The curves separate on paper but my clinic doesn't feel like that. Hard to sell it to patients as a big step up.

Early dose reductions for neutropenia, and then the response seems to wobble, or at least I wonder. Nobody can show me that benefit holds at the lower dose on SG.
Community practice, two patients on it right now, both stable at the third restaging. That's more than I got from capecitabine or eribulin in the same setting. Small numbers, but I'll take it.
Everyone says 'clinically meaningful' about the PFS gain. Meaningful to whom? A few extra months with day 1 and 8 visits and scans every couple of months isn't an easy trade.

I was optimistic going in. In practice a good chunk of my HR+ patients on SG progressed by the first or second scan, and the ones who responded often lost it within a few months. The trial says benefit over chemo, fine, but chemo is a weak comparator there. I keep hearing about a tail on the curve and haven't seen one in my own clinic. Maybe my patients are sicker than trial patients, probably true.

Response depth is what I look at first. If there's clear shrinkage at the first scan I continue, and the benefit usually holds for a while. If it's just stable disease I get nervous, because those seem to turn quickly. I don't have a clean rule for it. I'd like to see outcomes broken out by visceral involvement, since that drives my decisions.

Honestly I'm a bit surprised. I was skeptical of yet another ADC, but the rapid symptom relief and shrinkage in liver mets are hard to ignore. Duration is still the open point and I won't claim more than the data show. Still, compared with sequential single-agent chemo, it feels like a real step forward for these patients.

Urothelial is where I'm frustrated. The response data are early and follow-up is short, so durability with sac gov is basically unknown. Patients come off enfortumab already worn out and a lot of them don't make it to a second scan. I can't tell them honestly how long it will help. Without randomized OS I'm not going to push it hard.

Cross-trial comparisons drive me nuts. Everyone lines SG up against the other ADC and the numbers look similar-ish, but the populations differ. Tumor board spent twenty minutes on it and landed nowhere. I think the benefit is real, durability is moderate, and sequencing matters more than the headline.

Our pharmacy committee asked for OS evidence before adding it to the pathway, and I definately understood why. The PFS gain is there but modest, and the OS picture is less clear to me. I've had patients respond nicely for a few cycles and then fall off a cliff. That makes planning next-line therapy a scramble, and I keep wishing for a biomarker to tell me who gets the long ones.
Responses seem quick, but I'm not sure how long they hold.

Happy with the PFS benefit of sacituzumab in his heavily pretreated HR+ patients.
OS signal not convincing enough for their tumor board yet.

Urologist said his urothelial experience is thin and he can't tell if responses last. After enfortumab and pembrolizumab, he sees patients fade fast no matter what comes next.

Academic breast oncologist noted deeper responses than with single-agent chemo in her pretreated patients. She thinks the PFS separation is real and sees it in clinic, with several patients getting extra months of stable disease.

Private practice oncologist uses it mostly fourth line, so he can't say much about long-term benefit. Responders tend to be those with good performance status, though he admits that's probably confounded.

Oncologist at a large community center described using sacituzumab govitecan once endocrine therapy and a CDK4/6 inhibitor had run out.
