Uro-oncology nurse practitioner described the setting where SG comes after platinum and a checkpoint inhibitor. Few patients have received it in their clinic, so her impression is anecdotal. One had a decent partial response and others stopped early. She can't speak to durability and would want more real-world experience before forming a view.

Oncologist at a rural satellite clinic said that for patients who can't travel easily, a response that lasts matters a lot. She's had a few patients with lasting disease control who avoided admissions for months. Compared with the chemo she used before, scans look better more often. She thinks the PFS benefit translates into real life. She wishes she had longer follow-up to say the same about survival.

Tumor board discussion ended in disagreement. One physician felt responses fade too quickly to justify the cost, particularly in patients with liver mets. Another pointed to the PFS gain but admitted OS is hard to interpret because later therapies muddy it. The first said a few extra months isn't a win for everyone. Overall mood was cautious, with no clear change in practice.
Honestly love the PFS story, just wish the OS picture were cleaner.
Responses with sacituzumab are real, but they fade sooner than I'd like.
Great when it works, and a decent number do get a good ride.
Want longer follow-up before I get fully excited about durability.
Durability in urothelial is the open question for me, everything else looks promising
Deep responses, short tails. That's my read so far.

Had a heavily pretreated HR+ patient in my community clinic who stayed on for many months and kept working. That kind of disease control is why I'm so enthusiastic about Trodelvy. My only caveat is that I can't promise that outcome to everyone.
After endocrine therapy and a CDK4/6 inhibitor, the PFS advantage over chemo feels like a real win to me. The OS gap seems smaller, though, and I'm not sure how much later therapy muddies it.

I'm a big fan of the ADC class, but in my academic clinic the responses often come fast and then patients progress not long after. It feels like we're buying time, just not always a lot of it. Wish the tail of the curve looked a bit fatter.
Tumor shrinkage on scans is very encouraging, especially in patients with heavy visceral burden. Whether that turns into meaningful extra months probably depends on the patient, I think.

A payer reviewer asked me how long the benefit really lasts and I didn't have a great answer. I love the efficacy signal, but the long-term plateau isn't convincing yet. Until then I'll keep hedging in those conversations.

In urothelial after immunotherapy, even a modest response feels meaningful because options are so thin. I find the efficacy exciting and I'd happily use it earlier. The caveat is that the numbers are small and I'm not sure how durable it all is.
Colleagues in my region get genuinely fired up about the PFS gain with this drug. A few of them wonder, though, whether the extra time is good-quality time once dose reductions kick in.

Time to progression feels short in my later-line pts, even when the first scan looks fantastic. I'm excited about the drug overall, but I'd love to see more true long-term responders. Right now I can name only a handful.

One of my favorite cases is a woman with HR+/HER2- disease who had run out of reasonable options. She got a clear response by her first restaging and held it for a long stretch, which honestly surprised the whole team. It reminded us why we push for new mechanisms. The caveat is that she's the exception in my practice, not the rule. Still, seeing that kind of benefit is energizing.

In tumor board we keep coming back to the same point. The PFS signal from TROPiCS-02 is encouraging and fits what we see clinically. Responses often look good early, then the question becomes how long we can hold them. I'm optimistic, but the OS data feel less decisive to me, and I'd like to see how real-world patients compare. For now I describe it as a meaningful step, not a game changer.

I really want this drug to deliver more durable control, and sometimes it does. But in my clinic a lot of patients respond quickly and then relapse within what feels like a short window. That makes the conversation about expectations harder, especially with younger patients hoping for years. I still think it's a valuable option. I just can't oversell the duration.

Our oncologists are excited about the response depth, but several told me the benefit seems uneven. Some patients melt down on imaging and others barely move. Without a good way to predict who will get the long ride, it's tough to set expectations. I'm not sure biomarkers will fix that anytime soon. Great efficacy on paper, but the variability bugs me.

I'll say it plainly, I'm impressed. In the clinic we see more disease control than I expected from a post-chemo setting, and that stable disease often holds for months. Patients tell me they feel they got time back. My one hesitation is that I don't yet know how the benefit looks past the first year or so.

What I hear from the infusion center is mixed but warm. Nurses see patients doing well on therapy for a while, and that gets everyone upbeat. The doctors, however, keep asking whether PFS translates to OS in a way that matters for their patients. I think it probably does for some and not for others. We just don't have a clean way to tell them apart yet.

efficacy|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: Responses look deep, but I'm not sure they hold.
Durability in HER2-low is what impresses her most.
OS signal still too immature for him to lean on.
Honestly, PFS gain over chemo feels modest in his practice.
Long responders showing up in HER2-low, which surprised the whole team.
Depth of response good, tail of the curve unclear

Community oncologist said T-DXd shrinks tumors fast enough that patients with symptomatic liver mets feel better within a couple of cycles. She thinks that early depth is what keeps people motivated to stay on treatment.

Mixed feelings at the academic clinic: PFS looks clearly better than chemo after endocrine therapy, but he wonders how much of that carries into OS. Waiting on longer follow-up before changing his habits.
Several patients in her clinic progressed sooner than the published curves led her to expect. She suspects her real-world population is sicker, with more prior lines, though she can't prove it.
Describes the course as stop-and-start: a good response, then dose reductions creep in. Not sure whether reduced dosing erodes the benefit over time.
Doesn't see the point of chasing PFS if toxicity makes people stop early. Durability on paper, he said, is not durability in the infusion chair.
He has a handful of patients on it well past a year with stable disease, which in his experience of later-line chemo is rare. That makes him more comfortable recommending it earlier.

Patient selection drives everything for her. In low-burden, indolent disease endocrine-based therapy can still give long control, so she doesn't see ADC durability as directly comparable. I think she'd want a cleaner head-to-head picture before shifting those patients.
Payer pushed back, saying the OS evidence isn't there yet for the earlier line. He half agreed that PFS alone is a hard sell in that conversation.

After a long discussion, this medical oncologist said what keeps standing out is how often responses are both quick and lasting in patients who had run out of good endocrine options. She described a few HER2-low patients who were back to normal routines for many months, which she did not expect from an ADC. She still wants OS to mature, but day to day she feels the PFS benefit is real and clinically meaningful. I think she would use it earlier if access allowed.

Spent a good while with a hospital-based oncologist who split the question in two. For depth of response he's impressed, especially with visceral disease, where scans often look better than he'd hoped. For durability he is more guarded, because he has seen control slip once treatment is held for ILD concerns or nausea. He wasn't sure whether those interruptions really matter long term. Probably needs more real-world follow-up before he forms a firm view.

Her main worry is that the curve looks great early but she hasn't seen proof it translates into living longer. A few of her patients responded nicely and then progressed fairly abruptly, with little warning on imaging. She also pointed out that later therapies muddy any OS signal, so she isn't convinced we'll get a clean answer. Until then she keeps T-DXd for patients who truly need a response, not as a default.

Talked for most of an hour with a physician and an infusion unit lead; both felt the efficacy story gets overstated in presentations. Patients arrive expecting a near-cure result, and when progression comes at what feels like an ordinary interval they are devastated. The physician said the duration of benefit isn't that different from some other later-line options she sees. Expectation managment is becoming a big part of the consult.

Community practice view: efficacy isn't in doubt for HER2-low after endocrine therapy, but how long it lasts seems to depend on who you treat. Younger patients with good performance status tend to stay on longer, while frail ones usually drop off early, often not from progression. He thinks the trial population is cleaner than what walks into his clinic. Not sure published data will fully reflect that.

She summarised the conversation as cautious optimism. The PFS signal is convincing and she's seeing deep responses, but she keeps coming back to sequencing: if the drug works this well early, what is left afterwards, and will later lines work as well? She wasn't certain how durable benefit from a second ADC would be. In the meantime she is comfortable using it and watching closely.
PFS looks fine on paper, but my real patients don't always read the paper.
Responses with T-DXd come fast, no argument there.
Still not convinced the OS story is there.
Depth of response with T-DXd is impressive, but durability is the open question.
When it works, it really works.
Waiting on mature survival data before I change anything.

Our community practice sees the shrinkage on T-DXd early, usually by the first scan. What I don't see is how long it holds once we get into dose reductions for nausea or fatigue. The trial curves feel a lot cleaner than my clinic does.
Had a HER2-low patient on T-DXd, heavily pretreated, who stayed on well over a year, which frankly surprised me. One case, I know, but it sticks with me.

Everybody quotes the PFS benefit over chemo after endocrine therapy. I think it's real, I'm just not sure how much of it turns into OS once you factor in crossover and later lines. Probably needs longer follow-up before anyone can say.

My patients are mostly chemo-naive after endocrine progression, so DB06 is relevant to us. Still, a PFS gain that comes with ILD vigilance and extra monitoring visits isn't automatically a win in my book. It depends on how long the benefit actually lasts.
Tumor board consensus is that responses are deep, nobody disputes that. The argument is always whether that depth buys real extra time. The room was pretty evenly split.
Durability with T-DXd looks better than what I get from sequential single-agent chemo, I'll give it that. I'd still want to see it hold up in HER2-low patients outside of trial selection.
Payers keep asking me for proof of OS before they approve earlier lines, and I can't hand them that yet. PFS alone doesn't move them. Frustrating.

We're an academic center, so we see a lot of the progressors. Time to progression on T-DXd seems shorter than I'd hoped when brain mets are in the picture, though that's purely anecdotal. In the patients without CNS disease it looks better.

I keep hearing 'practice-changing' and it irritates me a bit. The response rate is high, fine, but I've had several patients respond beautifully on T-DXd and then progress faster than expected, and then we're out of good options. Trial populations are fit and mine often are not. When someone stops at month four over pneumonitis concerns, the PFS curve doesn't help them. I want real-world durability data before I buy in fully.

I'm mostly a convert. In my HER2-low patients who had already burned through endocrine plus CDK4/6, the radiographic responses on T-DXd were rapid and symptoms improved within a couple of cycles. A good chunk stayed on for many months, longer than I'd expect from capecitabine. I still caveat it with the OS uncertainty, but day to day it's the first option that feels like it changes the trajectory.

Mixed feelings here. The PFS data with T-DXd are consistent and I trust the direction. What bugs me is the lack of clear OS separation so far, and I'm not sure if that's immaturity or later-line treatment diluting it. For limited visceral burden I'd probably still try endocrine-based therapy first. For fast-growing disease I lean toward it because of the depth of response.

Community oncologist here, and we don't have much time to wait and see. First restaging scans often look great, then by the second or third I get the feeling the benefit is fading in some patients. Nobody can tell me which ones. I'd like a biomarker or at least a pattern, and without that I'm just hoping. Some of them recieve it for months and others barely get through a few cycles.

In HER2-positive disease the benefit after prior lines of T-DXd-naive therapy is well established and I won't argue with it. What I'm skeptical about is extrapolating that durability to HER2-low, where the baseline biology is different. IHC 1+ patients in particular, I'm not sure they get the same staying power. Maybe I'm being overly cautious.

Dose holds and delays make me doubt that the trial durability applies in my clinic. Patients miss cycles, get reduced, and I dont know if the benefit survives that. Nobody is showing me that breakdown. Until someone does, I read the headline PFS with a grain of salt, and my patients' actual time on treatment is what I trust.
T-DXd responses in HER2-low are deeper than we got with chemo.
Durability after the first scan is what worries me, honestly.
Waiting on mature OS before changing anything in our community practice.
Seen a few patients stay on well past a year.
Not convinced the PFS gain on T-DXd turns into living longer.
Depth of response looks good, duration still unclear to me.
At the community oncology clinic, the doctor said most of her HER2-low patients on T-DXd respond by the first scan. Whether that holds beyond the first year, she's not sure yet.
Two of his patients progressed fast after a good initial response. He thinks the tail of the curve matters more than early shrinkage, and he isn't seeing that tail yet.
Academic breast clinic physician says disease control in chemo-pretreated patients on T-DXd tends to last longer than she expected. She would use it earlier if the payer allowed.
He looks at PFS first and OS second, and says OS will probably be muddied by later therapies. His tumor board mostly agrees with that.

The regional payer wants proof of durable benefit before approving earlier use, and the HCP says the current data doesnt really give that yet. Prior auth denials are delaying starts for some patients.
Oncologist in a hospital-based practice noted that responses he sees on T-DXd come early and tend to stick. The first restaging scan is usually already convincing.
Teaching clinic with lots of fellows: they say the ultralow patients seem to respond, but they've treated too few to say anything about duration.

Private practice oncologist is cautious about durability. In her clinic a handful of patients had a nice early response, then came off treatment within a few months because of ILD concerns or dose holds. She feels that cuts into any PFS advantage in real life. She also pointed out that trial populations are fitter than who walks in on a Tuesday. She wants longer follow-up before calling it a durable option.

Mostly treats HR-positive HER2-low disease and compares T-DXd against the next chemo options in his head. Response depth seems better, and he's fairly confident about that. The PFS benefit looks real to him, though he's unsure how much patients feel it day to day. OS is the open question, probably, since people get many lines afterward. He'll wait for updates before shifting his sequencing.

Infusion center staff told the HCP they see patients coming back cycle after cycle with stable or shrinking disease. A couple of patients with liver mets had clear reductions that lasted many months. He thinks it's the most convincing efficacy story in HER2-low so far. He still hedged on OS, but thinks it will probably follow.

Concerned that response looks strong but the story after progression is poor. In her tumor board, patients who progress on T-DXd seem to go downhill quickly with few good options left. That makes the length of the first benefit even more important to her. She's not sure the data answers that and thinks the field is overselling depth.

Regional hospital oncologist said scan intervals decide a lot of what looks like PFS in practice. His group scans every few cycles, so progression gets caught at about the same time as in trials. He isnt sure real-world durability will match the trial. Nobody there has treated enough patients yet to say.
Long responders are the exception in her clinic, from what she described. Most of the T-DXd patients she follows progress sooner than she hoped.

Talked through how DESTINY-Breast06 is being read in his group. The earlier-line PFS signal is taken seriously, especially for patients whose endocrine therapy has stopped working. People are less sure on OS because later treatments muddy it. In clinic he tells patients shrinkage is likely but can't promise how long it lasts. He added that earlier use also depends on how quickly the payer approves.
Community onc: PFS gain vs chemo feels real in HER2-low, pts stay on longer.
Durability? HCP unsure, wants longer f/u before calling it.
OS still immature, HCP won't change practice on PFS alone.
Fast shrinkage, pts feel better quickly. How long it holds is the open question.
Responses just don't last long enough in her heavily pretreated pts.
Impressive scans at first restaging, HCP said nothing else does that.

Academic breast onc says the PFS benefit in HER2-low after endocrine tx looks convincing on paper. Not sure it carries over to pts w/ slow bone-predominant dz. Probably still tries endocrine-based sequencing first.

HCP worried benefit fades once T-DXd gets held or dose-reduced for lung tox concerns. Says real-world pts are older and sicker than trial pts, so duration is likely shorter. No local data, just gut feeling.
Tumor board last wk: several members cited depth of response as the reason to move T-DXd earlier. HCP agreed, esp. when pt has visceral burden and needs a quick response.
Brain mets pt came up. HCP saw decent intracranial control in a couple of pts but calls it anecdotal, not enough to hang a PA letter on.
Payer pushback on PA when PFS is the main argument, since there's no OS signal yet. Reviewers keep asking for survival. HCP finds this frustrating but understands it.
Private practice onc likes the response data but wants to see how many of his own pts reach a second restaging w/o a tx break. Waiting on his own experience before forming a view.
HCP: 'when it works it works'. Has a few pts on tx for a good while now, longer than she'd expect on chemo, and AEs manageable so far. Says that's what keeps her using it.
HCP said PFS bump is modest in abslute terms for HER2-low, not sure its worth the tox trade for every pt. Would reserve it for those who really need a response.

Regional hospital onc was skeptical that trial durability will hold outside study centers. Says the pts who do well on T-DXd are often fit, good PS, close monitoring. Her clinic has less imaging access, so progression may be caught later and benefit looks shorter. Also felt that without OS data she can't tell pts with confidence that they will live longer. Remains cautious, uses it selectively.

HCP described a split picture. Some pts have deep, early responses and she's happy, but a handful progressed fairly quickly and she can't predict who. Thinks HER2 expression level probably matters but isn't sure how much in practice. At tumor board people debate whether PFS is enough to justify earlier use. She's leaning toward using it but wants more follow-up first.

Very positive from a high-volume breast center. HCP said response rate and depth are the first thing pts and families notice, with tumor markers dropping fast. Several pts have stayed on well beyond what he'd predicted from prior-line experience. He thinks DESTINY-Breast06 context supports moving it ahead of more chemo in appropriate pts. Still watches for ILD but says benefit is hard to ignore.

Concern: HCP feels responses are impressive early but plateau, then pts progress and options are limited. Post-T-DXd tx is the unknown, so she worries about what comes next. Says a few pts went from great response to rapid progression with little warning. Doesn't want to burn the best option too soon. No OS data yet to settle it for her.

Hospital-based onc said clinic experience is mixed but mostly fine. Responses seem to match what he expected from the data, nothing shocking either way. Pts often need dose adjustments, which he thinks may blunt duration a bit but can't prove. Says he'd like registry-type data on how long pts really stay on. Currently uses it in 2nd line plus.

HCP asked how T-DXd durability compares in pts who got prior CDK4/6 vs those who didn't. Thinks it could matter for who benefits most. Said current data don't really answer it, so she relies on case-by-case judgement at tumor board. Interested in any subgroup looks but expects them to be thin.
Responses look deep, but not sure they hold past a year.
Honestly the PFS in pretreated low-expressers has been underwhelming for us.
T-DXd gives the longest disease control I see in later lines.
waiting on mature OS before changing anything
Fast shrinkage with T-DXd, but treatment stops early so the benefit doesn't last.
A few good responders still going after a long stretch.
Community oncologist said the first scan on T-DXd usually shows clear shrinkage. What he can't tell yet is how long it lasts, since a lot of patients come off for dose holds before any progression.
Academic clinician felt the PFS gain in HER2-low is real on paper but modest in practice. Her patients with visceral disease seem to progress sooner than the curves suggest on T-DXd, I think.
Regional hospital oncologist described a patient with liver mets who had a lasting partial response on trastuzumab deruxtecan. She now expects that kind of outcome more often than she did with chemo.
At tumor board, people said OS is the missing piece. Without it the payer pushes back on using this ahead of further endocrine-based options.
Infusion nurse lead mentioned that several patients needed earlier restaging because of new symptoms. She wasn't convinced the benefit lasts as long as it's presented.
Private practice doc said brain mets are his question mark. Systemic response on T-DXd is great, but he's unsure about intracranial durability.
Younger patient who progressed fast on CDK4/6 had a quick, clear response. Her oncologist said it bought enough time for her to get back to work.
Hard to judge durability on T-DXd when so many of our patients stop over lung safety worries. Probbaly underestimates the PFS we'd see otherwise.

Rural clinic oncologist said she's seen a mix in her HER2-low patients. A couple had striking shrinkage on the first scan, and a couple progressed within a few cycles. She thinks selection matters, like how much prior endocrine therapy they'd had. She's waiting for more follow-up before calling anything durable.

At a large cancer center, the clinician said the efficacy story feels front-loaded. Patients respond, but a good chunk seem to lose control after some months, and then options are thin. He worries T-DXd in earlier lines just moves the problem down the road. He's also not sure a PFS benefit will turn into an OS benefit given later therapies.

Community breast specialist said T-DXd has changed how she talks to patients about prognosis. Her HER2-low patients with prior endocrine progression often show a clear response by the second scan. Several have stayed on treatment much longer than she expected from chemo experience. She still wants OS data, but day to day she's happy with the disease control.

A hospital oncology lead described how they track outcomes informally. Time on treatment looks decent for most, though a handful stopped early for reasons unrelated to progression. He said comparing that to chemo in their own records is messy since the populations differ. Probably need a longer window before drawing conclusions.

Oncologist in a small group practice felt the data don't translate cleanly to her older patients. Many are frail and end up on reduced doses, and she suspects the benefit shrinks as a result. She's had a couple of responses that were short-lived and not worth the burden. The trial population seemed fitter than her waiting room, she said.

An oncologist on a hospital formulary committee said they accepted the PFS signal but kept asking about OS. Approvals are going through with an expectation of review after a year. He personally sees good responses with T-DXd in clinic, though duration is still being learned. Not sure how the committee would react if OS ends up flat.

guidelines|osimertinib.t: Pathway committee hasn't touched it yet, probably next quarter.
NCCN listing was enough for their P&T, no pushback at all.
Label wording on the chemo combo is still vague, which bugs them.
Waiting for ESMO to catch up before changing anything locally.
Honestly dont read the updates, just goes by what tumor board decides.
Preferred-category status made the payer conversation easy.

Community oncologist said the pathway vendor still shows osimertinib alone as the default first line, and the combo needs a peer-to-peer every time. She finds that exhausting, especially for patients with brain mets where she'd lean toward adding chemo.

Academic thoracic lead says their internal guideline group only meets twice a year, so the FLAURA2 data was discussed but not voted on. He expects a 'preferred but not exclusive' kind of wording eventually.
Likes that NCCN now gives the combination a clear place next to single-agent osimertinib. Says it simplifies talks with her pharmacy director about off-pathway requests.
Concerned that ASCO guidance seems slower than NCCN, so the fellows get mixed messages. Not sure which one the hospital will anchor to in the end.
Said compendia listing matters more to him than the guideline text, because the billing team only checks that. Wasn't sure the combo was fully captured there yet and didn't want to guess.

Pharmacist on the pathway committee worries the label talks about chemo-related adverse events but says little about who the right candidate is. They want clearer selection language before adding the combo, otherwise it becomes a free-for-all. Teh committee would rather wait than write vague criteria.
Regional practice follows ESMO more than NCCN, I think because of how their national body works. Nothing changes until the local reimbursement decision comes through.

Told me the updated recommendations gave him cover to offer the combo to younger fit patients with heavy disease burden. He still individualizes, but having it in the guidelines helped with the hospital administrators.

This was a long talk and she kept coming back to how fast the guideline landscape moves versus her institution's pace. The pathway committee wants to see both NCCN and a second source agree before editing the lung pathway. She thinks that is reasonable but admits it leaves a gap of several months. In the meantime she documents rationale in the chart and goes through the exception process. Not thrilled, but not angry either.

He was frustrated, I'd say, after we talked for a good while. His health system's pathway still doesn't mention the osimertinib plus platinum-pemetrexed option, so every case becomes an exception request. The nurses handling prior auths now keep a template just for it. He feels the guideline bodies moved but the local machinery did not. He worries some patients get default monotherapy simply because the paperwork is easier.

Pleasantly surprised by how smoothly it went at her center. The pathway group reviewed the NCCN update, looked at the label, and added the combination as an option within a couple of meetings. She credits a pharmacist who prepared a one-page summary beforehand. Tumor board still decides case by case, but nobody has to argue about legitimacy now. She thinks this will probably spread to the affiliated community sites.

Spent a while on the mismatch between guideline language and the label. As he reads it, guidelines allow flexibility but the label and some payer policies are narrower, so he's unsure which he'd be defended by in an audit. His compliance team leans conservative. He said he'd happily use the combo more if the wording were aligned, but for now he hedges and picks monotherapy in borderline cases. Frustrating, in his words.

Thoughtful conversation about how his group uses guidelines. He treats NCCN as the main reference, glances at ESMO for context, and mostly ignores society statements unless a pathway committee forwards them. On the combo, he feels the recommendation is sensible but wants more guidance on follow-up and sequencing after progression. He said the current texts are probably fine for now, just not complete. No plan to change his default this quarter.

She was concerned that guideline updates arrive faster than her tumor board can digest them. Several colleagues cite different versions of the NCCN document in the same meeting, which wastes time. She'd like the institution to name one owner for guideline monitoring, but nobody has volunteered. Meanwhile the combo discussion gets postponed again. I think she sees it as a process problem more than a data problem.
Pathway committee hasn't touched osimertinib plus chemo yet.
NCCN listing was enough for their pharmacy to approve it.
Waiting on the ESMO update before changing anything.
Label wording is vague on who should get the combo.
Compendia listing came through, so billing is fine now.
Not sure their community group even looked at the new guideline
Academic thoracic group follows NCCN closely and said the chemo combination is listed as an option next to osimertinib alone. They still decide case by case at tumor board.
Payer in their region wants the compendia entry in writing before approving pemetrexed with osimertinib. Prior auth took a couple of weeks last time and the patient started late.
Community oncologist said the guideline update gave her cover to offer the combination to a younger patient with brain mets. Her pharmacy just pointed to the listing and signed off.
Their health system's pathway committee meets quarterly, so anything new waits months. Doc finds that frustrating since colleagues elsewhere are already using the combo.
He said ASCO guidance reads more cautious than NCCN on adding chemo. I think he's leaning toward the conservative read for older patients.
Pharmacist on the pathway committee wasn't sure the label update had made it into their order sets. She thought it was still being reviewed internally.
Nurse navigator mentioned the EHR order sets still list osimertinib alone. Nobody has updated them since the guideline changed, so docs type in the combo by hand.
Rural clinic doc appreciated that the guidelines spell out testing and first-line choices clearly. Makes the conversation with patients easier.

Large hospital-based practice told me their pathway committee is split on the chemo combination. Some members worry about extra infusion visits, and the chair wants more follow-up before adding it. The medical oncologists feel held back for patients with high-risk features. He thinks the committee will list it as optional only. Not a fun conversation for the clinic.

Private practice group reviews NCCN updates at a monthly lunch meeting. They noted the combination is listed, but osimertinib alone still sits in the preferred category, I think. Most of the docs said they'd choose by patient fitness and disease burden. One partner asked how ESMO frames it and nobody had read it yet.

Thoracic oncologist said the recent guideline revision matched what her group was already doing. With osimertinib plus chemo in the listing, the pathway committee approved it in one meeting. The pharmacy team stopped asking for extra justification. She mostly uses it in patients with CNS disease. Overall pretty happy with how it went.

Oncologist at a smaller hospital said the guideline language on who benefits from adding chemo is too loose. Patients and families ask why he picks one approach, and the guideline doesn't give him a clean answer. Reviewers at the payer pick up on that vagueness too. He had one denial where they cited the compendia as supporting only certain patients, and the appeal dragged on.

Fellow-led clinic said they check NCCN, then ESMO, then the institutional pathway. Mostly they line up. Where they differ the attending decides. Osimertinib alone is still the default for most older or frail patients, in their words.

Pharmacy director said compendia updates tend to lag the guidelines, so for a few weeks they cover the combo case by case. Not sure how long that window usually lasts. Teh team keeps a running list of those approvals. It works but it's a lot of manual checking.
Pathway committee still hasn't touched the chemo combo, no timeline given.
NCCN lists osimertinib combos, but the wording leaves too much room for interpretation.
Honestly the NCCN update made my payer fights easier.
Label language on who actually needs chemo added is vague.
Waiting to see if ESMO follows NCCN here.
Compendia listing lag is what kills us at prior auth, every time.

Our community practice pathway committee meets quarterly and apparently missed the cycle, so osimertinib plus platinum-pemetrexed is still 'off pathway' on paper. I end up writing an exception for every single patient. Frustrating when it's already in NCCN.
I think the ESMO language is more cautious than NCCN, which is probably fair. Still, nobody at my tumor board can tell me which patients they'd actually reserve the combination for.
Fine, I'll admit the guideline update helped. Once the combo showed up in NCCN, our infusion pharmacy stopped pushing back on chair scheduling. Not perfect, but better than last year.

ASCO updates feel slow to me, and then they hedge anyway. Some academic colleagues are already giving osimertinib with chemo to brain mets patients, so there's a gap between what's written and what's done. I'm not sure which one I should be following.

Payer medical policy cites compendia, not the guideline directly, as far as I can tell. So the NCCN change only matters once the compendium entry catches up. No idea how long that takes, nobody tells us.

The label reads clunky on the combination. It helps with coverage, I'll give it that, but osi monotherapy still feels like the assumed default in the wording while the guidelines read differently. My staff gets confused when they're building the auth packets.

Our pathway got updated recently. They kept monotherapy as the default and added the combination for 'select' high-risk patients, and select isn't defined anywhere. Typical commitee move, punt the hard part to the treating doc.
Credit where due, our pathway group actually listened this time. They added the combination option within a couple months of the NCCN change, no endless back and forth.

My issue is that the guideline endorsement feels like it outran the long-term data. Overall survival is still a question mark for me, and the guidelines don't spell that out well. Community practice here, we basically follow NCCN and that's it. If it's listed after endocrine therapy and prior chemo, fine, but I'm not sure how a reviewer reads 'prior chemo in the metastatic setting' for someone who progressed fast after adjuvant.
I'll admit the guideline inclusion helped. Once it showed up in NCCN for HR+/HER2- disease, our pharmacy stopped pushing back on the first auth.
ASCO guidance tends to trail everyone else. It's useful as a reference, but by the time a rapid update lands we've already made decisions on a bunch of patients, so it doesn't help in real time.
Urothelial is murkier for me. Guidelines mention it, I think after enfortumab and a checkpoint inhibitor, but teh sequencing is still an argument at our board and nobody wants to commit.
Our payer goes by the compendia, not the guideline. So a patient gets denied even though NCCN supports use, and then we wait weeks for an appeal. Not sure whose job it is to fix that.
I read the ESMO piece, probably should reread it. They were cautious with the data, which I respect, but it left me unclear on where a TROP2 ADC sits versus more chemo in later lines.
Institutional pathway still lists physician's choice chemo as the default for pretreated HR+ patients. Nobody updated it after the new data and I'm tired of asking.

Honestly the boxed warning language is what our pathway reviewers fixate on. Neutropenia and diarrhea get read as a reason to restrict use, not as something we manage with growth factor support and dose changes. I keep hearing the committee wants 'more real-world experience' before they'll move, but how do we get it if we can't use it? Patients recieve whatever the pathway allows, and that's often not what the guideline would suggest. It feels circular.

We're an academic center and the pathway committee is slow but thorough. They compared the NCCN entry with the label and with the ESMO view, and the discussion was mostly about sequencing. I think they'll list it for HR+/HER2- after endocrine and CDK4/6 plus chemo. Not sure on urothelial, since the committee seems to want to see how the field settles. Fair, but it means another couple of cycles of waiting.

I was skeptical that guidelines would ever catch up with how we actually treat these patients. But the NCCN listing did give me cover with our pathway committee, and the conversation changed from 'why' to 'which patients'. That's progress. I still wish the guidance were more specific about who benefits most, but I'll take it. Prior auth is less of a fight than it was.

The label says one thing about number of prior systemic therapies in the metastatic setting and the guideline reads a little looser. In a small rural practice with a single pharmacist that mismatch is a real headache. The payer sticks to the label wording, so I end up documenting every prior line to show it counts. I'd like the sources to line up, but I doubt they will anytime soon.

NCCN and ASCO don't read identically on this and I think people gloss over that. At our tumor board we mostly default to NCCN because it's updated more often. The ESMO framework gets mentioned when someone wants to be cautious. Overall it's workable, though I'd say the guidance is clear for the typical patient and fuzzy for anyone with unusual prior therapy.

Our urothelial pathway added sacituzumab govitecan as an option after platinum and the other approved agents, and that was a relief. It took a few meetings and some pushing from the GU group. The wording is still pretty conservative and I'd like it broader, but having it on the page means I'm not writing an exception request each time. Pharmacy seems fine with it now.
Not sure yet if our pathway committee has even looked at it.
Pathway still lists older chemo first, I think.
NCCN listing seems to be enough for their P&T, probably.
Would need to see the next ESMO update before anything changes here.
Compendia status unclear to me, billing team may know more
Category listing seems supportive, which should help with prior auth.

Our community practice follows the NCCN algorithm pretty closely, but I'm not sure where SG sits for HR+ patients after endocrine therapy and a CDK4/6 inhibitor. It may be listed, but the line-of-therapy wording seems loose. Would need to see how payers read it.
Pathway committee meets quarterly, so any change probably won't land until later this year. Urothelial seems like a separate conversation, since everyone keys off the enfortumab-based sequence first.

I think the guideline inclusion gave the team confidence to consider it earlier than they otherwise would have. Seems like the academic group was waiting on that. Still some hesitation about toxicity, though that's not really a guideline issue.
The pharmacist wasn't sure how label language on prior chemo maps to patients who only got chemo in the adjuvant window. Might turn into a payer headache. Not sure yet.
ASCO guidance seems to lag behind NCCN on this, at least from what she showed me. She mostly checks NCCN and only glances at the others. That may change if ESMO adds a clearer benefit rating.
Formulary committee wanted to see compendia listings before even discussing it. Apparantly it may not be in all of them yet, so they're holding off for now, though nobody seemed opposed.
Fellow mentioned the updated guideline made tumor board discussions easier, since there's finally something concrete to point to. I think it probably helps with insurance appeals too.

Their integrated system has a pathway committee that seems to move slowly, and I got the sense sacituzumab hasn't been formally reviewed. The medical director thought it may be listed as an option, not a preferred step. He wasn't sure who owns the update process. Until the pathway changes, I think most community sites in the network will default to the older regimens. He said he would need to see the committee minutes to know for sure.

In urothelial, the discussion seems to hinge on where the ADC fits after platinum and checkpoint therapy, and the guideline wording doesn't feel settled to her. She thinks the NCCN position may firm up as more data mature. For now it seems to be used case by case. The tumor board tends to follow whatever the guideline says, so she'd want clearer language. I couldn't tell if the pathway group has even raised it.

She was fairly upbeat about the guideline status in HR+/HER2- disease. In her view, having a recommendation in the major guidelines probably makes it easier to justify after progression on endocrine and chemo. I think her team has started to bring it up earlier in treatment planning conversations. She still wasn't sure how the pathway would treat sequencing against other ADCs. But overall the listing seems to be helping, not hurting.

Label language came up repeatedly, especially the warnings around neutropenia and diarrhea. The nurse lead said the guidelines seem to mention supportive care, but she wasn't sure how prescriptive it is. That may matter for infusion center staffing and protocols. I think some of the group worry that a guideline listing makes it sound simpler to use than it really is. They would need to see clearer monitoring guidance before feeling comfortable.

He compared the ESMO and NCCN positions and thinks they may not line up perfectly, though he admitted he hasn't read the newest versions closely. Reimbursement bodies in his region seem to lean on the ESMO benefit scale. If that rating is modest, access could be slower. He's not sure yet whether local committees will wait for it. I'd guess it varies by center.

Small rural clinic, no real pathway committee, so the physician basically relies on whatever NCCN says that month. He said he's not sure when updates get noticed there, and a new listing may take a while to filter down. Nobody on staff tracks compendia, I think. He also worried that patients who could benefit might be missed becuase the referral center decides first.
Their pathway group seems interested but wants more real-world experience before moving it up. I'm not sure what would count as enough. Probably a couple of quarters of local use first.

guidelines|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: Still waiting on NCCN to say something clear about HER2-low after chemo.
Pathway committee approved it, finally. Took forever though.
ESMO wording is fine, doesn't change what I do.
T-DXd compendia listing lagging behind the label, so payer denials follow.
Honestly the category 1 vs 2A thing drives our P&T discussion.
T-DXd in the pathway now, one less peer-to-peer fight.
Our pathway committee meets quarterly and nobody has put HER2-low endocrine-refractory disease on the agenda. So we're stuck with exception requests case by case. Gets old.
I read the ASCO update and I think it nods to the newer data, but it's vague on sequencing. Not sure it moves my community colleagues much either way. Enhertu is on their radar regardless.

The label says HER2-low, but the pathology reports I get say 'score 1+' or 'equivocal' with no clear category. Guidelines assume everyone's IHC is clean, which isn't my reality in a small practice. T-DXd eligibility ends up a judgment call.
Good to see NCCN catch up for the earlier-line setting. My pharmacy director was waiting on exactly that before bringing it to P&T.
Guideline panels move slow, I'll say that. By the time the ESMO text caught up we'd already been debating these patients for months. Still, I'd rather have it in writing late than never.
Our payer follows compendia, not the guidelines per se. If it's listed we're mostly fine, if it's not it's a fight, and sometimes it's listed with odd wording that they read narrowly.
The pathway vendor's version is out of date and still lists older sequencing. I flagged it to the committee twice and got no reply. Hard to trust the tool after that.
Tumor board uses NCCN as the tiebreaker. For borderline cases, like ER-positive with few options left, they'll go with it for T-DXd. Some people still argue about the ILD monitoring wording.

We run an academic-affiliated clinic and the pathway committee is the real bottleneck. They want guideline support in black and white before T-DXd moves earlier, and the NCCN wording isn't strong enough for some members. I think a couple of them are also worried about budget, though nobody says it. Meanwhile I'm sending patients through exception requests that take weeks. It feels like the guideline is being used as a reason to wait.

Surprisingly smooth experience here. Our pathway lead pulled the latest ESMO and NCCN text side by side and both supported T-DXd for the HER2-low, endocrine-pretreated group. Committee signed off in one meeting. I'm not saying every site will see that, probably depends on who's chairing. For us it removed a lot of friction.

The label language on ILD monitoring is vague, honestly. Guidelines say monitor closely but don't say how often or who owns it, oncology or pulmonary. We have no pulmonologist on site, so the nurses end up improvising a protocol. I'd want deruxtecan guidance to be more concrete before I'm comfortable expanding use.

I'm pretty happy with where the guidelines landed. Having it in NCCN made the P&T discussion easy, and T-DXd now sits in our pathway as a preferred option for the right patients. Reviewers still want IHC documentation, but that's reasonable. Feels like the field finally caught up with what we were seeing in clinic.

Pathway committee keeps asking for ASCO guidance first, then ASCO is slow, so we go in circles. Our payer reps say they need a compendia entry, and the compendia supposedly wait on the guidelines. Everyone points at someone else. Meanwhile pateints with few options are waiting.

ESMO and NCCN don't line up perfectly on where HER2-low and ultra-low fit with trastuzumab deruxtecan. I've been going with NCCN since our payers reference it. Not sure the ultra-low piece is settled enough to put in a pathway. Probably need another update cycle before our committee touches it.
Waiting on NCCN update before changing pathway for T-DXd, per HCP.
Pathway cmte hasn't touched HER2-low yet, no timeline given.
NCCN listing enough for this group, PA easy now.
Label wording on ultralow unclear to HCP, not sure T-DXd is covered there.
ESMO nod noted but community onc says NCCN drives their orders.
Compendia listing lag = first-round payer denials, HCP annoyed
Academic breast onc said NCCN category made tumor board discussion quick for T-DXd. No one pushed back on using it post-endocrine tx. Pathway cmte basically rubber-stamped, I think.
HCP follows ASCO updates closer than NCCN for HER2-low. Says both probably align but hasn't compared line by line. Plans to check at next journal club.

Community practice, pathway cmte meets quarterly, so any new indication sits a cycle or more before adoption. HCP frustrated, pts wating on PA in the meantime. Pharmacy lead wants compendia entry first.
Not sure guideline wording covers HR+ pts w/ only one prior endocrine line. HCP reads it as maybe yes, pharmacist reads it as no. Wants clarification.
ESMO guidance clear on HER2-low sequencing. HCP said it helps when explaining tx plan to pts, uses it almost like a handout.
Payer cites compendia only, ignores ESMO. HCP says appeals eat staff time, PA nurse overloaded.
Health system pathway added T-DXd w/ restrictions, needs ILD monitoring plan documented up front. HCP ok w/ it, just extra paperwork.
HCP thinks guidelines undersell ILD mgmt for T-DXd. Wants clearer monitoring and AE grading language, esp. for community sites w/o much experience.

Large community clinic. Pathway cmte chair not convinced the newer HER2-low data justify moving T-DXd ahead of chemo. Wants to see NCCN preferred language first. HCP personally disagrees but has to go thru cmte. Pts get chemo by default meanwhile. Maybe revisit in a few months.

HCP at big academic center very positive. NCCN update came out, tumor board adopted it within weeks. Order set changed same month, PA templates updated. Pharmacy supportive. HCP says guideline backing is what got payers to approve w/o much fuss, mostly.

Mixed feelings from HCP. Guidelines list T-DXd for HER2-low post-endocrine, which is good, but preferred vs other-recommended distinction matters for their pathway. Not sure where cmte will land. Label vs NCCN differences also confuse the staff. Thinks it'll sort out by next review.

HCP: IHC variability is a guideline gap. Guidelines say HER2-low but path labs report inconsistently, esp. 0 vs 1+. Borderline pts get missed. Tumor board wastes time arguing retest. No clear rec in NCCN or ESMO on retesting as far as HCP knows.
Private practice onc, no formal pathway cmte, relies on NCCN plus whatever payer policy says. Payer policy updates lag by months. Uses peer-to-peer when denied. Fine overall but a big tiem sink.

Pt scenario: HR+ HER2-low, progressed on CDK4/6 + AI, no chemo yet. HCP said guideline now supports T-DXd and pathway agreed fast. Label language matched what they needed for PA. Approved first pass. Would like more of that.
Waiting on the next NCCN update before adding T-DXd to our order set.
Pathway committee hasn't touched HER2-low since last year, so no change yet.
T-DXd's NCCN listing made the P&T conversation much easier.
Pharmacist still unsure how label language handles HER2-ultralow.
Mostly follow NCCN here, ESMO only comes up at journal club.
Compendia listing lag is what holds up their prior auths

At their community practice the pathway committee added T-DXd for chemo-naive HR+ HER2-low after the guideline update. It went through in a single meeting, which surprised the physician. Nurses are now building the infusion templates.

The oncology pharmacist said the label wording on prior endocrine therapy is the first thing she checks. She thinks guideline and label mostly line up, but wasn't sure about patients who progressed quickly on a CDK4/6 inhibitor.

Academic clinic says the institutional pathway still lists chemo ahead of the ADC for HR+ HER2-low in the first chemo setting. Committee meets quarterly, so any change is months away. Frustrated but resigned.
ESMO guidance came up, and the physician said she reads it but her payer follows NCCN categories. So ESMO is background only for her.
Doctor worried that the ILD monitoring language in the guidelines is vague on scan frequency. His clinic ended up writing its own protocol, probably different from the neighboring practice.
Medical oncologist at a regional hospital found the ASCO update clear and printed it for tumor board. She has already used it to justify moving T-DXd earlier in two case discussions.

Payer in their region reportedly accepts a compendia listing alone, no label match needed. The practice manager still checks alot of cases, since IHC 1+ vs 2+/ISH-negative documentation gets questioned sometimes.
Community group said their pathway vendor platform hasn't been updated, so staff are working from a PDF memo.

Breast team at a large hospital said their pathway committee is cautious about the ultralow category. They feel the guideline wording leaves room for interpretation, and pathologists aren't routinely reporting it. Without a clear pathology report nobody wants to write it into the pathway. I think they're also worried about budget impact. They'll revisit after the next NCCN cycle.

Oncologist in a mid-size private clinic said the recent guideline changes let him stop arguing with the payer. He used to write long letters, now he cites the NCCN category and the label. Approvals come back faster, though he isn't sure if that's the guideline or just payer workload. Staff like it. He'd like ESMO to catch up on the same indication.

Interesting split at a cancer center. The breast chief follows NCCN closely, but the pharmacy lead wants the pathway to stay strictly with label language. They're still debating whether T-DXd after endocrine therapy for HER2-low should be a preferred option. Both agree the evidence is solid. The holdup is process, a form for the committee, and the next meeting isn't until spring.

Nurse navigator said patients get confused when guidelines differ from what their insurer lists. A few cases last month were denied because the HER2 result in the chart wasn't phrased the way the compendia entry reads. They resubmitted with a pathology addendum, which takes a couple of weeks each time. She thinks it's a documentation problem more than a guideline problem.

A hospital-based oncologist said she checks NCCN first, then the label, then ESMO if a trial question comes up. For HER2-low she thinks the recommendations are fairly consistent across them. Where they differ is sequencing T-DXd after CDK4/6, which she finds a bit fuzzy. She'd probably wait for the next ASCO update before changing how she sequences.

Tumor board at a rural affiliate used the updated NCCN language to agree on T-DXd for a patient with HER2-low disease progressing on endocrine therapy. They didn't have to refer out for pathway approval, which was a big deal for them. The pharmacist added it to the order set that same week. Overall they felt the guideline made a hard conversation simple.
Pathway committee meets quarterly, so nothing changes until the next cycle.
Still waiting on compendia listing before our payer will move.
NCCN listing for HER2-low made the T-DXd conversation much easier.
Honestly havent looked at the latest ESMO update yet.
Label language on HER2-low still feels vague to most of our group.
Pathway committee approved T-DXd for HER2-low after a fairly short review.
Our pharmacy lead said the NCCN category made the P&T discussion straightforward. I think T-DXd will go on formulary without much pushback now.
Seeing HER2-low in the ASCO guidance reassured the younger oncologists, who had been hesitant to move past chemo after endocrine progression. They said they'd probably reach for T-DXd more readily.
Guidelines read as if written before people had real-world experience with ILD on T-DXd. The group wants clearer monitoring language, not just a line about vigilance.
Their payer cites the label, not NCCN, and the label wording on HER2-low is narrower than clinicians assume. Denials happen, then get overturned on peer-to-peer, which eats a lot of staff time.
Compendia listing came up briefly. One physician assumes coverage follows if NCCN lists it, but the billing manager wasn't so sure.
We talked about whether ESMO frames sequencing differently from NCCN for T-DXd. Probably a minor difference, but the fellow thought the ESMO scale was easier to explain to patients.
The network pathway commitee reviews oncology drugs twice a year, I think, and HER2-low is on the agenda for the next round. No sense yet of how it will go.
Clinic manager said the EHR order set still reflects the older pathway, so T-DXd orders for HER2-low need a manual override. A fix is apparently queued but has no date.

We spent a good while on how guidelines are actually used in her community clinic. She said NCCN is the reference everybody opens, but the pathway vendor their network uses lags behind by a few months. For HER2-low after endocrine therapy she feels comfortable following NCCN and documenting her rationale. What she's less sure about is earlier-line use, where she'd want ESMO and the pathway to catch up before changing habits. Overall not negative, just cautious.

Long conversation with a breast oncologist at an academic center who sits on the pathway committee. Her frustration is that the committee wants guideline support before adding anything new, while the guidelines seem to wait for more mature data, so it feels circular. She worries that patients with very low HER2 expression get left in limbo because nobody knows how to classify them. I think she'd support T-DXd there but can't push it through alone. She also said committee members disagree on cost versus benefit.

It became clear over a long chat that this physician has really embraced the updated recommendations. She said the ASCO and NCCN language gave her tumor board a shared reference, and arguments about off-pathway use mostly disappeared. For HER2-low patients who progress on endocrine therapy, T-DXd is now just part of the standard discussion. She still flags ILD counseling as something to build into the workflow. On the guideline front, though, she feels things have moved the right way.

The main theme was a mismatch between what guidelines say and what the label supports. Prior auth staff at the practice are told to cite the label, and the HER2-low wording doesn't map neatly onto how their pathologists report IHC. A couple of patients had treatment delayed while paperwork went back and forth. She thinks NCCN carries clinical weight but not much administrative weight with some payers. She sounded worn down by it, and said alot of newer colleagues don't see how much of the job this is.

This oncologist trained somewhere that follows ESMO closely and now practices where NCCN dominates, so he had a useful comparison. He thinks the two broadly agree on HER2-low, but the emphasis on sequencing and the tone around evidence level differ a bit. Not sure the differences change what he'd actually prescribe. He'd like a clearer statement for hormone receptor positive patients who haven't had much endocrine therapy yet. He said he'd wait for the next update before shifting anything.

Pathway committee came up again, this time from a community hematologist who chairs a small one. They'd include T-DXd but want explicit ILD monitoring and a documented plan, and the guidelines don't give them much to copy from. He said members are nervous about owning a toxicity protocol nobody has standardised. So the listing is stuck in draft. He thinks it will eventually pass but isn't hopeful about timing, and the lack of a clear pulmonology referral route is a real obstacle.

patient_selection|osimertinib.t: Mostly ECOG 0-1 patients get the combo here, PS 2 usually stays on single agent.
Frailty is the main reason they skip adding chemo.
Osimertinib alone works well in our older patients with brain mets.
Worried about kidney function with platinum in the elderly.
Prior adjuvant osimertinib makes them hesitate on first-line choice, not sure how to classify.
Clear win for young, fit patients with CNS disease at baseline.

One community oncologist in a small practice said he only offers platinum-pemetrexed to patients under about 70 who walk in without a cane. Everyone else gets osimertinib alone. I'm not sure he applies that consistently.

Cardiology referrals came up a lot. Patients with a prior MI or reduced EF make the team nervous about osimertinib and the LVEF monitoring. Echo access at their practice is slow, so some just avoid starting it.

At the academic thoracic clinic, the tumor board likes adding chemo when brain mets are present at diagnosis, especially if symptomatic. They felt the extra infusion visits are worth it when the patient is otherwise fit.
Nurse navigator said transport is the real selector. Patients who live far from the infusion suite tend to stay on oral therapy only, and perfomance status is second after that.

Lots of uncertainty about patients who relapsed on adjuvant osimertinib. Nobody is sure if they count as treatment-naive for the combo. The payer has also been asking for extra documentation in those cases.
Leptomeningeal disease is a gray area for them. They would probably still use the combo if the patient can tolerate chemo, but nobody sounded confident about it.

Several clinicians said a history of ILD or prior chest radiation pneumonitis makes them stop and think before starting osimertinib at all. In that situation they lean toward close imaging follow-up and avoid stacking chemo on top.

A community doc described his best candidates for the chemo add-on as stable ECOG 1 patients in their 60s with liver mets. He thinks those patients can handle the extra toxicity. He said the discussion is easier when family are in the room.

The thoracic nurse said that frail patients are the ones she worries about. Lots of them are underweight, living alone, and already struggling with appetite at the first visit. Adding platinum means more labs and more infusion days, and she doubts many would keep up with it. The physicians there mostly agree and default to the oral drug by itself. A few said they'd like a simple frailty screen in the new patient workflow, but there isn't one now.

Workflow for brain mets at this center is MRI at baseline, then a neuro-oncology and rad onc discussion before choosing a regimen. If lesions are small and asymptomatic, they usually start the TKI and delay radiation. For larger or symptomatic lesions they tend to consider radiation first. Whether chemo gets added seems to depend mostly on how well the patient looks that day. They said there's no firm rule so its case by case.

The neuro-oncology group was positive about osimertinib in patients with brain mets at diagnosis. They said intracranial responses are often quick enough to hold off on whole brain radiation. A handful of their patients have stayed on it a long time with few neurologic problems. They would still want the chemo add-on reserved for fit patients. Overall they see CNS disease as a reason to choose a strong first-line regimen, not a reason to avoid it.

Age by itself doesn't drive the decision at this clinic, but it comes up a lot. Patients over 75 generally get osimertinib alone unless a geriatric assessment looks good. The geriatric assessment isn't routine, though, so it depends on which physician sees them. One doctor said some of her 70-something patients are fitter than people ten years younger and she doesn't want to under-treat them. Hard to say how often that happens.

Comorbidities were the main complaint from the community group. Patients with CKD, poorly controlled diabetes, or borderline blood counts are hard to fit into a platinum regimen. A few mentioned low albumin and recent weight loss as red flags. Several said that by the time the molecular results return, the patient has often declined and is no longer a candidate for combination therapy. They felt the data they've seen doesn't speak much to this real-world group.
Fit PS 0-1 only for the chemo combination, that's their line in the sand.
Over 75 with a shaky PS, they just won't add platinum.
Baseline CNS disease actually pushes them toward adding chemo, they said.
Prior adjuvant osimertinib? Still a grey zone for them honestly.
Renal function is what kills the pemetrexed conversation for a lot of their patients
Young, fit, brain involvement at diagnosis: easy yes for the combination.

Busy community practice, and the oncologist said selection often comes down to who can realistically get to infusion visits every three weeks. Older patients living far away tend to stay on osimertinib alone. Not really a clinical judgement, more logistics.
She worries about stacking chemo on top of existing heart disease or a reduced ejection fraction. With the QTc and cardiac warnings already on her mind, those patients default to single agent TKI.
His typical candidate is a younger patient, PS 0, high-burden disease or brain mets. For them he is comfortable pushing the combination. He feels the extra chair time is justified.

Frailty scoring isn't formally done in their unit, it's gestalt from the consult. I think the rule of thumb is: if they walk in alone and look robust, chemo gets discussed. Otherwise it doesn't come up.

Multidisciplinary board decides the borderline ones, especially with a history of ILD or prior chest radiotherapy. Radiation oncology opinion carries a lot of weight there. He said it's very much case by case, with no firm template.
Payer pre-authorisation is slowing things down. If PS is borderline the insurer questions the combo and the team just defualts to single agent to avoid the delay.

We spent a long time on brain mets. Her instinct is that patients with multiple asymptomatic lesions are the ones she most wants to intensify, but she is unsure how to weigh that against age. If the patient is symptomatic she would want radiotherapy sorted first, and then decide on chemo. She admitted she isn't sure whether prior local treatment changes her appetite for the combination. Probably it does, but she couldn't say how.

He kept coming back to frailty. In his clinic a lot of EGFR patients are elderly, often with a spouse who is also unwell, and the idea of adding platinum and several extra visits feels unrealistic. He worries about falls, poor appetite, and cytopenias in people who already have little reserve. Osimertinib alone is tolerable for them, so he sees no reason to risk it. He is not against the combination, he just thinks the eligible group is small.

Overall quite upbeat after a long chat. She sees a clear subset, fit, motivated, not too old, good organ function, where she would offer the combination without much hesitation. Patient preference matters a lot to her and the ones who want the most aggressive approach tend to be the same fit ones. She thinks word will spread once more colleagues see a few patients go through it comfortably. Still wants to watch tolerability closely in the first cycles.

Comorbidities came up repeatedly: diabetes, mild CKD, neuropathy, some hearing loss. He said none is an absolute barrier on its own, but together they tip him away from platinum. Pemetrexed with borderline eGFR is the one he worries about most. For these patients he usually starts the TKI and keeps chemo in reserve, though he admitted that reserve plan is a bit vague.

He is uneasy about PS 2 patients, particularly those whose performance status is poor because of the cancer itself. There is a temptation to go aggressive because they might improve fast on a TKI, but he fears being wrong with chemo on board. Nobody he knows has a clear framework for this. He said guidelines feel silent on it and he ends up deciding mostly on gut feeling, which bothers him. He'd welcome clearer thinking but didn't expect it soon.

Positive on osimertinib monotherapy for older or PS 2 patients, since it is well tolerated and oral. For him that remains a perfectly good choice and he doesn't feel guilty about not adding chemo. The combination is for a different, fitter patient. Having both options makes his selection conversations easier, he thinks.

Decisions are usually shared with the patient and family, and the discussion starts with what the person wants from the next year. Fitness matters, but so does how someone feels about hospital visits. He said the final call is rarely driven by one factor.
Fit, ECOG 0-1, no major cardiac history: fine, add chemo. Everyone else, no.
Frail 80-year-olds are not getting the chemo combo from me.
Baseline brain mets is the one group where I'd seriously consider the combo.
Honestly osimertinib alone does the job for most of my older patients.
Nobody can tell me who actually needs the add-on chemo.
Relapse after adjuvant osi, no idea what to do with them honestly
My ECOG 0 patients under 65 with good kidney function tolerate osimertinib plus a platinum doublet better than I feared. I still pick them carefully, and I won't pretend that's most of my clinic.
Comorbidities are what kills this for me. Half my referrals have CKD or heart failure on top, and a platinum-pemetrexed regimen is a hard sell for them.
Community practice here, and patients drive an hour each way. Several weeks of chemo visits for someone with ECOG 2 is just not realistic, so they get the single agent.
I was told large symptomatic brain mets are where the combo shines, but I haven't seen anything that convinces me yet. Probably needs longer follow-up. Until then I'm not changing a stable plan.
Age alone doesn't decide it for me, frailty does. I've had a 78-year-old walk in looking better than a 60-year-old smoker with COPD, so a chronological cutoff feels silly.
For a young never-smoker with multiple brain mets I'd happily start osimertinib upfront, with or without chemo. CNS control is what I care about most. Radiation can often wait.
Prior therapy muddies everything. A patient progressing after earlier TKI or adjuvant treatment isn't the population anyone studied properly, I think, and the payer wants a clean label anyway.
Pretty sure my tumor board splits on this every single week. Some want chemo added for high-burden disease, others say PS 2 ends the conversation.

Let me be blunt about selection. The trial population looks nothing like what I actually see: older, diabetic, some renal impairment, maybe a prior cancer. Adding chemo for those people means more admissions for cytopenias and fatigue. I'm not convinced the benefit justifies it outside a very fit group. Nobody gives a clear cutoff, just 'use your judgment'.

My rough checklist: ECOG 0-1, adequate marrow and kidney function, family support at home, and either high disease burden or brain involvement. If they tick most of those I'll discuss the combo. If it's only one or two, probably osimertinib alone and revisit at progression. The catch is that 'revisit' often means they're too sick for anything else. I'm not sure that sequencing logic holds up.

I've had a decent experience in a couple of younger patients with brain mets at baseline. They were ECOG 1, started osimertinib with chemo, and the headaches settled quickly. The infusion side was manageable with good nursing support. It's anecdotal, I know. But it has made me less skeptical than I was six months ago.

Infusion capacity is my real bottleneck. Even when a patient qualifies clinically, we're booking chair time weeks out, and borderline PS patients deteriorate while they wait. Then the payer wants a written rationale for the combo over single agent, and 'high-risk brain mets' gets bounced sometimes. Frustrating

On brain mets I'm torn. Osimertinib gets into the CNS well, so for small asymptomatic lesions I'd rather skip upfront SRS and watch with MRI. For symptomatic or numerous lesions I still lean on radiation first. Whether chemo adds real intracranial benefit on top, I just don't know. It looks suggestive to me but I don't think it's settled.

I keep hearing about 'ideal candidates' but the definition shifts depending on the speaker. At meetings it's under 70 and ECOG 0-1, then teh slides quietly stretch it. Real patients show up with ECOG 2 from bone pain, and I can't tell if that's reversible once the TKI kicks in. So I treat with single agent first and see.
Fit younger pts: osi+chemo an easy yes for this HCP.
ECOG 2+ and frail: wouldn't add platinum, TKI alone.
Brain mets at dx pushes HCP toward the combo, no hesitation.
Elderly w/ CKD, chemo add-on a hard no for most of his clinic
Prior adjuvant osimertinib then relapse: HCP unsure where combo fits.
Cardiac hx makes HCP nervous re QT on osimertinib.
Community onc, mostly 70+ pts. HCP said ECOG and social support drive the choice more than age itself. A fit 75 yo gets looked at same as a 60 yo.
Academic HCP likes osi+chemo for pts w/ CNS mets at baseline, esp. multiple lesions. Says the PFS gain feels meaningful enough to tolerate extra AEs in a fit pt.
HCP worried about anemia and nausea in pts w/ poor marrow reserve. Prior chemo-RT for another cancer makes him skip the pemetrexed combo. Prefers single agent there.
Tumor board handles borderline cases. If PS 2 is due to tumor burden they'll try osi alone first and reassess, I think.
PA delays for the combo at a rural clinic mean symptomatic pts get started on mono TKI anyway. HCP not thrilled but cant wait weeks.
Pts w/ prior ILD or pneumonitis: HCP cautious, wants pulm input first. Otherwise comorbidities like DM and HTN not a barrier.
Leptomeningeal disease pts are tough per HCP, no good data in his view and combo probably too much. Treats case by case, some recieve TKI alone.

Saw HCP at a large cancer center clinic. Says he now defaults to osi+chemo for fit pts under 70 w/ brain mets or high-volume disease. Thinks CNS benefit is the clincher, and baseline MRI findings often tip it. Pts w/ good PS handle pemetrexed fine in his experience, w/ dose reductions as needed. Wouldn't hesitate to offer it.

Concerned about the real-world pt. HCP said most of his EGFR pts are older w/ COPD or heart disease and don't look like trial pts. Adding platinum feels risky when PS is borderline and family is far away. Probably ends up w/ mono osimertinib in a good chunk of them. Wishes there was clearer guidance on who to skip.

Asked about sequencing. For tx-naive pts HCP is open to either mono or combo depending on PS and CNS status. Pts who had chemo for early stage disease, he's less sure and leans mono. Wants to see how peers handle it before shifting much. No strong view yet on an age cutoff.

Small community practice, no onsite tumor board. HCP says referring combo candidates to a bigger center is a hassle and many pts won't travel. Infusion chair capacity is limited, so q3w visits are a barrier for frail or rural pts. Not convinced the added burden is worth it for low-volume disease. Probably keeps them on oral tx alone.

Talked brain mets. HCP would treat small asymptomatic lesions w/ osimertinib up front and hold off on SRS, but symptomatic ones get RT first. Not sure if adding chemo changes that call. Neuro-onc input helps when lesions sit near eloquent areas. Overall comfortable but wants more clarity.

Positive convo. HCP has a handful of pts who were ECOG 2 from disease burden and improved fast on osimertinib. Said that changed how he thinks about PS, doesn't write them off now. Also noted younger never-smokers w/ CNS mets are his ideal combo pts. Nurse navigators help screen fitness and catch issues early.

HCP always checks renal and hepatic function at baseline, mostly for chemo eligibility. If CrCl is marginal, platinum is out and he goes mono. Not much concern for osimertinib itself on that front. Age alone changes nothing, though a frailty screen (G8) is sometimes used.
Fit pts, ECOG 0-1, no-brainer for osi + chemo.
Frail elderly = osi mono only, chemo add-on not realistic.
Baseline CNS mets is main reason HCP would add chemo.
Worried about renal fx in older pts on pemetrexed.
Honestly not sure where PS 2 fits.
Young never-smoker w/ brain mets, easy call for the combo imo.
Community onc, most of his pts are 75+ w/ COPD or cardiac hx so combo rarely even discussed. Defaults to single-agent tx. Sees combo as for the 'fit minority' only.
Academic thoracic HCP: tumor board flags baseline CNS disease or big tumor burden for combo. Says PS and marrow reserve decide in the end, age alone doesn't.

Likes the combo for pts w/ multiple brain mets or leptomeningeal concern, thinks extra intracranial control is worth the tox. Will still check LVEF and counts first. Said she'd rather start strong than chase progression later.
Pt w/ prior QTc prolongation, so HCP hesitant on osimertinib and wants cards input before starting. Not sure how often this comes up in his clinic, maybe a handful of pts a year.
Prior adjuvant osi pts came up. HCP unsure how to treat if relapse happens soon after stopping, no clear approach yet. Waiting to see what peers do.
PA for the combo goes smoother when chart clearly documents brain mets and good PS. Otherwise payer pushes back or asks for peer-to-peer. Clinic has a nurse who just handles these.
Had a 60 yo, ECOG 1, w/ brain mets, got carbo/pem + osi and AEs were manageable. Thinks she'd do it again for similar pts. Still picks carefully.
Diabetes and CKD pts make her nervous about adding chemo so she sticks w/ osi alone, no real debate. Says dose reductions get messy in those pts

Rural practice, so chair time and travel matter a lot. Many pts have a spouse who is also elderly and can't drive them for q3w infusions. HCP thinks this limits who realistically gets combo, even if PS is fine. Probably picks oral-only for those pts. Feels the data are good but access is the real filter.

Tumor board does a quick triage: PS, brain mets yes/no, organ function, pt preference. If CNS disease and ECOG 0-1, combo gets discussed first. Older pts w/ comorbidities usually go to osi alone. HCP said it's not a hard rule, more like a default that gets overridden sometimes. Thinks a frailty score would help but nobody uses one routinely.

Very enthusiastic for younger, fit pts, esp. those w/ brain mets at dx. Says they tolerate pemetrexed fine and want max PFS. Pts often ask about the longest benefit up front. HCP said fatigue and cytopenias are manageable w/ close follow-up. Would not offer it to a pt w/ poor PS though.

Concerned about pts w/ ILD history or prior pneumonitis, would avoid osi or at least monitor very closely. Also nervous about older pts w/ poor reserve if chemo adds toxicity. Thinks real-world pts look nothing like trial pts. Said some pts she sees are ECOG 2 w/ multiple comorbidities. Unsure what the evidence means for them.

HCP described pts who started on osi mono because PS was poor and later improved. Wonders if adding chemo then makes sense, but nobody really knows. Also asked about pts who got prior chemo for other reasons. Said she handles these case by case at tumor board. Would like more guidance but not expecting any soon.

Cancer center HCP does geriatric assessment for pts over 70 before choosing. Fit elders can get the combo, vulnerable ones get mono. Brain mets push toward intensification but not always. Says the assessment adds time to visits but he finds it useful. Still no consensus in his group on cut-offs.
ECOG 2 or worse, I'm not adding chemo. Period.
Age alone doesn't scare me off osimertinib; frailty is the real filter.
