Brain mets patients: osimertinib covers most, but the combo question is still unresolved for me.
Fit, young, brain mets at baseline? Easy combo conversation.
Honestly the chemo add-on feels like a stretch for my older pts.
Kidney function is what usually stops me, not the TKI itself.

Community practice here, so most of my EGFR patients show up ECOG 2 because they were unwell for weeks before the diagnosis. The trial population just doesnt look like them. I'm not convinced the combination data transfer.
Osimertinib alone is still my default for anybody over seventy-five. If they're fit and the brain imaging looks ugly I'll at least raise adding platinum-pemetrexed, but I'm not sure I'd push it.
For a fit 55-year-old with CNS disease at baseline I'm a lot more open to the combo than I was a year ago. Infusion chair time is the annoying part, but I can live with it.

Comorbidities nobody wants to talk about: CKD, heart failure, a prior ILD scare. Osimertinib already makes me watch the heart, and then you stack cisplatin or carbo on top. My cardiology colleagues just roll their eyes at me.
Patients who relapse after adjuvant osimertinib? Nobody has given me a clear answer. I treat them case by case and it feels a lot like guessing.
Prior auth wants ECOG documented, and I swear the combo only gets approved if the note reads perfectly. Borderline PS patients sit in limbo for weeks while the paperwork goes back and forth.
Asymptomatic brain mets, I'd probably go single-agent osimertinib and re-image early. Symptomatic ones get radiation first, then I think about the rest. Not sure the combo changes that calculus.

Our tumor board has gotten better at flagging who's really suitable for the combination: younger, good PS, high-volume disease. Still very selective, but at least it's a structured discussion now instead of gut feel.

Nobody in my clinic does a real geriatric assessment, we eyeball it from the doorway. ECOG gets charted as 1 because that's the box that keeps people on the pathway. Then I add chemo to someone far frailer than the chart says and they're in the ED by cycle two. I think we overcall fitness all the time. The TKI alone is tolerable enough that I'd rather not gamble.

Prior therapy is where it gets murky. Someone who comes to me after a first-gen TKI with T790M is a completely different conversation from the treatment-naive patients the combo data are built on. I tend to use osimertinib alone there. And people treated elsewhere with unclear records? I honestly don't know what to do with them.

Everyone says osimertinib penetrates the CNS well and I mostly believe it. But the moment there's leptomeningeal disease or lots of lesions, the talk turns to adding chemo, and I haven't seen anything that convincingly tells me who benefits. Neurosurgery and rad onc want my input and I can't give them a clean rule. Frustrating to be asked to choose without a selection tool.

I'll give credit where it's due: for the right patient the combination makes sense to me. Younger, ECOG 0-1, big burden, brain involvement at diagnosis. They tolerate it and I feel I'm giving them the best shot. I just don't pretend that's most of my patients, it's a minority.

Elderly patients with hypertension, diabetes, a bit of kidney trouble, that's my actual clinic. Anemia and nausea from chemo are not small things for them. I get that fitness matters more than birth year, but nobody gives me a threshold so I default to osimertinib alone and move on

Rural satellite clinic, so the practical side matters: patients driving a long way for infusions every three weeks. Even if they'd be clinically suitable, logistics knock a lot of them out. I'll offer the combo to those with family support and a reliable ride. Everybody else gets the tablet alone, and I think I'm okay with that.

patient_selection|pembrolizumab.t: ECOG 2 pts = HCP not comfortable w/ periop IO, too fragile for surgery.
Fit ECOG 0-1, resectable NSCLC = easy yes for pembro per HCP.
Age alone not a dealbreaker, frailty is what matters.
Brain mets? HCP says he just excludes, no data to lean on.
Autoimmune hx - case by case, tumor board decides.
Borderline PFTs, many pts never reach surgery anyway per HCP.

Community onc, says most of his stage III resectable pts are fit enough once cardiology clears them. Pembro periop is basically his default there. Thinks selection really comes down to whether the pt can handle lobectomy.
HCP mixed on 75+ pts. Chronological age less of an issue than comorbidities, esp COPD and CKD. Probably would offer if gait speed ok, not sure how he actually measures it.
Pts w/ prior transplant or chronic steroids = too much PD-1 risk imo of HCP. Sends every one to tumor board and it usually ends w/ no IO.
Gastric: many pts present w/ poor nutrition, low albumin, wt loss. HCP says that's the real barrier before even thinking about adding pembro to chemo. Gets dietitian involved first.
Thoracic surgeon type HCP would push good-PS pts toward periop IO. Likes that neoadjuvant tx lets him see who tolerates it before the OR. Says that helps him pick candidates.
HCP worried about pts who drop out after neoadjuvant, AEs then deconditioning then no longer fit for resection. Wonders if older pts get hurt more than helped. No clear answer in his mind.
Treated brain mets in gastric are rare in his clinic. For lung he'd send to rad onc first and then reconsider IO, I think. Said he's definately not enrolling anyone w/ active symptomatic dz.
Prior autoimmune dz (RA, colitis) = HCP hesitant, plus PA hassle. Hx of ILD is basically a no for him.

Rural clinic HCP, pts mostly 70s w/ CAD, DM, COPD. Says trial pts look nothing like his waiting room. Hesitant to offer pembro periop to anyone ECOG 2. Travel distance also makes monitoring for irAEs hard. Thinks real-world uptake will end up narrower than label.

HCP sees mostly gastric/GEJ. Selection hinges on HER2, PD-L1 status and whether pt can eat. Frail pts w/ obstruction get stent or feeding tube first, not sure pembro even makes sense for them. Would consider it for fit pts after tumor board review.

Very positive HCP. Over the last yr he's seen younger fit stage II-III lung pts do well through neoadjuvant and surgery on pembro-chemo. Doesn't exclude by age alone, 70s ok if PS 0-1. Only uses it in tx-naive pts. Would like more guidance on borderline cardiac pts.

Prior tx came up a lot. HCP says pts who already had chemoradiation or IO for something else dont fit the periop setting, so what to do w/ them? Also tests for EGFR/ALK first since driver+ pts probably wont benefit, but waiting on NGS delays tx. Some pts start chemo before results and it gets messy.

Tumor board POV. Surgeons, med onc, rad onc weigh in on resectability, then med onc looks at PS and comorbidities. A handful of pts get dropped for lung function. Age rarely the sole reason. HCP unsure how to handle mild renal impairment on cisplatin, often swaps to carbo.

Community HCP says elderly but fit pts surprise him. Does a quick frailty screen in clinic before deciding. Pembro tolerated better than expected in a few 70+ pts. For brain mets he'd treat locally and still consider IO. Overall comfortable picking pts.
ECOG 0 or 1 only, realistically, for the perioperative approach.
Cisplatin eligibility is the real gatekeeper here, not the checkpoint inhibitor itself.
Fit resectable stage III patients with good lung function are an easy yes for him.
Active autoimmune disease, he just doesn't go there with a PD-1.
Brain mets pretty much take them out of his perioperative pathway, treated or not.
Frailty worries me more than chronological age, honestely, and the clinic seems to agree.

The thoracic surgeon at their tumor board is keen to push IO in the neoadjuvant setting when the patient is fit and the nodes look clearly resectable. They see it as a good fit for anyone who can handle cisplatin. Younger patients with few comorbidities are the obvious group.

Honestly a lot of her gastric patients arrive already weak, with poor intake and weight loss, and that makes any combination hard to justify. She'd be reluctant to add pembro to chemo in an ECOG 2 patient. Not sure the benefit holds for that group.

Older patients aren't excluded on age alone in his clinic. It mostly comes down to cardiac and renal function and whether they'd tolerate a platinum. He thinks community colleagues are more cautious than the big-centre folks.

Prior therapy matters for him. In lung, someone who already had an immunotherapy for another indication probably wouldn't be a candidate in the perioperative setting. For gastric, he mostly talks about it in the first line, where prior exposure is rarely an issue.

COPD and poor lung reserve are what stop a lot of people from reaching surgery at all, so the perioperative regimen becomes moot. He also worries about pneumonitis in patients with baseline interstitial changes on CT. That combination makes him quite conservative.

Good chat with a gastric oncologist who feels comfortable using pembrolizumab in HER2-negative disease when the PS is decent. Having a CPS result in hand makes him feel more confident about who is likely to benefit. He said it takes some of the guesswork out.
Transplant history and chronic steroids came up and he avoids PD-1 in both unless there is truly no other option. Hepatitis and HIV status he would check but doesn't see as automatic exclusions

Renal impairment kills the cisplatin plan for a good chunk of his older patients, and then the whole KEYNOTE-671 style approach is off the table. He wondered about carboplatin swaps but said he has nothing solid to lean on.

We spent a long time on who actually gets offered perioperative pembrolizumab with chemo in lung. His view is that PS 0 or 1 is non-negotiable, and then the real filter is whether the patient can get through cisplatin and still be operable afterwards. Age by itself rarely changes his mind, but cardiac disease and borderline kidney function do. I think he is still unsure what to do with the patient who finishes neoadjuvant treatment but is too deconditioned for the adjuvant phase. That was his biggest open question.

She described her gastric clinic as mostly frail, often malnourished patients who are diagnosed late. Many are ECOG 2 by the time they reach oncology, and she feels the trials simply didn't represent them. She is cautious about adding an immune agent when a patient may not manage a second cycle of chemo. Brain mets are rare in her practice, so that isn't the worry, it's nutrition and general reserve. She would like clearer guidance for the borderline-fit group but isn't expecting it soon.

Very positive discussion with a thoracic oncologist who runs a busy multidisciplinary clinic. He finds selection fairly straightforward: resectable stage III, good PS, adequate organ function, no active autoimmune disease. Because surgeons and medical oncologists meet weekly, he can spot the fit patients early and start neoadjuvant therapy quickly. Older but fit patients are not excluded just because of birth date, in his experience. His main ask was more clarity on managing immune-related adverse events before surgery.

Mixed feelings in this one. For gastric he uses pembro mostly when the tumor is HER2 negative and CPS is meaningful, and he gets more hesistant when CPS is low. Treated, stable brain mets he would probably still consider, but active symptomatic ones go for radiation first. Comorbidities like diabetes and mild heart failure make him think twice but don't veto treatment.

Practice pattern from a community oncologist who gets lung patients referred after a CT-detected nodule. Mostly smokers with COPD and coronary disease, so many are ruled out before anyone even talks about IO. When they are fit, he sends them to surgeons quickly and then wants pembrolizumab started, but payer prior auth sometimes delays things. He said the delay alone can change whether someone stays a candidate. Not sure how common that is elsewhere.

Encouraging conversation with a gastric oncologist who feels the field is becoming more inclusive. He said older patients with a decent PS and reasonable organ function are offered treatment more often than a few years ago. For brain mets he would treat locally first and then reconsider, which he finds reasonable. He likes that biomarker testing gives him a cleaner basis for deciding than guessing from how the patient looks. He still wants real-world experience in the frail group.
Mostly ECOG 0-1 going forward, and the 2s get a longer conversation first.
Cisplatin eligibility is the real gate here, not pembro itself.
Fit patients under 70 with resectable stage III are easy yeses for pembrolizumab.
Chronic steroids for COPD flares make docs hesitant on pembro, understandably
Brain mets? Those go down a separate pathway, not periop.
Frail elderly gastric patients rarely get offered the periop sequence at all.

Community clinic had a patient in her late 60s with good PS and clean PFTs who went through neoadjuvant pembro plus chemo without much trouble. Surgery happened on schedule and the surgeon was comfortable. That's now the profile the team thinks of first.

At the cancer center clinic the group is split on patients over 75. Some say frailty scoring matters more than age, others just default to chemo alone. Not sure anyone is doing a formal geriatric assessment routinely.
Pre-existing autoimmune disease, like lupus or active colitis, is a hard stop for most of the docs I spoke with. They worry about flares mid-treatment and losing the surgical window.

Payer prior auth in the lung setting asks for documented PS and stage, so the clinic nurse pulls those before tumor board. Borderline PS patients tend to stall at that step. Probably more paperwork than clinical objection

One gastric surgeon said many of his patients show up malnourished and sarcopenic, so they often can't finish a periop sequence anyway. He thinks nutrition is the bigger barrier than which drug is on the table.

Academic thoracic group likes that most resectable patients are fit enough for the full periop plan, including pembrolizumab. They said selection is simpler than in metastatic disease. Prior therapy is rarely a question because these are treatment-naive.
Pulmonologist said that with prior chest radiation he would want to look closely at lung reserve and any pneumonitis history first. Not a firm exclusion, more case by case.

A medical oncologist at a regional hospital described the typical problem patient: early 70s, diabetic, borderline kidney function, mild heart failure. Cisplatin is out, carboplatin sometimes gets swapped in, but he isn't sure the pembro data really cover that substitution. Tumor board usually ends up cautious. He worries about starting and then having someone too deconditioned for surgery.

Brain mets came up in a neuro-oncology-heavy clinic. Stage III patients get a baseline brain MRI, and anyone with a positive scan is moved off the periop path entirely. A couple of docs wondered about oligometastatic cases treated with SRS, but nobody had tried it. I think they'd want to see more before changing that.

A smaller private practice oncologist said selection has gotten more straightforward. He checks ECOG, cisplatin fitness, and autoimmune or transplant history, and I don't think PD-L1 drives it much for him in this setting. If those are fine he proposes pembro. Patients are generally relieved to have something beyond chemo alone. Overall he feels comfortable with it.

In gastric, several docs said their patients are older with multiple comorbidities, so the periop approach is hard to apply. One described a typical case: 78, ischemic heart disease, poor appetite, family wanting something gentle. They'd rather go straight to surgery or use a doublet. Few seemed to see pembro as a fit for that group, definately not the frailest ones.

Endocrine history came up at a hospital clinic. Patients with existing thyroid disease or diabetes aren't excluded with pembro, but the nurse navigator flags them for closer labs. They also check baseline steroid use and hepatitis status. The workflow adds a few visits before cycle one. Docs didn't seem bothered, they just want it organized.

A thoracic surgeon at a large hospital said his biggest worry is patients whose PS drops during neoadjuvant treatment and who then can't have surgery. It has happened to a few, and the curative window was lost. He's not sure how to predict who will decline. Lung function and age both seem to play in but nothing reliable. He'd be more cautious with marginal patients.
A geriatric-leaning clinic said fit patients in their 70s did fine on pembrolizumab, so age alone isn't a reason to skip it. They check PS and heart function first. Seemed pleasantly surprised.
Frail 78-year-olds? Nobody wants to give cisplatin there, so the question is moot.
PS 2 patients basically get excluded by default in our clinic.
Brain mets still a grey zone, and nothing I've seen really settles it.
Fit, under 70, resectable, no autoimmune history: easy yes for pembro.
Real-world patients are sicker than trial patients, and we all know it.
Depends on whether cisplatin is even on the table.

Our tumor board keeps debating whether a borderline PS 1 with COPD should get perioperative pembro at all. Nobody wants to cause a pneumonitis that blocks surgery, but I think we probably under-treat out of fear.

Older patients, say mid-seventies, I check renal function first and fitness second. If they cant take cisplatin I'm not convinced pushing the chemo-IO combination is worth it. Pembro on its own isn't really what the neoadjuvant story is built on.
In a community practice we've had a few younger, fit gastric patients get through pembro with chemo without drama. Selection was strict, mind you. The good ones were obvious from the first visit.
Prior autoimmune disease, especially anything on active treatment, is where I stop. Payers also want every detail documented and I don't have time for that fight over a marginal patient.

Patients with treated, stable brain mets sometimes get through, but I'm not sure anyone can say what to do with new lesions. We usually radiate first and reconsider afterwards. Neuro input is slow, which doesn't help.
Transplant patients? Forget it, the rejection risk scares everyone. Nobody has given me a clear answer on that and I'm tired of askin.

An elderly patient with ECOG 2 and heart failure was referred to me for periop IO. The surgeon wasn't even sure they'd survive the resection. The referral pattern ignores reality and that frustrates me.

The trial population looks nothing like who walks into my clinic. We see alot of smokers with heart disease, poor PFTs and borderline kidney function. By the time they're staged, many can't tolerate the platinum backbone. So when people ask who a good candidate is, I say a small slice. The rest get surgery alone or something gentler, and I'm not sure that's wrong.

I'll give credit where it's due: for a fit patient with resectable disease and good organ function, the perioperative approach with pembrolizumab is something I'm comfortable offering. PS 0 or 1, adequate lung reserve for resection, no steroid requirement. The conversation is simple with those people. It gets messy with everyone else, but that's a different discussion.

For gastric we mostly see older patients with nutritional problems, so frailty screening matters more than age on paper. Albumin, weight loss, can they eat. Plenty are in rough shape at diagnosis and never make it to the periop plan. I'd probably treat a robust 75 over a deconditioned 62. Biomarker status plays in too, though I'm vague on how much weight colleagues give it.

Timing kills us with immunotherapy. Patients wait weeks for staging and molecular results, deteriorate, and PS has slipped by the time we're ready to start. Then the neoadjuvant window is gone. Nobody mentions that in selection discussions. It's logistics, not biology, that screens out a lot of people.

Younger patients with no comorbidities, I'm happy. Pembro in that group seems manageable and my nurses know the toxicity drill. Prior therapy isn't an issue since they're treatment-naive in the periop setting. I do wish the guidance on edge cases were clearer, but practical selection is straightforward for these folks.

Prior chest radiation, ILD, any baseline lung issue makes me hesitate with a PD-1. I'd get the CT reviewed and probably ask pulmonology. Not saying never, but it adds time and I'm skeptical it's worth it for every borderline case.

We run a busy thoracic clinic and honestly selection has gotten easier. We screen for autoimmune history, baseline steroid use and lung function up front, and the ones who pass go ahead. Pembro in that group has been less painful than I expected. Not everyone is convinced, me included on some days, but I'd rather treat the right few than hedge on everyone.
Probably fine in fit patients, not sure about ECOG 2.
Frailty worries me more than age, I think, with pembro.
Seems like a decent option for younger fit patients perioperatively.
Brain mets cases, would need to see more before anyone considers it.
Age alone doesn't seem to be the deciding factor for most of them.
Not sure yet how they handle pts with prior autoimmune disease on pembrolizumab.

In their community clinic the oncologists seem to pick perioperative candidates mostly by whether the patient can tolerate cisplatin. If not, I think pembrolizumab alone just isn't on the table for them, though nobody was certain.

One doctor mentioned that elderly patients with COPD and heart failure may not get through the full neoadjuvant phase. Not sure the adjuvant part even happens for a lot of them. Worried that real-world selection is a lot narrower than the trial population.

Thoracic surgeon thinks pembrolizumab seems a reasonable fit for resectable patients who are fit for surgery with good lung reserve. Would still want to see how it plays out in routine practice, but overall encouraged.
Gastric team said PD-L1 status may drive who gets considered, more than performance status. Still unclear to them how to weigh that against nutrition problems at diagnosis.

Pt scenario raised: borderline PS after big weight loss, probably from gastric outlet issues. They'd hesitate to add an IO there, mostly because toxicity could knock the patient out of surgery. Not sure there is any guidance for this.

Younger patients with no major comorbidities seem to tolerate it well from what she has seen, so she may be more open to using it earlier. Wants to see more follow up first though, and says a academic center like hers would probably adopt it faster than smaller sites.
They weren't sure whether earlier chemo exposure changes who they'd consider for pembrolizumab. Would need clearer data before forming a view.
Concerned about steroid use in brain metastases patients, it might blunt benefit but they're not sure. Most would probably avoid IO in that group for now

Spoke with a medical oncologist running a busy day clinic. She said she mostly looks at performance status and whether the patient lives alone before deciding on perioperative immunotherapy. Frailty scoring isn't done formally, it's more gestalt, I think. Comorbidities like diabetes seem to matter less to her than prior autoimmune issues. She wasn't sure if older patients are being under-offered.

Pleasantly surprised: the team seems fairly comfortable using pembrolizumab in patients past their mid seventies as long as they are active with no major organ issues. They feel chronological age may matter less than functional status. They said they'd probably check in more often with older patients early on. Might be a comfort-level thing that grows with experience.

Brain mets came up repeatedly. The group feels those patients are mostly absent from what they've seen, so they're not sure what to tell them. Treated, stable lesions may be okay but nobody wanted to commit. There seems to be real reluctance here. They would need real-world experience before changing practice.

Payer angle from the clinic pharmacist: approval in the perioperative lung setting seems to depend on documented PS and surgical eligibility. They aren't sure how denials would go for borderline cases. Timing matters too since the neoadjuvant start can't wait very long. They may end up choosing only clearly fit patients to avoid delays.

The tumour board seems fairly supportive overall. Thoracic colleagues said most resectable patients they see are decent candidates for pembrolizumab, with prior smoking-related lung disease the main thing they'd watch. They think good baseline function and a clear surgical plan matter most. Nobody raised age as a big barrier, though I'd guess that may change once they see a few toxicity cases.

Gastric surgeon said patients who already had treatment for another cancer or have poor oral intake are the ones he hesitates over. He isn't sure whether an anti-PD-1 helps them or just adds risk before an operation. Wants to see how others are managing these cases. For now he seems to default to leaving them out.

patient_selection|sacituzumab govitecan.t: ECOG 0-1 only, anyone worse and he'd hesitate.
Fit pts post-CDK4/6 + endocrine, SG an easy sell for him.
Elderly frail pts: not touching SG, neutropenia fear.
Active brain mets = no clue what to do, data thin imo.
Prefers it for pts w/ visceral burden who still walk into clinic.
Good fit when pt is 2L+ and still ECOG 1, I think that's his sweet spot.
Community onc, 70s pt w/ HR+ MBC, several chemo lines already. Would consider SG if ECOG 1 and counts OK, but wants a G-CSF plan upfront. Not sure about dose reductions in older pts.
Worried re: pts w/ prior bad diarrhea or IBD hx, the payload reminds him of irinotecan. Would just skip SG there.
Academic HCP: endocrine-resistant pts, visceral disease but still fit, are who he'd move to SG quickly. Tumor board usually agrees after CDK4/6.
UC pts post-platinum and IO, he'd only think SG if PA gets through. Renal fxn matters to him, CKD pts a grey zone.
Age alone not the issue, frailty is. But most of his 80+ pts are frail enough that he'd go oral tx or BSC instead.
UGT1A1 testing isnt routine at his site. Worried about pts w/ known Gilbert's, so he'd wait on tox picture before offering SG.
Says prior tx matters more than age for him. If pt had many chemo lines already he's less keen. Wants to see earlier-line use before changing habits.
Stable brain mets post-RT not an automatic exclusion in his mind, I think. Would still want neuro-onc input at tumor board before using SG.

Main barrier for him is comorbidities. Many of his pts have cardiac or diabetes issues plus poor reserve, and he feels the AEs (neutropenia, fatigue, diarrhea) could tip them over. Infusion center staffing is also thin so close monitoring is hard. He'd rather keep SG for the fittest pts only. Not convinced it fits real-world pts, honestly.

Mixed view. For HR+/HER2- pts after endocrine + CDK4/6 and a chemo line, he'd consider SG if ECOG is 0-1 and marrow looks ok. Older pts he'd treat case by case, probably with upfront dose discussion. Brain mets he sends to rad onc first, then reassesses. Payer PA delays are the thing that actually decides timing for him.

Very positive on pt selection. His ideal pt is HR+ MBC, progressed on endocrine + CDK4/6, 1-2 chemo lines, ECOG 0-1, good counts. He said these pts do better on SG than another single-agent chemo, in his experience. Age 70s is fine if they're robust and have family support. Uses a tumor board check for anyone borderline.

Doesnt see SG as suitable for most of his pts. Typical clinic pt is 75+, frail, with CKD or HF, and some have untreated brain mets. He worries about hospitalization from neutropenic fever and says caregivers can't manage that. So he mostly goes with palliative approach or oral options. Would reconsider only if a clearly fit pt shows up.

Thinks the 'good candidate' is mostly about trajectory, not birthdate. A pt with rapid progression but ECOG 1 gets considered, a slow-burn pt on endocrine stays there. He mentioned prior ADC exposure as an open question, not sure how he'd sequence. Pts w/ liver issues make him pause, would want hepatology input. Overall open-minded but cautious.

Mostly neutral, he said selection is basically ECOG, counts and prior lines. UC pts are rarer in his clinic so no strong view there. Wants a clear G-CSF and diarrhea protocol before starting anyone. Would revisit after a few pts in his own practice.
ECOG 0-1 only, that's who they would put on it.
Worried about older patients with poor marrow reserve and neutropenia.
Fit HR+ patients after endocrine plus CDK4/6 are the obvious fit for SG.
Brain mets patients mostly get left out, no real confidence it works there.
Depends on how many prior lines, honestly.
Frail 80-year-olds in her community clinic? She wouldn't start it.

In the academic breast clinic, the patients who do well are ECOG 0 or 1 with decent liver function and no big diarrhea history. Those are the ones she feels comfortable starting on sacituzumab. She said age by itself doesn't put her off.
Community oncologist checks UGT1A1 status when she can, but it isn't routine in her practice. Mostly she looks at age and how the patient handled prior chemo.

Urology group said a lot of their bladder patients are cisplatin-ineligible with poor kidney function already, so adding another toxic drug after enfortumab makes them hesitate. Not sure they'd use it beyond second line.

For a patient with stable treated brain mets, the doc would consider it if systemic disease is driving things, but it wouldn't be first pick. He wants fresh CNS imaging before starting and would reassess every couple of cycles.

Infusion nurses at a busy center flagged that older patients with diabetes or prior bowel problems worry them because of diarrhea and dehydration. The physician agreed and said it makes him pick patients carefully. He tends to avoid anyone living alone without family nearby.
She's been pleasantly surprised how some 70-somethings tolerate it with G-CSF support. Starts full dose in fit patients and dose reduces later if needed.
Payer prior auth in their region requires documented endocrine and chemo lines before approving, so selection ends up driven by that as much as by clinical judgment.
Prior pelvic radiation or a history of colitis would be a no for her. She's also hesitant with anyone whose baseline ANC is borderline, since delays tend to pile up.

Seen in a mixed academic and satellite HR+ practice. The oncologist mainly thinks about SG for patients who have progressed on endocrine therapy with a CDK4/6 inhibitor and at least one chemo. She also looks at visceral burden, since fast-moving disease makes her more willing to accept the toxicity. Comorbidities like heart failure don't worry her much with this drug, but marrow and gut issues do. Overall she sees it as a reasonable option for a fairly fit group rather than a broad default.

Medical oncologist in a rural clinic said the travel burden is a real selection issue. Patients who live far away and recieve care across two sites struggle with the day 1 and day 8 schedule. Add frailty and a caregiver who can't drive, and he usually chooses an oral or less frequent option. He also doesn't feel comfortable managing febrile neutropenia calls overnight. So even good-performance-status patients sometimes don't get it.

Breast specialist said her best experiences have been with patients who are ECOG 1, have already had several lines, and are motivated to keep going. She sees prior CDK4/6 exposure as a clear marker for who qualifies. Even a few patients in their mid-70s did fine once the team set up early antidiarrheal plans. She thinks the key is a good baseline conversation about what to expect. She'd happily use it earlier if access allowed.

Urothelial team said they mostly see patients after platinum and a checkpoint inhibitor, and by then performance status has often slipped to ECOG 2. Those patients are usually steered to supportive care. The few who stay ECOG 1 with adequate renal function are considered case by case. Nobody there felt strongly that prior enfortumab rules a patient out or in. It just comes down to who is still well enough.

Pharmacist at a large cancer center said they run a quick pre-treatment screen covering baseline counts, bowel history, and what the patient has already had. The workflow flags anyone with prior irinotecan intolerance for a doc review. It's been smooth and the oncologists seem comfortable with it. Patients who pass it generally start without much drama, which has made the team more confident using sacituzumab in a slightly broader group.

Palliative-leaning oncologist says he thinks twice about any patient with multiple comorbidities, like COPD plus CKD, in later lines. His worry is that a hospital admission from toxicity could wipe out whatever benefit they get. He'd rather have an honest talk about goals than push another ADC. Not against the drug, just very selective, and probably a handful of his patients ever qualify.
ECOG 2 with a neutropenia history? Hard no from me.
Honestly only my fit ECOG 0-1 patients ever get considered.
Brain mets patients basically get left out of the conversation.
Fit, post-CDK4/6 and post-chemo? SG is an easy sell there.
Not sure anyone over 80 should be on SG at all.
Prior enfortumab makes the sequencing murky, that's my main hang-up.

Community clinic, no smooth growth factor workflow, so I'm wary of anyone with borderline marrow reserve. The neutropenia and diarrhea risk worries me more in frail patients than the discussion at congress lets on. For a marginal patient I'd rather just use capecitabine.

Age alone doesn't stop me. I look at who's at home and whether they'd actually call at 2am with a fever. I had a 76-year-old do fine and a 68-year-old who crashed, so it's more frailty than birthdate, I think. Recieving that kind of toxicity at home is the real worry.

HR+ patients who've gone through endocrine therapy, a CDK4/6 and a couple of chemo lines? I'm happy to use sacituzumab govitecan. They're usually still fit enough, and I don't have much else that feels meaningful at that point.

Payer wants documentation of two prior chemo lines and the prior auth drags on for weeks with SG. By the time it comes through, the performance status has slipped and they're no longer candidates. Frustrating loop, and nobody upstream seems to care.

UGT1A1 testing comes up, but nobody in my practice orders it routinely. I'm not sure it should change who I pick, probably only for very frail patients or anyone with a history of severe chemo toxicity.
Chronic diarrhea or IBD history, I'd probably skip. Honestly nobody can tell me how often that actually bites in real practice, and I haven't had to test it myself yet.

With sacituzumab in urothelial, brain mets is where I get frustrated. Anyone with active CNS disease is basically excluded from the data I trust, so I have nothing solid to counsel with. Even treated and stable lesions leave me guessing. I end up sending those patients to radiation or a trial and moving on. It's a big gap for a population that isn't small.

In urothelial, most of my patients arrive after platinum and a checkpoint inhibitor, and a good chunk are already worn down. The real question is whether they're fit enough for another line at all. Some had an enfortumab-based regimen too, and then I'm unsure about order and overlap of toxicity. I take it case by case, but I don't feel the selection rules are clear. SG is an option, just not a confident one.

I came in skeptical, but my best experience was a patient with good performance status, no major comorbidities, and heavy pretreatment who stayed on for a while. She kept her routine and didn't spend her life in the infusion chair. That's the patient I'd choose again. I still wouldn't stretch it to marginal patients because the downside is bigger.

Elderly patients are where I see the most mess. Nobody does a proper geriatric assessment in my clinic, so we eyeball frailty in a ten minute visit and hope. Then teh first cycle goes badly and we backpedal with dose cuts or stop. I think we're picking by gut feel, and that isn't good enough for a drug with this toxicity profile. Families deserve better counseling than we give.

Stable, treated brain mets with systemic disease driving things? I'd consider sacituzumab govitecan, but I'm not totally comfortable. I'd want imaging recently clean and the neurologic picture quiet. Unclear to me if the ADC does anything intracranially, so I'd be treating the body and watching the head. I'd probably tell the patient we're extrapolating.

I expected renal and cardiac comorbidities to rule out a lot of patients, but they've been more manageable than I feared. Dose adjustments and close lab checks got most of them through. Still not a drug for someone who can't make visits or follow instructions. For a motivated patient with some comorbidity, I'd still go ahead.
I was skeptical, but one ECOG 1 patient with heavily pretreated HR+ disease stayed on for months and kept working. That shifted my view for similar fit patients.
Prior ADC exposure is rare in my clinic, so I've no real experience. I'd probably hesitate and look at the interval since the last therapy.
Brain mets are the sticking point; most colleagues won't offer it with active CNS disease.
ECOG 0-1, no visceral crisis, post-CDK4/6 and endocrine: SG feels like an easy yes.
Age alone doesn't stop me, it's frailty and bowel history that decide
Honestly, anyone ECOG 2 or above, I'd hesitate given the neutropenia risk.
Depends how many lines they've already had, probably third or later for most.
Worried about older urothelial pts with poor renal function and no G-CSF support.

A fit 58-year-old with HR+ disease progressing after endocrine plus CDK4/6 and a chemo would be a natural SG candidate in her community clinic. She likes that there's a clear post-chemo slot. Her one condition is that the patient lives close enough to call in quickly about diarrhea.

Comorbidities worry him more than age. He'd avoid SG in anyone with inflammatory bowel disease or recurrent diverticulitis, since diarrhea can turn serious fast. Also not sure what to do about UGT1A1 questions, nobody tests routinely where he works.

Tends to reserve SG for patients who've already been through endocrine therapy, a CDK4/6 inhibitor and at least one chemo. Prior taxane exposure doesn't bother him much. Beyond that it's about whether the patient can realistically manage day 1 and day 8 visits.

Said elderly but fit patients do better than people expect, as long as dose reduction is discussed early and G-CSF is ready. Biological age matters more than the birth date to him. He'd happily use sacituzumab in a 75-year-old who walks into clinic alone.

Stable treated brain mets are a gray zone for her team. She thinks the evidence is thin, so she'd probably only consider it if the CNS disease were controlled with radiation and the extracranial disease was driving things. Payers also tend to ask about it.

In urothelial the conversation is mostly about who is left after enfortumab and a checkpoint inhibitor, and many cisplatin-ineligible patients with poor kidney function never get that far. He'd consider SG for those who still hold ECOG 1 but is unsure about marrow reserve after so many prior lines.

Frail patients coming through the nursing home referral route rarely get sacituzumab, the infusion schedule and infection risk just don't fit. He mentioned families often push for 'one more try' and thats where it gets uncomfortable.

After a long chat, her view is that selection is mostly about reserve. ECOG 0 to 1 is the baseline she wants, and she looks hard at counts, albumin and how they tolerated prior chemo. Age by itself isn't a reason to say no, though she admits to being more cautious past about 75. Liver mets with some bilirubin elevation make her nervous. She'd like clearer guidance for borderline patients but isn't sure it exists yet.

He came across as quite enthusiastic by the end. For HR+/HER2- patients who've run out of endocrine options and had a chemo, he sees SG as the obvious next step when ECOG is 0-1. Several of his heavily pretreated patients kept good function and wanted something active. He thinks proactive antiemetics, G-CSF and early loperamide teaching make the difference. Even so, he'd keep it away from anyone with uncontrolled infection or active colitis.

She was candid that she's hesitant overall. Her patients tend to be older with cardiac disease, diabetes and CKD, and she worries a toxic regimen will land them in hospital. Neutropenic fever is the scenario she dreads, especially for rural patients an hour from the ED. In many of those cases she'd rather offer gentler single-agent chemo or supportive care. Brain mets pretty much end the discussion for her.

Prior therapy sequencing came up repeatedly. In breast he thinks SG belongs after endocrine/CDK4/6 and a chemo, but he wondered whether patients who progressed quickly on first-line chemo would do well. In urothelial he sees it after platinum and immunotherapy, with local EV access changing the picture. Comorbidity-wise he wants a reasonable marrow and no chronic diarrhea. In the end he said he'd go partly on gut feeling about the patient in front of him.

What bothers him most is how little guidance there is outside the studied population. Real-world patients are older, more often ECOG 2, and frequently have stable or untreated brain mets, which I think were largely not represented. He doesn't feel comfortable extrapolating, so he tends to avoid the drug for them. Pharmacy and payer pushback on anything that looks off-label adds friction. He'd want more real-world experience before widening his selection.

At her tumor board, SG gets raised early for fit patients, and she's pleased about that. She likes that it's an option for people who've had endocrine therapy and don't want to go back to older chemo. Patients in their 60s and some 70s have done fine, she said, when family support is good. Dose delays and reductions are used without much fuss. She thinks the main barrier is identifying the right patient before they decline.
Patients with Gilbert's or a known UGT1A1 variant make him pause; he's not sure whether to start lower or skip it. Otherwise he mostly looks at ECOG and counts.
Frail 80-year-old with ECOG 2? Honestly wouldn't go near it.
Fit ECOG 0-1 patient post CDK4/6 and chemo is the obvious candidate for sacituzumab.
Treated, stable brain mets probably fine in practice, but the evidence feels thin to them.
Anyone with a history of significant bowel problems or bad diarrhoea makes him hesitant, he said he'd probably recieve it only with close monitoring.
Mostly comes down to how much marrow reserve is left after earlier lines.
Younger, motivated, good PS: happy to use it early after progression.

Community oncologist said most referrals arrive already ECOG 2 after several chemo lines, so he rarely feels comfortable starting it. His main worry is neutropenia in that group. The day 1 and day 8 visits are also a lot for people who are already tired.

She looks at prior therapy history much more than age. If a patient has been through endocrine therapy, a CDK4/6 inhibitor and a couple of chemos, she'd consider it. Chronological age alone isn't a deal-breaker for her.

At their academic breast clinic they're comfortable treating older patients as long as they're fit and independent. They use G-CSF support readily and feel that takes the edge off the neutropenia concern. I got the sense the real selection filter is how the patient looks in the room, not the birth year.

In urothelial, nearly everyone he sees has already had platinum, a checkpoint inhibitor and often enfortumab. By then renal function and PS have usually slipped. He thinks the truly fit patient for this drug is the exception rather than the rule.
Not sure whether UGT1A1 status should change who gets treated. They don't test routinely and said they would like clearer guidance. For now they just dose-reduce at the first sign of toxicity.

Likes having an option once endocrine therapy is exhausted, especially in visceral disease where a response matters. The patients he'd pick are those with good PS who are symptomatic and need disease control. He thinks that group is where the drug is easiest to justify.

Payer pre-authorisation wants documented prior lines and sometimes takes weeks. By the time it comes through, a few of his borderline patients have dropped a PS point and are no longer candidates. He called that the most frustrating part of selection.

Older patients with cardiac comorbidities don't worry her much with this drug. Her concerns are infection risk and whether the patient lives far from the clinic if they get febrile. She thinks social support often decides candidacy more than the cardiac history does. Overall she lands somewhere in the middle: open to it, but cautious.

We talked for a long time about who she'd actually start. A fit patient with HR+ disease, several prior lines and no major organ dysfunction is straightforward. The grey zone is the person with ECOG 1 going on 2, mild renal impairment and limited family help. She said she would probably go with a reduced starting approach there, but isn't sure that's right. Mostly she feels the label doesn't help her draw the line.

His view is that real-world patients look very different from the ones in the trials. Many are older, have multiple comorbidities, and have had treatment-related cytopenias already. He worries that expecting a good outcome in those people is optimistic. He would rather save it for a narrow group and said he'd be nervous about a first-cycle neutropenic admission. Honestly he sounded more concerned than excited about broadening use.

This was an encouraging conversation overall. She has treated several patients who were older but physically active, and they tolerated it better than she expected with dose adjustments and growth factor support. She now looks at function and independence first and age second. Patients with a limited number of remaining options and good PS are the ones she now flags early. She said she wishes she had started considering it sooner for a couple of them.

Brain metastases came up repeatedly. He is reluctant to use it with active or progressing CNS disease because he doesn't know how well it works there. Leptomeningeal involvement is an absolute no for him. For treated, stable lesions he would still discuss it, but he'd want local therapy sorted first and frequent imaging. In practice most of his patients with CNS disease also have worse PS, so the question rarely comes up cleanly.

They use a formal geriatric screen for anyone over a certain age, mainly to separate fit from vulnerable. A fit older patient gets the same discussion as a younger one. Vulnerable patients are usually steered toward gentler options or best supportive care. She felt the ADC sits in between: effective enough to want to offer, but toxic enough that frailty matters a lot. I think she would welcome simpler tools to make that call quickly in a busy clinic.

Prior therapy sequencing was the thing he kept returning to. In breast he wants to see endocrine-based options truly used up before moving on. In urothelial he is unsure where it fits relative to the other ADC, and that uncertainty makes him cautious. He also pointed out that heavily pretreated patients are the ones most likely to have poor marrow. So the people who qualify on paper are not always the people who qualify clinically.

patient_selection|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: Fit, good PS, no lung history: an easy yes for T-DXd.
Any prior ILD and he won't even consider it.
Stable brain mets after local therapy? Open to it, but cautiously.
Frail patients in their eighties, no. He would go endocrine first.
Likes it after CDK4/6 progression in HER2-low, as long as ECOG is 0-1.
Cardiac history makes her pause especially in older pts with no recent echo

Says most of her patients are a bit older and carry several comorbidities, so she screens hard. Probably only about one in three looks like the clean candidate she imagines for T-DXd. She does not think that is a bad thing.

Infusion chairs and nursing time are the limit in his small community unit. He worries about managing nausea and early pneumonitis symptoms in people who live far away, so he picks patients carefully.

Thinks the HER2-low group after endocrine therapy is where this finally fits. Patients who are fit, still working and want something active get it first in his mind. He said it feels like a real option for them, not a last resort.

Prior lines matter to her less than how the patient tolerated them. If someone is worn down after chemo or has marrow issues, she hesitates. A fresher patient after endocrine therapy is a much easier conversation, I think.

Long-term smokers and anyone with COPD or reduced lung reserve are her red flag group. She said she cannot tell the difference between a flare and drug-related lung toxicity in them, so she mostly avoids T-DXd there.

Payer prior auth is shaping who gets it, he says. The staff must have clear IHC documentation of HER2-low status on file, and when the pathology report is vague the patient waits. That delay biases him toward patients with tidy records.
Active, untreated brain mets are a no for him until the CNS is dealt with. He does not trust that he can sort out new neuro symptoms from treatment effects. He said the data feels thin to him there.
Young, fit, with symptomatic visceral disease: she would reach for it quickly. She values the speed of response she expects and is comfortable with the monitoring plan.

We talked for a long time about performance status, and her view is nuanced. ECOG 0-1 is clearly fine, while ECOG 2 depends on why the patient is declining, whether tumor burden or other illness. If it is the cancer she might still try it with close follow-up. If it is cardiac or pulmonary disease she would not. She admitted that this is a gut judgment rather than a rule.

She is mainly concerned about frailty in older patients, which she thinks gets underestimated in clinic. Age alone is not her issue, but a patient who lives alone, struggles with transport and cannot report symptoms quickly is a real worry. Scan schedules for ILD surveillance add burden, and nausea can tip a marginal patient into hospital. Honestly she'd rather offer them something gentler than risk a bad toxicity. She still feels uneasy about that choice.

Overall he was quite positive after we went through his caseload. Most of the patients he would offer T-DXd to are HER2-low, endocrine-pretreated and otherwise well, with good organ function and a reliable family. He said that for them the benefit versus risk balance feels favorable. He would still do a baseline lung assessment and a clear conversation about symptoms. For the right person it is simply an easier decision than another chemo.

Comorbidity screening is his sticking point. Prior chest radiation, autoimmune disease needing steroids, or a history of drug-induced pneumonitis all push him away from it. He's not sure how much any one factor matters, but together they make him nervous. He said he'd rather lose a candidate than manage a fatal lung event. Some colleagues in his group are more relaxed, apparently.

On brain mets, she was balanced. She would consider T-DXd in patients with treated, stable lesions who have no steroid requirement, and she likes that the drug may have some CNS activity, though she isn't certain how strong. Untreated or symptomatic disease would go to radiation or surgery first. Follow-up imaging would need to be tight. She admitted that her comfort depends on neuro-oncology input being easy to get.

Sequencing is what she keeps coming back to. She doesn't want to use T-DXd too early in someone who could still do well on endocrine combinations, but waiting too long means patients are too sick to receive it. So the 'right' patient is a moving target for her. Probably after one or two lines, if PS holds. She wasn't sure the clinic has a clean way to decide that moment.
Fine with ECOG 0-1, hesitant beyond that.
Stable treated brain mets patients are the ones she'd put on it first.
Any history of ILD and T-DXd is a no for him.
Older but functionally fit patients shouldnt be excluded, in her view.
Frail patients with bad COPD? Not for T-DXd.
After endocrine and chemo are done, HER2-low patients are an easy yes for him.

Small community clinic with only one infusion chair for long visits. He'd use T-DXd for fit patients after endocrine therapy, but scheduling the monitoring scans is a hassle. Sounded more like a logistics issue than a question of who qualifies.
Cardiac comorbidity comes up a lot in her older patients. With a borderline EF she'd rather stay on older HER2 agents, though she's not sure how much the LVEF concern really matters for T-DXd.
For brain mets he does radiation first, then considers the ADC if systemic disease is progressing and the CNS is quiet. He doesn't feel there's enough to use it in active untreated lesions.

Academic oncologist said she's using T-DXd in HER2-low patients who are still ECOG 0 or 1 and have already had endocrine therapy plus a CDK4/6. She's pretty comfortable with that group and doesn't see it as a stretch.
Prior auth is the main barrier for patients who haven't had enough prior lines, according to the nurse navigator. Lots of back-and-forth with the payer, and a couple of patients got delayed by weeks.
Doesn't use an age cutoff. Looks at gait speed and whether the patient lives alone, and runs a quick frailty screen at the first visit.
Pulmonary history worries him. A former smoker with mild emphysema was passed over for T-DXd last month because he didn't want to risk pneumonitis in that setting.
A few patients with stable treated brain mets have done fine on it in her practice, I think. She'd keep offering it to that group.

Rural practice, no pulmonologist nearby. He says that makes him cautious about starting anyone with a lung history, since he'd have to send them far for a work-up if symptoms appear. Baseline CT is easy enough to get, but follow-up imaging is inconsistent. He also admitted some patients dont come back promptly when they have a cough. Overall he picks only the most reliable patients for T-DXd.

Her older patients usually get a geriatric assessment before anything new is started. If they score fine, she's open to the ADC, sometimes with an early dose reduction to be careful. Family preference carries a lot of weight in these visits. She wasn't sure whether being 75 or older should change anything on its own, probably not.

By the time many patients reach T-DXd they've had several lines and are already ECOG 2. He feels the drug gets used too late in a lot of cases. The ones he'd really like to treat are too tired to tolerate it well. He thinks earlier sequencing might help, but local habits and referral patterns keep pushing it back. Frustrating for him.

Selection for HER2-low is still messy in her clinic. Pathology sometimes reports IHC 0 on an old biopsy, and she isnt sure whether to re-biopsy or just proceed. Patients who are fit and clearly 1+ or 2+ are straightforward. For borderline reports she waits for the tumor board, which adds a week or so.

Her main worry is the frail patient with diabetes and kidney disease. Nausea and the antiemetic burden can tip those patients into the hospital. On the other hand, she says her fitter patients with normal organ function handle it reasonably well. She'd weigh comorbidities more heavily than age. Still not sure where to draw the line for borderline renal function.

Their neuro-radiology meeting happens weekly, so brain mets cases get a quick decision. If lesions are treated and stable, he's happy to move forward with T-DXd. If there are new symptomatic lesions he waits for local therapy first. He'd like more clarity for the in-between cases, like small asymptomatic lesions found on routine MRI, but he just discusses those one by one.
Fit ECOG 0-1 pts = easy yes for T-DXd.
Prior ILD hx = hard no, full stop.
Stable brain mets ok if neuro sx controlled, I think.
Elderly pts? Not sure, would go cautious.
Worried about pts w/ poor lung reserve
No formal frailty screen, mostly gestalt per HCP.
Community onc, says HER2-low pts post-endocrine tx w/ good PS are ideal for T-DXd. Fewer prior chemo lines = better tolerance, in his view. Would move it earlier.
Age alone not a dealbreaker for HCP. Looks at comorbidities first, esp cardiac and lung baseline. Probably wants echo and baseline CT chest before starting T-DXd.
HCP concerned re: pts w/ COPD or prior RT lung changes. Says most of her older pts have some lung issue so the eligible pool shrinks fast.
Brain mets: tumor board decides case by case. Active/symptomatic = local tx first (SRS), then consider T-DXd. Unsure how much CNS activity to expect.
HCP uses T-DXd in pts w/ stable treated brain mets, seeing decent responses anecdotally. Says it changed how he thinks about CNS dz in HER2+.
PA deneid for pts who haven't had enough prior lines, esp HER2-low HR+ dz. HCP frustrated, says selection ends up payer-driven not clinical.
Prefers to save it for pts after progression on endocrine + CDK4/6. Before that, hesitant. Wants more clarity on sequencing
Nurse-led infusion clinic flagged that frail pts struggle w/ N/V and fatigue. HCP often just skips them for T-DXd.

HCP runs a busy community practice, sees mostly 70+ pts. For T-DXd she looks at PS first, then renal fx and heart. Probably would treat a fit 75 yo but not a borderline 85 yo. Wants dose-reduction guidance for older pts, not sure it exists. Says families often drive the final decision.

HCP not comfortable w/ T-DXd in pts w/ lots of prior lines, thinks marrow reserve is poor by then. Also worried re: borderline LVEF after anthracycline. Says ILD monitoring and AE visits add burden that frail pts can't manage. Ends up using it in a small subset only. Cardiology input is slow to get.

Positive overall. HCP says pts w/ good PS and HER2-low after endocrine tx are the sweet spot, would rather use this before more chemo. Younger pts tolerate it well in his experience. Stable brain mets after RT not a barrier for him. Main need is close AE f/u and a team that knows ILD signs.

Concerned re: real-world selection. HCP thinks trial pts were healthier than what walks into clinic. Many of her pts have PS 2, multiple comorbidities, some active brain mets, so T-DXd is often off the table. Feels evidence is thin for those pts. Wouldn't extrapolate, probably defaults to single-agent chemo.

Tumor board at his site reviews every T-DXd start. Criteria informal: PS 0-1, no ILD hx, LVEF ok, brain mets controlled. Borderline pts get discussed, sometimes 1-2 cycles w/ close f/u then reassess. Unclear if that's too cautious. Said a written checklist would help.

Oncologist at a regional hospital sees T-DXd as a real option for pts previously thought too sick. Even some PS 2 pts, if the decline was disease-related, got a go. Says responses can be quick, which helps symptomatic pts. Still screens hard for lung and heart. Likes that the selection conversation is getting broader.
Anyone with ILD history, I'm just not giving them T-DXd.
ECOG 0-1 only, honestly. ECOG 2 I'd think twice.
Frail 80-year-olds? Not touching it.
Fit, HER2-low, endocrine-exhausted patients are the easy yes.
Stable brain mets, maybe. Active ones, no clue.
Baseline lung disease makes me nervous every single time.

Every time I see a post-CDK4/6 patient with a bit of COPD, I stall. The label doesn't tell me who's too risky, and the monitoring burden in a small community clinic is real. Most of us just default to chemo.
I use T-DXd in the fit ones, basically. Age alone isn't the issue for me, it's whether they have reserve if they get pneumonitis. That's hard to judge in a 15-minute visit.
For my younger HER2-low patients with good PS who've progressed on endocrine therapy, T-DXd is a no-brainer. I'd rather use it early than after three lines of chemo have ground them down.

Liver function is my sticking point. Patients with liver mets and borderline bilirubin end up in a grey zone, and I don't have a clean rule. Usually I wait for another set of labs and hope it settles.

Cardiac comorbidity is what slows me down, especially prior anthracycline with a lowish EF. I'd probably still consider the drug with cardiology on board but that adds delays. Payer prior auth is slow enough already
Elderly patients, I think we're basically guessing. Trials pick fit people and then we're told to extrapolate to the 78-year-old with diabetes and CKD. Doesnt sit right with me.
Honestly surprised how well a couple of my older but fit patients handled it with good antiemetic cover. I'd still pick carefully. But I wouldn't rule someone out just on birth date.

My issue is sequencing. Patients reach me after multiple lines, with ECOG already slipping, and by then T-DXd is hardly a realistic option. If it's meant for earlier use, community referrals need to happen sooner, but they don't. Then I get the 'she's too sick now' conversation. Frustrating, and kind of a wasted chance.

Pathology is a bigger headache than PS for me. Half the time I can't tell if a case is 0 or 1+ and re-testing delays alot. Once I'm sure it's HER2-low, I look at PS, lungs, and how fast the disease is moving. Rapid visceral progression pushes me toward the ADC, slow bone-only disease pushes me toward more endocrine. Not sure my colleagues agree.

Prior chest radiation worries me, like left-sided breast cancer survivors with lung changes on CT. Nobody gives clear guidance on where to draw the line. I end up arguing with radiology over whether it's scarring or something else. If I'm wrong, the patient pays for it. So I'm conservative, probably more than I need to be.

We built a checklist in clinic: PS, baseline CT chest, echo, and whether the patient can call in symptoms. It does filter people, which is probably good. But a couple of patients who live far away got excluded because they couldn't get in fast with cough or fever. Is that fair? I don't know. It's a practical selection factor nobody puts in the guidelines.

The sweet spot is clear to me now: post-endocrine, HER2-low, ECOG 0-1, clean lungs, and visceral disease that needs a response. Those I send straight to T-DXd without much debate. I used to push chemo first out of habit, and I think that was wrong for a good chunk of them. The grey-zone patients are still tough, but the clean candidates are easy.

I was skeptical going in, to be fair. But the fit, not heavily pretreated patients did better than I expected, and the ones with stable treated brain mets weren't a disaster either. I still screen hard for lung issues and I still worry about the older group. For the right person I'd stop dragging my feet.

Brain mets patients keep coming up at tumor board and opinions are split. Some want systemic therapy first if CNS disease is stable, others want local treatment before anything. I go along with whatever the neuro team prefers.
PS 2 patients? I don't put them on T-DXd.
Brain mets stable and treated, fine, I'd still use it.
Honestly it depends on the lungs, nothing else matters much to me.
Elderly with COPD, no way, not worth the T-DXd ILD gamble.
Post-CDK4/6, HER2-low, ECOG 0-1, easy yes for me.
Frailty scoring in clinic? We eyeball it, nobody does G8 propely.

We get asked about brain mets a lot, and the honest answer from my side is I'm not sure how much to trust it in active lesions. Stable after radiotherapy, sure, I'd go ahead. Untreated and symptomatic, neurosurgery and rad onc see them first.
Community practice here has no pulmonologist on site, so anyone with baseline lung issues just gets passed over. I get why, but it narrows the pool a lot more than the label suggests.
T-DXd has been my go-to for the fit 60-something with HER2-low whose endocrine therapy stopped working. Tolerability was better than I feared as long as we scan on schedule.

Everyone talks about 'good candidates' but the real patient is 78, on a blood thinner, with a bad heart and a daughter worried about hospital visits. Not sure the trials look anything like her, though I dont see a better option for her either.
Prior therapy matters to me mostly as a count of lines. If they're still fairly well after two or three lines I'll consider it. Otherwise the palliative care conversation comes first.
Payer wants proof of prior endocrine and chemo before approving T-DXd, and by the time the paperwork clears the patient's PS has slipped. Then they aren't eligible in my eyes anyway.
Renal function doesn't worry me much. Liver I check more carefully, probably overly so
Our tumor board has settled into a pattern: ECOG 0 or 1, no ILD history, no uncontrolled CNS disease, then T-DXd is on the table. It makes decisions quicker.

My worry is ILD, plain and simple. I saw one case in clinic go downhill fast on T-DXd and it changed how I pick patients. Now anyone with prior chest radiation, a smoking history or shaky lung function I steer elsewhere. People say monitoring solves it, but our CT access is slow and patients don't always call when they start coughing. I'd rather not gamble on someone who's already fragile.

Older patients are the grey zone for me. Age by itself isn't the issue, I think, but at 75 plus you rarely have just one problem. If they're independent and live alone I'll offer T-DXd and be ready to delay doses. If they need help dressing, I probably don't. Nausea and fatigue hit them harder, and the family usually ends up deciding.

HER2-low selection is messier than the slides make it look. Our pathology reports bounce between 0 and 1+ depending on the sample, and I'm not convinced the borderline ones are reproducible. So I end up deciding on a fuzzy score, sometimes for someone with poor PS as well. For the DESTINY-Breast06 type patient, endocrine-resistant after CDK4/6, I want a clear call and rarely get one. Frustrating.

Brain mets used to be an automatic exclusion in my head, but I've softened. I had a patient with treated brain lesions who stayed stable on T-DXd for a good while, and that stuck with me. I still want a baseline MRI and agreement from rad onc. For someone otherwise active who has already had endocrine therapy and chemo, I'd reach for it sooner than I used to. Not blindly, but with more confidence.

Trial populations are healthier than my clinic. Almost nobody in my waiting room is ECOG 0 with normal everything. We see diabetes, cardiac history, previous chest radiation, sometimes all three. When I try to extrapolate I feel like I'm guessing, and the usual answers I get don't help. I end up defaulting to chemo for the sicker ones.

In our day unit the practical filter is a baseline echo and a reliable way to get to scans. If a patient lives far away and can't come in for imaging, I hesitate to use the ADC. Treated, quiet brain mets are okay by me, active leptomeningeal disease is not. Past that, it's mostly whether they can tolerate the nausea.

pulm_surveillance|osimertinib.t: CT every 12 weeks is fine, honestly. Nobody I know does more.
Our triage line is basically a voicemail. Not reassuring for ILD.
Pneumonitis worries me less than the wait to see a pulmonologist.
Osi-related ILD has been rarer in my clinic than I feared.
Steroid taper protocols? Everyone just wings it, I think.
Baseline CT plus symptom checks at each visit works ok for us, no drama

We scan roughly every couple of months early on, then space out if stable. The trouble is the radiology read says 'ground glass, nonspecific' and I'm left guessing between pneumonitis, infection and progression.

On the combo with chemo, patients have so much cough, fatigue and dyspnea that I can't tell what's drug-related lung injury. Nurses either call me about everything or nothing. There's no middle ground.
Pulmonology here answers within a day or two when I flag a new opacity. That co-management is the only reason I tolerate the gap between scans.
Payer wanted a chest x-ray before approving an extra CT for a patient with new cough on osimertinib. Three days lost, and the film told us nothing. Then the CT got approved anyway.

I start prednisone fairly quickly for grade 2 if infection is reasonably excluded. Not sure how slow the taper should be though, probably depends on who you ask. Adn nobody has shown me anything solid.
We're a community practice with no in-house pulmonologist. Referrals take weeks, so I end up managing suspected pneumonitis mostly alone, which I really don't love.
Handing out a wallet card with a direct number for new breathlessness has worked well for us. Fewer surprise ER visits, I think. Patients actually use it.
Home pulse ox seemed gimmicky to me at first. A few patients did catch drops early, so I'm undecided. I wouldn't mandate it.

With the chemo combo the pulmonary risk conversation feels muddier, not clearer. Everyone says watch for ILD, but nobody tells me how often to image once someone is stable on osimertinib plus chemo. I end up improvising per patient. When a scan shows something borderline, I don't know whether to hold just the TKI or everything. That call is mostly gut.

The guidance on CT timing is vague and I'm tired of pretending otherwise. Some say fixed intervals, others say symptom-driven only. I split the difference, which probably means I over-scan some people and under-scan others. Real-world practice seems to vary a lot between centers. Until someone shows a surveillance schedule that changes outcomes, it's opinion.

Our workflow is a nurse call at the first couple of weeks, then check-ins at each cycle. It catches cough and exertional dyspnea reasonably well. What it misses is the quiet patient who doesn't want to bother us. I'm not sure a script fixes that. Some of it is just luck.

Last year a routine scan on osi showed asymptomatic ground glass changes. We held the drug, got pulmonology involved the same week, and it settled without steroids. After that we restarted carefully with closer imaging. That case made me more of a believer in scheduled CTs, even if I grumble about the cost.

Many of my patients live a long drive away, and a same-week CT just isn't realistic for them. The after-hours triage line is staffed by people who aren't oncology-trained, so 'new shortness of breath' gets treated like any other call. I worry we'll miss early pneumonitis that way. Telehealth visits don't help when you can't hear the lungs. Frankly the system is built for the clinic downtown, not for them.

Pulmonology wants a bronchoscopy before committing to steroids, and I want to start steroids if the picture is classic. We go back and forth for days. Meanwhile the patient is off treatment and breathing worse. I'm not saying they're wrong, but the disagreement costs time, and nobody has agreed a shared protocol.
CT every 12 weeks on osimertinib, same as restaging, nothing extra for ILD.
Honestly we only scan when the patient calls with a cough
Our nurse line catches breathlessness calls early, works well for us.
Osimertinib plus chemo makes it hard to tell pneumonitis from infection.
Pulmonology only gets pulled in at grade 2 or above, I think.
Haven't had to stop osimertinib for ILD in my community clinic so far.
In our community practice patients get a wallet card listing cough, fever and new shortness of breath. They're told to call the same day. Whether they actually do is a different story.

Baseline CT is fine, but extra chest imaging between restaging scans depends on what the payer approves. Prior auth can take days, and that delay worries me when an osimertinib patient sounds short of breath.
Our thoracic clinic has a pulmonologist sit in on the weekly tumor board, so any suspicious ground-glass change gets looked at fast. The steroid taper is usually started the same week.

With FLAURA2-style combination patients I probably look harder at every scan, since pemetrexed and platinum are on board too. Not sure it changes the schedule though, still roughly every 8 to 12 weeks.
Telehealth follow-ups make this tough, I cant listen to the chest and home pulse ox readings are unreliable. A couple of patients had mild symptoms for a week before we knew.
Our steroid protocol is weight-based prednisone with a taper over several weeks, after holding the drug. Rechallenge is decided case by case, usually with pulmonology input.
The triage line staff aren't oncology trained, so a call about dry cough often gets sent to primary care. I hear that a lot from our rural satelite clinics, and it's a gap.
A low threshold for CT has worked for us. A few patients with only a mild cough got scanned early and the changes were caught before they felt really unwell.

At our infusion center the nurse runs a respiratory symptom checklist at each chemo visit for patients on the combination. That's a better touchpoint than osimertinib alone, where visits are less frequent. CT is tied to restaging, roughly every three months. If anything looks off the case goes to a pulmonologist we share patients with. I think it's okay but depends a lot on the nurse noticing.

Telling ILD from radiation pneumonitis is a recurring problem for us, especially in patients who had thoracic radiation for oligometastatic disease before starting. Radiology reports often say nonspecific ground-glass and leave it to us. Then we wait on pulmonology, sometimes two weeks, with the drug held in the meantime. Patients get anxious and so do I. Not sure there's a clean answer

Our practice built a simple pathway: baseline CT, symptom screen at every visit, and a direct pager to pulmonology for any new infiltrate. Decisions are faster now. Osimertinib gets held right away, steroids start if it looks like ILD, and we re-image in a few weeks. Patients seem reassured knowing there's a plan.

Practice varies a lot in our group. Some colleagues scan every 8 weeks in the first months, others stick to 12. I follow restaging and only add imaging if there are symptoms. Most cases I've seen on osimertinib were mild and settled after a hold, and a handful needed steroids.

Patient education is the weak spot. Handouts mention ILD in one line among a lot of side effects, and people skip over it. I had a patient wait until the weekend and show up in the ED with real hypoxia. ED staff didn't know about the EGFR TKI at first. We put a chart note in now but it's patchy.

Our pulmonologist prefers bronchoscopy only when the picture is unclear, so most suspected cases are managed on CT and symptoms alone. We stop osimertinib, start steroids, and wait for improvement. When the patient is on chemo as well, infection gets ruled out with cultures first. Restart is discussed afterwards, and I'm not sure we're consistent about it. Reasonable but a bit ad hoc.
Honestly the baseline CT is where we stop; nothing scheduled after unless symptoms.
Pulmonology picks up the phone same day, which makes me comfortable.
Osimertinib restaging scans every couple of months double as our ILD check, I think.
No dedicated triage line for cough or dyspnea, patients just ring the front desk
Steroid taper length is still pretty much gut feel here.
Nurse-led symptom call a couple of weeks into osi has caught things early for us.

Community practice, so we rely on the radiologist flagging ground-glass changes on routine scans. If something looks off we hold osimertinib and get a pulmonary opinion within a few days. Not sure that counts as true surveillance though.

With osimertinib plus chemo I worry more about telling pneumonitis from infection or chemo-related changes. Patients show up febrile with a new cough and the workup becomes a muddle. We usually end up covering with antibiotics and steroids both.

Our thoracic group built a shared pathway: baseline high-res CT, a symptom card for patients, and a named pulmonologist for referrals. It's been smooth so far and patients seem to actually read the card.

Payer pushback on extra CTs is a real thing for us. Auth for off-schedule chest imaging sometimes takes days, which is awkward if someone is short of breath. We often route them through the ED in those cases, probably not ideal.

Rechallenge after grade 1 pneumonitis divides our group. Some will restart the drug at the same dose once the steroid course is done, others would never go back. I lean cautious but honestly don't have a firm rule.

Mostly we educate at the first visit and repeat at each cycle. Patients on osimertinib alone get less frequent contact than the ones on platinum doublet, so the chemo patients are probably watched more closely for breathlessness by default.
Home pulse oximeters have been a nice addition for a handful of our osi patients. They call if sats dip, and that triggers a same-week CT. Fairly low effort for us.
Rural clinic here, the nearest pulmonologist is a long drive away so co-management is mostly by telehealth and its not great when you really need someone to listen to the lungs.

We talked for a while about how ILD surveillance actually works day to day. On paper it's symptom-driven with a baseline CT and imaging at restaging. In reality the oncology nurses are the early warning, because patients mention a dry cough to them before they mention it to the doctor. If new dyspnea is reported, the plan is chest CT within the week and hold the TKI until it is read. What was less clear is who owns the follow-up CT after a mild finding, oncology or pulmonology.

The main frustration was the lack of a standard steroid protocol. Prednisone dose and taper seem to vary a lot between prescribers, and this physician has seen overly long tapers lead to infections and too-short ones lead to relapse. There's also uncertainty about PJP prophylaxis, whether it's needed for every taper. Pulmonology is helpful but they don't agree among themselves either. Would love consensus guidance, though not expecting it soon.

Overall quite upbeat. Their center runs a joint thoracic oncology and pulmonology clinic once a week, so suspected ILD cases get seen together within days. He feels that has probably prevented a few unnecessary permanent discontinuations, since mild cases get managed and osimertinib is restarted. Patient education sheets go out at start and nurses phone during the first cycles. His only wish is a quicker route to bronchoscopy slots when the picture is unclear.

Interesting discussion on CT frequency. On osimertinib he doesn't do routine surveillance scans just for pneumonitis, because the yield is probably low and the radiation and cost add up. But he admitted incidental asymptomatic changes make him anxious when they appear, so he repeats imaging in a few weeks and watches. Elderly patients and those with prior lung disease or chest radiation get a lower threshold. Not sure if that is evidence-based or just habit.

Concerned about telephone triage. Our after-hours line is staffed by generalist nurses who tend to treat cough like a cold, so someone with early pneumonitis may be told to wait it out. A couple of patients, I think, arrived later than ideal last year with significant hypoxia. We are drafting a script that asks about exertional breathlessness and fever but nothing is in place yet. Frankly it worries me more than the drug itself.

He raised how patient-reported symptoms get captured. They tried a short questionnaire at each visit about cough, breathlessness and fever, which works when patients attend but not between visits.
