An app was floated, though the admin side seems heavy and he's unsure older patients would use it. For now it's the clinic nurse and a paper handout. He thinks that is adequate for most, with a few likely to slip through.
Baseline CT only, then symptom-driven. No scheduled scans unless pt complains.
Osimertinib ILD rare in his practice, pts educated upfront, no issues so far.
Pulm consult only if grade 2+, otherwise onc manages.
Triage line swamped, cough calls pile up on chemo weeks, osi pts get lost in the mix
CT q3 months w/ restaging on osi, nothing extra. Not sure that's enough.
Pt handout w/ red-flag sx works well in clinic.
Worried the FLAURA2 combo muddies the picture. Pemetrexed pts get dyspnea/cough for other reasons, so hard to tell ILD from infection. HCP holds tx and orders CT early, probably overcalls.
Community onc, no in-house pulm. Refers out for HRCT when pt has new O2 sat drop on osimertinib, wait is a couple weeks which HCP hates.
Has standing pathway w/ pulm: new cough + ground glass on CT = same-week visit. Says it's smooth and tx rarely interrupted long.

Steroid approach: starts prednisone once pneumonitis confirmed, taper over several weeks, defers specifics to pulm. Stops osimertinib permanently if severe. Rechallenge only 'maybe' in mild cases, I think.
PA for extra CT keeps getting denied by payer when pt asymptomatic. HCP says surveillance imaging beyond restaging is basically clinic goodwill. Osimertinib pts end up scanned late.
Academic site, tumor board flags any radiology 'pneumonitis' wording on restaging. Good safety net. Radiologists now comment on ILD pattern routinely.
Pts w/ prior chest RT get extra attention. Not sure whether to scan earlier on osi, usually just lowers threshhold to call pulm.
Telehealth f/u misses early sx. Pts say 'just a cough' and HCP can't listen to lungs, bothers him.

Had one pt w/ osimertinib pneumonitis caught late, was traveling and ignored SOB for a week. Admitted, steroids, tx stopped. Since then HCP gives wallet card and calls at week 2. Still thinks most clinics lack bandwidth for that. Concerned elderly pts under-report.

Likes osimertinib safety overall, ILD on radar but manageable. Workflow: baseline CT, then q8-12 wks w/ restaging, nurse phone check first month. Any new dry cough or fever goes to same-day triage line. Pulm co-manages grade 2+. Feels this catches most cases early.

Split on adding chemo. W/ FLAURA2 regimen pts come in more often anyway so AE checks are built in. Unsure if CT interval should shorten, no data in mind. Pulm colleagues say wait and see. Probably keeps same schedule for now.

Steroid taper protocols vary across docs in the group, no consensus. Some taper over weeks, others longer, and a few pts relapse sx. HCP wants shared SOP w/ pulm but nobody owns it. Osi rechallenge decisions mostly gut feel at tumor board.

Rural clinic, pts drive far. Triage line is just front desk, not RN, so sx calls get delayed. HCP coaches pts to call at first fever or cough. CT done locally, read remotely, can lag. Ok overall but not ideal.
Piloting app-based sx diary for pts on TKI. Flags cough or SOB score to nurse. Early days, not sure it cuts missed ILD. Pts like it, some don't log. Would want pulm input on thresholds.

pulm_surveillance|pembrolizumab.t: Honestly our triage line just tells people to go to the ER.
Baseline CT, then whenever someone coughs. That's the real protocol.
Pulmonology answers within a day here, which is rare and appreciated.
Not sure anyone owns the pneumonitis follow up after surgery
Pembro, then steroids with a taper. Standard, nothing exciting.
Low-grade ILD on a scan in a pembro patient, we usually just watch. Bit nervous about it.
Community practice, no in-house pulmonologist. Referral takes weeks, so I end up starting prednisone myself and hoping the CT clarifies things later. Not ideal.
We do a CT roughly every other cycle in the neoadjuvant phase on pembro, mostly because the radiologists ask. In adjuvant it drifts. Probably depends on who's covering that week.
Our nurse-led symptom line actually works, I'll admit. Patients call with a new dry cough or breathlessness and get a same-day slot. Fewer surprises than I expected with pembrolizumab.

Everyone says 'educate the patient' but the handouts end up in a draw. Gastric patients already have poor appetite and fatigue, so breathlessness gets blamed on anemia. We miss early pneumonitis that way, I think.
Radiology reports often say 'nonspecific groundglass' and we're left guessing between infection, ILD and radiation change in someone on pembrolizumab. Pulm review helps but slows everything down.
Insurers push back on extra CTs for pembro patients who are asymptomatic so surveillance is basically symptom-driven whether we like it or not.
Once pulmonology started joining our tumor board monthly, steroid decisions got cleaner. Grade 2 gets a clear plan now rather than a debate.
Steroid taper length is all over the place in my clinic, four to six weeks depending on the doc. Nobody has data that convinces me either way, and pembro restarts make it murkier.

Perioperative lung patients worry me most. They've had surgery, maybe radiation, reduced lung reserve, and then we add pembrolizumab on top. When they get short of breath, is it the immunotherapy, a post-op issue, or a clot? Nobody agrees who works that up first. Surgeons point at oncology, we point at pulmonology, and the patient waits.

We have a written pathway: baseline CT, symptom check at each infusion, and a low threshold for a scan if sats drop. In practice the infusion nurses do the checking, and it's hit and miss on busy days. I think the pathway is reasonable on paper. Whether it catches grade 1 early, I really can't say. We haven't audited it.

Telehealth is a problem for this. You can't hear crackles or do a walking sat over video. A couple of patients on anti-PD-1 therapy that we caught late were on remote follow-up between cycles. I'd want an in-person check, but staffing doesnt allow it, so we accept the risk and feel uneasy about it.

Grudgingly, the pneumonitis pathway we built last year has helped. Home pulse oximeters for the gastric patients, a direct pager route to pulmonology, and a standing steroid order set. Most low-grade cases get picked up before they turn nasty. I still doubt it scales to smaller sites, though.

My main frustration is rechallenge. After a grade 2 pneumonitis resolves on steroids, do we restart pembro or not? Pulmonology says wait, oncology says the patient has limited options. I tend to go case by case, probably more cautious in lung than gastric.

Compared with what I feared, pulmonary toxicity has been manageable. Patients who report cough early get a CT within days and we start steroids fast, so most recover without drama. I'm skeptical of anyone claiming it's rare, though. The key for us is that radiology flags new groundglass the same day. Without that the whole thing falls apart.
CT q3 mo is default, nobody deviates unless sx.
Pneumonitis triage line works well, pts actually call.
No formal ILD pathway here. Ad hoc.
Pulm co-mgmt only after G2 on pembro, too late imo.
Pembro pts get baseline CT + PFTs, then symptom-driven only.
Steroid taper per guideline, no local tweaks.
Community clinic, no pulmonologist on site. Refferal takes weeks so they start pred first and hope for the best. Not ideal.
HCP said nurse-led phone triage catches cough/dyspnea early, pts told to call same day. Thinks it prevented a couple of admits. Fairly happy w/ it.
Unsure whether routine CT between cycles adds anything vs just symptom checks. Radiology wants a clear reason on the order or PA gets pushed back. Mixed feelings.
Post-op KN-671 pts: concern re telling surgical changes from pneumonitis on CT. Tumor board reviews scans when unclear. Helps but slow.
Pulm joins tumor board monthly and reviews any ground-glass finding. HCP finds this really useful, wants it weekly.
Steroid taper length varies by attending, usually 4-6 wks I think, after pembro hold. No written local protocol. Some pts flare when taper is fast.
Payer denied extra CT for pt w/ new cough, delayed about a week. HCP frustrated. Ended up doing CXR instead.
Academic center, ILD clinic fast-tracks IO pts within days. Pts hav a direct line. HCP says this changed comfort level w/ continuing tx after G1.

HCP worried about under-reporting. Pts on pembro often blame cough on a cold or post-op recovery and don't call. Clinic gives a handout but not sure anyone reads it. Pneumonitis probably gets picked up late in a good chunk of cases. Wants a symptom checklist at every infusion visit.

Workflow: baseline CT, then imaging w/ restaging roughly every 2-3 cycles, earlier if sx. Pulse ox at each visit. G2 means hold pembro, start pred 1 mg/kg, pulm consult. Not sure bronch is used much. Most resolved pts restarted tx but with some anxiety

Very comfortable w/ AEs now. Team has standing order set for pneumonitis: hold Keytruda, CT, labs, start steroids, pulm referral same wk. Pharmacy flags pts on infusion day. HCP feels pts trust the line. Would like to share the pathway w/ other sites.

Concern in gastric pts, older and frail w/ baseline COPD. Hard to tell pneumonitis from exacerbation or infection on PD-1. Pulm often says 'treat empirically'. HCP nervous about steroids and infections in these pts. No clear guidance on rechallenge.

Radiology reads vary. Some call 'possible ILD' on every small opacity, which triggers holds. HCP thinks probably overcalling but not comfortable ignoring it. Tumor board sometimes sorts it out. Wants standardized report language.

Asked about home monitoring. HCP likes idea of home pulse ox but unsure pts would use it consistently. Nursing bandwidth limits calling every pt weekly. Rural pts live far so they prefer phone triage over coming in. Probably a hybrid is realistic.
Baseline CT only, repeat if symptoms.
Pneumonitis calls go straight to our nurse triage line, works fine.
No formal ILD surveillance for pembro here, honestly.
Pulmonology co-management has been smooth for us.
Not sure when to rescan after steroid taper
On pembrolizumab we mostly rely on patients reporting cough early.
In our infusion suite the nurses ask about cough and breathlessness at every cycle, and it's built into the checklist. Probably caught a couple of early pneumonitis cases that way.

Surgical group wants a CT after neoadjuvant pembrolizumab and before resection, which doubles as the pneumonitis check. Medical oncology adds scans only if something changes. Works okay but the two services don't always talk.
Our rural satellite clinic has no pulmonologist on site, so any suspected pneumonitis means sending the patient to the main hospital. That delay worries me, especially on weekends.
Steroid protocol for pembrolizumab pneumonitis is standard-dose prednisone once grade 2 is confirmed, then a slow taper over several weeks. I think we taper too fast sometimes.
Gastric patients tend to be frail and underweight, so it's hard to tell pneumonitis from aspiration or plain deconditioning. We keep a low threshold for CT. Pulm weighs in on the unclear ones.
Payer pushed back on an extra chest CT for a patient on pembrolizumab with a mild dry cough, took a week of back and forth. Patient ended up fine but I didnt like waiting.
Our symptom hotline is staffed by oncology nurses with a short script for new cough, fever or shortness of breath. Any positive answer gets a same-day visit. Patients seem to like it.

Perioperative lung patients get a CT at restaging, and I go over possible ILD changes with the radiologist. Reports vary a lot in wording though, which makes follow-up decisions harder than they should be.

Since we set up a joint pneumonitis pathway with pulmonology, things have improved. Any grade 2 or higher is seen within a couple of days, with bronchoscopy only if infection is a real possibility. The steroid taper is written into the order set so nobody improvises. Pembrolizumab patients get a handout about breathing changes at the first cycle. Honestly it feels like we catch things earlier than before.

We got burned last year when a patient with a mild cough was told to wait over a long weekend and came back hypoxic. Since then I'm nervous. His DESTINY-Breast06 type patients, mostly pretreated with endocrine therapy, are tolerating it fine so far. Patients like having a direct number for the nurse. I think that helps with early reporting.

Practice manager and doctor both flagged staffing. Triage nurses rotate, so the cough-or-breathlessness script isn't applied consistently. One patient called twice about shortness of breath before being brought in. By then the CT showed changes and the drug was stopped permanently. The doctor feels the process failed more than the drug did. They're discussing a pulmonary flag in the chart but nothing is agreed.

Pulmonologist at a regional hospital said she gets very few refferals from oncology for this and would like baseline PFTs on file. The oncology team doesn't usually order them because of scheduling delays. She co-manages when called, with bronchoscopy only if infection is unclear. She starts steroids promptly and reviews weekly. In her view communication between the two teams is the real variable.
CT q3 mo on T-DXd, no exceptions in our clinic.
Pt education on cough/SOB is the weak link imo.
Pulm referral only after grade 2, not before.
No baseline PFTs at our site, never been asked for them eveer.
Nurse triage line catches most early symptoms, works well.
Steroid taper too fast = relapse, seen it once
Community practice, no in-house pulm. If pt calls w/ dry cough we hold tx and send for same-week CT, then sort out the rest. Radiology turnaround is the bottleneck.
PA delays for repeat CT are annoying, payer sometimes questions scans in asymptomatic pts. We argue it's label-driven surveillance. Eats a lot of staff time.
Tumor board now flags every T-DXd pt for an ILD check-in each cycle. HCP feels it cut down on missed cases, I think. Pulm joins the discussion when imaging is equivocal.
Worried about older HER2-low pts w/ COPD hx. Hard to separate baseline lung changes from new ILD. Probably need pulm input before starting tx.
Per HCP, prednisone-equivalent starts at grade 2 per label, but unsure how fast to taper. Pulm usually decides. Rechallenge after grade 1 is case by case.
Pt-reported symptom app being piloted for resp AEs. Too early to say if it helps, adherance seems patchy.
Pulm colleagues are very responsive, same-day slots for T-DXd pts. That makes HCP far more comfortable prescribing in earlier lines. Wishes all sites had this.
HCP says fear of pneumonitis makes part of the team default to chemo in HER2-low even when DB06 profile fits. Not everyone agrees tho.

Infusion center nurses call every pt mid-cycle to ask about cough, fever, SOB. Any yes = same-day visit and CT. Smooth so far and pts like the check-in. Pulm co-manages anything grade 2+ and steroids start fast. I think this is why the team feels okay using T-DXd more broadly.

Rural clinic, nearest pulm is a long drive. Pt had low-grade cough for a week before calling, thought it was a cold. By the time CT was done it was symptomatic ILD. Team now nervous about every new start. Not sure what else they can do without more resources, tbh.

Surveillance varies by oncologist here. Some do CT aligned w/ restaging, others baseline plus symptom-driven only. No consensus, probably needs a clinic SOP. Pulm wants early loop-in but oncs say it clogs their schedule. Tumor board discussed it, no decision yet.

HCP concerned steroid AEs (infection, glucose) pile on top of ILD in diabetic pts. Long tapers mean pt off tx for weeks, PFS impact unclear. PA for extra imaging was denied once too. Feels like the burden lands on community sites.

Joint onc/pulm clinic slot monthly for T-DXd pts w/ any lung findings. Works ok but capacity is limited. Grade 1 findings get tx held and repeat CT in a few wks. Unsure whether to resume at same dose, decided case by case w/ pulm.

Their protocol: baseline CT, restaging CTs on schedule, low threshold for extra imaging. Pulm reviews any ground-glass finding at a weekly huddle. Caught a couple of grade 1 cases early this way and tx resumed after. HCP says it gave pts and staff confidence. Offered to share their SOP.
Rural satellite clinic can't realistically do CT every three months, per the oncologist.
Feels confident spotting grade 1 pneumonitis since the nurse line was set up.
Unsure whether baseline PFTs add anything before starting, he said.
Thinks patients underreport cough, so ILD gets caught late.
Same-week pulmonology review of suspicious scans, he said, has been a game changer.
Holds T-DXd at grade 1 and rescans in a week, nothing fancier.

The oncologist described a patient who had a dry cough for two weeks before anybody called, and by the time the CT was done it was already grade 2. She said the phone triage script they use is probably too vague about what counts as a respiratory symptom.

He said his academic center does CT chest roughly every nine to twelve weeks on T-DXd, matching restaging, but he isn't sure that's frequent enough. Pulmonology only gets pulled in once something shows up.
Told me the steroid taper protocol they wrote with pulmonology is simple and the whole team follows it. Honestly it has removed a lot of the anxiety around starting prednisone early.

Community practice physician said insurers sometimes push back on extra CT scans outside the restaging window, which makes off-cycle imaging for mild symptoms a hassel. She ends up ordering anyway and dealing with the denial later.
Pulse oximetry at every infusion visit is now routine for them, he said, though he admitted it probably catches very little early. Patients with a COPD history get a lower threshold for a scan.

Reported that once more HER2-low patients began getting T-DXd, her clinic trained infusion nurses to ask about breathlessness and cough every cycle. She thinks it's working because a couple of cases were flagged early by nurses rather than by the patients themselves.

Nervous about giving T-DXd to anyone with prior chest radiation, he said, and nobody has clearly told him how often to scan those people. He'd like pulmonology to co-manage but they are stretched thin.
Mentioned the handout with warning symptoms goes home at cycle one, but he wonders if anyone really reads it. Thinks a midweek text check-in could help, not sure the staff has capacity

For her, ILD is the thing that keeps her up with this drug. Their pathway has a CT at baseline and then with restaging, but she feels that leaves long gaps where a low grade could quietly progress. Pulmonology at her hospital is by referral only, with a wait of a couple of weeks. She said she has sometimes started steroids herself before the pulmonologist even saw the patient. Overall she called the setup improvised and hoped for clearer guidance.

Their center built a joint ILD huddle with pulmonology and radiology that meets weekly for anyone on T-DXd, he said. Radiologists now flag subtle ground glass changes using a standard template, which he thinks makes reads much more consistent. Patients with any new cough get a same-day nurse call and usually a low-dose CT within a couple of days. He felt the whole thing has made the team more comfortable using the drug in earlier lines. His only complaint was the extra workload for the nurses.

A community oncologist said she follows the label guidance for holding and steroids, but in practice grade 2 decisions vary a lot between her partners. Some start prednisone at once while others wait for a repeat scan. She thought a shared protocol would probably help, though she wasn't sure the local pulmonologists would agree to one. On imaging she does CT every other cycle for the first few months and then eases off. Patients generally tolerate that fine, she said.

According to him, the biggest gap is nights and weekends. Patients with new shortness of breath call the general hospital line and get told to go to the ER, where nobody knows about T-DXd or ILD. A couple of patients apparently waited too long that way. He wants a wallet card but admitted nobody has made one. Pulmonology is helpful during office hours only.

She's torn about steroid dosing, she told me. Her pulmonology colleague likes to start high and taper slowly over several weeks, while she worries about infections and glucose in her older patients. They have settled on case by case decisions, usually after a repeat CT and sometimes bronchoscopy if there's fever. She thinks T-DXd is worth the risk in HER2-low disease but wants clearer evidence on the best taper.

Their practice moved to home symptom diaries on an app for patients on T-DXd, but uptake is mixed. Younger patients log daily and older ones mostly don't, he said. He thinks it probably helps for catching cough or low-grade fever, but he can't say it has changed the CT schedule. Pulmonology only sees the flagged ones. For now he's keeping the standard scans and treating the app as an add-on.

safety|osimertinib.t: Rash and paronychia, same old story, and nobody warns patients enough.
Honestly the tolerability is fine on single agent, my patients barely complain.
Too early to say if the toxicity of adding chemo to osimertinib is worth it.
Anemia with the pemetrexed combo is what worries me most.
Osimertinib alone? Boring, in a good way.
Diarrhea calls to my nurses nevr stop.
We see dose holds mostly for low counts or a cough that makes us worry about ILD. Most restart fine after a short break, but the scare itself eats clinic time.

Combination with a platinum doublet means weekly labs and chair time for patients who were previously on a pill at home. A community practice like mine doesn't have the infusion slots. Frankly I'd think twice for anyone over 75.
Compared with the older generation TKIs I used, osimertinib is easier on skin and gut. I haven't had to reduce the dose in most patients.

Nobody told me how much nausea and fatigue the chemo add-on would bring. Patients come in wiped out in early cycles but most settle after a few, so I'm unsure the extra benefit justifies it for everyone.
QTc monitoring with routine ECGs feels like box ticking to me, I think very few ever need a change. Cardiology referrals though, those are a headache whenever an EF drops.
Discontinuations on osimertinib have been a handful, mostly pneumonitis. Not sure if that's lower than I'd expect, I've no real comparison in my own practice.

Payer wants documented toxicity before they'll cover anything else, so every dose delay turns into paperwork. The adverse events themselves are mostly manageable with osimertinib plus chemo. It's the supportive-care load and admin that wear on us.
Our nurse-led toxicity call has been working well. Most issues like dry skin get sorted by phone, and the osimertinib patients stay on schedule.

I'm frustrated by how the safety discussion gets glossed over. In the combination, cytopenias show up early, and I've had two or three patients delayed because of platelets. Then you're juggling transfusion thresholds, growth factor and antiemetics on top of a TKI. Patients tell me they feel worse than they were led to expect. Probably still right for fit, younger patients, but it's a lot.

My experience is mixed. Single-agent osimertinib is well tolerated, with the usual rash, dry skin and diarrhea that we manage with topicals and loperamide. When chemo is added, fatigue and low counts are what cause the holds. I haven't had many permanent stops, I think because we're quick to reduce the pemetrexed rather than the TKI. Not sure that's evidence-based, just what we do.

Surprised, actually. I expected a mess with the combination, but the patients I've started have mostly coped. Antiemetic prophylaxis up front made a big difference. Labs are a burden but our nurses have a rhythm now. Still skeptical about the long term, but short term I can't complain.

Cardiac and lung monitoring feels endless. Baseline echo, repeat if symptoms, CT whenever a cough shows up, and every time it's a toss-up between ILD and a plain chest infection. Patients get anxious and so do I. We've stopped osimertinib on suspicion more than once and I think later regretted it. No clear guidance, just gut feel.

Rural clinic here, so monitoring is the real issue. Patients drive far for labs during chemo cycles, and some skip them. The toxicity itself is manageable. When I get a grade 3 event I hold, reduce and restart, and it mostly works out.

Paronychia is the one nobody takes seriously until a patient can't wear shoes. We lose weeks to it, with interruptions on osimertinib and derm referrals that take forever. Its not life-threatening but it wrecks quality of life and adherence. Honestly the trial reporting undersells it, in my view.
Rash and paronychia are what make patients want to quit, honestly.
Osimertinib alone is easy to manage in our clinic.
Mostly mild diarrhea, loperamide at home usually enough
Adding chemo means a lot more nursing time on infusion days.
Not many dose reductions so far, a handful at most.
Repeat echos for LVEF are hard to book in their small unit.

A community oncologist said most of her osimertinib patients stay on full dose for months. Skin issues get handled with an emollient and doxycycline routine run by the nurse. She finds it far easier than the older TKIs.

Seen mostly in the combo setting: cytopenias drive the delays, not the TKI part. Pemetrexed cycles get pushed a week now and then when counts are low. He thinks it's workable if the lab schedule is clear.
Nurse lead at an infusion centre said the extra chair time and lab checks are stretching the schedule. Patients on the combination call in more about nausea and fatigue. Hard to staff for it.
Pulmonologist said ILD is what she worries about most, even though she has rarely seen it. Any new cough gets a low threshold for CT. Not sure how many of those turn out to be real pneumonitis.
Pharmacist phone check at week two catches most problems early in this clinic. Discontinuations for toxicity have been rare there, I think.

Patient on the combo stopped the chemo after two cycles because of fatigue and mouth sores, but stayed on the TKI. The oncologist felt the trade-off wasn't explained clearly to patients at the start. He's unsure who will tolerate it long term.
Payer in his region wants documented monitoring before approving the combo, which adds paperwork for the nurses. Clinically he says tolerability is acceptable.
Older patients with poor PS worry him, and he'd probaly avoid the chemo add-on because of falls risk and low counts. Osimertinib alone he is fine with.

Her practice found the combo heavier than expected. Infusion days now need labs, a chair, and a nurse who can check in on nausea and mouth sores. Her two infusion nurses are already stretched, so she has been spacing out new starts. A couple of patients delayed a cycle for low counts. She still thinks the TKI part is fine, it's the added chemo load that worries her.

Reported a few osimertinib dose reductions this year, mostly for diarrhea and skin, nothing dramatic. Most patients just need a short hold and then return to full dose. One patient needed a lower dose after a long-running rash, and I think that went fine. He isn't tracking it formally, so it's more a gut feeling. Overall mixed but leaning acceptable.

A rural clinic with limited staff said osimertinib is the main reason they can keep these patients local. The nurse does a phone check every few weeks and sends rash photos to the doctor. Most problems are mild and sorted with creams and diet advice. She said patients rarely miss work because of side effects. Not sure the same would hold with chemo added.

Dermatology referrals are piling up from their lung patients. Paronychia and dry skin are the main complaints, and some say it affects gripping and walking after a few months. The oncologist said dose holds help but patients hate pausing. He thinks supportive care for nails is under-resourced. A few have stopped the drug altogether over this.

Clinic runs ECG and echo at baseline and then only if symptoms come up. The nurse said that keeps the burden low for osimertinib patients. With the combination they add blood counts every cycle, so visits get busier. The pharmacist helps with the schedule. Overall she thinks it's manageable, just more admin.

Thoracic nurse navigator at a large centre said most patients on osimertinib alone barely call about side effects. Diarrhea and rash show up but get settled with a handout and a phone call. Combo patients call more, mostly about tiredness, but few have quit. She feels the team has found a rhythm. Stopping for toxicity has been uncommon on her list.
HCP worried about cytopenias w/ chemo combo, esp. in older pts.
Osimertinib alone = easy tx, minimal AEs in his experience.
Rash/paronychia manageable, but pts do complain about it.
Nursing capacity is the bottleneck for adding chemo, per HCP.
Diarrhea common, usually mild, loperamide enough for most.
No d/c for tox in her osimertinib pts so far, I think.
Pt on combo needed 2 dose delays for low platelets in first few cycles. HCP says community onc nurses already stretched w/ extra labs. Probably would think twice before offering it to frail pts.
Community HCP: tolerability better than expected w/ pemetrexed + osi once antiemetics were sorted. Most pts stayed on full dose. Thinks monitoring is doable w/ existing infusion chairs.
Baseline echo and ECG before start, repeat only if symptoms. Not sure how often QTc gets rechecked, HCP said it varies by pt cardiac hx
ILD is the AE that keeps HCP up at night. Any new cough/dyspnea = hold osi + CT same week. Had one pt d/c permanently, no rechallenge.
Academic HCP: dose reductions rare on osi mono, more common w/ chemo partner, and chemo usually gets trimmed first. PFS gain seems worth the AEs for younger pts but unsure for 75+.
PA for pemetrexed + carbo slows tx start, and AE mgmt calls pile up. Nurse navigater overloaded, per HCP. Wants more staff before taking on more combo pts.
Tumor board consensus: combo OK for pts w/ brain mets despite added AEs. Supportive care plan in place, G-CSF if needed. HCP comfortable w/ that.
Skin and nail tox: derm referral only if severe. Most pts handled w/ topical + doxy. Pt QoL complaints are more about fatigue than rash, I think.

Rural clinic, many pts 2 hrs from center. Adding chemo means q3w visits + labs, and HCP doubts pts will keep up. One pt skipped cycle 3 bc of transport and nausea. Anemia needing transfusion in another strained the small infusion unit. Leaning toward osi mono for most there unless high-risk features

Few discontinuations on osi in this clinic over past couple yrs. Most AEs G1-2: rash, dry skin, loose stools. RN phone triage covers it, no extra visits. A handful needed dose reduction, usually after stomatitis. HCP sees tolerability as main reason pts stay on tx and adhere.

Mixed feelins re FLAURA2 regimen. HCP likes the PFS signal but says nausea, fatigue and cytopenias add real burden early on. Would consider for fit pts w/ high tumor load. Pharmacist helps w/ DDI checks and antiemetic plan. Unsure how long pts tolerate pemetrexed continuation, no clear sense yet.

One pneumonitis case on osi, steroid taper took weeks. Tx stopped, rechallenge discussed at tumor board but declined. Now HCP is cautious w/ pts who have prior lung disease or RT. Frequent CTs also a hassle, payer pushed back on extra scans first time. Fear of ILD colors how HCP counsels everyone.

Hospital-based HCP, infusion suite already full. Combo needs extra chair time and nursing hrs, so scheduling is the real q. AEs themselves seen as manageable, e.g. paronychia, mild diarrhea. Probably would phase in 1-2 pts per month to see how team copes.

Pt-driven dose decisions came up. Some pts ask to stop pemetrexed after cycle 4 bc of fatigue, osi usually continued at full dose. Labs every cycle plus monthly LFTs seem OK to most pts. Not sure if stopping chemo early hurts PFS, HCP brought it to tumor board. Pts w/ renal issues handled case by case.
Rash and paronychia are the main thing patients complain about, honestly.
Osimertinib alone is easy to live with for most of her patients.
Diarrhea manageable with loperamide rarely a reason to stop
Chemo add-on means nausea and cytopenias; clinic chairs already full.
Not sure yet how many will stop early, too soon to say.
Worried about ILD, every new cough gets a CT now.

Her view, after a long chat, was that osimertinib itself is well tolerated in a community practice, with diarrhea and dry skin the usual suspects. The burden comes from the schedule rather than severity: baseline and periodic ECGs, bloods, and the odd echo if symptoms arise. She isn't sure the monitoring is justified for every patient, but nobody wants to skip it. Nurses handle most of the phone triage, and that seems to work. Discontinuations for toxicity are uncommon, though she admitted she hasn't tracked this formally.

He kept coming back to the platinum doublet. Adding it to osimertinib means anemia, nausea, fatigue and more frequent counts, and he thinks a good chunk of his patients would struggle by cycle three or four. Dose delays on the chemo side are almost expected, and he worries about people dropping off the whole regimen rather than just the chemo. Infusion chairs and nursing time are tight already. He would reserve the combination for fitter patients with high-burden disease.

Their academic unit built a simple toxicity pathway: skin care started on day one, a pharmacist call at two weeks, and a named nurse contact. In their hands few patients have needed dose reductions on osimertinib, and stopping for adverse events has been the exception. They think the structure matters as much as the drug. Even with chemo added, the team felt it was realistic as long as antiemetics were front-loaded. Probably a selected population though, they admitted.

Travel is the issue for her rural patients. Every extra lab draw or ECG on osimertinib means a long drive, and with combination therapy the visits multiply. She said some patients quietly skip monitoring, which worries her more than the adverse events themselves. Cardiac checks came up briefly, but mostly she fears pneumonitis symptoms being reported late. Telehealth helps a bit, not for bloods though.

Pharmacist-led toxicity clinic described in some detail. They phone before each cycle, grade rash, diarrhea and mouth sores, and decide whether to hold. Holds are usually brief and most patients restart at the same dose. Permanent stops were described as rare, mostly lung events or cytopenias on the chemo side. He felt the workload is acceptable but depends on having a dedicated pharmacist, which not every site has.
Dose reductions have been rare in my experience with the single agent, she said. Most patients carry on at full dose for a long time, and the skin and nail issues settle with basic topical care.
Once patients are on the combination, it's tough to separate what is from the TKI and what is from chemo. I think thier team just treats the symptom and moves on. Dose holds happen but usually short.
Nurses said the toxicity calls are quicker than expected because patients already know what to look out for. Education at baseline seems to pay off, they felt.
Stomatitis and mouth sores were raised as a real quality-of-life hit, especially in people also getting chemo. One patient stopped the pemetrexed early because she couldnt eat properly.

Hard to give one overall impression, said the oncologist. Single-agent tolerability looks fine, and the nail and skin problems are annoying more than dangerous. With chemo the picture is mixed: some sail through, others need holds and transfusions. He thinks selection is everything. He'd like a clearer sense of which drug to reduce first, as in practice it varies by clinician and by day.
Payer prior-auth for the combination adds admin, but the toxicity side is mostly the same as before, according to the nurse lead. Extra infusion visits are the part that stretches scheduling.
Honestly pleasantly surprised: the combo is more work, but the patients who stay on seem to tolerate it fine once the first couple of cycles are over. Supportive meds sorted out early help a lot.

Concerned about older patients with comorbidities; the thought of adding chemo to osimertinib makes him hesitant. Anemia and fatigue would probably lead to delays, and he doesn't want these people landing in hospital.
Pneumonitis is rare in his clinic but when it happens it ends osimertinib for good, I think. He keeps a low threshold for imaging but doesn't scan routinely just to look for it.
Rash seems manageble so far, not sure about long term.
Honestly the cytopenias with the chemo combo worry me a bit.
Tolerability looks fine to me, probably better than expected.
Paronychia may be what patients complain about most, I think.
Not sure yet if the extra infusion visits are sustainable for us.
Osimertinib alone seems pretty well tolerated, few holds I can recall.

Community oncologist said nausea and fatigue from the pemetrexed on top may push some older patients to stop early. She isn't sure the benefit would justify it in frail ones. Would need to see more real-world experience first.
Dose reductions seem rare on single agent, at least from what this academic clinic sees. With the combo she thinks reductions will probably happen on the chemo side first, not the TKI.
Nurse lead mentioned that after the first couple of cycles the supportive-care load seems to settle. She thinks the education sheet helps, and it may be why the phone calls dropped.
ILD is what keeps him up at night, even one case on osimertinib means stopping for good I think. He's not sure how often to image outside the routine scans
Seems like QTc monitoring is done inconsistently here. Some sites do an ECG at baseline only, others repeat it, and nobody seems sure what is really needed.

Payer pushback on antiemetics and growth factor support might become an issue with the combination, not sure yet. Pharmacy team said prior auths already eat a lot of time, though so far they get through them.
He feels diarrhea and skin toxicity on osimertinib are mostly mild in his patients, and loperamide plus moisturizer seems to be enough. Maybe he's biased by a small sample, he said.
Treatment delays for anemia in combo patients probably happen, but she couldn't say how often. Would need to do a chart review first.

Thoracic oncologist at a large hospital is concerned about the monitoring burden of the combo. Bloods before each cycle plus the usual TKI checks seem like a lot for a clinic that is already stretched. She thinks some patients may drop out simply because of travel and chair time. Not sure yet whether toxicity itself or logistics will be the bigger driver of discontinuation. Would need a few months of her own experience.

Infusion nurse manager said the first few weeks are the heaviest, with calls about mouth sores, rash and tiredness. After that it seems to quiet down, though she can't say if that holds for everyone. Staffing is the open question, they may need a dedicated phone line. She thinks upfront education probably matters more than extra visits.

Patients on osi mostly keep working and don't miss much, according to a community physician. A handful needed a hold for rash or low platelets, but went back on without much drama. He thinks the combo may be tougher but isn't convinced it's unmanageable. Would want to see how his first few patients do. For now he feels cautiously okay.

Pulmonologist raised concern about telling pneumonitis from infection in patients on the combination, since cough and dyspnea overlap. It seems like that could lead to unnecessary holds, or worse, missed ILD. She's not sure there is an agreed pathway locally. Referrals to her may rise, and she doesn't think her service has the capcity.

Mixed feelings from a practice pharmacist. Single agent osimertinib seems to need little beyond routine checks, which is nice. With chemo added the workload probably changes a lot, e.g. antiemetic plans, renal function checks and the vitamin supplement schedule. Not sure if dose reductions will be common, would need to see.

Oncologist in a rural clinic said patients travel far, so any extra monitoring visit seems hard. Cardiac checks, bloods and infusion days stack up. I think some will decline the combo just for that reason. She also isn't sure what to do when a patient has a delay mid-cycle, as the TKI and chemo schedules may not line up well.

safety|pembrolizumab.t: HCP: pembro mostly well tolerated in periop pts, few delays.
Immune colitis = biggest worry, esp. after FLOT.
Thyroid AEs common w/ pembro, easy replacement, no big deal per HCP.
Some pts dropping out pre-op bc of tox, not sure how many.
No discontinuations on pembro in her clinic this yr so far.
Steroid taper burden on nursing > the AE itself imo.
Community onc, no in-house endo. TSH q cycle is fine but cortisol checks fall thru the cracks. Thinks hypophysitis probably under-picked
Worried re pneumonitis in NSCLC pts post-lobectomy w/ reduced lung reserve. Hard to tell from infection on CT. Tends to hold pembro and start steroids empirically, which delays tx.
Academic center, tumor board feels AEs are manageable w/ their pathway. Nurse-led triage line catches rashes early. Delays rare in his experience.
Gastric pts often cachectic so fatigue is hard to attribute, chemo vs IO. HCP not sure what's driving the delays. Mixed picture.
PA for steroids and admissions after irAE hospital stays = headache, payer pushback. Clinic eats cost of extra visits.
Says pts do better in adjuvant phase than chemo phase. Mostly fatigue and some itch. Still flags that late AEs need watching, so happy but cautious.
Had 1 pt w/ myocarditis, scary, stopped tx permanently. Now checks troponin more often than guidelines say I think. Nursing team stretched by teh extra labs.
Rural site, pts drive far for labs. Monitoring burden is main issue, not severity of AEs. Uses local lab draws where possible, results sometimes late.

HCP concerned re late-onset irAEs showing up months after periop tx ends. Pts already back in community, PCP doesn't recognise hypothyroid or colitis. A few ER visits where nobody knew about prior IO. Wants better pt wallet cards, unsure who owns that. Sees tox as more a coordination problem than a drug problem.

Infusion nurse manager feedback: pembro chair time short, few infusion rxns. Pts like q3w schedule vs chemo. Rash and pruritus mostly mild, handled w/ topical steroids. Fewer triage calls after IO cycles than chemo cycles. Tx completion looks good in her view.

Mixed bag. In gastric, HCP says delays mostly from chemo (neutropenia, neuropathy), IO just gets held along. Couple pts had hepatitis needing a hold, resolved w/ steroids. Stopping for irAE not common, but she's unsure how many stops are really due to IO.

Thoracic surgeon POV: worried IO AEs push back surgery date. A few pts had pneumonitis or hepatitis pre-op, anesthesia unhappy. Unsure about steroid effect on wound healing. Probably more reluctant to give pembro neoadj in borderline pts. Tumor board debates this a lot.

Pharmacist-led monitoring clinic set up for IO pts. Checklist: LFTs, TSH, glucose, cortisol if sx. Works but staff time is substantial, esp w/ adjuvant running long. HCP thinks worth it, maybe cost-neutral if it avoids admissions, not sure.

Private practice onc surprised how few pts stopped pembro for tox. Endocrine AEs most common, replacement and move on. Upfront nursing education on sx reporting helped a lot. No dose reductions w/ IO, just hold or stop, which he finds simpler than chemo.
Thyroid issues common but manageable, usually just replacement and carry on.
Pembro tolerability has been better than the chemo backbone, honestly.
Colitis cases scare the whole team, and the steroid taper takes forever.
Mostly fatigue and rash, nothing that has changed dosing so far.
Pneumonitis in the perioperative lung patients is what keeps me up at night.
Very few of ours stopped early because of immune toxicity.
Their community clinic runs TFTs and LFTs before every cycle, which the nurses accept but it eats chair time. Probably worth it, though I think scheduling is the real bottleneck.
Delays are the bigger problem than discontinuations for them. A hepatitis flare pushed one gastric patient's surgery back, and the surgeon was not happy about it.
Patients in the adjuvant phase tolerate single-agent pembrolizumab maintenance well. Most just need a phone check between visits, which the nurse navigator handles.
Getting patients to report diarrhea early is hard. They assume its the chemo, wait several days, and then arrive quite unwell.
Not sure the endocrine follow-up is organized properly after discharge. Primary care often doesn't know who owns the thyroid monitoring, so it falls between the cracks.
Infusion reactions have been rare in his experience. The bigger nursing load is education: teaching patients what counts as an immune-related symptom and when to call.
Payer pushback on admissions for steroid-requiring toxicity is a headache. The hospital team says those inpatient days are rarely reimbursed well, so they hesitate to admit early.
She finds the safety profile predictable, which helps with counseling. Once patients know the usual suspects like rash, thyroid and fatigue, they seem less anxious.

We talked for a good while about how the toxicity picture differs between gastric and lung patients. In lung, the perioperative timing makes everyone nervous, because an immune event before surgery could derail the whole plan. In gastric, the issue seems to be patients already frail from chemo, so even mild fatigue gets noticed. I think pembrolizumab itself is fine for most, but the combination makes attribution tricky. Not sure anyone is fully comfortable saying which drug caused what.

She was candid that the monitoring burden is wearing the clinic down. Every cycle needs bloods, symptom review and often a nurse call in between, and staffing hasnt grown to match. Late-onset events worry her most, since patients may be months out and no longer seeing the team regularly. A few dose holds turned into long steroid courses that created their own problems, like infections and glucose swings. Overall she feels the safety workload is underestimated once pembro is added to the pathway.

Overall he was upbeat. In his practice most patients complete the planned pembrolizumab course without major interruption, and immune events are usually caught early by the nursing team's phone triage. He credited a simple symptom card handed out at the first infusion. Steroids are needed occasionally but tapers are generally uneventful. He stays vigilant, but says it is not the barrier he expected when they started.

Discontinuations were described as rare but disruptive. One lung patient developed pneumonitis after surgery and never got back onto adjuvant therapy, and the team still debates whether it was avoidable. She finds it hard to separate the imaging from post-operative changes. Because of that she tends to hold at the first cough or breathlessness, which probably means some patients miss doses unnecessarily. It is a judgment call she finds uncomfortable.

He split the safety question into two buckets: the dramatic but rare events and the chronic low-grade ones. Colitis, myocarditis and hepatitis get all the attention, yet what he actually manages week to week is hypothyroidism, itching and joint aches. The chronic stuff rarely changes dosing but does drive calls and extra visits. Supportive care is mostly emollients, replacement hormones and reassurance. I think the pathway documents give too little weight to that everyday layer.

Nurses in the day unit told him the workload shifted rather than grew. There is less antiemetic and growth-factor effort than with chemo alone, but more triage of vague symptoms that could be immune-related or not. Dose delays are usually tied to the chemo partner, I think, not the checkpoint inhibitor. Pharmacy flags liver test thresholds before release, which slows things a little. Net feeling was mixed: manageable but not trivial.
Thyroid problems are what we see most, and they're easy enough to manage.
Pembro tolerated well in our older gastric patients, mostly.
Colitis scares the nurses more than anything else on the list.
Honestly the steroid tapers are the real burden, not the infusion visit.
Few delays so far, mostly for liver enzyme bumps.
Pneumonitis worry makes some of the team hesistant in patients with poor baseline lungs.
Community clinic oncologist said most of his perioperative lung patients got through pembrolizumab without missing a cycle. Fatigue came up, but nothing that needed a hold.
Monitoring is TSH and LFTs before each cycle, and their lab draws them the same morning as the infusion. Logistically it's fine, but the nurses say phone triage for rash and diarrhea adds up.

Two patients stopped pembrolizumab after surgery because of immune-related hepatitis, and she thinks that made the surgeons nervous about the adjuvant phase. Hard to restart anyone once high-dose steroids are on board, I think.

Academic center with a weekly tumor board. For gastric patients on chemo plus immunotherapy, most delays seem to come from the chemo side rather than immune AEs, though it's tough to separate the two.
Nurse lead said the education handout on immune side effects works well and patients call early. Most issues get caught at grade 1 or 2 because of that
Payer wants a new prior auth if pembrolizumab is held for more than a few weeks, so a steroid-related pause turns into paperwork. The infusion center pharmacist finds this very frustrating.
Endocrine referrals have gone up a bit since they started using immunotherapy perioperatively. Hypothyroidism is mostly levothyroxine and carry on, so they don't see it as a reason to stop.

There's no real dose reduction with pembro, so the conversation is just hold or continue. He finds that simpler than juggling chemo dose levels. Overall he rates the tolerability as good for his gastric patients.

Rural cancer center, and patients often drive a long way for infusions. The oncologist said her main concern with pembrolizumab is that immune side effects show up at home on a weekend, and the local ER doesn't always recognize colitis or hepatitis. They hand out wallet cards but she's not sure patients carry them. Two or three patients were admitted before anyone called the clinic. Staffing is thin, so better early detection is hard.

Medical oncologist at a mid-size practice said the safety profile is about what he expected. Pembrolizumab in the perioperative lung setting brings the usual thyroid, skin and occasional liver issues, and most are handled with a hold and a short steroid course. He thinks the bigger variable is how fast patients report symptoms. Discontinuation happens, but only in a handful of his patients. The labs aren't burdensome, though tracking them probably is.

Infusion nurse manager at a large cancer hospital was upbeat. Her nurses run a standard symptom checklist at every visit and it has become routine. Gastric patients on pembrolizumab mostly sail through, and holds are uncommon and short. Steroid courses were needed now and then but resolved without drama. She feels the team's comfort level has gone up a lot over the past year or two.

Thoracic surgeon is cautious about pneumonitis in the perioperative setting. After a lobectomy the lung reserve is lower, and he said it's hard to tell pneumonitis from infection or postop change on CT. In one case pembrolizumab was stopped for good after a long steroid course. He thinks that kind of case makes colleagues wary of the adjuvant phase. Not sure how common it really is, just that it sticks in people's minds.

Day unit charge nurse said the infusion itself is quick, but the follow-up calls take alot of time. Every patient gets a toxicity call between cycles, and one nurse mostly covers them. It works, though they'd struggle if volumes keep rising. Nothing specific to one drug, more the general load of immune AE triage.

Gastric oncologist said older, frail patients on chemo plus pembrolizumab sometimes stop early. It's usually fatigue, poor appetite and low counts rather than a clear immune event, and it's hard to say which agent is responsible. He tends to hold everything and reassess. Immune-related events are fewer than he feared, I think, though a few needed steroids.
Thyroid issues keep popping up and nobody wants to own the follow-up.
Pembro tolerability is fine until it isn't, then it's steroids for weeks.
Honestly, fewer problems than I expected with the periop schedule.
Pneumonitis on pembro scares me more than any other immune toxicity, full stop.
Delays happen mostly from labs, not real toxicity, i think
Nursing triage line gets hammered after cycle two.

Community site, no on-call endocrinology. Every fatigue complaint turns into a TSH, cortisol and glucose workup, and I'm not convinced we catch the real adrenal cases any faster. The burden on the nurses is real.

We've had a handful of dose delays for rash and diarrhea in the gastric patients, mostly sorted with topical steroids or a short hold. Colitis versus chemo diarrhea is the part that muddies things. Hard to say which is which on day five.
For most of my patients, pembro added little on top of chemo in terms of how they felt. I was skeptical going in, but stopping for immune AEs has been rare in my clinic. Still watch closely.

Payer wants documentation for every steroid taper and it eats clinic time. Patients end up with extra visits that nobody reimburses properly, and frankly that's why some colleagues hesitate to use IO in borderline-fit patients.

In the neoadjuvant lung setting my worry is whether toxicity pushes surgery back. A couple of patients had a hold but still made it to the OR, I think. Not sure anyone really knows how often that goes wrong.

Thankfully the periop patients tolerated pembro better than the metastatic ones I see, probably because they're fitter. Rash and itch were the usual complaints, all manageable. Pharmacist-run phone check-ins help a lot.
Late-onset events bug me. Someone finishes adjuvant therapy, we relax, then colitis shows up months later at a different clinic that doesnt know the history. Patient education only goes so far.
Dose reductions aren't a thing with a flat-dose PD-1, so it's hold or stop. That binary choice makes me hesitant with grade 2 events in older patients, and I go back and forth on re-challenge.

The monitoring burden is underestimated, I think. Labs for thyroid, liver, kidney and glucose, plus a nurse symptom check before each infusion. In a busy unit that adds chair time and phone calls. Patients also land in the ER with vague symptoms and nobody there thinks of an immune cause. It feels like we're always one missed call away from a bad outcome.

Mixed feelings. In gastric, chemo toxicity dominates, so it's hard to say what pembrolizumab itself adds when someone is nauseated and losing weight. The immune events I see are usually thyroid or skin, annoying but not dangerous. Hepatitis and pneumonitis worry me most, though they've been uncommon in my hands. Discontinuations seem driven more by chemo than by the IO, but I haven't tracked it formally.

I'm frustrated that steroid complications get ignored in the conversation. Patients with a grade 3 event end up on long tapers, then infections, high glucose, mood swings. We call that 'managed' but it's weeks of misery. Caregivers pay for it too. Hard to sell the benefit to a family when the first thing they remember is the hospital stay.

I'll give credit where due: the safety profile in KEYNOTE-671 style periop lung has been more predictable than I feared. Most patients got through neoadjuvant cycles with only mild fatigue or rash. Our nurses built a simple checklist and that cut the surprise calls. I still don't love the endocrine follow-up, but it's workable. Tolerability isn't what holds me back.

Academic clinic, so we have a toxicity nurse, which is a luxury. Even so, grading disagreements between oncology and the organ specialists slow things down. Pulmonology says pneumonitis, radiology says maybe infection, and treatment sits on hold while everyone argues. Not sure whether that's the drug or just system friction.

Had a patient in her seventies finish all cycles with just hypothyroidism, which we replaced and forgot about. That's why I push back on the idea that IO is too toxic for older gastric patients. Sure, a couple of others had to stop early, but that's true with chemo alone too. The key for me is early reporting, and our nurse-led calls catch most things. I remain cautious, just less than before.
Immune-related AEs have been very manageable in her community practice, mostly low grade.
Pneumonitis worries him most in the perioperative lung setting.
Thyroid checks every cycle, nobody minds anymore, it's routine now.
Fatigue and diarrhea clustering after cycle three, not sure which is which
Mostly delays rather than outright discontinuation, in his experience.
Infusion nurses say pembro days are easier on them than the chemo days.
Colitis in a gastric patient already on chemo is hard to untangle from plain chemo diarrhea. The steroid taper kept one man off schedule for weeks, and the surgeon got nervous about timing.
Their day unit runs a nurse-led toxicity phone line. It probably cuts down ER visits, though she couldn't say by how much. The nurses clearly carry a heavier call load because of it.

Most of his patients tolerate pembrolizumab better than he expected after neoadjuvant chemo. Rash and mild hypothyroidism are common, plus a handful of hepatitis cases that settled with a short steroid course.
Pre-auth for managing irAEs, like infliximab for refractory colitis, drags on with the payer. Meanwhile the patient just sits in hospital waiting.
The adjuvant phase is where people drop off, I think, from cumulative fatigue more than any single event. He wasn't sure whether that is immune-related or just slow recovery from surgery.
His rural clinic has no endocrinologist nearby, so hypophysitis could easily be missed. He admitted he'd probaly refer late, once the patient was already quite unwell.

Liver enzymes get checked before every infusion, and for him that's the least annoying part of the monitoring. Pulmonary symptoms are different, since they need a low threshold for a CT and a same-day call.
Said the lab and visit schedule is heavy for frail gastric patients, but nobody has actually refused treatment over it. Mostly it's a scheduling headache for the clinic staff.

She kept returning to pneumonitis once we had talked for a while. In lung patients with limited reserve after lobectomy, even a grade 2 event feels like a big deal to her. She holds the drug early and starts steroids, then worries the patient won't get back on. Radiology reads are often ambiguous, which delays decisions. Overall she feels the perioperative setting leaves less room for error.

With gastric cancer, he finds it hard to say what belongs to chemo and what to the checkpoint inhibitor. Nausea, fatigue and diarrhea overlap so much that he often delays everything and then restarts one agent at a time. That is not elegant, but it's what the team does. He thinks the dose reductions are mostly chemo-driven and the immunotherapy part gets held or stopped. Not sure the records capture that distinction properly.

Their nursing team has really adapted over the last couple of years. They use a standard grading checklist at each chair visit and escalate quickly, which she thinks has prevented a lot of hospital admissions. Patients get a wallet card and a number to call. She said the supportive-care load is real but predictable. In her view the AE profile is something the clinic can plan around, which makes her comfortable offering pembrolizumab broadly.

His older patients worry him most. A few stopped treatment early after colitis or pneumonitis, and the long steroid courses brought infections and weakness on top. He feels the discontinuations are quietly under-discussed at tumor boards. Nurses spend a lot of time on phone triage that never shows up as workload. I think he'd like better tools to identify who is at risk before starting.

In the perioperative lung patients he has treated, surgery was rarely pushed back because of immune toxicity, which surprised him a little. Most events were skin or thyroid and were handled in clinic without a hospital stay. He still checks baseline cortisol and thyroid because he'd rather catch problems early. Patients seem relieved that the side effects feel different from chemo. He called the overall experience better than he had feared.

Travel distance shapes everything about monitoring for his patients. Many live hours away, so bloods are drawn at local labs and results arrive late, sometimes after the infusion has already started. He accepts that and relies on patients reporting symptoms by phone. Nothing dramatic has happened, but he feels it's luck as much as design. He'd call tolerability acceptable and the logistics the real burden.

safety|sacituzumab govitecan.t: Neutropenia is manageable for us with G-CSF built in from cycle one.
Diarrhea calls are what eat up my nurses time.
SG tolerability better than I feared, honestly.
Alopecia is what patients raise first, not the labs.
Sacituzumab day 8 visits get skipped or pushed far too often here.
Few discontinuations in my panel so far, mostly just dose reductions.

We run a small community practice, and the day 1 and day 8 schedule is hard on our two infusion chairs for sacituzumab. Patients who live far away sometimes skip day 8. The nurses also say the premeds add a lot of chair time.

In our academic clinic the team got comfortable with SG after the first few patients. Early loperamide and premedication seem to blunt most of the GI problems. I think the dose reductions are mostly for neutropenia and not much else.
One dose level down usually keeps patients on sacituzumab, at least in the ones I have seen. Whether efficacy holds after the reduction I'm not sure. The payer now wants a note for every reduction.
Febrile neutropenia scared one older patient's family off treatment. She stopped after two cycles and wanted nothing more to do with it. The team is now more cautious about who they offer it to.
The hospital-based urothelial clinic says the SG toxicity profile feels familiar from other ADCs. Their nurses already ran a diarrhea protocol, so it slotted in without much fuss.
Nausea and fatigue seem mild for most of our SG patients, probably grade 1-2 though I didn't look at charts. The biggest complaint is the tiredness after day 8.
The infusion pharmacist flagged hypersensitivity risk with SG and the need for emergency meds on hand. That means extra setup at every visit. Smaller sites might struggle with it.
Pre-dose labs, mainly CBC, are fine for us since patients come in anyway. A telehealth check between cycles for diarrhea would help but we dont have the staff for it.

Our rural satellite clinic struggles with the monitoring load on sacituzumab. Patients need a CBC before day 1 and day 8, and several live over an hour away. A couple had delays simply because of transport and weather. The nurses also field a lot of calls about loose stools in the first few cycles. I think without extra staff it won't scale for us.

Overall I'm happy with how patients tolerate it in HR+/HER2- disease after several chemo lines. We use primary G-CSF in anyone with prior heavy myelosuppression, and that cut down on delays. Diarrhea is handled with loperamide, and atropine is on hand for early cholinergic symptoms. A handful needed a dose reduction but stayed on treatment. Patients accepted the hair loss better than I expected.

Mixed feelings from the breast team. Neutropenia is the main reason for holds, and a good chunk of patients get G-CSF at some point. Discontinuations for toxicity seem uncommon, probably because they reduce early. On the other side, the nurse navigator spends a lot of time on phone triage and I'm not sure that's sustainable.

A urologist told me his older, cisplatin-ineligible patients have a hard time on sacituzumab. Diarrhea plus dehydration led to two admissions last quarter, I think. Kidney function is already borderline in several, so any GI loss worries him. He would rather reserve it for fitter patients. Supportive care is also poorly reimbursed.

Infusion nurses at the day unit said the learning curve was short. They built a standing order set for premeds, antidiarrheals and growth factor. After a month nobody was paging the on-call doc for routine issues. Patients mostly complain of tiredness. Her view was that the burden is real but predictable.

Dose delays are what this physician tracks most. In the practice, most delays are one week for counts, which is annoying but not a dealbreaker. Reduction conversations usually happen around cycle two or three. Patients who stop tend to stop for fatigue plus the clinic burden, not one dramatic event. Overall tolerable but demanding.
Neutropenia drives nearly every dose delay in my clinic, he said.
Manageable once G-CSF is built into the SG order set.
Diarrhea counseling takes more chair time than the infusion itself, honestly.
Alopecia is what patients bring up first not the labs
Sacituzumab dose reductions were uncommon in her hands; delays were more frequent.
Fewer SG discontinuations than he expected going in.

Community practice, two nurses covering infusion. Every day-8 visit needs a CBC review and the neutropenia calls land on the same people, so scheduling is a constant squeeze. Not sure they could take on more patients on this drug without adding staff.

Her heavily pretreated HR+/HER2- patient tolerated the first few cycles on SG with a single dose reduction. Diarrhea was handled with loperamide plus an atropine backup, and she stayed on therapy for months. He called that a reasonable trade.

At the academic center they premedicate for infusion reactions and rarely see them after cycle one. The bigger issue is fatigue, which patients describe vaguely and which is hard to grade. Probably underreported to the team.

Urothelial patients tend to be older with poor renal reserve, so she worries diarrhea turns into dehydration fast. They've had a couple of admissions for it already. Makes her hesitant to start frail pts on this ADC.
Payer prior auth isn't the problem, it's G-CSF coverage afterward. Some patients get primary prophylaxis, others wait for a neutropenic event first. Depends entirely on the plan, I think.

Nurses keep asking about UGT1A1 and what to tell patients about it. I think most of them don't test, but one physician wondered if they should after a severe neutropenia case on the TROP2 ADC. No firm view either way.
Telephone triage for diarrhea has worked better than he feared. Patients get a written plan and call early, so most episodes stay low grade. Nursing load is real but predictable.

Delays mostly show up around cycle 2 or 3 when counts hasn't recovered by day 8, and they just hold and resume at a reduced dose. With sacituzumab it's an annoyance rather than a deal breaker. Patients accept it if it's explained up front.

Spent a long time on this with the oncologist, who kept returning to the cost of toxicity in a palliative setting. Patients on sacituzumab govitecan lose hair, get diarrhea, feel wiped out and need frequent labs, and she questioned whether that is justified in later-line HR+ disease. She doesn't doubt efficacy but feels the quality-of-life hit gets undersold in clinic discussions. I think she'd still use it, just more selectively and with a lower threshold to reduce dose. Discontinuations in her practice were mostly for fatigue rather than lab values.

Overall he was upbeat. The adverse events with sacituzumab are well characterized, so the team knows what's coming: neutropenia, diarrhea, nausea, alopecia. With early growth factor use and a standing antidiarrheal plan, most patients stay on schedule, he said. Dose reductions happen but he doesn't see them as a failure. He felt the monitoring burden is comparable to other chemo he already gives.

Mixed view from the nurse manager. The infusion itself isn't hard, but the first two cycles are heavy on phone calls, and first-dose chair time is long because of observation. After that it settles for most patients. She wasn't sure the later visits could be shortened, and said staffing for day 1 and day 8 is the sticking point. Acceptable overall, but not light.

A patient on treatment presented febrile on a weekend, and the practice has no after-hours oncology line, so it all went through the ED. Since then he has been cautious about starting new patients unless they live close by. He thinks the drug is active but the safety net has to exist first. Not sure how many community sites can offer that. He also sounded wary about adding other myelosuppressive agents down the line.

We talked at length about urothelial versus breast. For breast she has seen the toxicity pattern enough to anticipate it; for urothelial she has fewer patients and feels less sure. She suspects baseline renal function and prior therapies may shape tolerability but has no data of her own. Nausea and fatigue seem about equal across both in her limited experience. She'd like a clearer dose-modification roadmap for the ADC.

Looking back across her patients, the ones who stopped early mostly did so because of how they felt, not progression. Persistent diarrhea and fatigue wore people down even at reduced dose, and a couple declined further cycles after a hospital stay. The supportive-care list gets long, with antiemetics, antidiarrheals and growth factor, and patients find it overwhelming. I got the sense she'd welcome better guidance on when to stop rather than keep titrating. Frankly she sounded a bit disillusioned.
Neutropenia is the main worry, G-CSF basically mandatory in his clinic.
Diarrhea manageable w/ loperamide + early call-in, per HCP.
Alopecia bugs pts more than HCP expected.
Too many delays by cycle 2, HCP thinks PFS gain gets diluted
UGT1A1 testing? Not sure anyone orders it here, HCP said.
Fewer d/c than feared w/ SG, most pts stay on tx.
Community onc, 2 infusion chairs blocked for SG days 1 and 8. Nursing time heavy w/ premeds + monitoring. Probably workable if scheduling is planned ahead.
HCP saw febrile neutropenia in a heavily pretreated HR+ pt. Hospitalized, counts slow to recover. Now hesitant in anyone w/ poor PS, wants clearer guidance on primary G-CSF.
Academic center, urothelial pts post EV/pembro. HCP says AEs are predictable, nurse phone triage catches most diarrhea early. One dose reduction level usually enough.
PA from payer asks for supportive care plan upfront, HCP thinks that's fair. Delays mostly come from day 8 counts, not paperwork.
Pts report fatigue and nausea more than the label suggests, I think. QoL vs PFS benefit keeps coming up at tumor board.
Alopecia aside, HCP finds sacituzumab more tolerable than the later-line chemo they used before. Some pts kept working through tx.
Rural clinic, labs must be drawn locally before day 8. Missed draws = skipped doses sometimes. Not a safety signal per se, but a monitoring headache.
Nurse lead is worried about teach burden, diarrhea plan, when to call, when to hold. Takes a long first visit. Staffing is already thin and she isn't sure the clinic can absorb more SG pts.

Had a pt w/ severe diarrhea on a weekend, ER had no idea what to do w/ an ADC pt. HCP feels the after-hours gap is a real risk. Neutropenia also made her dose reduce twice. Eventually d/c'd for tolerability, not progression. Says defintely makes him more selective on who gets it.

Mixed view from community HCP. Dose delays are common, esp. around day 8, but most pts get back on after a short hold. He uses G-CSF secondary prophylaxis in a good chunk. Reductions rarely seem to hurt disease control, in his experience, though he can't prove it. Overall tolerable if you stay ahead of the AEs.

HCP was upbeat. In HR+/HER2- pts after endocrine + CDK4/6 and chemo, SG was easier to live with than expected. Premeds and early loperamide kept nausea and diarrhea low-grade in most. Few d/c, a handful of dose reductions. Nurses got comfortable w/ the routine after the first several pts.

Concerned re: older urothelial pts, often w/ renal issues and low reserve. HCP saw dehydration from diarrhea tip one into AKI. Neutropenia and fatigue stack on top. Starts at full dose only in fit pts now, unsure if that's the right call.

Infusion center manager said SG chair time is predictable but monitoring is not. Labs, vitals, post-infusion observation all add up, esp. first two cycles. Reactions have been rare so far, in her words. Pharmacy flagged the premed bundle as a bit of a hassle but nothing blocking. She'd like a standard order set.
Neutropenia is the thing that keeps biting us, honestly.
Diarrhea is manageable with SG if loperamide is already in the patient's hands on day one.
SG? Dose reductions in a good chunk of my patients, no way around it.
Hair loss is the complaint patients bring up first, not the labs.
Honestly less drama than I expected from the label.
Nurses hate the day 8 visit simple as that.
We pretty much always run primary G-CSF prophylaxis on SG now, otherwise delays pile up by cycle 2. I'm not convinced the benefit offsets the extra injections and clinic calls.

Had an older urothelial patient land in the ED with severe diarrhea despite the handout and loperamide. After that I stopped assuming patients understand the plan. Probably need a nurse call at 48 hrs for everyone.
Compared with what these pts had before, sacituzumab tolerability is fine for me. Neutropenia is predictable and we know what to do about it, and most stay on treatment.
Community practice here, so no in-house infusion reaction team. The premeds add chiar time and the first infusion makes everyone nervous. After that it settles down.
Fatigue gets underplayed in the papers imo. Paitents tell me they're technically on therapy but sleeping half the day.
Stepping down a dose level on SG usually rescues the patient, I think, without an obvious loss of control. Still, I don't love guessing whether I'm undertreating.
Payer pushback on growth factor support is a pain. We burn a day on prior auths just to protect counts.
Our nurses got comfortable with the protocol after a few patients. Atropine for the early cholinergic stuff, a loperamide kit at home, and the phone calls go down.

I'll be blunt: the monitoring is a lot with sacituzumab. CBC before every dose, day 8 visits, calls about diarrhea, and somebody has to chase the labs when a patient is borderline. We're a small clinic with two infusion nurses and it strains the schedule. Delays happen mostly for counts, and then the whole chair calendar shifts. I'm not saying it isn't worth it for some patients, but the burden is real and rarely acknowledged.

Metastatic HR+ patients who've been through chemo and a CDK4/6 inhibitor tolerate it okay-ish. The neutropenia and GI effects are what we expected from the class, nothing shocking. What surprises me is how many stop early for cumulative fatigue rather than a lab event. I'm not sure the trial population reflects my real-world folks, who are older and frailer. We reduce early rather than wait for something severe.

In urothelial my patients often have poor kidney function and prior platinum, so I worry about sacituzumab. Diarrhea plus dehydration plus renal issues is a bad combo. We've had a couple of admissions I'd consider avoidable. Honestly I hesitate to offer it to anyone with borderline performance status. Maybe I'm too conservative.

Surprisingly good experience this year. A handful needed dose reduction, one or two delays for counts, but nobody in my small group discontinued for toxicity. I think proactive G-CSF and telling them about diarrhea up front made the difference. Alopecia bothers them more than anything else. For a TROP2 ADC I expected worse.

Not sure how to feel about UGT1A1. We don't test routinely, and colleagues argue both ways. When someone has awful early neutropenia and diarrhea I wonder if genotype explains it, but it wouldn't change much in our payer setup. So we just watch closely and reduce. Would like cleaner guidance.

Nausea and vomiting get brushed off but they drive the phone calls. We premedicate heavily, yet a few patients still end up needing IV fluids on an off day. That means an extra chair, extra nurse time, and a patient who's already fed up. Discontinuation for tolerability isn't common in my hands, but the quality of life hit is what makes people quit with SG. Frustrating.
Neutropenia is what we watch most and G-CSF is basically routine now
Diarrhea is manageable on SG once patients have loperamide at home from day one.
Sacituzumab delays for low counts happen often enough to wreck our scheduling.
Hair loss is the first thing patients complain about, honestly.
Few of ours stopped SG for toxicity, mostly just dose reduced
Infusion reactions haven't been a big deal, but we still keep the premeds.

We run a community practice with only two chairs suited to long infusions, and sacituzumab days are hard to fit around premed and observation time. Nurses say the first cycle is the heaviest on their schedule.
Most of my breast patients on SG seem to get a dose reduction by cycle three or four, I think. It's usually neutropenia or fatigue, and they tend to do fine afterwards.
In the urothelial patients I see, who are older with limited renal reserve, diarrhea worries me more than the counts. Admissions for dehydration were only a handful, but they stuck with me.
Our oncology pharmacist set up a standing order for G-CSF and antiemetics. Since then the treatment delays have dropped noticeably.
Weekly labs before day 8 are a pain for patients who live far away. We sometimes let them use a local lab and then chase the results by phone, and the results don't always recieve on time.
Payer pushback on primary G-CSF prophylaxis with sacituzumab comes up now and then. It usually gets approved after a peer-to-peer, but it adds days to the start.
Nausea and vomiting were less of an issue than I expected with the standard premed. Fatigue is the one that lingers, especially for patients who are still working.
Compared with the older chemo options they've had, SG is tolerated better in my experience. The toxicities are predictable, which makes counseling easier.

Our infusion center is a small hospital outpatient unit and the monitoring burden is real. Day 1 and day 8 visits both need labs reviewed before the chair is released. When a patient shows up neutropenic on day 8 we hold, and the slot goes unused. The nurses have started to dread the after-hours diarrhea calls. I think it's workable but only with extra staff.

Overall I'm comfortable with the safety profile of sacituzumab now. We front-load education: loperamide plan, when to call, the fever rule. Most patients got through the first few cycles with a delay at most. Only one or two came off for toxicity, and I think both had a lot of prior lines.

In our academic clinic the toxicity discussion is mostly about when to reduce the dose. Some colleagues cut early after a bad neutropenia episode, others push on with G-CSF support. I lean toward reducing once and then staying put. Hard to say which approach is right. Patients' quality of life seems to decide it in the end.
