Older urothelial patients on sacituzumab worry me. Several had diarrhea that needed IV fluids in the day hospital, and one family struggled with the home care. We lose alot of time on phone triage. Discontinuations seem more frequent in this group than in my breast patients, though I haven't counted.

Private practice here, so we run our own labs on site and the day 8 checks stay simple. The harder part is the nurse phone line, which gets a steady stream of calls about diarrhea and hair loss. Some patients get an on-body G-CSF injector, others come back the next day. Mixed feelings on SG, but no big surprises.
Neutropenia worries the whole team on SG more than anything else.
Once G-CSF is built into the order set, most patients get through fine.
Diarrhea is manageable with SG if patients call early, otherwise it snowballs
Hair loss is what patients push back on, more than the labs.
Dose reduction by cycle two is almost routine on sac gov in our hands, I think.
Too many unplanned chair visits for IV fluids; infusion nurses are stretched thin.

In my community practice the tolerability has been a pleasant surprise for pretreated HR+ patients, honestly better than I feared after reading the label. Most stayed on therapy without drama, and SG discontinuations for toxicity have been rare so far. Small numbers though.
Day 8 is the pain point for us. We have to hold chair slots and get a CBC the day before, and when counts are borderline the sac gov dose gets pushed, which throws off the whole nursing schedule.

Honestly I hesitate to offer sacituzumab govitecan to frail, cisplatin-ineligible urothelial patients. Febrile neutropenia ending in an admission is the scenario I worry about, and many of them live far from us. I'd only go ahead with solid support at home.

Our infusion nurses run a premed protocol with antiemetics and steroids, and infusion reactions have been uncommon after the first cycle. Nausea is mostly controlled. The bigger workload is phone triage for loose stools between cycles.
The payer keeps denying G-CSF for secondary prophylaxis, so we end up delaying doses instead. It feels backwards. Prior-auth staff have become part of our toxicity management.
Our nurse navigator calls patients around day 3 and day 10 of each cycle, and that has cut emergency visits quite a bit. Patients feel looked after and we catch problems early.

For anyone over 75 I'd probably start at a reduced dose, though I'm not sure there's real data behind that. My gut says the neutropenia and fatigue hit them harder. I'd rather keep them on drug at a lower dose than see them stop.

After a long discussion, her view was that the toxicity profile is demanding but predictable, and that's what matters to her. With sacituzumab, neutropenia is anticipated, so primary G-CSF is just part of the order set and the team no longer panics. Diarrhea teaching at cycle one, with loperamide already in the patient's hands, seems to prevent most of the bad calls. She's done a few dose reductions but only a couple of patients came off for toxicity. Overall she finds it more manageable than the older chemo options in this late-line setting, I think.

Her main concern, after we went through several cases, is cumulative fatigue and the grind of the visit schedule. Heavily pretreated HR+ patients already feel worn down, and two had severe diarrhea that landed them in hospital for fluids. She said the nursing team doesn't have capacity to phone-check everyone. Delays have become frequent enough that she wonders whether patients get the intended dose intensity. Hair loss adds to the emotional burden. She isn't against the drug but is wary.

He compared it with the other ADC he uses in urothelial disease, where skin and nerve problems dominate; here it's blood counts and the gut, so sequencing depends on the patient's comorbidities. Pre-dose labs are fine in a hospital setting but harder for people who travel a long way. He has had few discontinuations, but dose reductions are common. Mixed overall: not worse than other ADCs, just different.

Bit of a vent after a long chat: she feels real-world patients are sicker than trial patients, so toxicity with SG will be worse than people expect. She described neutropenic fever admissions and patients who just can't recieve full doses for more than a couple of cycles. Nurses are tired of the constant calls. She worries that supportive care costs and clinic time are being underestimated in the planning, and said she'd think twice before using it in anyone with poor performance status.

Their clinic closes early on Fridays and has no weekend coverage, so a day 8 hold often slips to Monday. That means a gap nobody planned for. Nurses try to pre-empt it by checking counts early in the week, which helps somewhat. He thinks the toxicity itself is acceptable, but the logistics around it are what make him hesitate. He wasn't sure how smaller practices without an on-call nurse would cope.

She said her nurses were anxious at first, but after a few cycles of sacituzumab govitecan they got comfortable because supportive care is protocolized: premeds, G-CSF, early anti-diarrheal instructions. Dose reductions let most patients continue rather than stop, which she sees as a real advantage. A handful needed delays but came back on treatment. In her view the burden is real but worth it for patients who have run out of good options.

Pharmacy tells him most dose modifications come from neutropenia rather than non-hematologic events. He's not sure how often SG is reduced versus simply held. Either way he tracks it in a spreadsheet.

safety|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: ILD fear is still the main reason they hold off on T-DXd in older patients.
Nausea manageable with the triple antiemetic setup they use now.
Dose reductions happen, but mostly after cycle four or so, not early.
Fatigue and hair loss are coming up more than patients expected.
No discontinuations so far in their small T-DXd group, just a handful on treatment.
Not sure how often they repeat CT, they just follow the label.
Community practice with only two infusion chairs for this. Nurses say premeds and observation add maybe an extra half hour per visit. Not a dealbreaker, but Tuesdays get tight.

A pharmacist at a regional hospital said grade 1 ILD gets picked up late with T-DXd because patients blame a cough on a cold. They'd like a clearer symptom handout. Payer delays on scans slow things down too.

Breast clinic lead described tolerability as better than the chemo they used before in HR+ disease. Most patients stay on schedule, with antiemetics doing the heavy lifting. Only an occasional delay for low counts.
Thinks neutropenia is the usual cause of delays on T-DXd, and they just push a week. Dose reduction is rare in their hands, though they've only treated a few patients.

The pulmonology referral pathway is slow at their site, so any suspected pneumonitis means a few days of waiting. That makes the oncologist hesitant to start T-DXd in patients with COPD. Says it comes up alot in clinic.
Day unit manager said the extra monitoring is mostly echo and baseline lung checks, which fit into existing routines. Staff training on ILD signs was the main upfront effort.
The team has gotten used to it after a few months. Nursing flags symptoms early, and so far nobody has had to stop for toxicity.

An academic oncologist treated a HER2-low patient who developed grade 2 ILD after about three months on T-DXd. She needed steroids and the drug was stopped, with no rechallenge. Since then the team orders scans at tighter intervals than before. Nurses now phone patients between cycles to ask about cough and breathlessness. I think that has noticeably increased the workload, but they feel it's justified.

Private practice physician said patients tolerate T-DXd better than the warnings suggest. Nausea is the main complaint, and it's usually controlled when olanzapine is added early. Delays are uncommon and he has had only one dose reduction. Monitoring feels okay once the routine is set. He's comfortable continuing in suitable patients.

The nurse practitioner described a typical week: a couple of T-DXd patients, each needing antiemetic prep, vitals and a symptom checklist. Nothing dramatic, but it's one more thing to track alongside the oral therapies. Some patients vomit on day two or three at home and call the triage line. Not sure how many ultimately stop for GI reasons, probably few.

Hospital team worries about cumulative fatigue and poor appetite in frail patients on T-DXd. A couple of them dropped out of follow-up visits because they felt too tired to travel. Last-minute dose changes also mean pharmacy has to re-prepare the infusion, which annoys everyone. Overall the oncologist sees tolerability as the limit for some patients, not efficacy.

Rural clinic where patients drive a long way, so an unscheduled visit for suspected lung toxicity is hard. They rely on phone check-ins between cycles and a low threshold to send people to the nearest ED. Haven't had a serious event yet. The doctor said it's manageable but depends heavily on patients actually calling.

Several patients in the infusion suite asked about hair loss and vomiting before agreeing to start. The oncologist feels counselling takes much longer than with endocrine-based therapy, and a few declined.

Hospital pharmacist said the dose modification rules in the label are clear and the team follows them closely for T-DXd. Delays for blood counts are tracked in a simple sheet, and reductions are logged for audit. It adds some admin, though nothing the pharmacy can't absorb. She's unsure whether other sites are as strict about the lung monitoring schedule.
The ILD worry is what keeps me up, honestly.
Nausea manageable with upfront triple antiemetics, fewer calls than I expected.
T-DXd tolerability fine so far, it's the CT surveillance schedule that's heavy.
Community nurses still not confident spotting early pneumonitis symptoms.
Dose reduction rarely needed with T-DXd in my hands, most stay on full dose.
Alopecia less of a deal than patients feared, fatigue more so.
Seen a handful of delays for low counts, mostly around cycle two or three. Usually a one-week hold and then back at the same dose, I think. Nothing that made anyone stop.

Chair time in our infusion suite is already stretched, and the extra monitoring for T-DXd patients is a real strain. Nurses end up doing symptom phone checks between infusions on top of everything else.
Honestly, compared with the older chemo options, my patients tolerate this better than I expected. Vomiting is controlled with prophylaxis and very few have needed admission.
One patient had grade 2 pneumonitis, steroids, permanent stop. Since starting T-DXd I scan more often and I'm more hesitant in anyone with prior lung disease.

Payer approval is not the issue, supportive meds are. Getting the olanzapine plus 5-HT3 combo covered every cycle takes admin time, but once it's set up it works. Not sure all clinics have that workflow.
Cardiac monitoring with echo every few months is accepted by most T-DXd patients, though a few older ones find the extra trips annoying. I'd call it an inconvenience rather than a barrier.
Patients in the HER2-low group may be less fragile, but I still see persistent fatigue and appetite loss that wear them down. Some ask to stop after several months even wihout a dramatic event.

After talking it through, my main concern with T-DXd is how unpredictable ILD is. It can show up quietly, like a dry cough patients dismiss, and by the time they call it may be further along than we'd like. We counsel everyone at baseline but I'm not sure the counseling sticks. Rural patients living far from us worry me most. I'd probably use it more freely if there were a simpler way to screen between scans.

I've been pleasantly surprised overall with trastuzumab deruxtecan. Early nausea is what everyone warns about, but with a proactive antiemetic plan most of my patients get through cycle one fine. We've had a few dose reductions, usually for fatigue or counts, and they stabilised afterward. Discontinuation for toxicity has been rare. The nurses like that the pattern is predictable, so they know what to ask on the phone call.

Our team debated this for a while. The toxicity profile of T-DXd is clearly different from taxane chemo, with less neuropathy and less hair loss. But the pneumonitis vigilance adds a layer of work: baseline imaging, symptom checklists, quick access to a pulmonologist. I think it's worth it for the right patient, but the burden lands on nurse navigators who aren't funded for it. Net, mixed.

Nursing load is where I hear the most frustration. Each cycle needs premeds, longer chair time than people assume, and then follow-up calls for T-DXd related nausea, constipation and fatigue. Nurses told me these patients need more hand-holding than the others. Without extra staffing I don't see how smaller sites scale this up. Thats not about efficacy at all, just practicalities.

Thinking about discontinuations, I can recall only a couple, and both were for lung findings rather than GI. Delays are more common, usually a week, usually for neutropenia or plain patient exhaustion. I don't track it formally so this is impression only. Dose reductions seem to happen after the second or third cycle, if at all.

For patients who've had multiple prior lines, the tolerability is reassuring. A good chunk tell me they feel better than on previous chemo, apart from the first few days after infusion. We watch the lungs and heart per protocol, and so far nothing alarming in our clinic. The monitoring feels routine now on T-DXd, which wasn't the case at the start.

The ILD monitoring plan sounds fine on paper, but in practice scans slip, patients miss visits, and nobody really owns symptom triage. I had a near miss where a cough was put down to a viral infection for two weeks. It resolved, thankfully, but it shook the team. I think we need clearer ownership before we start more patients.
ILD is what worries me most w/ T-DXd. Every new cough = hold and scan.
Nausea manageable w/ triple antiemetic prophylaxis, pts tolerate fine.
Dose reductions rare so far, delays more common. T-DXd pts mostly stay on.
Infusion nurses stretched thin on chemo days, honestly
Echo every few months, not a big burden I think.
Fatigue and nausea mostly cycles 1-2, then settles, probably.
Community onc clinic, q3wk schedule fits our chair availability fine. T-DXd AEs mostly low grade nausea and fatigue, pts stay on tx. Happy w/ tolerability compared to prior chemo options.

Tumor board debated pneumonitis risk for older pt w/ COPD hx. Consensus was OK to treat w/ baseline CT and pulm input, low threshold to hold T-DXd. Not sure how many practices would actually do that outside big centers.
Had 2 pts d/c'd on T-DXd for ILD this past yr, both caught on routine CT. Scary for the whole team. Now hesitant in pts w/ lung mets.
PA office wants baseline LVEF and lung status documented before approval. Adds admin but nothing crazy. Probably same as other ADCs.
Nausea breaks thru olanzapine in a few pts, then tx delays follow. Nurses burn lots of phone time on day 3-5 check in calls.
HER2-low pt, minimal prior chemo, tolerating T-DXd better than I expected. One hold for low counts, back on within a week. Would use again.
Pharmacy flagged emetogenic risk so we built an order set w/ premeds. Still tweaking it. Dose reduction usually just one step when needed.
Monitoring is a real burden for rural pts. CT plus echo means lots of travel and some of them just skip visits, I think.

Pulm referral pathway is our bottleneck w/ T-DXd. Pt gets new dry cough, we hold, order CT, then wait days for pulm to see them. Steroid debate meanwhile, pt anxious, family calling the clinic. Two pts ended up off tx for what was probably not ILD but we couldn't be sure. Team is gun-shy now.

Quick chat w/ infusion nurses re T-DXd. They said infusion itself is easy, no big reactions, but after-care calls are the load. N/V, fatigue and constipation questions come in day 2-4. Not sure more staff is needed, maybe just a triage script. HCP thinks its doable if volume stays small.

Honestly pleasantly surprised. Most pts on T-DXd in her clinic stay on full dose a long stretch w/ routine antiemetics. A couple of delays for low counts, one reduction for fatigue, nothing dramatic. ILD vigilance is built into visits now so it feels routine. Pts value the PFS benefit enough to put up w/ nausea.

HCP says most stops are for progression not AEs, but the ILD ones are the memorable ones. Dose reduction rules are clear and she follows them. Unsure how to handle G1 ILD in pts w/ prior chest RT. Wants more real-world data on that. Tumor board usually splits.

Oncologist in small practice said monitoring is less painful than feared. Baseline echo, CT every couple cycles, CBC before each tx all slot into existing workflow. In her view T-DXd pts handle supportive care better than prior chemo pts. No extra nursing hires needed. Would move T-DXd earlier in HER2-low if PA allowed.

Worried about cumulative tox. Pts on T-DXd for many months get progressively fatigued, nausea never fully goes away for some, and a handful stop because QoL tanks. Hard to justify in frail pts. Nurses see this first and tell me. Payers dont care tho, PA just asks for HER2 IHC.
ILD risk is what stops me reaching for it earlier in the HER2-low setting.
T-DXd nausea is manageable if we front-load antiemetics, but that means extra chair time and extra calls on day two. Our infusion nurses are already stretched thin.

Had a woman in her sixties, HER2-low, who developed a dry cough and low fever after a few cycles. Everyone panicked: drug held, urgent CT, steroids, the whole circus. It was probably mild ILD, but she never went back on treatment. I get the risk, I just find the monitoring burden hard to justify in a community clinic with no pulmonologist on site. Not sure how other practices cope.
Tolerated better than I expected, honestly. Fewer holds than with the chemo I used before.
Alopecia gets glossed over in the pitch. My patients hate it, and a few stopped over it even when the scans looked fine.

To me it's a trade-off. In the post-endocrine DB-06 type patient the efficacy is attractive, but I'm not convinced T-DXd is kinder on quality of life than oral capecitabine. Fatigue and nausea are the main complaints in my clinic. Dose reductions have happened, a handful so far, mostly for GI issues and low counts. I'd use it, but only in people who live close enough to reach us fast if symptoms start.
Scans and symptom calls add up, though I'd rather catch pneumonitis early.
Most of my T-DXd patients cope fine once olanzapine is on board. The nurses got comfortable after the first handful of cases.

Payers want an echo and a baseline CT on file, and then any hold for suspected pneumonitis triggers more paperwork. Rescheduling chairs after an unplanned delay is a mess. Our scheduler spends half her week chasing authorisations for T-DXd restarts. Meanwhile the patient sits at home anxious and nobody is happy. I wish the administrative load matched the clinical reality a bit better.
Nausea common, ILD rare but frightening. Acceptable overall, I think.
I don't love the neutropenia plus nausea combo in older pts. We end up reducing early and then wondring if we're underdosing.

We built an ILD pathway at our center: baseline CT, a symptom card for the patient, and a nurse call after the first week. Since then I feel much more at ease. Discontinuations have been few, mostly out of pneumonitis caution rather than confirmed events. I'm still skeptical about long-term use, but the supportive-care package works better than I assumed it would.
Vomiting despite triple antiemetics; she refused cycle three.
Not sure dose delays are as rare as the slides imply. In my practice a fair few get pushed a week for counts or fatigue. It doesn't bother me much, though.

Our infusion nurses dislike the whole routine. The premed protocol is long, the vigilance for infusion reactions and later respiratory symptoms is constant, and the follow-up calls pile up. We have no extra staff for any of it. When two or three of these patients land on the same day the unit just gets overloaded. I'm not against the drug, but somebody has to pay for the nursing time.
Fewer ER visits with T-DXd than I feared.
Echo monitoring is routine here anyway, so that part isn't new. What's new is pulmonary vigilance, and I'm not sure the local ED or primary care would recognise early ILD.

In a small community setting I can't easily send patients for urgent imaging, so I tend to be conservative. Most of the toxicity I see is GI and fatigue, handled with antiemetics and the odd dose reduction. G-CSF has been needed occasionally. I'm not seeing many discontinuations, but I suspect I'd see more if I were screening harder for lung changes. That uncertainty is what I wrestle with.
Our pharmacist says the supportive-care checklist is longer than for most regimens we run. Fair enough. Still, once it's in the order set it mostly runs by itself.
Honestly the safety profile has been less dramatic than I braced for. Patients who stick with the antiemetic plan usually stay on schedule. I'd still keep a close eye on cough and breathlessness.
ILD fear is the main reason he hesitates with T-DXd, full stop.
Tolerability better than expected in her community pts.
Nausea manageable w/ triple antiemetic prophylaxis, mostly.
Too many baseline CTs, pts grumbling and nurses chasing schedulng.
T-DXd delays happen, true dc's not so many imo.
Only low-grade GI AEs so far, pt kept working.

Community onc, 2 NPs, no dedicated infusion pharmacist. Worried about catching early ILD sx between cycles since pts don't always call in. Wants a clear pathway before starting more than a couple pts on Enhertu.
Dose reduced once for fatigue + nausea in an older pt, then stable. HCP thinks PFS gain probably worth it but still watching closely. Not sure how typical that course is.
Academic HCP says AE mgmt got easier once the team built a standing order set for antiemetics and labs. Pts mostly tolerate the ADC and few dc'd. Nurses now comfortable w/ it.
Alopecia a bigger deal than HCP expected for younger pts, a few declined tx over it. Also says explaining the nausea timeline eats chair time at every first cycle.
Pulm referral loop is the bottelneck I think. If pt has new cough HCP holds first and asks questions later, which he feels is the right call.
Enhertu-related cytopenias caused delays in a couple pts, which wrecks scheduling. Infusion center is already jammed Tues/Thurs.
Tumor board debated HER2-low pts w/ prior lung issues (RT, COPD). Consensus was case by case and cautious, no blanket rule.
Small practice but HCP is happy. AEs predictable, early grade 1-2 stuff, supportive meds sorted at cycle 1 so pts rarely call.

HCP candid: ILD monitoring is what wears the team down. Needs regular imaging, symptom check calls, and a low threshold to hold T-DXd. Nurses make extra calls between cycles, not reimbursed as far as she knows. One pt scare turned out to be an infection but tx was delayed several wks anyway. Probably worth it, she said, but it's a lot.

Compared w/ prior ADC, GI tox on deruxtecan is more front-loaded, HCP thinks. Nausea peaks first few days then settles for most. They add olanzapine to the standard combo, not sure that's universal. Dose reductions rare-ish, delays more common. Net workload about same as chemo.

Very positive on T-DXd tolerability in earlier-line setting, esp. vs chemo. Pts keep working and neuropathy worry is gone. Nausea and fatigue are there but supportive care handles them. Only a handful needed a reduction. ILD still on radar so they screen sx every visit, but nothing derailed.

Concerned about a long-term pt who developed grade 2 pneumonitis, got steroids, tx stopped permanently. HCP says that kind of event changes how the whole clinic thinks. Now every cough = hold. Pts are scared too after reading online. Wonders if benefit is durable enough to justify the dc risk.

Rural clinic, pts travel far. Extra visits for labs and scans are hard so they use local lab + tele check-in. HCP not sure the monitoring is feasible for everyone on Enhertu. Echo schedule adds more burden. Still uses it for fit pts.

AEs mostly lead to delays, not dc, per HCP. Vomiting rare w/ prophylaxis but fatigue lingers. Nurse navigator logs every pt call and flags to MD same day. Payer hasn't pushed back on monitoring scans so far. Unsure how it holds up w/ bigger volume.

sequencing|osimertinib.t: Still defaults to osi alone first, chemo held back for progression.
Worried that adding chemo upfront burns the platinum option for later.
Likes the idea of hitting hard in first line with the combo.
No clear next step after osi plus chemo progresses, honestly.
Depends on brain mets at baseline, that drives everything for him.
Prior auth for the combination is the sticking point, so it rarely happens here.

Community practice, mostly older patients. Tends to start osimertinib alone and keep a platinum doublet in the back pocket for progression, though she said she'd reconsider for a younger patient with a heavy disease burden.

Thinks the combination makes sense for high-risk presentations like liver mets or a TP53 co-mutation, since you get one real shot at the best first line. Has started a couple of patients on it and tolerability has been manageable so far.

Academic thoracic clinic. His concern is that once someone has had chemo plus osi, second line is basically more chemo or a trial, and that feels like a thin bench. Not sure the sequencing logic holds up for the average patient.

Wants to see ctDNA clearance a couple of months in before deciding whether chemo gets added at all. The idea is to escalate only the ones who don't clear. Not standard, I think, just how he'd like to run it.
Tolerability drives his decision. Anemia and fatigue from pemetrexed/carbo in frail patients mean he'd rather go sequential with osi. Infusion chair time is also a real bottleneck in his clinic.
Reports being comfortable with osimertinib as the backbone in any scenario. After progression he rebiopsies and goes by mechanism, so the first-line choice doesn't worry him much.

Asked whether pemetrexed maintenance continues indefinitely alongside osi or gets dropped at some point. Currently he stops it when toxicity piles up and carries on with the TKI alone. Open question for him.
Sequential feels safer to me, he said, since we dont know yet how much the combination really helps overall survival.

After a long chat, the picture is that he splits patients into two groups. For small-volume disease with no CNS involvement he is comfortable with osimertinib alone and saving chemo for later. For brain mets or a large tumor burden at diagnosis he leans toward the combination up front. He admitted the dividing line is fuzzy and mostly gut feel. He'd like a clearer framework from the tumor board rather than deciding case by case.

Their tumor board has not agreed a standard yet. Some members want to add chemo for everyone fit enough, others want to hold it until progression, and the discussion tends to go in circles. She said the default ends up being whatever the treating oncologist prefers. Probably settles once there's more local experience, but for now it's inconsistent.

He looks at the whole sequence rather than first line alone. If a patient progresses on osimertinib by itself, platinum-based chemo is still available, maybe with local therapy for oligoprogression. If they progress on the combination, he's less sure what he would do next. So he sees the combo as a trade: possibly better first-line control but a narrower menu afterwards. Still undecided which side wins.

Came across as quite enthusiastic. She now offers the combination to most fit, younger patients because she wants the deepest response possible before resistance emerges. Her view is that the chemo cycles up front are a limited price, with osi carrying on afterwards as familiar maintenance. Patients accept the plan better when it's framed as a defined chemo period followed by a pill. Her nurses adapted the scheduling without much fuss.

Continuity matters to him, which is why he's positive on osimertinib in first line regardless of chemo. In his experience a good chunk of patients stay on it a long time, so he doesn't want to complicate things without a clear reason. When progression does come, he likes having NGS on tissue or plasma to guide what's next. Overall the sequence feels more predictable than it did a few years ago.

Frustrated about what happens after osimertinib. Post-progression options are limited and anything newer, like ADCs or bispecifics, is hard to get through his hospital formulary. That makes him hesitant to use up chemo early, because he may need it later and there isn't much else. He also mentioned patients who decline quickly after progression and never reach a second line. He'd rather give the strongest regimen first, but couldn't reconcile that with his worry about toxicity.
Osi 1L, chemo add-on only for high-burden pts. Still deciding.
Prefers sequential, chemo kept in back pocket for after progression.
Not convinced adding chemo upfront is worth the AEs.
Happy w/ osimertinib alone in 1L, no plans to change.
Post-osi options unclear, that's what worries me most
Combo upfront for pts w/ brain mets, yes.
Community clinic, limited infusion chair capacity. Combo w/ chemo is hard to schedule, so most pts get TKI alone and chemo is saved for progression. HCP said it's workflow, not philosophy.
HCP likes hitting hard upfront in younger fit pts w/ CNS disease. Thinks the extra tx burden is acceptable if it buys more time before 2L. Would want tumor board buy-in first.
PA for the combo regimen was delyed a few weeks, so pt started osi alone. HCP unsure whether to add chemo later or just wait. Frustrated w/ payer.
Academic center, tumor board decides case by case. Mentioned ctDNA clearance as a possible factor but not routine yet, I think. Neutral on combo vs sequential.

After 1L progression HCP goes to platinum chemo if rebiopsy shows no actionable target. Rebiopsy often not feasible, so chemo is the default anyway. Not sure what to do w/ pts who can't be biopsied, and that bothers them.
Sees the combo as moving chemo earlier rather than adding a new line. That actually simplifies things since 2L is less crowded. Cautiously positive.
Worried that using chemo upfront burns the one good option left post-progression. Sequential keeps flexibility, in their view. Esp. in elderly pts.
Some pts on mono doing well for a long time, HCP wouldn't touch them. Only considers adding chemo if slow radiographic progression, and oligo-progression gets local tx. Continues TKI beyond that.

Pt in 60s, PS 1, started osi + chemo. Cytopenias after cycle 2, had to hold the chemo component. HCP now unsure whether to drop chemo and continue osi alone or stop everything. Felt guidance on de-escalation is thin. Makes them hesitant to offer combo to the next pt.

Joint rad onc + med onc clinic. Pts w/ brain mets at dx go combo, they feel CNS control matters most early. Chemo for a limited number of cycles then TKI maintenance, easy for pts to grasp. Sequencing feels logical: strongest hit first, simple maintenance after. Would use more if infusion access improves.

Mixed view. Uses osi mono for low-volume stage IV, combo for high volume. Not sure if mutation subtype should drive the choice. Interested in ADC options after TKI progression and hopes for access. Waiting on more data before changing practice for everyone.

Rural practice, pts travel far for infusons. Combo means more visits, so default is osi alone and chemo held. After progression many are too frail for chemo, which HCP admits is a problem. Thinks the sequence looks good on paper but real-world drop-off between lines is big. No clear fix.

HCP asked how others handle the switch off osi. Theirs: scan q3 months, switch at clear progression, not for minor asymptomatic growth. Plasma NGS first, tissue if neg. Occasionally continues TKI + local tx. Said 'it depends' a lot.

Pt progressed on osi, HCP considered adding chemo vs full switch. Tumor board split. Some wanted to keep osi + chemo, others a full switch. HCP leans toward continuing osi beyond progression if slow and asymptomatic. Honestly not sure there's a standard.
Honestly, I'd still hold chemo back for second line.
Osimertinib first, full stop, nothing else convinces me yet.
Adding chemo upfront feels like overtreating most of my patients.
Not sure the post-osimertinib options are good enough to justify any delay in switching
Fine with osimertinib upfront and chemo later, it's worked for my people.
Sequence matters less than getting a rebiopsy at progression, which almost never happens.

Community practice here, and for fit younger patients with CNS disease I'm fairly comfortable going osimertinib plus platinum doublet from the start. Fewer people reach second line anyway, so I'd rather front-load. Still wish the toxicity picture were cleaner.
Payer approval is the real gatekeeper for me. If the combo gets denied I just start the single agent and keep chemo in my back pocket. Probably ends up the same sequence in the end, I think.
Everybody talks about the combination, nobody talks about what comes after it. If someone progresses on osimertinib plus chemo, what's next, more chemo they've already had? That hole bothers me.

I tend to ask whether the patient can realistically tolerate pemetrexed before even raising the combination. Older folks with borderline kidney function go straight to osimertinib alone. Younger, high burden, then I'll have the conversation.
Our tumor board keeps debating this and never lands anywhere. One camp says upfront combo, the other says sequential, and nobody has anything that settles it for my typical 70-something patient.
I like a clean first-line story with osimertinib alone: scans stable, patient still working, no infusion chair time. When it eventually fails we rebiopsy and decide. Simple works.

Switch point is murky. Do I move off osimertinib at radiographic progression, or wait for symptoms? Slow oligoprogression gets local therapy and I just keep going, which probably isn't evidence-based but it's what I do.

Patients show up already on the combo from another practice, and then I'm inheriting someone whose maintenance phase I don't fully know how to manage. Do we drop the pemetrexed at some point or not? Different docs tell me different things.

I'm frustrated with how little guidance there is on where chemo goes once the TKI stops working. It used to be simple: TKI, rebiopsy, then platinum if nothing targetable. Now with upfront combination in the mix, I'm not sure we haven't just pushed the same problem later. A lot of my patients have poor performance status by progression, so the 'save it for later' chemo never actually gets given. I worry we pretend sequencing is a choice when attrition decides it.

I've moved a handful of patients to osimertinib plus chemo, mostly baseline brain mets and heavy liver disease. They've tolerated it better than I feared, though I do reduce the chemo dose early. My comfort is growing. Still skeptical about doing it for everyone, but for the right profile front-loading makes sense to me.

My workflow is staging, NGS back, then decide in one visit. If NGS is delayed I sometimes start chemo first and add the TKI once results land, which is messy. Pharmacy and infusion scheduling can add most of a week. Not ideal, but the alternative is leaving someone untreated and they recieve nothing while we wait.

Payers are driving sequencing more than biology in my clinic. Prior auth for the combo takes forever, and for post-progression regimens they want a documented resistance mechanism that we often can't get because tissue is insufficient. So patients stay on the TKI well past when I'd have wanted to switch. Frustrating.

I don't think there's a right answer yet. For a lot of patients, osimertinib alone then chemo is perfectly reasonable, and the combo is for the sicker ones. What I don't know is whether delaying chemo costs anything in the end. I'll probably keep individualizing and see what longer follow-up shows.

Lost track of how many patients I've seen who never made it to second line. Brain progression, rapid decline, whatever. Makes me doubt the 'sequential is equivalent' argument alot. But then combo toxicity scares me for the frail ones, so I end up stuck in the middle.
Osimertinib alone first, chemo held back for progression.
Community practice here defaults to single agent, add-on chemo rarely comes up.
Would go osi plus chemo upfront for anyone with brain mets.
No clear idea what comes after progression on the combination.
Sequence is settled in his clinic, second-line evidence is what's missing.
Fit, younger patients probably get the combination first, I think.

The thoracic group at their regional hospital reviews every new EGFR case at tumor board and mostly lands on a single-agent TKI. Chemo gets added to the discussion when disease burden is high. The decision usually comes the same week the NGS result is back.
Infusion chair capacity is the sticking point. Adding platinum chemo up front means several extra visits, and the day unit is already booked out weeks ahead.

Saw a couple of patients on the combination whose first scans looked great, so the doctor is warming to it up front. Plan would be to stop the chemo after the initial cycles and carry on with teh TKI.
Prior auth for the combination takes a couple of weeks with the main payer there. Some physicians start osimertinib alone in the meantime and add chemo once approved.

Concerned that using chemo up front uses up the main option for later. After progression on osi, a platinum doublet is mostly what's left unless a resistance mechanism turns up, so this oncologist prefers keeping it in reserve.
Re-biopsy at progression is the plan, but tissue is hard to get so they usually try plasma first. Then it's chemo or a trial, depending on what comes back
Having a clear first-line choice, single agent or with chemo, keeps tumor board discussions short. Nobody argues about the next step anymore, at least at the start.
Older patients with poor performance status only get the single agent, the combination is seen as too much. Not sure there's a middle option for them.

At the academic clinic, sequencing is decided by disease burden and patient age. Younger patients with brain involvement are offered the combination, older ones get osimertinib alone. The physician said she is not sure the split is evidence-based, it just feels right. Chemo after progression is the default either way. Nobody there has tried a different order.

A rural clinic doctor said distance is the main barrier to the combination. Patients drive a couple of hours each way for infusions, and some decline chemo for that reason alone. He ends up starting a TKI by itself and hoping for a long run. If it stops working he worries the patient will be too frail or too far away for chemo later. He called it a practical problem, not a clinical one.

Nurse-led workflow in this oncology office makes the combination manageable. Chemo teaching happens the same day as the osimertinib start, and the first infusions are booked before the patient leaves. The oncologist said patients tolerate the early cycles better than expected. He now offers it to most fit, newly diagnosed patients. Moving to the TKI alone after the chemo phase is straightforward for them.

Progression is where this physician feels stuck. Patients who progress slowly are sometimes kept on the TKI while chemo is added, but there's no agreement in her group on whether that's right. Some colleagues stop it right away. She said she mostly follows the molecular report and otherwise improvises. Honestly it feels like guesswork past second line.

For oligoprogression, the usual approach in this center is local radiation and carrying on with osimertinib. A systemic change is saved for when several sites grow or symptoms appear. The radiation oncologist is involved early in these cases. The physician thought this buys time but isn't sure it changes the overall sequence. Brain-only progression is handled the same way.

A community pulmonologist refers EGFR patients to oncology as soon as the mutation is confirmed, so he rarely makes sequencing decisions himself. He hears back about a month later which regimen was picked. From what he sees, most go on a single agent first and chemo shows up at progression. He's not sure whether that reflects preference or just access to infusion services. He'd like to know more about when the combination gets chosen.
Honestly, I'd still rather hold chemo in reserve for second line.
Osi alone first, chemo later. Not convinced adding it upfront is needed for everyone.
Too many unknowns about what comes after progression on the combo.
Fine for the young, fit, brain mets patients. That's about it.
Upfront combination makes sense to me for high-risk disease, yes.
Payer fights me on every single step after first line

Had a patient with baseline brain mets who did great on osi plus chemo, and I liked not having to wonder about timing of the next line. For that type of patient I'd go combo again. Still choosing case by case though.
Community clinic here, so logistics matter. Pemetrexed visits every three weeks plus scans is a lot for someone living two hours away. I weigh that against any benefit of going combo first.

Nobody can tell me what the best option is after osi plus chemo. We'd probably rebiopsy and chase a resistance mechanism, but the tissue is often inadequate and the NGS wait drags on while the patient gets worse.

I think sequential is perfectly reasonable if the patient is elderly or frail. You keep chemo in your back pocket. The risk is that a good chunk never make it to the next line because they decline too fast.
Frustrated by how immature the data feel for sequencing questions. We're making switch decisions on gut feel, mostly. Tumor board ends up split every time.
Moving to platinum doublet once osi alone fails is something I'm comfortable with. The workflow is straightforward and our infusion team knows it cold. No drama, which I appreciate.
If we put chemo up front what do we give at progression? Same question every time and I dont hear a clean answer from anyone.
Oligoprogression on osi, I'd just add local therapy and keep going rather than switch. Switching too early burns an option. Combination upfront doesn't change that thinking much for me.

My main gripe is that the upfront combo front-loads toxicity in patients who might have done fine on osi alone. I've seen anemia and fatigue push people off the chemo part within a few cycles. Then what, we're back on single agent anyway? I'm not sure that counts as a real combination strategy. Maybe I'm cynical, but selecting who actually benefits feels hand-wavy.

I've shifted a bit. For heavy burden or CNS disease I now lean toward starting osi with chemo together, since you only get one shot at first line. After induction I treat the maintenance phase as osi plus pemetrexed until it stops working. It's a clearer plan than waiting and hoping second line is tolerable. Still skeptical about doing it for everyone.

Academic setting, so we see both approaches. Residents ask why we pick one over the other and honestly the answer is patient preference and performance status. Insurance pre-auth has delayed the combo in a few cases. After progression we repeat NGS and, if nothing actionable, go to platinum-based chemo, maybe with immunotherapy, though I'm not sure about that last part.

Third line is a mess. Once a patient has had a TKI and then chemo, there's basically nothing evidence-based and trials are far away. I get referrals where they've burned through everything in under a year. The sequencing debate feels academic when the back end is so thin. I'd like someone to show me what changes outcomes after first progression.

Typical month, I see maybe a handful of new EGFR patients. Older ones I start on osi alone, no debate. Younger, fit, big burden, I raise the combo and let them decide after hearing about the infusion schedule. I worry the choice locks in the next step, but I'm not sure that's really true. Time will tell.

Positive on osi as the backbone regardless. Whether chemo is layered in at the start or held until progression, a TKI-first plan is solid in my hands. A few of mine have stayed on it a long stretch, which makes later lines feel less urgent. My frustration is the in-between cases where there's no clear rule.

sequencing|pembrolizumab.t: Chemo plus pembro first, ramucirumab-paclitaxel after progression. That's their default.
Honestly no clear plan for what comes after relapse on adjuvant immunotherapy.
Starting neoadjuvant makes the whole sequence much easier to explain to patients.
Not convinced rechallenge with a PD-1 after progression is worth the effort, probbaly just adds toxicity.
Depends on PD-L1 and whether HER2 is positive, really.
Perioperative approach feels natural now, surgeons are on board.

In their community clinic the surgical slot often slips by several weeks after neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy. A good chunk of patients then arrive at the adjuvant phase deconditioned or not at all. They worry the intended sequence rarely survives real scheduling.

For gastric second line they usually stop the PD-1 and move to a taxane with ramucirumab. They said they'd consider continuing the PD-1 beyond progression but have no real basis for it. Not sure anyone in their group has tried it deliberately.

Their tumor board has a clean pathway: chemo-immunotherapy before surgery, resection, then adjuvant pembrolizumab. Everyone knows their role and the handoffs are clear. They said it's the first lung sequence where nobody argues about order.

Payer paperwork for the neoadjuvant combination is eating days, so the start date moves and the whole timeline shifts. They think prior auth is now the main thing that dictates sequencing, not biology. Frustrated that surgery gets scheduled around approvals.

For frail older gastric patients they'd lean toward sequential single agents rather than a full combination up front. They admitted it's a gut call, I think based more on tolerability than on any data. Fit patients get the combination, no debate.

Their worry is that a heavy combination before surgery leaves some patients unable to complete the adjuvant part. They've seen a handful stall after surgery with poor recovery. So the plan on paper and what gets delivered are different things.

They hold off on any perioperative decision until EGFR and ALK results are back, even if that adds a week or so. Once those are negative they go straight to chemo-immunotherapy before surgery. In the rare case results are late, they'd rather delay than risk the wrong sequence.

If the patient tolerates the neoadjuvant phase well and imaging looks good, they feel confident carrying on with adjuvant pembrolizumab afterward. They like that the logic is continuous rather than a string of separate decisions. Said patients seem reassured too.

We spent a while on HER2-positive gastric disease, where they said the order is not obvious to them. They'd start with trastuzumab, chemo and a PD-1 in suitable patients, but check PD-L1 first and weigh the added burden. After progression they'd go to second-line chemo and probably drop the immunotherapy. They're unsure whether a different switch point would help anyone. Mostly they follow local guidance and the tumor board.

The question that kept coming back was what to do when disease returns after a full perioperative course including adjuvant PD-1. They said there's no agreed next step, so it falls back to chemo, often a platinum doublet again if the interval was long enough. They don't think reusing the PD-1 makes sense but admit they've got nothing better to offer. Patients who finish adjuvant and relapse early are the hardest conversations. Sequencing feels well defined up to that point and then it just stops.

At their large referral centre the perioperative lung pathway has become routine. Chemo-immunotherapy goes first, then surgery in a defined window, then adjuvant treatment. Nurses and surgeons both know the timings, which they think matters as much as the drug. They feel the option to operate after downstaging has changed how they talk to borderline resectable patients. Overall they're clearly pleased with how it fits together.

They raised a concern about what happens after neoadjuvant treatment when the response is unclear. Should adjuvant PD-1 continue regardless, or does a poor pathological response suggest changing course? They said they currently continue by default because nothing else is established. They are uneasy about that, since it feels like automatic sequencing without a real decision point. They'd like some guidance on switching but aren't sure what it would be based on.

Their workflow is pretty practical: first-line gastric patients get chemo with pembrolizumab if CPS is above their usual cutoff, otherwise chemo alone. At progression they move on to the second-line regimen without much fuss. The grey zone is low CPS, where some colleagues still add the PD-1 and others don't. They think consistency matters more than the exact rule, though I'm not sure the group agrees on that.
Pembro periop then adjuvant fine, but what after relapse? No clear answer.
Not comfortable rechallenging IO after progression on adjuvant, no data.
Happy w/ neoadjuvant chemo-IO before surgery, sequencing is intuitive.
Depends on PD-L1 and tumor board consensus, case by case.
PA delays push them to start chemo first, add IO later.
HER2+ gastric: trastuzumab + pembro + chemo 1L, then ramucirumab-based 2L I think.
Community onc, lung. Pt had pembro periop, recurred within months of finishing adjuvant. Team unsure whether to call that IO-refractory or go straight to chemo; no consensus at their tumor board.
Thoracic surgeon likes the periop pembro sequence, neoadjuvant first means pt actually gets tx before surgery. Fewer drop-outs vs adjuvant-only in his experience, anecdotally.
Gastric 1L, HCP said he'd use chemo + pembro if CPS high, otherwise probably chemo alone. Not sure how to place IO if CPS borderline.
Concerned that pts who don't make it to surgery after neoadjuvant never get the adjuvant half. Unclear to HCP whether to continue IO if surgery gets cancelled. Seems like a gap.
Academic GI onc: 2L usually ramucirumab/paclitaxel after 1L chemo-IO. Doesn't think IO beyond progression adds much but admits no data either way.
Likes that periop pembro keeps sequencing simple: one regimen start to finish, then maintenance. Easier to explain to pts and nursing, infusion scheduling smoother.

Payer pushback on adjuvant IO continuation when neoadjuvant response was strong. HCP says reviewers ask why continue. Ends up w/ peer-to-peer calls every time. Sometimes he just stops, then worries about it.
Would do EGFR/ALK testing before any IO in lung, obvioulsy. Thinks some pts get IO first then turn out driver+, messy for next line.

Rural clinic, limited surgical access. Pts often wait weeks between neoadjuvant pembro and resection, HCP worried about the gap. Some progress during the wait, then no adjuvant IO because surgery never happens. Not sure what to do w/ them, switch to chemoRT? Feels like the sequencing was designed for big centers.

HCP split on adjuvant duration. Thinks continuing IO post-op is logical but toxicity matters, esp. AEs like pneumonitis or colitis that show up during neoadjuvant. If pt had a grade 3 AE pre-op he'd probably stop. Otherwise carries on, I think. Wants guidance on restarting after AEs resolve.

Very positive on moving IO earlier. In gastric, HCP uses chemo-IO 1L for most and feels pts tolerate it well. Keeps ramucirumab combos for 2L, trastuzumab deruxtecan later if HER2+. Says the line order feels logical now.

Radiation onc unsure where RT fits when pt on periop pembro. Concurrent vs sequential unclear, pneumonitis risk worries him. Has seen a pt where RT came after IO and AEs were rough. Tends to avoid combining unless tumor board pushes.

Pharmacist, infusion center. Workflow wise, neoadjuvant cycles then surgery then adjuvant cycles = lots of hand offs. Pts sometimes lost between surgeon and med onc. Pembro sheduling is fine, it's the transitions that slip. Missing a few weeks probably not huge but nobody knows.

Tumor board at their large center now defaults to periop pembro + chemo for resectable stage II-III lung unless contraindicated. HCP says discussion is shorter and surgeons are on board. Post-recurrence they go to platinum doublet if not already used. Seems settled, they're comfortable.
Most of our gastric patients get pembro with chemo up front, nothing fancy.
Not sure where to slot it after progression on first-line.
Community oncologists here just want a clear switch point after adjuvant.
Perioperative approach makes sense to me, fewer dropouts before surgery.
Honestly sequencing after relapse is a mess, no clear next step.
Tumor board prefers neoadjuvant for anything borderline resectable, works well for them.
At their small satellite clinic the surgeon wants patients back in the OR quickly, so chemo plus IO before surgery gets squeezed. Scheduling gaps mean a few never recieve the adjuvant part, I think.
Medical oncologist said she runs neoadjuvant chemo with pembro, then goes straight to adjuvant pembro if the patient recovers well. If recovery is slow she waits and sometimes drops it.

Gastric team at a regional hospital moved pembro into first line for HER2-negative, PD-L1 positive patients and likes the simplicity. Second-line planning is easier because everyone knows what has already been used.
Worried about patients who progress within months of finishing adjuvant immunotherapy. Nobody in the group knew whether to rechallenge with a PD-1 or move to chemo alone.
Payer in his region wants line of therapy documented before approving the combination, so the team sometimes starts chemo alone and adds the IO at the second cycle. Not ideal but it avoids denials.

She said combining versus sequencing is mostly decided by toxicity in frail patients. For older gastric patients she would rather start chemo and decide on pembro later, though she admitted that's probably not what the evidence favors.
Thoracic group likes that the perioperative regimen keeps one drug backbone from pre-op to post-op. Makes infusion scheduling easier for the nurses at their academic center.

Pharmacist in a hospital infusion unit noted adjuvant pembro continues after surgery on a different schedule from the chemo combo, so orders get confusing. They built an order template to handle the changeover.

Oncologist in private practice described a lung patient who had neoadjuvant chemo-IO and then a post-op complication. Adjuvant pembro was delayed for weeks and he wasn't sure whether to start it at all. He thinks this happens more often than the trials suggest. The group has no agreed rule on how late is too late. He would like some guidance on what to do when the adjuvant phase gets missed.

In gastric, the team treats pembro mostly as a first-line add-on to chemo. After progression they move to a taxane-based option or ramucirumab, usually without another checkpoint inhibitor. A couple of them wonder if continuing beyond progression has any role, but nobody does it routinely. PD-L1 and HER2 get checked before first line so the order is settled early.

A surgeon at a high-volume hospital said neoadjuvant chemo plus pembro has changed how he plans resections. Patients arrive in the OR already treated systemically, and he feels more comfortable taking borderline cases. He still wants adjuvant pembro to start as soon as wound healing allows. Overall he sees the sequence as one flow rather than separate decisions.

Several attendees at the local lung tumor board said stage III patients who may or may not be resectable are the hard ones. If chemo-IO is started and the response is poor, they are unsure whether to pivot to chemoradiation. I think nobody wants to lose the surgical window. Radiation oncology tends to prefer going straight to chemoradiation then durvalumab, which creates friction.

One physician in a rural practice said he follows whatever the guideline lists but is unsure about gastric patients who had perioperative therapy without immunotherapy. For those who relapse he would treat as first-line metastatic, probably adding pembro. A late relapse seems easier to him than an early one. For an early relapse he'd likely pick a different regimen. The lack of clear direction leaves him improvising.

Infusion nurse manager said sequencing matters for chair time. Neoadjuvant visits are long because of the chemo, while adjuvant pembro alone is quick, so they plan slots around that. Some patients get confused when the visit suddenly becomes short and think something was missed. Teh oncologists don't always explain that change beforehand. She thinks a clearer handover would help.
Honestly, nobody agrees where it sits after neoadjuvant chemo-IO fails.
Pembro upfront, then chemo at progression. Simple enough for me.
Still unclear what we do second line after perioperative pembro.
Depends on PD-L1 and what the tumor board feels like that week.
Fine with continuing adjuvant pembro if they tolerated the neoadjuvant part.
Rechallenge after IO progression? I wouldn't bother, tbh.

We get gastric patients who go straight from first line chemo-pembro to ramucirumab plus paclitaxel, and nobody has a clear view on whether anything was lost by that. Community oncologists mostly just follow the pathway.
Our surgeons want to operate fast after neoadjuvant, then medical onc wants to restart the PD-1 afterwards, and the gap in between is a mess. Nobody owns the handoff.
Combination with chemo in the neoadjuvant phase makes sense to me. What annoys me is that we still have nothing solid on what to do when someone relapses a few months after finishing adjuvant.
I'd say sequential beats stacking everything at once for frail patients, but that's more gut feel than evidence. Our elderly clinic usually drops the chemo and keeps the IO going.
Payer approval for the adjuvant phase takes weeks in our practice, so patients sometimes lose a cycle or two. It breaks the sequence in a way trial patients never had to deal with.
Pretty happy with how perioperative pembro lines up for resectable NSCLC. Pathologic response at surgery gives us something to hang the next decision on.
For gastric, I'm not convinced the PD-L1 cutoff should decide whether IO goes first line at all. Later lines are where I'd rather see something targeted, honestly.
If a patient progresses on adjuvant pembro we're basically guessing. Probably platinum doublet again, not sure, and I haven't heard anyone defend it convincingly.

Biggest frustration is the lack of guidance on switch points. A patient finishes neoadjuvant, has surgery, and the margin is borderline, so do we go to adjuvant pembro, add radiation, or change course entirely? Our tumor board gave three different answers last month. I think we're all improvising and calling it individualized care. Wish someone would just admit that.

In our high-volume thoracic clinic the perioperative sequence has become routine. Neoadjuvant chemo with pembro, surgery within a reasonable window, then adjuvant pembro for those who recover well. Most patients get through it. I was skeptical early on, but the workflow is cleaner than I expected. My remaining worry is what comes after, but upfront I'm on board.

For HER2-negative gastric we put pembro with chemo up front when the CPS looks supportive, otherwise I hesitate. Second line is the usual taxane plus ramucirumab whether or not IO was used. I don't see much reason to continue IO beyond progression, but some colleagues do it out of habit. Not sure anyone can defend either approach with real evidence.

Rural practice here, so sequencing often gets decided by logistics, not biology. Patients travel far for surgery, come back weeks late, and the adjuvant start drifts. Then somone gets a bad immune-related toxicity and the whole plan collapses. Was that a failure of the sequence or just bad luck? Nobody can tell me.

I treat sequencing as a trade-off between early benefit and keeping options open. Giving IO before surgery feels logical because the tumor's still there and the immune system has something to see. But once we commit, later lines get narrower, especially for people who relapse fast. I probably lean toward neoadjuvant anyway. Still, I'd like to see how patients do after IO exposure before I'm fully comfortable.

Gastric first-line combination has simplified my life, to be fair. Before, sequencing was chemo, then chemo, then maybe something else. Now a pembro-containing first line is the anchor and everything after slots in more clearly. I still grumble about the later lines being thin, but at least the front end is settled. My nurses like the predictable schedule too.
Honestly no clue what to give after pembro progresses in second line.
We just keep IO going with chemo until something breaks.
Adjuvant phase after neoadjuvant is a coin flip for us, depends on recovery.
Neoadjuvant then adjuvant pembro is at least easy to explain to patients.
Stopping IO after surgery if toxicity hits is decided case by case here.
Nice that CPS at least gives a clear first-line gastric starting point.

Tumor board keeps arguing over whether FLOT should come first and IO gets bolted on later. I don't see clean data for gastric perioperative IO, so most of us just stay with chemo alone there. Frustrating when the lung colleagues get a clear path.

For resectable NSCLC we do neoadjuvant chemo-IO, then surgery, then adjuvant pembro if the patient is fit enough. The problem is a good chunk never make it to the adjuvant part because of slow post-op recovery or immune side effects.
Community clinic, so the payer fight eats weeks. By the time prior auth for the adjuvant phase clears the patient is already drifting, and I'm not sure that delay is harmless.
I like having a defined order in KEYNOTE-671 type patients. Chemo plus pembro before the OR, same drug after, and I can plan around it. Simple is good.

If someone relapses within months of finishing adjuvant IO, I honestly don't know whether to call that IO-refractory. We usually go back to a platinum doublet and hope. Rechallenge is basically guesswork, though sometimes it works.
Second line gastric after chemo-IO is ramucirumab plus paclitaxel for us, mostly out of habit. Not sure thats evidence-based after PD-1 exposure, but nothing else is clearly better.
HER2-positive gastric is a mess, trastuzumab plus pembro plus chemo up front, and then what? Third line is pretty barren. I'd rather teh options were mapped out before I commit to anything.
Giving IO early, before surgery, makes more sense to me than waiting. Patients who respond pre-op seem easier to keep on track, I think. Still a small group in my clinic.

My frustration is the handoff between surgeon, med onc and sometimes a separate thoracic team. Neoadjuvant pembro and chemo gets started, but nobody owns the decision on adjuvant restart. Surgery gets delayed, the window slips, and then we debate skipping adjuvant IO or giving it late. I've seen patients just fall through. The pathway looks tidy on a slide and sloppy in real life.

In gastric, first-line I check HER2, then CPS, then MSI before picking anything. If CPS is low I lean chemo alone, or maybe chemo with IO anyway depending on how the patient looks. Second line is usually ramucirumab-based. I think the real question is whether IO beyond progression adds anything, and I haven't seen anything convincing. So we mostly stop it at progression.

The switch point is what bothers me most. In lung, if a patient progresses during adjuvant pembro, is that a failure of the whole neoadjuvant approach? We treat it like metastatic first-line, but with chemo-IO already used it's murky. Some colleagues want repeat molecular testing, some want docetaxel-based regimens. Nobody agrees and the guidelines don't help much.

Overall I'm pretty happy with how IO has slotted into perioperative lung care. Starting before surgery gives me a read on response, and continuing after feels logical. Most of my patients tolerate chemo-IO ok, though a few have stopped early. When that happens I still feel fine carrying on with single-agent adjuvant. It's cleaner than what we had before.

Elderly gastric patients, ECOG 2, are where line placement falls apart for me. Do I give chemo and PD-1 together or start with a doublet and add IO later? Most trials didn't enroll people like this, so I'm extrapolating. Families want aggressive, the patient can barely eat. I usually compromise with a dose-reduced regimen and revisit the IO question at first scan.

We run combination, not sequential, whenever the label allows it. Waiting to add IO later seems pointless to me since the tumor doesn't wait. That said, in patients with an autoimmune history I'll hold the PD-1 and go chemo first, probably reassess after a couple cycles. It's a judgment call each time.
No idea what to do after pt relapses on adjuvant pembro, tbh.
Waits for CPS result before deciding 1L chemo alone vs chemo + IO.
Likes neoadj pembro + chemo then adj pembro as one continuous plan.
PD-1 rechallenge after relapse soon after finishing adjuvant? HCP skeptical, probably wouldn't.
Tumor board sets the order, usually surgery first if clearly resectable, but not always.
PA timing decides if IO starts w/ chemo or only by cycle 2, I think.

Community onc, sees perioperative approach as cleaner than surgery-first then adjuvant. Pts get systemic tx earlier and tumor board likes that later options stay open. Would use pembro up front for most resectable stage III.
HCP: gastric 1L, low CPS pts = debate chemo alone vs adding pembro. Thinks adding IO is probably fine but not sure it's worth the AEs in frail pts. Defers to PS in the end.
Worried neoadj pts who have post-op complications never recieve the adjuvant phase. Then the 'perioperative' plan is really neoadj only. Wants to know how much the adjuvant part actually matters.
Academic thoracic surgeon says OR timing after last neoadj cycle varies, usually a few wks. Med onc tries to start adjuvant once pt has recovered. Handoff between the two is the sticking point.
HER2+ gastric: HCP unclear on order of trastuzumab + pembro vs chemo backbone. Says local pathway doesnt spell it out, so ends up case by case. Slightly uneasy about that.
Pt w/ PD-L1 high lung ca, finished neoadj, pCR on path. HCP happy to continue adj pembro anyway, sees it as logical continuation. Keeps chemo in reserve for relapse.
Said sequencing after IO in gastric is mostly 2L chemo, ramucirumab/paclitaxel type, so nothing changes because of pembro. Not sure if prior IO affects response to those. Waiting on more data.

Rural practice HCP says pts travel far for surgery so the perioperative sequence breaks down. Neoadj cycles done locally, then OR at a referral center, then back home for adj IO, and handoffs get lost. A handful never restart adjuvant. Thinks plan looks great on paper but logistics decide. Wants clarity on who owns the adj start.

Large cancer center HCP uses pembro + chemo 1L gastric for PD-L1 positive pts. Wonders if MSI-H pts should get IO alone earlier, not sure though. Most colleagues stop IO at PD when switching to chemo. Feels evidence for continuing beyond progression is thin. Open to hearing more.

Pulm onc really likes KN-671 style sequencing. Neoadj, surgery, adj flow fits how tumor board already works. Pts see response before OR, which helps counseling. Main caveat: EGFR/ALK results must be back before starting anything.

Payer issue: PA for adj pembro often requested separately from neoadj, causing gaps. HCP had a pt wait several wks post-surgery. Thinks this undermines the whole sequence. Practice now submits both PAs upfront but not every payer accepts that. Frustrated.

Cis-ineligible pts are the gray zone. HCP unsure whether to go surgery first then adjuvant, or still do neoadj with carbo. Depends on PS and comorbidities, tumor board split. Pembro isn't the issue, the chemo partner is. Would like more real-world experience.

Sequencing after relapse on perioperative IO: nobody in the group has a good answer. Some go straight to chemo, some try other IO combos, a few push for trials. Worried about burning the PD-1 option early. Unclear when relapse counts as IO-refractory. Pts want a decision fast.
Gastric 1L w/ good CPS: HCP comfortable starting chemo + pembro together day 1 rather than staged. Says it avoids losing pts to fast progression before IO gets added.

sequencing|sacituzumab govitecan.t: Usually after CDK4/6 and at least one chemo, not before.
Still unclear to me where it goes once EV has already been used.
SG slots in fine as the next step after endocrine plus CDK4/6 stops working.
Can't see them using it ahead of capecitabine, honestly.
Depends on how fast the disease is moving at the switch.
Payer wants two chemo lines first, so it ends up late.

Community practice, mostly HR+ patients. Once they've progressed on CDK4/6 and a couple of endocrine switches, the oncologist said sacituzumab govitecan is what she goes to before other chemo. She likes that it's a clear slot.
For urothelial they see it after platinum and a checkpoint inhibitor, and after EV if the patient got it. The order of EV versus SG is still close to a coin flip for them, I think.

Academic clinic, worried about neutropenia in patients already worn down by earlier lines. They hold the ADC back until performance status is clearly good, which pushes it later than they'd otherwise place it.
Combination with pembrolizumab came up, but he would only do that in a trial. Outside of that he thinks purely in sequential terms.
The infusion nurses prefer a plan set early, so the practice lines up SG right after progression on first chemo. There is less of a gap between lines and alot less scrambling for chair time.
Not convinced about moving it earlier in HR+ disease. In his view endocrine-based options with targeted agents should be used up first, and the ADC stays for later.
She is unsure what comes after an ADC, probably another chemo. Not sure a second ADC makes sense wiht what she has seen so far.

Tumor board discussion at a large hospital. They generally agree SG comes after endocrine therapy and CDK4/6 are done, but argue over whether it goes ahead of other single-agent chemo. The medical oncologists lean toward using it first, while a few colleagues prefer to save it. Nobody was keen on combining it with anything outside a study. The group seems comfortable with the order but not with the reasoning behind it.

Rural clinic where many patients drive a long way for infusions. Because SG means two visits per cycle, the physician often tries oral options first and brings it in late. He worries that by then some patients are too frail to get it. Sequencing ends up being driven by logistics as much as biology. He said this is probably true for a good chunk of his panel.

Urothelial-focused physician at a cancer center. After progression on EV and pembro, he sees SG as the natural next option, since there is little else with a similar rationale. He would like to see it earlier but accepts that label and access keep it behind those two. For fit patients he moves quickly, usually within a couple of weeks of scan progression. He called it a reasonable third-line slot.

Prior auth is the bottleneck. At her practice the payer review can take long enough that patients progress further before the switch happens. Sometimes they give a bridging chemo while waiting, which muddies the sequence. She feels the switch point is set by paperwork rather than the clinical picture.

They debate whether to switch at imaging progression or wait for clear symptoms. In the hospital's HR+ patients, the team usually moves at scan progression if the liver is involved and waits a bit longer for bone-only disease. Sacituzumab govitecan is considered once endocrine options are exhausted. No one at the clinic had tried it alongside another agent. They described their approach as pragmatic and a little inconsistent.

Concern about using it after another ADC with a similar topoisomerase payload. He suspects cross-resistance but admitted he's guessing. For now he would rather put a non-ADC chemo in between, which lengthens the sequence. He also said it makes planning a third or fourth line really hard for these patients.
Private practice, HR+ patients. The oncologist said sacituzumab is now his default after CDK4/6 and chemo. It gives him a straightforward answer when families ask what's next.
Honestly can't tell where SG fits after CDK4/6 and one chemo.
Probably third line for most of my pts, not earlier.
Too many options post-EV, no clear order.
If they've failed endocrine plus CDK4/6, I'd go ADC before capecitabine.
Combos with pembro? Sequential only, the tox stacking worries me.
Depends which way the tumor board leans that week.

We're a small community practice and I'm wary of putting SG in early, because the neutropenia management is a lot for us. If they still have endocrine options left I'd rather exhaust those first. Jumping to an ADC after one chemo feels premature to me.
In urothelial the order is a mess since EV plus pembro moved up front. After that I'm not sure what comes next, probably sacituzumab if they're fit enough, but I haven't actually done it yet.
I like having SG right after progression on CDK4/6 when visceral disease is moving fast. Rather than burn through single-agent chemo that does little, I'd switch sooner in those pts.
Our payer wants two prior chemo lines documented before approving, so the sequence is dictated by paperwork, not biology. Patients lose weeks waiting. Really frustrating.
My switch point is usually liver mets progressing or symptoms climbing, not just a scan change. If it's imaging alone I'd probably keep going on endocrine a bit longer.
Everyone talks about ADC after ADC, but I haven't seen anything convincing on what works after the first one. Cross-resistance worries me. Until that's clearer I wouldn't run two back to back.
At our hospital clinic we've used it after only one prior chemo in a handful of fast progresors and it went better than I expected. Not a rule, just an impression so far.
Seen a few pts do well enough on SG after CDK4/6 and one chemo that I'd now move it up a bit. Still skeptical overall, but what usually follows is worse.

The trial population was heavily pretreated, so using it after just CDK4/6 feels like extrapolation to me. I keep hearing 'earlier is better' and nobody shows me that. My patients are older with more comorbidities, and I doubt many would reach a later line anyway. So I default to what I know best, usually capecitabine, and revisit at the next progression.

Cisplatin-ineligible pt, got EV plus pembro, progressed in a few months. Now what? Platinum if they never had it, otherwise SG, but nobody has a clear answer. I asked around at tumor board and got three different opinions. Feels like we're guessing at every step.

I'm fairly convinced sacituzumab belongs after endocrine-based therapy stops working in the metastatic setting, ahead of most older chemo. My reasoning is partly practical: patients who get it earlier are fitter and tolerate it better. I can't prove that, so I hedge. But compared with the usual chemo carousel it feels like a more rational place to put it.

People keep asking me about adding SG to endocrine therapy or rolling over to a second CDK4/6. I wouldn't do either outside a study. Some colleagues do the CDK4/6 rollover and I'm skeptical. Combination versus sequential will probably only get settled when real data show up, not opinion.

Honestly the logistics drive sequencing more than anyone admits. Day 1 and 8 scheduling is hard for patients who travel far, and our chairs are always full, so I offer oral chemo first. By the time they come around to SG a lot have lost performance status and it's too late. That's the part that frustrates me

We can't pick by biomarker since TROP2 isn't tested routinely, so line placement ends up being about prior therapies and how fast the disease is moving. I think that's fine, but it's not very satisfying. In HR+ I lean toward using it after endocrine and CDK4/6 are done. In urothelial I just don't have a rule yet.
Post-CDK4/6i with fast progression, SG would be my pick for next tx.
Too many pts crash befor 3L, never even get to SG.
Still deciding T-DXd vs SG order, not sure which goes first.
No clear data on what follows after this ADC, bugs me.
UC: EV/pembro first, SG after. Standard in my clinic.
Visceral crisis post-CDK4/6i? Straight to sacituzumab, I think.
Community onc, mostly 2 endocrine-based lines then chemo. SG would probably go ahead of capecitabine for some pts, but PA delays make it hard to say. Depends on payer, honestly.
Tumor board split on UC sequencing. Some want SG only after EV and pembro, others say pts are too frail by then. Not sure we ever get a clean answer.
Likes SG as first chemo once endocrine options are used up, esp. rapid progressors. Felt PFS was meaningfully better than single-agent chemo in his own pts. Would move it earlier if access allowed.
Worried neutropenia and diarrhea early on drop PS, so the next tx options shrink. Prefers holding SG later for frail pts. Doesn't want to burn the fit window.
Combo with pembro in UC? Curious but says trial setting only, sequential for now
Academic HCP, HER2-low pts: unsure if T-DXd should precede SG. Feels the order is guesswork right now. Wants real sequencing data before changing anything.
Switching at first radiographic progression on ET+CDK4/6i to SG has worked ok in a handful of pts. Easy to explain to pts too, clear next step.
Would consider SG after EV only if PS 0-1 and counts still good. Otherwise platinum rechallenge if not already used. Hedged a lot on this one.

Large group practice runs 3L+ HR+ pts through chemo mostly by habit. Capecitabine or eribulin usually first, SG considered when those are exhausted or pt is symptomatic. Thinks that probably undersells it but admits PA burden shapes the order. Would revisit if pharmacy could pre-clear. Not sure leadership would back a protocol change.

Tox concerns dominate for this HCP. Diarrhea and neutropenia in a pt who already had EV neuropathy and rash seems like stacking AEs. So SG goes to the very end, if at all. Also unclear to him what comes after, so he hesitates to use it early. Wants clearer guidance on post-SG options.

Tumor board last month moved a pt straight from CDK4/6i progression to SG, skipping more endocrine tweaks. Pt had fast liver mets so waiting felt wrong. Response was quick enough that the team now flags similar pts earlier. Still individualized, he stressed. Wants to do more of this if PA stays smooth.

Rural clinic, infusion chair capacity limits things. D1/D8 visits for a pt living far away is a real issue so he often picks oral chemo first. Sequencing is more logistics than biology bc of this. Feels guidelines ignore that. Pts drop out before 3L anyway.
