For UC, HCP described a pretty standard flow: platinum, maintenance, then EV+pembro, with SG as a later option. Not sure where the line sits if pt progresses on EV, honestly. Combining ADCs seems premature to him, sequential feels safer. Waiting on more real-world experience.

Breast specialist, hospital-based clinic: sequence depends on HER2-low status, PS, and how fast things are moving. Endocrine+targeted first, then ADC, then single-agent chemo if pt still fit. I think SG vs T-DXd comes down to HER2 IHC. Wasn't sure about going back to endocrine after ADCs. Tumor board usually settles it.

Talked for a good while about where SG fits in HR+/HER2- after CDK4/6 and endocrine therapy. In his view it sits after at least one chemo, probably capecitabine or a taxane, since TROPiCS-02 was a heavily pretreated group. He wouldn't jump to it straight after CDK4/6 progression unless the disease is clearly visceral and moving fast. He's still unsure whether it belongs before or after the HER2-low ADC and said the data to decide just isn't there. In the end he chooses by what toxicity the patient already tolerated.
Not keen on stacking ADCs back to back, cross-resistance is a black box.

Community oncologist who sees SG as a clean option after endocrine plus CDK4/6 and one chemo line. Easy to slot in, predictable schedule, and she likes that it doesn't force her to pick a combination partner.

In urothelial the sequencing is a mess right now. Most of his patients get platinum, then maybe PD-1 maintenance, and by the time the nectin-4 ADC comes in there's little room left for anything else. He thinks SG would end up fourth line in practice, by which point performance status is often gone. Payer pre-auth delays add a couple more weeks, which he said can decide whether a patient gets another line at all. Overall pessimistic about it being more than a late salvage choice.
Happy to use it right after first chemo if the disease is aggressive.

Honestly I switch based on how fast things are moving, not on a fixed line. Slow bone-predominant disease stays on endocrine swaps longer, while a visceral crisis goes to chemo or an ADC much earlier.

After a long chat he summed up that he's fairly comfortable using SG as the first ADC in later-line HR+ disease. His reasoning is that the TROPiCS-02 population looked like the patients he actually sees, heavily pretreated and running out of endocrine options. He'd rather give it before a patient is too frail for anything, and keep other chemo in reserve. Dose reductions and G-CSF support are things his nurses already handle, so workflow isn't a barrier. He would like clearer guidance on what follows it, but that doesn't stop him from starting.
Sequence depends mostly on HER2-low status and prior chemo exposure.
I'm not sure the data supports putting it ahead of other chemo options for most of my patients. Also nobody can tell me what works after it, so I hesitate to use it early and burn the bridge.
Combination with endocrine therapy or immunotherapy comes up at tumor board, but we mostly stay sequential because there's no real evidence for combos. Maybe within a trial, not in routine care.
Too many ADCs competing for the same slot, and we lack a clear order.

Her clinic runs a molecular tumor board, so line placement is usually argued case by case. For HR+ disease SG tends to come after endocrine therapy with a CDK4/6 inhibitor and at least one chemo, though a few patients get it earlier when liver involvement is heavy. She said the biggest open question is the order relative to the HER2-low ADC, and her group is split. In urothelial she sees it mostly after platinum and checkpoint therapy, with the nectin-4 option going either before or after depending on access. Comfortable overall, but wants prospective sequencing data.
For a fit patient who progressed on CDK4/6 and a single taxane, SG is my natural next step. Having a clear switch point, like progression with visceral spread, makes the decison simpler.

Patients who already had a rough time with neutropenia on earlier chemo worry me for sacituzumab. If they arrive after capecitabine and a taxane with poor marrow reserve I'd probably lean to supportive care rather than another cytotoxic line
Still deciding case by case, no fixed place for it yet.

Cost and access drive a lot of this in his setting. The hospital pharmacy committee wants proof that SG beats cheaper chemo options before it gets a slot, so in practice it comes late, if at all. He thinks that undermines thoughtful sequencing, because patients reach it after two or three other lines and just aren't fit. I asked whether he'd move it earlier if access improved and he said probably, but he's not convinced the benefit would hold up in an earlier line. I left the conversation feeling he's skeptical rather than opposed.
We tend to treat the ADC as a bridge to trial enrollment, so placement depends on which studies are open. If nothing is open it goes after the second chemo. Not sure thats ideal but its how we work.
Moving SG earlier makes sense to me, especially with visceral disease.

Switching after only two cycles feels premature to me, but scans are slow to get and some patients clearly go downhill anyway. That grey zone about when to call it failure and change course bothers me with this drug.

Mixed feelings overall. On one hand he likes having a mechanistically different option after CDK4/6 and endocrine therapy, and thinks sacituzumab govitecan fills a real gap in later lines. On the other, he worries the order of ADCs will be decided by availability rather than biology, and he doesn't know how to counsel patients on that. In urothelial he sees it as a post-platinum, post-checkpoint option, probably after the nectin-4 ADC. He'd want head-to-head or at least real-world order data before changing his habits.
Probably after CDK4/6 and one chemo, but not sure it's that clean
Would need to see more before moving SG ahead of chemo.
Seems like a reasonable pick once endocrine options run dry.
Not sure about combining it with anything yet, sequential feels safer.
I think post EV/pembro is where it lands in urothelial, may be
Honestly unsure where it fits after another ADC. Sequence feels murky.

Our community clinic mostly sees it as a third-line-ish option in HR+ disease, after endocrine plus CDK4/6 and maybe one chemo. I think that may shift if earlier-use data firm up, but nobody here is rushing.

Seems to me that for a patient who progressed quickly on endocrine plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor, SG would probably be my next move rather than another single-agent chemo. Fatigue and counts would need watching, but sequencing-wise it feels natural.

Payer prior auth tends to want two prior chemo lines documented, so I may end up using it later than I'd like. Not sure that's right clinically. It's frustrating when the order gets dictated by paperwork.
In urothelial I'm not sure whether SG goes before or after a platinum rechallenge for patients who already had enfortumab. Probably depends on fitness and how long the last response lasted.
Worried about going straight from another topoisomerase-based ADC to SG, since the payload overlap might blunt benefit. Would need to see real-world sequences before I try it.
I think SG may be a good bridge for people who aren't trial candidates but have run out of standard choices. Seems to fit after a couple of lines where we can monitor closely.
Pairing with immunotherapy in urothelial is tempting on paper, but I'd stay sequential for now. Overlapping toxicity, diarrhea and neutropenia mostly, may be hard for frail pts.
Tumor board usually lands on this after chemo, then it depends on performance status. Not sure we have a consistent rule yet, kind of case by case

For HR+/HER2- patients I lean on endocrine plus CDK4/6 first, then usually a single-agent oral chemo if disease is slow. SG seems to come in once visceral spread picks up or chemo stops working. I'm not sure jumping it ahead of oral chemo is justified, though a few colleagues hint at it. TROPiCS-02 looked like a pretty pretreated population, so I'd hesitate to extrapolate earlier. Probably need more sequencing data before I change habits.

We had a patient who got SG right after a different ADC and the response was short. One case proves nothing, but it made me cautious. I think the order may matter more than we admit, and I'm not sure anyone knows the best gap between agents. So I tend to delay SG and use something else first, which probably isn't ideal. Would need to see actual sequencing data.

Honestly I'm fairly optimistic about SG as the next step after CDK4/6 failure plus one chemo. Patients seem to tolerate it okay if we get ahead of the GI side effects and use growth factor support. I think it may even earn a spot before more chemo lines, but I'd want to see that play out. In my infusion-heavy practice the day 1 and 8 schedule is managable. Overall a sensible slot, not sure about earlier yet.

Switch points are what bother me. When to call endocrine therapy exhausted and move on isn't obvious, especially with slow bone-dominant disease. I may be moving too late for some and too early for others. Imaging in our clinic is about every three months, so progression gets spotted late. Not sure the guidelines help much here.

In urothelial the sequence is crowded: platinum, then maintenance immunotherapy, then enfortumab-based treatment, and SG seems to sit after all that. A few of my pts never make it past two lines because of performance status, so it may rarely get used. I'd probably consider it for fit patients with decent liver function. Not sure about combining it with anything, would need to see safety first.

Our infusion nurses felt things went smoother when SG followed a short break from chemo rather than back-to-back. I think a bit of recovery time may help patients get through the first cycles. It seems like a decent argument for placing it after a chemo line, not stacked directly onto one. Still just an impression from a handful of cases. If that holds, I'd be comfortable using it that way.

sequencing|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: Honestly, I don't know where HER2-low fits after endocrine therapy fails.
Probably after one endocrine line, but I'm not convinced yet.
Payer wants two prior lines documented, so sequencing is decided for me.
Fine with T-DXd earlier if disease is clearly progressing.
Too many unknowns about what comes after the ADC.
Sequential works fine for us; combining feels unnecessary.

Community practice here, so we can't just jump to T-DXd after CDK4/6 failure when the prior auth team wants chemo documented first. A few weeks of delay matter when someone is symptomatic. I'm tired of redoing the same appeal.

I'd put it ahead of chemo in a HER2-low patient with visceral disease, I think. For slow, bone-only disease I'd still run another endocrine option first. Not sure the guidelines make that distinction clear.
Nobody can tell me what to give after progression on this drug. Another ADC? Chemo? It feels like guessing, and I don't love starting something when the next step is a blank.
For my fit, younger patients with fast-moving disease, moving it up has been reasonable. Response seems to show up quickly, which lets me decide the next step sooner. I'd keep doing that.
My switch point is second progression on endocrine plus CDK. Before that I'd rather stay oral. Tumor board usually agrees, though not always.
Combining it with anything feels like a stretch given my lung worries. I wouldn't stack agents outside a trial. Sequential is simplier to monitor.
Having an option before chemo in HER2-low is a real change for our clinic. Pharmacy and infusion scheduling adapted fine. I'm more comfortable moving it earlier now than I was a year ago.
Waiting on more data in the HER2-ultralow group before I change anything. For now those patients get endocrine-based sequencing like before, and I'd revisit it later.

My issue is that the sequencing evidence comes from trials with comparators that don't match what I actually use. Real patients show up after three or four lines, with mixed receptor status and poor performance status. I'm not sure the earlier-line story translates to them. The scan schedule and ILD vigilance also eat clinic capacity. So I tend to hold it until options are clearly narrowing.

We have a rough pathway: endocrine plus CDK4/6 first, then re-check HER2 on a new biopsy if feasible, then the ADC if HER2-low and progressing. The biopsy step is a pain because many patients are bone-dominant with thin tissue. When we can't get one, we go off the old pathology. I think that's probably okay but I'm uneasy. Pathologists vary a lot on the low calls.

Our pharmacy lead and I argued last week about positioning. In HER2-positive disease it already sits after the first-line regimen, and now people want it pushed further forward. I'm skeptical, since the standard first-line is working well for a lot of my patients. Why swap out something good and burn through options faster? Maybe I'm just being conservative.

I've changed my approach this year. After endocrine therapy stops working, I now go to the ADC rather than single-agent chemo for most HER2-low patients. They tolerate it better than I expected, and nausea is manageable with prophylaxis. It also keeps chemo in reserve for later, which I like. Still watching the lungs closely.

Sequencing after T-DXd is the part that keeps me up. We're a rural site, patients travel far, and if they progress I've little to offer locally besides chemo. Referral to a trial center means a long drive and many decline. So starting early has a downside that nobdy talks about.

Honestly it depends on who's in front of me. Elderly, frail, ER-positive and slow: endocrine again. Young, in crisis, liver mets: ADC now. The in-between folks are where we argue, and I don't think one rule fits them. Insurance sometimes breaks the tie.
Wants T-DXd after 1 line endocrine+CDK4/6 at most, not earlier.
Not moving T-DXd earlier till 1L data mature, per HCP.
HER2-low = clear 2L slot post-endocrine, no debate for this HCP.
Sequence depends on pt. Visceral crisis goes straight to ADC.
Worried about what's left after ADC. Nothing great.
PA denials for T-DXd before ET exhausted, constant headache
Community onc, mostly HER2+ pts. Uses T-DXd 2L after taxane/trastuzumab/pertuzumab now, no longer waits for T-DM1 failure. Says AEs manageable w/ early antiemetic plan.
Tumor board split on HER2-low, ER+ pts w/ no chemo yet. Some want ET + CDK first, others jump to ADC if liver mets. HCP leans ET first, probably.
Concerned re ILD risk in pts w/ prior chest RT or recent CDK4/6i. Would rather space tx out, not stack. Not sure how long a gap is needed.
Academic HCP asked about T-DXd then TROP2 ADC vs reverse. No clear answer in practice, picks by tox profile and pt preference I think.
Likes having an ADC option post-endocrine. Changed how she counsels pts on 'what's next'. Sequencing feels less like a cliff now.
Payer wants 2 lines endocrine before approving. HCP says pts lose weeks waiting on appeals, some progress meanwhile.
Combo w/ IO or TKI? HCP says trials only, not routine. Sequential still default.
Brain mets pts: unsure if T-DXd goes before or after tucatinib regimen. Usually defers to neuro-onc and RT timing, esp. if pt did not recieve SRS yet.

Regional hospital HCP, HER2+ mets. Currently 1L THP, then T-DXd 2L, T-DM1 later if at all. Says order feels right but not sure it's evidence-based vs habit. Pts w/ residual disease after neoadjuvant are a gray zone since T-DM1 already used. Wants tumor board input case by case.

HCP frustrated w/ lack of guidance on switch point. Pts stable on endocrine but slowly creeping up, when to pull trigger on T-DXd? Wait too long and pt too sick for tx, switch early and you burn the endocrine option. Infusion nurses also worry re ILD monitoring load if use moves earlier. No one has a clean answer rn.

Large cancer center HCP, very upbeat. Moves T-DXd up for HER2-low once endocrine-based tx stops working, esp. w/ symptomatic liver disease. Says responses tend to come fast, which helps pt morale. Keeps chemo as later option. Sequencing talk is much easier than before.

Workflow comment from infusion side. Going from oral tx to ADC needs chair slots and pharmacy prep, so switch isn't same-day. HCP now flags likely progression early to line things up. Says this works ok but depends on clinic size. Smaller sites struggle more.

Older pt scenario, ECOG 2, HER2-low, post CDK4/6i. HCP would still offer T-DXd but maybe single-agent chemo first, not sure frailty changes order. Wants geriatric assessment before deciding. Probably more cautious than trial pop.

Private practice HCP says T-DXd after endocrine progression is an 'easy call' now. Likes that it comes before further chemo lines. Pts tolerate nausea w/ prophylaxis. Wonders about later options after ADC but happy w/ current order. Tumor board only for odd cases.
Would use T-DXd right after progression on endocrine plus CDK4/6, before any chemo.
Still unsure where it fits after a second endocrine line.
Sequencing after T-DXd is a big unknown for us.
Honestly chemo first for most of my HER2-low patients.
Fine with it second line, no strong feeling about third.
Easy slot after progresion on first-line CDK inhibitor combo.

Community practice, three oncologists. We usually run endocrine therapy until there is visible progression, then talk about T-DXd. Hard to justify skipping another endocrine line if the patient feels fine.
Our infusion center is booked about two weeks out, so the switch often waits on scheduling rather than a clinical decision. Patients on oral therapy just stay on it longer than I'd like.
I like that it can come after endocrine-based treatment without going through chemo first. For a patient with low-volume visceral disease I'd move quickly.
One payer here wants documented prior chemo in the metastatic setting, which pushes us to give a taxane first. Annoying for HER2-low patients who would otherwise go straight to the ADC.
Not sure about combining it with anything, I think sequential is the only realistic option right now. Nobody here has paired it with endocrine therapy outside a trial.
We stopped T-DXd in one patient over lung toxicity worries and I had no clear idea what to give next. Went with single-agent chemo, probably not ideal.
Tumor board usually lands on the ADC after one endocrine line if disease is moving fast. Slower disease gets more endocrine options first.
Younger patient with symptomatic liver mets, so we used T-DXd earlier than we would have a year ago. She responded quickly and it let us keep chemo in reserve.

Small hospital-based clinic. My default for HR+ HER2-low is endocrine plus CDK4/6, then another endocrine option if there is an actionable mutation, then T-DXd. For HER2-positive, second line after a taxane with trastuzumab and pertuzumab feels settled. The grey zone is HR+ HER2-low with only one prior endocrine line. A few of us would go earlier if symptoms are present, and a lot of it comes down to the patient's tolerance for infusions and nausea.

My worry is what comes after. If T-DXd moves earlier, patients reach later lines with fewer good choices, and I have no data on how other ADCs behave after it. Our pharmacy also flags that back-to-back ADCs may not be covered. I tend to hold it a bit longer than guidelines might suggest. Probably overly cautious, but that's where I am.

Our nurse navigator flags progression scans, so we can switch patients to T-DXd within about a week. That has made second-line use straightforward for HER2-positive disease. For HER2-low I'm now comfortable using it once endocrine therapy stops working, before chemo. I think patients prefer skipping a long chemo stretch first. The main prerequisites are a baseline lung check and a monitoring plan.

Rural satellite clinic, and patients drive a long way. Moving to T-DXd means three-weekly infusions plus scans for lung monitoring, so I hesitate to switch anyone who is stable on oral endocrine therapy. I'd rather wait until it's clearly needed. That means some patients probably recieve it later than ideal.

The combination question comes up at our conference. I said I don't see a role outside trials, so for us it's sequential. We usually finish endocrine options, then T-DXd, then chemo. Whether the order should flip for HR+ HER2-low with high disease burden, I'm not sure, and the team splits on it.

For HER2-positive after first-line progression, T-DXd second line is what we do and nobody argues. The debate is third line, where I have mixed feelings about other HER2 options versus staying on the ADC longer. Our oncologists tend to pick based on brain mets and how the patient handled the last regimen. I'd like clearer guidance on switching points but I don't expect it soon.
Would rather use it second line than hold it back for later.
Slots it after endocrine plus CDK4/6, not before.
Honestly no clear idea what should follow it if she progresses.
Chemo first for HER2-low, T-DXd later; that's the tumor board habit.
Worried about burning the ADC option too early.
Earlier use makes sense to me, especially with visceral disease.
Our payer wants documented progression on endocrine therapy and at least one chemo before approving T-DXd in HER2-low. That basically dictates the line, whatever I'd prefer clinically.
In the community setting patients usually get referred once they're already on second-line chemo, so T-DXd ends up third by default. Not sure that's ideal but it's the workflow we have.
I like moving it up in HER2-low once endocrine options are used up, particularly if the patient is symptomatic and I need a response. Capecitabine can wait. That's my current thinking anyway.
Combining it with anything else makes me nervous, tbh. I'd worry about overlapping GI and lung toxicity and wouldn't stack agents outside a trial.

For HER2-positive I still see it after first-line taxane plus dual blockade, but I think the second-line conversation is shifting. Where it sits relative to other ADCs is probably the open question for most of us.

If she gets it early and develops ILD, we lose a really effective drug and I'm left with chemo. That risk of having to stop pushes me toward being conservative about line placement. I'd rather have it in reserve for a bit.
Older patients with slow luminal disease would still get an endocrine switch first, I think. T-DXd can wait until it's clearly endocrine-resistant and symptomatic.
For patients with brain mets I'd probably go earlier. Knowing it's an option for second line feels reassuring.

We talked for a good while about where it fits after endocrine therapy. His view is that for HR-positive HER2-low disease the order is endocrine plus CDK4/6, then another endocrine line if there's a targetable alteration, then T-DXd. He admitted the switch point is fuzzy because it depends on how fast the disease is moving. Visceral crisis would pull it forward, otherwise he tends to wait. He expects guidelines will settle it eventually.

Frustrated, mostly. Her group has no agreed sequence, so each patient's line gets decided by whoever sees them that week. She worries that using T-DXd early closes doors because she doesn't know what comes after it, and the evidence for later ADC use seems thin to her. Infusion nursing capacity also limits how many she can start at once. Her words were that she'd rather be wrong late than early.

He was quite upbeat and said he now moves T-DXd up as soon as endocrine therapy stops working in HER2-low, rather than pushing through several chemo lines first. In his experience patients who get it earlier are fitter and cope better with the nausea plan. He thinks sequential use is cleaner than any combination attempt. He still isn't sure what he'd do after progression, but feels that's a good problem to have.

She's skeptical about jumping straight to it after CDK4/6 failure. Many of her patients still have decent endocrine options and she feels we're skipping them. She also fears payers may refuse anything similar later, so she'd hate to spend the one shot too soon. Teh whole thing feels premature to her without clearer guidance.

In HER2-positive he sees T-DXd mainly as a second-line choice after taxane plus dual HER2 blockade. It gets murky for patients who relapse quickly after adjuvant therapy, where he'd probably still go early. He wasn't sure whether to hold a TKI-based regimen for third line or use it before the ADC. Overall comfortable with the approach, but waiting for more data before changing habits.

He kept coming back to combination versus sequential. In theory pairing it with endocrine therapy is attractive, but nobody in his unit would do that off trial. So in practice it's sequential: endocrine, then T-DXd, then chemo, and he's fine with that for now. The one exception might be a rapidly progressing patient, though even there he'd just go straight to the ADC alone.
Still sorting out where it fits after CDK4/6 failure, honestly.
Too early before endocrine options are used up imo.
Happy to move it up ahead of chemo in HR+ low pts.
Payer wants two prior lines so it ends up 3rd line regardless.
Depends on pace of disease, visceral crisis means go sooner.
Worried about what comes after, nothing obvious post ADC.

Community practice, so sequencing is mostly dictated by what the infusion suite can handle. They'd probably slot T-DXd after one endocrine-based line if scans look bad, but not sure about using it before a CDK4/6 inhibitor.
She now thinks of it as the natural next step once endocrine therapy stops working in HER2-low disease. Prefers it over going straight to single-agent taxane for most pts.
Concerned about ILD monitoring if it goes earlier, since those pts may stay on it a long time. Their scan schedule is every 3 months and that feels thin. Would rather wait for later lines tbh.
Asked whether to combine with endocrine therapy or go sequential. In her mind there's no real data for combining, so she keeps them separate and stops the endocrine agent when the ADC starts.
Nobody at tumor board could say what to give after progression on this, so people hesitate to use it early. Everyone says 'save it' which I think is kind of backwards but thats the mood.
Academic breast clinic. For HER2+ pts after first-line trastuzumab/pertuzumab she'd go to T-DXd second line without much debate. Easy decision for her team now.
Switch point is mostly clinical. Rapid progression or symptomatic liver mets pushes her to the ADC sooner, while slow bone-only disease stays on endocrine longer.

Prior auth delays are the real sequencing issue for them. Pt progressed, chemo was started as a bridge, and by the time approval came the pt had already recieved a taxane. Frustrating and it happens a lot.

Really positive on moving earlier. In HR+ HER2-low pts who've stopped responding to endocrine therapy she would now go to T-DXd before any chemo. A good chunk of those pts were getting chemo anyway, so she'd rather give the more active agent first. Still wants baseline echo and lung imaging sorted before start. Said her nurses are comfortable with the antiemetic plan.

Fairly upbeat. For HER2+ metastatic disease she treats T-DXd as the default after first line and doesn't wait for a second progression. Her real question is what follows it, and she mentioned maybe a tucatinib-based regimen, not sure. Says early use gives pts the best shot at a long response before performance status drops. Team seems aligned on this.

Unsure how to handle the HER2-ultralow group. Pathology reports are inconsistent, so she hesitates to place the ADC ahead of chemo. Some pts she'd go ahead with, others she'd keep on another endocrine-based combo first. Probably waits for clearer guidance before changing habits. Overall mixed, not opposed.

Rural practice, pts travel far. Sequencing is shaped by how often they can realistically come in, so q3w infusions vs oral endocrine pills matters a lot. She'd likely use oral options first in older pts and keep the ADC for when a response is needed. Not against earlier use, just logistics. Depends on day-care capacity too.

Skeptical about jumping it ahead of other options. Too many unknowns about what comes next, like whether another ADC after this one would work as well. She also worried that giving it early burns the best option for a pt who might do fine on endocrine plus targeted therapy longer. Prefers to hold it until chemo is clearly needed. Said a few colleagues feel the same way.

Discussed combo vs sequential in HER2+ disease. She said she'd never combine it with other cytotoxics outside a trial because of tolerability, and keeps things strictly sequential. Maybe revisit if new data shows up. For now it's one agent at a time, with a clear break before the next one.

trial_design|osimertinib.t: OS still immature, so I can't tell my patients much yet.
Comparator is fair, single-agent osimertinib is what we'd use anyway.
Baseline brain MRI built into the design reassured me, honestly.
Trial patients look a lot fitter than half of my clinic.
Subgroup numbers probably too small to say anything firm about L858R.
PFS benefit without a clear survival signal, our tumour board is split on whether that's enough.

I think the control arm was the right call. Osimertinib alone is the standard people actually prescribe, so the comparison feels clean and I don't have to argue about a weak comparator when I present it to colleagues.

Crossover is what I keep coming back to. Not sure how many control patients really got chemo at progression, and if only a few did, then a later survival difference may be hard to interpret either way.
Our payer reviewer asked straight away where the overall survival data were. PFS alone isn't persuading them to fund adding chemo for everybody, and I can see why they're cautious.
From a community practice view, the scan schedule in the trial is tighter than what we do. Real life we scan when we scan, so I wonder if the PFS gap would look the same for us, not sure tbh.

Having PFS2 reported alongside the primary endpoint helps me. It at least hints at what happens after first progression, which is where my patients' decisions actually get made, and I'd like to see more of that.

The performance status cutoffs bother me. Older, frailer patients with comorbidities are who I see most days, and they're exactly who the trial barely enrolled, so I'm hesitant to extrapolate the chemo combination to them.

Subgroup power is the weak spot for me. Things like TP53 co-mutations or detectable ctDNA at baseline are what I'd want to use to pick patients, but I doubt the trial was sized to answer that, and any signal there is hypothesis generating at best.

Open-label design with investigator-assessed progression leaves me a little uneasy. I'd feel better with more blinded central review. Knowing who has chemo could easily nudge scan reading and timing of discontinuation.

We talked for a good while about what the trial can and can't tell us. Overall I'm somewhat torn. The progression benefit looks real to me, and the control arm is reasonable, but the survival story isn't there yet and crossover muddies it. I'd probably want the final analysis before telling the group that it changes practice across the board. For selected younger patients with high-burden disease I'm more open to it, though that's my impression rather than something the data cleanly show.

The enrolled population doesn't look like my waiting room. Most of my patients are older, have renal or cardiac issues, and many are diagnosed on small biopsies with limited molecular work-up. I don't think many of them would have met the entry criteria. Even if the headline result holds, I'm not sure it transfers. The extra toxicity from chemo, with anemia and fatigue, would hit my group harder, and the trial can't really tell me by how much.

Honestly I thought the design was quite thoughtful. Randomising against osimertinib alone avoids the old argument about a weak control, and including patients with brain metastases at baseline matters a lot for what I treat. The endpoints are sensible for a first-line study, and PFS is a reasonable primary when survival takes years. I'd still like longer follow-up, but I don't feel the trial was set up to flatter the combination, which is more than I can say for some others.

My concern is that the endpoints don't capture what patients feel. A longer time without progression is good, but if people spend that time on chemo infusions with cytopenias, is that a win? Quality of life data seemed secondary in the way it was presented. I'd want patient-reported outcomes treated as central, not an add-on, and time off treatment or treatment-free intervals discussed too. Without that I find it hard to counsel anyone properly.

We spent most of the discussion on CNS disease and subgroups. The CNS data are encouraging in direction, but I suspect the numbers in any given subgroup are modest, so I wouldn't lean on them for exon 19 versus L858R decisions. Still, I think it's reasonable to see them as signals. I'd like a pooled look or real-world cohort to confirm. For now it nudges my thinking but doesn't change what I do for most patients.

Overall I came away positive. The question the trial asked, adding chemo to osimertinib versus osimertinib alone, is the one I face in clinic, and the answer seems clinically meaningful for fitter patients. I appreciate that the comparator wasn't a straw man. The remaining gaps, like survival and crossover, are acknowledged rather than hidden, and I think that honesty builds trust with my colleagues.
Osimertinib alone as the comparator is the right call, honestly.
Not enough brain mets patients in there for me to extrapolate.
Crossover question still open, so OS is hard to read.
PFS as primary endpoint is fine by me, our patients move on fast.
Mixed feelings on the enrollment mix, unsure how it maps to osi patients here.
Too early to say if the chemo add on holds up in older pts.

Our clinic sees a lot of patients over 75 with borderline PS, and the trial population looks fitter than that. I'd probably still consider the combination for a younger patient with CNS disease. Not sure about everyone else.
In real life the osimertinib-alone patients get chemo after progression, and I'm not sure the trial reflects how many actually did. So the comparison feels a bit artificial to me.
The tumor board at our regional hospital liked that the comparator was osimertinib monotherapy, since that's what we all prescribe. It also makes the result easy to bring to payers.
Subgroups like L858R and baseline brain mets look underpowered to me. People at our weekly thoracic meeting keep asking and I have no firm answer.
OS data are still maturing, and the pharmacist running our formluary review wants to see them before adding anything. I think that's reasonable.
Excluding poor performance status patients means we're guessing for a good chunk of our walk-ins on osimertinib. Also the scan schedule in the trial is tighter than what we do in routine follow-up.
Nice that they stratified by things we care about, like CNS status and mutation type. Makes it easier to explain to patients in clinic.
Crossover wasn't really built in, so a survival difference may be tricky to interpret down the line. I'd wait and see. Patients at our infusion center mostly ask about side effects first anyway.

Honestly I struggle with the endpoint story. PFS looks good, but patients on the doublet need extra chair time every three weeks, and the trial can't tell me if that's worth it if OS ends up similar. Quality of life data exist but I don't know how much weight to give them. We're a small practice with one infusion nurse most days, so workflow matters. I'd want more than PFS before changing my default.

I think the design is solid for what it set out to do. One comparator everyone recognizes, randomized, with brain imaging built in, which matters because a lot of my EGFR patients end up with CNS disease at some point. The population looks reasonably close to the people in my academic clinic, minus the frail ones. I'd still like longer follow-up, but I have no major complaints about the structure.

My take is the trial answers a narrow question well. It tells us adding chemo to osimertinib delays progression in a selected group, but not which patients actually need it. Our molecular tumor board has been talking about using ctDNA clearance to pick people, and the trial wasn't set up for that. Probably a hypothesis for later studies. Until then we decide case by case.

Several colleagues in community practice say the enrolled patients don't look like theirs. Many of their patients are older, have comorbidities like COPD, and travel a long way for treatment. The visit schedule in the trial may not be realistic there. They worry the toxicity picture in routine care will be worse than reported. Nobody I spoke to thought it was a bad trial, just not a perfect fit.

Payer reviews are where the evidence gaps show up for me. The plan we deal with most asked whether the benefit holds for exon 19 versus L858R, and I had to say the subgroups weren't powered to answer that. They also asked about crossover and OS, and I explained the data are still immature. They'll probably approve case by case for now.

An oncologist at a rural satellite clinic said she likes the combination idea but can't tell from the trial how to sequence later lines. After osimertinib plus chemo progresses, what then? The control arm gives more of a roadmap since most would go on to platinum doublet. She thinks the design is fine but silent on that point. Probably needs real-world data.
Osimertinib mono as control = fair, that's what he uses now.
No OS yet, so osi + chemo is a hard sell.
Crossover at progression muddies the OS read imo.
Brain mets subgroup too small to lean on.
Clean design, clean comparator. No complaints.
Not sure PFS alone convinces payres.
Community onc says trial pts look fitter than his walk-ins. Mostly ECOG 0-1 in the study, he sees plenty of 2s. Probably applies to maybe half his panel.
Tumor board pointed out the protocol scan schedule was way tighter than real life. So the PFS gap might look different in routine practice. Wants to know how much is just imaging timing.
Likes that the control arm was actual current SOC with osi, not an old-gen comparator. Says it makes the add-on question answerable. Would've liked longer f/u but fine for now.
Academic thoracic doc: L858R vs ex19 split looks underpowered for firm conclusions. Sees it as hypothesis-generating only. Still reads the overall trial as positive.
PA team at a payer-heavy practice keeps getting denials citing immature OS on osimertinib combo requests. HCP feels the endpoint choice leaves them exposed. Pts sometimes wait weeks for approval.
Asked whether post-progression tx was balanced between arms, didnt remember from the data. Said it matters for how to read the later endpoints, I think.
Rural clinic doc says trial pop mostly resembles his EGFR pts, never/light smokers, mostly adenocarcinoma. Feels fine extrapolating to osi pts he sees.
Frail elderly pts basically absent from the trial in his view. Thinks AEs with osi+chemo in the 75+ group are unknown territory. Would stay with mono there.

Pulm-onc, large center. Main gripe = no OS and PFS as primary. Says PFS2 or time to next tx would speak more to him. Also wonders if frequent brain MRI in the trial pulled forward progression events in the mono arm, not sure on that. Wants mature data before changing his default with osimertinib.

Discussed crossover at length. HCP thinks since mono pts could get chemo at progression, the real question is upfront vs sequenced. Fair design for that question. But in his clinic many pts never make it to 2nd line, so the sequencing argument cuts both ways. Leaning toward combo for high-burden pts only, tbh.

Very positive on design overall. Randomized, open label but he accepts that since IV chemo can't be blinded. Likes that the PFS benefit looked consistent across a good chunk of subgroups. Thinks trial pts reasonably reflect his de novo stage IV cases. Still wants OS but not a dealbreaker for osimertinib combo.

Tumor board discussion: ctDNA clearance not a stratifier or endpoint, which they see as a gap. TP53 co-mutation and other high-risk features subgroup too small as far as they recall. Group split on using combo for those pts. Consensus = trial answers the average pt, not the individual one.

Small community practice. Worries trial excluded poor PS pts and some comorbidities he sees weekly. Open-label so investigator bias on progression calls possible, I think he said central review helped but not fully. Chair capacity and travel burden for pts not captured in any endpoint. Hesistant to move off osi mono for most pts.

Rad onc input: trial didn't really address local consolidative tx for oligoprogression, so fit with osi is unclear. HCP says that's a real-world workflow issue, esp. brain. Probably outside trial scope anyway. Still wants to know if pts on combo handle SRS timing differently. No data he knows of.
Osimertinib alone as control is fair, though it's a pretty undemanding comparator.
OS immature, so I'm not convinced yet.
Crossover limited so any OS story is hard to read
Trial patients are nothing like who walks into my clinic.
Design was clean enough that the PFS gap is hard to wave away.
Brain mets subgroup probably too small to conclude anything.

Most of my community referrals are ECOG 2, older, with comorbidities the protocol would have excluded. So I really can't say the chemo add-on applies to them. Frustrating to see the slides ignore that.

Using PFS as primary makes sense to me with osimertinib, since the control arm does well for a long time. But patients don't live for scan intervals. I want quality of life and time to next treatment before I shift anything.
Credit where due, they compared against osimertinib alone rather than an old first-gen TKI. That's the real standard of care, so the data are actually usable at our tumor board.
Subgroups like L858R and CNS disease are underpowered, everyone knows it, yet people present them as conclusions. Teh forest plot looks tidy but I wouldn't build a decision on it.
A payer reviewer asked me last month for survival data on the combo and I had nothing mature to offer. The trial design is okay, it's just early. I'll probably hold off for now.
Post-progression therapy wasnt tightly controlled, I think, so the crossover picture is muddy. Hard to say whether combining upfront beats giving chemo later.
Routine brain imaging in the protocol is something I appreciate, since real-world data rarely has it. Makes the CNS findings more believable to me, at least on paper.

The enrolled patients look like the fittest slice of what I see. A good chunk of mine have effusions, borderline renal function, or just won't tolerate a platinum doublet on top of osimertinib. Those people barely show up in the eligibility picture. So when colleagues say 'the trial supports it', I ask for whom. I'm not saying the result is wrong, just that the population match is thin.

Open-label design bugs me a little. Investigator-assessed progression can drift when everyone knows who's getting chemo, though I assume there was some central review as a check. I don't think it sinks the result. Still, I'd take the primary endpoint with a pinch of salt and wait to see how the secondary endpoints settle.

The comparator is a low bar in my view. Single-agent TKI first, with chemo held back, isn't how a lot of us would sequence anyway, and the trial can't tell me whether everyone needs the combo or just high-risk patients. Osimertinib monotherapy already works fine for plenty of mine. Without that answer I'm reluctant to push extra toxicity on all of them.

I came in skeptical, but the question being asked is a real one: does adding chemo to osimertinib upfront beat osimertinib alone. Comparator is right, endpoint is reasonable, eligibility wasn't absurdly narrow. Crossover is imperfect, sure. But I'd say it's one of the better-designed studies in this space, and I'd happily go through it with a young patient with high-volume disease.

Endpoints don't capture the burden. My infusion chairs are booked, patients drive long distances, and nobody in the trial had to sweat about that. Cytopenias and extra visits matter to people on a drug that is otherwise a pill a day. Osimertinib alone is easy; the combo changes the whole workflow. I'd want some measure of that, not just scans.

Biomarker side is where I'm unsure. Co-mutations and ctDNA clearance came up as exploratory, but nothing was powered for it, I think. They might identify who gains most, or it might be noise. Right now I can't use them in clinic and I doubt anyone can. Interesting for generating hypotheses, though.
For once the endpoint choice felt defensible. Progression-free survival against a strong control arm, plus real attention to CNS progression, is what I'd have asked for myself.

trial_design|pembrolizumab.t: Placebo + chemo comparator fine, but no neoadj-only IO arm to isolate the adjuvant piece.
HCP says EFS as primary makes sense for a periop design.
Not enough EGFR+ pts in there, so unclear for those pts.
Crossover probably not a big issue here, I think.
Trial pts way fitter than what walks into my clinic, per HCP.
Subgroups underpowerd, wouldn't over-read any forest plot.

Pembro periop design is clean imo: placebo-controlled, blinded, same chemo backbone both arms. Tumor board likes that it answers the 'does IO add anything' question directly. Still wants longer f/u on OS tho.
Community onc, mostly 70s pts w/ COPD. Trial excluded a lot of the borderline PS group, so extrapolating is a judgment call. Uses it anyway when the pt is cisplatin-fit.
Unsure how much benefit comes from the neoadj vs adjuvant phase, design can't split it. Payer PA reviewers ask this exact q sometimes. HCP has no good answer for them.

Gastric: chemo backbone in the trial isn't what HCP uses day to day (FLOT-ish instead), so pt match is imperfect. Still thinks the IO signal is directionally interesting. Would love an MSI-specific look but guesses it's too small to say anything.
Likes that pCR and EFS were both reported, gives the surgeon something concrete at tumor board. Thinks pCR as a surrogate is still unproven but supportive.
EFS definitions differ across periop trials so cross-trial comparison is messy. HCP wasn't sure which events counted, e.g. pts who never made it to surgery. Makes pt counseling frustrating.
Crossover unclear to HCP: did placebo pts get IO at recurrence? Probably some did, which might blunt OS. Not sure how the trial handled it.

Thoracic surgeon worried about pts who progress or drop out during neoadj. ITT counts them, but he wants clearer resection rates and any OR delays from AEs. Not sure delays were captured well. Probably fine at trial sites, but at his hospital scheduling is tight and a delay can mean a lost window. Wants that spelled out before he's fully comfortable.

Rural community oncologist, lots of heavy smokers w/ comorbidities and borderline organ function. Trial required good organ function, so she's unsure the pts match. N2 stage III is also a heterogenous group and she doesn't think the trial split it enough. Still offers pembro to fit pts. Says she mostly relies on the tumor board to sort who is a real candidate.

Overall pleased with the design. Blinded, placebo-controlled, clear primary endpoints, and the population looked a lot like her stage III pts at the academic center. She said the endpoint hierarchy made the OS read-out easier to trust. Only wish was more real-world data on older pts. Not a dealbreaker, she said, and she'd use it in most eligible pts.

HCP skeptical about giving IO to everyone regardless of PD-L1. Regional payer wants a cutoff for PA, and the trial wasn't powered for that question. Low-expressors are a small slice so any signal there is soft. HCP said she doesn't want to deny tx based on an underpowered subgroup. But also can't argue strongly with the payer w/o better data.

Molecular mix in his gastric pts doesn't match the trial much, HER2+ and MSI-H especially, since those get handled separately in his clinic. I think he said the trial didn't carve them out clearly, but he wasn't sure. Wants to know if those pts were just a handful. Neutral on the whole, waiting to see how guidelines treat them.
Follow-up still short for OS imo, esp. late tox. Pts ask 'how long on tx' and the fixed adjuvant duration doesn't tell him if less would do.
Placebo plus chemo is a fair comparator, just not a real-world one, I think.
EFS looks convincing to me, OS maturity is the only open question.
Our patients are older and frailer than anyone enrolled, simple as that.
Control arm was reasonable for its time, no complaints from me there.
PD-L1 low subgroups are far too small to say anything, frustraing.
Data look clean on paper, pembro included, I'm just unsure who it applies to.
Crossover is the thing I can't get past. If control patients could get a PD-1 later, I'm not sure the survival curves show the full picture, and I haven't seen how many actually did.

In my community practice a lot of patients have borderline renal function and would never pass cisplatin eligibility. So I'm not sure the perioperative pembrolizumab data speak to them. Probably some benefit but it's a guess.
I'll give them credit: the placebo plus chemo control was clean and the endpoints were things I can actually explain to patients. Event-free survival matters to my surgeons too.
Pathologic response as a surrogate keeps getting oversold. Nobody has shown me it tracks with survival here, and our tumor board treats it like gospel anyway.
Gastric trials skew heavily toward patients from certain regions, as far as I can tell. I think that limits how I counsel my western patients, though I'm not claiming it sinks the result.
Pembro in gastric: the PD-L1 cutoffs keep shifting between trials and it's maddening. Hard to compare anything across them when the scoring changes every time.
Using a chemo backbone I actually prescribe made the comparator feel credible. That's more than I can say for a lot of studies.
Stage mix bugs me a bit. The lung trial had plenty of stage III, and I see more stage II than III in practice, so extrapolating is a judgment call.

I keep coming back to the control arm. Placebo with chemo is a clean design, but my payer contacts ask whether that's really the baseline for a prior-auth appeal. I'm also not convinced we can tell what the neoadjuvant phase contributed versus the adjuvant phase with pembrolizumab. Plenty of my patients never finish the adjuvant part, and the design doesn't tell me much about them. It feels like a gap that gets glossed over.

Small community clinic here, so my patients look different from trial participants. A lot of them are older, have COPD, and live a long drive from the treating center. I think the benefit probably carries over to the fitter ones. For the rest I'm extrapolating, and pembro labeling doesn't help with that. I'd like to know how many comorbid patients were actually in the trial, but I couldn't find it.

Where I get frustrated is subgroup analyses. Everyone quotes forest plots, but nothing is powered for the small groups, so an interval crossing one is just noise to me. When a never-smoker or someone with a driver alteration shows up in my clinic, I can't tell from the pembrolizumab data whether they benefit. Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence, sure, but I won't pretend the plot answers it.

I came in skeptical, honestly. But the more I look at the design, the less I can pick at: the endpoints were hard ones, the blinding held up, and the comparator was standard chemo. My main gripe is only generalizability. Still, for a fit patient with resectable disease I think pembro is hard to argue against based on how the trial was built.

Endpoints bother me in the gastric setting. Response and progression get quoted a lot, but my patients care whether they're alive and eating. Crossover to a PD-1 after progression in the control arm probably muddies overall survival, and I haven't seen anyone quantify it. Quality of life data felt like an afterthought. I'd want that answered before I tell a frail patient the extra toxicity is worth it.

Biomarker subgroups in gastric are tiny, MSI-high especially, so whatever we say about them is shaky. I tend to believe the signal is real but can't prove it from the pembrolizumab trial data. Tumor board keeps asking me and I just say 'probably'. Also teh enrolled patients seemed healthier than what walks into my infusion unit.
Placebo comparator makes sense to me, nothing odd there.
Not enough PD-L1 low patients to say much, honestly.
EFS is fine but I'd still like OS to mature.
Trial patients looked fitter than the ones coming through our door.
Pembro design was clean and big enough to trust the main result.
Crossover wasn't really part of that design I think, so not a big worry

At his community clinic a lot of the resectable stage III patients have COPD or borderline kidney function. Many of those would have been excluded from the pembrolizumab trial, so he's not sure how much applies. The tumor board mostly goes by gut feel on them.

In gastric, the comparator was chemo alone in most of the older studies, which was standard when they were designed. Now that other PD-1 options are in the mix, her group wonders if that's still the right control. She said it's hard to judge from the clinic side.

The perioperative structure, with a neoadjuvant phase and an adjuvant phase, matched how his team actually treats these patients. Having EFS as a primary endpoint alongside OS made the data easier to bring to the multidisciplinary meeting.

Subgroup numbers for never-smokers and driver-positive patients were small, so nobody at the academic clinic would lean on those cuts. They said they'd just use the overall result and keep an eye on real-world data.

A payer reviewer asked her whether pCR can stand in as a surrogate. She thinks it's supportive but not a replacement for EFS yet. She also said pathology reporting varies between sites, which muddies the comparison.
Seems well run to him. The blinded placebo control limited bias in how EFS was assessed, and for his thoracic clinic that is enough to start the conversation with surgeons.

He's concerned that the adjuvant contribution can't be separated from the neoadjuvant part because the trial wasn't built to ask that. In his clinic a few patients never make it to surgery after neoadjuvant therapy, and he can't tell from the design how pembrolizumab helps or hurts them. That's the question he gets from surgeons most.

Rural practice, so most of his gastric patients are older and frailer than a typical trial enrollee. He's unsure the pembro data cover them and said he'd extrapolate cautiously, probably with a lower threshold to stop.

Oncologist at a regional hospital talked through the gastric data. The CPS subgroups seemed underpowered to her, especially the lower cutoff groups. She suspects the benefit signal mostly comes from higher-expression patients but isn't certain. The mix of Asian and Western enrollment also makes her hesitant to apply results to her own patients. She'd want more data before using pembrolizumab broadly there.

He said crossover is less of an issue in the perioperative lung setting because control patients get placebo and treatment at recurrence is left open. Still, he thinks many control patients probably got immunotherapy after relapse, wich could dilute OS. He expects OS to be hard to interpret for that reason. He's comfortable with EFS as the main endpoint. For now he reads OS as supportive only.

Thoracic oncologist at a large referral clinic said the trial answered a practical question: does adding an immunotherapy to platinum chemo around surgery help? She liked that surgery had to actually happen on a set schedule, because that matches how her team plans cases. The placebo-controlled structure gave her confidence in the EFS result. She'd still like longer follow-up, but she's already presenting it to her surgical colleagues.

A hospital pharmacy lead pointed out there's no direct comparison to neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy followed by observation, which some centers do. The control arm was placebo plus chemo, so it can't tell them whether the adjuvant phase is needed. Their formulary committee keeps asking for that. He said without it they approve cautiously and track outcomes locally.

Her clinic sees many stage IIIA patients with bulky N2 nodes, while the trial covered a wider stage range. The tumor board isn't sure benefit is the same across the stage subgroups, since each one is fairly small. She thinks it probably holds but wouldn't say so confidently. For borderline-resectable cases they still debate case by case.

Said the trial population is not what he sees at his safety-net clinic. Lots of ECOG 2 patients, uncontrolled diabetes, patients who dont return for follow-up visits. He doubts they'd finish the adjuvant phase of pembro as scheduled. Without data in those patients he sees the evidence as a good starting point but a real gap for his practice.
Crossover handling still bugs me, honestly.
EFS as the primary made sense for perioperative pembro.
Not sure the pembro subgroup numbers are big enough to say much.
Our older, frailer gastric patients basically weren't in that trial.
Comparator was right, a cisplatin doublet is what we'd give anyway.
Waiting on longer survival follow-up before I fully trust the signal with pembro.
Honestly the ECOG 0-1 restriction is the thing for me. Half my referrals at the community site would never have qualified for pembro, so I'm extrapolating a lot.

Adjuvant phase being continued regardless of pathologic response makes it hard to know which part did the work. I think that's a design limit rather than a flaw, but the contribution question stays open
Having placebo plus chemo as the control, rather than chemo alone, gave a clean comparison I could show at tumor board without caveats. That matters more than people think.
Payer reviewers keep asking about control-arm crossover in the gastric studies and how it muddies overall survival. I don't have a great answer for them.
In gastric, I'm not sure how much the PD-L1 cutoffs were really powered for. The pembro subgroups looked interesting but are probably hypothesis-generating only.
Staging was probably more uniform than what we see, since plenty of our stage III patients have borderline CT staging and no mediastinal sampling. Trial selection feels tidier than real life.
Surgeon colleagues liked that the trial tracked whether patients actually made it to resection. Feels relevant to how we plan timing with pembro on board.
Biomarker-negative patients are my worry, as the study wasn't built to say much about them as far as I can tell. I'd want that gap acknowledged, but I wouldn't withhold pembro over it.

We talked for a good while about whether the control arm reflects practice. In lung, placebo plus platinum doublet seems fair to me, although I think some colleagues would have liked a a adjuvant-only comparison. In gastric the chemo backbone varies a lot by region, so I'm not convinced one comparator can speak for everyone. Pembro might still be the right call, but the design leaves me with more questions than answers about sequencing.

By the end of the discussion, what stuck was how selected the population felt. Patients in our clinic are often older, with COPD or renal issues that limit cisplatin, and some can't finish the full adjuvant course. The trial seemed to assume most would get through everything. I'm not saying the benefit isn't real, just that I can't tell how much carries over to the people I actually see. Pembro in that setting feels like an extrapolation.

Overall I came away reassured. The double-blind placebo design, event-free survival as primary, and the focus on resectable disease all seem sensible to me. I like that pathologic response was captured too, since it helps me counsel patients before surgery. There are gaps, sure, but for a perioperative trial it was well thought through, and I'd be comfortable citing it to my tumor board.

Endpoints were a recurring theme. EFS is reasonable, but I wonder whether it stands in for survival in gastric, where recurrence patterns differ from lung. Pathologic response is nice, probably, but as far as I know it isn't validated as a surrogate across these settings. I'd wait for mature overall survival before changing anything for gastric patients, though I'm already comfortable in lung.

My main frustration is subgroup power. Stage, histology, and PD-L1 splits all show up in forest plots, but nobody can read much into small slices, especially squamous versus nonsquamous. Then clinicians and payers lean on them anyway. For gastric, the regional split worries me too, as I think enrollment wasn't balanced. Pembrolizumab might behave differently across those groups and we simply can't tell.

Spent a long time on real-world fit. At our academic center most patients are fit enough to look like trial patients, so I think the data translate reasonably well here. Smaller affiliate clinics are a different story, with delays to surgery and more missed adjuvant doses. Nobody knows how much those delays blunt the benefit. Probably the next evidence has to come from regsitries rather than another RCT.
Placebo-controlled is fine, but chemo alone isn't what everyone uses as the modern standard.
Crossover barely matters in a perioperative design, so OS probably reads cleaner here.
Subgroups far too small to say anything about PD-L1 negative patients.
EFS is reasonable but I'd wait for OS maturity before getting excited
Pembro design was clean, comparator matched what most clinics already use.
Our frail, borderline-PS patients just aren't represented in that trial.

In gastric, the chemo backbone used in the trial differs from what they give much of the time in the community unit. Not sure how much that changes interpretation, but it keeps coming up at tumor board.

Honestly the randomization against placebo plus chemo was the cleanest way to isolate what pembrolizumab adds. For resectable lung, I think EFS made sense as the endpoint given how long OS takes to mature.

Nobody in the room felt the trial told us whether the adjuvant phase actually matters. Without a design that separates the neoadjuvant and adjuvant contributions, they're guessing when a patient can't finish the post-op portion.

A payer reviewer asked whether pathologic response could stand in for survival, and the oncologist wasn't sure. The design relied on EFS and OS, which the reviewer accepted, but they wanted longer follow-up before committing.

She pointed out that the stage III patients in the trial seemed fitter and more selected than the ones coming through her thoracic clinic. Many of hers have borderline lung function and wouldn't tolerate cisplatin, so she questions how far the data stretch.
Subgroup data by nodal status are interesting but I think underpowerd to guide anything. He'd use them for hypothesis generation only, never to withhold treatment.

The surgeon liked that the design tracked whether surgery still happened on schedule. He said it reassured him the neoadjuvant approach is workable, though he admitted that's an impression and wants to see real-world timing.
HER2-positive gastric patients complicate things, and she wasn't sure how the trial handled them. Overall she feels the evidence in that subgroup is thin, though she wouldn't call it a deal-breaker.

After a long back-and-forth, his main point was that the trial answers a narrow question well. Pembrolizumab added to chemo versus chemo alone is a sensible comparison for resectable disease, and the endpoints are defensible. What it doesn't tell him is the best sequencing against newer approaches he sees locally. He also wondered how much of the benefit sits in the neoadjuvant versus adjuvant phase, and I think he's right to. Overall he's comfortable using it but keeps a list of open questions.

We spent a good while on OS interpretation. Her worry is that control-arm patients who relapse may later get an immunotherapy outside the protocol, which could blur the survival comparison over time. She isn't sure how often that happens in practice. Since crossover wasn't built in for the periop design, shes inclined to treat OS as supportive rather than definitive for now. She'd want a sensitivity look at post-relapse treatment before quoting it to patients.

He was more positive by the end than at the start. Initially he assumed a perioperative design would be messy, but he came around to seeing the placebo-controlled structure as a strength because it limits bias in assessing event-free survival. He liked that the population was resectable stage II to IIIB and looked a lot like the mix at his multidisciplinary meeting. Pembro in that setting feels evidence-based to him, with the caveat that he'd like longer follow-up. He said the gaps are real but not disqualifying.

Community oncologist in a rural practice, long chat about who actually enrolled. Her patients tend to be older, heavy smokers with COPD and cardiac comorbidity, and a fair number can't get through the platinum cycles before surgery. Trials like this pick fit patients with good performance status, so she feels the headline benefit may overstate what she'd see. Many of her patients are also never even discussed with surgeons. Until there's real-world data she stays cautious about generalizing.

On the gastric side, he feels the evidence base is patchier than lung. Trial populations seem to reflect regional differences in disease biology and surgical practice, so he's unsure how neatly they map onto his Western patients. The chemo-alone comparator is reasonable, but biomarker selection, particularly PD-L1 and MSI status, shapes how he reads subgroup results. He thinks most subgroups were too small to be confident. He'd call it promising but not settled.

Endpoint choice was where she pushed hardest. EFS is useful, but she argues patients care about whether they'll live longer and feel well, and quality-of-life data seemed secondary in how the trial was reported. She also felt that late immune-related toxicities may not be captured with the follow-up available so far. Combined with the lack of head-to-head data on treatment duration, she thinks the trial leaves gaps that matter in the clinic. She would like a patient-reported outcome analysis before changing her default.

Her main question was how HER2-low status was handled, because a good chunk of her HR+ patients fall in that category. She wasn't sure if the analysis allowed a clean read there. Neutral overall, waiting for more detail.

After a long chat, he kept returning to the same point: the population is very selected. She felt the design answered the question that matters in her clinic: what to do after endocrine therapy and chemo have run out. At the end of a long discussion she said the evidence package is stronger than she first assumed. Randomized, a sensible chemo control, and endpoints she can explain to a tumor board. Her residual worry is just how many of her patients really match that profile.

The HER2-low subgroup analyses look underpowered to me, probably exploratory only. I wouldn't change how I pick patients based on them, but they are interesting.

Concerned about subgroup claims. HER2-low and TROP2 level come up at every tumor board, but trial wasn't powered for those, so we're eyeballing forest plots. Mixed feelings on endpoints. PFS primary is okay but I'd want OS maturity and QoL before changing all my 3rd-line habits. Positive take on the sample: big enough that I trust the overall result. The subgroups I'm less sure about, but the main comparison looks clean.

Presented at tumor board, mixed room. Med oncs liked the HER2-low data for T-DXd, rad onc asked about CNS outcomes, which weren't a design focus. HCP would probably use it for HR+ pts after endocrine fails but unsure about earlier. Pathologist raised IHC scoring variability between labs. No consensus by end.

Pt scenario from community HCP: 60s, HR+, HER2-low, progressed fast on CDK4/6 + AI. Said that's basically the trial pt. Comparator chemo is what he'd offer otherwise, so the result feels relevant. PFS benefit probably matters for pt QoL too, I think. Would like OS but not waiting for it.

Payer issue came up. HCP's practice gets PA pushback when real-world use is wider than what the trial enrolled. Staff spend a lot of time on appeals and pts recieve tx late. He feels evidence gaps (OS immature, small subgroups) give payers an easy reason to say no.

HCP flagged exclusion of pts w/ significant lung disease. In her clinic a good chunk of older pts have COPD or prior chest RT, so T-DXd eligibility isn't a clean fit. Not sure how to read ILD from a selected pop. Thinks registries will fill in. For now she screens case by case.

PROs felt thin to him. PFS ok as primary, but for 3rd+ line pts QoL and tolerability matter as much. Not clear AEs like nausea and fatigue were captured in a way he can use for counseling. Wonders if dose reductions skewed things. Evidence feels incomplete for his frailer pts.
Chemo comparator is reasonable but not what everyone here actually uses.
Not convinced the trial patients look like my Friday clinic.
PFS gain with T-DXd after prior chemo is convincing enough for me.
Crossover question remains, so OS will probably be messy to interpret.
Ultralow subgroup feels small, wouldn't build practice on it yet.
Good that a real HER2-low population was enrolled prospectively.

Physician's-choice chemo as comparator makes sense to me, since that's what I'd truly offer once endocrine therapy stops working. T-DXd beating it head to head feels more honest than any indirect comparison.

We're a community practice and our HER2-low patients are often older, with comorbidities and borderline performance status. The trial group looks fitter than who walks through my door. I worry about extrapolating T-DXd results, especially around ILD monitoring.
PFS as primary endpoint is fine for me in this setting, but I'd want mature OS before telling a payer it changes survival. Immature OS is probably the biggest gap right now.
Subgroups by IHC category are underpowered I think, so I wouldn't read much into differences between them. Hypothesis-generating at best, even if T-DXd looks consistent across them.

At tumor board we debated whether the chemo arm reflected the sequencing we use. Some of us go to capecitabine early, others straight to a taxane, so the control mix is hard to map onto our own patients.
A payer reviewer asked me for quality of life data and honestly the patient-reported outcomes felt thin to me. Without that I cant argue easily for earlier use

Prior CDK4/6 use was common in the trial, which fits my patients, but I'm unsure how many had been through several endocrine lines. Probably need real-world data before I'm comfortable with T-DXd in everyone.
Enrolling after endocrine therapy with only limited prior chemo is exactly where I see the decision point. That makes the T-DXd results feel applicable to the patients I actually treat.

We talked for a good while about the control arm. The physician's-choice chemo was sensible on paper, but my own sequencing varies a lot depending on tolerance and prior taxane exposure. So I'm not sure the comparator maps cleanly onto what my patients would have received. That said, I can't think of a better single standard to pick. I'd just want to see how results looked by which chemo was actually used.

After going through the publication together, my main worry was the narrow window of who got enrolled. Our clinic sees a lot of patients with brain mets history, poor marrow reserve, or prior lung issues, and those are probably underrepresented. With ILD being a known concern for T-DXd I'm hesitant to assume the trial safety picture holds for them. I think a handful of my colleagues feel the same. Real-world cohorts would help but they're likely a while off.

Honestly I came away more positive than I expected. Defining HER2-low and even the lower-expression group prospectively, and using an endpoint like PFS that matters clinically here, fills a gap we've had for years. The control arm was something I'd actually use. Not perfect, OS will matter, but for a patient running out of endocrine options I feel the design justified the question it asked.

What bothers me is how we'll interpret survival data later. If therapies after progression weren't balanced, any OS signal could get dilluted or confounded, and I'm not sure anyone can untangle that. Also HER2 testing in the trial was central with tight standards, whereas in my lab the IHC 0 versus 1+ call is pretty subjective. That gap alone makes me cautious about selecting patients for T-DXd outside a study.

We went back and forth on whether the trial population reflects my clinic. Most of my HR+ patients with low HER2 had a couple of endocrine lines plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor, which seems to match decently. The ones I'm unsure about got chemo early because of visceral crisis. I'd say the answer is mostly yes with caveats, and the ultralow group probably needs longer follow-up before I treat it as settled.

Cost and access came up repeatedly in our chat. Payer reviewers here ask about head-to-head evidence against what we'd otherwise give, and they pick on immature OS and small subgroup numbers. I explained the design, but I can tell these evidence gaps will slow approvals for T-DXd in HER2-low. Meanwhile patients wait, and that frustrates the whole team.
Not enough HER2-ultralow patients to say much, honestly.
PFS benefit over chemo is what my tumor board cares about with T-DXd.
Unsure how crossover would have changed the OS picture.
Trial pts look fitter than what walks into my comunity clinic.
Comparator was reasonable, though payers may want something different.
Primary endpoint of PFS is clean enough for me to start T-DXd discussions.

At our community practice a lot of the HER2-low patients have been through several endocrine lines before chemo. The trial seems to fit that group reasonably well, I think. What I can't tell is how it maps to the ones who progressed quickly on CDK4/6.

Physician's choice chemo as the comparator makes it hard to explain to our pharmacy committee why we'd skip the cheaper option. They keep asking for OS before they'll approve T-DXd. Without mature survival data it's a tough conversation.
A chemo-only control in a pretreated metastatic population is what I'd want to see. It makes the PFS result easy to present at our weekly conference.
Subgroups by IHC score look small, so I wouldn't lean on them for borderline cases. I had a patient with 1+ on one biopsy and 0 on another, and T-DXd data don't really settle that.

Crossover didn't come up much, probably because the control arm was chemo and access to T-DXd afterward varies by country. For my patients it'd be available later anyway. Not sure that matters for the endpoints.
Brain mets patients were mostly not in the trial from what I recall. A good chunk of my practice right now is stable treated CNS disease so I'm cautious about T-DXd there
In our small infusion center the comparator regimens are all things we already give, so the comparison felt practical. I'd say the design matched how we actually treat.
I like PFS as the primary endpoint with T-DXd but I keep coming back to quality of life data. Patients ask about that more than scan reults. I haven't seen enough on it yet.

Main gap for me is the population. Our patients are older, often with kidney or heart issues, and the trial pts were selected pretty carefully. I had a woman in her late seventies with borderline EF who probably wouldn't have qualified. So when someone says the data support it, I want to know how it translates. It probably works, but it's unproven in that group.

Spoke with a medical oncologist at a hospital-based practice about the comparator. She thinks chemo of physician's choice was reasonable but wishes there had been a clearer split of capecitabine versus taxane. In her clinic a taxane is common once endocrine options run out. She also felt the HER2-low subgroups were underpowered for anything beyond hypothesis. Overall she's comfortable using it, just with caveats.

Community oncologist said the design answered the question he cares about: does T-DXd beat the chemo he'd otherwise use? He liked that the endpoint was PFS in a population that looks like his pretreated hormone-receptor-positive patients. He still wants longer follow-up for OS. For his next eligible patient he'd go ahead. Pharmacy sign-off is the only bottleneck.

Concerned about the open-label design, since investigators knew who got the ADC. Imaging was centrally read, I think, but dose reductions and early discontinuations could still differ between arms. In my clinic ILD monitoring adds extra CT visits and I wonder if the trial captured that burden accurately. Not saying the result is wrong, but I want to read the methods closely.

Our tumor board talked about whether ultralow should be treated as its own group. Some think the trial is thin there, others think it's enough to extrapolate. Pathology reporting is the practical problem because our lab doesn't always call a 0 with faint staining consistently. I think the trial assumed more consistent testing than we really have.

Last month a prior auth reviewer asked whether the control chemo reflected current practice. I said mostly yes, though some of my pts would get a different sequence. Documenting prior lines is what moved the T-DXd request through. I don't think the design is the real issue for them, it's more the lack of OS.

unmet_need|osimertinib.t: Post-progression options still feel thin once chemo is the only thing left.
Brain mets are what keep me up at night, more than systemic control.
Osimertinib has made CNS control much less of a worry in my clinic.
No clear plan for C797S patients outside a trial, as far as I know.
Rebiopsy at progression is still hit or miss in our community practice.
Patients on the combo keep asking how long the chemo part has to last.
Our academic thoracic clinic likes having the combination for patients who present with brain mets at baseline. It seems to give a bit more reassurance, though we're still watching how long it holds.
Seen a couple of patients progress on osimertinib with MET amplification showing up on the NGS panel. Combination options exist, but access is by trial or off-label, so it depends on the payer.
Neuropathy and low counts from the platinum-pemetrexed part are limiting for older patients. For a lot of them I probably wouldn't even offer the chemo add-on.
Liquid biopsy at progression is quick for us, turnaround is around a week. But when it comes back negative we're guessing whether to just continue and add local therapy.

Leptomeningeal disease is the scenario where I feel we have almost nothing reliable. I've seen it in a few patients on first-line osimertinib, and they went downhill fast. Intrathecal options are patchy and not every center offers them.
With oligoprogression on osimertinib we usually do SBRT to the one spot and carry on with the TKI. That has worked well for quite a few patients and keeps them on a pill.
