Infusion nurses tell me the quality of life trade-off is the main complaint with the combo. The extra visits every three weeks add up for people who live far from the clinic. Some are fine with it, some clearly aren't.

A community oncologist told me that once patients progress they mostly end up on a platinum doublet and that's about it. He's not sure newer agents are reachable for his patients becuase of prior auth delays.

Resistance is so heterogeneous that it's hard to know what to do at progression. In our tumor board we often see more than one mechanism, or a histologic transformation, on the same rebiopsy. Then we're picking between chemo, local therapy and a trial slot that may not be open. I think a single targeted next step is unrealistic for most of these patients. It feels like we're improvising a bit each time.

Our workflow for CNS disease is a baseline brain MRI and then repeat imaging every few months, even if the patient feels fine. If something new shows up, it goes to a joint neuro-onc discussion. Radiation is usually the first move for a focal lesion, and the TKI continues. It works but it's heavy on scheduling, and some patients drop off the imaging calendar.

I have a younger never-smoker with exon 19 who has been on osimertinib a long time and is still working full time. She has mild rash and dry skin, nothing that gets in her way. Her brain mets from diagnosis stayed quiet. Honestly she's the reason I'm fairly optimistic about where first-line therapy is now, though I know not everyone does this well.

A lot of our progressors come back with no actionable target on NGS, or the tissue is too scant to test at all. We then fall back on empiric chemo and hope for the best. Plasma testing helps sometimes but I'd say it misses a good chunk. The gap is really for the patients where we can't identify why they progressed. That's a frustrating conversation to have with them and their families.

The mono versus combo discussion is where I see the most uncertainty. If we use chemo upfront, I'm not sure what we hold in reserve for later lines. Some colleagues think that's fine given the better disease control, others worry it burns the one option left. Patients mostly ask about side effects and time in the chair rather than sequencing.

Our radiation oncologists are really positive about how the TKI and focal radiation work together for brain lesions. Patients often keep their cognition and independence, which was not the case a few years ago. We now treat many CNS relapses as manageable rather than end of the road.

We spent a long time on what happens once osimertinib stops working, and the honest answer from this physician was that there's no real standard. Platinum doublet is the default, but it feels like a step backwards for patients who've done well for years on a tablet. Rebiopsy gets attempted, though in practice it's patchy, and even when a MET or other bypass signal turns up, access to anything targeted is hit or miss. The physician said the real gap is a clear, evidence-based second step that doesn't depend on which centre the patient walks into.
Honestly, after osimertinib it's still mostly chemo and hope.

Osimertinib's CNS activity is the reason this physician is comfortable starting it in patients with brain mets at baseline. Said it has cut down on whole-brain radiation referrals in their clinic, and they see that as a real quality of life gain.

The conversation kept coming back to resistance biology, and I think the physician was trying to be balanced about it. They see MET amplification and the occasional C797S on plasma testing, but a good chunk of progressors have nothing clearly actionable. Histologic transformation is on their mind too, mostly because it needs tissue and tissue is hard to get from some sites. Liquid biopsy helps when it's positive; when negative they're not sure whether to trust it or push for a repeat procedure. Overall they felt our understanding of resistance is ahead of our ability to act on it.
Brain mets remain what keeps me up at night, per the physician.

With the FLAURA2 combination the physician worries about the cumulative toxicity burden, especially in patients over 70 or with borderline performance status. Anemia, nausea and the infusion visits all chip away at quality of life, and they're not convinced every patient needs that upfront.

This was a younger patient-focused discussion, and the physician was fairly positive about adding chemo to osimertinib for high-risk presentations, such as multiple brain lesions or a heavy liver burden. They said patients who are motivated and have family support usually cope with the pemetrexed visits fine. Their hope is that deeper early control means fewer patients end up needing a rushed second-line decision. Still, they admitted this is more instinct than proven for now, and they'd want longer follow-up before making it routine for everyone.
Intracranial control has honestly changed how I counsel newly diagnosed patients.

In their community practice, repeat tissue biopsy at progression is difficult to arrange and often delayed by weeks. Plasma testing is the fallback but comes back negatve more often than they'd like, which leaves them guessing about the mechanism.

The payer side came up at length. After progression, the next-line agents they'd like to use often need prior authorization, and the delay can be two or three weeks. In that window patients can decline quickly, particularly those with CNS symptoms. The physician said their nurse navigator spends more time on appeals than on patient education now. They see this as a gap in the system as much as in the science, because even a good option doesn't help if the patient is too unwell by the time it's approved.
Not sure sequencing after the combo will look any different; no data yet.

Fatigue, rash and diarrhea add up for patients who stay on treatment for years. The physician said a couple of patients asked to stop chemo early becuase of how they felt, and they struggle with how to weigh that against disease control.

At their tumor board the discussion on progression usually splits into two camps: those who want to rebiopsy every time and those who treat empirically. The physician sits somewhere in the middle. Small cell transformation worries them most, since it changes management completely and is easy to miss without tissue. They said they'd love a reliable non-invasive marker to flag it. Until then, a lot of decisions are made on imaging pattern and gut feeling, which they find unsatisfying.
Oligoprogression in the brain: we improvise with SRS and continue the TKI, no clear rule.

Patients are living long enough on osimertinib that the conversation has shifted toward long-term tolerability and keeping people working. The physician sees that as a good problem to have and feels monotherapy still fits many patients well.

The physician wondered whether adding chemo upfront changes the pattern of resistance that eventually emerges. They haven't seen enough progressors on the combination to say, and I think they'd want that information before changing their sequencing habits.
Leptomeningeal disease is where they feel most stuck. Few options, patients decline fast, and intrathecal approaches are not available everywhere. Probably the biggest unmet need in their view.
Infusion chair time for rural patients is the real barrier to combination therapy.
The physician is optimistic overall. Between better CNS control and new bispecific and antibody-drug conjugate options coming, they feel the post-progression picture is slowly improving.

We ended on biomarkers. The physician said the biggest gap is knowing, at diagnosis, who truly needs intensification and who will do fine on a single agent. Right now it's mostly clinical features like brain involvement and tumor burden, and those are crude. They also mentioned that circulating tumor DNA clearance might help, but they don't trust it enough to act on it. Without something better, they feel they're either over-treating some patients or under-treating others, and they can't tell which until progression happens.
Nothing good after progression, honestly. Chemo and hope.
Brain mets control has been better than I expected, fair enough.
Re-biopsy at progression: coin flip whether tissue is even usable.
Older pts on osimertinib plus chemo just look wiped out, QoL question is real.
Liquid biopsy helps, but a negatve result tells me nothing
Fewer early CNS relapses in my clinic, which is the one thing I like.

We're a community practice, so NGS at progression takes weeks and the patient has usually decliend by the time it's back. Then we're picking chemo blind anyway. Not sure the resistance workup changes much for us.

Honestly I like that the CNS protection is built in with first-line osimertinib. Most of my brain met patients stay off radiation for a good while. Still don't love what happens once they do progress though.
Payer pushback on the combo is the issue for me, not the biology. If a patient progresses early on the doublet, what's the next step? Nobody has a clean answer.
Probably the biggest gap is the patient with C797S or MET amplification, which I see a handful of. Trials are the only route and the nearest site is hours away. It is what it is.

Quality of life matters more than people admit in these slides. Patients on osimertinib plus chemo get tired of infusion visits, esp those still working. I think it's worth it for high-risk CNS disease but I'd want to pick carefully.
Tbh the data on what comes after osimertinib is thin. Platinum doublet is the default, maybe with bev, and we just copy what was done years ago. Not exciting

Had a patient on osimertinib with oligoprogression in one lung nodule. We did SBRT and she stayed on the TKI for months, which worked well. I wish there were clearer guidance on when that's reasonable versus switching.
Skeptical about the combo for everybody. A lot of my patients would do fine on single-agent osimertinib and I'd rather save chemo for after progression. Hard to know up front who those are.

My frustration is the CNS question. Everyone talks about brain mets control, but nobody talks about the patient who does fine systemically and then develops leptomeningeal spread. We have few good options there and intrathecal approaches are clunky. Neuro-onc referral takes ages in our setup. By then the patient has lost function that doesn't come back.

I'll say something positive for a change. Since moving to osimertinib first-line, I'm seeing far fewer patients present with symptomatic brain disease at relapse. Patients keep working and driving longer, which they care about. Tolerability is manageable with dose holds and skin care. My gripe is only about what comes after.

At progression we re-biopsy when feasible, send NGS plus plasma, and wait. Sometimes we find MET or something targetable, more often it's nothing clear or a histologic transformation. Small cell transformation is the one that scares me. I'm not convinced the extra testing always changes management, but I'd feel worse not doing it. Access to matched combinations is patchy depending on the site.

The combo adds toxicity and I don't think we have good tools to select who benefits. Anemia, nausea and the infusion chair time all hit QoL. Patients ask me wether it's worth it and I give a hedged answer. I'm also wary that using chemo up front leaves us with less to offer later. Payers approve it inconsistently as well.

Elderly patients are my main worry. They usually tolerate osimertinib fine, but add pemetrexed and platinum and I see falls, poor appetite, delayed cycles. I think the benefit in CNS-heavy disease is real, I just can't tell how it applies to frail folks. We end up individualizing and that feels like guessing.

Resistance mechanisms are messy and mostly not actionable in practice. A good chunk of cases have no clear mechanism at all. Then there's heterogeneity, where plasma shows one thing and tissue another. Trials would be the answer but slots are scarce and my patients can't travel easily. So for most I fall back on chemo and decide on the TKI case by case.
No clear standard after progression on osimertinib, mostly just chemo.
CNS progression still the scariest thing for pts.
Likes how CNS control holds up on osimertinib 1L.
Wants repeat biopsy at PD but PA/logistics a pain.
Tox from chemo add-on worries him for older pts.
Honestly not sure which resistance mech matters most clinicaly.
Community onc, sees lots of brain mets at dx. Says osimertinib + chemo gives him some comfort for those pts, esp. symptomatic CNS. Would use it upfront more if AEs stay manageable.
Tumor board usually pushes NGS on tissue + plasma at PD. HCP says results often come back w/o a clear actionable target, so default ends up platinum doublet. Not thrilled but that's reality.
Pts on osi do fine QoL-wise until PD, then fall off a cliff. HCP feels 2L options just don't match what pts had before.
Academic HCP mentioned MET amp and C797S as the ones he sees, I think. Says the rest is a mixed bag and often no driver found at all.
Thinks combo tx could delay CNS relapse, which is his biggest worry. Pts who had SRS earlier like the idea of avoiding WBRT. Wants more f/u before saying for sure.
Payer pushback on newer agents after PD, PA denials common in his practice. Delays of a few wks mean some pts decline before they ever start.
Asked about leptomeningeal dz, says no great option. Sometimes uses higher dose osimertinib off-label, unsure how much it really helps.
Rural clinic, pts travel far for infusions. Chemo combo = more visits, more fatigue, caregiver burden. Wonders if QoL tradeoff is worth it for pts w/ low-volume dz, but sees the PFS rationale.

HCP frustrated w/ post-osimertinib landscape. Most pts end up on chemo ± bev and responses are short-lived in his experience. Resistance is heterogeneous so there's no single next step. Re-biopsy often not feasible in frail pts, so he leans on ctDNA, which probably misses things. Biggest gap for him is CNS-only progression.

Overall positive on 1L osimertinib. Pts stay on tx a long time, keep working, travel, AEs mostly rash and paronychia. For CNS dz it's his go-to since intracranial control seems robust. Still wants a better plan for when it stops working, but doesn't regret the 1L choice.

Discussed sequencing. HCP split: fit pts w/ big tumor burden or brain mets lean combo upfront, older pts get osi mono. Worries chemo upfront leaves less for 2L, not sure that matters. Wants data on what happens after PD on the combo. Also unclear to him if resistance mechs differ between arms.

Recent pt, 50s nonsmoker, ~2 yrs on osimertinib then oligo-progression in brain. SRS done, TKI continued, but systemic PD a few months later. No good trial access nearby, tumor board kind of shrugged. Pt ended up on chemo w/ rough AEs and QoL tanked. He feels there's nothing solid for these pts.

Rad onc and neurosurg collab is good at his center, so CNS oligoprogression gets SRS and osimertinib continues. HCP sees that as a real win for QoL, pts avoid switching tx too early. Says it buys time and keeps pts functional. Still wishes there was more for when systemic dz breaks through.

Not sure resistance testing changes mgmt much outside trials. Does send plasma NGS at PD bc pts ask. Sometimes finds MET or something, sometimes nothing. Turnaround ~2 wks is a problem when pt is symptomatc. Would want faster results and a clearer 2L algorithm.

unmet_need|pembrolizumab.t: Once they progress on pembro after periop, we've basically got chemo and hope.
Brain mets in gastric are rare in my clinic, but I've got nothing good to offer.
Honestly, quality of life data in the periop setting is what I wish I had more of.
Fewer early relapses is real progress, even if the next step stays murky.
No biomarker tells me who will be resistant and who won't, zero help there
Cutting recurrence risk with perioperative IO is a step forward, finally.
For fit patients, the perioperative approach has changed how we talk about cure, which I didn't expect to say. Still waiting to see how people function long term, but early impressions are good.
Community colleagues keep asking me what to do with early relapse within months of finishing adjuvant pembro. Rechallenge? Switch? Nobody has a straight answer and I'm tired of shrugging.
Leptomeningeal spread after IO in lung is the thing that scares me. I think radiation helps focal lesions, but the systemic options feel thin.
Gastric patients are often too frail by the time they progress to even get second-line. Nutrition and fatigue wreck quality of life way before scans do, and trials barely capture that.
Payer pushback on anything beyond standard second-line is constant for us. Even if there were a decent option after progression we'd be fighting for access, and prior auth takes weeks.
Immune-related toxicity is manageable in most of mine, so quality of life during periop treatment is better than I feared. Not perfect, but I'd definately take it over what we had before.
Resistance mechanisms, I think it's probably a mix of tumor microenvironment stuff and loss of antigen presentation. We don't test for any of it routinely though. Research question for now.
Our clinic does brain MRI surveillance for stage III lung patients, but teh frequency is all over the place. Some colleagues skip it entirely, tbh.

Gastric after progression on a PD-1 plus chemo backbone is a wasteland, frankly. Second-line is mostly the same cytotoxics we used a decade ago, and a lot of patients can't tolerate them. I see them in a busy outpatient unit where performance status drops between one visit and the next. By the time we've sorted scans and consent, a good chunk are hospice candidates. We keep having the same conversation and it doesn't get easier.

On the lung side, my main worry in the periop setting is the patient who gets neoadjuvant pembro and then never makes it to adjuvant because of complications or slow recovery. I'm not sure how much that matters biologically, probably some. The CNS question comes up too, since a handful relapse in the brain first. We screen mostly on symptoms. I don't think anyone has this nailed.

Trials love to exclude active brain mets, and then we're expected to extrapolate. I get that it keeps the data clean, but my real patients don't come clean. Radiation helps locally, sure, yet nobody can tell me whether pembrolizumab is doing anything intracranially in the gastric patients I see. Neurologic decline wrecks quality of life faster than anything else. Feels like a blind spot the field ignores.

I'll give credit where it's due: the perioperative approach has genuinely changed what I tell lung patients in clinic. More of them reach surgery and stay disease-free longer than I'd have guessed a few years back. Yes, there's still a gap after progression, but that's true of nearly everything in oncology. Quality of life on treatment has been acceptable for most, with the usual thyroid and skin issues. I'm cautiously optimistic, and I don't say that often.

Patient-reported outcomes are what I'd want to see, and they're thin. Everyone quotes survival-type endpoints, but my patients ask whether they'll be able to work, climb stairs, travel. Fatigue and low-grade immune toxicity linger for months in some and nobody tracks it. I think quality of life is probably fine for most, but 'probably' isn't data. Maybe real-world registries will fill that in.

Nobody rebiopsies at progression where I work, mostly because tissue is hard to get and payers balk at the cost. So resistance stays a black box, and we just guess and switch to chemo. I keep hearing talk about antigen loss and other mechanisms, but none of it changes what I do on Monday. Feels like a lot of science with no bedside payoff yet.
No clear tx after relapse on adjuvant pembro. Big gap.
Brain mets surveillance schedule unclear in resected NSCLC, per HCP.
QoL on pembro maintenance generally good, fewer AEs than chemo phase.
Resistance biology still a black box per HCP. Rebiopsy sometimes helps, not always.
Wants rebiopsy at progression on pembro but PA hassles slow it down
CNS relapse is what worries this HCP most.

Community onc, says most pts tolerate periop IO fine and recover function after surgery. Likes that pts aren't on intensive tx for long in the adjuvant phase. Still wants durability info but QoL piece is a win for them.
Gastric HCP: after PD-1 progression it's mostly taxane +/- ramucirumab, nothing new. Not sure sequencing matters much. Tumor board usually defaults to a trial if one is open.
Thoracic surgeon concerned that early recurrences post-neoadj tend to show up as distant mets, often brain. Hard to counsel pts preop on that. No good predictor of who does this.

HCP thinks resistance is probably loss of antigen presentation or TME stuff, admits not their area. Would love a biomarker to guide next tx for pts progressing on pembro. For now it's just imaging q3mo and hoping.
Saw a few pts w/ small brain mets where SRS plus IO went well, anecdotal only. HCP wants that clarified in a real dataset. Encouraged overall.
HCP feels periop QoL talk is underdone. Fatigue and neuropathy from the platinum part linger for months in some pts. Pts ask 'is it worth it' and HCP says they don't have a great answer.
PA for 2L after IO failure takes weeks, tx gets delayed while pt declines. HCP says unmet need is partly access, not only new drugs. Mentioned payer denials for off-label combos come up a lot.

Gastric clinic, mostly HER2-neg pts. After progression on 1L chemo-IO, PS drops fast so a good chunk never get 2L. HCP cited dysphagia, nutrition and ascites as the blockers. Not sure continuing IO beyond progression helps, tried it a couple times w/o clear benefit. Wants anything that works post-IO. Palliative referral also comes too late, I think.

Community HCP, periop NSCLC. Says the KN-671 regimen changed the pt conversation, more going to surgery w/ curative intent and doing ok. Baseline brain MRI is routine now. Thinks relapses are less frequent than before but can't quote numbers. Thyroid AEs manageable w/ replacement. Gaps post-relapse remain but feels better than 2 yrs ago.

Tumor board case: pt relapsed a few months after finishing adjuvant. Debate over calling it IO-refractory vs resistant since that changes next line. HCP thinks rebiopsy + NGS is probably worth it but tissue is often scant. Some favored local tx for oligo progression. No consensus, ends up case by case.

HCP w/ neuro-onc overlap. Pts progressing on IO w/ brain mets get SRS, but steroids for edema may blunt IO effect, I think is their worry. Whole-brain avoided where possible yet cognitive issues still show. Pts lose driving and independence. No clear pathway between med onc and rad onc at their site. Wants prospective CNS data in periop setting.

Gastric periop: HCP says FLOT is still the backbone and the IO add-on question is unsettled, waiting on more. Worried immune AEs could delay surgery. Pts who progress during neoadj mostly go straight to surgery if resectable, otherwise switch chemo. Gap = no biomarker beyond PD-L1/MSI to say who benefits.

Rural clinic HCP, pts drive 2+ hrs for scans and many skip follow-up becuase of cost and travel. Relapses get caught late, sometimes w/ symptomatic brain mets. No local rad onc for SRS so referral adds weeks. HCP says post-progression options matter less when pts can't even reach them. Feels the system gap is as big as the drug gap.

Resected NSCLC pt doing well on adjuvant pembro, back at work. HCP cited this as why they're optimistic. QoL is a bigger part of the conversation now and pts value it. Would still want better options if relapse.
Nobody has a good answer once brain mets show up after surgery.
Second-line after IO in gastric is still mostly chemo, I think.
Fewer early recurrences on periop pembrolizumab, so fewer hard second-line talks.
No clear biomarker for who will progress on PD-1
Most periop pembro patients I follow are back to normal routine by month three.
Post-progression options in gastric are limited, especialy for PD-L1 low patients, but trials are enrolling.

In our community oncology clinic, most gastric patients who progress on first-line chemo plus a checkpoint inhibitor go straight to taxane-based therapy. Rechallenge with another checkpoint inhibitor comes up occasionally, but nobody is confident it helps. They'd like some actual data.

Pembro in the periop lung setting has been well tolerated in the patients followed at the academic center, and most are working or driving again within a few months. That is a real quality of life gain compared with what they saw after chemo alone.
Payer prior auth delays hit them when a patient progresses and needs a next-line drug. Two weeks of waiting in someone with CNS symptoms is a long time.
Resistance mechanisms are still a black box for this clinic. I think loss of antigen presentation plays a part, but nothing like that is tested in routine practice
Leptomeningeal disease after resected lung cancer is rare but devastating. They have almost nothing to offer beyond radiation and comfort care, and the neuro-onc board usually has no new ideas.

Their tumor board often debates continuing pembrolizumab beyond progression when only one lesion grows. Usually they treat that lesion with SBRT and carry on. The evidence for this is anecdotal at best.

Brain imaging at baseline and in follow-up has become routine for their stage III lung patients on periop pembrolizumab. Catching small asymptomatic mets early means SRS rather than whole brain, which patients tolerate far better.

Elderly gastric patients in this clinic often can't get through the perioperative regimen, so the question of what comes next never even arises. The gap is probably more upstream than people admit, and I'm not sure it's solvable.

Seen mostly in a regional hospital oncology unit. When lung patients relapse after periop pembrolizumab, they don't really know whether it's primary or acquired resistance, because re-biopsy is rarely done. Pathology turnaround is slow and patients are often too frail. Next line is usually platinum doublet re-treatment or docetaxel, and the physician wasn't sure that's right. It feels like guessing.

Per one gastric oncologist, HER2 and claudin testing is now part of the baseline work-up, which helps first-line, but after progression the menu shrinks fast. Ramucirumab with paclitaxel remains the default. Patients with peritoneal disease do worst and often can't eat, so nutrition and quality of life dominate the visit. She'd like supportive care brought in at first progression. There isn't much to offer for peritoneal spread right now.

Positive overall from a thoracic surgeon at a high-volume center. After periop pembro, more of his resections show a major pathologic response, and he feels the post-op follow-up visits are calmer. He still worries about the small group who relapse in the brain. Fast access to SRS helps them. He thinks a standing neuro-onc slot would be the next improvement.

Quality of life in the adjuvant phase came up first. Several of his patients stopped pembrolizumab early because of thyroid problems, joint pain or plain exhuastion, and then worry about whether stopping hurts them. He doesn't have a good answer for them. Endocrine follow-up is also hard to arrange in a rural practice with long drive times.

From the community side, access is the main issue. PD-L1 results come back fast, but anything beyond that, like NGS after progression, takes weeks and sometimes isn't covered. By then the patient is already on something else. I think trial referral would help, but the nearest site is a long drive. So most stay local and get standard chemo.

CNS progression in gastric is uncommon but they are seeing it a bit more as patients live longer. When it happens there is no real systemic option and the team falls back on radiation. Families ask whether immunotherapy could have prevented it and nobody can say. Pretty unsatisfying conversation, tbh.
Brain mets after neoadjuvant pembro are the scenario nobody has a clean answer for.
Second line after IO in gastric is still basically chemo, in most clinics.
Perioperative IO has spared some of her lung patients a much harder palliative course.
No reliable way to know early who will relapse after surgery.
Fatigue and slow recovery after surgery come up more often than efficacy questions.
Leptomeningeal spread, thats where we run out of options entirely.

He mostly worries about the gap between finishing adjuvant treatment and the first surveillance scan, because anxiety in that window is huge. Not sure there is anything formal for support there, probably varies by centre.

Pretty encouraged that more resectable lung patients now reach surgery with a real chance of cure. Toxicity has been manageable in her clinic, and most people get through the preoperative phase without long delays.

Rapid progression on pembrolizumab plus chemo in HER2-negative gastric leaves a lot of people too frail for anything else. By the time it shows on imaging, performance status has often dropped. Third line is a hard conversation.

Resistance came up. He thinks the tumor microenvironment and loss of antigen presentation are probably relevant, but nothing he can act on in clinic. Wants biomarkers that change a decision, not ones that just describe biology.
Access is a real barrier for anything beyond standard second line, becuase payer approvals drag and trial sites can be far away. Patients often progress before the paperwork clears.
Radiation colleagues have been good at CNS control with SRS, so he feels oligometastatic brain relapse is more manageable than a few years ago. Systemic control outside the brain is the harder part.

Asked about immune-related adverse events as a quality of life issue: endocrine problems tend to be lifelong, and he wonders whether cured patients accept that trade. They seem fine with it so far, but follow-up is short.

After a long talk, what stood out was how stuck he feels when a patient relapses early after perioperative pembrolizumab. Rechallenge with the same class seems unreasonable to him, yet he has no good alternative beyond another platinum doublet or a trial. He thinks we under-discuss how many people relapse in the brain or bones rather than locally. I think he would like clearer sequencing guidance, probably from real-world data. For now he leans on tumour board opinions and a lot of improvisation.

She split her concern into two buckets. For gastric it is mostly nutritional status and whether people are fit enough for anything after first-line progression. For lung it is what happens once the perioperative course is done and relapse occurs, since options depend a lot on the molecular profile. She felt both settings share the same gap: very little guidance on what comes next. Reasonably optimistic about future combinations but not holding her breath.

He was upbeat overall. In his lung clinic, patients on the perioperative regimen seem to tolerate surgery fine, and the multidisciplinary team feels the pathway is smoother than before. He said quality of life during the neoadjuvant phase has been better than he feared, mostly because side effects were caught early. The remaining worry is the unknown long-term picture. He would still rather have that worry than the old one.

Brain involvement dominated the discussion. She sees patients whose extracranial disease is quiet yet who develop symptomatic CNS lesions, and she feels systemic options penetrate poorly. Local therapy buys time, but repeated courses are limiting, especially with cognitive effects. Families ask what quality of life will look like and she struggles to give an honest, hopeful answer. She would like CNS endpoints reported more routinely in studies

Our conversation circled around resistance. He thinks primary resistance in gastric is probably tied to biology we only partly measure, like PD-L1 status or microsatellite stability, and acquired resistance looks messy. He was cautious about repeat biopsies at progression, since many patients are frail and the yield is uncertain. Still, he sees value in collecting tissue where feasible for future trials. Not convinced anything actionable exists today.

She felt the unmet-need picture is slowly improving. Her centre now gets patients into trials after progression more often, thanks to a coordinator who screens every relapse at tumor board. Supportive care has also helped, with early palliative referral and dietitian input making follow-up feel less bleak for gastric patients. She still wants better options, but described the mood in clinic as cautiously hopeful rather than resigned.
The cost of frequent imaging and visits for surveillance after resection is a burden for rural patients, and some skip scans. Not sure it changes outcomes, but it clearly affects their wellbeing.

unmet_need|sacituzumab govitecan.t: Nothing good after SG in HR+ disease, mostly back to single-agent chemo.
Resistance question comes up a lot, nobody knows what to sequence next.
Brain mets patients are mostly excluded from studies so we just dont know.
Glad to have another option after CDK4/6 and endocrine failure.
Alopecia and diarrhea drive most of the QoL talk.
No clear next step once a TROP2 ADC stops working.

Community practice, two patients on sacituzumab beyond third line for HR+/HER2-. Both kept working part time, which they valued a lot. The doctor feels it fills a real gap after endocrine therapy and CDK4/6.
At the urology clinic the discussion was what comes after enfortumab and a PD-1. SG is seen as a possible option but they aren't sure where it fits. Payer approval can add a couple of weeks.

Older patients have a lot of dose delays from neutropenia and fatigue. HCP worries any QoL benefit gets eaten up by extra growth factor visits and cytopenias. Not sure it is worth it for frail ECOG 2 patients.

Tumor board mostly asks about repeat biopsy at progression. It is hard to get approved and the logistics slow things down, so most patients are treated empirically. They would like markers to guide the next line.
Had a patient with leptomeningeal disease and nothing to offer beyond radiation and supportive care. HCP said ADC penetration into the CNS is basically unknown to them and wants any data available.

Infusion nurse-led clinic says patients tolerate the day 1 and day 8 schedule better than expected once premeds and growth factor are set up. That keeps people out of hospital. The physician thinks this matters a lot for QoL in later lines.
Thinks resistance probably involves lower TROP2 expression or a payload problem, but admits that is speculation. Would not change practice based on it.

Large hospital breast clinic keeps a running list of patients who stop SG for toxicity rather than progression. Those patients have no obvious fallback. They would like guidance on dose reduction timing and rechallenge.

Seeing a few HR+ patients progress fast on sacituzumab, within the first couple of scans. After that it is usually single-agent chemo again and performance status drops quickly. Nobody in the clinic has a good answer for why some don't respond. They said biomarkers for selection are the biggest gap. Honestly the post-ADC space feels empty to them.

Medical oncologist in a regional clinic sees mostly cisplatin-ineligible urothelial patients who already had enfortumab and a PD-1. SG is what they think of next, but access varies by payer. Some patients wait weeks for authorization and deteriorate in the meantime. When it is approved, they feel it is worth trying. What happens after SG in urothelial is still unclear to them.

Private practice oncologist said sacituzumab gives her a real choice in pretreated HR+/HER2- patients who used to get a third or fourth chemo. A few of her patients have stayed on it for months with manageable side effects and recieve fewer admissions. She thinks the extra time with family counts. She still wants better CNS data but overall sees it as a step forward.

Neuro-oncology referrals are the pain point in this clinic. Patients with active brain mets usually get local therapy and then systemic options run thin. The HCP doesn't know if SG helps intracranially and has no way to tell families. They said most trials leave these patients out. Tracking CNS progression separately would be useful in their view.

QoL conversation in a small oncology practice is mostly about trade-offs. Patients accept hair loss if scans are stable, but diarrhea and fatigue make them reconsider. The nurse manager says phone triage calls go up in the first two cycles. The HCP thinks it is probably still better than another round of conventional chemo. Not sure how to measure that in routine care.

Palliative care team at a community hospital noted that patients on SG describe less of the cumulative neuropathy they had with taxanes. Hair loss is still a complaint. Overall the patients seem to prefer it to more chemo. The team is unsure how that holds up over a longer time on treatment.
Nothing good after SG fails, honestly; mostly back to single-agent chemo.
CNS progression is the blind spot nobody has a plan for.
Says QoL on SG beats what chemo gave her patients.
Alopecia and diarrhea still drive early discontinuation in her clinic.
Unsure whether TROP2 expression even matters for resistance.
Worried about having no sequencing data after an ADC.

Community oncologist said sacituzumab has given her a real option for endocrine-resistant patients who have run out of CDK4/6 steps. Even when progression comes, she feels the patient had decent months with fewer hospital visits than before.
For urothelial, he sees it as a bridge after EV and pembro but isn't sure what follows. Probably a clinical trial if the patient is fit enough, otherwise supportive care.

Brain mets in HR+ patients are showing up more often as people live longer. Nobody on her tumor board believes the ADC reaches the CNS well, so they default to radiation and hope. She was frustrated by how little data there is.

Team speculates about TROP2 downregulation or payload resistance, but without repeat biopsies it's just guessing. His academic-type setting might get a re-biopsy approved, a community practice wouldn't.
Payer prior auths for the next line after progression take wekks, and the patient deteriorates in between. He called that a bigger gap than the drug itself.
Thinks the QoL story is underrated; patients on SG keep working part-time more than he expected. Still wants something for after, but that's a good problem to have.
Fatigue is what patients complain about, not the labs. She said dose reductions help but then she worries about efficacy, and nobody can tell her where teh trade-off sits.
He asked whether switching to a different-payload ADC after SG is reasonable. Thinks maybe, but would want data first; unclear to him if cross-resistance exists.

Spent a long time on what happens when sacituzumab stops working in HR+/HER2- disease. Her honest view is that the options after are thin: another chemo, maybe a different ADC if she can get access, and hospice conversations earlier than anyone wants. Patients are often heavily pretreated by then, with poor counts and little marrow reserve. She also pointed out that nobody tells patients clearly what to expect at third or fourth line. Overall she called it the biggest hole in the pathway.

After a long discussion he was more upbeat than expected. In his GU clinic, patients who had been through platinum and checkpoint therapy used to have almost nothing, and now a TROP2 ADC gives them a credible later-line step. He still worries about diarrhea and neutropenia, but thinks supportive care protocols are mature enough. What he'd like next is clarity on sequencing relative to other ADCs. Said it's the first time in a while he can offer hope rather than just comfort.

We talked mostly about CNS disease. In her practice a good chunk of HR+ patients who progress do so intracranially, and she's not sure whether that reflects drug penetration or just biology. SRS handles limited lesions fine but leptomeningeal disease is basically a dead end. She'd like patients with stable brain mets included in studies rather than excluded. Until then she is unsure how to counsel them about SG.

Biggest frustration is that we don't know why it stops working. No biomarker to tell who will respond, no good way to track resistance, and ctDNA isn't reimbursed in his setting. He treats on imaging and symptoms which feels crude. When progression happens he usually moves to a chemo he would have used anyway. Honestly it feels like the ADC is a detour rather than a platform.

The conversation turned to logistics. Her infusion center runs at capacity, and day 1 and day 8 visits are a burden for patients who live far away, so some stop for that reason alone. She thinks the QoL trade is acceptable if the benefit is meaningful, but less so in late lines. Probably what she would want is a less frequent schedule, though she doesn't know if that's feasible. Hair loss came up more than expected.

Described a patient with HR+ disease and several prior lines who got real disease control and kept gardening through it. That sort of story shaped his view that the drug fills an important gap after endocrine and CDK4/6 failure. He is realistic that it isn't durable forever and that what comes after is murky. Still, he'd rather have this problem than the old one. He expects younger colleagues to use it earlier, probably.
Post-SG progression = basically no good next option, per HCP.
Wants a biomarker to pick pts for TROP2 ADC. None yet.
CNS mets pts get excluded from everything, big gap.
Likes SG for HR+ pts who've run out of endocrine options.
Unsure what resistance looks like after a topo-I payload ADC.
Neutropenia and diarrhea hit QoL, pts dread the later cycles.
Community onc, mostly sees HR+ pts after CDK4/6 and chemo. Says SG fills a spot but what comes after is a blank. Wary of back-to-back ADCs, not sure if payload cross-resistance matters.
Urothelial HCP happy to have SG after EV/pembro progression. Pts who'd otherwise go to hospice get some more time. Still wants better data on how long the benefit lasts.
Brain mets in HR+ pts: HCP thinks SG probably doesn't do much there, not sure. Ends up with SRS and then nothing systemic. Tumor board keeps asking the same question.
Hair loss and fatigue are what pts bring up first, not PFS. HCP thinks QoL on tx is under-measured. Would probably trade some efficacy for fewer AEs in older pts.
PA delays for ADCs at her practice, pts progress while waiting. She calls it an access gap more than a science gap. Payer keeps asking for a biomarker she doesn't have.
HCP said TROP2 targeting gives a real mechanism-based option after endocrine resistance. Thinks pts feel ok on tx w/ G-CSF support. Wants to see it used earlier in the sequence.
Asked whether TROP2 expression loss drives resistance. He doesn't know and neither do I tbh. Would want rebiopsy at progression but community pts rarely get one.
Elderly urothelial pts w/ poor PS, cis-ineligible, hardly any options after progresion. HCP worried SG toxicity is too much for them.

Large community clinic, HR+ MBC. Most pts have been through endo, CDK4/6 and a chemo before SG gets discussed. After SG progression she mostly falls back on single-agent chemo and responses are poor. No clear sequencing guidance and tumor board doesn't help much. Resistance mechanisms are a black box to her. Pts ask 'what's next' and she has no good answer.

Academic breast HCP, optimistic overall. Thinks SG moved the bar for pretreated HR+/HER2- pts, esp. w/ visceral disease. Sees the next frontier as combos and earlier use, not post-progression rescue. Still wants clarity on sequencing vs other ADCs, but calls it a good problem to have.

GU onc, urothelial. After EV and IO, SG is what he reaches for, though access depends on the payer. Brain mets are rare in his pts, but when they happen he has little systemic to offer. On QoL, pts tolerate the first cycles ok, then fatigue accumulates. Not sure how to balance dose delays vs keeping intensity. Would like real-world data.

Worried about CNS progression. Several HR+ pts came in w/ headaches while stable systemically, what she called discordant progression. Brain-directed tx then interrupts systemic tx for weeks. Doesn't know if ADCs penetrate meaningfully, probably not. Trials exclude active brain mets so she's extrapolating. Biggest hole in her view.

Rural practice, long drive for infusion. Pts weigh travel plus AEs vs benefit and some choose to stop. HCP thinks SG works but the day 1/day 8 schedule is a burden. G-CSF support helps but adds complexity. Mixed feelings overall.

Breast MD shared a heavily pretreated HR+ pt who did well on SG and kept working part-time. He thinks this QoL angle is under-appreciated. Yes, neutropenia needs active management, but with dose reduction most of his pts stayed on. Unmet need for him is what follows, but he's glad to have something. Would use again in similar pts.
Nothing good after SG fails, honestly.
CNS mets are still a black hole for ADCs, in my experience.
Sequencing after progression is basically guesswork right now.
Manageable with G-CSF and early loperamide, QoL better than I feared.
Fine, it buys time when chemo options are thin.
Resistance biology? We just don't know, and no one's testing for it.

Community practice here, so we get HR+ patients who've already burned through endocrine plus CDK4/6 and a couple of chemos. By the time sacituzumab is on the table they're ECOG 2 and fragile. Then they progress and we have nothing to offer except hospice talk.
I'm not sure whether TROP2 expression drops at progression, nobody rebiopsies where I work. Would be useful to know, but payers don't love paying for repeat biopsies anyway.
For my urothelial patients post-enfortumab and pembro, having something with a different target is a relief, I'll admit. Doesn't solve what comes after, but it beats the empty chair we had before.
Brain mets patients get excluded from everything, then we're asked to extrapolate. I treat them anyway and just hope. Its frustating that the data are silent.
Alopecia and fatigue matter more to my patients than the slides suggest. Some accept it for a few extra months, others stop after two cycles. I think the QoL conversation up front is under-done.

Everyone talks about the next ADC after progression, but cross-resistance to a similar topoisomerase payload worries me. Probably the payload is the issue and not just the target, though I haven't heard a convincing answer.
The gap feels smaller than it used to; HR+ patients who've exhausted endocrine therapy at least have a real option now. I still want something better for the line after that.
Prior auth and pharmacy delays eat weeks, and these patients don't have weeks after progression. Nobody budgets for that in the pathway.

Let me be blunt: the unmet need isn't another line, it's knowing who will respond. We give sacituzumab to HR+/HER2- patients and some progress by the first couple of scans, with no biomarker to predict it. Meanwhile they've lost weeks, needed G-CSF, and had diarrhea. I'd want a TROP2 or resistance signal before committing. Until then it feels like a coin toss with a toxic drug.

Tumor board discussions after progression always go in circles. Options are chemo rechallenge, a trial if the patient is fit enough, or best supportive care. Trial access is the real issue since most of us are nowhere near a research site. I think the gap is practicl more than scientific, because patients live hours away and can't travel weekly.

I'll give credit where it's due: a few of my patients with long prior treatment histories got meaningful extra time on SG with decent function. One kept traveling to see family. That matters more to me than a scan. Still, when it stops working I have nothing equivalent to move to, and that's the part that bothers me.

Leptomeningeal and parenchymal disease is where I get most frustrated. Our urothelial and breast patients develop brain mets while systemic disease is stable, and then we radiate and shrug. I doubt a big ADC penetrates well, but I have nothing to point to. Nobody can tell me whether to keep the ADC going while we treat the brain, so I make the call on instinct.

In urothelial the sequence is crowded now. After platinum, EV and checkpoint, sacituzumab is one of few things left, but I'm hesitent using it that late. These patients are usually cachectic with poor marrow reserve. If it fails there's no plan B, so I probably move to hospice earlier than I'd like.

Nobody sends anything for resistance testing in my clinic. People mention TROP2 downregulation, payload efflux, topoisomerase changes, but none of it is actionable for me. I wouldn't know what to do with a result anyway. So at progression I'm basically guessing the next line.

unmet_need|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: Sequencing after T-DXd = big question, no clear answer yet per HCP.
CNS mets still the main worry, esp. pts progressing in brain on tx.
Pt QoL on T-DXd better than HCP expected, nausea well controlled.
No good option once the ADC fails, HCP said bluntly.
Likes that brain mets pts can often stay on T-DXd, fewer switches
ILD fear limits T-DXd use in older pts, HCP admits it's a gut call.
Community clinic HCP: HER2-low pt progressing after 2L mostly goes back to chemo. Not sure what else to offer, trial sites are too far for most pts. Feels stuck.
Tumor board chat: HCP thinks resistance probably involves HER2 loss or payload handling, but nobody tests for it routinely. Wants more re-biopsy at progression, though pts hate it.
HCP says fatigue and alopecia hit QoL more than the label suggests. Still prefers it to older chemo for PFS reasons, overall a trade-off.
Academic HCP encouraged by intracranial responses in a handful of pts w/ stable brain mets. Wants prospective CNS data tho, not just anecdotes.
PA delays a few wks for 2L approval and pts progress while waiting. HCP frustrated, says its an access gap more than a clinical one.
HCP unsure about rechallenge w/ another HER2 ADC after T-DXd. Would probably try if pt fit and nothing else left, thinks evidence is thin.
HER2-low, bone-only pt: HCP would do endocrine + CDK4/6 first and save T-DXd for later. Real unmet need is better markers to pick who needs the ADC early.
Younger pts on tx worry about fertility and long-term AEs. HCP says counseling resources are patchy, some support exists but not consistent.

Infusion-center-heavy practice. HCP says pts tolerate T-DXd better than expected once antiemetics are tight. Fewer admissions vs prior chemo regimens. Some pts keep working, which HCP values a lot. Still wants a plan for post-progression but feels the QoL trade-off is fine.

HCP very concerned re CNS. Brain mets show up in a good chunk of HER2+ pts and SRS gets repeated again and again. Systemic options w/ real CNS activity are limited imo. Neuro-onc referrals are slow too. Not sure T-DXd fully solves this, wants dedicated CNS data before changing practice.

Rural clinic, one med onc. Resistance mechanisms discussed only in theory, no NGS at progression for most pts bc of cost and tissue. Follows guideline sequence and switches on clinical gut. Thinks HER2-low heterogeneity is probably part of it. Would like a simple tool, maybe ctDNA, but payer coverage unclear.

After T-DXd progression pts are often too sick for next line. PS drops fast and the hospice convo comes sooner than anyone wants. Few trials open locally. HCP feels field moved on 1L/2L but nothing real for 3L+. Frustrated tone throughout.

Tumor board HCP optimistic. Thinks HER2-low opened a whole pt group w/ no prior HER2 option, which was a huge unmet need. Seeing pts stay on tx longer than on chemo, from what he recalls. QoL mostly ok, AEs manageable w/ dose reductions. Hopes earlier use in HR+ disease shrinks later gaps.

ILD monitoring burden: CT every few cycles, pts anxious, scheduling a mess. HCP says workflow is heavy for small centers w/o extra staff. Likes the efficacy impression overall but unsure how to cover monitoring. Probably some pts get undertreated bc of this
Brain mets are still the big hole after T-DXd progression.
Not sure what sequencing comes next once HER2-low disease progresses.
Patients on T-DXd say the visit schedule is easier than weekly chemo.
Nausea management is eating up chair time in her infusion suite.
Resistance mechanisms come up at every tumor board and nobody has a clear answer.
Leptomeningeal disease: honestly nothing good to offer these patients.
Community oncologist described two patients with stable brain mets on T-DXd, which surprised her. She said it may change how she times local therapy. Still anecdotal, she added.
After T-DXd progression she mostly goes to single-agent chemo, picking the agent by how fast things are moving. She would like a biomarker to guide that choice, but there isn't one she trusts.

Worried about the ILD follow-up burden with T-DXd. Her clinic has one nurse doing symptom calls, and CT scans get delayed by prior auth. Because of that she hesitates in older patients with existing lung problems.

At his academic breast clinic, HER2-low patients are progressing on endocrine plus CDK4/6. He is unsure when to move to the ADC versus trying another endocrine line. He thinks it comes down to visceral burden and what the patient prefers.
Fatigue and hair loss are the first things patients bring up at follow-up. The oncologist feels those day-to-day issues don't get enough weight when options are compared.
Oncologist in a hospital infusion center said the every-three-weeks schedule suits patients who still work. She sees fewer unplanned visits than with her previous chemo patients, I think.
Resistance is the part nobody can explain, one oncologist said, why some HER2-low tumors just stop respondng after a good first few scans

Radiation oncologist at a regional center likes that small intracranial lesions can sometimes be watched instead of irradiated right away. He sees that as a real step forward for patients who want to put off whole-brain treatment.

The oncologist at a large cancer center said CNS progression on T-DXd is where the plan falls apart. Neuro-oncology referrals take weeks, and by then the patient has often lost function. Systemic options after that feel thin to her. She would like some way to catch brain involvement earlier, but routine MRI surveillance isn't covered consistently.

Her practice rebiopsies when it's feasible after progression, but it's often a liver lesion that is hard to sample. HER2 expression may have shifted, though she isn't sure it would change management. For now the next line is chosen mostly by prior treatments and performance status. She said a clearer sequencing framework would help the whole group.

A rural clinic nurse practitioner reported that most patients on T-DXd keep doing their normal routines between cycles. A few had to stop because of nausea, but most managed with the antiemetic plan they were given. Families like that the travel to the infusion site is every three weeks. She said overall quality of life is better than she expected for this setting.

Payer hurdles were the main complaint from the practice manager. After T-DXd progression, the next-line drugs often need new authorizations, and trial slots are far away for most of their patients. Patients sometimes wait weeks with active disease. The oncologist said that gap in care is her biggest frustration right now.

For older patients she is torn. Several are doing well and would prefer to stay on treatment, but she worries about lung toxicity and has reduced doses in a handful. Dose reductions seem to help tolerability, though she is unsure what that means for control. She would like more real-world data in people over 70 before she feels settled.
Nothing good to offer after T-DXd progression, really.
Brain mets are still the elephant in the room for us.
Fewer chemo-type side effects than I feared, and patients notice.
No clue what to give once ILD forces us to stop early.
Resistance biology? Mostly guesswork in a community setting.
QoL data is thin beyond 2nd line and nobody seems botherd.
Sequencing after T-DXd is basically a coin toss in my clinic. We rebiopsy when we can, but the tissue is often inadequate and the result rarely changes what we do.
I'll give it credit: for HER2-low patients who'd run out of chemo, it bought real time and a few are still working. My gripe is what comes next, but at least we start from a better place.
Neuro-onc wants baseline and serial MRI for anyone with HER2 disease. Sounds sensible, but scanner slots and payer pushback on frequent imaging make it hard to do routinely.

Nausea and fatigue are manageable on paper. A patient vomiting through cycle two doesn't care about response rates, though, and some of them do still feel better overall. I think the QoL conversation needs to be more honest in both directions.
Not sure resistance comes from HER2 loss or from how the payload is handled, probably a mix. Nobody can tell me which, so I treat empirically.
Seeing intracranial responses in a few patients with stable-ish brain mets has been encouraging. Small numbers in my practice, but more than I used to see.
prior auth delays for the next line eat weeks when someone is already progressing and then the patient deteriorates before we start anything
We refer for trials after progression when slots exist. Most of my patients live too far away for that to be realistic, so it stays a nice idea.

Honestly the ILD issue keeps me up. We counsel everyone, scan on a schedule, and still catch some cases late because patients ring the wrong number or put a cough down to a cold. Once treatment stops they've lost their best option and there's nothing obvious behind it. Nobody has a clean answer on rechallenge either. I think the field undersells how much this limits who we dare to treat.

For CNS disease the workflow is messy. Rad onc wants to go first with local therapy, medical oncology wants to keep systemic going, and the patient waits in the middle for referrals. I think the systemic activity in the brain is probably real, but I wouldn't skip radiation on a symptomatic lesion. There's no clear rule on timing, so it gets decided case by case at tumor board.

HER2-low is a shaky category to me. Scoring at the low end varies between pathologists, and a sample from years ago may not reflect what's growing now. So when someone progresses I can't tell if the biology changed or if we mislabeled the tumour at the start. That uncertainty makes resistance discussions feel hollow. I'd want better re-testing guidance before anyone claims to understand failure.

Of everything we've used, this is the first that lets some of my patients keep going to family events between cycles. That matters more to me than waterfall plots. Yes, there's nausea and hair thinning, and I'm wary of the lung risk. But the day-to-day experience is better than I expected. My frustration is that we still can't say what follows when it stops.

The trial populations don't look like my clinic. My patients are older, carry comorbidities, and often arrive with brain or liver disease that would have excluded them. So when I hear about benefit I assume it's somewhat smaller for them, though I can't prove that. Quality of life in these real-world folks is rarely reported. Until it is I'll stay skeptical of the headline message on T-DXd.

Tumor board has turned a bit more hopeful lately. T-DXd gives us a credible option in HER2-low where we used to just cycle chemo. Younger patients especially tolerate it well, and pharmacy and infusion staff have gotten comfortable with premedication. We still lack a plan for progression, but I'd rather have that problem than none.
Sequencing after T-DXd is basically a blank page right now.
CNS progression is the thing that worries this community oncologist most.
Brain mets responding on T-DXd has genuinely shifted their thinking on radiotherapy timing.
Nausea and tiredness still cut treatment short for some patients on this ADC.
Not sure what resistance looks like biologically, probably heterogenous HER2 loss.
Nothing good for HER2-low patients whove progressed through chemo and an ADC.

Academic breast clinic sees T-DXd as a real step forward for HER2-low, because options used to run out fast. Quality of life on treatment is acceptable for most as long as antiemetics are front-loaded. Still wants to know what comes next, but today feels better than a couple of years ago.

Tumor board discussion: when a patient progresses on an HER2-directed ADC, nobody agrees on whether to rebiopsy. Some push for repeat HER2 testing, others say it rarely changes the plan. I think it depends on whether the lesion is accessible.

Worried about the ILD monitoring burden for rural patients who live far from imaging. Frequent scans are hard to arrange and a delay in reporting symptoms could be dangerous. Payer pushback on extra CTs slows things down even more

Regional hospital oncologist finds the CNS data encouraging but incomplete, mostly because patients with active brain disease seem underrepresented in what she reads. She would still treat, probably with SRS alongside.

Cumulative toxicity is the quiet issue. Patients on long courses get worn down by the cycle, and dose reductions blur whether they're still getting full benefit becuase nobody has a clear approach to treatment breaks.

Nurse-led symptom checks have worked well for their T-DXd patients in a busy community practice. Problems get caught early and patients feel looked after, so this clinician is hopeful that model eases the quality-of-life burden.
Asked about the next line after progression, said they'd probably go to another HER2-directed agent or chemo depending on performance status. Admitted it's mostly habit rather than evidence.
Leptomeningeal disease is basically a dead end in their experience. Systemic options feel inadequate, intrathecal approaches are inconsistently available, and families want answers that aren't there.

After a long conversation, the main frustration was what happens once T-DXd stops working. This clinician said resistance seems to arrive quietly, often with a mix of responding and progressing lesions, which makes picking the next line hard. Rebiopsy is rarely feasible in frail patients. Chemo afterwards feels like a step back, and patients notice. They'd love a biomarker that flags early who will fail, but don't think anything like that is close.

Spent most of the visit on CNS disease. This oncologist treats a lot of HER2-positive patients and has seen brain mets both respond and flare while systemic disease stays controlled. Probably the right answer is local therapy plus systemic treatment, but the timing of radiation relative to the ADC is still debated in her group. She'd welcome prospective data, especially for untreated lesions. Until then it's case by case.

Thoughtful, fairly upbeat discussion. In HER2-low this physician feels patients now have a real option where before it was serial single-agent chemo, and she sees fewer people sliding into hospice early. Quality of life is better than expected when GI side effects are managed proactively. The remaining gaps are real, mainly what follows and brain disease, but she framed them as the next problems to solve rather than reasons to hold back.

Quality of life came up repeatedly. Patients tolerate infusions, but hair thinning, nausea and tiredness add up, and a few in the clinic stopped for fatigue rather than progression. She thinks the benefit still justifies it for most, though she isn't sure how to weigh it in older patients with comorbidities. Wished for better tools to capture this in routine visits, since clinic notes mostly don't. Overall mixed, leaning cautious.

We talked through earlier-line use in HR-positive, HER2-low disease once endocrine therapy stops working. This physician sees the appeal of an ADC before standard chemo but worries about sequencing afterward, since options get narrower. Also unsure how to approach very low HER2 expression, where the testing itself feels shaky. Pathology variability was a practical headache. Likely to use it, just with lots of caveats.

Long, friendly chat with a breast specialist who works closely with neuro-oncology. She has seen intracranial responses she didn't expect, and with T-DXd some patients with stable brain mets are getting more time with decent function. That changes how she counsels families, who used to hear only bad news. She still wants better answers at progression, but it was a notable shift in tone from earlier discussions.
Nobody has a good answer for what comes after T-DXd progresses.
Sequencing of ADCs after the first one is still guesswork, honestly.
Brain mets control with T-DXd has surprised me in a good way, said the neuro-oncology lead.
ILD worry still limits who gets offered it in her practice
Rebiopsy at progression would help but patients often decline
Hair loss and fatigue weigh more on younger patients than we admit, I think.

We talked for a long time about what happens once the disease finally escapes. She felt the honest answer is that we don't really know whether resistance is HER2 loss, a payload problem, or heterogeneity that was always there. Rebiopsy is rarely done because of logistics and patient fatigue, so decisions are mostly empirical. She would welcome guidance on whether another HER2-directed ADC makes sense or whether to switch payload class. Probably the biggest gap, in her words, is a biomarker that tells you at progression what to do next.

Community oncologist with a large HER2+ population, and we spent a while on brain mets. In his experience T-DXd has changed how he approaches patients with stable or small CNS lesions, and he is more comfortable delaying whole-brain radiation than before. He still coordinates with radiation oncology and keeps MRI surveillance tight. I think he sees it as a real step forward, though he admitted his numbers are small. His remaining worry is leptomeningeal disease, where he feels nothing works well.

Long conversation on T-DXd tolerability in HER2-low patients, who are often still fairly well. Nausea is manageable with prophylaxis, but the monitoring burden for ILD (scans, symptom calls) wears on patients and nursing staff alike. She worries we ask patients with a few good years ahead to accept fatigue and hair loss without much discussion of trade-offs. Not sure the current QoL data capture what her patients actually describe. Some stop early not because of progression but because they're exhausted.

We discussed access after progression. In his hospital the pathway for a second ADC is unclear, and the payer often wants documentation that nothing else is suitable. He thinks that delays treatment by weeks, which matters in fast-moving visceral disease. Clinically he would like to move straight to the next option but is unsure which has the best rationale. Probably a tumour board decision for now.

Pathology interplay came up again and again. IHC 0 versus 1+ calls are inconsistent, and she feels patients near the cutoff fall into a grey zone where it's hard to say who truly benefits. After progression the HER2 status on a new biopsy may have shifted, but nobody knows what to do with that information. She also pointed out that endocrine-resistant patients who have already used up their options have few alternatives. Overall she is cautious rather than dismissive.

He was upbeat after a long chat about earlier-line use. His view is that moving T-DXd earlier in HR+ HER2-low disease could delay chemo for many patients, which they really value. He still has questions about what follows but feels a strong option sooner leaves more room to sequence. I think he would use it more if the ILD monitoring workflow were simpler. Overall the tone was optimistic with realistic caveats.
Patients progressing on T-DXd often return with new liver lesions and few good choices. We mostly fall back on chemo, which feels like a step backward for quality of life.
Her main concern is the unknown overlap in resistance between ADCs. If the topoisomerase payload is the problem, she doesn't see why a similar ADC would work, but nobody has shown otherwise.
Likes that CNS activity gives her something to offer patients who used to have almost nothing. Still sends everyone for a baseline MRI, mind you.
Every-three-week dosing is convenient but the ILD vigilence is a lot to ask of rural patients on T-DXd who live far from the clinic. Phone check-ins only go so far.
In the academic clinic they would enrol anyone progressing after T-DXd into a trial if one existed. Otherwise it's a case-by-case chat about chemo versus best supportive care.
Thinks the HER2-low label gives false hope to some patients. Durability of response is the unmet piece, and she has seen several relapse in the brain after good systemic control.
Patient preference matters a lot after progression, especially for older women. Some choose fewer visits over a marginally better option, which I think we underplay.
Seeing fewer treatment-related hospital stays on T-DXd than expected with proper antiemetics, so QoL has been better than he feared. Still keen on real-world data about long-term fatigue.

why_high|osimertinib.t: Brain met control has been consistently good in my hands.
Score is high mostly because nothing better exists, not out of real enthusiasm.
Fine with osi alone; chemo add-on only for select fit pts.
Worried about the anemia and nausea but I'd still offer it.
Single agent tolerability is why I keep reaching for it.
Payer hoops for the combo make me hesitate, so only 'likely'.

Mostly a community practice, so my patients are older and often have comorbidities. Osimertinib is easy to hand over and monitor with the nurses we have. I'd add chemo only if the person is clearly fit, and I'm not sure how many would be.

I'm thinking of a young never-smoker with an exon 19 deletion and baseline brain lesions. For her I'd be quite comfortable adding chemo to osimertinib, because the CNS question worries me more than a few cytopenias. Probably the easiest yes I have.

Infusion chair capacity is a real limit for us. Even if I believe in the combination, scheduling every three weeks for several cycles is a hard sell for patients who travel far. So my confidence is more about the drug than the logistics.

At tumor board people generally defaulted to the TKI alone, with the combo discussed for high-risk features. I go along with that. The score reflects trust in the backbone drug, less so in the add-on.

My concern is cumulative toxicity once chemo is layered on a drug people take for years. Fatigue and low counts early on can derail patients who would otherwise do well. I'd still use osimertinib, but my confidence in the combination is a notch lower.

I'm waiting for longer follow-up before using the combination broadly. Still, osimertinib alone has been so dependable in my clinic that I score high anyway. Doubt is about patient selection, not the TKI.
Having a strong first-line option makes sequencing less stressful for me. I can plan later lines calmly, and patients come back to clinic mostly feeling normal. That predictability is a big driver.

My frail ECOG 2 patients are what come to mind. With chemo on top I think I'd be asking for trouble, and families tend to want the gentler path anyway. I'd use osimertinib alone and be fairly cautious about the rest.

Honestly, my score is high but a bit uneasy. I've seen a handful of patients do remarkably well on osimertinib for a long time, which anchors me. But the combo means more visits, more labs, and more phone calls to my team. I think I'd use it in maybe a minority of new starts, and I'm still working out which ones. Confidence in the drug is strong; confidence in my own selection criteria is not.

We talked for a while about where I'd actually use it. Patients with brain mets at diagnosis or a high tumor burden are the ones I picture for the combination. The others I'd probably keep on osimertinib alone, since they tend to do fine and avoid the chemo burden. I'm not sure that split is evidence-based, it's more a gut sense from clinic. Overall I'm likely to use osimertinib either way.

What drives me is the experience of treating a few younger patients who stayed on therapy, working and traveling, for a long time. That is what I want for everyone with an EGFR mutation. The chemo addition feels reasonable for those with a worse outlook, and I'd discuss it openly with them. Side effects are manageable if we catch them early. I'd say I'm confident, with the usual caveat that real life is messier than a trial population.

My academic clinic sees many referrals after progression elsewhere, so I notice what first-line choices have meant downstream. That makes me value an approach with good durability and CNS protection. At the same time, I worry we might overtreat people who'd have done well with the TKI alone. Not sure there is a clean way to tell them apart yet. I'd lean toward using it, mixed with some hesitation.

Cost and coverage are what hold me back, not clinical belief. Our payer often asks for extra documentation for the combination, and a delay of even a couple of weeks makes patients anxious. I've had cases where we started the TKI alone just to avoid waiting. Fatigue from chemo is another worry in people who still work. So I'm likely to use it, but with a lot of friction and probably less often than I'd like.

I think the main reason is that my patients with CNS involvement have done well, and that's what scares them and me the most. When a pt walks in with headaches and multiple small brain lesions, I want the strongest option up front. I'd explain the extra chemo burden plainly and let them decide. A few have chosen the TKI alone and I respected that. Still, I feel good recommending it.
Osi track record + CNS control = HCP comfortable, easy call.
Will use, but only for pts fit enough for the chemo add-on.
Likely to use, still nervous about AEs w/ chemo combo.
PA delays only thing holding HCP back from combo
Brain mets pts, no-brainer for HCP, wants that CNS coverage.
Tolerability known, PFS benefit convincing, OS still pending per HCP.
Score high mostly bc of familiarity. A good number of pts on single-agent osimertinib for yrs, few progressed early. Would add chemo for high-risk ones, not everyone.
Academic HCP, tumor board pushed combo for L858R pt w/ brain mets. Personally worried about cytopenias and infusion chair time. Still scores high bc the PFS gain looks real to them.
Younger pt, good PS, multiple brain lesions at dx. HCP thinks this is exactly who FLAURA2 is for. Would start combo tomorrow if PA clears.
Rural clinic, pts drive far. q3w chemo visits a burden so HCP only likely to use combo selectively. Mono osi remains go-to.
I think confidence comes from data matching what HCP sees in clinic. Not sure re OS yet tho. Payer hasn't pushed back so far.
Elderly pts w/ comorbidities worry HCP, would stick w/ TKI alone. High score is for the TKI itself, lower for adding chemo on top.
Pts stay on osi a long time w/ few dose mods, HCP likes the QoL. Combo seen as option for right pt, not default.
Private practice oncologist, buy-and-bill makes combo workable. Infusion nurses already comfy w/ platinum regimens, no workflow change needed. Mostly a pt selection question for HCP.

High score but w/ caveats. Likes CNS activity, esp. a pt w/ leptomeningeal picture who stabilized for a long stretch. Concerned combo AEs (anemia, nausea, fatigue) lead to early dc and lose the benefit. Also unsure how to sequence after progression since chemo already used. Probably offers combo to fit pts only, rest mono, wants more real-world data.

HCP very positive. Several pts w/ exon 19 del doing well on osimertinib for a long time, w/ minimal fuss. Sees combo as logical step for pts w/ high burden disease or CNS involvement. Says teh PFS signal is what gets pts to accept chemo. Team already used to managing the AEs.

Community HCP, relies on tumor board for 1L decisions. Board generally favors osi for all EGFR+, combo discussed case by case. HCP thinks the combo is reasonable for pts w/ brain mets or big tumor burden. Not sure about pts w/ borderline PS. Scored high but says it depends on the pt in front of them.

Payer is the main issue. HCP confident in the science but had two combo PAs denied or delayed, pts waited weeks. Meanwhile mono osi gets approved w/o a fuss. So realistically HCP will use combo less than the score suggests. Frustrated w/ admin burden.

HCP likes having ctDNA to monitor response, helps decide who needs the extra chemo. Pts w/ persistent detectable levels would be considered for combo. Still unclear if that approach is validated, said so openly. Overall comfortable w/ osimertinib as backbone, combo is case-by-case

Scored high for osi, honestly less sure on combo. Saw a pt w/ bad nausea and neutropenia who had to stop pemetrexed early. HCP wonders whether most pts will tolerate it long term. Also thinks QoL matters more than extra PFS in older pts. Will probably reserve it for a handful of younger pts.
Brain mets patients do well on it, that's my main reason.
Osimertinib alone is my default; chemo add-on only for high-risk disease.
Likely to use osimertinib, but the extra infusion visits worry me.
Familiarity mostly. Everyone in our group knows the toxicity profile.
Not sure I'd add pemetrexed for anyone over 75.
Easy once daily pill, patients stay on it with no fuss

Community practice, two oncologists, no thoracic specialist. We stay with what we know, and osimertinib is on our pathway so approval is rarely a fight. For the chemo combo I'd want the patient to have a big tumor burden or brain mets first.
I have a 52-year-old nonsmoker with L858R and a few small brain lesions in mind. Combination seems reasonable there given the CNS risk, and she is fit with good family support for infusion days.
Payer pushback on the combination is my main hesitation, prior auth for platinum and pemetrexed can take weeks. I'd still use osimertinib on its own without a second thought.
Probably will use the combo in selected cases, i think younger patients with baseline brain mets. The rest I'd keep on single agent and watch.

Cytopenias and nausea scare me a bit with the doublet in older patients. Still confident in the TKI backbone, just not sure about the add-on at my rural clinic where lab turnaround and infusion chairs are limited.
Our tumor board generally favors it, and I go along with that. Mostly I start after a plasma ctDNA result comes back showing an exon 19 deletion.
Follow-up for the combination still feels early to me. I like osimertinib but would wait for more survival data before changing my usual first-line approach.
Clinic runs a Friday infusion block, so adding chemo fits our schedule, which helps. Whether patients tolerate it is another matter; I'd see how the first two cycles go.

My go-to example is a retired teacher in her late 60s who has been on osimertinib a long while with very little trouble. She's kept up her gardening, no real rash issues. That experience shapes how I see it for newly diagnosed patients. For someone younger with higher-risk features I'd consider adding chemo, and I feel okay about that because the TKI part is familiar. Our nurses also know what to watch for.
