Mainly the brain. Two of my recent patients presented with multiple small mets and responded without needing radiation upfront, which made a lasting impression. Because of that I trust the drug as a first-line backbone. I'm more open to the combination for those presenting with CNS disease, and families seem to like having a more aggressive plan on paper.

I'd say likely, not certain. Osimertinib alone is what I'm comfortable with and it's what most of my EGFR patients are on. The combination I'd discuss case by case, mostly with fit patients who live close enough to come in for infusions. A couple of my patients work full time and wouldn't want the extra visits. We usually talk it through at the first visit and decide then.

My high score is mostly for osimertinib itself, not the chemo version. Honestly the combination worries me: anemia, fatigue and the nausea burden on top of a TKI that was already well tolerated. I keep thinking of a patient in her 70s who stopped chemo early in another setting. Insurance delays add to it. I'd offer the combo to only a small handful.

Our hospital pharmacy wants a formal request for the pemetrexed combo, and the pathway comittee only meets monthly. That slows everything down and patients are anxious in the meantime. I'm confident the drug works, but the logistics make me hesitate to start combo. Typical case would be a younger patient with exon 19 and bone mets. I'd probably start osimertinib alone and revisit.

Mostly habit and guidelines. We follow the national guideline sheet pinned up in our clinic and osimertinib sits at the top for first-line EGFR. I haven't prescribed the combination much yet, maybe one or two patients. Those went okay so far, though follow-up is short. I think I'd keep selecting on disease burden.
Nothing else I use covers brain mets this reliably, that's the whole story.
Only because the alternatives are worse, not because I love the data.
Oral, familiar, good CNS coverage. Fine, that's enough for me.
Chemo add-on is still a hard sell in my older folks.
Payer approves it without a fight, which is rare these days.
mostly the young never smoker with brain mets, nobody else comes close

Osimertinib is my default in the community clinic because I know the toxicity playbook cold. Rash and diarrhea I can handle. Adding platinum and pemetrexed is where I get nervous, so I'd only do it in selected patients.

Frankly the confidence comes from a lack of better options. The progression benefit with chemo is interesting but I'm not convinced it turns into living longer. The infusion chair time is a real burden for my rural patients.
I've had a few patients with baseline brain lesions who did remarkably well on osi for a long time. That's who I picture when I say yes. Hard to argue with that at the bedside.
Testing is back before I start anyway, so slotting in a TKI is easy workflow-wise. The combo needs infusion scheduling and our unit is slammed, so that part is a headache.
I'd use it, sure, but resistance always shows up eventually and then we're stuck with chemo anyway. So why not chemo upfront? I honestly haven't settled that in my own head.
Stage IV, exon 19, fit, sixties. I'd go straight to single-agent osimertinib. The combo I'd keep for high-burden disease or when CNS involvement worries me, and I'm not selling it to everyone.
Prior auth paperwork for the combo eats staff time. I'd still use it for someone with big-volume disease, but I'm irritated that I have to justify it twice.
Patients stay on it for ages with side effects that are mostly manageable. I think of a retired bus driver who is still doing his garden years in. Hard to be cynical about that.

My score is high mostly by default. Osimertinib is what everyone expects me to prescribe, and the payers know it. I do worry about the cardiac and lung warnings, and my staff hates the monitoring logistics. Still, when I think about the actual patients in my waiting room, I can't name a first-line option I'd trust more. That's not enthusiasm, it's resignation.

I think about the patient who just finished resection and is scared of recurrence. In that setting I'm comfortable because I've seen how people tolerate it long term. Where I'm less sure is sequencing, because whatever I use first changes what's left later. So the confidence is real but it has limits, and I'd say that's true of most of my colleagues too.

I'm a skeptic by nature, but osimertinib has earned its place in my clinic. Most of my patients get a quick symptom response and go back to normal life. The brain mets patients are the ones who convinced me. I still grumble about cost and the slow resistance work-up afterward, but the day-to-day experience is good. Probably my easiest first-line decision.

We talk about it at tumor board for nearly every new EGFR case now. I lean yes when imaging shows a lot of disease or CNS spread, and the group usually agrees. For lower-burden patients I'm less convinced the extra chemo is worth it. The plasma result and the patient's tolerance for infusions usually tip me. Not a clean rule, more a gut call with some evidence behind it.

I'm likely to use osimertinib but I'm honestly worried about the combo. I've watched people get anemic and nauseated, and one patient just stopped coming because the visits wore her out. The data look attractive on paper, but paper doesn't sit in my chair. If I use it, it's only with a very frank talk about what they're signing up for. Otherwise the TKI alone does fine.

I run a small practice and don't have much support staff. Osimertinib is easy for me because it's a pill, the follow-up is predictable, and patients rarely need urgent visits. The combo is where my capacity gets stretched, with scheduling, labs and managing counts. I'd probably still offer it to someone young with heavy disease, becuase I'd regret not trying. For everyone else I'd keep it simple.

why_high|pembrolizumab.t: Pt selection easy here: resectable, PD-L1 pos, fit for periop tx.
Familiar drug, team already comfy w/ irAE mgmt.
Score high mainly bc not much else to offer these pts.
Likely to use, but worried abt pts never making it to surgery after neoadj.
Pembro already default at our tumor board for stage III NSCLC.
PA usually goes thru w/o a fight so no real barrier
Community clinic, mostly older gastric pts w/ HER2-neg dz. Would use when CPS looks decent, hesitant if borderline. Probably a good chunk of them end up on it.
HCP trusts the efficacy story but not sure re AEs in frail pts. Thyroid and pneumonitis keep coming up in his head. Would still use w/ close f/u, just not happily.
Thoracic surgeon is on board, says pts get to resection w/o major delays in his experience. Tumor board consensus makes starting neoadj simple.
Infusion suite already gives it in met setting so infrastructure is there. Unsure about completing the full adjuvant course if pt struggles w/ fatigue.
Fine w/ the drug on paper. Real issue is surgical delay when AEs hit, sx team gets annoyed. Still using in most fit pts bc curative intent.
Large center w/ pharmacist-led tox clinic, so scaling use is easy. Slight worry re pt copay but fin counselors usually sort it. Overall likely to keep prescribing.
Thinking of a younger pt, stage II resectable lung ca, curative intent so tolerates risk of tx. Unsure how much it adds if PD-L1 neg, but would lean to use anyway.
Stage III resectable, good PS, motivated pt who wants best shot at cure. So yes, pembro in the periop plan.

Mostly comfortable bc we've used PD-1 for yrs in other settings. Nurses know the tox calls and steroid pathways. Concern is gastric, where pts often have poor intake and weight loss before tx. Not sure they tolerate it any better than chemo alone. Still would offer it to most w/ decent PS.

Honestly my score is high more out of habit and lack of options. Pt had pneumonitis last yr and now whole team is jumpy. Steroid tapers drag on and delay adjuvant plans. I think I'd use it again but only in pts w/ good lung reserve and reliable f/u. Rural pts w/ long travel worry me most.

Rep of the group here, I'd say pembro is easy yes for resectable NSCLC. Tumor board, surgeon and med onc all aligned on sequencing. Pts handle neoadj fine in most cases and make OR dates. Pathology response feedback is encouraging impression-wise. Would use again w/out much hesitation.

Confident re using it, but logistics are a pain. Scheduling neoadj cycles around scan, PFT and surgical slot is chaos in our small clinic. Also unsure what to do w/ pts who have a great response but poor tolerance. Some pts drop out before adjuvant. I'd still use, mostly bc alternative is less appealing.

Reasoning is mostly practical. PA approvals now routine, pharmacy stocks it, and pts know the name from media. Not totally sure on gastric subgroups tho, esp low CPS, so I'd be selective there. For lung, less hesitation. Will keep using, prob steady rather than growing.

Worry is long-term tox, esp endocrine stuff showing up months later in pts we consider cured. Pts get lost to f/u w/ PCPs who miss it. Using it anyway for stage III but wish there was better guidance on duration. Not a super enthusiastic yes.
Pembro is already routine for my resectable lung patients.
Mostly comfort from using it in the metastatic setting already.
High score only because alternatives are thin, toxicity still bugs me.
Tumor board keeps recommending it so I go along with that.
Easy to slot into our infusion schedule, the nurses know the drill.
Not sure how much PD-L1 matters in gastric, but I'd still offer it to most.

We're a community clinic with a fair number of stage III NSCLC patients who are fit for surgery. The perioperative approach makes sense to me and the KEYNOTE-671 data were enough to change what we offer.
I think it depends on the patient. Younger, good PS people with resectable disease, I'm quite comfortable. Older ones with bad COPD I'd hesitate.
Score is high but I worry about the ones who never get to the adjuvant phase. Had a couple last year who were too deconditioned after lobectomy to restart anything.
Payer approval has been smooth in our practice, which honestly drives a lot of it. Prior auth takes a few days with no real fights so far.
Gastric is where I'm less certain, probably because HER2 and MSI status complicate the picture. For the right biomarker profile I'd still use pembrolizumab.
One patient with locally advanced lung cancer got through the neoadjuvant cycles with few issues and made it to surgery on schedule. That experience made me more confident with the next few.
Mostly because guidelines list it and our pharmacy already has the pathway built in. I'd say I'm following the standard more than being excited about it.
Immune-related AEs are my main hesitation, thyroid and colitis especially. We're a small rural clinic and the nearest endocrinology is a long drive for patients, so follow-up is hard.

I see mostly stage II and III lung patients in a hospital-based clinic. Surgery usually gets scheduled within a few weeks of finishing neoadjuvant treatment, and the thoracic surgeons are on board with that. I like that the plan is clear from day one. What I'm still unsure about is how long to keep going in the adjuvant part if the patient is struggling. Overall I'd say I'm fairly confident.

My score is high on paper but I have reservations. The surgeons in our group don't love operating after immunotherapy, and a couple of them have mentioned more difficult dissections. I've also had one patient whose surgery got pushed back because of a pneumonitis scare. Cuz of that I'm cautious about who I pick. I still think it's the right default, probably.

In my practice most of the lung patients I'd consider are motivated and have good family support, which really helps with the longer treatment course. I feel the perioperative concept is logical, giving it before and after surgery. Our infusion center handles the schedule well and the team is good at catching early side effects. That combination is why I scored high. I'd be happy to use it more broadly.

For gastric I'm a bit of a mixed bag. I use pembro when the biomarkers line up, usually in combination with chemo, and our oncology pharmacist helps check eligibility. Honestly most of my confidence comes from familiarity with the drug rather than gastric-specific experience. I'd probably use it more if I saw more of these patients, but we only get a handful a year.

Confidence is there for lung but not as much as the score suggests. Many of my patients are frail, smokers with comorbidities, and I'm not sure they'd tolerate the whole sequence. Mixed feelings overall. He rates it high because guidelines and peers seem to be moving in that direction, and he doesn't want to be the outlier. Nausea and fatigue worry me for older patients, tbh. I'd still use it in fit 60-somethings who progress on first-line endocrine therapy, probably.
Mainly the HER2-positive patients after progression on prior anti-HER2 therapy, thats where I have the most experience. HER2-low I'm less sure about but willing to try in chemo-naive cases.
Our hospital tumor board treats it as a go-to option now. I think that consistency matters, and I have three or four patients who would fit right now.
Honestly my confidence comes from the HER2-positive setting, not the low-expression one. For ultralow I can't tell if it's worth the toxicity, so I'd hold off on those.

We run a mid-size oncology clinic with a dedicated infusion nurse for ADCs. Most of my candidates are HER2-low patients who've had endocrine therapy and are now facing chemo. I think T-DXd gives them something better than a taxane, but I haven't seen enough of my own patients to be fully sure. The scan schedule and symptom checks add work for us. Still, I'd start it in the next suitable patient.

I scored high mainly on the efficacy story. In practice our formulary committee is slow, and one patient waited weeks for approval, which cost her time. The ILD risk also makes me cautious with anyone who has prior chest radiation. I'd use it in a younger patient with good performance status and clean lungs. Everyone else I'm hesitant about.

My clinic sees a lot of metastatic HER2-low disease sent over from smaller practices. Several arrive after endocrine therapy has stopped working and they're anxious about standard chemo. I've treated a few with T-DXd and the response on imaging was clear in most of them. Patients and families notice that too. I'd now consider it ahead of a taxane in the right person.

Rural satellite clinic, so travel is the big issue for me. Efficacy-wise I'm comfortable, and I'd pick it for HER2-low patients progressing on endocrine therapy. But the nearest scanner is an hour away, and that affects who I'd put on it. Probably three or four patients on my list qualify, maybe fewer once logistics are sorted.

My score is a seven-ish, not a ten. Reasons to use it are limited choices after CDK4/6 and the benefit seen in HER2-low. Reasons for caution are pneumonitis, cost to the center and cumulative nausea. I have an older patient with COPD in mind and I'd likely not give it because she wouldnt cope with a lung event.

I use it a lot already in HER2-positive after progression, so adding HER2-low feels like a natural step. Our pharmacist built an order set, which removed a lot of friction. I'm still working out sequencing in the endocrine-resistant group. Most of my patients are in their sixties and fairly fit, so they'd probably do OK.
T-DXd is my go-to once chemo is the next step in HER2-low.
Mostly the lack of good options after endocrine therapy stops working.
Likely to use T-DXd, but the ILD worry keeps me cautious.
Fit, younger patients with fast-growing visceral disease, that's who I picture.
Honestly tumor board consensus pushes me there more than my own gut
Score is high only because the alternatives feel weak, not thrilled about the nausea.

Community practice here, and I've watched a couple of patients on T-DXd hold disease control longer than I'd expect from standard chemo. That experience is a big part of my score. Mostly HR+ patients who have exhausted endocrine options.

I think the evidence is persuasive enough for HER2-low, though I'm not sure how far to stretch it to the very low expression group. Pathology reporting is inconsistent in our lab, so I'd probably want a repeat read first.

Prior authorization is what I keep coming back to. I'd use it for the right patient, but a couple of weeks waiting on the payer is rough when someone is symptomatic. I'm thinking of a woman with liver mets who can't really wait.

Patients who are worn out by sequential oral endocrine combos and need something more active, that's the group. I'd still want baseline lung imaging and a clear monitoring plan in place before starting.
Our infusion nurses aren't very familiar with T-DXd yet, which tempers me. Still my score is high because a few of my patients are progressing quickly and need something stronger than what I've got.
What sells me is the feedback from colleagues on how quickly symptomatic disease shrinks. For a patient who needs a response fast, T-DXd is what I'd reach for.
Younger patients with good performance status, definately; older ones with comorbidities are a harder sell for T-DXd, and lung history matters a lot.
Two patients come to mind, both HR+ with a heavy visceral burden after several lines. I'd offer trastuzumab deruxtecan, with a frank talk about GI side effects and lung risk.

Long conversation, and the thread was consistent: for HER2-low patients who have run out of endocrine-based options, this is the first thing that feels clearly better than yet another single-agent chemo. The physician pictures a woman in her fifties with symptomatic liver and lung disease who needs a response soon. Comfortable with the ILD risk because the clinic already does regular imaging and the team knows what to look for. Probably would move it earlier rather than later if payers allow.

Said he's somewhere in the middle but still scores high. Main reason is that there aren't alot of convincing choices after a CDK4/6 inhibitor and a couple of endocrine partners, so he'd rather try T-DXd than go straight to older chemo. He's less sure about borderline expression, since in his experience the pathology result can change between samples. He'd also want to see baseline lung status first. So yes, likely, but with a checklist in his head.

Score is high but the tone was uneasy. She keeps picturing a patient who developed lung toxicity and how frightening it was for the family, and that memory colors every decision. Still, she admits the disease control she has seen is hard to ignore, especially in rapidly progressing visceral disease. She would use it mainly in patients who are otherwise well and can be seen often. For anyone living far from the clinic she's honestly not sure.

Reasons were practical and a bit grudging. Hospital-based oncologist; pharmacy has to approve and prepare a costly ADC and the formulary committee only recently okayed T-DXd, so access isn't guaranteed for everyone. He still rates himself high because the patients he has in mind, HER2-low with progression after endocrine therapy and a lot of disease burden, have little else. Nausea and fatigue worry him in frail patients, so he'd likely reserve it for those who can tolerate it.

She thought about it a long time before answering. Likelihood is high because her tumor board now discusses T-DXd by default for HER2-low patients after first-line endocrine-based therapy, and she follows that culture. She doesn't have a personal stack of cases yet, so some of her confidence is borrowed from colleagues. The patient she imagines is postmenopausal, HR+, with bone and liver spread. She'd like a few more months of real-world experience before calling herself very confident.

He's likely to use it, but wanted it known that the high score reflects unmet need rather than enthusiasm. Mostly he's thinking of two patients whose cancers are growing despite endocrine treatment and who aren't good candidates for more oral therapy. What bothers him is the monitoring burden, repeated CT scans and symptom calls, in a small practice with one nurse for this. He also worries patients will stop early if nausea hits. Still goes ahead, I think, with close follow-up.

why_low|osimertinib.t: Toxicity of adding chemo worries him more than any benefit he has seen so far.
Wants to see how it plays out in older patients first.
Happy with the drug; score is low only because few eligible patients come through his clinic.
Payer still refuses the combination upfront, so for him it's a moot point.
Waiting for longer survival follow-up before he changes anything.
Mostly comfortable, just wants a clearer way to pick who actually gets chemo.

Community practice, so infusion chair time is the bottleneck. Osimertinib alone is easy to manage by phone, whereas adding pemetrexed and platinum means more visits and nursing capacity he doesn't really have. Probably would consider it if chair slots opened up.

Thinks the extra benefit is real but isn't sure it's big enough to justify anemia and fatigue in patients who are doing well on a single agent. He has seen a couple of patients stop the chemo early and wonders what that means for the benefit.

Very keen on the data in principle, especially for patients with brain mets at baseline. The score is held back mainly because the tumor board hasn't agreed a standard approach yet. He sees it as a process issue, not a doubt about the drug.

Unsure how to choose patients. L858R versus exon 19 and CNS involvement keep coming up but he has no clear rule, so he defaults to single-agent for frail or older people. A simple selection framework would help him.
Reimbursement is the wall. The hospital pharmacy commitee has not approved the combination, and requests take months, by which time the patient has usually already started on a single agent.

Feels osimertinib monotherapy already works well for most of his patients, so he doesn't see the urgency. He would want to know what happens at progression after the combination, and whether later-line options get harder. Open-minded but waiting.
Honestly quite confident already; the gap is just time to counsel patients properly about the chemo part. Once the clinic has a nurse-led education slot he thinks he'd use it more.
Worried about patients who can't tolerate platinum, which is a good chunk of his clinic. Doesn't want to start the combination and then de-escalate halfway through, as that feels messy.

After a long discussion it came down to tolerability and the real-world picture. He treats a lot of patients in their seventies, and in his experience adding chemotherapy to a targeted agent changes quality of life quickly. The trial population felt fitter than the people he actually sees. He also worries about cumulative cytopenias and the knock-on for scheduling. Not against it, but he'd reserve it for a small slice and doesn't expect that to grow soon.

Overall supportive, and he said so several times. The low score reflects workflow rather than evidence: imaging, MDT discussion and consent all have to line up before cycle one, and in his unit that tends to slip. He thinks that with a dedicated pathway he would move his score up. He also mentioned that patients are often keen once they hear about the brain-metastasis angle.

Sat on the fence throughout. He likes the idea of deeper early control but isn't convinced the benefit shows up equally in everyone, and he'd like more clarity on overall survival. There are practical concerns too, since his day unit is small and already stretched. He said he'd use the combination for younger, fit patients with high-risk features and keep single-agent osimertinib as the default for the rest. Whether that changes depends mostly on the next data cut.

His main hesitancy is that the trade-off feels unresolved. Patients ask whether they'll live longer and he cant answer that honestly yet. He has also seen how hard the first few chemo cycles hit people who felt fine on the TKI alone. Because of that he tends to offer it only when the patient pushes for the most aggressive option, and he isn't comfortable making it routine.

Wants the biomarker picture settled before he commits. Tissue versus plasma, turnaround time for NGS, and whether co-mutations should change the decision all feel vague to him. In practice he often starts osimertinib before the full report is back, which makes adding chemo at the outset awkward. I think he'd be more willing if testing were faster and the guidance on co-alterations were clearer. For now he's neither for nor against it.

Pretty positive about the combination and said the score is low only because of his referral pattern. Most of his EGFR patients arrive already established on osimertinib from elsewhere, so the window to add chemo has passed. When he does see someone newly diagnosed, he considers it seriously, especially with a heavy disease burden. He expects his use to go up as earlier referrals become more common. It's a numbers issue for him, not a confidence one.
Toxicity with chemo added, honestly. My frail patients just wouldn't tolerate it.
No OS data yet so I'm holding back.
Payer keeps rejecting the osimertinib combo, end of story.
Brain mets control is good, just waiting on more follow-up.
Not sure the extra benefit justifies the infusion chair time
Happy with osimertinib alone, just don't see who needs more.

Pemetrexed plus platinum on top of osimertinib, which is already working well, feels like a lot to ask. Anemia and nausea are what my patients remember, and they tell me so. I'd need a clearer picture of who actually gains.

Community setting here, so infusion capacity is the bottleneck. I like the osimertinib combo concept, but fitting three-weekly visits around our chair availability is a mess. Probably would use it in a very select few.
Honestly the combo data feel immature to me. Progression-free looks nice on paper but I've been burned before by curves that never turned into people living longer.
I'm generally positive and already use it in younger, fit patients. What holds my score down is that I can't tell which lower-risk patients would be overtreated.
Depends on the patient, I think. With high tumor burden or CNS disease I'd consider adding chemo, but otherwise osimertinib alone does the job and I don't see a reason to complicate things.
Prior auth for osimertinib plus chemo takes weeks, and by then the patient is anxious and wants to start. Frustrating. Our pharmacy team also has no clear pathway for the chemo piece.
Good tool, no complaints on efficacy. My hesitation is that NGS turnaround is slow, so I often start treatment before I know the full molecular picture, which muddles who qualifies for what.
Not convinced on sequencing. If they progress on the osimertinib combo, what's left besides more chemo? Nobody has given me a satisfying answer on that, so I stay cautious.

Look, I've treated EGFR patients a long time and most do well on osimertinib alone for a good while. Adding a platinum doublet means more visits, more labs, more dose delays, and I see the dropouts in my clinic. Elderly patients especially. The trial population looked fitter than what walks through my door, I think. Until something clearly picks out who benefits, I'm not changing much.

Mixed feelings. Part of me sees the appeal for poor-prognosis features like TP53 co-mutations or liver mets. But the evidence in those subgroups is thin, and subgroup claims always make me nervous. I also worry about quality of life, since people on osimertinib alone are basically living normally. Might use it in a handful of cases, not routinely.

I actually like the combination and have started a couple of patients on it. What keeps me from scoring higher is practical: our oncology nurses are stretched and chemo education takes time we don't have. The cost conversation with patients is also awkward when coverage isn't certain. If those got easier I'd go up.

Frustrated that follow-up is so short for such a big change in treatment. Everyone quotes progression benefit but my patients care about how long they live and how they feel. Side effect burden is real, fatigue and low counts especially. And the gudiance from our tumour board is all over the place. So I default to what I know.

Referral patterns are part of it. A lot of my patients arrive from regional hospitals already on osimertinib, so adding chemo midstream isn't really a thing. The ones I start fresh I'd consider for the combo, but I don't see many new starts so my usage stays low. Also unclear how to handle pemetrexed when kidney function dips.

Nothing wrong with the drug itself, I'm skeptical about how it's being positioned. The messaging makes it sound like everyone should get chemo added, which isn't how I practice. Where I do see value is bulky or CNS-involved disease, and there I'm comfortable. For the rest I'd keep it simple.
Worried about anemia and nausea from the chemo add-on in frail patients.
Our unit is a small community clinic with limited chair slots. Adding platinum-pemetrexed to osimertinib means rebooking people every three weeks, so I'd only do it for a select few.
Already use osimertinib alone in most eligible pts, little room to go higher.

Not convinced the added benefit of the combo outweighs the extra toxicity in my typical patient, who is in their late seventies with other comorbidities. I had one patient stop chemo after two cycles because of fatigue and worsening kidney function. I'd want longer follow-up on survival before changing practice. Until then osimertinib alone stays the default and chemo is for heavy brain or liver disease.
Payer in our region still questions the combination and prior auth takes weeks. Symptomatic patients can't wait, so they start on single agent.
Not sure which patients actually need the combo, no clear selection criteria
Comfortable with the drug itself, and the team handles rash and diarrhea well. Score is lower only because I haven't had many new EGFR starts lately.

I think the data are interesting but I'm waiting to see how the CNS patients do over time. Our tumor board generally prefers to start with the oral drug and keep chemo in reserve for progression. Nurses are stretched too, and chemo teaching adds time. If the pathway for who gets the combo were clearer I'd probably use it more. Not a hard no.
Had a stage IV patient with a long commute who flatly refused infusions. Most of my patients want pills only and I don't push it
Waiting on more mature survival data before shifting.

Confident in osimertinib as the backbone, no concerns there. What holds me back on the combo is logistics at our hospital-based clinic, where the infusion suite is booked out. With faster chair access I'd use it more.

Biggest issue is tolerability. Several of my patients on osimertinib alone already have paronychia and diarrhea, and adding chemo feels like piling on. I also worry about blood counts when I can't see them weekly. In a rural practice labs are often drawn locally and results come back late. I'd rather keep it simple for now.
Unsure how to sequence after progression if chemo is used upfront.
Happy with how my single-agent osimertinib patients are doing, so I don't feel pushed to change. The few I put on combo tolerated it okay.
Cost is a problem for uninsured patients at our safety-net type clinic. Two drugs plus infusion visits adds up, and teh social worker already struggles with copays.

I use the combo more in younger fit patients with brain mets, but that's a small slice of my panel. Most are older and I default to osimertinib alone. I'd like a simple way to flag who might benefit at the first visit. Pathology sometimes takes so long that the patient is already on the oral drug by the time I decide. That timing limits how often combo even comes up.
Satisfied with current osimertinib use, would only go up if more pts presented.

Mixed experience. One patient on the combination ended up admitted with neutropenia, and since then my staff is nervous. Our oncology pharmacist asked for extra monitoring steps and that slowed things down. I'm not against it but the confidence isn't there yet. I'd probably need to see a few more people do well locally.
Still comes down to NGS turnaround. Without the result at the first visit I can't decide on osimertinib plus chemo, so people start whatever is quickest.

I think the benefit is real for some, but the toxicity discussion takes a long time in a 20 minute slot. Patients leave overwhelmed and I'd rather not add to that. Then the follow-up call load goes up for my nurse. Probably I'd use it more with a dedicated educator.
Chemo add-on tox worries me, esp in older pts.
Happy w/ osi results so far, no reason to push use higher.
Already uses osimertinib in nearly all eligible pts, no room to go up.
PA for combo tx takes forver at our site.
Not sure which pts actually need the chemo combo.
Infusion chair capacity, simple as that.
Says mono osi works fine for most of his ex19del pts. Would only add pem/platinum if high-burden or brain mets, but unsure how to define that cutoff. Tumor board split on it.
Community practice, no infusion nurse bandwidth for q3w chemo visits. HCP also worried abt anemia and nausea stacking on top of TKI AEs. Prob stays w/ single agent for now
Score low only bc HCP already uses osimertinib first line in everyone EGFR+. Very happy w/ PFS and CNS control in his experience. Nothing missing, just no more pts to add.
Payer pushback on the combo, PA denied twice last quarter per HCP. Staff spends hours on appeals. Not worth it unless pt is clearly high risk.
Wants longer f/u on QoL w/ chemo added. Thinks PFS gain is probably real but not sure it's meaningful for a pt who feels fine on TKI alone.
Likes the combo concept, esp for younger fit pts, but few new EGFR pts walk in each month. Low score = volume not hesitation, I think.

HCP burned by a pt who needed dose holds for cytopenias in the first cycles. Since then hesitant to start chemo w/ osimertinib outside of very fit pts. Also unclear on when to drop the platinum and how this affects sequencing at progression. Pts' families ask abt hair loss and hospital visits, tough sell.

Mixed. HCP sees value in combo for pts w/ brain mets, thinks CNS benefit probably matters. But rural clinic, pts drive far, so extra visits are a barrier. Pharmacy not set up for pemetrexed prep on site. Would refer out for osimertinib plus chemo maybe, not sure pts would go.

Fairly confident overall, rates low just bc waiting on tumor board consensus. Once criteria agreed, expects to use more combo in L858R pts w/ high burden. Says data mostly convinced him. Just needs internal protocol and pharmacy order set built.

Doesn't think benefit justifies tox in his typical pt, 70+ w/ comorbidities. Renal fxn often borderline so pem/platinum is tricky. Seen too many pts stop tx early becuase of AEs. Prefers osi alone, chemo held for progression. Not convinced early combo changes long term outcome.

Wants a biomarker to pick who gets chemo, ctDNA clearance maybe? Not routinely available at his center. Without it he defaults to mono. Open to changing if something practical shows up, too many unknowns for now.

Cost and reimbursement main issue. Hospital admin questioning the osimertinib combo budget, HCP can't commit to more pts w/o approval. Nursing time also limited. Open to it clinically but feels stuck.
Unsure if pt in front of him is 'high risk' enough. Probably uses combo for a few, mostly sticks w/ osi alone. Wants clearer rule of thumb.
Resistance mechanisms after combo not clear to HCP. Wants to know what next-line options look like, rebiopsy etc. Until then, cautious.
Chemo add-on tox probably too much for older pts.
Waiting for OS to mature before changing anything in 1L.
Score 7 only bc PA delays, otherwise happy w/ osimertinib.
Not convinced PFS gain justifies extra infusion visits.
Community site, no chiar capacity for chemo days. Logistics issue mostly.
Brain mets pts do fine on mono, so why add chemo? Not sure.
HCP says osimertinib mono still default for most pts. Would consider combo for high-burden dz or CNS involvement but wants clearer way to pick. Tumor board hasn't agreed on criteria yet.
Worried about AEs stacking (anemia, nausea, fatigue) in pts who are doing well on TKI alone. Feels QoL gets lost in the PFS conversation.
Confident in the data, honestly. Score held back by payer only: PA for combo takes a while and sometimes denied w/o peer-to-peer.
Unsure how to sequence after progression if pt already got platinum upfront. Thinks that probably limits later options. Wants more discussion on what comes next.
Academic HCP, sees mostly 75+ pts. Frailty and renal fx mean combo rarely feasible, so osimertinib mono it is.

Rural clinic but infusion RN team is solid now, so logistics not a barrier. Score not higher just bc very few pts actually started on combo so far. Limited personal experience, wants to see a few more real-world cases first.
Wants NGS/ctDNA back faster before committing to 1L plan. Currently starts tx before full report so combo decision gets muddied. Says it's a workflow gap not a drug problem
Thinks benefit is mostly in a subset, not clear who. Hesitant to expose everyone to chemo. Open to it if biomarkers or risk features get better defined.

HCP not comfortable adding pemetrexed/platinum in pts w/ good PS and low-volume dz. Those pts sit on osimertinib for a long time w/ few issues. Mixed feelings. Likes the PFS story and has started combo in a couple of younger pts w/ CNS dz. But nursing time, chair scheduling and extra labs are a real burden in a busy private practice. Pretty positive overall, uses osimertinib in nearly all EGFR+ pts. Main limit is pt selection: some refuse chemo outright after hearing about hair loss and nausea. Others live far away. Concerned about cumulative cytopenias and the need for dose reductions that may compromise efficacy. Saw one pt stop the TKI early due to chemo-related AEs, and it stuck with the HCP. HCP split on this. Reimbursement fine in their setting, tolerability seems manageable per colleagues. Real hesitation is uncertainty about who truly needs intensification vs who is fine on mono. Tumor board discussions go back and forth every time. Would like a practical algorithm, maybe based on baseline brain imaging and tumor burden.

Low score is mostly lack of experience, not doubts. HCP sees maybe a handful of new EGFR pts per quarter so combo exposure is small. Team is keen and nurses are trained. Feels comfortable w/ the rationale and expects to use it more as case numbers grow. Would value a peer case discussion to build confidence.
Added chemo toxicity worries me for my older patients.
Waiting for more mature overall survival follow-up before I change what I do.
Already using osimertinib in nearly everyone eligible, so not much room to grow.
Payer keeps denying the pemetrexed combo here.

Community clinic with only a few chairs, so fitting in platinum-pemetrexed visits every three weeks is hard to schedule. I'd use the combo for fit, younger patients with brain mets, but not across the board.
Happy with single-agent osimertinib for most of my stable patients, which is why the score isn't higher. I'd only add chemo for high-risk presentations, and that's a small group in my practice.

Confident in the drug itself. The limit is that most of my EGFR patients are already on it, and only newly diagnosed ones with CNS disease would be candidates for adding chemo.

Patients hear 'chemo' and say no, even when I explain it's time-limited and then back to the TKI alone.

I run a rural clinic where most patients drive a long way for treatment. Adding infusion days on top of the daily tablet means extra trips, and a few have already told me they can't manage that. Biggest hurdle is workflow. Prior auth for the combination takes a while, pharmacy needs lead time to prepare pemetrexed, and our nurses are already stretched. None of it is a clinical objection. I think I'd use it more if the logistics were smoother, but right now I'm not sure it's worth the friction for borderline cases.

My patients do well on osimertinib and I'm pleased with the CNS control I see. The score is held back mainly by uncertainty over who gains enough from adding chemo to offset the extra burden. I can see myself offering it to a few more patients with a heavy tumor load. For the rest, I don't see a reason to change a regimen that is working.

I'm skeptical about the cost versus the benefit when survival numbers aren't mature yet. Our hospital is tight on budget, and I'd have to justify every combo start. Our formulary committee is still reviewing the combination, so for now I can only use it case by case with extra paperwork. Until that's settled I'm holding back. Once it's on formulary I think I'd be more comfortable, particularly for patients with a lot of metastases at diagnosis.

I'm keen to use the combination more. The only thing holding me back is that our infusion unit is expanding next quarter and slots are limited until then. Once capacity opens up I expect to offer it to more of my newly diagnosed patients, especially the younger ones who tolerate chemo well. Timing, not conviction, is the issue.

We talked for a good while and it kept coming back to tolerability in her older patients. She worries that adding platinum-pemetrexed to osimertinib means more admissions for anemia and fatigue, and her day unit already has very few free chairs. Already uses osimertinib first-line for nearly everyone eligible, so little room to increase.
Not sure the extra benefit justifies the infusion burden for most of his patients. He wants longer follow-up on overall survival before he changes habits.
Worried about stacking chemo toxicity on top of the TKI.

Waiting for more mature survival data before shifting.

Happy with osimertinib alone for most patients, whose responses in his experience have been durable. He sees no pressing reason to add anything unless something clearly goes wrong.

Convinced by the concept, just doesn't have the eligible patients right now.

I'm comfortable with osimertinib itself, it's the combination logistics holding me back. Once our pharmacy sorts out the pemetrexed pathway I'd probably use it more.
Frustrated that the data don't tell me who benefits. Everybody gets lumped together and I'm supposed to guess. I won't put a frail patient through teh combo on a maybe.

Results are encouraging and my patients tolerate osi well. What's missing for me is a clear plan for sequencing after progression, since chemo would already be used up.
Cytopenias scare me, esp. in patients with renal issues. Pemetrexed dosing gets messy and the monitoring burden lands on me, so I'm hesitant.

Mixed feelings. We're an academic-type clinic and get brain mets referrals, and for those I lean toward adding chemo. For the incidental, low-volume ones I really don't. The cutoff is fuzzy, so I end up deciding on gut feel. I'd use it more if selection were clearer and follow-up matured.

Reimbursement is the wall for us. Prior auth for the combination takes forever, and by the time it's approved the patient has already started osi alone. Overall pretty confident in osi. My hesitation is narrow: I want a better handle on managing overlapping side effects like rash and mucositis once chemo is added. Probably the only thing really keeping me from using it more.

Not convinced. Everything I hear is PFS, and PFS alone doesn't move me when the downside is real. Time toxicity, hospital visits, cost to the system. I also worry about what's left for second line if chemo is already used. Until someone shows me a survival signal I'm staying put.

Waiting for guideline update. Until then tumor board defaults to chemo-only in most gastric cases.

Works well for my patients, I just don't see enough eligible ones.

Pembrolizumab is in my toolbox for sure, but I want clearer subgroups in gastric before going beyond the obvious PD-L1 positive, HER2-negative cases. Probably staying cautious for now.
I like it and use it when I can. What holds me back is logistics, mainly infusion chair capacity and the long adjuvant course for older folks. Not really a drug problem.

Everyone calls it a game changer but my patients with bulky nodal disease still come back with relapse. Frustrating. I'm not convinced the benefit justifies the hassle in every case.
Confidence is decent actually. What I lack is guidance on what to do after recurrence on adjuvant treatment, rechallenge or not? That's the gap for me.
Cost and reimbursment are the issue, our hospital pharmacy wants extra paperwork every cycle. Clinically I'm fine with it.

Honestly I'm tired of the perioperative story being sold as simple. In practice a good chunk of my lung patients never make it to the adjuvant part because they're wiped out after surgery. Gastric patients here are often frail and diagnosed late. By the time they reach me performance status is borderline and families want comfort over aggressive combos. I'd use pembro more if I felt the benefit held up in that population, but I'm not sure it does. Maybe there is data I haven't seen, thats part of my hesitation.

No real complaints about efficacy from what I've seen. The hesitation is that our tumor board is split on who goes perioperative versus upfront surgery. Patient selection is vague and that bugs me. I get told to use it broadly but nobody can say clearly who won't benefit. Then I'm the one managing colitis or thyroid problems at 2am. I use it, but not as often as reps would like. Long-term toxicity and what happens to these patients years down the road is thin in my mind. Combined with chemo the side effect burden is alot, especially for older patients. Maybe my confidence goes up with more follow-up.

I'm fairly positive overall. Patients tolerate it better than I feared and the surgeons have been cooperative. What keeps my score down is not knowing the optimal duration and whether everyone really needs the full adjuvant course. If that was clearer I'd use it more across both lung and gastric.
Mostly a lack of eligible patients in our small community clinic.

Happy with it, score is low only because few resectable cases come to us.

Concerned about patients who never make it to the adjuvant phase after a big lobectomy. A few of mine were too deconditioned, so they only got the neoadjuvant part. Not sure how to counsel them on that.
Feels like a solid option and I'd use it more. The limit is referral flow, since most of our lung patients get staged at the regional hospital before they ever see me.
Payer in our area wants prior auth with documented PD-L1 for gastric cases, and that slows everything down. Once it's approved I'm fine with the drug itself.
Hard to tell which patients truly benefit versus just get extra toxicity. Without a clearer biomarker beyond PD-L1 I stay cautious, especially in older patients.

I think the drug is a good fit and my experience so far has been decent. The low score is really about logistics, not belief. Our hospital pathway for perioperative lung cases isn't formalized, so each patient gets discussed ad hoc. Once there's a standard order set I'd likely use it a lot more.

Patients ask how long they will be on treatment and I never have a clean answer. Some stop early for side effects, others complete everything, so I tell them it depends. I'd feel more confident with a clearer picture of who finishes the full course. I'm also unsure what to do for those who don't.

Cost conversations are the main issue in our clinic. Many patients have high deductibles and the copay assistance paperwork is a chore for my staff. A few have declined pembrolizumab outright once they heard the total. I don't love starting a regimen I know they might not finish financially, so I stay selective.

Generally positive on pembro in this setting. What holds my score down is limited local experience, since our surgeons are still getting used to timing after neoadjuvant therapy. Honestly it's just that very few of my patients get to the resectable stage.

Told me the biggest unknown is how to choose between pembrolizumab and other options when PD-L1 is low. She thinks a benefit might be there but isn't sure it justifies the toxicity. Big fan of the class overall. What I'd want is a clearer view of immune-related adverse events when it's given with chemo before surgery, since my surgeons get nervous about delays.
Great option on paper, but our payer pushes back on pembro approvals and the paperwork delays the start by weeks. By then some patients have progressed or changed their minds.

I like it a lot for resectable disease. My thoracic surgery colleagues vary on timing between the last cycle and the operation though, and until we align I hold back a bit.

Overall I'm a big supporter of pembrolizumab and it's already a default in my head for eligible patients. Very excited about where pembro is heading, but I worry about late immune toxicities like thyroid problems or colitis showing up once the patient is back home. Our community follow-up is patchy. I'd want more real-world color on pembrolizumab before pushing harder.
