Not sure how to think about patients with low PD-L1 expression, so he hesitates to offer it widely.
Pretty comfortable overall, she said, but a small clinic just doesn't give her many eligible patients.

Dr. said a good chunk of her perioperative patients arrive frail after neoadjuvant treatment, and she's not convinced they'd finish the adjuvant part. She worries about stopping early and having exposed them to the drug for little gain.

The tumor board at his community hospital is split on this. He mentioned that the surgeons don't want to commit before seeing how patients tolerate the neoadjuvant cycles, so he tends to wait and see.
Felt the data are encouraging and said he'd use pembro more if more patients actually made it to the OR. In his view the limit is late referral, not the drug itself.

Told me gastric is the harder area: he thinks biomarker selection is still murky and he doesn't want to give pembro to everyone. He's also unsure how older patients cope with chemo plus immunotherapy toxicity.
Said she'd probably use pembro more once local guidelines are updated. For now pharmacy wants a formal protocol, and that apparently takes months.
Said the cost-benefit talk with patients is difficult, espcially when the benefit seems modest for some subgroups. Reimbursement is also uncertain in his region, which makes him cautious.
He explained that infusion chair capacity at his day unit is stretched, and adding long immunotherapy courses is a logistics headache. Clinically he said he's fairly open to it.

The HCP said they don't feel confident managing late immune-related adverse events, particularly endocrine ones, because there is little endocrinology support nearby. With anti-PD-1 therapy they'd rather limit use for now.

Said his main hesitation is that he can't tell which patients truly need the immunotherapy component. He thinks a fair number of early-stage patients do well with surgery alone and he fears overtreating. He'd like clearer markers or more subgroup detail. He also said patients ask about quality of life and he has little to tell them beyond 'it varies'. Overall he's not against pembrolizumab, just cautious.

Reported being fairly positive but not highly confident yet. She said her multidisciplinary team hasn't aligned on sequencing, and the thoracic surgeon wants a shorter interval before surgery. She isn't sure how to handle equivocal scans after neoadjuvant therapy with the KEYNOTE-671 type regimen. A shared pathway would help her use it more, but for now it's case by case.

Said she's actually quite happy with how pembro has worked in her practice. Most eligible patients got through the neoadjuvant part fine, so her lower score is mostly because she sees few new cases each month. She thinks word of mouth from colleagues will eventually bring more referrals. No major safety concerns so far, she said, just wants to keep watching longer-term outcomes.

Patient anxiety is a big thing for him: people hear 'immunotherapy' and expect either a miracle or a disaster. He struggles to set expectations because he has no long-term real-world experience in gastric. He also said two of his patients had rough colitis episodes and that stuck with him. So he's more selective now and probably won't broaden use soon.

Dr. said they're waiting on the hospital formulary committee, and until then each case needs an exception request. That's time-consuming and she's not sure she'll keep doing it. Clinically she believes in it for resectable lung, less so for gastric where she feels the evidence is thinner. If access gets easier she'd probably raise her score, unsure about the timeline though

Said her experience so far has been good and she'd happily recommend it to colleagues. The low score is simply about volume: she works in a small regional clinic and rarely sees resectable cases. The patients she has treated tolerated it reasonably well and the surgeons were supportive. She figured that if referral patterns improve she'd use it more. No real reservations about the drug itself.

why_low|sacituzumab govitecan.t: Neutropenia with sacituzumab worries me in my frail community patients.
Still prefers endocrine-based options until they run out.
Likes the data, just waiting on formulary approval.
No clear sequencing guidance after CDK4/6 and chemo.
Infusion chair capacity is the bottleneck at their site.
Diarrhea management plan is not something the nurses are comfortble with yet.
Small private practice, so G-CSF support and same-day labs are already in place. Happy with how the few patients did on sacituzumab. The only limit is that few patients reach that line of therapy.
Academic center, and the tumor board tends to favor trial enrollment first. SG comes up after that, probably third line or later.
Two infusion visits per cycle is hard for patients who live far from the hospital. Several declined and chose oral options instead.
Not sure how sacituzumab fits against the newer HER2-low ADC for the same patients. Would want a clearer picture of which one goes first.
Comfortable with the efficacy story in pretreated HR+/HER2- disease. The hesitation is only the prior auth turnaround, which can run over a week and delays the start.
Mostly sees urothelial patients after progression on enfortumab plus pembrolizumab. Isn't sure what SG adds there and wants more clarity before using it.
Hair loss is the first thing patients ask about and it puts some of them off. I think it weighs more in the decision than it should
Community practice with one infusion nurse on chemo days. Adding a regimen with premeds and close toxicity monitoring is a stretch right now.

Solo practice, mostly older HR+/HER2- patients. Has used SG in a couple of cases and the response was acceptable. The score isn't higher because most patients are still on endocrine therapy plus CDK4/6 and never reach chemo. Will probably use it more as they progress. Would like a simple dose-reduction guide for the older ones.

The hospital pathway committee has not added it to the order sets, so each use needs a manual request. The pharmacist supports it but setup is slow. The oncologist sees it as a reasonable option, just not the default. Would use it more if the pathway were updated, I think.

Early on the team had two patients with severe diarrhea and one admission for febrile neutropenia on SG, and they still remember it. Now reluctant to offer it outside clearly fit patients. Not sure if that was typical or bad luck. Wants a more reliable way to pick who can handle it.

Likes having a TROP2-directed option and talks about it positively with patients. The reason for not scoring higher is logistics. The infusion center runs full on Mondays and Tuesdays, which is when day 8 visits land. Rural patients also drive a long way. Easier scheduling would put more patients on sacituzumab.

Unsure about choosing between sacituzumab and further chemo like capecitabine or eribulin in a patient with slow-growing visceral disease. Quality of life matters more to her than response. The oncologist says it depends on how fast the disease is moving. Doesnt see a clear rule yet.

Payer mix is the issue. A good chunk of patients are on plans that deny first and approve on appeal. Office staff spend a lot of time on peer-to-peers. The doctor still thinks the drug has a place. Starts it only when the patient is stable enough to wait for approval.
Neutropenia worries me too much in older, frail patients.
Waiting on more real-world data before I move it any earlier.
Diarrhea management is a burden for my small clinic, honestly.
Happy with SG, just limited by chair slots and approvals.
Sacituzumab sits behind too many other options in my sequence right now.
Payer pushes it later until other lines are exhausted, so access is the limit.

I think the benefit in pretreated HR+/HER2- disease is real, but I'm not sure how to pick patients who will tolerate the toxicity. Probably need clearer guidance on dose reductions and G-CSF use before I'm more comfortable.
Alopecia and fatigue put a lot of my patients off, they'd rather stay on oral therapy as long as possible. Hard to push an IV treatment like sacituzumab when they're still doing fine on endocrine.

My score is lower than my actual view of the drug. Efficacy looked convincing to me with sacituzumab govitecan, it's mostly that our infusion unit is booked out and starting a new patient takes weeks.
In urothelial I'm unclear where sacituzumab sits relative to the other ADC and checkpoint inhibitors. Until sequencing is clearer I'll use it case by case, mainly after those have failed.
Community setting, no on-site support for febrile neutropenia out of hours. I'd rather refer than risk it.
Cost-benefit discussion with the hospital pharmacy committe hasn't happened yet, so for now it's restricted to select cases. Not against it, just waiting.
Overall positive on the TROP2 ADC concept and I'd use it more. I'm just unsure who is at higher risk of severe toxicity, and UGT1A1 testing isn't routine for us.

Patients I see are usually heavily pretreated by the time we get there and performance status is poor. I worry about giving something that knocks them down fast, and the quality-of-life trade-off isn't clear to me.

Long chat, and what came out is that this HCP isn't against the drug at all. In HR+/HER2- disease it seems a reasonable option after endocrine therapy and a CDK4/6 inhibitor, but the line-of-therapy decision is where things stall. A few patients did well and a few stopped early because of GI effects and low counts, so the gut feeling is mixed. A simple practical protocol for premedication and monitoring would be needed before expanding use. Time spent in the infusion chair also has to be weighed against any survival gain.

She was frank that her confidence is low outside the trial population. Her patients tend to be older with comorbidities, and she thinks the toxicity would hit them harder than published experience suggests. A couple of her patients needed repeated dose delays, and they lost trust in the treatment. The reimbursement paperwork also drains her nurse team. For now she keeps it for fitter patients only.

Fairly upbeat conversation overall. The low score was really about capacity, not doubts about sacituzumab. Her unit has limited nursing and pharmacy hours, and each cycle needs close lab review plus supportive meds prepared in advance. With a nurse navigator or a more flexible schedule she'd probably offer it to a good chunk more patients. She added that the patients who responded became vocal advocates, which makes her want to use it more.

In urothelial the discussion was mostly about positioning. He feels the landscape moved quickly, with new ADCs and combinations, so it isn't obvious where sacituzumab govitecan belongs. Tumor board discussions default to what's familiar and reimbursed. He'd like data in his exact patient type, post-platinum and post-IO, before changing habits. Not negative, just cautious, and he said he'd revisit in a few months.

Biggest barrier for him is the side-effect profile in day-to-day practice. Patients call the clinic a lot with diarrhea and low counts, and the team spends a lot of unreimbursed time on phone triage. I think he also feels the benefit over the chemo he knows well isn't big enough to justify the extra workload with SG. he'd consider it only with a clear selection biomarker or a way to predict who will struggle.

Relatively favorable view, but her confidence is limited by lack of clarity on dose modification. She treated one patient with long disease control and was impressed, which is why she'd like more patients on SG. What holds her back is not knowing how aggressively to reduce dose when neutrophils drop, since she doesn't want to lose benefit by being too cautious. She also asked about practical sequencing with later chemo. With clearer guidance she thinks she'd use it earlier in suitable HR+/HER2- patients.
Sacituzumab PA delays, pt progresses before approval comes thru.
Few pts fit right now, most still on endocrine or CDK4/6.
Like SG overall, just not enough eligible pts in my clinic.
Worried about SG neutropenia in my frail pts.
Sequencing unclear vs. enfortumab in UC, waiting on tumor board consensus.
Diarrhea mgmt scares community staff, no real protocol in place.
Community practice, no chair capacity for the D1/D8 schedule. Would use SG more if scheduling were easier, I think. Pts also hate coming in twice every 3 wks.
Honestly pleased w/ the pts I've treated, PFS benefit seemed real in my hands. Score is low only because the 2L slot is crowded. Most pts get other tx first and I'm not sure where SG fits.
Not convinced the benefit outweighs tox for SG in pts already worn down post-chemo. Probably stay with other options unless PS is good.
Payer keeps asking for step therapy docs. Takes staff time, probably limits how many I start. Once approved pts do ok.
Would use more if I had more HR+/HER2- pts progressing post endocrine + CDK4/6, my panel is small. Team is comfortable w/ AEs now, so it's a numbers issue.
Alopecia and fatigue are dealbreakers for some pts, esp. younger ones. Also unsure re G-CSF prophylaxis, no clear guidance in our group.
Urothelial is where I'm least sure. No clear pt selection and no biomarker to help. Waiting on more real-world exp before expanding.
Academic center, tumor board favors trial enrollment first. SG is the fallback after that, so volume stays low.

Main hesitation = tox. A couple of pts had bad neutropenia early on and one was admitted w/ fever. Since then I dose reduce up front, which makes me wonder if I'm undertreating. Nurses are anxious too. Would need clearer guidance on who tolerates it before I use it more.

Overall positive on SG. Responders seem to keep decent QoL vs chemo. What holds my score down is access: buy-and-bill cash flow, PA turnaround and the occasional denial. Also need a way to ID pts earlier so I'm not using it after PS has dropped. If those get fixed I'd use it more.

Mixed feelings. Efficacy seems reasonable but pts in 3L are few. Surgery and rad onc colleagues dont refer early so I see pts late. Unsure if TROP2 expression matters, probably not, but pts ask. Prescribing is still driven by habit tbh.

Cost is the issue for our underinsured pts. Safety net clinic so copay assistance doesnt solve it. Also no oral or home option, travel is hard for many. Honestly would default to chemo most times. Not likely to increase until access changes.

Other ADCs are coming and I'm unsure where SG ends up. Sequencing after another ADC is unclear, and I think cross-resistance is a real question. Nothing I trust yet on that. Holding off on expanding till clearer.

Fairly confident in the drug itself, rating held down by logistics. Infusion reactions manageable w/ premeds and the team knows the drill. Biggest gap is a simple pt-ID checklist and a nurse navigator for PA paperwork. Once we have that it probably ramps up. Pts still ask about hair loss tho.
Sacituzumab neutropenia management is a headache for my small community clinic.
Dose delays with SG have been frequent in my hands, not sure that's typical.
Waiting on more real-world experience before I move it up
Happy with it overall, just can't get approvals through fast enough.
Calls about GI side effects flood the nurses, nobody wants more of that.
Not sure where it sits after EV in bladder.

Frankly the toxicity scares me for my older, frail patients. I'd rather stick with a chemo I know than risk admissions for febrile neutropenia. Not convinced sacituzumab is worth that trade in this group.
Payer pushback is the main thing. Prior auth takes forver and patients progress while we wait. If that were smoother I'd probably use it more.
I think the drug works fine for the right patient, I just don't see enough of them. Most of my HR+ patients are still on endocrine plus CDK4/6 or earlier chemo lines.
Sequencing is a mess. After CDK4/6 and a couple of lines nobody can tell me whether to go to SG or T-DXd first, and the guidance reads vague. Until that's clearer I'm staying with what I know.
Chair capacity is tight and the day-8 visit is a pain for patients who travel far. G-CSF logistics add to it. Not a dealbreaker, but it makes me hesitate.
Efficacy impression is decent. My hesitation is mainly alopecia and fatigue in younger patients, they really hate it. I'd use SG more if I could counsel better on what to expect.
Bladder data feel thin to me. Nothing I've seen convinces me it beats what we already have post-platinum and post-EV. Tired of hearing that it's 'promising'.

Two of my patients ended up in hospital in the first cycles and that sticks with you. The nurses now push back when I bring SG up. Nobody in my centre is sure whether to test UGT1A1, and the lab turnaround is useless anyway. I'm not against it, but until I trust I can handle early toxicity without drama I'll keep it for a narrow group.

Durable benefit is the open question for me. Patients still progress and quality of life feels like a trade-off. For HR+ disease I want a clearer signal on who benefits most, maybe a biomarker, but nothing practical yet. So I decide case by case, usually when chemo alternatives are nearly exhausted. Probably a handful of patients a year.

Clinically I rate it fairly well. What holds me back is workflow: our day unit is overbooked, and pre-meds, growth factor support and monitoring need dedicated nursing time. Reimbursement approval is slow too, and I've lost a couple of patients to deterioration while waiting. Fix those and I'd use it a lot more.

I'm skeptical it changes much for my patients. They come to me late with borderline performance status, and a drug with this much GI and marrow toxicity is hard to justify. The GP then handles the diarrhea at weekends and I get the angry calls Monday. TROPiCS-02 looked fine on paper but the population seemed fitter than what walks into my clinic. I'd want to see it work in the real world before pushing it.

Communication with the MDT is the sticking point, in my view. Urology wants EV first, breast asks about T-DXd, and nobody owns the third-line decision so the referral just stalls. I'd use sacituzumab more if there were a local pathway but right now it's ad hoc and teh champion isn't obvious.
It's not a clinical issue for me, it's supply. We had a stock delay once and had to postpone a cycle, which made me wary of starting new patients on SG.
Results speak for themselves to me. The problem is I only get a few eligible patients referred per quarter, so my confidence stays limited by my own experience.
Not sure yet where it fits after CDK4/6, sequencing seems unclear to me.
Probably just waiting for more real-world data before I use it more.
Neutropenia worries me in my frail patients, I think.
Would need to see a clearer OS benefit in my pts.
Seems fine clinically, honestly just hard to get approved quickly.
Unsure the label covers my typical patient, so I'm hesitant.
I think the efficacy looks reasonable for later-line HR+ disease, but I'm not sure how it compares with the chemo options I already know well. Would need to see more on quality of life.
We're a community setting, so managing febrile neutropenia and diarrhea overnight is a real concern. Sacituzumab seems to need more support than our nurses can probably give right now.
Sacituzumab govitecan seems to work well in the few patients I've tried it on. My hesitation is mostly timing in urothelial after enfortumab, I'm not sure of the best slot so I'm holding back a bit.
Not convinced the benefit justifies the alopecia and fatigue for every patient, may depend on goals of care. Some pts probably yes, some probably no.
Hospital pharmacy committee hasn't signed off yet so it may be months. Until then I can't really say I'd use it more.
Fairly positive overall. I'd just need a clearer picture of who benefits most, maybe some kind of biomarker, before I increase use.
Dose reductions seem common from what I hear and I'm not sure how that affects outcomes. Would need to see how other centers manage that in practice
Chair time and G-CSF support make it harder to schedule, I think. Our infusion unit is already packed and adding this may stretch it.

My main hesitation is toxicity in older patients. I see a lot of people in their late seventies at a regional clinic, and I'm not sure they'd tolerate the GI effects and low counts. It may be workable with an upfront dose reduction, but I haven't seen clear guidance on that. I'd probably keep it for fitter patients until I see more. It's also unclear how much it adds over what I already use.

In urothelial it seems to be a later-line option, and by the time pts progress many are too sick or have declined quickly. I think the data are still maturing there. Not sure yet whether I'd use it before or after the immunotherapy combos. Would need to see how colleagues sequence it. Interested, just not confident yet.

I like the mechanism and the TROP2 targeting seems sensible. What's holding my score down is mostly logistics, as payer approvals vary a lot and the paperwork may take weeks. In HR+/HER2- patients with visceral disease that delay matters. If access were smoother I'd probably use it earlier.

Not sure the survival gain is big enough to change my habits. Patients often ask about hair loss and how long they'd stay on treatment, and I don't have a clean answer. A few colleagues seem reluctant too. I think longer follow-up would help, plus clearer sequencing versus other ADCs. For now I stay with what I know.

Honestly it's a mix for me. Efficacy seems decent, but two visits per cycle may be hard for patients who live far away, and rural pts espcially. I'd also want to know how much lab monitoring the local clinic can realistically do. Probably I'd use it more if travel were less of a barrier.

I'd use it more if I had a better sense of patient selection. The ADC seems promising and the patients who responded did well, as far as I can tell. My uncertainty is mostly about how long responses last and what to do afterwards. Probably I'll wait for more follow-up before moving it earlier.
Said neutropenia management in his community clinic worries him.
Not sure where it fits after CDK4/6 and endocrine therapy, he said.
Happy with it clinically; only held back by prior auth delays.
Felt the diarrhea burden is too much for frail pts.
Wants more real-world experience in urothelial before using it wider.
Thinks standard chemo is cheaper and good enough for most later-line patients.

He explained that most of his HR+ patients go to chemo after endocrine progression anyway, so the real question is sequencing against other ADCs. Not sure which one belongs first and would like clearer guidance.

According to the HCP, the nurse-led infusion unit is already stretched, and adding a regimen with premeds and close neutropenia follow-up is hard to absorb. Probably only a few select patients for now.

Reported being impressed by the benefit in pretreated patients, but the score is middling because pharmacy hasn't added sacituzumab to the formulary yet. Expects that to change within a few months, I think.
Mentioned that the alopecia and fatigue conversation puts some patients off. Said he would still offer it and just needs better tools for setting expectations.

Said the urothelial patients he sees are often older with poor renal function, and he doesn't know how the drug behaves there. Feels the evidence in that group is thin, so he wants more experience before prescribing.
Payer in his region apparently wants documentaton of prior lines at every cycle, which slows things down. He called it a hassle but not a dealbreaker.
Generally positive and would use it more, but said the urothelial space is crowded with other ADC and checkpoint options, so patients rarely get to this line.

Said her main hesitation is tolerability. She has seen patients on chemo-like regimens end up with dose delays and G-CSF use, and expects the same here. Her patients are mostly older and prioritize quality of life. She admitted she hasn't treated many yet, so it's mostly impression. Would wait to hear from colleagues first.

The HCP described a split feeling: efficacy in the TROPiCS-02 setting looked meaningful, but the benefit seems modest next to the toxicity burden in his view. He'd like to know which subgroup gains most, maybe by prior CDK4/6 duration or TROP2 expression. Without a biomarker he picks patients on gut feel, which keeps him cautious about broad use.

Reported that logistics at his small private practice are the barrier. No on-site growth factor protocol, patients live far away, and a weekend neutropenic fever would land in an ER that doesn't know the drug. He said he'd rather refer to a bigger center. Stressed it's not about the drug itself.

She likes it and uses it in select patients; the score is lower only because she doesn't see enough eligible ones. Most of her HR+ patients stay on endocrine-based combinations for a long time. When chemo is finally needed, performance status is often too poor. She'd use it more if progressors were easier to catch earlier.

He said he is waiting for longer follow-up to see how durable the benefit really is before changing habits. The tumor board is split too, with a couple of colleagues enthusiastic and others sticking with what they know. Also unsure how to weigh it against other options coming up after endocrine therapy. Sounded open but not ready to commit.

Said patient pushback is the main issue. Hair loss and cost-sharing worries come up in nearly every conversation, and a good chunk decline once they hear the schedule and side effect list. He feels he spends a lot of visit time just talking people into it. Not sure that's sustainable in a busy clinic.
Felt nobody in his group has real hands-on experience with sacituzumab so everyone defaults to the regimen they already know and that inertia is hard to shift
Neutropenia worries me in my frail pts, esp. the 70+ group.
Prior auth takes too long, pt is often worse by the time we can strt.
Happy with SG, just limited by how many pts actually fit.
GI tox and diarrhea mgmt is a hassle for my small clinic, honestly.
Not sure where SG sits vs the other ADCs now
SG: too many delays and dose holds in my hands, not convinced yet.
Pts who got it did better than I expected, so I'd use it more if I had infusion slots. Chair time is the bottleneck, esp. the day 8 visits.
Mostly an urothelial question for me. After EV and pembro I'm not sure of the right sequence with sacituzumab, so I tend to wait for more data. Would consider it in a fit pt.
Community practice, no routine G-CSF plan yet and I've seen a couple of bad neutropenia cases with SG. Makes me hesitant to push it earlier.
Prob would use more in HR+ post CDK4/6 and chemo, but colleagues in my group still default to capecitabine or similar first. We need to agree a pathway before I change habits.
Score is low only because of volume, not doubt. I see maybe a couple of pretreated HR+/HER2- pts per quarter. When they show up I'd reach for it.
Alopecia and fatigue are what pts push back on with sacituzumab, esp. younger women. They've had plenty of chemo already and want to protect QoL, so its a tough conversation.
Reimbursement for 2L bladder is unclear at our hospital, pharmacy still reviewing. Until then I cant commit.
No TROP2 selection bugs me. I can't tell who benefits most, so picking the right pt feels like guesswork, but the activity is real I think.

Rural clinic, one infusion nurse on Fridays. The day 1 and day 8 schedule is hard to staff and pts travel far. Two pts missed day 8 because of transport and then the next cycle slipped. The logistics alone make me pick oral options first. Also unsure how to handle pts who already needed dose reductions.

Interested but not fully confident. TROPiCS-02 looked reasonable to me, but I think the benefit is modest vs the toxicity burden for some pts. I'd like more on duration of benefit and QoL. Also unclear how sacituzumab compares with newer ADCs my colleagues keep mentioning. Probably selective use until then.

Overall I like sacituzumab, my few pts tolerated it ok with growth factor support. What holds me back is admin: prior auth takes a week or more and the pt keeps progressing meanwhile. If pharmacy could pre-clear it I'd go earlier. Would also want a simple nurse handout on diarrhea. Not really a clinical objection.

One pt had severe diarrhea and an admission in cycle 1 of SG and it stuck with the team. Now nurses are nervous and ask me to avoid it unless nothing else is left. I understand the data but real world feels rougher. Pts also hate the hair loss. Need reassurance on practical tox mgmt before pushing it.

Tough one. In urothelial I'd use sacituzumab after platinum and checkpoint if EV isnt an option, but that group is small. In breast there are several options post endocrine and I'm not sure it always goes first. Depends on PS and how fast disease is moving. Probably a few more pts per year, not a big shift.

Honestly it's timing, not belief. Our tumor board only just added it to the protocol so I haven't had many chances. Once the pathway is set I expect to use it more, esp. in visceral crisis pts after chemo. Waiting on pharmacy to stock it.
Efficacy impresses me, but I worry about neutropenia in my frailer pts.
Honestly the prior auth delays are what hold me back, otherwise I'd use it far more.
Sequencing after enfortumab still isn't clear to me, otherwise keen.
Very positive overall, only real limit is chair availability early in the week.
Would happily use sacituzumab more if the diarrhea plan for nurses were simpler.
Excited about it but alopecia puts a lot of patients off, tbh.
I'm a big fan of this drug in later-line HR+ disease. My only hesitation is that our small community site has no standing G-CSF routine yet, but that's fixable and I expect to ramp up.
Pretty enthusiastic after seeing how some of my pretreated patients did. That said, I'm not sure where it fits against T-DXd for the HER2-low group, so I tend to pick case by case.
Realy want to use it more. The trouble is the day 1 and day 8 schedule for patients who live far away; a couple declined because of travel and I can't blame them.
Data are exciting, I think, but the picture in my urothelial patients feels less settled than in breast. Until I see more there I'll stay selective with sacituzumab govitecan.
Love the concept of a TROP2 ADC. Biggest worry is infusion reactions and dose delays when the pt is already beaten up from prior lines, and I'm not confident handling that outside the main hospital.
Enthusiastic about it, honestly. Our hospital pharmacy committe still wants more justification before adding it to the formulary, so for now it's limited to a few patients.

Honestly I'd love to prescribe it more but I don't feel confident managing febrile neutropenia in the evenings with our on-call setup. The drug itself is exciting, the safety net around it isn't there yet.
Keen on it for second-line urothelial, though the guideline position still feels a bit fuzzy to me. So I hesitate to go beyond a handful of cases

I'm excited about this ADC and have told colleagues so. The caveat for me is who owns toxicity. In our clinic the nurse navigators are stretched, and early calls about diarrhea or low counts tend to land late. Until we have a clear escalation pathway I'll keep it for fitter patients. Once that's in place I'd expect to offer it much more broadly.

Really like what sacituzumab brings to heavily pretreated HR+ patients and I plan to use it more. One thing I keep going back and forth on is whether to test UGT1A1 up front. Colleagues seem to do different things and nobody in my group has a firm view. A simple agreed approach would remove my last bit of hesitation.

Our patients are mostly on plans with big co-pays, and that is the main wall for me. I'm enthusiastic about the drug, truly, and I've seen it help people who had run out of options. But when a patient hears the out-of-pocket estimate they often go quiet and ask about oral options instead. Social work is overloaded so nobody follows up properly. I end up offering it less often than I'd like.

We get referrals late. By the time a lot of these women reach me their performance status has slipped, and I'm wary of starting an ADC with real toxicity in someone that fragile. I do think it's one of the better things we have post-endocrine. But the window to use it well feels narrow, and earlier referral from the community would probably change my usage.

Tumor board is very pro-ADC here and I share that. My one open question is duration, i.e. when to pause if someone is doing well but worn down. I'd probably use it more broadly with some clearer real-world guidance. For now I keep a close eye on quality of life.

The drug is great on paper and I like talking about it with patients. What holds me back is where it sits after CDK4/6 and endocrine therapy versus other chemo options I know well. Some patients are chemo-averse from the start and don't want another IV regimen. I'll use it in the right fit, though not routinely yet.

why_low|trastuzumab deruxtecan.t: ILD risk still keeps me cautious, especially in older pts.
Waiting for clearer guidance on HER2-low sequencing after endocrine therapy.
Nausea and fatigue make my patients dread infusion days.
Happy with T-DXd overall, just limited by payer approvals.
Not convinced the HER2-low benefit holds up outside a trial population.
Too many other options I'd try first, so it feels early to me.
We're a community practice with no easy pulmonary access, so I hesitate to start T-DXd in anyone with lung history. Scans every few months plus symptom check calls is a lot for our small staff.
The data look interesting for HER2-low, but I'm not sure who truly benefits after endocrine-based therapy. IHC scoring is inconsistent at our lab, so I don't fully trust the 'low' label.
I've had a few great responders and would use it more. Prior auth delays are the only real brake, and waiting two weeks for a progressing patient feels wrong.
Oral options are simply easier for patients to stay on. The three-weekly chair time and GI side effects mean a lot of them push back, and frankly I'm tired of managing the nausea.
Cost conversations with our pharmacy are awkward. Clinically the case seems fine to me, but admin keeps flagging it every cycle.
Hair loss and antiemetic planning put off my younger patients. Not sure the benefit justifies that in someone working full time, but I go back and forth on it.
Mostly confident in the ADC. I just want longer follow-up on what comes after it before I move it earlier, as I don't love guessing at the next line.
Response rates in my own clinic have been better than I expected. Honestly the only thing stopping me from using it more is bed capacity in the infusion unit.

We had one pneumonitis case last year and it shook the whole team. Steroids, a held dose, and a patient who never wanted to restart. Now every cough in a T-DXd patient triggers a flurry of calls and a CT. I believe in the drug on paper, but I'm wary of putting more people on it without a tighter monitoring routine. The reality is we don't have one yet.

Tumour board is split on this. Some colleagues want it right after first line for HER2-low, others prefer to exhaust endocrine and chemo options first. I sit in the middle, I think. Without a clear consensus on timing I end up deciding case by case, which isn't very confident prescribing.

My patients travel a long way, some over two hours, for treatment. If they develop breathlessness at home they may not call straight away. That worries me more than efficacy. Nobody has given me a practical plan for remote monitoring in a rural setting, and teh nurse line we have is stretched already.

I'm quite positive on T-DXd in general and the responses can be striking. My hesitation is narrower than most: I want a cleaner picture of duration of benefit in the pretreated HER2-low group. Once I see that, I'd use it more readily. Until then I keep it for patients who are clearly progressing and fit.

Most of my HER2-low patients are still on endocrine plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor and doing OK, so there's no trigger to switch. When they do progress, I weigh it against chemo options I know very well. I'm not against deruxtecan. It just hasn't become my reflex yet. Probably need a few more cases that go well, and some reassurance on recieving it safely in frail patients.

Frankly, I feel the messaging oversells it. Tolerability in the real world looks harder than the slides suggest, and patients drop off quicker than I'd like. Add the cost and the monitoring burden and it's a tough sell to my team. I'd use it for the right patient, but not broadly.
Worried about ILD, honestly.
Prior auth takes too long in our clinic, so starts get pushed back.
Happy with it, just limited by infusion chair slots.
Not sure our HER2-low IHC calls are reliable enough.
Patients dread the nausea on T-DXd, so I hold it back.
No real hesitation, only waiting for more survival follow-up.
Most of my HER2-low patients are still on endocrine therapy plus a CDK4/6, so they haven't reached the chemo stage yet. I'd consider T-DXd later, but not many are there right now.
Small rural practice with no on-site CT, so the ILD scan schedule is a headache. Patients would have to travel for imaging every few cycles. That makes me reluctant to start more.
Very comfortable with the efficacy I've seen so far. The only thing holding me back is that our pharmacy needs a few days' lead time to prepare Enhertu, so starts get delayed.
I think the data are good, but I'm unsure where it fits against other options after progression on endocrine therapy. Tumor board discussions usually end up split.
One patient stopped early with lung toxicity on T-DXd and it shook the team. The nurses are nervous now and I'm probably more cautious with new starts.
A lot of my older patients have COPD, so I tend to steer away from it. For the fitter ones I'd be fine with it.
Insurance denies it at first pass, often needing a peer to peer. Staff time is limited and somtimes we just pick a cheaper regimen instead.
Waiting to see how sequencing with other ADCs shakes out. I don't want to burn the option early in someone who might need it later.

Lots of my patients are doing fine on oral endocrine combos and I don't want to jump to an ADC too early. Hair loss is less of an issue, but fatigue and nausea affect work and family life. I'm also not sure how long people can stay on T-DXd before dose reductions pile up. Our nurses need more training on spotting ILD symptoms. Until that's sorted I'll keep use selective.

I trust the drug and have used it in a handful of patients with good response. The barrier is logistics, not belief. Our infusion center runs full, and a three-weekly schedule with premeds takes a lot of chair time. With more capacity I'd use it more. Pharmacy also wants a clear antiemetic protocol first.

It comes down to how I read the HER2-low label. A few biopsies came back as 0 on repeat testing, which makes me uneasy about who really qualifies. Pathology is helpful but turnaround is slow. I'd use it more if the IHC call were more consistent. No real concerns on efficacy otherwise.

Follow-up is the issue for me. Many patients live far away and miss visits, and with ILD you want early reporting of cough or breathlessness. I worry they'd sit on symptoms until it's too late. Phone check-ins help but we're short staffed. So I'm choosing patients for Enhertu very carefully.

Chemo-naive metastatic HR+ is where I'd think about it, but I still lean on endocrine-based treatment first. I'm not sure the benefit justifies earlier chemo in patients who feel well. We discuss it at tumor board and opinions differ. Might change as more real-world experience comes in.

Overall positive. I've seen it used with good supportive care and it was tolerable. The main reason I'm not scoring higher is that reimbursement for earlier-line use isn't settled in our region. That means I can only use T-DXd in selected cases for now. Once that clears I expect to use it more.
ILD risk worries me, esp in older pts w/ lung comorbidities.
PA turnaround is slow at our clinic. Pt often already started chemo by the time T-DXd approval comes through.
Very comfortable w/ tx, just not many eligible pts.

Honestly not convinced yet for HR+/HER2-low pts who still have endocrine options left. Sequencing unclear to me, would I burn T-DXd too early before other lines? Nausea and fatigue also hit QoL, and a few pts hate the idea of alopecia. Want more real-world data in my type of pt before pushing harder.
Waiting on guideline update for T-DXd before changing practice.
Community setting, so no on-site pulm for baseline/monitoring CT. Would have to send pts out, which complicates things, probably why I only use it selectively.
Score lower only because of drug access, not efficacy. If PA were smoother I'd use T-DXd earlier in most eligible HER2-low pts, I think.

Tumor board is split on T-DXd. Some prefer chemo first for pts w/ visceral crisis, others want it up front. I'm in the middle tbh. Need clarity on which HER2-low pts benefit most, and how to handle ultralow. Until then I pick case by case.
Not sure about pt selection, IHC 1+ vs 2+ confuses my team.
Pts on a long CDK4/6 response, I don't want to switch them early. Fear of AEs outwieghs unknown PFS gain in that group, at least for me.

Infusion chair capacity is the bottleneck for T-DXd. Q3W visits plus monitoring labs and scans add up, and pts living far away struggle with the schedule. Payer also pushes back sometimes on off-pathway cases. Would use more if logistics were easier.
Results impressed me, and my pts tolerate T-DXd ok w/ good antiemetics. Main thing holding me back is awareness among referring docs, so pts reach me late.
Cost and PA hassle, plain and simple.
Not enough personal exp managing ILD grading yet for T-DXd. Would want a clear algorithm and a pulm contact before ramping up.

Had one pt w/ grade 2 pneumonitis last yr and it shook the whole team. Since then nurses are nevrous and ask for extra scans. I get that, but it slows uptake. Pt also stopped tx and family was upset. Hard to feel confident after that, tbh.
Mostly positive on T-DXd. Only hesitation is long-term safety in real world, so waiting a bit before using it in earlier lines.
Depends on pt fitness and prior tx lines.

Elderly pts are my main issue. Frailty, cardiac hx and poor reserve make me nervous about AEs. Palliative focus often wins in clinic. No data I trust for that group, so I default to single-agent chemo or endocrine. Not saying never, just not now.
I think T-DXd is a real step forward and want to use it more. Limiting factor now is our pharmacy stock and ordering lead time, which is fixable.

Mixed feelings overall. Data seem solid, but I'm unsure where it sits vs other options after endocrine progression. Pts ask about hair loss and nausea first. Some pref oral tx if possible. Will probably use more once colleagues share their experience.
ILD risk still makes me hesitant outside clear-cut cases.
Keen to use it more, just need a bit more local experience first.
Happy with T-DXd, only limited by chair availability in our day unit.
Honestly the nausea and fatigue put a lot of patients off.
Payer aproval is slow so I default to what I can start now
Unsure where it fits versus endocrine-based options after progression on a CDK4/6.
Monitoring burden is my main sticking point in a small community practice. We don't have easy access to rapid chest imaging, and I worry about missing early pneumonitis symptoms between cycles.

HER2-low patients who are still responding to endocrine therapy are hard to move over, in my view. I'd rather save T-DXd for after endocrine options run out, though I accept that thinking on sequencing may shift.
I like what I've seen in my own patients so far. What holds me back is mostly logistics, like infusion chair time and pharmacy prep, not the drug itself.
Hair loss and the need for antiemetic planning make some older patients refuse. A few prefer oral options even when I think the ADC might do more for them.
Not sure how to choose between HER2-low patients when IHC scoring seems to vary from one report to the next. Until pathlogy is more consistent I'm hesitant to expand use.
Reimbursement is the blocker. Our payer wants prior lines documented and appeals drag on for weeks, so patients end up on chemo first.

I'm comfortable with the efficacy story, but ILD keeps me cautious. Most of my patients are managed in a busy community clinic where a cough or mild breathlessness might be phoned in days late. I worry about being the one who misses early pneumonitis until it progresses. Until there's a tighter shared protocol with radiology and our nurses, I probably won't offer T-DXd to anyone with prior lung problems or borderline lung function.

I think the post-chemo data are convincing in principle, but I'm still working out which HER2-low patients benefit most. A lot of them look similar clinically, yet the IHC picture is not always clean. Earlier in the pathway I'm not sure the extra toxicity justifies leaving endocrine-based options. T-DXd is on my radar, but for now I use it selectively and mostly later. More discussion at tumour board would probably steady me.

Overall I'm quite positive about deruxtecan, and patients who received it generally did well in my experience. The reason I scored lower is practical. I work in a regional hospital and patients often travel a long way for infusions, which some can't manage. We share care with a bigger centre, but that adds delay. If local delivery were simpler I'd use it a lot more.

Brain metastases are the grey zone for me. A good number of my HER2-positive patients develop CNS disease, and I'm not certain how much I can rely on the evidence in that setting. I don't want to switch from a regimen that is controlling the brain just to try something new. So I wait, review imaging, and discuss with neuro-oncology colleagues before committing.

Frailty is the issue. Many of my patients are in their late seventies and already struggling with fatigue, so adding a drug with nausea, possible lung toxicity and regular cardiac checks feels heavy. I'd rather keep quality of life stable. Families often ask for the gentlest option, and I tend to agree. Maybe I'm being too conservative, not sure.

I'm fairly confident in T-DXd and would give it more often. The limiting factor is that few of my patients reach that line in good enough shape, because earlier treatment takes a lot out of them. Where they are fit, I rarely hesitate. A couple of colleagues feel the same, so it's more about timing in the pathway than doubts about the drug.
Oncologists in my group disagree on whether to use it before or after other HER2 options, and I'm somewhere in the middle. Without a clear local pathway I tend to individualise case by case.
Follow-up scans and visits come so often with this that my nursing team struggles. I'm okay with the drug, I just don't have the capcity to run more patients through at the moment.
ILD worry. T-DXd pts need too much monitoring for my clinic.
Waiting on PA approvals, slows everything down.
Great drug, just very few eligible pts in my practice.
N/V in elderly pts, hard sell for them.
Not sure HER2-low bx result is reliable enough to act on.
Would keep it for later line, probably.
Community setting, no pulm on site for ILD workup. Would use more if rapid CT access. Currently refers a lot of these pts out.
Pts on 1L CDK4/6 doing fine so no reason to switch yet. HCP wants longer f/u on PFS before moving T-DXd earlier. Tumor board generaly agrees.
Very comfortable w/ T-DXd after several pts, outcomes good. Only limit is infusion chair time, schedule is packed. Not a clinical issue.
Concerned about cumulative AEs, esp fatigue and alopecia, in pts who want to keep working. Tends to pick oral options first.
HER2-low scoring varies between path labs I think. Wants clearer IHC guidance b4 sending more pts. Otherwise fine with the tx.
Payer denied twice last quarter for HER2-low pts. Office staff now reluctant to even start a PA. Frustrating for HCP.
Likes the efficacy signal and would use more. But only a handful of chemo-naive pts post endocrine, rest already got chemo.
Unsure how to sequence other ADCs after this. Tumor board split on it. Wants data on tx after T-DXd before committing more pts.

Rural clinic, older pt population. Many have cardiac and lung comorbidities. HCP afraid pts won't report cough early enough for ILD. Travel is long so a grade 2 event could be missed. Probably stays with endocrine + CDK until clear progression.

Mixed feelings overall. HCP sees benefit in HER2-low and has used it a few times w/o major issues. But the nausea mgmt takes nursing time and the clinic is understaffed. Also unsure if pts with slow-growing disease really need chemo-based ADC this early. Would reconsider if more pts were clearly visceral crisis.

Positive experience so far, pts tolerated it better than expected. HCP says low score is purely about volume, not confidence. Most HR+ pts still respond to endocrine tx for a long while. Would escalate usage once those pts progress. Expects numbers to rise next year.

Worried about long-term tox, esp lung and cardiac echo burden. Pts already on multiple visits for scans. HCP feels the trade-off isnt clear for those with low symptom burden. Wants more real-world experience first. Colleagues locally share the same hesitation.

Academic-type referral center, so HCP sees mostly later-line pts. Early-line HER2-low use is rare there since community docs treat first. Not against T-DXd at all. Would need referral pattern to change, and not sure that will happen soon.

Cost and co-pay a big barrier for pts w/o good coverage. Several declined after financial counseling. HCP also thinks the ILD risk makes it hard to justify when alternatives are cheaper. Doesnt feel confident pushing it. Would want clearer guidance on who benefits most.
ILD worry still dominates my thinking, especially in older patients.
Not sure where it fits after CDK4/6 failure in my HR+ patients.
Happy with it, just limited by chair slots in our unit.
Payer keeps pushing back so I hold it back
Waiting for more real-world experience before I move it earlier.
Nausea and fatigue make patients reluctant, honestly.

I'm fairly confident in the efficacy story, so my low score is really about capacity. Our infusion suite is small, and a q3w ADC with pre-meds and observation squeezes the day. If that eased I'd use it more.
HER2-low is a moving target in my practice. Pathology reports are inconsistent on 1+ versus 0, so I hesitate to commit. Probably need a clearer local testing pathway first.
Honestly the ILD monitoring burden worries me in a community setting. We have no easy access to quick CT or pulmonology input, and I'd hate to be the one who catches pneumonitis late.
The data look encouraging, but in slow-burning disease I still reach for endocrine-based combinations first. T-DXd feels like a later-line step to me, not an earlier one, though I could be convinced.

Several patients decline once we discuss hair loss and nausea, particularly when they feel well on oral therapy. I think that conversation is harder than people admit. It limits how often I even propose it.

Score is middling only because of reimbursement lag, as the approval came before our formulry caught up. Clinically I'm keen and have a couple of patients lined up. Once access is sorted I expect to use it more.
I'm unsure about sequencing and what I'd do after progression on it. My team also hasn't agreed how to think about the gap before the next ADC or chemo. Until that is clearer I'm cautious.
Mostly frail, elderly patients in my rural clinic, and I'm not sure they'd tolerate it. Nobody checks in between cycles, so early symptoms might get missed. I'd probably wait.

After a long chat, the main thing holding me back is pneumonitis. I've seen one case that went badly in a previous role, and it stays with me. Our clinic has thin nursing coverage for phone triage, so I don't trust us to pick up early cough or breathlessness. I'm also unsure how it compares with the oral options my patients already tolerate. Until I feel safer on monitoring, I'll keep it for clear-cut situations only.

I like the direction of travel but I'm torn. The activity in HER2-low is clearly meaningful, and I think it will change practice. But my patients are often doing fine on endocrine therapy, and I don't want to burn the ADC too early. I'd like better guidance on who truly needs it sooner. Toxicity counselling also eats clinic time we don't really have.

Honestly my score is low only for practical reasons, not because I doubt the drug. The tumor board is supportive and I've used it in a few patients with good experience. What slows me down is scheduling and the pre-authorisation paperwork, which our admin team handles slowly. If I could get decisions turned around faster I'd offer it far more often. I just don't want patients waiting weeks.

Access is the problem. Every request needs prior authorisation, and the payer often asks for evidence of prior lines in a way that doesn't match the newer indication. Denials then mean appeals, and patients can wait weeks. By then their disease has sometimes moved on. I'm confident in principle but tired of the fight, so I default to alternatives that get approved quickly.

The multidisciplinary meeting is where this stalls for me. Our pathologists are careful, but the IHC scoring for low versus zero isn't always reproducible, and I'm not convinced we're calling the right patients. That makes me hesitant to offer an expensive ADC with real toxicity. I think a standardised approach would help, and I'd likely use it more with that. Not a criticism of the drug itself, more of our diagnostic pathway.
ILD risk worries me with T-DXd in older patients who already have lung comorbidities.
Most of my HER2-low patients are still doing fine on endocrine therapy plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor.
Great drug, I just don't see many eligible patients in my clinic.
Nausea and fatigue are manageable, but I'm not sure our small clinic can support T-DXd patients.
Prior aproval for T-DXd takes weeks here and that slows me down.
Not convinced the IHC 1+ calls from our local lab are reliable.

We're a small community practice with only one infusion chair free for this kind of regimen. Fitting in the q3w visits and the monitoring scans is a squeeze. I'd probably only add a few more patients.
Pathology reports in our setting often just say 'HER2 negative' with no clear split between 0, ultralow and 1+. Until that's sorted I can't pick the right patients with confidence.
I like what I've seen with T-DXd so far, honestly. My score is lower only because the payer keeps denying it after endocrine therapy and the appeals take forever.
One patient developed grade 2 pneumonitis early on and it shook the whole team. The nurses are nevrous now, and I'm slower to start new patients.
I think I'd use it more if there were clearer guidance on sequencing versus other chemo options. Right now it depends on who is at tumor bord that week.

Tolerability in the two patients I've treated with trastuzumab deruxtecan was better than I expected, apart from nausea that premeds handled. I just haven't had enough suitable patients to feel highly confident yet.
Long-term safety feels thin to me for patients who might stay on treatment for years. I'd want more reassurance on lung and cardiac monitoring over that time, especially in my older patients.

Our hospital pharmacy is strict on cost. Every T-DXd request goes to a committee and it's been slow. Meanwhile a patient with symptomatic disease can't wait, so they get a chemo they can start Monday. I understand the reasoning, but it limits how much I can use it. I also don't know how to explain the cost to patients with weak coverage.

I work in a rural clinic and many patients live a couple of hours away. If someone gets a new cough, I need quick imaging and a fast decision, and that's hard to arrange. Weather and transport make it worse in winter. I'm fine with the drug itself, but logistics hold me back. I would probably use it more in patients who live closer.

Overall I'm positive on T-DXd. The data made sense for my HER2-low patients who progressed on endocrine therapy. What holds me back is practical: HER2 retesting takes a long time to come back here. I often have to decide before the result is in. If that got faster I'd likely go up a point.

A lot of my patients are in their late seventies and frailty is a real issue, I'm not sure how deruxtecan would go in someone who is barely independent. Family members often ask about hospital visits and side effects and I don't have a lot of real-world examples to share. I think I'd start with the fittest ones and see how they do. Right now I hold off on the rest.

A good chunk of my patients push back on anything that causes hair loss, even when I explain the benefit. Several have said they'd rather try a gentler option first. We spend most of the visit on this. Some of them also worry about the lung risk after reading online, which makes the conversation longer.

Results from my own patients have been encouraging and the team is comfortable with it now. The limit is how many people fit the label, since many of mine are already on endocrine therapy and doing okay.

Mixed feelings. The HER2 biopsy was done years ago in several of my patients and I'm not sure it still reflects the disease. Rebiopsy isn't always feasible in our small hospital because radiology availability is limited. Without that I hesitate to switch someone who is stable. I'd probably use T-DXd more if the testing criteria were clearer.
ILD risk still scares me for anyone with a lung history.
Payer keeps pushing back on T-DXd for HER2-low after chemo so I hold off
Frail patients get so nauseated they stop coming back, and that's hard to ignore.
Love the T-DXd efficacy, but my pharmacy can't stock it reliably.
Unsure where it fits versus endocrine plus CDK4/6 in HR+ HER2-low.
Great drug, just not enough eligible patients walking in yet.

We have no pulmonologist on call in our community practice, and I'm not comfortable monitoring for ILD on my own. Every cough turns into a CT and a treatment hold. Frankly it's a lot of workload for something I can't always manage locally

I think T-DXd works, I just don't know how to sequence it after CDK4/6 in HR+ HER2-low. Nobody has given me a clean rule for when chemo should come first. Probably I'll keep it for the sicker, fast-progressing patients.
Results have impressed me, no real complaint about the drug itself. My low score is more that I only see a few eligible patients a month, so there's not much room to use it more.
Prior auth takes weeks and patients in visceral crisis can't wait. By the time approval comes through they're already on something else.

Alopecia and fatigue matter more to patients than the papers suggest, at least from what I hear in clinic. A few decline T-DXd once hair loss comes up. Not sure how to counsel the ones who need to keep working.
HER2 IHC 1+ versus 0 reads are inconsistent in my experience. Reports vary a lot between readers, and I'm not sure the category is reliable enough to start an expensive ADC.
Cardiac monitoring is manageable, an echo every few months is fine. What holds me back with T-DXd is infusion chair capacity, we're booked solid. I'd use it more if scheduling were easier.
Elderly patients with comorbidities make me cautious. Dose reductions seem to happen often and I'm unsure how much benefit survives them.

Honestly, I'm tired of hearing T-DXd is the new standard when the toxicity is what lands on my desk. A grade 2 ILD means stopping, steroids and a very scared patient. Follow-up scans every few cycles add cost and anxiety. I'd also like to know how many patients really stay on long enough to benefit. Until that's clearer I'll reserve it for clear-cut cases.

Our hospital formulary committee hasn't added T-DXd for the HER2-low indication yet, so I need case-by-case exceptions. That eats admin time I don't have. Clinically I'm fairly open to it. If the process were simple I'd probably double my use, but right now patients fall through the cracks. Not sure when that changes.

I think T-DXd is a real step forward and I've seen a couple of great responders. My hesitation is patient selection, I don't want to use it on everyone just because HER2-low is technically eligible. Some people do fine on endocrine therapy for a long time. I need clearer markers for who needs an ADC earlier. Otherwise I'd use it more.

Neutropenia and nausea hit more people than I expected, and we dont have good support staff for phone triage. Patients call at night, nobody knows the ILD red flags, and I end up handling it. The pitch sounds smooth but the follow-through falls on us. T-DXd doesn't convince me the benefit justifies that burden in later lines.

Cost conversations are awkward. Insurance covers some patients while others face big copays, and I can't predict which until late. I feel stuck describing a drug I may not be able to deliver. It's also unclear to me how long to continue if they're stable but exhausted. Probably I'll wait and gather more experience first.

Brain mets patients worry me. The data feel thin for active CNS disease, and I don't want to promise something I can't back up. Neurology wants frequent imaging anyway. I'd rather stay with a regimen I know than use T-DXd there. Maybe that's conservative, but that's where I am.
